title: Can't Terminate a Tenancy Solely for Domestic Abuse / Sexual Violence Victim Status
bodyText: Wyoming law prohibits terminating a tenancy based solely on a tenant's, applicant's, or household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence (W.S. 1-21-1303(c)). This does not prevent an adverse housing decision based on other lawful factors you're otherwise aware of — it specifically targets using victim status itself as the reason. Also logged as a standing cross-check: any future WY clause or custom termination language should be checked against this rule before use.

title: Safe Homes Act Rights Can Never Be Waived or Modified
bodyText: The protections in Wyoming's Safe Homes Act (W.S. 1-21-1301 through 1304) cannot be waived or modified by a lease or any separate agreement between landlord and tenant (W.S. 1-21-1304). Keep this in mind for any custom termination or waiver language you write yourself — attempting to contract around these protections would be unenforceable. Also logged as a standing cross-check, same pattern as CO's deposit-nonwaiver rule.

title: You May Refuse an Uneconomical Repair and Terminate Instead
bodyText: If a tenant notifies you of a habitability issue and the cost to fix it would be unreasonable relative to the rent charged and the nature of the property, Wyoming law lets you refuse the repair and terminate the rental agreement instead (W.S. 1-21-1203(d)). You must notify the tenant in writing and give them no less than 10 and no more than 20 days to find substitute housing. Rent is prorated to the tenant's move-out date, and any balance plus the deposit gets refunded per the standard deposit-return rules. This is a real option worth knowing about for a low-rent unit facing a major, disproportionate repair cost — not something to state to the tenant in the lease itself, since it only becomes relevant if you choose to invoke it.

title: Give Separate Written Notice of Nonrefundable Deposit at Collection Time
bodyText: Wyoming law requires you to give the tenant separate written notice that a portion of their deposit is nonrefundable at the time you actually collect the deposit — not just state it in the lease itself (W.S. 1-21-1207). Stating it in the lease satisfies one part of the requirement; you should also hand or send the tenant a standalone written notice when you take the deposit, to be safe.

title: Valid Ways to Serve the Abandoned-Property Notice
bodyText: Wyoming recognises three ways to serve the abandoned-property notice, and any of them starts the seven-day clock: certified mail to an address the renter gave you in writing specifically for that purpose, personal service under Rule 4 of the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure with a copy delivered to the renter personally, or publication in a newspaper published in, or widely circulated in, the county where the unit is (W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)(A)-(C)). Publication is the fallback when a renter vanishes without leaving an address. One trap in the same section is worth knowing before you dispose of anything. If the renter answers in writing within the first seven days saying he intends to collect the property, W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(iii) tells you in one sentence to hold it 'for an additional period of seven (7) days', and in the next sentence refers to 'the additional fifteen (15) day period'. The statute gives two different numbers for the same hold, and no Wyoming court has sorted it out. Hold for the longer period: the extra storage is chargeable to the renter under W.S. 1-21-1210(b), while disposing too early is conversion of someone else's property, and nothing caps what that costs you.

title: Habitability Duties Don't Cover Trivial Issues
bodyText: Wyoming's habitability requirements don't apply to breakage, malfunctions, or conditions that don't materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary renter (W.S. 1-21-1202(c)). A minor cosmetic issue or trivial malfunction isn't a habitability violation under this statute — useful context if a tenant frames something minor as a habitability problem.

title: Habitability Duties Can Be Reassigned by Written Agreement
bodyText: Unlike some states, Wyoming lets you reassign or modify the habitability-related duties under this article by explicit written agreement signed by both parties (W.S. 1-21-1202(d)) — for example, shifting responsibility for a specific utility or system to the tenant where that makes practical sense for a given property. This flexibility isn't automatic; it requires an explicit written agreement, not just silence in the lease.

title: How to Respond to a Tenant's Habitability Notice
bodyText: If a tenant who is current on rent gives you written notice of a suspected habitability problem, you must either start fixing it or notify them in writing that you dispute the claim, within a reasonable time — sent by certified mail or in the manner used for eviction notices (W.S. 1-21-1203(b)). You are not required to fix anything caused by the tenant's own misuse of the property (§1203(c)), and you are never liable under this article for a tenant's claims of mental suffering or anguish (§1203(e)).

title: Tenants Have No Self-Help Repair-and-Deduct Remedy
bodyText: Wyoming gives tenants no self-help repair-and-deduct remedy. If you don't fix a notified habitability issue, the tenant's only recourse is to send a follow-up 'notice to repair or correct condition' giving you 3 more days to act, then file a civil action in circuit court (W.S. 1-21-1206). If a court finds you unreasonably refused or failed to use due diligence to correct the condition, it can award the tenant costs, damages (including rent improperly retained), and affirmative relief — including terminating the lease and ordering you to refund the rent balance and deposit within 30 days, with the tenant required to vacate 10 to 20 days after that court-ordered termination.

title: Deposit Duties Carry Over to a New Owner
bodyText: If you sell the property or transfer your interest in it, whoever holds the owner's interest at the time a rental agreement terminates is bound by the nonrefundable-deposit-notice and deposit-deduction rules (W.S. 1-21-1207, 1-21-1208) — meaning deposit obligations carry over to a buyer or successor, not just to you as the original landlord. Worth flagging in any sale or transfer paperwork so a new owner knows they're inheriting this duty.

title: Penalty for Unreasonably Withholding the Deposit
bodyText: Wyoming's deposit penalty is blunt: if you unreasonably fail to comply with either deposit duty, the renter may recover the FULL deposit plus court costs -- not just the amount in dispute (W.S. 1-21-1208(c)). Note that it reaches both limbs. Subsection (a) is the ordinary deposit: the balance, prepaid rent and a written itemization of every deduction with reasons. Subsection (b) is a separately identified utility deposit, with its own 10-day, 45-day, 15-day and 7-day clocks. Missing either one exposes the whole deposit. Get the (a) deadline right, because it is not a flat thirty days. The balance and itemization are due within 30 days after termination OR within 15 days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, WHICHEVER IS LATER -- so a forwarding address that arrives late pushes the deadline out, not in. If there is damage to the unit, the period is extended by a further 30 days. If you are the prevailing party and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs in addition to any other relief. These rules come from Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act, which covers a renter's principal place of residence, not a mobile home lot or recreational property rented on an occasional basis (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(iv)); the eviction procedure applies either way.

title: No Deposit Cap, No Interest Requirement, No Separate-Account Requirement
bodyText: Wyoming law places no cap on the amount you can charge for a security deposit, does not require you to pay the tenant interest on it, and does not require you to hold it in a separate or interest-bearing account (W.S. 1-21-1207–1211, read in full — none of these appear anywhere in the article). You can set the deposit amount at your discretion and hold the funds however you choose.

title: No Statutory Advance-Notice Period for Landlord Entry
bodyText: Wyoming law does not set a specific number of hours or days of advance notice you must give before entering the property — the only statutory rule is that Tenant can't unreasonably deny you access for repairs, inspection, or showing the unit (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(iii)). Many landlords choose to state a specific notice window (commonly 24–48 hours) in the lease itself as a practical courtesy and to set clear expectations, but Wyoming law does not require it.

title: No Statutory Rent-Increase Cap, Frequency Limit, or Notice Period
bodyText: Wyoming has no rent control, no cap on how much you can raise rent, no limit on how often you can raise it, and no statute requiring a specific notice period before a rent increase takes effect. Rent can't be increased during a fixed-term lease unless the lease itself allows it; for month-to-month tenancies, most landlords give at least one full rental period's notice (commonly 30 days) as a matter of practice — tied to the same convention used to end a month-to-month tenancy — but this is not a codified requirement.

title: No Separate Mobile-Home-Park Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Unlike some states, Wyoming does not have a distinct landlord-tenant act specifically for mobile-home-park lot rentals — mobile home lot tenancies fall under the same Residential Rental Property Act (Article 12) as any other rental. Separate rules exist for mobile homes, but they aren't landlord-tenant law: titling and taxation of the home itself falls under Title 31, Chapter 2, and health/sanitation standards for parks fall under Title 35; siting and zoning are handled locally by individual cities and counties.

title: No Comprehensive Anti-Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Wyoming does not have a standalone statute prohibiting retaliatory rent increases, service reductions, or eviction threats in response to a tenant exercising a legal right (such as reporting a habitability issue). This is different from most states. That said, courts generally disfavor retaliatory conduct as a matter of common-law principle, and a tenant facing eviction may still be able to raise retaliation as a defense if they can show the landlord's action was motivated by the tenant exercising a protected right — so the practical exposure isn't zero even without a codified statute.

title: Carbon Monoxide Detectors Come from Building Code, Not the Rental Statute
bodyText: Wyoming does not address smoke or carbon monoxide detectors anywhere in the Residential Rental Property Act (Article 12). The requirement instead comes from Wyoming's adoption of the International Residential Code, which generally applies to new construction with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage — not automatically to existing rental housing. Enforcement and any additional requirements are set locally by individual cities and counties, not by one uniform state rule. Practically: don't assume a detector requirement doesn't exist just because it's absent from the landlord-tenant statute, and check your specific city/county's building and fire code rather than relying on a single statewide answer.

title: No Statutory Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, which requires a radon disclosure on every lease regardless of term length, Wyoming has no statutory radon disclosure requirement at all — not even the lighter-weight version some states use (a standard disclosure form promoted by the state real estate association rather than by statute). Wyoming is one of only a handful of states with no radon disclosure obligation of any kind. This doesn't mean radon isn't a real risk in Wyoming housing — it just means there's no legal requirement to test for it or disclose it before renting the property.

title: No Statutory Bed Bug Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, which requires disclosing a property's bed bug history within the past 8 months, Wyoming has no statutory bed bug disclosure requirement. Wyoming's only two state-mandated lease disclosures are the federal lead-based-paint disclosure and the written notice of any nonrefundable portion of the security deposit. If your property is within a city or county that has its own bed bug or pest-notice ordinance, that would be a local requirement layered on top — not something imposed by Wyoming state law.

title: No Statutory Right for Tenants to Install EV Charging
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, Wyoming has no 'right-to-charge' statute giving tenants a legal right to install an electric vehicle charging system at a rental property. You're not obligated to allow, accommodate, or reasonably consider a tenant's request to install one — whether to permit it, and on what terms, is entirely your call. If you do choose to allow it, spelling out the terms (who pays for installation, who owns the equipment, what happens at move-out) in the lease is still a good idea, since nothing in Wyoming law will fill those gaps for you.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection — Voucher Applicants May Be Declined
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where accepting Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) applicants is legally mandatory, Wyoming has no source-of-income protection law. You are free to decline an applicant solely because they use a housing voucher, and doing so is not a form of discrimination under Wyoming or federal fair housing law. If you do choose to accept a voucher tenant voluntarily — which some landlords find attractive for the guaranteed, predictable monthly payment — none of Colorado's specific subsidy-tenant protections apply here: there's no Wyoming equivalent to a capped late fee for subsidized tenants or a mandated habitability-proration formula. Ordinary lease terms and Wyoming's standard Article 12 rules govern the tenancy the same as any other.

title: No Statutory Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a tenant has a statutory right to elect to pay the security deposit in installments over at least six months, Wyoming has no such right. You can require the full deposit upfront before occupancy, or choose to offer an installment arrangement voluntarily — but nothing in Wyoming law obligates you to accept installments if a tenant asks.

title: No Rental-Fee-Specific Transparency Law — General Consumer Protection Act Only
bodyText: Wyoming has no rental-fee-specific transparency law comparable to Colorado's Honest Pricing Act. There's no requirement to display a single all-in advertised price including mandatory fees, no requirement to offer at least one fee-free payment method, and no specific statutory prohibition on charging a fee for a service you don't actually provide. Wyoming does have a general Consumer Protection Act (Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-101 et seq., enacted 1973) that prohibits broadly deceptive trade practices — misrepresenting what you're offering, in general terms — and a tenant or the Attorney General's office could theoretically pursue a complaint under it if a rental fee practice were clearly deceptive. But this is a much weaker, more general protection than Colorado's specific mandates, not a real substitute for them.

title: No Tenure-Based Cause Requirement — Landlords Can End Without Cause at Any Point
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a tenant who has lived in a property for 12 months or more generally can't be removed without a specific legal cause or defined no-fault reason, Wyoming has no tenure-based cause requirement of any kind. You can end a month-to-month tenancy without cause by giving written notice, and you can decline to renew a fixed-term lease without cause once it expires — regardless of how long the tenant has lived there. No length of tenancy changes this. Ending a tenancy without cause is not the same as skipping notice. Before filing a forcible entry and detainer action you must still serve a notice to quit at least three days beforehand, by leaving a written copy with the tenant, or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found (W.S. 1-21-1003). That three-day notice is a precondition to filing, not a right to cure: Wyoming gives a tenant no statutory opportunity to cure a nonpayment by paying up. You are always free to give more notice than the statute requires, and often should.

title: No Dedicated Tenant-Death Lease-Termination Statute
bodyText: Unlike Colorado's 'Letty's Act,' Wyoming has no dedicated statute addressing what happens to a lease when a tenant dies during the term. Article 12 (all 11 sections) never addresses tenant death. In practice, if a tenant dies mid-lease, the estate generally remains liable for the remaining lease term under ordinary contract principles, subject to your general duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit (a broad contract-law mitigation-of-damages principle, not a landlord-tenant-specific statutory duty). There's no Wyoming equivalent to Colorado's specific protections against liquidated damages, accelerated rent, or clawed-back move-in concessions when a lease ends this way.

title: No Requirement to Provide Alternate Housing During Major Repairs
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, which can require you to provide comparable alternate housing or a hotel room at your own cost when a condition materially interferes with a tenant's health, life, or safety, Wyoming has no such requirement. A Wyoming tenant's only remedy for an uncorrected habitability issue is the judicial path described elsewhere in this library — sue for costs and damages, or seek a court order — not a self-help or automatic alternate-housing obligation on your part.

title: No General Deposit-Rights Nonwaivability Statute
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, which makes it explicitly unenforceable for a lease to waive a tenant's security deposit rights, Wyoming has no equivalent statute making deposit-related rights nonwaivable. This is separate from the Safe Homes Act's own nonwaiver provision, which only covers domestic-abuse-related protections, not deposit rights generally. That said, a lease provision that conflicts with a mandatory requirement — like the 30-day return deadline — would likely still be unenforceable under ordinary contract-law principles, even without an explicit statutory nonwaiver rule; Wyoming just hasn't codified that protection the way Colorado has.

title: No Broad Notice Requirement When Ownership or Management Changes
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where any change of landlord or property management company triggers a requirement to notify each tenant within 1 business day, Wyoming's only related rule is narrower: a successor owner is bound by the nonrefundable-deposit-notice and deposit-deduction duties under W.S. 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208 (see this library's edu-successor-owner-bound-wy). There's no broader Wyoming statute requiring you to proactively notify tenants of a change in ownership or management generally. Doing so anyway is still good practice — tenants need to know who to pay and who to contact — but nothing in Wyoming law requires it on a specific timeline the way Colorado's rule does.

title: No General Prohibited-Lease-Provisions Statute in Wyoming
bodyText: Unlike Colorado (C.R.S. §38-12-801), Kansas (K.S.A. 58-2547), and Nebraska (§76-1415), Wyoming has no equivalent statute banning categories of lease provisions outright — no attorney-fee-shifting ban, no confession-of-judgment ban, no exculpation/liability-limitation ban. All 11 sections of Article 12 (W.S. 1-21-1201–1211) were read directly from primary source during Wyoming's original verification pass, and no such section exists. This means the liability-disclaimer exposure found for Kansas and Nebraska in `tenants-property-insurance`, `services-utilities-provided`, `parking`, `storage-space`, and `pet-policy` doesn't apply to Wyoming — those clauses' generic language is safe to keep as-is for WY leases.

title: No Immigration-Status Inquiry Prohibition
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute prohibiting landlords from asking about immigration or citizenship status. Wyoming does have its own fair housing act (W.S. 40-26-101 through 40-26-145), which covers national origin among other classes, but immigration and citizenship status are not among its protected classes. Federal fair housing law applies as well.

title: No State-Level Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Wyoming has no state-level statute establishing a non-waivable tenant right to call police or emergency services. Any protection here would exist, if at all, at the municipal level — not audited here, consistent with how this category of question has been treated for other states in this project.

title: No Dedicated Tenant-Screening Fairness Act
bodyText: Wyoming has no rental-application or tenant-screening fairness statute — application fees are uncapped, with no requirement that the fee track the actual cost of a background/credit check. Landlords do not need tenant consent to run background and credit checks. Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act obligations still apply regardless of state law.

title: Returned Check Fee Cap
bodyText: Wyoming caps at $30 the collection fee you can charge on a bounced rent check, on top of the check's face value, and you only get it by making a written demand that follows the statute (W.S. 1-1-115(a)). The demand has prescribed content and a prescribed delivery: it must be mailed to the drawer by United States Postal Service certificate of mailing, at the address on the check or the last known address, or served personally under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure; and it must state both that the drawer has to pay the value of the check and the collection fee, and what that collection fee is. A casual email or a line on a ledger will not do. The part most landlords miss is what happens next. If the tenant does not pay the check plus the $30 within 30 days of that demand, W.S. 1-1-115(b) makes them liable for three times the amount of the check -- never less than $100 -- plus the $30 fee and court costs, and in a case where the court finds the tenant raised dilatory or bad-faith defenses it may award the prevailing party reasonable attorney fees (subsection (c)). You can bring it in small claims court if it fits that court's limit. None of this stops a criminal prosecution, though restitution paid in a criminal case is set off against a civil judgment on the same facts. This is a general bad-check statute, not a landlord-tenant one, but a bounced rent check is a dishonored check like any other.

title: No Reciprocal Attorney-Fee Statute — One-Sided Fee Clauses Are Enforceable
bodyText: Unlike Colorado, where a lease clause awarding attorney's fees only to the landlord is void (C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)), Wyoming has no reciprocity statute. Wyoming follows the American Rule - each side pays its own fees unless a contract or statute says otherwise - and the Wyoming Supreme Court requires that a contract 'unequivocally provide' for fee recovery before fees can be awarded. A landlord-only fee provision would be enforceable in Wyoming. Note that your Steinoak lease nonetheless uses mutual prevailing-party language, which gives the tenant a reciprocal right Wyoming does not require. That is a deliberate choice, not a legal obligation.

title: Wyoming Has No Holdover Rent Multiplier
bodyText: Wyoming does not provide a doubled or trebled rent penalty against a holdover tenant. A holdover is grounds for a three-day notice to vacate and a forcible entry and detainer action, and Wyoming's residential rental statutes contain no holdover damages formula at all — so plan on recovering the rental value of the holdover period and your costs through ordinary damages, not a penalty multiple. Do not confuse this with Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b), which is about PROPERTY DAMAGE: if the renter damages the unit, you may apply the deposit and the renter stays liable for damages beyond it, plus ten percent annual interest on unpaid amounts. That provision says nothing about rent for a holdover period.

title: Wyoming Imposes No Storage Duty on Removed Possessions
bodyText: Wyoming is unusually spare about what happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(a), if the renter does not vacate as a court order requires, the sheriff may remove the renter's possessions and prevent the renter from reentering, without any further action by the court. Wyoming's residential rental statutes impose no storage period, no inventory requirement, no duty of care over removed property, and no notice-before-disposal obligation on the owner. That is far less prescriptive than neighboring states — Minnesota, for example, requires a signed inventory prepared in the officer's presence, mailed notice, a care standard, and either a 28-day hold or a 60-day lien-and-sale track depending on where the property is stored. Wyoming's silence is not permission to be careless: ordinary conversion and bailment principles still apply, and documenting what was removed and its condition protects you if the tenant later claims property was lost or destroyed.

title: No Statutory Notice Period to End a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Wyoming sets no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy -- not for month-to-month, not for week-to-week, and not for a periodic tenancy of a year or more. The widely repeated "30 days" is common-law practice and the expectation of Wyoming courts, not a statute you can cite. The common-law rule scales with the tenancy: one full rental period's notice, with the termination date falling at the start of a new period. So month-to-month runs about thirty days and week-to-week about seven. Because there is no statute, the lease itself is doing the work -- state the notice period in writing rather than relying on a default that does not exist.

title: Your Property Manager Is You, for Notice Purposes
bodyText: Under W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i), a managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager counts as the "owner" for every notice and communication required or allowed under Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act -- unless the agent or manager says otherwise in writing in the rental agreement itself. Two practical consequences. If you use a property manager and the lease is silent, a tenant's written notice of a habitability problem, a deposit demand, or a forwarding address is effective when it reaches the manager, and your statutory clocks start running then, whether or not the manager has passed it along to you. And if you want notices to come to you directly, the lease is the only place you can say so -- a side agreement with the manager will not do it, because the statute requires the designation to be in the rental agreement.

title: Towing and Disposing of a Vehicle Left on Your Property
bodyText: Wyoming's rules for a vehicle abandoned on a rental property sit in the motor-vehicle title, not the landlord-tenant title, and they are more procedural than most landlords expect. To have an abandoned vehicle removed by law enforcement, you make a written request on a form the department prescribes; a police officer then places a notice of intent to impound on the vehicle, and on private property that notice must stay there at least five days before removal (W.S. 31-13-104). The towing service has its own duty to notify the registered owner and lienholders by certified mail within three business days of identifying their latest known addresses. If instead you want to clear title by selling the vehicle yourself, W.S. 31-13-109 sets the track: wait 30 days from when you knew the vehicle was left unattended or unclaimed, give written notice to the sheriff of the county of sale and to the owner and any lienholder by certified mail with return receipt, publish notice once a week for two consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, and hold the public auction no sooner than ten days after notice. Your total recoverable expenses for removal, towing, storage and sale are capped at $1,000. A court action is available but not required.

title: If the Property Is Foreclosed, Federal Law Protects Your Tenant
bodyText: Wyoming's foreclosure statutes say nothing about tenants. The foreclosure-by-advertisement chapter (W.S. 34-4-101 through 34-4-113) covers notice by publication and service, the sale, and the proceeds, with no tenant-notice step and no provision on what happens to an existing lease. The protection that does apply is federal: the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which lapsed in 2014 and was restored permanently in 2018, requires whoever takes title at foreclosure to honor a bona fide tenant's existing lease through the end of its term, and to give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate. The main exception is a purchaser who will occupy the property as a primary residence, who may end the lease early but still owes the 90 days' notice. Practically: a Wyoming lease does not evaporate at the foreclosure sale, and neither you nor a buyer can treat the tenant as a holdover on the strength of the sale alone.

title: No Statute Bans Lockouts -- and That Is Not Permission
bodyText: Wyoming gives you a court route to recover possession: a notice to quit under W.S. 1-21-1003, a forcible entry and detainer action under W.S. 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, and a writ of restitution the sheriff executes. W.S. 1-21-1211(a) is explicit that it is the sheriff, acting on a court order, who removes a renter's possessions and prevents reentry. What Wyoming does not have is the express statutory ban on landlord self-help that thirteen other states in this library carry: no located statute prohibits changing the locks, removing a door, or cutting off utilities to force a tenant out, and none sets a penalty for it. Do not read that silence as permission. For a tenant, the FED process is the route the statutes actually provide, and a landlord who locks a tenant out instead is exposed to ordinary civil claims -- wrongful eviction, trespass, and conversion of the tenant's belongings -- none of which carries a statutory cap on what a court may award. The cheap, fast-looking option is the one with the open-ended downside. Wyoming does have one non-court route, but it is not for tenants: since 2025, an owner may ask law enforcement to remove a person who unlawfully entered and remains in a dwelling, but only if that person is not a current or former tenant under a written or oral rental agreement, is not a family member or cohabitant of the owner, and no litigation over the property is pending; a person wrongly removed can recover actual damages plus triple the fair rental value for the period, with costs (W.S. 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403). Never use it against a tenant or former tenant.

title: Safe Homes Act: A Tenant Who Leaves Because of Abuse Owes No Later Rent
bodyText: Under Wyoming's Safe Homes Act (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1303), a tenant who moves out because of a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property, or because the tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the property within the preceding 60 days, is not liable for rent accruing after moving out. The tenant must give you written notice at least 7 days before moving out, stating the reason and, where applicable, the date of the incident with supporting medical, court or police evidence. If hospitalization, or seeking shelter or counseling, prevented notice within the 60 days, notice given as soon as practicable afterward still counts. Rent owed for the period before the tenant moved out and gave the notice is still owed, and your remedies for it are unaffected. These rights can't be waived (see the Safe Homes nonwaiver note).

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: Wyoming puts two different duties on you in one subsection, and they are not equally firm. The first is absolute: you must maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation (W.S. 1-21-1202(a), first sentence). Nothing in the statute lets a lease undo that one. The second is the utilities list -- operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water -- and that sentence, and only that sentence, ends 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. See the separate note on what that escape hatch actually does before you consider using it. Separately, the section does not prevent renting seasonal units such as summer cabins that were never intended to have those amenities, so a genuinely seasonal property is outside the utilities requirement without any agreement at all. The tenant must cooperate in maintaining the property (W.S. 1-21-1202(b)). See also the notes on responding to a habitability notice, on trivial conditions, and on reassigning a specific duty by written agreement. These rules come from Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act, which covers a renter's principal place of residence, not a mobile home lot or recreational property rented on an occasional basis (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(iv)); the eviction procedure applies either way.

title: Returning a Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: If you hold a deposit identified separately as a utility deposit, refund it within 10 days after the tenant shows that all utility charges they incurred are paid. If the tenant hasn't shown that within 45 days after the lease ends, apply the deposit to the tenant's outstanding utility debt within 15 days after that period ends, then refund any remaining balance within 7 days after applying it, or within 15 days after receiving the tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(b)).

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Itemization
bodyText: Within 30 days after the lease ends, or within 15 days after receiving the tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later, deliver or mail the balance of the deposit and any prepaid rent with a written itemization of any deductions and the reasons for them. If the property is damaged, the period is extended by another 30 days (Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a)). See the penalty note for what happens if you miss it. Two things Wyoming allows that the library's deposit clause deliberately does not use, both in the tenant's favour: Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct the cost of cleaning the unit back to its condition at the start of the tenancy, where the library's clause allows cleaning costs only if the unit is substantially less clean; and it lets you apply the deposit to any other costs the lease provides for, which the library's clause doesn't list. Both are lawful, so a landlord who wants them can add a custom clause. These rules come from Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act, which covers a renter's principal place of residence, not a mobile home lot or recreational property rented on an occasional basis (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(iv)); the eviction procedure applies either way.

title: When Your Tenant Causes the Damage
bodyText: Wyoming law is unusually good to the landlord here, and it works without any lease clause. A renter must not intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly let anyone else do so (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(i)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit to the damage, and the renter stays liable for whatever the deposit does not cover, plus interest at ten percent a year on the unpaid balance, and you may take any legal action available to recover it (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). Two defences the tenant would otherwise have are switched off. You are not required to correct any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees through inappropriate use or misuse (W.S. 1-21-1203(c)). And the renter's repair remedies -- the notice-to-repair ladder, the civil action, the court-ordered termination -- are available only to a renter who is in compliance with the renter-duty and prohibited-act sections (W.S. 1-21-1206(a)), so a renter who caused the damage is generally outside them. What Wyoming does not give you is a rule about rent. There is no casualty or untenantability statute in Wyoming at all, so nothing in the statutes says whether rent keeps running while a unit the tenant wrecked is repaired, or whether you can recover the rent you lose if the lease ends. That is left entirely to the lease, which is why the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause exists. Without it you are arguing common-law damages and mitigation from scratch.

title: What You List, You Must Maintain
bodyText: Wyoming turns part of your own lease into a statutory duty. W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv) requires an owner to 'maintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement' -- so whatever you list in the lease stops being a courtesy and becomes an obligation under the Residential Rental Property Act, enforceable through the renter's remedy ladder in W.S. 1-21-1206: written notice, then a formal notice to repair, then a civil action in circuit court that can award the renter costs, damages, rent improperly retained, an order to repair, or termination of the lease. List the window air conditioner and you have to keep it running. Two related levers run the other way. The baseline in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) -- operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water -- applies 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. And W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in the article be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Wyoming is unusually permissive on this; most states make habitability non-waivable. Both are real, and both are blunt instruments: a lease that contracts away heat or hot water is a lease you will have to defend. The practical rule is to list appliances deliberately rather than generously, and to treat any shifting of a core duty as a decision to take advice on, not a form field.

title: Which Notices You Cannot Send by Email
bodyText: Wyoming's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-101 through 40-21-119) is broad: it excludes only wills, codicils and testamentary trusts, most of the Uniform Commercial Code, and the Uniform Computer Information Transactions Act (W.S. 40-21-103(b)). Unlike some states, it carves out nothing for eviction, default or cure notices, and nothing for residential leases. That does not make email safe for the notices that matter, because the landlord-tenant statutes prescribe their own service. The three-day notice to quit that must precede any forcible entry and detainer action is served 'by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business' (W.S. 1-21-1003) -- a physical delivery. The habitability notices under W.S. 1-21-1203(b) and the renter's notice to repair under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) must go by certified mail or in the manner W.S. 1-21-1003 specifies. The abandoned-property notice under W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i) is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. UETA itself says a transaction it covers is still subject to other applicable substantive law (W.S. 40-21-103(d)), so these methods control. Two further limits. The act applies only between parties who have each agreed to conduct transactions electronically, judged from the context and the parties' conduct (W.S. 40-21-105(b)). And a party who has agreed may still refuse to conduct other transactions electronically -- a right the statute says in terms 'may not be waived by agreement' (W.S. 40-21-105(c)). A blanket lease clause consenting to electronic notice for everything cannot take that away.

title: Does Consumer Law Reach Your Lease?
bodyText: Wyoming has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts, so there is no readability test to meet and no required statement of the rights a tenant is giving up. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act (W.S. 40-12-101 and following) is the only general consumer statute in play, and no Wyoming case deciding whether it reaches a residential lease was reviewed. It defines 'merchandise' to include 'any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed' -- real property is expressly in. But it reaches only a 'consumer transaction', defined as the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of merchandise to an individual for primarily personal, family or household purposes. Renting a home is plainly for household purposes; the Act does not say whether letting it is a 'sale or distribution', but its exemptions section (W.S. 40-12-110) contains no exemption for real property or for landlords, so assume it can apply. It is also the only Wyoming statute aimed at a landlord's knowing misconduct: its unlawful practices are gated on acting 'knowingly'. Before suing under it a consumer must give written notice of the practice and the damage within one year of discovering it or two years of the transaction, whichever is first, which gives you a chance to cure (W.S. 40-12-109). What the Act does not contain is worth knowing, because other states do have these: there is no provision making it unlawful to leave blank spaces in a contract to be filled in after signing, and none requiring that the consumer be given a copy at signing. The unlawful-practice list in W.S. 40-12-105 runs to misrepresentation, false pricing, bait-and-switch and the like, with a catch-all at (a)(xv) for 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. If the Act does reach leases, that catch-all is the realistic exposure -- a lease term or a rental advertisement that misleads -- rather than anything about formatting. Practical reading: draft honestly and fill in every blank before signing, but do not expect a Wyoming consumer-law formatting rule, because there is not one.

title: No Algorithmic Rent-Setting Rule
bodyText: Wyoming statutes do not regulate the use of algorithmic or software pricing tools to set residential rents. Wyoming regulates rent lightly in general: there is no rent control, no rent-increase notice period and no cap. Federal antitrust law and any city ordinance may still apply.

title: Fees Are Not Rent in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act never defines 'rent', and no statute converts a fee into rent. That matters most at the eviction door. A forcible entry and detainer action for nonpayment is available only 'after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due' (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(i)); unpaid late fees, pet fees or utility charges are not rent, and calling them 'additional rent' in the lease does not make them the thing the statute names. Trying to evict on unpaid fees alone is how a Wyoming nonpayment case gets dismissed. The statutes keep the two apart elsewhere too: a deposit may be applied to 'accrued rent' and separately to 'other costs provided by any contract' (W.S. 1-21-1208(a)), and in an FED judgment the court finds 'the amount of rent due and payable' and adds costs and attorney's fees as the lease provides (W.S. 1-21-1008(b)). You can still collect fees -- sue for them, deduct them from the deposit, or treat them as a lease breach. What you cannot do is run them through the three-day nonpayment route.

title: No Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Some states let a landlord give notice, do work the tenant should have done, and add the cost to the next rent payment. Wyoming does not. Nothing in the Residential Rental Property Act gives an owner a self-cure right, a notice period for one, or a way to bill the cost as rent. What you do have: the renter owes the statutory duties in W.S. 1-21-1204 and must not commit the prohibited acts in W.S. 1-21-1205, and may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make repairs or inspect (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(iii)). Breach of either section is a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action in its own right (W.S. 1-21-1002(a)(vi)). If the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit and sue for the rest plus ten percent interest (W.S. 1-21-1211(b)). So the Wyoming route is entry, then damages or possession -- not self-help repair billed forward as rent. A lease clause purporting to make repair costs 'additional rent' would also run into the point that Wyoming's three-day nonpayment eviction reaches rent only.

title: No Blank-Space or Lease-Copy Rule
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no statutory requirement that a written lease have every blank space completed, and none that the landlord give the tenant a signed copy. Neither failure is a statutory breach the way it is in some states. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act does not list either one among its unlawful practices. Two things still bite. Wyoming recognises oral rental agreements -- the Act's definition of 'rental agreement' covers 'any agreement, written or oral' (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(ii)) -- so an incomplete written lease does not leave you with no lease; it leaves you arguing about terms. And several Wyoming rights turn on something being in the rental agreement in writing: the nonrefundable-deposit statement (W.S. 1-21-1207), the agent notice opt-out (W.S. 1-21-1201(a)(i)), appliances you must maintain (W.S. 1-21-1203(a)(iv)), the occupancy number (W.S. 1-21-1204(a)(v), which separately requires the tenant to occupy the unit in the manner for which it was designed, whatever the lease says) and any reassignment of duties (W.S. 1-21-1202(d)). A blank left in one of those is a right left on the table. Fill in every blank, bracket and placeholder before signing, and give the tenant a copy -- not because a statute says so, but because the statutes that matter all point back at the document.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: Wyoming's Residential Rental Property Act contains no covenant of quiet enjoyment or quiet possession running from the landlord to the tenant. The Act's only 'peaceful enjoyment' language runs the other way: it is a renter's duty not to 'interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property' (W.S. 1-21-1205(a)(ii)), which protects neighbouring tenants from this one, not this tenant from you. A tenant's possession is protected instead by the shape of the eviction process: the three-day notice to quit, the court action, and a sheriff acting on a court order (W.S. 1-21-1003, 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, 1-21-1211(a)). Wyoming attaches no statutory damages to an unlawful ouster, which is the gap covered separately in the self-help row; that row also explains the 2025 law-enforcement removal route for a person who was never a tenant, which never applies to a tenant (W.S. 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403). Whether a covenant of quiet enjoyment is implied in a Wyoming lease as a matter of common law was not researched and is not answered here.

title: Statutory Forms
bodyText: Wyoming prescribes no form for a residential lease, no form for an eviction notice and no agency-issued tenant-rights document that has to be attached to anything. There is no 'substantially in the following form' language anywhere in the residential rental statutes. What the statutes prescribe is content, not form, and in two places only. The abandoned-property notice must describe the property claimed to be abandoned and state that it will be disposed of seven days after service unless the renter acts (W.S. 1-21-1210(a)(i)), and it is deemed served only by certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for that purpose, by personal service under Rule 4, or by newspaper publication. The renter's own 'notice to repair or correct condition' has five prescribed contents under W.S. 1-21-1206(b) -- that one is the tenant's to draft, but knowing its required elements tells you whether a notice you received is effective. Outside the landlord-tenant title, the bad-check demand under W.S. 1-1-115(a) has prescribed content too: it must state that the drawer has to pay the value of the check and the collection fee, and state the amount of that fee.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Wyoming statutes do not address tenant-installed security cameras, video doorbells or similar devices. The lease's alteration and installation terms govern -- in this library, the Alterations section, which requires your written consent before a tenant adds or changes a fixture. Wyoming's recording and surveillance laws, and any homeowners-association rules, were not reviewed and may apply to what a camera records rather than to its installation.

title: The Utilities Waiver -- Legal in Wyoming, and Still a Bad Idea
bodyText: Wyoming lets a lease do something almost no other state allows. The sentence in W.S. 1-21-1202(a) requiring operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water ends with 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'. Read plainly, a signed lease can remove the requirement itself -- not shift who maintains the water heater, but agree there need not be hot water. Keep that separate from the other flexibility in the same section. W.S. 1-21-1202(d) lets you assign a specific duty to the tenant: the unit still has to have a working well pump, the tenant just looks after it. That one is in the lease library as an optional clause. The (a) waiver removes the amenity from the deal altogether, and it is not offered as a clause -- deliberately. Three reasons to leave it alone. The habitability duty in the first sentence of 1-21-1202(a) -- safe, sanitary, fit for human habitation -- carries no such escape, so a unit with no heat in a Wyoming winter may well fail that duty whatever the lease says, and you would be arguing the point in front of a judge. No Wyoming case law on this sentence was reviewed for this library, so how far a court would let it stretch is unknown. And a tenant's agreement to go without heat is exactly the kind of term that invites an unconscionability argument and reads badly to everyone who later looks at it. If what you actually have is a cabin, you may not need the waiver at all: the same subsection says it 'shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities'. A genuinely seasonal property sits outside the utilities requirement by statute. If after all that you still want the term, it is lawful and you can add it as your own custom clause. Put the specific amenity and the reason in writing, keep it off anything that touches safety, and get advice first.

title: What Happens When a Wyoming Tenant Walks Out Early
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute that tells you to re-rent after a tenant abandons, and no statute that keeps the lease alive for the rest of the term. The Residential Rental Property Act (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) says nothing about mitigation of damages, reletting, or avoidable loss. What the Act does do is define the event. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(v), "termination" means the lawful ending of a rental agreement "for any reason," and the definition expressly lists "abandonment of the leased premises by the renter prior to expiration of the rental period." That matters more than it looks. Every deadline in the Act that runs from "termination of the rental agreement" starts running on the abandonment, not at the end of the original lease term. So once you have lawfully regained possession of an abandoned unit, the clock in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) is already running: you have thirty days from termination, or fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, to deliver or mail the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent with a written itemization of every deduction and the reason for it. If the unit is damaged, that period is extended by another thirty days. You cannot hold the deposit open until the end of the term to see how much rent you ultimately lose. Do the itemization on the abandonment-date clock, deduct the accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition, and other contract costs that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) allows, and pursue anything beyond that separately.

For belongings left behind, follow Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210. Trash and anything you reasonably believe is hazardous, perishable, or valueless and abandoned can go immediately, and anything still in the unit after termination is presumed valueless and abandoned. For property you treat as valuable, serve written notice describing it and saying it will be disposed of after seven days, served by certified mail to an address the renter gave you in writing for that purpose, by personal service under W.R.C.P. 4, or by newspaper publication in the county. Silence for seven days makes the property conclusively abandoned. A written response claiming it buys the renter another seven days, and the statute caps the whole hold at fifteen days. You may charge reasonable or actual storage costs plus removal, payable before the renter takes the goods, and you are not responsible for loss during storage.

For the money, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b) lets you recover damage to the unit beyond the deposit, with ten percent annual interest on the unpaid balance, and preserves "any legal action available" to you. It says nothing about future rent. Because the statute is silent on both future rent and mitigation, your right to unpaid rent for the remainder of the term rests on your lease and on Wyoming contract common law, not on the Act; Wyoming has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so there is no statutory default to fall back on. Take the cautious course. Write an express survival clause into the lease stating that the tenant remains liable for rent through the end of the term, less sums actually collected from a replacement tenant, because nothing in the statute supplies that term for you. Then market the unit promptly anyway and keep dated proof of the listings, showings, and rent asked. A Wyoming court applying ordinary contract principles can impose an avoidable-consequences limit on your recovery even without a statute, and a documented re-rental effort costs you nothing if the court does not. Do not rely on a lease term purporting to waive any duty to mitigate; no Wyoming statute blesses one, and you would be litigating the question with no authority on your side.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Wyoming has no accessory dwelling unit (ADU) statute. The Wyoming Statutes never use the phrase "accessory dwelling unit," "accessory apartment," or any equivalent, and no state law requires a city, town or county to allow a second small dwelling on a single-family lot, caps what a local government may charge or require for one, or bars an owner-occupancy condition. Whether you may build an ADU, and whether you may rent it out, is entirely a question of your local zoning. Cities and towns get that power from Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-601(a), which lets the governing body regulate by ordinance the height, number of stories and size of buildings, the percentage of the lot that may be occupied, the size of yards and open spaces, population density, and the location and use of buildings, structures and land for residence or other purposes, and divide the municipality into districts; counties get the parallel power over unincorporated areas from Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-201(a). Neither statute mentions accessory units, so a local ordinance that prohibits them, allows them only with a conditional use permit, or requires the owner to live on the lot is valid in Wyoming and the state will not override it. Practical course: before you advertise or lease an ADU, confirm in writing with the city or county planning office that the unit is a permitted dwelling unit at that address, that it has been permitted and inspected as a dwelling (not as a garage, shop, basement or storage space), and that any owner-occupancy or parking condition attached to its approval is being met. Renting out a unit that local zoning does not recognize exposes you to an abatement or enforcement action, and in most Wyoming municipalities enforcement runs against the property owner, not the tenant. Note also that a city or town may act under Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-602 only after a public hearing with at least fifteen days' notice, so ADU rules can and do change locally - check the current ordinance, not an older copy. Once the unit is lawfully rented, the tenancy is an ordinary Wyoming residential tenancy and the rental statutes at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211 apply to it the same as to any other rental dwelling. LOCAL ORDINANCE: ADU permission, size, parking and owner-occupancy rules are set municipality by municipality and county by county and are not resolved here.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Method in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no "actual notice" standard in its residential rental law, and no provision letting you and the tenant agree in the lease on an extra way of giving a notice the statutes require, such as a text message or an e-mail. Instead, each Wyoming statute that requires a notice names how that notice is given, and you must use the named method. The tenant's written notice of an unsafe or unsanitary condition, and your written answer to it, are served by certified mail or in the manner set out in Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003 (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1203(b)); the tenant's follow-up "notice to repair or correct condition" goes the same way (§ 1-21-1206(b)). A notice to quit before a forcible entry and detainer action is served at least three days before you file, by leaving a written copy with the tenant, or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found (§ 1-21-1003). A notice that property left behind is treated as abandoned is deemed served only on the date it is mailed by certified mail to an address the tenant gave you in writing for that purpose, the date it is personally delivered under Rule 4 of the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, or the date it is published in a newspaper published or widely circulated in the county (§ 1-21-1210(a)(i)(A)-(C)). The lease cannot substitute a text or an e-mail for any of those. Wyoming's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 40-21-101 through 40-21-119) does let an electronic record satisfy a writing requirement, but only between parties who have each agreed to transact electronically (§ 40-21-105(b)), only if the record can be retained and printed by the recipient (§ 40-21-108(a)), and expressly not where another law specifies a transmission method — in that case "the record must be sent, communicated or transmitted by the method specified in the other law," and that requirement cannot be varied by agreement (§ 40-21-108(b)(ii), (d)). The practical course: you may add a lease term saying routine, non-statutory communications (maintenance scheduling, rent reminders, showing coordination) may be sent by text or e-mail to the address or number the tenant gives in writing, and that is enforceable as a contract term; but serve every statutory notice — notice to quit, the habitability responses, and the abandoned-property notice — exactly as the statute directs, on paper, and keep the certified-mail receipt or the server's return. Sending an extra courtesy copy by text or e-mail is fine and costs you nothing, but it never replaces the statutory service.

title: Claims and Foreclosure Against the Property
bodyText:
Wyoming does not require you to tell a tenant or an applicant that the property is in foreclosure, under a tax proceeding, or subject to anyone else's claim. There is no disclosure statute on the subject and no Wyoming statute on attornment, so nothing makes a tenant's agreement to treat a stranger as landlord void and nothing obliges the tenant to forward you a notice they receive. If you want either protection, the lease has to create it.

What Wyoming does do is make the foreclosing lender notify your tenant directly. Before a mortgage is foreclosed by advertisement and sale, the foreclosing mortgagee must serve written notice of intent to foreclose on the record owner and, separately, on "the person in possession of the mortgaged premises if different than the record owner" -- your tenant -- by certified mail, return receipt requested, at least ten days before publication begins (Wyo. Stat. § 34-4-103(a)(iv)). It must then serve a copy of the published notice of sale on the record owner, the person in possession, and subordinate lienholders by certified mail before the first date of publication (Wyo. Stat. § 34-4-104(a)). Expect your tenant to learn of a foreclosure from the lender whether or not you say anything, and expect to be asked about it.

Practical course: if the property is in or heading toward foreclosure, tell your tenants yourself rather than letting the certified letter be the first they hear of it, and keep collecting rent under the lease until a sale and the redemption period actually change who owns the property. Separately, note that federal law still protects a bona fide tenant after a foreclosure sale: FEDERAL: Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, 12 U.S.C. § 5220 note, which generally lets a bona fide lease run to the end of its term and otherwise requires 90 days' notice to vacate from the successor in interest. A Wyoming city or town may have its own notice or registration rule for foreclosed rental property; check the local ordinance where the unit sits.

title: Charging a Tenant for Alarm Tampering in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute on smoke or carbon monoxide alarms in rental housing at all, and therefore none that authorizes, sets or caps a lease fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with one. The words "smoke alarm," "smoke detector" and "carbon monoxide" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes in a dwelling-alarm sense — the only "carbon monoxide" reference in the whole code is the animal-euthanasia ban at Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-1003(a). Alarm requirements for Wyoming buildings come instead from the International Fire Code and International Building Code, which the state fire prevention and electrical safety council adopts by rule under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i), and which a municipality or county may enforce locally under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121. Those adopted codes and any city ordinance are outside this library — check them for whether your building must have alarms and who must maintain them.

Because no Wyoming statute creates a tampering fee, treat it as a contract and damages question, and charge your cost rather than a penalty. Three Wyoming provisions give you real leverage. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(i) forbids a renter to "[i]ntentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the residential rental unit or knowingly permit any person to do so" — a hard-wired or landlord-installed alarm is part of the unit, so pulling one off the ceiling breaches this statutory duty directly, with no lease language needed. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(iv) and (a)(vii) require the renter to use the unit's facilities reasonably and to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, so a written no-tampering rule in your lease is itself enforceable as a statutory duty. Third, knowingly defacing, injuring or destroying another person's property without consent is the crime of property destruction and defacement under Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-201(a) — a misdemeanor under $1,000 of damage — but any fine there goes to the state, not to you.

Practical course: put a no-tampering term in the lease and make the tenant liable for the actual, documented cost of repairing or replacing an alarm the tenant or the tenant's guest removed, disabled or damaged, keep receipts, and bill that cost or deduct it at move-out from the deposit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a). Do not write in a flat dollar "tampering fee": Wyoming has no statute blessing one, so its enforceability would turn on whether a court treats it as a reasonable liquidated-damages estimate or an unenforceable penalty — a case-law question this library did not research. A charge tied to your real loss is safe; a round-number penalty is not.

title: Animals Left Behind in a Wyoming Rental
bodyText: Wyoming gives you no right to enter a unit to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. The words 'animal' and 'pet' do not appear anywhere in Wyoming's residential rental article. The only access Wyoming law secures for you is in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii), which bars the renter from unreasonably denying entry 'for the purpose of making repairs to or inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale' — a closed list that does not include animal welfare. On the other hand, Wyoming has no statute restricting landlord entry either, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties modify the article's duties 'by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' So the practical answer is to put animal-care entry in the signed lease, with an emergency contact for each animal, rather than rely on the statute. Two traps. First, do not treat a live animal as abandoned property under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210. That section lets you presume property left in the unit is valueless and abandoned and dispose of it after a seven-day notice; applying it to a pet would put you in the position of the person with 'charge and custody' of the animal, and under Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-1002(a)(iv) failing to provide proper food, drink or protection from the weather, abandoning the animal, or failing to get care for an obviously seriously ill or injured animal is criminal cruelty. Relinquishing the animal to a public or private animal shelter is expressly not abandonment under § 6-3-1002(a)(iv)(B), so a shelter is your safe exit. Second, Wyoming's seizure procedure for mistreated animals runs through law enforcement, not through you: Wyo. Stat. § 11-29-109 lets a peace officer or an agent of the livestock board take charge of an abandoned, neglected or cruelly treated livestock animal, and there is no equivalent self-help power for a landlord or for a household pet. If you find an animal in distress, call animal control or a peace officer, document what you saw, and let them take custody.

title: Appliances Are Opt-In Under Wyoming Law
bodyText:
Wyoming runs the opposite way from most states on appliances. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) says you must "maintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." The duty is created by your lease, not by the statute: if the lease does not specifically contract for an appliance, you have no statutory duty to maintain it. There is no Wyoming statute presuming that an appliance sitting in the unit is yours, and no statute requiring you to supply a stove, a refrigerator, a washer, air conditioning or any other appliance.

That makes your appliance list the most important sentence in this part of your lease, and it cuts both ways. List an appliance you will maintain and you have taken on a statutory obligation you did not otherwise have. Leave it off and you have not. So write an affirmative list of what you supply and maintain, keep it short and accurate, and add a catch-all saying anything not on the list is excluded. Do not list an appliance you have no intention of servicing just to be thorough.

Four things the list cannot get you out of. Under § 1-21-1203(a)(i)-(iii) you must not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; you must maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition; and you must maintain the electrical systems, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water. Section 1-21-1202(a) adds the general duty to keep the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation. A water heater or furnace serving the unit sits inside those duties no matter how you label it, so do not try to exclude one as an "appliance."

Two real limits worth knowing. First, § 1-21-1202(a) allows hot and cold running water to be varied "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties," and § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty in the article be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by both parties. There is no anti-waiver provision in the article. That is a real power, but it is not a good idea for essential systems: the exception exists mainly for seasonal units such as summer cabins, which § 1-21-1202(a) names expressly. Second, § 1-21-1202(c) limits the whole article to conditions that materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter, so a broken dishwasher was never a statutory problem in the first place — it is a contract problem governed by whatever your lease says.

Practical steps. Remove an unwanted appliance before move-in rather than leaving it and disclaiming it, because an appliance you let the tenant use is an appliance a court may find you contracted to supply. If you leave one, name it in the lease as excluded, say the tenant uses it as-is, and offer to remove it on written request. Photograph the unit at move-in. And if a tenant installs their own appliance, say in writing that the tenant maintains it and restores the unit on removal.

title: No Wyoming Rule on Application or Screening Fees
bodyText: Wyoming does not regulate the rental application stage at all. There is no cap on what you may charge an applicant, no requirement that the fee match your actual screening cost, no refund duty if you rent the unit to someone else before spending the money, no bar on charging a fee when no unit is available, no exemption for minor household members, no portable-screening-report rule, no written screening-criteria disclosure duty, and no state adverse-action or denial-notice requirement. The phrases "rental application," "screening fee," "prospective tenant" and "holding fee" do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes; the only mention of "tenant screening" is in Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-505(d), which exempts public-records-only tenant-screening databases from the consumer credit security-freeze rules — so an applicant's credit freeze will not necessarily block that kind of search, though it will block an ordinary credit report pulled under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-503. What does constrain you comes from outside Wyoming's application-fee law. The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681 et seq., governs permissible purpose and the adverse-action notice you must give when you deny or charge more because of a consumer report. The federal Fair Housing Act and Wyoming's own Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, make it unlawful under § 40-26-103 to discriminate in rental on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin — which reaches a fee or screening standard applied unevenly, so charge every applicant for a given property the same amount under the same written criteria even though no statute makes you. One Wyoming trap does bite: if you credit an application fee toward a deposit, or call any part of it a deposit, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and requires separate written notice of that fact to the renter when the deposit is taken. Keep a true application fee separate from deposit money, label it plainly as a nonrefundable processing fee in your written application, and § 1-21-1207 stays out of it. Because no statute fills the gap, your application fee, refund policy and screening standards are set by the written application you hand the applicant — so put them in writing and apply them consistently. Municipal ordinances are not covered here and should be checked locally.

title: Asbestos in a Wyoming Rental
bodyText:
Wyoming has no asbestos law that touches you as a landlord. There is no statute requiring you to disclose asbestos to a tenant, to inspect a rental for it, to give notice before asbestos work, or to hire a state-licensed abatement contractor. Wyoming has no state asbestos abatement licensing or accreditation program and no clean-indoor-air or indoor environmental-quality act. The word 'asbestos' appears in the Wyoming statutes only in the Successor Corporation Asbestos-Related Liability Fairness Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-1-131 through 1-1-137, which caps the asbestos tort liability a corporation inherits from a company it absorbed before May 13, 1968. That act is about corporate successor liability in asbestos personal-injury suits; it imposes no duty on a landlord and gives a tenant nothing.

What actually governs you is federal, and it bites hardest when you renovate or demolish rather than when you rent. Under the EPA asbestos NESHAP, FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. § 61.145, before you renovate or demolish you must have the affected portion of the building thoroughly inspected for asbestos-containing material, and if regulated quantities are present you must file written notice with the regulator before work starts and follow the removal and wetting work practices. The threshold is low enough that an ordinary gut-renovation of an older apartment can cross it. Under FEDERAL: 29 C.F.R. § 1926.1101(k), a building owner must determine the presence, location and quantity of asbestos-containing and presumed asbestos-containing thermal system insulation and surfacing material, and must notify the employers of anyone who will work in or next to it — that reaches your own maintenance staff and every contractor you send in. Note also that the only federal pre-lease disclosure of this family is for lead, not asbestos: FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d and 24 C.F.R. part 35 subpart A require a lead-based paint disclosure and the EPA pamphlet for target housing built before 1978, and Wyoming adds nothing to it ('lead-based paint' appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes).

The practical course. Do not volunteer an asbestos statement in the lease; Wyoming does not require one and a loose or wrong statement can become a misrepresentation you have to defend. If you know the building has asbestos, say so accurately and in writing, keep the survey, and tell the tenant in the house rules not to drill, sand, scrape or remove ceiling or pipe-insulation material. Before any renovation of a building built before roughly 1980, get a survey from an accredited inspector and budget for the federal notification and work practices. If a tenant reports crumbling pipe lagging, popcorn ceiling or floor tile, treat it as a habitability repair under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203 (which applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence, per § 1-21-1201(a)(iv)) and do not let the tenant 'fix' it. Remember that § 1-21-1202(d) lets any Article 12 duty be reassigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, but never use that to push asbestos work onto a tenant — the federal work-practice rules run to the owner and the employer regardless of what the lease says.

title: Association Documents and Your Wyoming Tenant
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires a lease of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' or property owners' association to disclose the association's obligations, and none requires you to hand the tenant the declaration, the covenants or the rules. Wyoming's Condominium Ownership Act is unusually thin: it is four sections, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-20-101 through 34-20-104, and it stops at recognising condominium ownership, defining air space units and common elements, and handling tax assessment and recording. It creates no resale certificate, no offering statement and no bylaws regime — the word "bylaws" does not appear anywhere in Title 34. Wyoming has no common-interest-ownership act and no planned-community act at all. The county subdivision statutes, Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-306(a)(xii) and § 18-5-316(a)(x), do require a subdivider to show that recorded covenants create an entity (homeowners' associations are named as one option), but those covenants are made binding on "subsequent owners of the land," and nothing in them speaks to a lease or a tenant.

This matters more in Wyoming than in states with a full condominium act, because there is no provision anywhere that binds your tenant to the association's documents directly. In Virgin Islands, Guam and Hawaii style acts the tenant is bound by the declaration and bylaws whether or not the lease mentions them; Wyoming has no equivalent. The only Wyoming provision that makes association obligations run with the property is § 34-20-104(c), and it reaches "all condominium owners and their successors in interest" — an owner's obligation, not an occupant's. So if you want the association's rules to reach your tenant, your lease has to put them there. Attach the current declaration, covenants and rules to the lease as an exhibit, or state plainly where the tenant can read them, require compliance as a lease term, and send the tenant each amendment the association adopts. Rules given after signing are safest treated as binding only once the tenant has actual notice of them.

Do the same with money. The association assesses you, not your tenant, and will fine you for what your tenant does. You can pass a fine on only if the lease creates that charge — but if it does, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct "other costs provided by any contract" from the deposit, so a clearly drafted pass-through is collectable out of the deposit as well as recoverable as rent. A pass-through you never wrote down is not collectable at all. Note also that Wyoming law gives an association no right to collect rent directly from your tenant if you fall behind on assessments, so that risk stays between you and the association.

title: Automatic Renewal and the No-Implied-Renewal Rule
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute regulating automatic renewal clauses in residential leases. There is no bold-face type requirement, no separate pre-renewal reminder notice, no affirmative opt-in or initials box, and no general consumer automatic-renewal law that reaches a lease of a dwelling. The one place Wyoming legislates about an agreement that is "automatically renewable" is the Wyoming Consumer Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-19-101 through 40-19-120, and that Act is confined to rent-to-own of personal property: § 40-19-102(a)(x) defines "property" as personal property, so it cannot reach a residential tenancy.

What Wyoming does have is two old statutes that point the opposite way from most states, and landlords who bring a form lease in from elsewhere get them wrong. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that in Wyoming the relation of landlord and tenant does not exist by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, and that on expiration of a term created by a lease, verbal or written, "there shall be no implied renewal of the same, for any period of time whatever, either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent for or during any period of such holding over." Holding over plus your acceptance of rent creates a tenancy by sufferance only. Wyo.
