Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that a lease which has expired by its own limitation may be renewed only "by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto," whether the original lease was written or verbal, and that no tenancy other than sufferance exists after the original lease terminates unless created that way.

The practical consequences are real. You cannot let a term run out and assume the tenant's continued payment carries your lease forward; it does not, and the terms you care about most (late charges, the pet addendum, any attorney-fee provision, the deposit terms, rules incorporated by reference) stop binding the occupant as contract when the term ends. A sufferance tenancy also has no statutory notice period in Wyoming - no month-to-month statute exists - so ending it runs through the Article 10 route, a three-day notice to quit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 and then a forcible entry and detainer action.

Whether an automatic-renewal clause written into the original signed lease satisfies § 34-2-129 is unsettled, and this review covers statutes only, not Wyoming case law. The better reading is that a lease whose own terms extend it never "expire[s] by its own limitation," so § 34-2-129 is not triggered at all; but no Wyoming statute says so. The cautious course, and the one to build your process around: use an automatic renewal or extension clause if you want one, and also obtain a short renewal or extension addendum signed by every party before the current term ends. That way the renewal rests on an express signed writing whichever reading is correct, and you never find yourself holding a sufferance tenant you thought was under a lease. Finally, if you do use an auto-renewal clause, describe it plainly: the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches real property (Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi)), and a renewal term that is buried or misdescribed could be attacked under the § 40-12-105(a)(xv) catch-all, which is gated on knowing conduct and requires the pre-suit notice and cure period in § 40-12-109.

title: No balcony or deck inspection mandate, but exterior fire stairs must be kept in repair
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring you to have balconies, decks, porches, landings or other exterior elevated structures inspected by an engineer, architect or certified inspector, on a schedule or at all. The word "balcony" does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes, and there is no Wyoming counterpart to the California or Maryland balcony-inspection laws. There is also no reporting form, no filing, and no certification you must keep on file.

What Wyoming does impose on you is older and narrower. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-501, every apartment house or tenement house three or more stories in height must have safe and suitable metallic, tunnel, iron or fireproof ladder or stair fire escapes, fitted with a guard rail of sufficient strength, attached to the outside walls and running from at or near the ground to the top story, with platforms of at least six feet by three feet positioned near the windows of each story above the first, and you must post notices in every hall and in a conspicuous place showing where the fire escapes are on each floor. Under § 35-9-502, an apartment house, boarding house or tenement house of two stories or less with twelve or more rooms must have at least two stairways, hallways or other means of exit from each story. Section 35-9-504 is the maintenance duty that matters most here: all such fire escapes, stairways, hallways and means of egress must at all times be kept free from obstruction, in good repair and ready for use, and lit at night with a red light marked "FIRE ESCAPE". Under § 35-9-506 an owner, or anyone having the management or control of the building, who fails to comply commits a misdemeanor punishable by three to six months in the county jail, a fine of $100 to $500, or both, and every month the building stays in violation is a separate offense. Section 35-9-507 switches §§ 35-9-501 through 35-9-507 off entirely inside any incorporated city or town that has adopted a uniform building code by ordinance covering inside fire escapes, smoke towers and fireproof enclosed stairways, so in most Wyoming municipalities the local code, not these sections, is what governs you - and that local code is not something this review can resolve for you. Check with your city or town building department.

The general rental duties do not fill the gap either. Wyoming's rental-unit duty section, § 1-21-1203(a)(iii), carries a closed ongoing list - electrical, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water - and structural exterior elements are not on it. Section 1-21-1203(a)(i) requires the unit to be fit for human habitation when the tenant takes possession, and § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) reaches anything else only "as specifically contracted", so a balcony or deck becomes your maintenance obligation chiefly because your own lease says so. These Article 12 duties also apply only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence (§ 1-21-1201(a)(iv)). Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) has the state fire prevention and electrical safety council adopt minimum standards not exceeding the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code and International Fuel Gas Code - those model codes contain guard and railing requirements, but under § 35-9-108 the state fire marshal's plan-review and certificate-of-occupancy machinery is triggered by new construction and remodeling, not by periodic inspection of an existing balcony. If a failing structure becomes dangerous, the pressure comes from the nuisance side instead: § 35-1-105(a)(vii) allows a removal order with only a 48-hour compliance window, and §§ 35-9-111 through 35-9-113 allow fire-hazard condemnation.

Practically: inspect your own elevated wood structures on a schedule you set, document it, and treat ledger connections, flashing, fasteners and guard height as the failure points. Write the inspection and repair obligation into the lease if you intend the tenant to report problems, because § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) will not supply it for you.

title: No Bed Bug or Pest Statute in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no bed bug statute and no pest statute of any kind for rental housing. There is no disclosure duty, no inspection or treatment deadline, no rule on who pays, and no statutory tenant duty to cooperate with treatment or to prepare a unit. The words “bed bug” and “vermin” do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes; “infestation,” “infested” and “pest” appear almost entirely in Title 11 (agriculture, crop and livestock pests), and the Wyoming Pesticide Act’s only occupant-notice rule, Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-375, is limited by its own terms to school buildings and school property — it imposes nothing on a landlord or on a pest control operator treating an apartment.

What fills the gap. Four provisions do the work. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) bars you from renting a unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, so a known active infestation at move-in is your problem before the lease starts. Second, § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) requires you to maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition. Third, § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) is a closed ongoing list — electrical systems, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water — and pest control is not on it; § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) sweeps in “other appliances and facilities” only “as specifically contracted in the rental agreement.” So if your lease promises pest control, you have created the duty; if it is silent, no ongoing statutory extermination duty exists inside an occupied unit. Fourth, § 1-21-1203(c) says you are not required to correct any condition caused by the renter, the renter’s family, guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse of the property — your best defense when a tenant brings in infested furniture.

On the tenant’s side, § 1-21-1204(a)(i) requires the renter to keep the unit clean and safe and not unreasonably burden any common area, and (a)(ii) requires disposal of garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner. Neither mentions pests, and neither compels a tenant to prepare the unit. Access is better than you might think: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) forbids a renter to unreasonably deny access to, refuse entry to or withhold consent to enter the unit for the owner, agent or manager “for the purpose of making repairs to or inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale,” and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1205 a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action. That covers an inspection for pests. It does not expressly cover a treatment visit, it sets no notice period and names no hours, and it says nothing about preparing the unit. Put the cooperation and access duties in writing: § 1-21-1202(d) lets any Article 12 duty be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and a signed lease is the only instrument that will give you an enforceable right to enter, require preparation, or charge a tenant-caused treatment back.

Two limits. All of Article 12 applies only to a “residential rental unit,” defined by § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) as the renter’s principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally — so none of §§ 1-21-1203 or 1-21-1204 reaches a lot-only mobile home tenancy or a vacation rental. And a city or county ordinance or local health code may impose pest, sanitation or pesticide-notice duties that are not in the state statutes; check the municipality where the property sits.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Wyoming Leases
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute written for arbitration of landlord-tenant disputes. Nothing in the eviction chapter (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017) or the residential rental article (§§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) permits, requires or forbids an arbitration clause in a residential lease. What governs is the general Uniform Arbitration Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-36-101 through 1-36-119, and it is friendly to you. Section 1-36-103 says a written agreement to submit any existing or future controversy to arbitration is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on the grounds that would undo any contract — so ordinary defenses such as fraud, duress or unconscionability remain open to a tenant, but nothing in the Act singles leases out. Unlike some states, Wyoming's Act carves nothing out: there is no exclusion for personal injury or tort claims, and the only special subject the validity section names is employer-employee agreements. If a tenant sues you anyway, § 1-36-104(a) requires the court to order arbitration on your application, and § 1-36-104(c) requires the court to stay the lawsuit (or the arbitrable part of it).

Three hard limits you cannot draft around. First, § 1-36-108: a party may be represented by an attorney at any arbitration proceeding or hearing, and 'a waiver of representation prior to the proceeding is ineffective' — a lease term stripping the tenant of counsel in arbitration is void, and including one risks the whole clause. Second, § 1-36-107 fixes minimum process: at least five days' notice of the hearing served personally or by registered mail, and the parties are entitled to be heard, present material evidence and cross-examine witnesses. Third, § 1-36-119 preserves appeals from orders denying arbitration, staying it, confirming, modifying or vacating an award — you cannot make an award unreviewable.

The practical warning runs against you, not the tenant. Wyoming's forcible entry and detainer procedure is fast and cheap: a three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003, a hearing in a court of limited jurisdiction, and under § 1-21-1007 a tenant cannot get a continuance beyond two days without posting a surety bond for accruing rent. A broad arbitration clause gives the tenant a § 1-36-104(c) argument that your own possession case must be stayed while an arbitrator is appointed, which costs you exactly the speed the eviction statute gives you. No Wyoming statute says a possession action must stay in court, and no Wyoming case was reviewed, so this is unsettled. The cautious course is to exclude actions for possession and for unpaid rent from any arbitration clause you use, and to leave the clause optional. Separately, § 1-21-801 lets the parties to a civil case already pending before a judge agree to submit it to three arbitrators — that is a post-filing option, not a lease term. Whether the Federal Arbitration Act would enforce a clause Wyoming law would not was not reviewed, and Wyoming case law is outside this corpus.

title: Cannabis Is Still Fully Illegal in Wyoming and No Tenant Protection Exists
bodyText: Wyoming has no medical-cannabis program and no adult-use legalization, so none of the tenant protections that exist in legalizing states exist here. You may write a flat, unconditional ban on cannabis possession, use, smoking, vaping, edibles and cultivation into your lease, and you may enforce it like any other lease term. Three statutes carry the point. Marihuana and tetrahydrocannabinols are Schedule I under Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-1014(d)(xiii) and (d)(xxi). Possession is a crime under Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-1031(c) — a misdemeanor of up to twelve months and $1,000 at three ounces or less of plant material, a felony above that — and the same subsection says in terms that 'no practitioner shall dispense or prescribe marihuana, tetrahydrocannabinol, or synthetic equivalents' and that no such prescription 'shall be valid' unless the drug has final FDA approval (dronabinol, listed at § 35-7-1018(h)). Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-1039 makes merely using or being under the influence of a Schedule I, II or III substance a misdemeanor of up to six months and $750. So a Wyoming tenant cannot hold a cannabis card of any kind, and an out-of-state card gives them nothing here. Wyoming once had a narrow program — Article 19 of Title 35 was headed 'Supervised Medical Use of Hemp Extracts' — but §§ 35-7-1901 through 35-7-1903 were all repealed by 2019 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 173, § 3, and the article heading is all that survives. One thing is lawful and you should not ban it by accident: Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-1063(a)(i) exempts 'the possession or use of hemp or hemp products for any purpose or application' from the whole chapter and penalties, with hemp defined in (b)(i) as cannabis sativa L. with no synthetic substances and a THC concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis. A blanket 'no cannabis products' clause would on its face reach lawful CBD and hemp goods a tenant may buy in a Wyoming store; write the ban against marijuana, THC above the hemp threshold, and synthetic cannabinoids instead, and handle smoke and vapor through your separate smoking policy. You also have an affirmative reason to police this and not just paper it. Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-201 declares a nuisance anyone who 'maintains, uses, owns or leases any structure' for the 'manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of ... any controlled substance in violation of law', and § 6-6-202 lets the county attorney or any citizen of the county sue to enjoin the nuisance and name 'the owner or agent of the building or ground upon which the nuisance exists.' Abatement can reach building closure and a $300 tax with a perpetual lien. That exposure runs to you as owner, not only to the tenant, so a cannabis clause you never enforce is worse than useless. Finally, the one route a tenant may try is a disability claim: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation in rules and policies for a person with a disability. Nothing in the Wyoming act says cannabis is a reasonable accommodation, and the substance remains unlawful under both state and federal law, so the cautious course is to document the request, grant any accommodation that does not involve a controlled substance, and get counsel before refusing one outright.

title: Charging for Cleaning and Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: Wyoming has no carpet-cleaning statute — the words "carpet", "rug" and "floor covering" do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. What Wyoming gives you instead is broader and better. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) says that when the rental agreement ends, money or property held as a deposit may be applied to accrued rent, to "damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear", to "the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement", and to "other costs provided by any contract". Read the sentence carefully: the "beyond reasonable wear and tear" limit attaches to the damages item only. The cleaning item has its own, different yardstick — the condition the unit was in when the tenancy began. So in Wyoming you may charge the cost of returning the unit, carpets included, to its starting condition, and you do not have to prove the dirt went beyond ordinary wear. That makes your move-in condition record the single most valuable document you own: without it you cannot show what the starting condition was. Photograph or video every room at move-in, note the carpets specifically, and have the tenant sign the record. The fourth item, "other costs provided by any contract", is your authority for a lease term that requires professional carpet cleaning: if the lease creates the charge, the deposit statute lets you deduct it. Two limits to respect. First, § 1-21-1208 sits in Article 12, which under § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) reaches only a "residential rental unit" — the renter's principal place of residence, not a mobile home lot and not recreational property rented occasionally; outside that definition the deposit rules do not apply and you are on the lease alone. Second, the deduction must be itemized in writing with reasons and the balance delivered or mailed within thirty (30) days after the rental agreement ends, or within fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by another thirty (30) days if there is damage. Under § 1-21-1208(c) an unreasonable failure to comply lets the renter recover the full deposit plus court costs. Practical course: keep receipts, charge what you actually pay, and never charge a flat carpet fee when no cleaning was done — Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing (§ 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property) and a knowing misrepresentation about charges is exposed under § 40-12-105(a).

title: What a Wyoming Lease May Contract Around
bodyText:
Wyoming gives you unusually wide room to write your own rules, and one narrow place where you have none.

Start with casualty. There is no Wyoming statute governing what happens to a residential lease when fire, flood, or another casualty destroys or disables the unit. No rent-abatement rule, no tenant right to walk away, no landlord duty to rebuild. The Residential Rental Property Act (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) does not mention casualty, fire, destruction, or untenantability at all. That means your lease is the only document that answers the question, and if the lease is silent you and the tenant will be arguing common law in front of a judge with no statute to guide either of you. Write a casualty clause. Say who may terminate and on what notice, whether rent abates in whole or in part while the unit is unusable, how a partial casualty is handled, and what happens to the deposit and prepaid rent on termination. Also write it so it dovetails with Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), because a casualty termination is still a "termination of the rental agreement" and the thirty-day deposit-accounting clock will start on it.

Mitigation is the same story: no Wyoming statute imposes a duty to re-rent, and none forbids waiving one. But do not read that as permission to disclaim mitigation in the lease. Nothing in the Act authorizes such a waiver either, and a Wyoming court applying ordinary contract principles can still limit your recovery to losses you could not reasonably have avoided. The cautious course is to leave the waiver out and re-rent promptly with documentation.

Now the provision that makes Wyoming different. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." The phrase is "this article," not "this section," so it reaches every duty in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, including the owner's habitability duties in §§ 1-21-1202(a) and 1-21-1203(a) and the deposit mechanics in § 1-21-1208. Most states forbid exactly this. Wyoming permits it, but on three conditions you must actually satisfy: the agreement must be explicit, it must be written, and it must be signed by the parties. A general "tenant accepts the premises as-is" or a waiver buried in boilerplate is not an explicit modification of a named statutory duty. If you intend to shift a duty, name the duty and the statute, state plainly who now carries it, and get signatures. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) carries its own narrower version of the same idea for one item: hot and cold running water is required "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties." That trailing qualifier attaches to the operational-utilities sentence it sits in, not to the safe-and-sanitary duty in the sentence before it, so you cannot use it to contract out of habitability generally.

The one hard floor is the Wyoming Safe Homes Act. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 provides that "[t]he provisions of this act shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant." That covers the domestic-abuse and sexual-violence provisions in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304, including the tenant's affirmative defense to a rent claim after vacating and the bar in § 1-21-1303(c) on terminating a tenancy based solely on victim status. Those sit in Article 13, a different article from the one § 1-21-1202(d) opens up, so the modification power does not reach them. Do not put a waiver of them in your lease.

Two limits on how far to push § 1-21-1202(d). It is a grant of contracting freedom inside one article of the civil-procedure title; it does not override building, fire, or health codes, and it does not override a municipal or county housing ordinance, which you should check locally. And it says duties may be "assigned" or "modified," not extinguished. A clause purporting to leave nobody responsible for a safe and sanitary dwelling is a different thing from assigning the duty to the tenant, and is the kind of term a court is most likely to refuse to enforce.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Wyoming does not require you to tell a tenant anything about a certificate of occupancy. No statute makes you state whether one exists, whether it is valid, or hand the tenant a copy, and nothing in Wyoming's residential rental statutes (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) conditions your right to collect rent or to evict on holding one. You should still care about the certificate itself, for two reasons. First, the state fire marshal issues certificates of occupancy under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(n): after new construction or remodeling is finished the marshal inspects for conformance with the approved plan review and issues a certificate of occupancy for a new building or a letter of compliance for a remodel, and that subsection says in terms that no newly constructed or remodeled building may be used or occupied until one has issued. If it is occupied first, the marshal orders use and occupancy to cease until the certificate issues, and an order served on the owner that the owner does not obey within forty-eight hours is a misdemeanor (Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(m)). That duty reaches only buildings that needed a state plan review in the first place under § 35-9-108(a) - state or locally owned or leased buildings, public buildings over 5,000 square feet including basement, multistory public buildings, child care centers for more than ten children, public bars, restaurants, lodge halls, theaters, churches and public meeting places, and fuel dispensing facilities - and Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-102(xvii) defines a public building as one intended for access by the general public. An ordinary house or small apartment building is usually outside that list, but a larger multistory rental building is a judgment call, so if you are putting up or substantially remodeling a multi-unit property, ask the fire marshal's office in writing whether a plan review and certificate are required before anyone moves in. Second, under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121 the state fire marshal delegates complete fire, building and electrical enforcement to any municipality or county that adopts equivalent or stricter standards and keeps certified inspectors, and § 35-9-108(h) then takes the state requirement off the table entirely for that jurisdiction. In those places a local certificate of occupancy or rental inspection program, not state law, controls, and that is where any real occupancy-certificate obligation will be found. Practical course: get and keep the certificate of occupancy or letter of compliance for the building, and do not let a tenant move into new or newly remodeled space before the inspecting authority has signed off, even though no Wyoming statute makes you show the tenant the paper. LOCAL ORDINANCE: certificate of occupancy and rental licensing requirements in a jurisdiction with delegated authority under § 35-9-121 are flagged but not resolved here.

title: Occupancy by Children in Wyoming Leases
bodyText: Wyoming does not require your lease to say anything about children. There is no statutory required-content list for a residential lease in Wyoming, and the Residential Rental Property article (Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) never mentions children, minors or an occupancy standard. What does constrain you is the Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145. "Familial status" — one or more minors domiciled with a parent or another person having legal custody, or that person's written designee — is a protected class, and the protection also covers anyone who is pregnant or in the process of securing legal custody of a minor (§ 40-26-102(a)(ix)). You may not refuse to rent, make a dwelling unavailable, or discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the services or facilities you provide, because of familial status (§ 40-26-103(a), (b)), and you may not publish or post any advertisement indicating a preference, limitation or discrimination on that basis (§ 40-26-104). So do not advertise "adults only," do not set a different rent, deposit or rule for households with children, and do not confine families with children to particular buildings or floors. You may still cap total occupancy. Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) requires the tenant to occupy the unit in the manner for which it was designed and not to increase the number of occupants above the number specified in the rental agreement without your written permission — so state a maximum occupancy number in the lease and apply it to every occupant regardless of age. Section 40-26-113(a) confirms the Fair Housing Act "does not affect a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling or a restriction relating to health or safety standards," so an occupancy cap drawn from a local building or housing code is safe; one you invent to keep families out is not. Two exemptions may take you outside §§ 40-26-103 to 40-26-109 entirely: an owner renting a single family house who owns no more than three such houses, rents without a real estate broker or agent, runs no discriminatory advertisement, and uses the exemption for only one rental in any 24-month period if the owner was not the most recent resident (§ 40-26-110(a)); and an owner-occupied building of no more than four independent living quarters (§ 40-26-110(b), which still leaves § 40-26-104's advertising ban in force). Qualifying housing for the elderly is exempt from the familial-status and age provisions under § 40-26-112, but only on that section's terms, including the 80 percent occupancy and published-policy requirements for 55-and-older housing. Do not rely on any of these exemptions without checking the facts against the section text — and remember the federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq., applies on its own terms and has its own exemptions, so a property outside the Wyoming act may still be covered federally (§ 40-26-113(b) preserves other nondiscrimination law). The cautious lease term is a plain occupancy clause that names the maximum number of occupants and lists every occupant, child or adult, with no separate rule for children.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice
bodyText:
Wyoming has no cold-weather statute of any kind for rental housing. Nothing requires a tenant to warn you before leaving the unit empty in winter, nothing sets a minimum indoor temperature a tenant must hold while away, nothing makes failing to give that warning an offense, and nothing stays an eviction because of cold. This matters in Wyoming more than in most states: a unit left unheated in January in Laramie or Casper can freeze and split supply lines in a matter of hours, and the statute books give you no help.

The only statutory hook is indirect. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(iv) makes each renter use "all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner," and § 1-21-1204(a)(iii) makes the renter maintain all plumbing fixtures in a sanitary condition. A tenant who shuts the furnace off and leaves for three weeks in midwinter is arguably not using the heating facilities reasonably, but that is an argument, not a rule, and it gives you a damages theory after the fact rather than the advance warning you actually want.

So put it in the lease. A cold-weather notice-before-vacating clause, a duty to keep the heat at a set minimum, and a duty to report a heating failure immediately are all enforceable contract terms in Wyoming -- § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes the renter comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement. Note the limit on what the lease can do about your side of the bargain: if you list heating among the appliances or facilities you supply, § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes maintaining them your duty, so a freeze caused by a furnace you were supposed to maintain is not the tenant's problem. If the unit is master-metered or you hold the utility account, a winter vacancy also means you, not the tenant, are the one who must keep service on.

title: Charging a Tenant for Collection Costs in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming does not regulate what a residential landlord may charge a tenant to collect a past-due debt — there is no statute authorizing a collection fee, no cap on one, and no statute forbidding one. That cuts both ways: your lease is the only source of the right, so if the lease is silent you can recover the debt and nothing more.

Four Wyoming rules shape how you should draft and act.

1. Attorney's fees come from the lease, not the statute. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) says that in a nonpayment case the court, in addition to ordering restitution, "shall render judgment ... for the amount of rent found due, together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease." The qualifier "as provided by the lease" attaches to the fees. No fee clause means no fee award, even when you win. Note the limit too: subsection (b) applies only to a case "based on failure to pay rent," so an eviction for some other breach gets you restitution and costs under subsection (a), with fees only if the lease supplies them and the court applies them.

2. A dishonored rent check carries a real statutory remedy. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-115, after you mail a written demand by U.S. postal service certificate of mailing to the address on the check or the drawer's last known address (or serve it under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure), the tenant has thirty (30) days to pay the amount of the check plus a collection fee of up to thirty dollars ($30.00). The demand must itself state that the drawer must pay the check's value and the fee, and must state the fee the statute provides. If the tenant does not pay within those thirty days, the tenant is liable for three (3) times the check amount — never less than one hundred dollars ($100.00) — a thirty-dollar collection fee, and court costs; in an extraordinary case, such as dilatory or bad-faith defenses, the court may also award the prevailing party reasonable attorney fees. You may bring it in small claims court if the demand is within that court's limit. Get the demand letter's wording right: the statutory three-times recovery depends on it.

3. You generally do not need a collection-agency license to chase your own rent — unless you use another name. Wyo. Stat. § 33-11-102 requires a license to conduct a collection agency, and § 33-11-115(a) makes operating without one a misdemeanor (fine of $50 to $750, up to six months in jail, or both). But § 33-11-101(b)(i) and (b)(v) exclude a creditor's own officer or employee collecting in the creditor's name, and anyone whose collection activities "are carried on in the true name of the creditor, and are confined to the operation of a business other than a collection agency." Read § 33-11-101(a)(iii)(E) before you set up a collections alias, though: a person who "[u]ses a fictitious name or any name other than their own name in the collection of their own accounts receivable" IS a collection agency and does need a license. Collect in your own legal or registered name.

4. Wyoming has no mini-FDCPA. The Collection Agency Act is a licensing and bonding statute only — it has no list of prohibited collection practices and no bar on adding fees to a debt, so unlike Massachusetts or Puerto Rico, Wyoming puts no statutory ceiling on what an agency may add. The Uniform Consumer Credit Code in Title 40 does not reach you either: "consumer lease" in Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-206(a) means a lease of goods, not of a dwelling. What does reach you is the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act: "merchandise" in Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) expressly includes real property, and § 40-12-105(a)(xv) makes it an unlawful deceptive trade practice to knowingly "[e]ngag[ing] in unfair or deceptive acts or practices" in the course of business and in connection with a consumer transaction. Overstating what a tenant owes, or dunning for a fee the lease never authorized, is the kind of conduct that invites a claim. The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act does not cover a landlord collecting its own debt, but it does cover the agency you hire.

Practical course: put a collection-costs clause and an attorney's-fees clause in the lease, tie the collection charge to the actual fee the agency charges you rather than a round percentage, use your own name, and follow § 1-1-115 to the letter on bounced checks.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: Wyoming sets no footcandle level, no hours-of-operation rule and no fixture count for common-area lighting. What it does give you is a general safety duty and one narrow fire-escape rule. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) you must 'maintain common areas of the residential rental unit in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition,' and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) the common areas and grounds held out for renters generally are part of the rental unit, so a dark, unlit stair or entry is a safety problem you own even though no statute says 'light.' Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) separately requires each unit to have operational electrical service. Treat working lights at entries, stairs, hallways and parking approaches as part of the reasonably-safe-condition duty, keep a replacement log, and respond to a renter's written notice under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) within a reasonable time. The one hard rule is Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-504: in a building covered by the fire-escape article, the fire escapes, stairways, hallways and other means of egress must be kept free of obstruction, in good repair and ready for use at all times, and at night, or in the daytime where lights are necessary, a red light inscribed 'FIRE ESCAPE' must be provided. The article reaches an apartment house or tenement house three or more stories high (Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-501) and one of two stories or less with twelve or more rooms (Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-502); violation is a misdemeanor and each month in violation is a separate offense under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-506. Note Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-507: none of that applies inside an incorporated city or town that has adopted a uniform building code by ordinance, so in Cheyenne, Casper, Laramie or any other incorporated place you must check the local code, which this library does not resolve. Beyond the fire-escape article, the fire prevention and electrical safety council sets minimum fire and building standards by rule under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i), and Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) lets a municipality or county take over enforcement — again, rules and ordinances outside this library.

title: Wyoming Has No Communal Land System, But State Trust Land and Reservation Land Each Need Approval
bodyText:
Wyoming has no communal or native-family land tenure of the kind found in American Samoa or the Northern Marianas, and no Wyoming statute makes a private residential lease of private land wait on a government officer's signature. The word "communal" does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes or constitution. If you own the land in fee and rent a house on it, you need no state approval, and your lease is effective when the parties sign it.

Two kinds of land in Wyoming do carry an approval requirement, and both can hold a house. Find out which kind of land you have before you sign anything.

State trust land. The State Board of Land Commissioners may lease state lands for industrial, commercial and recreational purposes for up to 75 years under Wyo. Stat. § 36-5-114(a), and § 36-5-115 defines "recreational purposes" to include cabin sites, public camp sites, public parks and recreation areas, golf courses "and any associated residential development." So there are houses and cabins on Wyoming state trust land. If you hold one of those leases, Wyo. Stat. § 36-5-116 is the rule that matters to you: a lease issued under §§ 36-5-114 through 36-5-117 "shall not be assignable or transferable except with written consent of the board of land commissioners." You cannot assign or transfer that lease to a buyer, and you should not treat a long sublease as a way around it, without the board's written consent first. On agricultural and grazing state land the parallel rule is § 36-5-105(d): if you assign, sublease or contract any part of the lease area, the lease is subject to cancellation unless the director approves, approval cannot be arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld, and the land may not be subleased unless half the excess rental is paid to the state. The board also sets rental at not less than fair market value under § 36-5-114(c), and its rules under § 36-5-114(d) require compliance with applicable land use planning and zoning laws, so the board can set terms your private lease has to live inside.

Wind River Indian Reservation land. The Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho reservation covers a large part of Fremont and Hot Springs counties. A lease of tribal trust land or of an allotment held in trust or restricted against alienation is governed by federal law and requires Bureau of Indian Affairs approval, not state approval, and tribal law may apply as well. Wyoming's own statutes do not purport to regulate it; the only Wyoming provision that touches it is Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-121(a)(i), which merely lets a certified copy of a federal instrument affecting reservation real estate be recorded in the county records with the same effect as a conveyance acknowledged under state law. If your property sits on trust or restricted land, do not rely on a Wyoming lease form or on state eviction procedure without confirming jurisdiction first; a state court may have no power to hear the case at all.

The cautious course. Pull the deed or the lease and identify the landowner before you rent. If the landowner is the State of Wyoming, read your state lease for its assignment and sublease clause and get the board's or the director's written consent in hand before you commit to a tenant. If the land is on the reservation and held in trust or restricted, get advice on federal and tribal requirements before you sign or try to evict.

title: No Wyoming Bar on Collecting Rent After a Condemnation or Vacate Order
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute that stops you collecting rent or holding a deposit once a dwelling has been condemned, placarded or ordered vacated. There is no treble-damages penalty like Minnesota's, no advertising or re-renting ban like Wisconsin's, and no statutory rent abatement while a unit is legally unoccupiable. The phrases "unfit for human habitation," "unfit for occupancy," "unsafe building," "order to vacate" and "dilapidated" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and no provision pairs a vacate order with a limit on rent. Two things do exist and you need to know both. First, Wyoming's one state-level uninhabitability order is Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d): after a hazardous-material, weapons-of-mass-destruction or clandestine-drug-lab incident, the local incident commander may order that any portion of a building, structure or land is uninhabitable or contaminated and secure it. Under § 35-9-156(e) the written order must state its grounds, be filed with the clerk of the district court for the county, be served on the owner AND any occupants under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, and be posted conspicuously on the building. The owner or an occupant has twenty (20) days under § 35-9-156(f) to file an answer; with no answer the court affirms the order and fixes a time for enforcement, and with an answer the court must hold a hearing within eleven (11) days under § 35-9-156(g). Note that the duty to limit the declaration to the affected areas, and the written-specificity notice, are written only for COMMERCIAL real estate — a residential building can be declared uninhabitable in whole. Section 35-9-156 says nothing at all about rent. Second, condemning an ordinary unsafe dwelling is a municipal matter in Wyoming: Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xxvi) empowers a city or town to "provide for the repair, removal or destruction of any dangerous building or enclosure" by ordinance. Whether rent stops, and on what notice, therefore depends on the local code where the property sits — check your city's building and nuisance ordinances, which are not state law and are not covered here. Practically: if the unit is ordered vacated, keep charging rent only if you are prepared to defend it. The tenant is not without leverage — a condemned unit will usually breach the habitability duty in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203, triggering the notice-and-remedy track in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1205 and 1-21-1206, including the renter's right to terminate — and continuing to demand rent for premises the tenant is legally barred from occupying invites a failure-of-consideration defence and a counterclaim. The cautious course is to stop billing from the date of the order, refund any prepaid rent covering days the tenant cannot occupy, and handle the deposit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208 as if the tenancy had ended. Remember also that the Article 12 habitability machinery applies only to a "residential rental unit" as defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and occasionally rented recreational property.

title: Documenting Condition at Move-In and Move-Out
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no move-in inspection and no written inventory. There is no joint walkthrough, no signed condition statement, no deadline to deliver one, no duty to tell the tenant they may request an inspection, and no statutory damage list the tenant must sign or dissent from. Nothing conditions your right to keep deposit money on having documented the unit first.

But read the deposit statute before you conclude that documentation is optional in practice, because Wyoming twice makes the move-in condition the legal yardstick and then gives you no statutory way to prove it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii) makes it the renter's duty to remove all property and garbage placed in the unit by the renter or the renter's guests before the rental agreement terminates and to 'clean the rental unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement.' Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) then lets you apply the deposit to accrued rent, to 'damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear,' to 'the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement,' and to 'other costs provided by any contract.' Both tests run against the beginning condition. If the tenant disputes your charge, the burden of showing what that condition was falls on you, and you will have no statutory document to point to. A dated, signed move-in condition report with photographs is therefore worth more in Wyoming than in a state that mandates one, because it is the only record that will exist.

You can create the inspection duty yourself. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that any duty or obligation in Article 12 may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit cover 'other costs provided by any contract.' So a lease term setting up a joint move-in report, a move-out walkthrough, and the consequences of each is enforceable. Use the optional clause 'move-in-condition-report-as', which is sound Wyoming contract language as written.

Two cautions. First, Article 12 — habitability, renter duties and the deposit rules alike — applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence; § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally. Outside that definition you have no statutory deposit framework at all and the lease is the whole of your protection. Second, the only inspection-adjacent written-notice duty Wyoming actually imposes runs the other direction: under § 1-21-1203(b) a renter who is current on rent and has reasonable cause supported by evidence may serve you written notice of a health-and-safety defect specifying the remedial action requested, and within a reasonable time you must either begin correcting it or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim, served by certified mail or in the manner specified by § 1-21-1003. Your own hard deadline is at move-out, not move-in: § 1-21-1208(a) requires the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent plus a written itemization of every deduction with reasons to be delivered or mailed within thirty (30) days after termination, or within fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by a further thirty (30) days if there is damage. Under § 1-21-1208(c) an unreasonable failure lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText:
Wyoming has never abolished confession of judgment, but the two sections that authorize it do not support the clause landlords usually want, and you should not put one in a residential lease.

What the statute actually allows. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-16-201 a person who is indebted "may personally appear in a court of competent jurisdiction and with the assent of the creditor… confess judgment." Both halves are conditions: the debtor appears in court in person, and the creditor assents. That describes something the tenant does after a dispute has arisen, in front of a judge — not something a tenant signs in advance at lease signing. Wyo. Stat. § 1-16-202 is the one provision that contemplates an advance authorization: an attorney who confesses judgment must produce the warrant of attorney to the court when the confession is made, and the original or a copy must be filed with the clerk. So the old warrant-of-attorney (cognovit) device survives on the books in Wyoming, unrepealed. That is the authority cutting in a landlord's favour, and it is the reason this row says "do not use" rather than "is void."

Why you still should not use one. A confessed judgment for possession would skip the forcible entry and detainer procedure in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, and that procedure is not something your lease can contract around. The waiver provision landlords rely on elsewhere in the landlord-tenant law, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d), lets duties be reassigned or modified by explicit signed writing only within "this article" — Article 12 — and the eviction procedure sits in Article 10, out of its reach. A judgment taken without notice or a hearing also runs straight at Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 6, which forbids deprivation of property without due process of law. Expect a Wyoming court to be hostile, and expect to have litigated the clause's validity instead of your eviction.

When it is flatly void. If what you are really doing is a rent-to-own or lease-purchase deal on the home, a confession-of-judgment authorization can be void by statute. Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-249 says a buyer or lessee may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of a consumer credit sale or consumer lease, and an authorization that violates it is void. Two definitions decide whether you are caught. "Consumer lease" under § 40-14-206(a) is a lease of goods only, so an ordinary apartment or house rental is not one. But "consumer credit sale" under § 40-14-204(a) expressly includes a sale of an interest in land, and § 40-14-205(f) defines a sale of an interest in land to include a lease in which the tenant has an option to purchase and all or a substantial part of the rent already paid is applied to the purchase price. The escape is § 40-14-204(b)(ii): such a sale is not a consumer credit sale if the credit service charge does not exceed eighteen percent per year. So a lease-option home deal priced above that line, or one the parties opt into under § 40-14-256, carries a void confession clause. A separate rule reaches rent-to-own of furniture or appliances: § 40-19-108(a)(i) forbids a confession of judgment in a rental-purchase agreement outright, with no interest-rate escape.

The one confession-of-judgment mechanism worth knowing as a landlord runs the other way. Under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-10-103 and 1-10-104 a tenant you have sued, or are about to sue, may offer to confess judgment for a specified sum or for part of your claim. Do not ignore the offer. If you refuse it and then recover no more than was offered, § 1-10-104 makes you pay the tenant's costs incurred after the offer. Under § 1-10-105 the offer is not an admission and cannot be mentioned at trial.

title: Habitability Rules Wyoming Does Not Have
bodyText:
Wyoming's residential habitability law is Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, and it is much thinner than the URLTA-style codes most form leases are written against. Eleven habitability rules that exist elsewhere have no Wyoming counterpart.

(1) NO WARRANTY OF HABITABILITY BY THAT NAME. The word "habitability" appears nowhere in the article. What you owe is the list in § 1-21-1203(a): do not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; maintain common areas sanitary and reasonably safe; maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; and maintain other appliances and facilities only "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." Describe your duties that way, not as a warranty.

(2) APPLIANCES ARE OPT-IN. Under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) you have no duty to maintain an appliance or facility unless the rental agreement specifically contracts for it. Listing a refrigerator, range, washer, dryer, dishwasher or air conditioner in the lease is what creates the duty.

(3) NO NON-WAIVABILITY. This is the single biggest difference. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." There is no anti-waiver section anywhere in Article 12, so the habitability duties, the renter's duties, the deposit rules and the abandoned-property rules are all modifiable. The conditions are cumulative and strict: explicit, written, and signed by the parties. Note also that § 1-21-1202(a) already lets the parties agree in writing to do without hot and cold running water, and expressly preserves the rental of seasonal units such as summer cabins not intended to have those amenities.

(4) NO REPAIR-AND-DEDUCT, NO RENT WITHHOLDING, NO RENT ESCROW. Wyoming gives a tenant none of these. The tenant's only route is the two-notice sequence and a lawsuit: a written notice of the condition under § 1-21-1203(b), then after a reasonable time a "notice to repair or correct condition" under § 1-21-1206(b) giving you three days to commence reasonable corrective action, then a civil action in circuit court under § 1-21-1206(c). A tenant who simply stops paying loses the remedies entirely, because § 1-21-1203(b) requires the renter to be current on all payments and § 1-21-1206(a) conditions every remedy on compliance with §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205.

(5) NO MINIMUM INDOOR TEMPERATURE AND NO COOLING DUTY. No Wyoming statute sets a minimum heat temperature, a heating season, or any air-conditioning or cooling obligation. You must maintain heating under § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) because it is named; air conditioning becomes your duty only if the lease contracts for it under (a)(iv).

(6) NO ESSENTIAL-SERVICES REGIME. Wyoming has no statutory category of "essential services" and no special fast remedy for losing one.

(7) NO PEST OR INFESTATION RULE. Nothing on infestations, vermin, rodents or bed bugs - no inspection duty, no response deadline, no disclosure.

(8) NO SMOKE ALARM OR CARBON MONOXIDE STATUTE. Wyoming has no statewide smoke-detector, smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm requirement for rentals of any kind. Local building and fire codes are the only source, and they are outside this review.

(9) NO STATUTORY LIST OF IMMINENTLY DANGEROUS CONDITIONS AND NO CODE-VIOLATION PRESUMPTION. A code violation does not by statute prove a breach, and no statute defines imminent peril in a rental.

(10) NO DESIGNATED-REPAIRER RULE AND NO FIXED REPAIR DEADLINE. The statutory clock is "within a reasonable time after receipt" of the tenant's § 1-21-1203(b) notice, and your options are to commence corrective action or to notify the tenant in writing that you dispute the claim. Both are equally compliant at that step.

(11) NO MENTAL-SUFFERING DAMAGES. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) provides that the owner is not liable under the article for claims for mental suffering or anguish, and it applies to the whole article, not just § 1-21-1203.

Two things Wyoming does give you that other states do not. Under § 1-21-1203(d) you may refuse to correct a condition and terminate the tenancy where the cost of repair exceeds an amount reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property - you must notify the tenant in writing within a reasonable time of receiving the noncompliance notice, allow no less than ten and no more than twenty days to find substitute housing, prorate rent to the vacate date and refund the balance with the deposit under § 1-21-1208. And § 1-21-1203(c) relieves you of any duty to correct a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse.

Two limits on all of the above. Article 12 applies only to a "residential rental unit," which § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally - outside that definition these rules switch off, though Article 10 eviction procedure still applies. And this review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws only; case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched, and local codes may add requirements.

title: Other rules Wyoming does not have
bodyText:
Four rules that exist in other states are confirmed absent from Wyoming's statutes. Each one is a place where your lease, not a statute, has to do the work.

(1) NO SMOKE OR CARBON MONOXIDE ALARM STATUTE AT ALL, so nothing about evidence or insurance either. Some states make your compliance with an alarm mandate inadmissible in a later injury suit, or bar an insurer from cutting a payout over an alarm failure. Wyoming has neither, because Wyoming has no residential alarm mandate to attach them to: the words "smoke detector" and "smoke alarm" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and the single "carbon monoxide" reference is an animal-euthanasia prohibition in the criminal code. The only alarm obligation that can reach a rental building comes through Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i), which has the state fire prevention and electrical safety council set minimum standards not exceeding the International Fire Code and International Building Code, and through whatever your city or town has adopted by ordinance. Install and maintain alarms as a matter of ordinary care and insurance underwriting, not because a Wyoming statute tells you to, and keep your own dated installation and battery records, since no statutory presumption will help you.

(2) NO PAYMENT-METHOD FEE RULE IN EITHER DIRECTION. No Wyoming statute bans or caps a convenience fee or card surcharge on rent, and none requires you to accept any particular form of payment. "Convenience fee" and "checkout fee" appear nowhere; the 86 "surcharge" references are court, insurance, motor vehicle and fire-service surcharges, none of them a private merchant rule, and Title 40 contains the word zero times. So a card or processing fee is governed by your lease, your card-network rules and the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act's knowing-misrepresentation provisions (§ 40-12-105(a)), which means the fee must be disclosed plainly before the tenant pays. What Wyoming does give you is the other half of the payment problem: under § 1-1-115, if a rent check is dishonored for any reason, you mail or personally serve a written demand stating the amount and the collection fee, and if the drawer does not pay the check plus a collection fee of up to $30 within thirty days of that demand, the drawer is liable to you for three times the check amount (minimum $100), a $30 collection fee and court costs, with attorney fees available in extraordinary cases or where the court finds dilatory or bad-faith defenses. The claim can be brought in small claims court.

(3) NO STATUTORY RIGHT TO TERMINATE FOR A FALSE RENTAL APPLICATION. Wyoming has no counterpart to the states that let you end a tenancy because the application was untrue. The phrase "rental application" does not appear in the statutes, and the eviction grounds in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1002 and 1-21-1003 are built on nonpayment, holding over and breach of a lease condition, not on pre-lease misstatements. Your only reliable route is contractual: make the application part of the lease by reference, have the tenant warrant that every answer is true and complete, and state expressly that a material falsehood is a material breach and a ground for termination. Without that language a false application gives you no termination right at all.

(4) NO STATE RENTAL-HOUSING LICENCE, INSPECTION CYCLE OR MANDATORY LEASE FORM to carry any of this. Wyoming regulates residential landlords lightly: outside Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 to 1-21-1211 and the eviction procedure in §§ 1-21-1001 to 1-21-1017, nearly everything is left to the parties, and § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in Article 12 be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. That cuts both ways. It means your lease can reallocate most statutory duties, and it also means that anything your lease does not say is simply not covered.

Throughout, remember that ordinances are the real gap. Wyoming cities and towns can and do legislate on alarms, inspections and rental licensing, and no statewide statute displaces them.

title: Checked Across the Whole Wyoming Code
bodyText:
All 44 titles of the Wyoming Statutes, the Wyoming Constitution, the noncodified session laws and every 2025 and 2026 enrolled act were searched — not just the landlord-tenant chapters — for three things landlords ask about. Two are genuinely absent; the third is not, and Wyoming is one of the minority of states that has it.

(1) UNAUTHORIZED OCCUPANTS — WYOMING DOES HAVE A SPECIFIC REMEDY. Do not assume you must file an eviction case. Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, added in 2025, let an owner or the owner’s authorized agent ask the sheriff or city police in the county where the property sits to remove an unauthorized person immediately. You submit a sworn complaint containing the ten items in § 1-21-1402(b), signed under penalty of perjury; law enforcement verifies you are the record owner, then serves a notice to vacate by hand or by posting it on the front door and puts you back in possession. Under § 1-21-1403(a) an officer will then stand by to keep the peace while you change the locks and move the occupant’s belongings to the property line. CRITICAL LIMIT: this cannot be used against a tenant. Section 1-21-1402(a)(iv) and (b)(v) exclude any current or former tenant under a written or oral rental or lease agreement authorized by you, your predecessor or your agent; (a)(ii) requires that the person unlawfully ENTERED, which also keeps out a guest you let in; (a)(iii) requires that no litigation about the property be pending between you and the occupant; and (a)(v) excludes your own spouse, child, parent or cohabitant. Misuse is expensive: § 1-21-1403(c) lets the removed person be restored to possession and recover actual damages plus triple the fair market rental value, and it reaches the authorized agent personally. For anyone you ever rented to, the route is still the forcible entry and detainer chapter, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017.

(2) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY. Nothing in the Wyoming code requires you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, whether paid in cash or otherwise. Give one anyway. Wyoming has no statutory rent grace period beyond the three days in § 1-21-1002(a)(i), and your dated receipt is as much your evidence of what was paid and when as it is the tenant’s.

(3) NO RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LICENSE AS A PRECONDITION TO POSSESSION. Wyoming has no statewide rental registration, rental license or certificate-of-occupancy requirement, and nothing anywhere in the code makes holding one a condition of filing or winning a forcible entry and detainer case. The forcible entry and detainer chapter requires no pleading or proof of licensure. Three caveats. An out-of-state corporation or LLC that transacts business in Wyoming without a certificate of authority may not maintain a proceeding in any Wyoming court, including a forcible entry and detainer case, until it obtains one (Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-16-1502(a), 17-29-114); owning property "without more" is not transacting business, but leasing it out likely is (see `edu-landlord-registration-wy`). A city or town may impose its own registration, licensing or inspection scheme under its general municipal powers, and municipal ordinances are not state statutes and were not searched here — check the city or county where the property sits. And if you hold a real estate license and manage for others, Title 33 chapter 28 governs you separately; that is a licensing law about brokerage, not a rental registration law, and nothing in it conditions an eviction.

title: Contractor Liens for Work Your Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Wyoming's Revised Wyoming Statutory Lien Act has a section written for exactly this problem, and it is good news for you if you keep your hands off the tenant's project. Normally a contractor, subcontractor or materialman gets a lien on the interest of the 'owner' who contracted for the work (Wyo. Stat. § 29-2-101(a)), and 'owner' is defined broadly at § 29-1-201(a)(v)(A) as any person with a legal or equitable interest in the property. Because § 29-1-201(a)(xi) says 'real property' includes leasehold interests, a tenant who hires a contractor is the owner of the leasehold being improved, and § 29-2-102 extends a perfected lien to 'the entire interest of the owner' — meaning the tenant's leasehold.

Your interest is reached only through Wyo. Stat. § 29-2-105. It opens 'Notwithstanding the definition of "owner"' and gives the lien claimant a lien on 'the landlord's and the tenant's interest' when a tenant places improvements in, on or outside the building, but ONLY if (i) the landlord has agreed to pay the costs of the improvement, or (ii) the improvements are specifically authorized by the landlord. Those are the only two triggers. Wyoming has no 'knowledge' trigger of the Oregon kind — you do not lose your interest merely because you knew the work was happening and said nothing, and there is no three-day posting duty to protect yourself. The agency route is closed too: § 29-1-201(b) says 'Only the following agency relationships are presumed in this act' and lists spouses, joint tenants, tenants in common, and employee-employer. A tenant is not presumed to be your agent.

The practical risk is the word 'specifically'. A lease that permits alterations generally, or that requires your written consent before alterations, should not be 'specifically authorized' work — but a signed consent that describes the project, a work letter, a plan approval, or anything that reads as you asking for or paying toward the improvement can put you inside § 29-2-105(a)(ii). A rent credit or construction allowance is close to § 29-2-105(a)(i) outright. No Wyoming case law was searched, so treat the line as unsettled.

Wyoming gives you no recordable escape hatch. There is no statute letting a lease, a recorded memorandum or a posted notice declare your interest free of liens for tenant work — the Florida and Kentucky mechanisms have no Wyoming counterpart, and 'nonresponsibility' appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. Your protection is behavioral and contractual: keep consent general and in writing, say in the consent that you are not requesting the work, are not agreeing to pay for it and are not authorizing it within the meaning of § 29-2-105, and use the no-liens lease clause so the tenant must pay everyone it hires and clear any lien that is filed.

You will get warning. Under § 29-2-112(a)(i) every contractor, subcontractor and materialman must send written preliminary notice to the record owner or the owner's agent — that is you, not just the tenant — and § 29-2-112(a)(iii) says failure to send it within the time specified (the contractor before receiving any payment; a subcontractor or materialman within thirty days after first providing services or materials) bars the lien entirely. Under § 29-2-107(a) a claimant must also send you written notice of intention no later than twenty days before filing the lien statement. If you receive either notice about work you did not authorize, say so in writing at once. Deadlines then run short: § 29-2-106(a) gives a contractor 150 days and everyone else 120 days from the last work or substantial completion to file the lien statement, and § 29-2-109 kills the lien 180 days after filing unless a foreclosure action is started.

title: No Condominium Conversion Notice or Tenant Purchase Right in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no conversion disclosure on you, no advance notice period before converting a rental building to condominium or cooperative ownership, and no tenant right of first refusal to buy the unit. There is also no required first-clause conversion statement of the kind several states demand, and no statute barring conversion of rental housing to hotel or other transient use. Wyoming's Condominium Ownership Act is a four-section act — Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-20-101 through 34-20-104 — and Chapter 21 of Title 34 follows immediately after it. All four sections were read. § 34-20-102 recognizes fee simple ownership of air space and common elements; § 34-20-103 defines the terms; § 34-20-104 handles the notice to the county assessor, separate tax assessment of each unit, and the recording of the declaration and map. Not one of them mentions an existing tenant, a notice period, a purchase option or a disclosure. The notice § 34-20-104(a) does require goes to the county assessor so units can be taxed separately — it is not a tenant notice and does not become one. The practical consequence is that if you convert, your obligation to a sitting tenant comes entirely from the lease and from ordinary Wyoming landlord-tenant law, not from a conversion statute. That means two things in sequence. First, a fixed-term lease runs to its end; conversion does not shorten it, and a buyer takes subject to it. Second, when the term ends, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 are in your favour: holding over creates only a tenancy by sufferance, there is no implied renewal either by holding over or by your accepting rent, and an expired lease renews only by an express written contract signed by the parties. If you need possession for the conversion, you still have to take it through the forcible entry and detainer chapter, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 et seq., with the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003. The cautious course where the statute is silent is to give a sitting tenant written notice well before the end of the term, keep the notice separate from any solicitation to buy, and avoid any representation about the unit's future that could be read as a knowing misrepresentation under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a), which reaches real property through the § 40-12-102(a)(vi) definition of merchandise. Two things fill part of the gap. Municipalities and counties have independent zoning and subdivision power — Wyo. Stat. §§ 15-1-601 et seq. and 18-5-201 et seq. — so a local conversion ordinance, plat approval or moratorium can exist where state law does not, and nothing in the Condominium Ownership Act preempts one. Check the city or county before you convert; local ordinances are outside this library. And if a public agency rather than you is forcing the move, the Wyoming Relocation Assistance Act of 1973, Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-7-101 through 16-7-121, expressly reaches displaced residential tenants: § 16-7-105 pays a tenant a replacement-housing payment up to forty-two months' rent differential capped at $5,250, and the agency acquisition policies require at least ninety days' written notice before a lawful occupant must move. Those duties fall on the agency, not on you.

title: Terminating for Criminal Activity in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming gives you no crime-specific eviction machinery at all. There is no fast-track or expedited eviction for violent crime or drug sales, no statute that strips the tenant of a cure right because the breach was criminal, no statute making eviction a landlord DUTY, no statute letting a tenant organization, a district attorney or the Attorney General bring an eviction in your place, no crime of failing to make reasonable efforts to eject a tenant, and no statute that authorises, forms, requires or limits a crime-free lease addendum. The phrase "crime-free" appears nowhere in Wyoming law, and "criminal activity" appears nowhere in the landlord-tenant title.

A crime-free clause is nonetheless lawful and enforceable in Wyoming, as an ordinary contract term. The chain is short and worth knowing exactly. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a statutory renter duty to "[c]omply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement between the owner and the renter." Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) allows a forcible entry and detainer action "[a]gainst renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205." So a crime-free covenant you write into the lease becomes a lawful requirement of the rental agreement, a breach of it breaches § 1-21-1204(a)(vii), and that breach is itself a statutory FED ground. You are not relying on common-law forfeiture.

For conduct that affects other people you may not need the clause at all. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) independently forbids a renter to "[i]nterfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property," and § 1-21-1205(a)(i) forbids intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging, impairing or removing any part of the unit, or knowingly permitting any person to do so. Either is an FED ground under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) with no lease term written at all. That is your fallback when a tenancy began on a bare lease.

What the clause cannot buy you is speed. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires the same written three-day notice to quit before any FED action, served on the defendant or left at his usual place of abode or business, and Wyoming has no shorter notice for criminal conduct. You cannot contract around it: § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties modify a duty "in this article" by explicit written signed agreement, but it sits in Article 12 and does not reach the Article 10 notice. Do not write an immediate-termination or self-help clause; what Wyoming gives instead is that no statute creates a cure right for a § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) breach either. The three-day period in § 1-21-1002(a)(i) is a grace period for unpaid rent only, not a general cure right. So "no opportunity to cure" is already the statutory position for a crime-free breach, and saying so in the lease removes argument rather than creating a right.

The real reason to carry the clause is what criminal use of your property costs YOU. Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-201 makes anyone who owns or leases a structure used for lewdness, assignation, prostitution, gambling, or the manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of a controlled substance guilty of maintaining a nuisance, and declares the structure, the ground and the contents a nuisance to be abated — with closure, a $300 tax under § 6-6-207 and an action any citizen of the county may bring under § 6-6-202. And § 35-9-158(a)(ii) caps an owner's clandestine-laboratory remediation bill at one percent of assessed value only where the owner neither knew nor with reasonable diligence could have known. A written covenant, plus inspections you actually perform and record, is the documentary backbone of that defence.

FAIR HOUSING — read the carve-out precisely. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(a) and (b) forbid refusing to rent, or discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Subsection (c) then says: "This section does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been convicted under federal law or the law of any state of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance." Four limits sit in that one sentence. It protects only against "this section" — § 40-26-103 — not § 40-26-104 (advertising), not § 40-26-107 (disability), not § 40-26-144 (intimidation and interference). It requires a CONVICTION, so an arrest, a charge, a dismissed case or a police report is outside it. It covers only illegal MANUFACTURE OR DISTRIBUTION, so simple possession is outside it. And it covers only a CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE, so assault, theft, arson, weapons and sex offences are outside it. The phrase "illegal manufacture or distribution" occurs exactly once in the entire Wyoming statutes — here. Treat it as a narrow shelter for one screening decision, never as a general licence to exclude on criminal record.

DISPARATE IMPACT — unread doctrine, not a prediction. Wyoming's Fair Housing Act codifies no effects test; the word "disparate" does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. Whether a blanket criminal-record exclusion or an aggressively worded crime-free clause creates unlawful disparate impact is governed by federal Fair Housing Act case law and by HUD's rule and guidance, none of which is in this library's source material and none of which has been read here. We make no prediction about how it would come out. The cautious course, which also happens to be the best litigation posture under Wyoming law, is: make the clause about CONDUCT during the tenancy rather than about a person's record; do not treat an arrest, a charge or a record as itself a breach; apply the clause the same way to every household; and if you screen on criminal history at application, make the screen individualised and keep a written reason for each decision rather than running a flat bar.

TWO SCOPE LIMITS. First, Article 12 — which supplies § 1-21-1204 and § 1-21-1205 — reaches only a "residential rental unit", defined by § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally. Outside that definition the § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) hook is unavailable and you are back on holding over under § 1-21-1002(a)(i) and on your own lease. Second, a city or town may regulate here: Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xvi)(B) empowers municipalities to suppress or prohibit houses of prostitution and other disorderly houses and to punish the keeper, and (a)(xix) covers nuisances generally. Crime-free rental programs and rental-licensing ordinances exist at municipal level in some states and local ordinances are outside this library's sources — check your city before relying on, or being caught by, one.

Finally, do not overstate your rights in the clause itself. Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing — § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines "merchandise" to include real property and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110 — and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct. A clause claiming a self-help lockout or an immediate termination Wyoming does not allow is the kind of wording that hook is aimed at.

title: Grounds and Notice for Evicting a Wyoming Tenant
bodyText:
Wyoming does not give a residential tenant a statutory right to cure. There is no notice-to-cure anywhere in the eviction statutes, no cure window, and no two-track scheme with different periods for rent and non-rent breaches. What Wyoming gives you is a short list of grounds and one three-day notice to quit, and you need to get both exactly right because the statute is unforgiving about nothing else.

The grounds are closed. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a) lists every case in which forcible entry and detainer may be had, and three of the six matter to a residential landlord. Paragraph (i) covers two separate things in one sentence: tenants holding over their terms, and tenants who have failed to pay rent for three days after it is due. Paragraph (vi) covers renters in violation of any terms imposed under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205. The rest of the list is about execution sales, foreclosure sales, probate and partition sales, and settlers without color of title. Subsection (b) adds that the section is not to be read as limiting Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1210.
