Paragraph (vi) is the one to understand, because on its face it only reaches the statutory duties, not your lease. It gets you to your lease through a chain. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter's duty to "[c]omply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement between the owner and the renter." So a breach of a lawful lease term is a violation of § 1-21-1204, which is a ground under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi). Plead that chain explicitly in your complaint: the lease term, the breach, § 1-21-1204(a)(vii), and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi). The word "lawful" is doing work, so a lease term that is itself unenforceable will not carry the eviction. The other duties in § 1-21-1204 are independently available grounds: keeping the unit clean and safe, waste disposal, plumbing fixtures, reasonable use of the facilities and appliances, occupying as designed and not exceeding the stated occupancy without the owner's written permission, being current on all payments required by the agreement, and removing property and garbage and cleaning at the end. So is each prohibited act in § 1-21-1205: intentional or negligent destruction or defacement, interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment, and unreasonably denying the owner entry to repair, inspect, or show the unit.

On timing for nonpayment, there are two three-day periods and they do not overlap. First, under § 1-21-1002(a)(i) the ground does not exist until rent has gone unpaid for three days after it is due. Then, under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003, you must notify the tenant to leave the premises and that notice must be served at least three days before you commence the action. Count them separately. Serving the notice to quit on day one of the delinquency does not work, because on that day you have no ground to notice. For a holdover or a § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) breach there is no waiting period before the notice; serve the three-day notice to quit and file after three days.

The notice itself is lean. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires only that you notify the adverse party to leave the premises, in writing, served by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at the defendant's usual place of abode or business if the defendant cannot be found. The statute does not require you to state the breach, the amount owed, or an opportunity to cure, and it does not offer pay-and-stay. Put the reason and the amount in anyway. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) makes the court find the rent due and the payment terms in a nonpayment case, and a notice that already recites them is easier to prove than one that does not.

Can your lease set its own cure period and service method instead? Partly, and only in one direction. The three days in § 1-21-1003 is a floor, written as "at least three (3) days before commencing the action," so a lease may promise the tenant a longer notice or a cure opportunity and you will be held to it, but a lease cannot shorten the period or substitute a weaker service method. Do not try to use Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d), which lets the parties modify duties by explicit signed writing, to cut the notice down; that subsection reaches duties "in this article," meaning Article 12, and § 1-21-1003 sits in Article 10. If you do write a longer cure period into the lease, it becomes a lawful requirement of the rental agreement and you must honor it before the eviction will stand.

From there the process is mechanical. The summons states the cause, the time and place of trial, and must be served not less than three nor more than twelve days before trial, and the tenant is not required to file a written answer to participate fully (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1004, 1-21-1006). A no-show does not win it for you automatically: under § 1-21-1005 the court tries the case as though the tenant were present, you must file a complaint, and the complaint must be sustained by proof or be dismissed, so bring the lease, the ledger, and proof of service. A continuance longer than two days requires the tenant to post a bond for accruing rent and costs (§ 1-21-1007). On a finding for you the court enters judgment for restitution and costs, and in a nonpayment case also for the rent found due together with costs and attorney's fees "as provided by the lease" (§ 1-21-1008(b)) - so if your lease has no attorney-fee clause you will not get fees. The court issues the writ of restitution at your request (§ 1-21-1012), and absent an appeal the officer executes it within two days of receiving it, Sundays excepted (§ 1-21-1013). An FED action does not bar a later ejectment action (§ 1-21-1016). Finally, if you hold through an LLC or corporation, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1017 lets the entity appear without an attorney through an owner, shareholder, member, or partner, provided the entity holds a majority interest in the property, every owner, shareholder, member, or partner signs a written notice to the court and all parties, and the judgment sought does not exceed the W.S. 1-21-201 limit; if your attorney does appear, the tenant is entitled to a continuance to get one too.

One ground you do not have: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(c) bars terminating a tenancy based solely on the tenant's, applicant's, or a household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 makes that unwaivable by lease. Adverse decisions on other lawful factors within your knowledge remain available.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure Statute
bodyText: Wyoming has no defective drywall statute of any kind. The word "drywall" does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and neither does "wallboard" or any definition of corrosive, sulfur-emitting or so-called Chinese drywall. There is no disclosure form, no remediation standard, no special limitations period, and no rent abatement tied to it. Wyoming also has no general residential property condition disclosure statute that would pick the subject up indirectly - the phrases "property condition disclosure," "residential real property disclosure" and "latent defect" appear nowhere in the statutes either. What actually governs is your habitability duty. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) says each owner renting a residential rental unit shall maintain that unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) says you shall not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. Corrosive drywall that emits sulfur gases, pits copper wiring and plumbing, and makes occupants ill is the kind of condition that can breach both. Note the statutory escape hatch in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(c): the article does not apply to breakage, malfunctions or other conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter - so minor cosmetic drywall damage is outside this entirely, while a genuinely off-gassing wall is not. Note also Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d): a duty under the article may be assigned to a different party or modified only by explicit written agreement signed by both parties, so you cannot shed the habitability duty by a one-line lease disclaimer the tenant never separately signed. Practical course: Wyoming does not make you volunteer anything about drywall, but if you actually know a unit has defective drywall that has not been remediated, say so in writing before the tenant signs and keep the acknowledgment. Renting a unit you know is off-gassing is a § 1-21-1203(a)(i) problem whatever the lease says, and a knowing misrepresentation about the condition of property in a consumer transaction can also draw the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a), whose definition of merchandise at § 40-12-102(a)(vi) expressly includes real property - whether a residential lease is a covered consumer transaction under § 40-12-102(a)(ii) is not settled by the statute's text, so treat it as a risk rather than a certainty. If a tenant gives you written notice of a drywall condition under § 1-21-1203(b), you must within a reasonable time either start correcting it or notify the tenant in writing that you dispute the claim, by certified mail or in the manner of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds Go to the State
bodyText:
A deposit refund you owe a former tenant and cannot get to them does not become yours. Wyoming's Uniform Unclaimed Property Act names security deposits outright: Wyo. Stat. § 34-24-102(a)(x)(B) puts "security deposits, refunds, credit memos" in the definition of intangible property. Under the general rule in § 34-24-103(a), intangible property held in the ordinary course of your business that stays unclaimed for more than five years after it became payable is deemed abandoned. The refund became payable when § 1-21-1208(a) required you to return it, so the five years run from that date, not from when you gave up looking.

At that point you are a "holder" and you owe the State Treasurer, who is the administrator, three things. First, notice to the tenant: not more than 120 days before you file, you must send written notice to the apparent owner at the last known address telling them you hold property subject to the act, if your records show an address you do not know to be bad, the claim is not time-barred, and the property is worth $50 or more (§ 34-24-118(e)). Second, a verified report, filed no later than November 1 each year for the reporting period ending the preceding June 30, listing the owner's name and last known address for each item of $50 or more, the nature and amount, and the date it became payable; items under $50 may be reported in the aggregate (§ 34-24-118(b), (d)). Third, payment: you pay or deliver the property to the administrator at the time you file the report (§ 34-24-120(a)). Keep the owner's name and last known address on file for five years after the property becomes reportable (§ 34-24-132(a)).

The penalties are real. Willfully missing the report or any other duty costs up to $100 per day (§ 34-24-135(a)(i)); willfully failing to pay over the property costs a civil penalty of 25% of its value (§ 34-24-135(a)(ii)); and late payment, willful or not, carries interest at 10 percentage points above the 52-week Treasury bill discount rate, compounding to a fresh rate each year it stays unpaid (§ 34-24-135(a)(iii)). The administrator can sue to compel the report, audit your records and get an injunction (§§ 34-24-131, 34-24-133).

Do not try to write around this. A lease term that says an unclaimed deposit is forfeited to you after 30, 60 or 90 days does not work in Wyoming: § 34-24-130(a) says the expiration of any period specified by contract, statute or court order does not prevent the money from being deemed abandoned or affect your duty to report and pay it over. The clause may bind the tenant; it does not bind the State. Two related points: § 34-24-109's one-year dormancy for utility deposits is for deposits made with a "utility" -- a person who owns or operates a plant or system "for public use" (§ 34-24-102(a)(xvii)) -- so a landlord who submeters its own tenants is not covered and a separately identified utilities deposit under § 1-21-1208(b) still falls under the ordinary five-year rule. And § 34-24-103(a) lets you take "lawful charges" off the top first, which is where your properly itemized damage and unpaid-rent deductions belong -- make the deductions when the tenancy ends, not five years later.

Practical course: close out every deposit when the tenancy ends. Use the forwarding address, mail the refund, and if the check comes back or is never cashed, keep the money segregated with the tenant's name and last known address attached, diary it, and report it on the next November 1 cycle once five years have run.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming never uses the phrase "last month's rent" in its statutes, and it places no restriction on collecting rent in advance or on applying a deposit to rent. The phrase "security deposit" does not appear in Title 1 either. What governs is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), which speaks of "property or money held as a deposit." Four things follow, and the third surprises most landlords.

First, you may apply the deposit to unpaid rent. Section 1-21-1208(a) says that upon termination of the rental agreement, the deposit "may be applied by the owner or his agent to the payment of accrued rent, damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement and to other costs provided by any contract." Accrued rent is first on the list. There is no Wyoming rule, as some states have, that walls the deposit off from rent.

Second, the right is yours, not the tenant's, and it ripens only at termination. The statute says the deposit "may be applied by the owner" — it gives the tenant no power to declare the deposit spent as the final month's rent, and it gives you no power to dip into it mid-tenancy. A tenant who skips the last month's rent is simply in default, and you may both apply the deposit afterward and pursue the shortfall. Put the no-self-help rule in the lease anyway: Wyoming attaches no statutory penalty to a tenant who does it, so the lease is your only lever.

Third — the trap — prepaid rent must come back on the deposit's clock. The second sentence of § 1-21-1208(a) requires that "[t]he balance of any deposit and prepaid rent and a written itemization of any deductions from the deposit together with reasons therefor, shall be delivered or mailed without interest to the renter within thirty (30) days after termination of the rental agreement or within fifteen (15) days after receipt of the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later." Prepaid rent is named alongside the deposit. So money you took up front as "last month's rent" that is not consumed by the final month's rent is a balance you owe back on the same 30-day / 15-day timetable — extended by another thirty (30) days if there is damage to the unit. The tenant must tell you within thirty (30) days of termination where to send payment and notice. If you unreasonably fail to comply, § 1-21-1208(c) lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs; if you prevail and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in suing, you may be awarded court costs on top of other relief. Wyoming does not add interest, and none is owed.

Fourth, if any of it is nonrefundable, say so twice. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires that the rental agreement state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable AND that written notice of that fact be given to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. Two separate acts — the lease term is not enough by itself. If you label a prepaid final month as nonrefundable, treat § 1-21-1207 as applying and disclose it both ways; the cautious course, since § 1-21-1208(a) sweeps prepaid rent into the refund duty, is not to call prepaid rent nonrefundable at all.

One more point for a buyer or lender: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209 binds "[t]he holder of the interest of the owner or designated agent in the residential rental unit at the time of termination" to §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208. Whoever owns the property when the tenancy ends owes the refund, whether or not the money was ever handed over at closing. Wyoming sets no cap on a deposit or on prepaid rent.

title: Move-Out Address Notice and the Deposit Clock
bodyText: Wyoming puts the move-out notice duty on the renter, not on you, and ties your refund deadline to it. Under the last sentence of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), 'The renter shall within thirty (30) days of termination of the rental agreement, notify the owner or designated agent of the location where payment and notice may be made or mailed.' Your side of the clock is in the second sentence of the same subsection: the balance of the deposit and any prepaid rent, together with a written itemization of every deduction and the reasons for it, must be delivered or mailed to the renter, without interest, within thirty days after termination of the rental agreement, or within fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later. If there is damage to the unit, that period is extended by thirty more days. A utilities deposit that was held and separately identified as such runs on its own schedule under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b). Two practical points. First, Wyoming's deadline is 'whichever is later,' so a renter who never gives you an address never starts the fifteen-day prong. Do not read that as licence to hold the money: the cautious course is to mail the itemization and the balance to the renter's last known address, and to the unit itself, at the thirty-day mark (sixty where there is damage), keep proof of mailing, and hold the funds if the mail comes back. Second, Wyoming does not require you to give the renter any move-out notice, inspection appointment, pre-move-out statement of anticipated deductions or demand for an address, and gives the renter no right to attend a move-out inspection. Asking for the address in writing is still the sensible step, because without it you cannot show when the fifteen-day prong began. If you unreasonably fail to comply with subsection (a) or (b), Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs — the full deposit, not a multiple of it, and Wyoming has no punitive multiplier here. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209, whoever holds the owner's interest at termination is bound by §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208, so selling the building does not move the obligation off you by itself.

title: You Control Who Does Repairs, Because Wyoming Gives No Repair-and-Deduct Right
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute that names who must do repairs, and no statute that stops you from naming one. More importantly, Wyoming gives a tenant no right to fix a problem and take the cost out of the rent. There is no repair-and-deduct remedy, no rent withholding and no rent escrow anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. That means a designated-repairer clause in Wyoming is not, as it is in a URLTA state, an attempt to narrow a statutory remedy the tenant has. It is simply a contract term, and it is enforceable on ordinary contract principles. Say plainly in your lease that you arrange all work, that only you or contractors you authorize may perform it, and that the tenant may not deduct anything from rent.

How the repair process actually runs here. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) sets a two-sided procedure, and it is narrower than landlords expect. A tenant who is current on all payments required by the rental agreement, and who has reasonable cause supported by evidence to believe the unit does not meet the article's health and safety standards, must advise you in writing of the condition and specify the remedial action requested. Only then does your clock start. Within a reasonable time after receiving that notice you must either begin action to correct the condition or notify the tenant in writing that you dispute the claim. Note what the statute requires of the tenant: being current on payments, writing, and specifying the remedy sought. A tenant in arrears has not triggered the procedure.

The statute is specific about service. Section 1-21-1203(b) says the notices it requires "shall be served by certified mail or in the manner specified by W.S. 1-21-1003." That applies to your dispute notice too, not just the tenant's. If you dispute a claim, send it certified mail or serve it the way § 1-21-1003 prescribes, and keep the receipt.

Who counts as you. Under § 1-21-1201(a)(i), for purposes of notice and other communication under the article, "owner" includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager "unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement." Read the direction of that default carefully. Your property manager is a proper recipient of the tenant's repair notice automatically. If you do not want notice at the manager's office to count as notice to you, the manager has to say so in writing in the rental agreement. You cannot fix it after the fact.

Your escape hatch if the repair is too expensive. Section 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse to correct the condition and terminate the tenancy instead, if the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement. You must notify the tenant in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance, and you must give the tenant time to find substitute housing — no less than 10 days and no more than 20 days from the date of your notice. On termination, prorate the rent to the date the tenant vacates, refund the balance, and return the deposit under § 1-21-1208.

Two more things in your favour. Section 1-21-1203(c) says you are not required to correct a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, or the renter's guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse of the property. And § 1-21-1203(e) says you are not liable under the article for claims for mental suffering or anguish, which caps a common category of tenant damages claim.

Practical limits on the clause. Wyoming licenses electricians, so electrical work should go to a licensed electrician; there is no state plumbing or general-contractor licence in the statutes, but a city may require permits of its own. Keep an emergency phone number in the lease alongside the written-notice address, because a tenant with a burst pipe at midnight will call, and you want the call. And do not write the clause so broadly that it reads as the tenant waiving habitability: § 1-21-1202(d) does let any duty in the article be modified by explicit written agreement signed by both parties, and the article has no anti-waiver provision, but a clause that looks like a habitability waiver is a fight you do not need.

title: Reasonable Accommodations and Modifications for Disability
bodyText: Wyoming has its own fair housing act, and Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107 is its disability provision — it operates on you independently of the federal Fair Housing Act. Under § 40-26-107(a) you may not refuse to rent, or make unavailable or deny a dwelling, because of a disability of the renter, of anyone who will reside there, or of anyone associated with the renter. Under § 40-26-107(b) you may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of the rental, or in services or facilities, for the same reasons. Section 40-26-107(c) then says what counts as discrimination. Two duties matter day to day. First, § 40-26-107(c)(i): you may not refuse to permit a reasonable modification of the existing premises, made AT THE TENANT'S OWN EXPENSE, where the modification may be necessary to afford full enjoyment of the premises — grab bars, a ramp, a widened doorway, lever handles. Second, § 40-26-107(c)(ii): you may not refuse a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices or services where it may be necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. That second duty is the one a request to waive a no-pets rule, assign a closer parking space, or accept a third-party rent payer falls under. Note the statutory threshold is "may be necessary," not "is necessary" — a low bar. Wyoming's definition of disability is in § 40-26-102(a)(v): a mental or physical impairment substantially limiting at least one major life activity, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having one. It expressly excludes current illegal drug use or addiction, and it expressly says the term does not apply to an individual because of sexual orientation or because the individual is a transvestite — that exclusion removes those from the DISABILITY definition only; it does not create any licence to discriminate on another listed ground. Assistance animals are governed separately and more strictly. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) says a person may not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, which must be permitted in leased residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act — and the same subsection makes the tenant liable for damage the animal does. "Assistance animal" is defined in Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-205(a)(iv) to include an animal that provides EMOTIONAL SUPPORT alleviating an identified symptom or effect of the person's disability, so emotional-support animals are inside the Wyoming rule, not outside it. Do not charge pet rent or a pet deposit for an assistance animal, and do not apply breed or weight limits to it. If you suspect a fake, Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(b) makes knowingly and intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service or assistance animal a misdemeanor punishable by a fine up to seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00) — but that is a criminal matter for law enforcement, not a self-help ground to refuse the animal. Section 35-13-201 sits in Title 35 and carries NO small-landlord exemption. The fair housing act does. Under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(a), §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109 — which includes the disability section — do not apply to an owner of not more than three single family houses renting without a broker and without a prohibited advertisement, and only to one rental in any twenty-four (24) month period if the owner was not the most recent resident. Under § 40-26-110(b), §§ 40-26-103 and 40-26-105 through 40-26-109 do not apply to rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of not more than four families — read that list carefully, because § 40-26-104, the advertising provision, is deliberately left OUT of the (b) exemption, so even an exempt owner-occupant may not publish a discriminatory notice or advertisement. Do not rely on either exemption without also checking the federal Fair Housing Act, which has its own narrower exemptions, and § 35-13-201(c), which has none. Two further limits you may invoke: § 40-26-107(f) says the section does not require a dwelling to be made available to an individual whose tenancy would be a direct threat to the health or safety of others or would result in substantial physical damage to others' property — this must rest on an individualised, evidence-based assessment of that person, never a generalisation about a condition. And § 40-26-113(a) preserves reasonable occupancy limits and health or safety standards. Finally, if you own newer multifamily stock, § 40-26-107(c)(iii) imposes design and construction duties on "covered multifamily dwellings," defined in § 40-26-107(g) as buildings of four (4) or more units with an elevator, plus ground floor units in other buildings of four or more units: accessible common areas, doors wide enough for a wheelchair, an accessible route through the dwelling, accessible controls, bathroom wall reinforcement for later grab bars, and manoeuvrable kitchens and baths. Section 40-26-107(d) treats compliance with the American national standard as it existed on July 1, 2015 as satisfying the adaptive-design requirement. Read § 40-26-107(e) carefully: by its literal words only the accessible-route requirement of subparagraph (c)(iii)(A) is switched off for a building first occupied on or before March 13, 1991 — the other adaptive-design features are not expressly exempted, even though federal law exempts pre-1991 buildings generally. The cautious course for an older building is to treat a modification request under § 40-26-107(c)(i) as the operative duty and not to assume the whole of (c)(iii) falls away.

title: A Tenant Who Takes In People Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about disaster-displaced guests. Nothing gives a tenant a right to house someone burned out, flooded out or evacuated, nothing suspends your occupancy limits during an emergency, nothing protects you from liability for letting it happen, and nothing requires you to allow it. There is no state price-gouging law and no emergency rent or eviction moratorium on the books either. Wyoming's emergency statutes operate at the government level: the interstate emergency management assistance compact in Title 19 plans how party states move, register, feed and house evacuees between themselves, and the relocation assistance act at Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-7-101 et seq. compensates people displaced by a public agency acquiring property. Neither says anything to a private landlord.

So the question is decided by your lease plus two ordinary provisions. The first is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v): the renter shall 'occupy the residential rental unit in the manner for which it was designed and shall not increase the number of occupants above that specified in the rental agreement without written permission of the owner.' The cap is whatever number your lease specifies — and if the lease specifies no number, this subsection caps nothing. That is the single most important point for this topic. If you want the power to say yes or no when a tenant wants to shelter a displaced family, you must state an occupant number in the lease; otherwise § 1-21-1204(a)(v) gives you no handle, and you are left with whatever guest or subletting term you wrote. Note also that the statute's cure is written permission from you, which means you can say yes to a temporary arrangement without rewriting the lease or creating a tenancy for the newcomer — put the permission in writing, date it, and state when it ends.

The second is that you remain covered for what the extra people do. Under § 1-21-1203(c) you are not required to correct or remedy any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, or the renter's guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse of the property. Under § 1-21-1204(a)(viii) the renter must remove all property and garbage placed in the unit 'by the renter or his guests' and clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement. Damage a displaced guest causes is the tenant's responsibility and is chargeable against the deposit under § 1-21-1208(a).

Do not plan on using Wyoming's new non-judicial removal procedure against a guest your tenant let in. Article 14, §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, lets an owner ask law enforcement to remove an unauthorized person immediately, but § 1-21-1402(a)(ii) requires that the person 'has unlawfully entered and remains or continues to reside' in the dwelling, and someone your tenant invited in did not unlawfully enter. Section 1-21-1402(a)(iv) separately shuts the door on anyone who is a current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement. Misusing the procedure is expensive: § 1-21-1403(c) exposes you to triple the fair market value of renting plus costs and fees, and the complaint you sign under § 1-21-1402(b)(x) is submitted under penalty of perjury and must expressly acknowledge that liability. Against a tenant who has overloaded the unit, your route is an ordinary breach — written notice, then the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 and a forcible entry and detainer action.

The cautious course when a tenant asks: say yes or no in writing, in advance, with an end date, and say in the same writing that the guest acquires no tenancy and that the tenant remains responsible for the guest's conduct and damage. Remember that all of Article 12 — occupancy, habitability, deposits — applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence under § 1-21-1201(a)(iv).

title: When Fire, Flood or Storm Damages the Property
bodyText:
Wyoming has no disaster statute for landlords and tenants. Nothing in Wyoming law ends a tenancy because a declared disaster destroyed the unit, abates or suspends rent while the tenant cannot live there, requires you to clean up disaster debris or test for mold, smoke or asbestos, or gives the tenant a right to return at the old rent. There is no rent-abatement provision anywhere in the Wyoming statutes, and no price-gouging law. If your lease is silent, there is no default rule waiting to fill the gap, which makes a written casualty clause more important in Wyoming than in most states. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty in the landlord-tenant article be reassigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so a casualty clause allocating risk, abatement and termination between you and the tenant is enforceable.

What actually governs, absent a clause, is the ordinary owner-duty section, and it works in a sequence you need to follow in order. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires you to keep the unit reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, to maintain common areas, and to maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. A fire or flood that knocks out any of those puts you out of compliance, and the damage being nobody's fault is not an excuse: the only fault-based escape, § 1-21-1203(c), covers conditions the renter, the renter's family or their guests caused by inappropriate use or misuse.

Your exit is § 1-21-1203(d), and it is the provision to know. If the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property, you may refuse to repair and terminate the rental agreement. That is the realistic answer after a serious fire or flood. But three conditions bind it. First, it is reactive, not free-standing: the ten-to-twenty-day clock and the right to refuse both run from your receipt of the renter's written notice of noncompliance under § 1-21-1203(b), so you cannot simply announce after a disaster that the lease is over. If the tenant has not sent that notice, prompt them to put the condition in writing, or negotiate a written surrender instead. Second, the tenant can only give a valid § 1-21-1203(b) notice while current on all payments required by the rental agreement, so a tenant already in arrears cannot start the sequence. Third, if you do terminate, you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time, give no less than ten and no more than twenty days to find substitute housing, prorate the rent to the date the renter vacates, and refund the balance along with the deposit under § 1-21-1208. Note also that § 1-21-1203(e) bars claims for mental suffering under the whole article, which limits what a tenant can recover from you over a disaster. All of this applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence, because § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" that way and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

Three other Wyoming provisions can matter after a disaster. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d), after a hazardous-material, weapons-of-mass-destruction or clandestine-laboratory incident, the incident commander may order that any portion of a building, structure or land is uninhabitable or contaminated and secure it. Read that subsection carefully if it happens to you: the requirement that the commander narrow the declaration to the affected areas, and the duty to give the owner written notice describing the extent, are written for commercial real estate only, so a residential building can be declared uninhabitable as a whole. Property ordered uninhabitable can be sold before remediation only with full written disclosure to the buyer, which under that subsection releases the seller and shifts liability to the buyer. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-140, a public utility is not liable for property damage or economic loss from a catastrophe caused by an act of God unless a negligent, willful, wanton or reckless act of the utility was a proximate cause, so do not assume you can pass your loss to the utility. And if you rent as a small business, the small business emergency bridge loan program at Wyo. Stat. §§ 11-52-101 and following, added in 2025, makes short-term loans available through the office of state lands and investments once the governor declares a natural disaster and designates the affected counties.

title: No Wyoming Rule on Double-Letting a Room
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute on double-letting - renting the same room or unit, or part of a room, to more than one tenant for overlapping periods. A searched canvass of all 44 Wyoming titles and the 2025 and 2026 session laws turns up nothing.

This matters because the states that do have a rule impose a severe one. The old field-code provision carried in California, Montana, North Dakota and elsewhere says that a person who hires part of a room as a dwelling is entitled to the whole room whatever the agreement says; that if a landlord lets a room as a dwelling to more than one family the first person to whom any part of it was let is entitled to possession of the whole room for the agreed term; and that every tenant in the building under that same landlord is relieved of all obligation to pay rent for as long as the double-letting continues. Wyoming imports none of that. There is no automatic rent abatement, no building-wide rent suspension, no statutory priority for the first tenant, and no statutory entitlement to a whole room for someone who rented part of one.

What fills the gap in Wyoming is ordinary contract and possession law, plus two Wyoming-specific points that cut in a landlord's favour and one that does not. (1) Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) caps occupancy only at the number "specified in the rental agreement," so the number of people lawfully in a unit is whatever your lease says and nothing more - if you want a per-room limit, write it. (2) Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 means that nothing about an overlapping occupancy creates a tenancy by implication; a second occupant you never contracted with holds nothing but a tenancy by sufferance at most. (3) Against you: double-booking a unit is a straightforward breach of the earlier tenant's lease, and the earlier tenant's damages are contract damages - the cost of substitute housing, moving costs, and the difference in rent - with no statutory cap. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) bars mental-suffering claims only for claims "under this article," so it does not shield you from an ordinary breach-of-contract or misrepresentation claim brought outside Article 12. And because the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches real property under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi), knowingly letting the same unit twice could be attacked under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105, subject to the pre-suit notice and cure period in § 40-12-109.

Practical course: never execute a second lease on a unit before the first is surrendered in writing or possession is actually recovered; make the lease identify the specific unit (and room, in a shared-housing arrangement) before signing; and if you do find yourself double-booked, relocate and compensate the later tenant promptly rather than litigating, because Wyoming gives you no statutory safe harbour and no statutory ceiling on the exposure.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: No drug-free or crime-free addendum statute, but drug activity on your property is a nuisance you own
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute that requires, authorizes, forms or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. There is no Wyoming equivalent of the Washington or Oregon drug-and-alcohol-free housing programs, no state-prescribed addendum text, and no statute that converts a drug charge into an automatic lease termination. The words "drug-free" and "crime-free" do not appear in the landlord-tenant statutes at all. So if you want a drug-free term, you write it yourself as an ordinary lease covenant and it is enforced as an ordinary lease covenant.

That is workable, because Wyoming's eviction statute reaches lease terms you create. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows forcible entry and detainer against tenants holding over their terms, and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) allows it against renters in violation of any terms imposed under § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205 - the renter-duty sections. Section 1-21-1204(a) is where your written rules and the terms of the rental agreement get their teeth, so a drug and criminal-activity covenant written into the lease, and into rules the lease incorporates, supports an FED action. You still have to serve the separate three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 before filing. Note the structural point: your addendum is only as strong as the breach-and-termination language you put in it, because no statute supplies a shortened notice or an automatic forfeiture for drug activity.

The real reason to have the covenant is what Wyoming does to the owner, not to the tenant. Two regimes:

NUISANCE. Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-201 declares that whoever maintains, uses, OWNS OR LEASES any structure for lewdness, assignation, prostitution or gambling, or for the manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of intoxicating liquor or any controlled substance in violation of law, is guilty of a nuisance - and the structure, the ground it sits on, and the furniture, fixtures and contents are declared a nuisance too, to be enjoined and abated. Owning or leasing is inside the definition. Under § 6-6-202 the county attorney or ANY citizen of the county may bring the action in the state's name. Under § 6-6-204 the order of abatement directs removal and sale of the movable property and orders the structure closed for a period the court sets. Section 6-6-206 is your escape: if the owner appears, pays all costs and files a bond with approved sureties in the full value of the property, conditioned on immediately abating the nuisance and preventing its recurrence for a period the court sets, the court may cancel the abatement order as to the property if satisfied of the owner's good faith - but the release does not discharge any judgment, lien or liability. Section 6-6-207 assesses a $300 tax against the building, the ground and the owner or agent whenever a permanent injunction issues. Acting promptly on known drug activity, and being able to show you did, is the practical defence.

CLANDESTINE LABS. If a methamphetamine or similar lab is found in your rental, the Wyoming Emergency Response Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-9-151 through 35-9-159, decides what it costs you. Under § 35-9-156(d) the incident commander may order any portion of the building, structure or land uninhabitable or contaminated, secure it, and take steps to limit exposure, and the order stands until the commander declares the threat to public safety ended. Property ordered uninhabitable or contaminated may only be transferred or sold before remediation if full written disclosure is made to the buyer and attached to the earnest money receipt, accompanying the sale documents but not forming part of the deed and not recorded. Then § 35-9-158(a) governs who pays: the governing body must first claim against the party responsible for the lab and apply any related asset forfeiture, and a claim against the OWNER of the building is allowed only through a court-approved expense account. The sentence to know is § 35-9-158(a)(ii): if the owner did not know and could not with reasonable diligence have known of the clandestine laboratory operation, the amount recoverable from the owner is limited to one percent of the county assessor's fair market value of the portion declared uninhabitable. If you knew, or reasonable diligence would have told you, that cap disappears. Whatever the court allows becomes a lien on the real property under § 35-9-158(a)(iii), and if the owner does not pay within six months of approval the sheriff may sell the property on court order. Section 35-9-158(b) entitles you to a reasonable opportunity for nonbinding mediation before suit, and § 35-9-158(c) awards the government its collection costs and reasonable attorney's fees if it prevails.

So the drug-free clause is not a formality. It is the documentary backbone of a reasonable-diligence defence that is worth, quite literally, ninety-nine percent of the remediation bill. Pair it with inspections you actually perform and record.

Federally assisted housing is separate: HUD's own lease requirements and drug-free addendum apply there and this library does not cover them.

title: No Landlord Confidentiality Duty for Domestic Violence Victims
bodyText:
Wyoming imposes no confidentiality duty on a landlord who learns that a tenant or applicant is a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence. The Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304, is only four sections long and contains nothing about secrecy: it defines terms, gives the tenant an affirmative defense to a rent claim after vacating, bars termination solely for victim status, and forbids waiver. It does not say the tenant’s status, notice, supporting medical, court or police evidence, or forwarding address is confidential, does not bar putting any of it in a database or a tenant-screening report, and creates no penalty or damages for disclosure. Wyoming also has no address confidentiality program and no substitute-address system — neither phrase appears anywhere in the statutes — so there is no state-issued proxy address a tenant can give you.

What the Safe Homes Act does do, and what you must honor. Under § 1-21-1303(a) a tenant who gives you seven days’ written notice before vacating, stating that the reason is a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the premises, has an affirmative defense to your suit for rent accruing after the tenant leaves, if the court finds the threat proved by a preponderance and demonstrated by medical, court or police evidence. Subsection (b) is a separate route for abuse that already occurred on premises you own or control: same seven days’ written notice, which must also state the date of the violence and that the tenant gave you the medical, court or police evidence, and the violence must have occurred within sixty days before the notice unless hospitalization or seeking shelter or counseling made that impracticable. Note that the defense cuts off rent only for the period after the tenant vacates: § 1-21-1303(d) expressly preserves your claim for rent accrued before the tenant gave notice and vacated, and preserves a forcible entry and detainer action for that earlier nonpayment. Section 1-21-1303(c) separately bars you from terminating a tenancy based solely on the tenant’s, an applicant’s or a household member’s status as a victim, while allowing adverse decisions on other lawful factors you know of. Section 1-21-1304 makes none of this waivable — “The provisions of this act shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant.” That is the one hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law; the general modification power in § 1-21-1202(d) sits in a different article and does not reach it. Do not put a Safe Homes waiver in your lease.

The one confidentiality rule that can bind you is a court order, not a standing duty. Wyo. Stat. § 35-21-112 lets a victim of domestic abuse move, at any point in any Wyoming court proceeding — including your eviction or rent case — for an order keeping her address, city and state of residence and any other residence-identifying information confidential. Under (c) the court must issue the order if she holds an unexpired protection order, or if it finds by a preponderance that she is a victim and may face further abuse without confidentiality. Subsection (d) limits the order to the action in which it is granted. So the obligation arrives only when a judge grants it, and then it binds you in that case.

Practical course. Treat victim information as confidential as a matter of policy even though no statute compels it. Keep the notice and supporting evidence out of shared databases and screening files, do not pass a forwarding address to a third party, and do not discuss the tenant’s status with other residents. Disclosure is not a statutory violation in Wyoming, but it can supply the facts for a sex-discrimination claim under the Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-103 and 40-26-105, or a common-law claim, and it is the kind of conduct § 1-21-1303(c) is aimed at. If you receive a § 35-21-112 order, redact the address from every filing and exhibit in that case.

title: Deposit Timing After a Domestic Violence Departure
bodyText:
Wyoming has no special security-deposit rule for a domestic violence or sexual violence departure. The Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304, is four sections long and never mentions a deposit: § 1-21-1301 is the short title, § 1-21-1302 the definitions, § 1-21-1303 the substance, and § 1-21-1304 the anti-waiver rule. The ordinary deposit statute, § 1-21-1208, applies unchanged, and nothing in it waits for other occupants to deliver possession the way Massachusetts does.

What makes this a trap in Wyoming is the shape of § 1-21-1303. It does not give the victim a right to terminate the lease. It gives the tenant an affirmative defense in an action you bring for rent: the tenant 'shall have an affirmative defense and not be liable for rent for the period after which a tenant vacates', if the tenant gave you seven days' written notice before vacating and proves the statutory facts (§ 1-21-1303(a) for a credible imminent threat; § 1-21-1303(b) for violence that already occurred on the premises, within 60 days of the notice or as soon thereafter as practicable). So the tenant leaves, but the rental agreement itself does not end by operation of the statute.

That matters because the § 1-21-1208(a) clock is keyed to termination of the rental agreement, not to move-out: the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent plus a written itemization of deductions and the reasons for them must be delivered or mailed, without interest, within 30 days after termination of the rental agreement, or within 15 days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later — extended by a further 30 days if there is damage to the unit. The renter has 30 days from termination to tell you where to send it. (Article 12 only reaches a 'residential rental unit', defined at § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and occasionally rented recreational property.) A separately identified utilities deposit runs on its own 10/45/15/7-day cascade under § 1-21-1208(b).

Because the statute is silent, two situations are genuinely unsettled and you should take the cautious course in each. If the victim was the only tenant and has vacated, treat the tenancy as terminated when you accept the surrender, start the 30 days then, and send the itemization — do not sit on the money waiting for the lease term to expire. If co-tenants remain and the tenancy continues, the deposit is still the tenancy's deposit; do not refund a share to the departing victim unless you release her from the lease in writing and reset the deposit with those who stay. In either case, put the decision in writing to everyone named on the lease.

Two more points. Section 1-21-1304 says the Safe Homes Act 'shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant' — this is the one hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law, so do not write a lease term that conditions, shortens or penalizes the § 1-21-1303 defense, and do not charge an early-termination fee for invoking it. The deposit rules are different: § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty in Article 12, § 1-21-1208 included, be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so you may fix the deposit clock contractually — but drafting the clock so that it defeats a Safe Homes departure would pull § 1-21-1304 back in. Finally, § 1-21-1303(c) forbids terminating a tenancy based solely on anyone's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence, while allowing adverse decisions on other lawful grounds you know of; keeping a deposit for actual rent arrears from before the notice is not a status-based decision, and § 1-21-1303(d) expressly preserves your claim for rent accrued, and your forcible entry and detainer rights, for the period before the tenant gave notice and vacated.

title: No Duty to Change Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming gives a tenant who is a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence no right to demand a lock change, and gives you no duty to change, rekey or add a lock, no deadline for doing so, and no immunity for doing it. The Wyoming Safe Homes Act is four sections — Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304 — and all four were read end to end. What it actually gives the tenant is narrower than most landlords expect: § 1-21-1303(a) and (b) each create an affirmative DEFENSE to your action for rent after the tenant vacates, not a right to stay and not a right to any physical change to the unit. Under (a) the tenant must have been under a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the premises, shown by medical, court or police evidence, and must have given you seven days' written notice before vacating stating that as the reason. Under (b) the abuse must have occurred on premises you own or control, the tenant must have vacated as a result, the same seven days' written notice must state the date and confirm the evidence was given to you, and under (b)(iii) the incident must have been not more than sixty days before the notice, extended only where the tenant could not reasonably give notice in time for reasons related to the abuse, such as hospitalization or seeking shelter or counseling. § 1-21-1303(c) separately bars you from terminating a tenancy based SOLELY on victim status, while expressly preserving adverse housing decisions based on other lawful factors within your knowledge. § 1-21-1303(d) preserves your claim for rent that accrued, and your forcible entry and detainer action for nonpayment, for the period BEFORE the notice and vacating. § 1-21-1304 is the only hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law: 'The provisions of this act shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant.' Nothing in those four sections mentions locks, keys, security devices or excluding a perpetrator. Wyoming has no general statutory lock or security-device standard either — the ongoing habitability duties in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) are a closed list of electrical, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water, and § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) sweeps anything else in only as specifically contracted. So what fills the gap is the protection order, not the lease. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-21-105(a)(i) a court finding domestic abuse may 'grant sole possession of the residence or household to the petitioner' for the life of the order, or order the respondent to provide alternative housing; § 35-21-105(a)(vi) allows other injunctive relief; and § 35-21-105(c) makes willful violation a crime under Wyo. Stat. § 6-4-404 with immediate arrest. Wyo. Stat. § 7-3-509 is the parallel order in a stalking case. Critically for you, § 35-21-105(d) says no order issued under that act affects title to any property — the order rearranges possession between the household members, it does not change who your tenant is or rewrite your lease. Act on this as follows. You have no obligation to change a lock, so do not promise one in the lease unless you mean to perform it; once you write it in, § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes it your contracted duty. If a tenant asks, the cautious and usually right course is to say yes, change the lock promptly at your own or the tenant's cost as you agree in writing, keep a key, and document the request and the date — Wyoming imposes no penalty for doing it and the alternative is a tenant who changes the lock themselves and locks you out of your own unit. Where the person to be excluded is a co-tenant named on the lease, do not change the lock on your own judgment: that person has a contractual right of possession, and shutting them out exposes you under Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-306 and under the forcible entry and detainer chapter, which Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1001 lets a locked-out occupant use against a landlord. Ask for the protection order first and act on its terms. Finally, if you want to offer a lock change as a lease benefit you may — § 1-21-1304 bars waiving or cutting down the Safe Homes Act, not adding to it.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText:
Wyoming has not moved or renumbered any of the protection-order law your lease and your notices depend on. Every citation below is current as of July 1, 2026, and you can use it without checking.

The two protection-order tracks are in different titles and have been for years. Domestic-abuse orders of protection issue under the Domestic Violence Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-21-101 through 35-21-112, which still names itself that at § 35-21-101 and still defines its own extent at § 35-21-102(a)(viii) as running 35-21-101 through 35-21-112. Stalking and sexual-assault orders of protection issue under a separate set in the criminal procedure title, Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-3-506 through 7-3-512, whose definitions section says so in terms at § 7-3-506(a). The two tracks mirror each other section by section — petition, temporary order, order, service and duration, emergency law-enforcement assistance, confidentiality — so if you are handed an order, read which statute it issued under before you assume what it does.

The cross-reference that matters to you is current. Wyoming's tenant-side domestic violence statute is the Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304 (its extent is fixed by § 1-21-1302(a)(v)). Section 1-21-1302(a)(i) does not define "domestic abuse" itself — it borrows the definition by citing W.S. 35-21-102(a)(iii). We checked that paragraph against the current statute text: § 35-21-102(a)(iii) is still "Domestic abuse", and still means one or more of three things done by a household member, excluding acts of self-defence — (A) physically abusing, threatening to physically abuse, attempting to cause or causing physical harm, or acts unreasonably restraining a household member's personal liberty; (B) placing a household member in reasonable fear of imminent physical harm; or (C) causing a household member to engage involuntarily in sexual activity by force, threat of force or duress. So the Safe Homes Act's pointer is live, not stale. Note that "household member" is itself defined, at § 35-21-102(a)(iv), and is wider than spouses: it reaches people living together as if married, former spouses and former cohabitants, parents and their adult children, other adults sharing common living quarters, unmarried co-parents, and people in or formerly in a dating relationship.

"Sexual violence" works differently and is the one definition not to look for in the protection-order chapters. Section 1-21-1302(a)(iii) defines it inside the Safe Homes Act itself, as any act of sexual assault, sexual abuse or stalking of an adult or minor, including any nonconsensual sexual contact or intrusion as those terms are defined in the Wyoming Criminal Code. If you quote a definition in a lease or a notice, quote this one for sexual violence and the § 35-21-102(a)(iii) one for domestic abuse.

The 2025 session amended protection-order law twice and moved nothing. 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 33 (SF0007) amended §§ 7-3-506(a)(i), 7-3-507(d), 7-3-510(a) and (b), 35-21-102(a)(ii), 35-21-103(a) and (e) and 35-21-106(a) and (b) — counsel appointment, filing, service and notice, service of an extension order by mail, and who may petition on a victim's behalf. Within § 35-21-102 it touched paragraph (a)(ii), the "Court" definition, and left the domestic-abuse definition at (a)(iii) where it was, so the Safe Homes Act cross-reference survived the amendment untouched. 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 34 (SF0008) added § 7-3-510(e) and § 35-21-106(f), both saying an order of protection stays effective during an appeal or review unless a court orders a stay — a useful point when a tenant shows you an order that is under appeal. No 2026 act touched the Safe Homes Act or the domestic-abuse definition.

What to do with this. Cite the Safe Homes Act by section number with confidence. When you need the substance of "domestic abuse" in a lease, a notice or a policy, quote the words rather than the number, so a future renumbering cannot strand you — but as of today the number is right. And remember the part of the Safe Homes Act that constrains you rather than the tenant: § 1-21-1303(c) forbids terminating a tenancy based solely on a tenant's, applicant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence, though it expressly does not prohibit adverse housing decisions based on other lawful factors within your knowledge; and § 1-21-1304 says the Act cannot be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement. That is the one hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law — § 1-21-1202(d)'s power to shift duties by written signed agreement reaches only Article 12 and cannot touch Article 13.

title: Proof a Wyoming Tenant Must Supply to Use the Safe Homes Defense
bodyText:
Wyoming's rule on domestic-violence documentation is narrow and specific, and it works differently from most states. The Wyoming Safe Homes Act (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304) does not create a tenant right to terminate the lease early. It creates an affirmative defense the tenant raises when you sue for rent after they have already moved out. So the documentation question is not "what do I have to accept at the counter" - it is "what will the tenant have to prove in court, and what must they have handed me first."

The only qualifying proof the statute names is "medical, court or police evidence of domestic abuse or sexual violence." That phrase appears twice, in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(a)(i) and § 1-21-1303(b)(ii), and it is the whole of the documentation standard. Wyoming does not recognize a certification from a victim-services agency or other qualified third party, does not supply a statutory form, and does not require you to accept a tenant's self-certification or sworn statement. If a tenant offers only their own written account, the statute's standard is not met. But do not treat a thin showing as the end of it, because federal law may independently constrain you - the Violence Against Women Act self-certification rules apply to covered federally assisted housing regardless of what Wyoming provides (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. S 12491), and fair-housing law can be implicated by a blanket refusal. Flagged: a municipal or county ordinance could also impose its own standard, which this review does not resolve.

Where the evidence has to go depends on which of the two tracks the tenant is on, and this is the practical difference for you.

Track one, credible imminent threat, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(a). The tenant must show that at the time they vacated, they or a household member were under a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the premises, "as demonstrated by medical, court or police evidence," and that they gave you seven days' written notice before vacating stating that the reason for vacating was a credible imminent threat. Read that carefully: the evidence demonstrates the threat to the court. Nothing in subsection (a) obliges the tenant to put the evidence in your hands before leaving. All you are entitled to in advance is the seven-day written notice and its stated reason.

Track two, abuse that already happened, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(b). Here the tenant or a household member must have been a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence on premises you own or control and have vacated as a result; the seven-day written notice must state the reason for vacating, the date of the sexual violence, and that the tenant provided medical, court or police evidence to the landlord supporting the claim; and the abuse must have occurred not more than sixty days before the notice, or, where the tenant could not reasonably give notice in that window for reasons related to the abuse - the statute names hospitalization and seeking shelter or counseling as examples - then as soon thereafter as practicable. On this track the evidence must actually reach you, and the notice must say so. If you receive a track-two notice, log the date, keep whatever documents came with it, and do not discard them; they are the record of whether the statute's own condition was satisfied.

"Domestic abuse" takes its meaning from Wyo. Stat. § 35-21-102(a)(iii): one or more acts by a household member, excluding self-defense, consisting of physical abuse or the threat or attempt of it or acts unreasonably restraining a household member's personal liberty, placing a household member in reasonable fear of imminent physical harm, or causing a household member to engage involuntarily in sexual activity by force, threat of force, or duress. "Household member" under § 35-21-102(a)(iv) is broad and includes spouses, former spouses, people living together as if married or formerly doing so, parents and adult children, other adults sharing common living quarters, unmarried co-parents, and people in or formerly in a dating relationship. "Sexual violence" is defined separately in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1302(a)(iii) as any act of sexual assault, sexual abuse, or stalking of an adult or minor, including nonconsensual sexual contact or intrusion as the Wyoming Criminal Code defines those terms.

Two more things you are bound by. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(c) forbids terminating a tenancy based solely on the tenant's, an applicant's, or a household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence, though it expressly does not prohibit adverse housing decisions based on other lawful factors within your knowledge - so document the independent ground if you have one. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 provides that the provisions of the act "shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant." Do not put a clause in your lease requiring a particular form of proof, requiring more than the statute requires, shortening the sixty-day window, or waiving the defense. Such a clause is void and its presence invites a challenge to the rest of your lease.

What the defense does not reach is worth knowing. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(d) nothing in the act is a defense against recovery of rent for the period before the tenant vacated and gave notice, or against forcible entry and detainer for failure to pay rent before the tenant gave notice and vacated. Arrears accrued before the notice remain collectible. Wyoming also has no statute entitling a victim to a lock change at your expense; the only lock-change provision in Title 1 is in the unauthorized-occupant removal article, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402, and has nothing to do with this.

title: Submetering and Reselling Electricity to Tenants
bodyText: Wyoming has no submetering disclosure form and no statute telling you what to put in the lease about a submeter - but it has something more important, and it cuts the other way. Under Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(C), anyone who owns or operates a plant, property or facility for the generation, transmission, distribution, sale or furnishing of electricity to or for the public is a public utility subject to the Public Service Commission. Subparagraph (H)(VI) then exempts the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, the manufacture or distribution of gas, and the furnishing or distribution of water, by a person for the use of that person's tenants and not for sale to others. That is the exemption a landlord lives under when utilities are included in the rent or the building is master-metered with no separate charge. But (H)(VI) ends with a second, separate sentence: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." Read as written, that sentence takes the exemption away the moment you sell electricity to a tenant on a metered or otherwise direct basis - which is exactly what submetering and billing by the kilowatt-hour is. The contrast inside the same subparagraph confirms the reading: subparagraph (H)(VIII) creates an express carve-out for metered and other direct sales of water by a person to that person's tenants, but only when the sales are solely for allocating usage among tenants and include no additional fees or charges, and (H)(IX) adds a second water-only carve-out for very small water systems. The legislature wrote a tenant-billing exemption for water and wrote none for electricity or gas. Practical course: in Wyoming, do not submeter and bill electricity or gas as a separate per-unit charge unless you have confirmed your position with the Public Service Commission first. The safe structures are (1) include electricity in the rent, (2) have each tenant open their own account directly with the serving utility in the tenant's own name, or (3) if you must allocate, get PSC guidance in writing before you start. Billing water by submeter is permitted, but only pass through actual usage allocation with no markup, administrative fee or service charge of any kind - adding even a small billing fee takes you outside (H)(VIII). Whatever you do, say plainly in the lease which utilities are included in rent, which the tenant must put in their own name, and how any permitted allocation is calculated; no statute requires that disclosure, but there is no Wyoming statute capping or policing a utility charge to a tenant either, so the lease is the only thing that will settle a dispute. Keep in mind that any separately identified utilities deposit is governed by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b), which has its own refund clock.

title: No Emergency Contact Requirement in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency telephone number, a 24-hour repair line, or a posted after-hours contact, and none requiring you to collect an emergency contact from the tenant. The Residential Rental Property article (Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) uses the word "emergency" nowhere, and Wyoming has no general disclosure section naming the owner or managing agent of the kind other states use. What the statute does do is make the address question matter. For every notice and communication required or allowed under the article, "owner" includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager — unless that agent or manager says otherwise in writing in the rental agreement (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1201(a)(i)). So a tenant's written notice of an unsafe or unsanitary condition, served on your on-site manager, is service on you, and your "reasonable time" to commence corrective action or to dispute the claim under § 1-21-1203(b) starts running from that moment. If you want notices to come only to you and not to your manager, the rental agreement has to say so in writing, signed by the party giving the notice-exclusion. Two more places an address does real work: the tenant's habitability notice and the follow-up "notice to repair or correct condition" are served by certified mail or in the manner of § 1-21-1003 (§§ 1-21-1203(b), 1-21-1206(b)), so certified mail has to reach a person who will act on it; and the tenant must tell "the owner or designated agent" within 30 days of termination where the deposit refund and itemization may be sent (§ 1-21-1208(a)), which only works if the tenant knows who the designated agent is. Practical course, none of it compelled by Wyoming law: put in the lease the name, mailing address and telephone number of the person who accepts notices and the number to call for a water leak, gas smell, no heat or no power; say plainly whether your manager is or is not authorized to receive statutory notices; keep that information current in writing; and remember that a 24-hour line costs you little and shortens the "reasonable time" the tenant can later say you let slip before acting on a habitability complaint. Check the city or county where you rent — a local rental-licensing or housing code may require a posted local contact, and local ordinances are outside this review.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText:
Wyoming has a statute on this, and the first thing it says is that your lease outranks it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-26-711(a): if the property taken includes a leasehold interest, the effect of the condemnation on the rights and obligations of the parties to the lease "is governed by the provisions of the lease, and in the absence of applicable provisions in the lease, by this section." So § 1-26-711 is a gap-filler. Write a condemnation clause and it controls; leave the lease silent and the court applies the statute.

What the statute supplies covers partial takings only. Under § 1-26-711(b), if there is a partial taking and the part taken includes a leasehold interest that extends to the remainder, the court may determine either that the lease terminates as to the part taken but stays in force as to the remainder -- in which case "the rent reserved in the lease is extinguished to the extent it is affected by the taking" -- or that the lease terminates as to both the part taken and the remainder, if the part taken is essential to the purposes of the lease or the remainder is no longer suitable for the lease's purpose. Note three things about that. It is "may," so the court chooses between the two outcomes. The rent reduction in (i) is stated as a proportion of what the taking affects, with no formula. And the subsection is written for a partial taking: a complete taking of the whole property is not addressed anywhere in § 1-26-711, so what happens to the lease and the rent in a total taking is left to the common law, which is not in this library's source material.

Timing is fixed: under § 1-26-711(c), termination or partial termination occurs at the earlier of the date the court's order lets the condemnor take possession or the date title transfers to the condemnor. Rent stops running from that date, not from the date the condemnor files or the date the tenant moves out.

The tenant's compensation is separate from yours and you cannot take it by lease. Section 1-26-711(d) says the section "does not affect or impair a lessee's right to compensation if his leasehold interest is taken in whole or in part." The award itself is computed on the property as a whole: under § 1-26-710, "[t]he amount of compensation for the taking of property in which divided interests exist is based upon the fair market value of the property considered as a whole," then apportioned among the interests, so you and your tenant are dividing one pot rather than each proving a separate claim against the condemnor.

If the condemnor is a government body, your tenant may also collect relocation money that has nothing to do with the award. The Wyoming Relocation Assistance Act of 1973 (Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-7-101 through 16-7-112) makes a residential tenant a "displaced person" (§ 16-7-102(a)(iv)), and § 16-7-105 requires the displacing agency to pay a tenant who lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least 90 days before negotiations began the amount needed to rent a comparable replacement dwelling for up to 42 months, capped at $5,250, plus relocation advisory services under § 16-7-106. Point your tenant at the agency for that, and do not promise it where the condemnor is a private condemnor rather than an agency.

Practical course: put a condemnation clause in the lease so you are not litigating which branch of § 1-26-711(b) applies, make it say what happens on a total taking since the statute does not, and have it preserve the tenant's separate claim rather than purport to assign it to you -- § 1-26-711(d) will not let you take it anyway.

title: Screening and Licensing Apartment Staff in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming does not require you to run a background check on anyone who works at a rental property. No statute obliges a landlord, property manager or apartment owner to screen a maintenance technician, leasing agent, groundskeeper or on-site manager, and none bars you from doing so. Wyoming has dozens of mandatory fingerprint-and-criminal-history provisions — for teachers and school employees, child care, health care, insurance, gaming, concealed carry, dozens of occupational licenses — but none of them reaches residential rental staff. Compare Florida, which requires every employee of a licensed apartment establishment to pass a background screening; Wyoming has no counterpart. Whatever screening you do is governed by employment law and the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, not by landlord-tenant law.

There is a different Wyoming requirement in this area, and it catches people out: a license, not a background check. Under the Real Estate License Act, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-101, it is unlawful to engage in "real estate activity" without a license. Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-102(b)(xlv) defines real estate activity as acting "for another and for compensation" to, among other things, rent, manage or lease real estate (subparagraph (A)), offer to do so (B), or collect rent (F); and § 33-28-102(b)(xlii) defines "property management" as the act of managing real estate for compensation for another, including collecting rents, maintaining the property and accounting for fees. "Real estate" expressly includes leaseholds, § 33-28-102(b)(xliv). So a person who manages or leases someone else's rental property for pay needs a Wyoming real estate license, and § 33-28-106(a) makes every applicant submit fingerprints and the information for a criminal history record background check under Wyo. Stat. § 7-19-201(a). That is the only mandatory screening in the chain — and it falls on the licensee, not on you as employer.

Two exemptions in Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-103(a) decide whether your own staff need licenses, and both have conditions worth reading closely.

Paragraph (a)(i) exempts "[a]n owner of real estate or ... a member of his immediate family or ... his regular employees with respect to property owned by him." "Regular employee" is defined at § 33-28-102(b)(xlviii) as an individual employed by an owner of real estate "on a salaried basis or paid wages which are not performance based, is subject to income tax withholding and FICA," whose duties are in the ordinary course of the owner's business or the management of the owner's investments. Read the three conditions together: a W-2 salaried or hourly employee managing your own buildings is exempt, but a leasing agent you pay per signed lease, or an independent contractor you 1099, is not a "regular employee" and is doing unlicensed real estate activity.

Paragraph (a)(vi) separately exempts "[a]ny person or employee acting as the resident manager for the owner or an employee acting as the resident manager for a responsible broker managing an apartment building, duplex, apartment complex or court, when the resident manager resides on the premises and is engaged in the leasing of real estate in connection with his employment." The trailing "when" clause is a condition on this paragraph only: the manager must actually live on the property. An off-site manager does not qualify here and must rely on (a)(i) or hold a license.

The penalties are real. Performing real estate activity without a license is a misdemeanor under Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-114(a) — up to a $2,500 fine or six months in jail for a first offense, up to $5,000 or a year for a later one, and up to $5,000 for a convicted entity.
