Under § 33-28-114(b), anyone who receives money as a result of a violation is liable to an aggrieved person for a penalty of between one and three times the sum received. And § 33-28-110(a) makes it unlawful for a responsible broker to compensate a non-licensee for performing real estate activity, so a licensed management company cannot pay your unlicensed helper either.

Practical course: screen anyone who will hold keys or enter occupied units, because nothing stops you and negligent-hiring exposure is a matter of common law rather than statute; comply with the FCRA if you use a consumer reporting agency; and before you hire or engage anyone to manage or lease property you do not own, confirm they are either a Wyoming licensee or squarely inside a § 33-28-103(a) exemption. If a city you operate in has its own rental-operator or business-licensing rule, check that too — municipal ordinances are outside this library.

title: No Energy Benchmarking or Tenant Usage-Data Release Law
bodyText: Wyoming has no building energy-benchmarking program and no statute letting a lease clause direct a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. Vermont has one (30 V.S.A. § 63(a)(2)); Wyoming does not. The phrases 'energy usage', 'usage data', 'energy use data' and 'consumption data' appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and there is no smart-meter or advanced-metering data provision. The state's only energy-performance law, the Wyoming Energy Performance Program at Wyo. Stat. § 9-12-1201 et seq., is about energy performance contracts for state agency and other public facilities; it does not reach rental housing and does not create any data right. The public service commission's authority over customer information is in its own rules and tariffs, not in the statutes. What this means in practice: if the utility account for a unit is in the tenant's name, the utility is the tenant's customer, not yours, and only the tenant can release the data. A lease clause is worth having, but treat it as the tenant's promise to cooperate rather than as something the utility must honor — the utility will almost always require its own signed release or online authorization from the account holder, and a sentence buried in a lease will not move it. Ask for the authorization on the utility's own form at lease signing, and renew it when the tenant renews. If instead the account is in your name and you bill the tenant, watch Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI): the exemption that keeps a landlord out of public-utility regulation 'shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants.'

title: When an LLC or Corporation Landlord Can Evict Without a Lawyer
bodyText:
Wyoming has a statute on exactly this question, and it is unusually generous — but it has four conditions and one cap, and missing any of them puts you back in front of a judge without standing to speak.

The statute is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1017. It says that, notwithstanding any other provision of law, a business entity may represent itself without an attorney in any proceeding under the forcible entry and detainer article (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017) that the entity brings, or has to respond to or take part in. That covers your eviction case, whether you filed it or you are defending an appeal. Subsection (b) adds that a person who represents the entity this way has not engaged in the unauthorized practice of law, as long as that person complies with Wyo. Stat. § 33-5-117 — which means simply that the person must not hold himself out or advertise as an attorney or counselor-at-law.

The four conditions, all of which must be met.

First, the person appearing must be an owner, shareholder, member or partner of the entity. Read that list narrowly. It does not include an employee, a bookkeeper, an office manager, a leasing agent or a hired property manager. If your properties are managed by a management company, the management company's staff cannot appear for your LLC under this section, even though Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) makes a managing agent a proper recipient of notices. Notice is one thing; appearing in court is another.

Second, the entity must own a majority interest in the lands or tenements that are the subject of the alleged unlawful and forcible entry. A minority co-owner entity does not qualify.

Third, if an attorney does appear on the entity's behalf, the opposing party is entitled to a continuance to get an attorney of its own. So do not file self-represented and then bring counsel in at the hearing expecting to proceed that day; you will hand the tenant a delay.

Fourth — and this is the one that catches people — the entity must give written notice to the court and to all parties that it is being represented by an owner, shareholder, member or partner, and that notice "shall be signed by every owner, shareholder, member or partner of the business entity." Every one. Not the one appearing, not a majority. If your LLC has four members scattered across three states, you need all four signatures before the hearing. Build this into your filing packet and get the signatures when you start the case, not the morning of.

The cap. Subsection (c) switches the whole section off for a business entity "seeking a judgment exceeding the amount specified in W.S. 1-21-201" in any action under the article. That amount is $6,000, exclusive of costs. So an entity that wants possession plus a money judgment over $6,000 in the same forcible entry and detainer case must hire a lawyer. If you want to stay self-represented, keep the money claim at or below $6,000, or take a possession-only judgment and pursue the balance separately.

Small claims is a separate and broader route. In small claims court, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-202(b) says that notwithstanding Chapter 5 of Title 33 (the state bar chapter), the state, governmental entities, natural persons, corporations, partnerships, associations or other organizations may litigate actions on their own behalf in person or through authorized employees, with or without an attorney — again with the opposing party's right to a continuance if an attorney appears. Note the difference: small claims lets an authorized employee appear, while § 1-21-1017 requires an owner, shareholder, member or partner. The small claims jurisdictional limit under § 1-21-201 is $6,000 exclusive of costs. Small claims will not give you possession, so it is the route for a deposit shortfall, unpaid rent or damage claim after the tenant has gone, not for the eviction itself.

An individual owner, of course, may always appear for himself. The problem only arises when title is in an LLC, corporation or partnership.

The cautious course. If your entity is a single-member LLC with you as the member, § 1-21-1017 is straightforward: sign the notice, file it, appear. If your entity has several owners, or you want more than $6,000, or a manager rather than an owner would be the one in court, hire a Wyoming lawyer. Court rules on filings and appearances are not in this library, so confirm the local circuit court's filing requirements for the § 1-21-1017(a)(iv) notice before your hearing date.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Right, But a Cost-of-Repair One
bodyText: Wyoming gives you no statutory right to end a lease because of a sudden environmental public health event, a wildfire, a flood, a smoke event or a government order that makes occupancy impossible or unlawful. There is no casualty-termination statute of any kind in Wyoming — "fire or other casualty," "destroyed by fire," "impossible or unlawful," "force majeure" and "frustration of purpose" return nothing in the Wyoming statutes, and no provision pairs a disaster with a termination right for either party. What Wyoming does give you is narrower and differently shaped, and it is the provision to reach for after a fire or flood: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d). It says the owner may refuse to correct the condition of the residential rental unit and terminate the rental agreement if the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement. Three things about it catch landlords out. First, it is reactive, not free-standing: by its words the termination notice must go out "within a reasonable time after receipt of the notice of noncompliance" — the renter's written notice under § 1-21-1203(b). If the tenant has not yet served that notice, § 1-21-1203(d) is not yet switched on, and the cautious course after a disaster is to invite the tenant's written notice, or to rely on a casualty clause you wrote into the lease, rather than to send a bare termination. Second, the notice must be in writing and must give the renter sufficient time to find substitute housing, which the statute fixes at no less than ten (10) days and no more than twenty (20) days from the date of the notice. Third, on termination you must prorate the rent paid to the date the renter actually vacates, refund the balance, and return any deposit due in accordance with Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208. Three limits worth knowing. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) says you are not required to correct a condition the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees caused by inappropriate use or misuse — so tenant-caused damage does not have to run through the § 1-21-1203(d) cost test at all. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) says the owner is not liable under the article for claims for mental suffering or anguish. And the whole of Article 12 applies only to a "residential rental unit" as defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and occasionally rented recreational property. Separately, if a hazardous-material, weapons-of-mass-destruction or clandestine-drug-lab incident is involved, a local incident commander can order the building uninhabitable under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d), with the court-filing, service and posting procedure in § 35-9-156(e) through (h). That order does not itself terminate the lease or stop rent — it just makes the premises unoccupiable, which is what you would then rely on. Because the state law is this thin, the gap is filled by your lease. Wyoming has no anti-waiver provision in Article 12, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) expressly allows any duty or obligation in the article to be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so a casualty and environmental-event termination clause is enforceable if you write one. Write it; do not assume the statute covers you. A note on COVID-era law, because landlords ask: Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-141 is an assumption-of-the-risk shield against COVID-19 exposure claims, not a lease-termination or rent-relief provision, and nothing in Wyoming excuses rent during a declared public health emergency.

title: EV Charging Equipment When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText:
Wyoming has no electric-vehicle charging law for rental housing. No statute gives a tenant the right to install a charger, requires you to allow one, sets who pays, requires insurance or a deposit, or says what happens to the equipment when the tenancy ends — nothing on removal, restoration, abandonment, or whether the charger becomes yours. Wyoming also has no common-interest or homeowners'-association statute that could override a no-charger rule, and the Condominium Ownership Act at Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-20-101 et seq. says nothing about charging. Wyoming's landlord-tenant articles contain no tenant-fixture rule at all: the only 'fixtures' in Title 1 are the plumbing fixtures a renter must keep sanitary under § 1-21-1204(a)(iii). End-of-tenancy treatment of a charger is therefore entirely a matter of your lease, and if the lease is silent you are arguing common-law fixture doctrine with no statute to point at.

Write the term before you let anyone drill into your wall. Say who owns the equipment during and after the tenancy; whether the tenant must remove it and restore the surface, wiring and parking area at the tenant's cost; the condition and deadline for that work; who holds the permits; and what happens if the tenant leaves it. You have two statutory hooks that make such a term stick. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that any duty or obligation in Article 12 may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties — explicit, written and signed are cumulative conditions. And § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit be applied not only to damages beyond reasonable wear and tear but to 'other costs provided by any contract,' so a removal-and-restoration cost your lease creates is deductible. If the lease creates no such cost, it is not deductible.

One limit you cannot contract around. If the charger is a disability-related modification, Wyoming's fair housing act controls. Under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(i), refusing to permit, at the expense of the individual having a disability, a reasonable modification of the existing premises is discrimination if the modification may be necessary to afford full enjoyment of the premises — and in a rental you may condition permission on restoration only 'when it is reasonable to do so' and only on the renter 'agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted.' Read that word 'interior.' A charger mounted in a carport, on an exterior wall or on a parking-lot bollard is not interior, so the statute's restoration carve-out does not reach it, and you should not assume you can demand restoration of exterior charging equipment installed as a disability modification. Section 40-26-107(c)(ii) separately requires a reasonable accommodation in rules and policies, which can mean waiving a blanket no-charger rule or reassigning a parking space.

If you intend to sell charging to tenants rather than just permit it, two provisions matter and they pull in opposite directions. The good news is that you will not become a regulated utility: Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(X) excludes from 'public utility' the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under Title 37. That is a genuine electric-vehicle exception, and it matters because the neighbouring § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) does the opposite for ordinary utilities, providing that the landlord's exemption 'shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants.' The bad news is tax. Effective July 1, 2026, 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 33 (HB0145) added Wyo. Stat. § 39-17-304(a)(iv): 'Notwithstanding paragraphs (i) through (iii) of this subsection, there is levied and shall be collected a license tax of three and one-half cents ($.035) per kilowatt hour on all electricity sold or dispensed for sale or use in this state to propel a motor vehicle except for electricity exempted under W.S. 39-17-305.' On its face that is not limited to DC fast charging stations, while the taxable-event provision at § 39-17-303(a)(iii) and the collection, metering and price-display duties at § 39-17-303(c)(ii) and (c)(iii) all still speak only of a DC fast charging station. The cautious course for a landlord with an ordinary Level 2 charger who bills tenants per kilowatt hour is to treat the $.035 tax as potentially applying, check the Department of Revenue and Department of Transportation rules that section 2 of HB0145 requires them to promulgate, and consider charging a flat parking or amenity fee rather than a per-kilowatt-hour price until that is clear. Note too that under § 39-17-303(b)(i) the state preempts the field, so no city, town or county may levy its own tax on these sales.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging and the Two Traps in Selling the Power
bodyText:
Wyoming gives your tenant no right to charge an electric vehicle and gives you no duty to allow it. There is no EV-charging provision in the landlord-tenant article, none in the property title, and no condominium or common-interest statute that could supply one. So whether a tenant may install or use charging equipment is entirely yours to decide, and whatever you decide belongs in the lease. If the lease is silent and a tenant installs a charger, you are arguing about alterations and damage after the fact with nothing to point to.

The risk in Wyoming is not refusing to allow charging. It is charging the tenant for the power by the kilowatt hour. Two separate regimes bite, and both turn on metered sale rather than on the charging itself.

First, public utility status, and here the answer is better than it looks at first. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H) opens "None of the provisions of this chapter shall apply to:" and then lists ten separate, independent non-applications. Subparagraph (H)(VI) exempts furnishing electricity "for the use of tenants ... and not for sale to others" and then takes that back: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." That clawback is the reason ordinary household submetering is dangerous in Wyoming. But it sits inside (H)(VI), it says "Such exemptions" — the exemptions stated in that same subparagraph — and it ends at a semicolon before (H)(VII) begins. It does not reach the later subparagraphs. The structure proves it: (H)(VIII) separately exempts "[m]etered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants", which is the exact thing the clawback names, so if the clawback reached forward, (H)(VIII) would cancel itself. And Wyoming wrote an electricity provision of the same kind: § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(X) exempts "the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under this title." So selling EV charging to your tenants by the kilowatt hour should not make you a public utility, provided you are not otherwise regulated. Household electricity submetering is a different matter and remains inside the (H)(VI) clawback — do not read (H)(X) as covering the apartment meter. Second, the alternative fuels license tax, which was reworked by 2026 HB0145 effective July 1, 2026. Read together, these sections do not say the same thing, and you need to know that before you price anything. The imposition provision, Wyo. Stat. § 39-17-303(b)(iii), levies the tax on electricity sold or dispensed for charging a plug-in hybrid or all-electric vehicle "at a DC fast charging station," and § 39-17-301(a)(lii) defines that term by reference to DC Level 1, 2 or 3 in SAE International Standard J1772. An ordinary Level 1 or Level 2 AC outlet in a parking stall is not a DC fast charging station, so on the imposition section you are outside the tax. But the rate provision, § 39-17-304(a)(iv), is written far more broadly: "Notwithstanding paragraphs (i) through (iii) of this subsection, there is levied and shall be collected a license tax of three and one-half cents ($.035) per kilowatt hour on all electricity sold or dispensed for sale or use in this state to propel a motor vehicle." That sentence has no DC fast charging limit and itself uses the word "levied." The exemptions section, § 39-17-305, is no help either way: both its subsections exempt only from "the license tax imposed under W.S. 39-17-304(a)(i) through (iii)," so they do not reach the electricity tax in (a)(iv) at all, and there is no residential, small-seller or incidental-use exemption anywhere in the article. The cautious reading is that any per-kilowatt-hour sale of charging electricity is taxable, whatever the equipment. Again, the way out is not to sell by the kilowatt hour.

If you do operate a DC fast charging station and sell the power, three duties attach directly. Under § 39-17-303(c)(ii) you collect the license tax as the dealer and are liable for the whole of it, and each station must be metered as to the electric energy sold or dispensed. Under § 39-17-303(c)(iii) you must conspicuously display the price per kilowatt hour including all applicable taxes. Two pieces of good news: § 39-15-105(a)(v)(E) exempts sales of alternative fuels taxed under this article from sales tax, so you are not taxed twice, and § 39-17-303(b)(i) preempts the field, so no city, town or county may levy its own tax on the sale. Local electrical permits and inspections are a different matter and do apply; get them before any work starts.

title: No Wyoming Rule on EV Charging in Shared Parking
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute on electric vehicle charging in shared or common parking at a rental property. There is no tenant right to install a charger in a shared lot, no obligation on you to allow one, no statutory right to charge a reasonable fee to reserve the space where a charger is installed, no default rule allocating damage from a shared charger, and no rule on how a charger is shared among tenants or what happens when one tenant installs at a space another later gets. Wyoming also has no condominium or common-interest statute that could supply any of it: there is no unit owners' association act, and the Condominium Ownership Act at Wyo. Stat. § 34-20-101 et seq. says nothing about charging equipment in common elements.

Everything in a shared area is therefore yours to set by lease and written rules, and if the lease is silent you will be arguing about alterations, common-area damage and exclusive use after the fact with nothing to point to. The clause to use is in the library's Wyoming electric vehicle charging row; the points specific to a shared area are these.

ASSIGN THE SPACE IN WRITING, OR NOTHING ELSE WORKS. Wyoming gives a tenant no claim to any particular space, so you may assign, reassign or reserve spaces, and may charge for a reserved space, purely as a matter of contract. Do it in writing in the lease or in a parking addendum, name the space, and say expressly that the assignment may be changed on written notice and that the tenant's charging equipment confers no permanent right to the space. Otherwise a tenant who pays to install at a shared stall will argue for a right to keep it.

SAY WHO OWNS AND WHO PAYS. Put in the lease, for the specific stall: who paid for the installation; whether the equipment stays or is removed at the end of the tenancy; who repairs it; who pays if it damages the building, the lot or another tenant's vehicle; and whether any other tenant may use it. A charger installed by tenant A at a stall later assigned to tenant B is the case that goes wrong most often - decide in advance whether it stays as your equipment or comes out.

THE REAL WYOMING RISK IS BILLING FOR THE POWER, AND FOR A SHARED CHARGER THE ANSWER IS BETTER THAN LANDLORDS EXPECT. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H) opens "None of the provisions of this chapter shall apply to" and then lists ten separate non-applications. Subparagraph (H)(VI) exempts furnishing electricity for the use of your tenants and not for sale to others, and then takes it back for landlords: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." That clawback is written as "Such exemptions" and sits inside (VI), so by its terms it reaches only (VI). Subparagraphs (VIII) and (IX) restore the exemption for water, and subparagraph (H)(X) does the same for this topic: "The retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under this title." A landlord is not otherwise regulated under Title 37, so the better reading is that selling power from a shared EV charger - including metered, per-kilowatt-hour sales - falls inside (H)(X) and does not make you a public utility. Note the limit in (H)'s own words: it disapplies "this chapter," meaning chapter 1 of Title 37, which is where the definition of public utility lives. That reading has not been tested in any Wyoming decision this review covers, so if you want certainty rather than the better argument, fold charging into rent or charge a flat monthly amount for stall access and say in the lease that you are not selling electricity by the kilowatt hour. Do not try to extend this to ordinary tenant submetering of household electricity: (H)(X) is confined to charging electric vehicles, and (VIII) and (IX) are confined to water, so metered household electricity sales to tenants remain caught by the (VI) clawback.

The tax is separate and is not avoided by any of this. Wyoming's alternative fuels license tax reaches electricity sold or dispensed for electric vehicles under Wyo. Stat. §§ 39-17-303 and 39-17-304, as reworked by 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 33 (HB0145) effective July 1, 2026, at $.035 per kilowatt hour under § 39-17-304(a)(iv). A shared charger that several tenants pay to use is exactly the arrangement that looks like dispensing for a fee. Price and register accordingly, and see the library's Wyoming electric vehicle charging rows for the detail.

Two other Wyoming points. A disabled tenant's request about a shared lot runs through the state fair housing act, not any EV statute: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation in rules and policies, and § 40-26-107(c)(i) requires you to permit a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense, with an express rental carve-out allowing you to condition it on restoration "when it is reasonable to do so." And a local ordinance, building code or EV-ready parking requirement may apply to your property; ordinances are outside this review and are not resolved here.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: No hardship stay of eviction, and every delay runs on a bond
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant no hardship stay of eviction. There is no provision letting a circuit court pause a writ of restitution because immediate removal would be a hardship on the tenant or the tenant's family, no stay for a tenant who cannot find other housing, no stay while a rental-assistance application is pending, and no winter or cold-weather stay. The words "substantial hardship" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and none of the seven "hardship" references in Title 1 is in the forcible entry and detainer article. Every delay Wyoming does allow is bought with a bond.

BEFORE JUDGMENT. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1007, no continuance may be granted the defendant for longer than two days unless the tenant gives a bond to you, with good and sufficient surety approved by the circuit court, conditioned for payment of the rent that may accrue and costs if judgment goes against the tenant. Two days is the free allowance; beyond that the tenant is securing your accruing rent or is not getting the continuance. If the tenant asks for more time, say on the record that § 1-21-1007 requires the bond and ask the court to set it.

AFTER JUDGMENT. Section 1-21-1012 says that when a judgment of restitution is entered, the court shall issue a writ of restitution at the request of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's agent or attorney - so ask for it, because it is not automatic. Under § 1-21-1013, unless the defendant takes an appeal, the officer shall execute the writ within two days after receiving it, Sundays excepted, by restoring you to possession, and shall levy and collect the execution for rent and costs. There is no discretion in that sentence for the officer and no hardship exception written into it.

ON APPEAL. Section 1-21-1014(b) is the only true stay in the article, and it is conditional: an appeal by the defendant does NOT stay proceedings on the judgment unless, within forty-eight hours after judgment, Sundays excepted, the appellant executes and files a bond to you with two or more sufficient sureties approved by the court, conditioned to pay all costs accrued or accruing and all damages you may sustain from the wrongful detention of the premises during the appeal. Only upon taking the appeal AND filing that bond are further proceedings stayed. The appellate court may require a new, larger bond if needed to secure the parties' rights, so ask for one if the first is thin. On top of that bond, § 1-21-1015(a) requires the appellant to deposit with the court the amount of rent specified in the judgment, and says in terms that unless the deposit is made the appeal is not perfected and proceedings on the judgment shall be had accordingly. Section 1-21-1015(b) then requires the appellant to keep depositing rent with the clerk of the appellate court as it comes due, and if the appellant misses any deposit, on your motion and proof the appellate court SHALL affirm the judgment with costs. That is a mandatory affirmance, and it is your most useful lever during an appeal: calendar every rent due date and move the moment one is missed. Section 1-21-1014(a) also tells the officer that if the premises have already been restored to you when a stay notice arrives, he must put the tenant back in possession - so a bond filed inside the 48 hours can undo a completed writ.

Do not confuse any of this with Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-17-201 et seq., the general stay-of-execution article. Section 1-17-201(a) applies to a judgment rendered in a DISTRICT court for the recovery of money or the sale of property, and even there the stay comes through the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure on a supersedeas bond. It is not a possession remedy and it is not a hardship provision.

THE ONE REAL EXCEPTION IS MILITARY. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act does allow a court to stay a residential eviction, and Wyoming extends those protections by statute: Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(a) gives Wyoming National Guard members ordered to active state service for more than thirty consecutive days all the protections the SCRA affords members of the armed forces. Section 19-11-122(b) makes a knowing violation of those protections a misdemeanor punishable by a fine up to $1,000, and § 19-11-122(c) lets them be raised as a claim or as a defence, with § 19-11-122(d) requiring courts to give scheduling preference on a servicemember's motion with certification of service. Screen for military status before you file and comply with the federal affidavit requirement.

A note on the Article 14 procedure: Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 to 1-21-1403 allow a sworn complaint to law enforcement and immediate removal of an unauthorized occupant, but § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement, so it is never a shortcut around a tenant's eviction, and § 1-21-1403(c) exposes an owner who misuses it to triple the fair market value of renting plus fees.

Finally, because Wyoming's timetable is this tight, the practical risk is procedural rather than substantive. Get the § 1-21-1003 three-day notice to quit right, and remember that § 1-21-1202(d)'s power to modify duties by signed written agreement is confined by its own words to Article 12 and is not authority to shorten or waive anything in the Article 10 eviction procedure.

title: No Ban on Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute voiding a lease clause that imposes a penalty on the tenant because you served an eviction notice or filed an eviction case. There is no list of prohibited lease terms anywhere in Wyoming’s landlord-tenant law, no “void and unenforceable” provision aimed at rental agreements, and no statutory eviction fee, filing-fee pass-through or liquidated-damages cap for residential leases. Wyoming law runs the other way: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says any duty or obligation in the landlord-tenant article “may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties,” and Article 12 contains no anti-waiver section. The only non-waivable provision in the field is the Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304, which sits in a different article.

That freedom is real but it is not unlimited, and three statutory limits decide what you can actually collect.

First, what a court will award you in the eviction case itself is fixed by statute, not by your lease. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(a), if the court finds your complaint true it renders judgment for restitution of the premises and costs — costs only. Attorney’s fees appear in just one place: § 1-21-1008(b), and only “if the case is one based on failure to pay rent,” where the court renders judgment for the rent found due “together with costs and attorney’s fees as provided by the lease.” Read that limit carefully. In a holdover or lease-breach case that is not about unpaid rent, subsection (b) does not apply and § 1-21-1008(a) gives you costs and nothing more, even if your lease promises fees. If you want fees in a non-rent eviction you must pursue them as a separate contract claim.

Second, a penalty you cannot collect in the eviction case you may still try to deduct from the deposit, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct damages, unpaid rent and “other costs provided by any contract.” That phrase is broad: a charge your lease creates is generally deductible. But the deposit is the ceiling, and § 1-21-1208 still requires you to account for it, so a large penalty clause will usually drive you into court anyway.

Third, the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential landlords and is the real outer boundary. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines “merchandise” to include property “real, personal or mixed,” and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110. Section 40-12-105(a) is gated on “knowingly,” and (a)(viii) plus the (a)(xv) catch-all can reach lease wording and advertising. A clause that charges the tenant a flat sum simply for receiving a notice, or that recovers more than your real loss, is the kind of term that invites a WCPA claim; § 40-12-109 requires the consumer to give you pre-suit notice and a cure period, and § 40-12-111 exposes you to restitution including reasonable attorney fees, with up to $15,000 per violation payable to the Attorney General.

Practical course. Draft the charge as a genuine pre-estimate of an actual cost — your filing fee, service fee, actual attorney time, the cost of reletting — itemized and tied to a real expense, and state that it is in addition to rent accrued. Do not write a flat “eviction fee” or a penalty that bites the moment a notice is served. Wyoming courts apply the ordinary common-law rule that a contract term operating as a penalty rather than a reasonable estimate of damages is unenforceable; that doctrine comes from case law, which is not in this statutory corpus, so treat the line as a litigation risk rather than a bright statutory rule. Note also that § 1-21-1202(d)’s modification power does not reach Article 10 — its words are “this article” and it sits in Article 12 — so no lease clause can shorten or waive the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 or any other part of the eviction procedure.

title: How a Wyoming Eviction Runs
bodyText:
Wyoming evictions are forcible entry and detainer (FED) actions under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, filed in the circuit court for the judicial district. Section 1-21-1001 lets the court inquire against a person who entered unlawfully and holds by force, or who entered lawfully and then holds unlawfully, and requires the judge to order restitution to the complaining party. Note that the chapter runs both ways: a tenant you lock out can use it against you, and taking or keeping possession by force is separately a crime under Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-306. There is no self-help eviction in Wyoming.

Grounds. Section 1-21-1002(a) lists them. For a landlord the live ones are (a)(i) — a tenant holding over after the term, or a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due — and (a)(vi), a renter violating the duties in § 1-21-1204 (clean and safe condition, waste disposal, plumbing fixtures, reasonable use of facilities, occupancy only as designed and not above the number specified in the rental agreement without written permission, being current on all payments, complying with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, removing property and cleaning at the end) or the prohibitions in § 1-21-1205 (intentional or negligent damage, interfering with another's peaceful enjoyment, unreasonably denying the owner access for repairs, inspection or showings). Section 1-21-1002(b) says the section does not limit §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1210. Wyoming has no for-cause or just-cause eviction protection of any kind, no matter how long the tenancy has run, and no landlord-retaliation statute — the word 'retaliat' does not appear anywhere in Title 1.

Keep two three-day periods apart. The § 1-21-1002(a)(i) three days is a grace period: rent must be unpaid for three days after it is due before a nonpayment ground even exists. The § 1-21-1003 three days is a separate pre-suit notice: you must notify the adverse party to leave the premises, served at least three days before you commence the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found. They stack. Section 1-21-1003 is a notice to quit, not a pay-or-quit cure notice — no Wyoming statute gives the tenant a right to cure by paying — but nothing stops you from offering a cure, and a lease that promises one binds you. A criminal trespass warning does not substitute: Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(c) does not supersede § 1-21-1003 as to the notice to quit.

The case. Under § 1-21-1004 the summons states the cause of complaint and the time and place of trial, is served and returned as in other cases, and service must be not less than three nor more than twelve days before the trial date the judge sets. The same section says the defendant 'shall not be required to file a written answer to the complaint as a condition of being allowed to participate fully in the trial' — expect a tenant to appear and contest with no pleading on file. If the tenant does not appear, § 1-21-1005 does not hand you a default: the court tries the action as though he were present, you must file the complaint you rely on, and the complaint 'must be sustained by proof or the action dismissed'. Bring your lease, ledger, notice and proof of service. Section 1-21-1006 lets a defendant who appears file an answer and lets either party amend. Section 1-21-1007 is your protection against delay: no continuance longer than two days unless the defendant gives a bond with surety approved by the court for rent that may accrue and costs.

Judgment. Section 1-21-1008(a) gives a general judgment for restitution of the premises and costs if the complaint is true, judgment against you for costs if it is not, and restitution of part only where the complaint is true in part. In a nonpayment case § 1-21-1008(b) requires the court to find the amount of rent due at the hearing and the terms of the parties' agreement on amount and timing, and to render judgment for the rent found due 'together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease', with execution issued separately from the writ of restitution. That phrase is the whole of your fee recovery: Wyoming has no attorney-fee shifting in Article 10 or Article 12, so if your lease does not provide for fees you will not get them. Either party may demand a jury (§§ 1-21-1009, 1-21-1010), and either may take exceptions on law or evidence (§ 1-21-1011).

Turnover. On your request, your agent's or your attorney's, the court issues a writ of restitution (§ 1-21-1012). Under § 1-21-1013, unless the defendant appeals, the officer must execute it within two days after receiving it, Sundays excepted, by restoring you to possession, and must levy and collect the execution for rent and costs. An appeal does not stay anything unless, within forty-eight hours after judgment, Sundays excepted, the tenant files a bond with two or more sufficient sureties approved by the court covering costs and your damages from wrongful detention during the appeal (§ 1-21-1014(b)); if the officer is told of a stay after you are already back in, § 1-21-1014(a) requires him to put the tenant back in possession. On top of that bond, § 1-21-1015(a) requires the tenant to deposit the rent specified in the judgment or the appeal is not perfected, and § 1-21-1015(b) requires further deposits as rent comes due — if the tenant misses one, the appellate court 'shall affirm the judgment appealed from with costs' on your motion and proof. Section 1-21-1016 preserves a separate ejectment action.

Representing yourself. Section 1-21-1017(a) lets a business entity appear in an FED case without a lawyer, but only if an owner, shareholder, member or partner appears (not an employee and not a property manager), the entity owns a majority interest in the property, and written notice signed by every owner, shareholder, member or partner goes to the court and all parties. Section 1-21-1017(c) switches this off entirely if the entity seeks a judgment above the small-claims amount in § 1-21-201, which is $6,000 — so a large rent claim means hiring counsel or splitting the claim.

What Wyoming does not have. There is no tenant counterclaim or pay-into-court provision for defending the possession action itself; 'counterclaim' and 'escrow' each return zero hits within Article 10. (Wyoming's rent-into-court mechanisms are the § 1-21-1007 continuance bond and the § 1-21-1015 appeal deposits, both of which run in your favor.) There is no statute reserving eviction procedure to the legislature or barring local or judicial modification, no rule against courts requiring a particular pleading form beyond § 1-21-1004's no-written-answer sentence, no restriction on process servers recording service or execution, no federal-shutdown continuance for federal employees or contractors, and no special wage-attachment rule or percentage cap for a residential-lease judgment — ordinary post-judgment garnishment under § 1-15-408 applies. Finally, do not reach for Article 14 (§§ 1-21-1401 to 1-21-1403, removal of unauthorized occupants by sworn complaint to law enforcement). It is real and it works, but § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement, and § 1-21-1403(c) exposes an owner or authorized agent who misuses it to triple fair-market rent plus fees. Against a tenant, the FED action is the only route.

title: Wyoming Has No Eviction Record Sealing or Expungement
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute that seals, expunges, masks or ages off an eviction record, and so there is also nothing for you to object to. A tenant cannot petition to seal a forcible entry and detainer case, a dismissed or settled FED case is not automatically expunged, there is no seven-year or other removal deadline for court indexes, and nothing requires you to agree to a sealing as part of a settlement. A Wyoming FED judgment is an ordinary civil judgment and the file stays a public court record. Wyoming's one expungement scheme is criminal only: Article 14 of Title 7 chapter 13, Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-13-1401 et seq., headed 'Expungement of Criminal Records', covering records of arrest, dismissal of charges and disposition. It has no civil counterpart. The only 'expunge' word anywhere in Title 1 is at Wyo. Stat. § 1-40-203(b)(xi), a crime victim's right to be notified that an offender has petitioned to expunge a conviction, and the only sealing provision in Title 1 is the adoption file under Wyo. Stat. § 1-22-104(d). Neither touches an eviction. Wyoming law in fact assumes tenant screening runs on public court records and leaves it alone. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-505(d)(iv) exempts from the security-freeze regime a consumer reporting agency's database of files consisting entirely of public records and used solely for criminal record information, tenant screening, employment screening or fraud detection, and (d)(v) repeats the exemption for a file of adverse information used for tenant screening or any purpose permitted by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681b. So a frozen credit file does not block a Wyoming tenant-screening pull. What this means in practice is simple. You may report, rely on and keep an eviction record indefinitely as far as Wyoming law is concerned, and you need not treat a tenant's request to seal as anything but a negotiating point. Three real limits sit outside this library and you should respect them. First, FEDERAL: the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681c, bars a consumer reporting agency from reporting most civil judgments and adverse items older than seven years, and 15 U.S.C. § 1681m imposes adverse-action notice duties on you when you decline an applicant on a screening report — those duties apply in Wyoming and are the real constraint here. Second, a Wyoming court retains its own inherent and rule-based power to restrict access to a file; the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure and the Wyoming Supreme Court's public-access rules are court rules and are not in this library, so if a tenant moves to seal, read the applicable rule rather than assuming no mechanism exists. Third, if you agree in a settlement to seal, dismiss or not report, perform it — a knowing misrepresentation about a tenant's record can reach the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a), which covers real property through the § 40-12-102(a)(vi) definition of merchandise. The cautious course for a landlord who wants the case to disappear from the tenant's record as part of a deal is a stipulated dismissal before judgment, which leaves no judgment to report, rather than a promise to seal a file you do not control.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute letting a lease name a person to accept eviction papers for the tenant, and no address-confidentiality program that would redirect service to the Secretary of State. The phrases "address confidentiality" and "substitute address" do not appear anywhere in Wyoming law, and "agent for service of process" appears 47 times without once reaching landlord-tenant.

What Wyoming does fix is the two separate steps before and at filing, and you must get both right.

Step one, the notice to quit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires the party who wants to bring a forcible entry and detainer action to notify the adverse party to leave the premises, served at least three (3) days before commencing the action, "by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found." Read the structure: handing it to the defendant is the first method; leaving it at the usual place of abode or business is conditional on the defendant not being found. There is no agent option here, no mail option and no posting option in the statute. A lease clause naming someone to take the notice to quit would be adding a method the statute does not give, so do not rely on one. Serve the tenant, and if you cannot find the tenant, leave the copy at the unit or at the tenant's workplace and record what you did, when and where.

Step two, the summons. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1004 says the summons shall state the cause of the complaint, the time and place of trial, and "shall be served and returned as in other cases", with service not less than three (3) nor more than twelve (12) days before the trial day the judge sets. "As in other cases" sends you out of the statute and into the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, which are court rules and are not part of this library's source material. We have not read them, so we cannot tell you whether a person the tenant names in the lease would qualify as an agent authorised to receive service under those rules. That is the honest answer, and it is why we do not offer a named-service-party clause for Wyoming.

The cautious course, which costs nothing. If you want a named-service-party clause, treat it as a belt-and-braces addition and never as a substitute: always serve the tenant by the statutory route as well, and let the named person be an extra copy. A default judgment taken on a defective service is worth less than no judgment, because § 1-21-1005 lets the court try the action as though the defendant were present only "in accordance with a properly served summons", and the complaint must still be sustained by proof or the action is dismissed. Note also that § 1-21-1006 makes a written answer optional and § 1-21-1004's last sentence says the defendant cannot be required to file one as a condition of participating fully at trial — so do not expect a non-answering tenant to be out of the case.

The mirror-image point, in your favour. Service running the other way IS addressed. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) provides that for purposes of notice and other communication required or allowed under Article 12, "owner" includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager — unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement. Two things follow. A tenant's Article 12 notice handed to your property manager is good notice to you, so your manager must know to pass it on the same day. And you as owner cannot switch that off by yourself: the statute puts the specifying in the hands of the agent or manager, in writing, in the rental agreement. If you want notices to come to you directly, have the managing agent say so in the lease itself.

What fills the gap. Nothing in a lease can change the § 1-21-1003 method or the § 1-21-1004 timing. What you can do by lease is make the tenant easy to find: require a current telephone number, a work address and an emergency contact, require written notice of any change, and keep the record. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) separately puts a duty on the renter to notify you within thirty (30) days of termination where payment and notice may be made or mailed, which is useful after the tenancy but not during it.

title: Limiting Your Liability in a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute bans exculpatory clauses in a residential lease. Wyoming has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and has no provision like the ones in most states voiding a lease term that relieves the landlord of liability or makes the tenant indemnify the landlord. The Residential Rental Property Act (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) contains no list of prohibited lease terms at all. So the question is not whether a statute forbids your clause; it is whether a Wyoming court will enforce it, and that is governed by common law your lease has to be drafted to survive.

Start with what the statute already gives you for free, because these are the two pieces of exculpation you do not have to argue for. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) provides that "[t]he owner is not liable under this article for claims for mental suffering or anguish" - the section's own heading ends with the words "liability limited." Note the scope precisely: it bars mental-suffering damages on claims brought under the article, not on an independent tort claim such as negligence causing personal injury. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210(c) provides that "[t]he owner is not responsible for any loss to the renter resulting from storage" of personal property left behind after termination, which pairs with your right under § 1-21-1210(b) to reasonable or actual storage costs plus removal, payable before the renter takes the goods back. Restate both in the lease. Restating them changes nothing legally but it tells the tenant and their lawyer where they stand before anyone files.

Next, Wyoming gives you a tool most states do not. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." That is a reallocation power, not a liability shield, and the distinction matters when you draft. Shifting a duty - for example, making the tenant responsible for maintaining a specific appliance - is squarely within § 1-21-1202(d) and is the stronger move. Saying you are not liable for the consequences of failing to perform a duty you still hold is a classic exculpatory clause and gets the harder common-law treatment. Where you can accomplish the goal by assigning the duty under § 1-21-1202(d), do that instead, and do it the way the subsection requires: name the duty and the statute, say explicitly who now carries it, put it in writing, and get both signatures. A general "as-is" recital or a waiver buried in boilerplate is not an explicit modification.

Now the limits, which are real even though no statute states them. Wyoming courts, like courts everywhere, read a clause exculpating a party from its own negligence strictly and against the drafter, and will not find such an intent unless the language is clear and unmistakable. Draft accordingly: say "negligence" in so many words rather than relying on a general "any and all claims" formula, and set the clause out conspicuously rather than burying it. Do not attempt to exculpate yourself from gross negligence, recklessness, or willful or wanton misconduct, and do not attempt to exculpate yourself from statutory violations; a court that is going to strike anything will strike that first, and an overbroad clause risks taking the enforceable part down with it. Add a severability clause so it does not. Be especially careful about exculpating yourself from the habitability duties in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1202(a) and 1-21-1203(a). § 1-21-1202(d) is on its face broad enough to let the parties modify them, but a clause that leaves nobody responsible for a safe and sanitary dwelling is the one most likely to be refused, and the renter's judicial remedy in § 1-21-1206(c) - costs, damages, and affirmative relief including an order to repair or a declaration terminating the agreement - exists independently of your clause.

Two hard boundaries. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 makes the Wyoming Safe Homes Act unwaivable: "The provisions of this act shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant." Nothing in your liability or indemnity language may touch the domestic-abuse and sexual-violence provisions of Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304. Second, federal law is untouched by any of this - fair housing and the lead-based paint rules in particular - and a municipal or county ordinance could impose its own limits, which this review flags but does not resolve.

On tenant indemnity running the other way, Wyoming has no anti-indemnity statute reaching residential leases, so an indemnity for claims arising from the tenant's own use of the premises is on ordinary contract footing and is the safer of the two devices. Keep it to the tenant's own acts and omissions and those of the tenant's household and guests, and do not write it so it sweeps in claims caused by your own conduct, which converts it back into an exculpatory clause with all the same problems. Finally, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) is a reminder that not every risk can be contracted away: it gives the renter the full deposit and court costs when the owner unreasonably fails to comply with the deposit-accounting rules, and a lease term disclaiming that exposure would be a modification of an article duty that a court is unlikely to treat as the kind of bargained exchange § 1-21-1202(d) contemplates.

title: No Expedited Eviction Track for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Wyoming has no fast-track eviction for drug activity, violent crime or other criminal conduct. There is no criminal-activity ground, no shortened notice, no accelerated hearing window and no no-cure provision anywhere in the statutes. The words "criminal activity" never appear in the landlord-tenant statutes at all. Every eviction, whatever the reason, runs on the one forcible entry and detainer track in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017. That track is already quick. You must first serve a notice to quit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003, at least three days before you file, by leaving a written copy with the tenant or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a) lists the cases in which the action may be had, and criminal conduct reaches the list only indirectly, through paragraph (a)(vi): against renters in violation of any terms imposed under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205. That matters, because § 1-21-1205(a)(i) forbids a renter to intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit or knowingly permit anyone to do so, and § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) forbids interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property. Most on-premises criminal conduct that actually harms you or your other tenants will breach one of those, and § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) separately requires the renter to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, so a well-drafted crime-free lease clause gives you a second route in. After filing, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1004 requires service not less than three nor more than twelve days before the trial date the judge sets, and the tenant need not file a written answer to participate. In other words, Wyoming's single track can get you to trial inside two weeks - but you get there the same way for a meth lab as for unpaid rent, and you cannot shorten the three-day notice. Three things to keep in mind. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) gives a separate nonpayment ground after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due, so if the tenant is also behind, plead both. Second, under the Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(c), you may not terminate a tenancy based solely on a tenant's, applicant's or household member's status as a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence, though that subsection expressly does not prohibit adverse housing decisions based on other lawful factors within your knowledge - so evict the perpetrator's conduct, document the lawful ground, and do not evict the victim for being the victim; and § 1-21-1304 says that act cannot be waived or modified in any lease. Third, do not confuse the criminal-activity question with Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, the law-enforcement removal remedy for unauthorized occupants: § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) makes it available only where the person is NOT a current or former tenant under any written or oral agreement, so it is a squatter remedy and never a shortcut around an eviction. Separately, be aware that a structure maintained, used, owned or leased for lewdness, assignation, prostitution, gambling, or the manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of intoxicating liquor or a controlled substance in violation of law is a statutory nuisance under Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-201, and the structure, the ground it sits on and its contents are declared a nuisance to be enjoined and abated - an action a county attorney or a citizen can bring against your property. That is a reason to act promptly on a drug tenancy, not a tool you can use to evict faster.

title: No Expedited Deposit Return Procedure in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no procedure letting a tenant ask you to settle up the deposit faster than the statute requires, and no statute authorizing you to charge an administrative, expediting or processing fee for doing so. The deadlines in Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1208 are outer limits, not minimums, so you are always free to return the balance sooner — but you may not bill the tenant for the privilege. Here is the clock you are actually on. On termination of the rental agreement, you may apply the deposit to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy, and other costs provided by the contract. The balance, together with any prepaid rent and a written itemization of every deduction with the reasons for it, must be delivered or mailed to the tenant, without interest, within 30 days after termination or within 15 days after you receive the tenant's new mailing address, whichever is later — and if there is damage to the unit, that period is extended by another 30 days (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1208(a)). The tenant has a duty too: within 30 days of termination the tenant must tell you or your designated agent where payment and notice may be made or mailed. A utilities deposit runs on a different and faster clock, but only if you held it separately and identified it as a utilities deposit: you refund it within 10 days of a satisfactory showing that the tenant paid all utility charges; absent that showing within 45 days of termination, you must within the next 15 days apply it to the tenant's outstanding utility debt, and any refund then due is paid within 7 days after you apply it, or within 15 days after you receive the new mailing address, whichever is later (§ 1-21-1208(b)). Two other termination routes carry their own deposit timing: if a court terminates the rental agreement on the tenant's habitability claim, the tenant is entitled to the balance of rent and the deposit within 30 days of the date the agreement is ordered terminated (§ 1-21-1206(d)); and if you terminate because repairs would cost more than is reasonable, the rent is prorated to the day the tenant vacates and the balance is refunded along with any deposit due under § 1-21-1208 (§ 1-21-1203(d)). Get this wrong and the price is steep: if you unreasonably fail to comply with subsection (a) or (b), the tenant may recover the full deposit plus court costs (§ 1-21-1208(c)) — not just the wrongly withheld part. The cautious course: diary the 30-day and 15-day dates the moment the tenancy ends, send the itemization and balance early if you can, and do not deduct any fee for processing or for returning the deposit ahead of schedule.

title: No Duty to Report an Extended Absence
bodyText:
Wyoming is not a URLTA state and has nothing like the familiar seven-day absence-notice rule. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 is the complete list of a renter's statutory duties -- keep the unit clean and safe, dispose of garbage, maintain plumbing fixtures, use the electrical, plumbing, sanitary and heating facilities reasonably, occupy the unit as designed and not exceed the occupancy specified in the rental agreement, stay current on payments, comply with the rental agreement, and remove property and clean at the end. Nothing in those eight paragraphs requires the tenant to tell you they will be away, and no other Wyoming statute does either. There is also no statutory damages remedy for failing to give such notice, so even where the lease requires the notice your recovery is ordinary contract damages, not a statutory penalty.

This matters more in Wyoming than it looks, because of how abandonment works here. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(v) makes "abandonment of the leased premises by the renter prior to expiration of the rental period" one of the ways a rental agreement terminates -- but no Wyoming statute defines abandonment, sets a number of days of absence that amounts to it, or tells you how to establish it. That is a gap you fill in the lease or you live with. The consequences of getting it wrong run in both directions. If you treat an absent tenant as having abandoned when they have not, you have taken possession of an occupied unit without the summary-eviction process in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017 and without a court order, and you have likely disposed of property you had no right to touch. If you wait too long on a genuinely abandoned unit, you carry the vacancy and the damage.

Once the agreement has in fact terminated and you have regained lawful possession, § 1-21-1210 gives you a procedure for what is left behind: you may immediately dispose of trash and anything you reasonably believe hazardous, perishable or valueless, anything remaining is presumed valueless and abandoned, and for valuable property you serve written notice describing it and stating it will be disposed of after seven days, with a further fifteen days to collect if the renter responds in writing. You are entitled to storage costs. But § 1-21-1210 operates "following termination of the rental agreement" -- it is not a tool for deciding whether a long absence terminated anything.

Practical course: put an absence-notice clause in the lease and tie it to an express definition of abandonment, so that absence plus unpaid rent plus some objective indicator is what triggers your rights, not absence alone. Keep the trigger conservative. Where the facts are genuinely ambiguous, serve the statutory notice and use the forcible entry and detainer process rather than self-help -- a wrong call on abandonment is the more expensive error. If your concern is specifically a winter vacancy and frozen pipes, see the cold-weather vacate notice clause, which handles that case directly.

title: Wyoming Fair Housing Act Protected Classes and Duties
bodyText:
Wyoming has its own fair housing statute — the Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145. It sits in Title 40 (Trade and Commerce), not in the landlord-tenant article in Title 1, which is why landlords often believe Wyoming has no state housing discrimination law. It does, and it has teeth.

The protected classes in the substantive provisions are race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, and national origin — the same seven as the federal Fair Housing Act, with no additions. Wyoming adds no class for age, marital status, source of income, sexual orientation, gender identity, ancestry or veteran status in §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109. The Act goes out of its way on two of those: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-102(a)(v) says "disability" "does not apply to an individual because of an individual's sexual orientation or because that individual is a transvestite," and excludes current illegal drug use or addiction.

There is one important exception, and it is easy to miss. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i) — the intimidation-or-interference offense — lists a LONGER set of classes than the rest of the Act: "race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin or status with respect to marriage or public assistance." So age, marital status and public-assistance status (effectively a source-of-income class) are protected, but only against intentional intimidation or interference "by force or threat of force," not against ordinary refusal-to-rent discrimination. § 40-26-144(b) adds, with no force requirement, that it is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone exercising or enjoying a right under the chapter, or for having aided or encouraged someone else to. § 40-26-144(c) makes an offense under (a) or (b) a misdemeanor. Treat harassment of a voucher holder, an older tenant or an unmarried couple as legally dangerous even though you may generally decline to rent to them.

What the Act forbids, in its own sections:
• § 40-26-103(a): refusing to sell or rent after a bona fide offer, refusing to negotiate, or in any other manner making unavailable or denying a dwelling because of a protected class.
• § 40-26-103(b): discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or in providing services or facilities in connection with it. This is the subsection that reaches different rent, different deposits, different rules, or unequal maintenance.
• § 40-26-104: making, printing or publishing — or causing — any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates any preference, limitation or discrimination, or the intention to make one. This is a separate, strict duty: it is violated by the words, with no need for anyone to be turned away.
• § 40-26-105: telling someone a dwelling is not available for inspection when it is.
• § 40-26-106: blockbusting — inducing someone for profit to sell or rent by representations about who is moving into the neighborhood.
• § 40-26-108 and § 40-26-109: discrimination in residential real-estate-related transactions (including brokering and appraising) and in access to multiple-listing services and brokers' organizations.

Disability carries extra duties under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107. You may not discriminate because of a disability of the applicant, of anyone who will live in the dwelling, or of anyone associated with them — § 40-26-107(a)(i)-(iii) and (b)(i)-(iii). § 40-26-107(c)(i) makes it discrimination to refuse to permit a reasonable modification of the premises at the tenant's expense, though in a rental "the landlord may condition, when it is reasonable to do so, permission for a modification on the renter agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted." § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services where necessary to give equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. § 40-26-107(c)(iii) imposes the familiar design-and-construct standards on "covered multifamily dwellings," defined in § 40-26-107(g) as buildings of four (4) or more units with an elevator, plus ground-floor units in other buildings of four (4) or more units; § 40-26-107(e) exempts a building first occupied on or before March 13, 1991, and § 40-26-107(d) makes compliance with the ANSI accessibility standard as it existed on July 1, 2015 sufficient.

Two carve-outs inside the duties themselves. § 40-26-103(c): the Act does not prohibit discrimination because the individual has been convicted, under federal or any state law, of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance — note the narrowness, it is manufacture or distribution, not possession and not any other crime. § 40-26-107(f): nothing requires you to rent to an individual whose tenancy would be a direct threat to the health or safety of others or would result in substantial physical damage to others' property. And § 40-26-113(a) says the chapter does not affect a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants, or a restriction relating to health or safety standards.

Practical course: use the same written screening criteria for every applicant, keep the advertising neutral in every medium, document reasonable-accommodation and reasonable-modification requests and your response in writing, and remember that § 40-26-113(b) preserves every other nondiscrimination requirement in state or federal law — the federal Fair Housing Act, Section 504, the ADA for public areas, and any city ordinance apply on top of this chapter, not instead of it. Wyoming's assistance-animal rule lives separately at Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c).

title: Wyoming Fair Housing Act Exemptions and Enforcement
bodyText:
The Wyoming Fair Housing Act's exemptions are narrow, conditional, and — critically — they do not all cover the advertising ban. Read which sections each exemption names.

The small-owner exemption, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(a), lifts "W.S. 40-26-103 through 40-26-109" for the sale or rental of a single family house by its owner, but only if every condition holds: the owner owns no more than three (3) single family houses at one time (and holds no interest in, and has nothing reserved on their behalf from, the proceeds of more than three); the house is rented without using the services or facilities of a licensed real estate broker or agent or of anyone in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or their employee or agent; and without "the publication, posting or mailing of a notice, statement or advertisement prohibited by W.S. 40-26-104." The exemption applies to only one (1) sale or rental in a twenty-four (24) month period if the owner was not the most recent resident of the house. So although the exemption's range nominally includes § 40-26-104, running a discriminatory ad destroys the exemption and leaves you exposed on every section. The advertising ban survives in substance. The subsection also defines who is "in the business": anyone who in the preceding twelve (12) months participated as principal in three (3) or more dwelling sales or rentals, or as agent in two (2) or more (other than selling their own home), or who owns any dwelling designed, intended for, or occupied by five (5) or more families. Owning one five-plex therefore strips the exemption from all of your single-family houses.

The owner-occupied exemption, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(b), is the clearer answer to the advertising question. It lifts "W.S. 40-26-103 and 40-26-105 through 40-26-109" for the rental of rooms or units in a dwelling of not more than four (4) families living independently, if the owner maintains and occupies one of them as the owner's residence. The list deliberately skips § 40-26-104. The advertising ban therefore applies in full to an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or fourplex: you may be permitted to choose your housemate, but you may not say so in the ad. Note that Wyoming's version covers up to four families, broader than the two-family "Mrs. Murphy" exemption some states use.

Two other exemptions. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-111(a) lets a religious organization, or a nonprofit it operates or controls, limit or prefer occupancy of dwellings it owns or operates for other than a commercial purpose to people of the same religion, unless religious membership is itself restricted by race, color or national origin; § 40-26-111(b) does the same for a genuine private club not open to the public that provides lodging incidental to its primary purpose. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-112(a) exempts housing for the elderly from the chapter's familial-status (and age) provisions if HUD or the enforcing authority has determined it is designed and operated for elderly individuals under a federal or state program, or it is intended for and solely occupied by people sixty-two (62) or older, or it is intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person fifty-five (55) or older per unit — and for that last route the enforcing authority's rules must require at least eighty percent (80%) of units occupied by someone fifty-five (55) or older and published policies showing that intent. § 40-26-112(b) protects the status of residents already living there as of July 1, 2015 and of unoccupied units reserved for qualifying occupants.

Enforcement, and why it matters to you as a respondent. A complaint goes to the "enforcing authority," which Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-102(a)(viii) defines as a Wyoming state agency or a Wyoming nonprofit accepted by HUD for that role — so whether one exists at any moment is a factual question; confirm it rather than assuming. A complaint must be filed within one year of the practice occurring or terminating, § 40-26-118(a). You get notice within ten days, § 40-26-118(b), and may file a sworn written answer within ten days of receiving it, § 40-26-119(a) — a short clock, so do not wait.

You have the election right. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-130 gives it to "[a] complainant, a respondent, or an aggrieved person on whose behalf a complaint was filed" — the respondent, meaning you, may move the charge out of the administrative hearing and into a civil action under § 40-26-136. You must elect no later than the twentieth day after service of the charge under § 40-26-126(b), and give notice to the enforcing authority and every other complainant and respondent. If you elect, the attorney general may file suit in district court within thirty days.

The exposure is substantial. In an administrative hearing the enforcing authority may order actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, court costs and injunctive relief, § 40-26-132(a), plus a civil penalty up to $11,000, or $27,000 with one prior discriminatory housing practice in the preceding five years, or $55,000 with two or more in the preceding seven years, § 40-26-132(b); under § 40-26-132(c) the time windows drop away if the same individual did it before. In an aggrieved person's own district-court suit — which may be filed within two years under § 40-26-139(a), with or without any administrative complaint, § 40-26-139(c) — the court may award actual AND punitive damages, attorney's fees, costs and injunctive relief, § 40-26-140. In an attorney general pattern-or-practice case, § 40-26-137(b)(iii) allows a civil penalty up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for a later one. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-143 lets the court or the enforcing authority award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party — which can run your way if you win. One shield: §§ 40-26-133 and 40-26-141 protect a completed lease with a bona fide tenant who had no actual notice of the complaint.

Finally, a drafting glitch to be aware of rather than to rely on: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-102(a)(vi) defines "discriminatory housing practice" as an act prohibited by §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109 "or conduct that is an offense under W.S. 40-26-145" — but § 40-26-145 is the records provision and creates no offense; the offense is at § 40-26-144. Do not assume intimidation falls outside the Act because of the misdirected cross-reference. § 40-26-144(b) independently labels coercion and interference a discriminatory practice, and § 40-26-144(c) makes it a misdemeanor.

title: Family Child Care in a Wyoming Rental
bodyText: Wyoming does not require you to let a tenant run a child care home in your rental. Oregon does (ORS 90.358); Wyoming's residential rental article says nothing about it, and nothing in the state's child care licensing law conditions a license on the landlord's permission — the words 'landlord' and 'lessor' do not appear in Title 14 at all. So the decision is yours, and it belongs in the lease. There is one Wyoming provision you must know about, and it cuts against a landlord who stays silent. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-501 says that 'For residential property subject to a covenant that does not clearly and expressly prohibit child care, the provision of child care in a family day care home is a residential use of property and is a residential purpose,' and defines a family day care home as a private residence or other structure where day care is provided to not more than ten children on a regular basis. The section sits in Title 34, chapter 1, article 5, which is headed 'Covenants' and deals with covenants on real property rather than lease terms, so whether it reaches a lease clause is not settled in the statutes. Assume it does. The consequence is that a generic 'the property will be used as a private residence only' or 'no business may be conducted on the property' clause will not reliably keep a ten-child day care out of your unit, because § 34-1-501 declares that very use residential. The remedy the statute itself supplies is in its own words: clearly and expressly. If you do not want child care in the unit, say so in those terms — name child care, day care and a family day care home, and do not rely on a residential-use-only clause to do the work. If you are willing to allow it, say that too, and attach your conditions. Separately, note that under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) a renter may not increase the number of occupants above the number specified in the rental agreement; children in day care are not occupants, so that paragraph is not a tool here. Operating a day care also engages licensing under Wyo. Stat. §§ 14-4-101 through 14-4-115 unless an exception in Wyo. Stat. § 14-4-102(b) applies — for example day care for fewer than three minors, or occasional care of a neighbor's or friend's child — and local zoning, which this library does not resolve.

title: In Wyoming Your Tenant Can Let Hunters On Unless Your Lease Says Otherwise
bodyText:
