Wyoming does not have the rule some states have, which keeps hunting and fishing on rented farmland with the owner unless the owner grants it in writing. Wyoming runs the other way, and if you rent out a house with acreage you need to know it.

Who can give permission to hunt. Wyo. Stat. § 23-3-305(b) makes it a low misdemeanour for anyone to enter upon, travel through or return across private property to take wildlife, hunt, fish, collect antlers or horns, or trap "without the permission of the owner or person in charge of the property." Note the second half of that phrase. A tenant who occupies the land is a strong candidate for "person in charge," and the statute does not say the permission has to come from the title holder. Nothing in § 23-3-305(b) requires the permission to be in writing either, so a verbal yes from your tenant may be all a hunter has.

The statute is even clearer about night hunting. Section 23-3-305(e) says no person may hunt at night on privately owned or leased lands "except with written permission of the landowner or lessee." The lessee is named as a grantor alongside the owner.

The licensing provisions do the same thing. Wyoming requires a hunter's licence to bear the signature of "the landowner, lessee, or agent of the owner on whose private property he is hunting," or other legitimate proof that permission was granted. Your tenant's signature is as good as yours for that purpose. See Wyo. Stat. § 23-2-401(c) and the parallel licensing provision in Title 23.

What this means for you. If you lease ground and say nothing about hunting, you have effectively handed the hunting to your tenant, and you may find strangers on your land with your tenant's blessing, or your tenant may lease the hunting out and keep the money. There is no Wyoming statute you can point to afterwards that says the right stayed with you. Put a reservation in the lease. Say that you reserve all hunting, fishing, trapping and antler-collection rights, that the tenant may not exercise them and may not grant them to anyone, and that the tenant will not sign a licence or permission slip as landowner, lessee or person in charge. If you do want the tenant to hunt, grant it expressly and describe the limits.

The liability side, which cuts in your favour. Wyoming's Recreation Use statute, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-19-101 through 34-19-107, says an owner of land owes no duty of care to keep the premises safe for recreational entry, and no duty to warn of a dangerous condition, to people who enter for recreational purposes (§ 34-19-102); and that inviting or permitting someone to use the land for recreation without charge does not assure the premises are safe, does not make that person an invitee or licensee, and does not make the owner responsible for injury or damage caused by that person's acts, including to third parties (§ 34-19-103). "Recreational purpose" expressly includes hunting and fishing, and since 2025 also rock climbing (§ 34-19-101(a)(iii), amended by 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws (HB0073)). Importantly, § 34-19-101(a)(ii) defines "owner" to include a tenant, lessee, occupant or person in control of the premises, so your tenant has the same protection you do.

Two things turn that protection off. Under § 34-19-105(a)(ii) the limitation does not apply where the owner charges people who enter for recreational purposes, so if you or your tenant start selling hunting access you lose it. And under § 34-19-105(a)(i) it never covers a willful or malicious failure to guard or warn against a dangerous condition, use, structure or activity. Keep access free, and warn about the real hazards — an open well, a rotten bridge, an unstable stand.

The cautious course. Reserve the hunting in writing, do not let anyone charge for access, mark the genuine hazards, and tell your tenant in the lease that you and the people you authorize will be on the land during specified seasons so that nobody is surprised.

title: No Wyoming Rule on a Fee in Lieu of a Security Deposit
bodyText: Wyoming has no fee-in-lieu-of-deposit statute. Nothing requires you to offer a deposit alternative, nothing requires you to offer a deposit option alongside a fee, nothing bars you from considering which option an applicant picks, no statute mandates disclosures about the two choices, no statute gives the tenant a right to switch from a fee to a deposit mid-tenancy, and no statute requires notice before you report a damage claim to a credit bureau or a collection agency. The phrases "in lieu of a security deposit," "rental security insurance," "deposit waiver," "rent guarantee," "lease insurance" and "credit bureau" return nothing in the Wyoming statutes. There is also no Wyoming equivalent of the Massachusetts problem where a fee is barred until a housing agency writes regulations — Wyoming has no such statute and no such agency mandate, so nothing is on hold. Wyoming also does not cap deposits at all, which removes most of the commercial reason landlords elsewhere reach for a fee-in-lieu product. What does bear on it is the wording of the two Wyoming deposit sections, and you should structure around both. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) attaches to "property or money held as a deposit" — that is the trigger phrase. Money genuinely earned on receipt as a non-refundable fee is not held as a deposit, so the thirty (30) day / fifteen (15) day itemisation cascade in § 1-21-1208(a), the thirty-day extension where there is damage, and the renter's recovery of the full deposit plus court costs under § 1-21-1208(c) should not reach it. But that conclusion depends entirely on how the money is characterised, and no Wyoming case in this corpus settles it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 is the trap: "Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or his designated agent." Two separate duties — a statement in the agreement AND a separate written notice when the money is taken. If you call your fee a deposit anywhere, or if a court treats it as one, § 1-21-1207 applies and you will have missed it. So: if you charge a non-refundable fee instead of a deposit, call it a fee and never a deposit in the lease, the receipt, the ledger or the application; state in the lease that it is non-refundable, is earned when paid, secures nothing, and does not limit the tenant's liability for unpaid rent or for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear; and give the § 1-21-1207 written notice at the time you take it anyway, as cheap insurance against the money being recharacterised. Remember too that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct from a real deposit not only accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and the cost to clean the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy, but also "other costs provided by any contract" — so in Wyoming a well-drafted lease already lets an ordinary deposit do most of the work a fee-in-lieu product is sold to do. Two outside constraints remain. If the fee funds a third party's insurance or surety product, that product and the person selling it are subject to the Wyoming Insurance Code in Title 26, including licensing — check before you act as anyone's producer. And if you report an unpaid damage claim to a consumer reporting agency, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2, governs what you furnish and how you must handle a dispute, because Wyoming imposes no notice duty of its own. The whole of Title 1, Chapter 21, Article 12, including §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208, applies only to a "residential rental unit" as defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and occasionally rented recreational property.

title: Charging for a Service the Tenant Does Not Get
bodyText:
Wyoming's landlord-tenant law does not regulate your fees. There is no statute barring a charge for a service that is not provided, no fee-itemization or mandatory-fee disclosure requirement, no cap on any fee, no junk-fee law, and no residential late-fee statute. The deposit statute runs the other way and is permissive: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to accrued rent, damages beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement, 'and to other costs provided by any contract.' In Wyoming, almost any charge your lease creates is a charge you can collect and deduct. The corollary is the one that catches landlords: a charge your lease does not create is not collectible at all, so if you want a trash, pest, amenity, technology or administrative fee, name it and price it in the lease.

The constraint is not in Title 1. It is the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114, and it reaches residential renting because of how two definitions are written. Section 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines 'merchandise' to include 'any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed' — services and real property both. Section 40-12-102(a)(ii) defines 'consumer transactions' as the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any merchandise to an individual for purposes that are primarily personal, family or household, which is what renting a home to a person is. Assume the Act applies to you, because the downside of assuming otherwise is larger.

What that means in practice. Under § 40-12-105(a) you commit an unlawful deceptive trade practice when, in the course of your business and in connection with a consumer transaction, you 'knowingly' do any of a long list of things. Four of them map directly onto charging for an unprovided service: (a)(i), representing that merchandise has 'accessories or uses it does not have'; (a)(iii), representing that merchandise is of a particular standard, grade, style or model if it is not; (a)(v), representing that merchandise 'has been supplied in accordance with a previous representation, if it has not'; and the catch-all at (a)(xv), 'Engages in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.' Advertising a building with a pool, gym, valet trash, covered parking or on-site laundry, charging a fee for it, and then not providing it is squarely within (a)(v) and (a)(xv). Note the scienter: the opening words of (a) require that you act knowingly, so an amenity that closes for a genuine repair is a different case from one you bill for and never intend to deliver. The honest and cheap fix is to stop billing the fee the day the service stops, and to put that in the lease so the tenant knows it.

The enforcement route is unusual and gives you a real chance to fix things. A private suit under § 40-12-108(a) lies only for an 'uncured' unlawful deceptive trade practice, and § 40-12-102(a)(ix) makes a practice uncured only if the consumer first gave you written notice under § 40-12-109 and then either you made no offer to cure within fifteen (15) days of that notice, or you did not actually cure within a reasonable time after the consumer accepted. Curing means, under § 40-12-102(a)(viii), offering in writing either to adjust the transaction to conform to the consumer's reasonable expectations, or to rescind it — and performing if the offer is accepted. So when a tenant sends you a letter complaining about a fee for something they never received, treat the fifteen (15) days as a hard deadline and answer in writing with a refund or an adjustment. Section 40-12-109 also limits the tenant: written notice must be given within one (1) year after initial discovery of the practice or within two (2) years following the consumer transaction, whichever occurs first, and suit must be filed within one (1) year after that notice. Damages under § 40-12-108(a) are the actual damages the consumer suffered; attorney's fees are available under § 40-12-108(b) only in a class action, which is the real exposure for a portfolio landlord billing the same dead amenity fee across a building. Separately, under § 40-12-102(a)(vii) the attorney general is the enforcing authority and can act without any tenant suing. Note finally the exemption at § 40-12-110(a)(i) for acts or practices 'required or permitted by state or federal law, rule or regulation or judicial or administrative decision' — do not read that as covering a fee merely permitted by your own lease; a contract is not a law, and that reading has not been tested.

title: Which Fire and Building Code Actually Applies to Your Rental
bodyText:
Wyoming's fire code is real but narrow, and most of what will actually be enforced against a residential rental is local, not state. Work out which layer you are in before you spend money.

The state standard. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) the fire prevention and electrical safety council adopts rules setting minimum fire standards "not exceeding the standards prescribed by" the International Fire Code, the International Building Code, the International Mechanical Code, the International Existing Building Code and the International Fuel Gas Code. Read that phrase carefully: for the state council the I-codes are a ceiling, not a floor. The rules reach new construction and remodeling under § 35-9-108(a), the protection of life and property from fire in all existing buildings, and hazardous substances. These are privately published model codes; you buy them from the International Code Council, you will not find them on a free state page, and the state's adopting rules are agency rules you must get from the department rather than from the statutes. Two overrides sit inside the same section: under § 35-9-120(a) the National Electrical Code controls over any of those I-codes for electrical installations, and under § 35-9-106(d) NFPA 58 and ANSI Z223.1/NFPA 54 control over the International Fuel Gas Code for liquefied petroleum gas, which matters on propane-heated rural property.

When the state actually touches you. State plan review under § 35-9-108(a) is required before new construction or remodeling only for a listed set of buildings: state or local government owned or leased buildings; public buildings over 5,000 square feet including basement; multistory public buildings; child care centers housing more than ten children; public bars, lounges, restaurants, night clubs, lodge halls, theaters, churches or public meeting places regardless of size; and fuel dispensing facilities. "Public building" is defined at § 35-9-102(a)(xvii) as "a building intended for access by the general public," which an ordinary apartment building is not, so a normal residential rental falls outside state plan review. Be careful at the edges: a mixed-use building with a public-facing ground floor, or a clubhouse or leasing office open to the public, can pull you in. The state fire marshal's inspection power under § 35-9-107(b)(ii) is drawn the same way — it covers "public, business or industrial buildings," not dwellings. And § 35-9-118(a)(i) exempts farms and ranches of forty acres or more on deeded land from the whole of §§ 35-9-106 through 35-9-117, so a ranch house you rent out on deeded acreage sits outside this regime entirely.

Where the real requirements live. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(a) directs the state fire marshal to delegate complete authority to any municipality or county that applies and qualifies, and § 35-9-121(a)(i) lets local standards be "equivalent to or more stringent than" the state's. So the ceiling in § 35-9-106(a)(i) binds the council, not your city. Your actual obligations are whatever your municipality or county has adopted by ordinance, enforced by inspectors who must be certified by the International Code Council or the International Conference of Building Officials under § 35-9-121(a)(iii). If a jurisdiction lets its standards lapse, § 35-9-121(a)(ii) returns enforcement to the department. Call your city or county building department and ask which edition of which codes they have adopted and whether they hold delegated authority — that answer, not the statute, tells you what you must build to. There is no statewide residential building code in Wyoming: Wyo. Stat. § 16-13-101 confirms the point by describing counties and cities "that ha[ve] adopted a version of the International Residential Code" as a subset.

A new deadline that works in your favour. Effective July 1, 2026, Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-13-101 and 16-13-102 impose permit timelines on any county or city that has adopted a version of the International Residential Code. They apply to a dwelling of one or two dwelling units, not more than three stories above grade plane, with not more than 3,000 square feet of finished floor area per unit — and the definition of "dwelling" in § 16-13-102(a)(iii) expressly includes a building "rented, leased, let or hired out," so your rental counts. The jurisdiction must tell you in writing within ten business days whether your application is complete, and must approve or deny a completed application within thirty calendar days, subject to suspensions for requested clarification or for required state or federal approval. If it denies, it must give written reasons within seven days. If it imposes conditions after approval that it did not raise in the initial review, § 16-13-102(f) cuts your application fee by ten percent unless the conditions respond to unanticipated property conditions. And under § 16-13-102(g), if it blows the thirty-day deadline your application is deemed approved as submitted the day after it lapses — though the building must still pass all safety and code inspections before a certificate of occupancy issues. Diary these dates; they are enforceable.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Wyoming Rentals
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires a residential landlord to install or retrofit fire sprinklers, and none requires you to disclose to a tenant whether the building has them. There is no retrofit mandate of any kind - not for high-rises, not for multifamily, not on sale or conversion, and not tied to any compliance date. The word "sprinkler" appears ten times in the entire Wyoming code and not once as a duty on a building owner.

Where sprinkler requirements actually come from in Wyoming, and what you need to know about each:

THE ADOPTED CODES, NOT THE STATUTE. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) directs the council on fire prevention and electrical safety to adopt rules establishing minimum fire standards "not exceeding" the standards prescribed by the International Fire Code, the International Building Code, the International Mechanical Code, the International Existing Building Code and the International Fuel Gas Code - for (A) all new building construction or remodeling under § 35-9-108(a), (B) the prevention of fire and the protection of life and property from fire and panic in all existing buildings, and (C) hazards from hazardous substances. Note what subparagraph (B) covers: all existing buildings, with no residential exclusion. Any sprinkler obligation you have therefore lives in those adopted rules and the model codes they incorporate, which are agency rules and model codes outside this review. The statute itself imposes nothing, and it caps the council at the model-code standard rather than letting it go beyond it.

STATE PLAN REVIEW PROBABLY DOES NOT REACH YOUR BUILDING. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(a) requires plans to go to the state fire marshal before new construction, remodeling, or installing an aboveground fuel storage tank, but only for six categories: buildings owned or leased by the state or a local government; public buildings over 5,000 square feet of total floor area including basement; multistory public buildings; buildings for child care centers housing more than ten children; public bars, lounges, restaurants, night clubs, lodge halls, theaters, churches or public meeting places regardless of size; and public and private aboveground fuel dispensing facilities. "Public building" is defined at Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-102(a)(xvii) as "a building intended for access by the general public," which an ordinary apartment building is not. So a privately owned apartment building, even a large multistory one, is not caught by the state plan-review list as such - though a mixed-use building with a genuinely public ground floor can be, and a child care use in a unit can be. Where plan review does apply, § 35-9-108(s) requires that plans for fire alarm systems and fire sprinkler systems be submitted as successive phase plans after the initial plans are approved, so sprinkler drawings are a second submission, not part of the first.

LOCAL ENFORCEMENT IS WHERE IT WILL BITE. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(a) requires the state fire marshal to delegate complete enforcement and interpretation authority to any municipality or county that applies and that has adopted, by ordinance or resolution, minimum standards "equivalent to or more stringent than" the state standards. Section 35-9-121(b) lets a local entity take sole plan review authority, and says in terms that "[i]f local code provisions are more stringent than adopted state codes, the local code prevails." Section 35-9-108(h) and (q)(iv) then switch the state plan-review requirement off entirely where the locality has that authority. The practical result for a landlord: your sprinkler obligations are set by your city or county, not by the state code, in most of populated Wyoming. Ask your local building or fire official in writing before you buy, build or remodel. Local ordinances are flagged here and are not resolved by this review.

REMODELING THRESHOLDS WORTH REMEMBERING. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(q), a plan review is not required for remodeling exempt from permitting under the International Code; is required, at a fee of no more than $50.00 per hour, for remodeling costing less than $40,000.00 that affects a built-in fire protection system; and is required, at the full fee, for remodeling costing $40,000.00 or more. Touching a sprinkler or alarm system pulls even a cheap job into review.

THE ENFORCEMENT TEETH. If you begin work without approved plans the marshal may order it to cease (§ 35-9-108(k)); orders are served as the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure require and failing to stop within forty-eight hours of service is a misdemeanor (§ 35-9-108(m)). A newly constructed or remodeled building may not be used or occupied until the marshal issues a certificate of occupancy or a letter of compliance (§ 35-9-108(n)). An owner aggrieved by an order has only forty-eight hours to appeal to the council (§ 35-9-108(p)), and the order stays in force meanwhile. Those are short clocks - diary them.

ONE EXEMPTION THAT MAY HELP. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-118(a)(i) provides that §§ 35-9-106 through 35-9-117 do not apply to farms or ranches of forty acres or more on deeded land. A ranch dwelling let to a hand or a tenant on qualifying deeded acreage therefore sits outside the state fire prevention scheme, though not outside any applicable local code.

AND A RELATED ABSENCE. Wyoming also has no statewide smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm requirement for rentals, so you cannot rely on a sprinkler system substituting for detectors the way some states allow - there is no state detector rule to substitute for. Local codes are again the only source.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Agency rules, model codes, case law, court rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: A Wyoming private landlord may restrict firearms, and the statute says so expressly
bodyText:
Wyoming is a strong firearms state, and a Wyoming landlord reading that may assume a lease firearm rule is unenforceable. The opposite is true, and the legislature said so in the same act that opened up public buildings.

Wyo. Stat. § 6-8-105 is the "Wyoming Repeal Gun Free Zones Act", added in 2025. Subsections (b) and (c) let permit and permitless carriers take concealed weapons into governmental meetings, public airports, public buildings, and public school and university facilities. Subsection (e) makes it a misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year, a fine up to $2,000, or both, to knowingly refuse entry to someone for lawfully carrying a concealed weapon into a place authorized under (b) or (c). But § 6-8-105(d)(ii) says in terms that nothing in the section shall be construed to "[p]rohibit a private property owner from restricting firearms on his private property" - and the (e) offence is expressly made subject to subsection (d). So a private residential landlord is outside the criminal provision and keeps the right to set a firearm rule on the property.

There is no counterweight anywhere else. Wyoming has no statute protecting a tenant's firearm possession against a lease term, no Texas or Tennessee style tenant firearm right, no statutory right to keep a firearm in a locked vehicle in a residential parking area, and no employer parking-lot firearm statute at all - the word "firearm" does not appear once in Title 27, the labour title. So nothing in Wyoming law supplies the "notwithstanding the lease" protection that Louisiana, Mississippi, Utah or Ohio tenants have.

ONE IMPORTANT EXCEPTION: GOVERNMENTAL LANDLORDS. Wyo. Stat. § 6-8-401(c) preempts firearm regulation to the state, and provides that except as authorized by § 15-1-103(a)(xviii) and § 23-1-302, "no state agency, city, town, county, political subdivision or any other entity shall authorize, regulate or prohibit the sale, transfer, purchase, delivery, taxation, manufacture, ownership, transportation, storage, use, carrying or possession of firearms, weapons, accessories, components or ammunition except as specifically provided by this chapter." Read alongside § 6-8-105(d)(ii), which preserves the private property owner's right, the sensible reading of the phrase "or any other entity" is that it catches other governmental bodies, not private owners. But the phrase is broad on its face, and no case has construed it in this corpus. If you are a housing authority, a municipal or county landlord, or any public body, assume § 6-8-401(c) binds you and do not write a firearm ban. Wyo. Stat. § 6-8-105(d)(vii)(A) points the same way: even where a governmental entity may require employees and students to store firearms in a biometric container or lock box, the rule may not prohibit the storage of firearms and ammunition in public campus housing by an authorized employee or student, and may not require that a firearm be stored unloaded or separate from its ammunition. Public campus housing therefore cannot be made firearm-free.

BACKGROUND YOU SHOULD KNOW. Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 24 provides that the right of citizens to bear arms in defense of themselves and of the state shall not be denied; that is a limit on government, and no Wyoming statute applies it to a private lease. Wyo. Stat. § 6-8-401(a) declares the right to keep and bear arms a fundamental right in every part of Wyoming. Wyoming is a permitless-carry state: under § 6-8-104(a)(iv) a United States resident who meets the disqualification criteria in § 6-8-104(b)(ii) through (vi), (viii) and (ix) may carry concealed without a permit. Possession by a person previously convicted of a violent felony is a felony under § 6-8-102, and possession of a deadly weapon with intent to threaten or injure is a felony under § 6-8-103 - so an unlawful-possession rule in your lease simply tracks Wyoming criminal law.

PRACTICAL ADVICE. You may lawfully impose a firearm rule, but the most defensible rule in Wyoming is the narrow one: no unlawful possession, no discharge except in a lawful act of defence, safe storage, and no display or handling that alarms other residents. A flat ban is lawful on its face as to a private landlord but it is unpopular, hard to police, invites disputes over what is inside the unit, and gives you nothing a conduct rule does not. Apply whatever rule you adopt evenly and make it part of the lease or of the written rules the lease incorporates, so that a breach is enforceable through Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) with the § 1-21-1003 notice to quit. This review covered the Wyoming statutes and constitution; it did not cover city or county ordinances, agency rules or case law, and § 6-8-401(c) in any event prohibits most local firearm ordinances.

title: No Flood Disclosure Requirement
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no flood disclosure to a residential tenant. There is no statute obliging you to say whether the dwelling sits in a 100-year floodplain or a FEMA special flood hazard area, no state model form or rider, no signature or point-size requirement, no prescribed heading, and no tenant right to terminate after a flood. Wyoming also has no residential seller-disclosure act, so there is no sale-side form to borrow from. The words “floodplain,” “flood hazard,” “flood zone” and “special flood” do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes. The one “flood plain” reference, in Wyo. Stat. § 16-10-102(a)(v), is a definition inside the surface water drainage act and describes a federal flood plain insurance area as part of a drainage district’s service area — it imposes nothing on a landlord. The only “flood insurance” reference is a permitted third-party fee in the mortgage lending chapter at Wyo. Stat. § 40-23-123. Every “flood disclosure” proximity hit in the code is in Title 31 and concerns the branded title of a flood-damaged motor vehicle.

One real duty can still apply, and it is easy to miss because it is in the real estate licensing law rather than the landlord-tenant law. If a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is involved in the rental, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-102(b)(viii) defines “buyer” to mean a person attempting to acquire real estate and expressly “includes a tenant as that term is commonly used in the rental, leasing or management of real estate.” That definition pulls prospective tenants into Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-310(a)(i)(F), which requires the licensee to disclose to all prospective buyers any adverse material facts actually known to the licensee, including adverse material facts pertaining to the physical condition of the property and any defects in the property. Note how that sentence is built: the qualifier “required by law to be disclosed” attaches only to the last item, environmental hazards — it does not limit the physical-condition and defects items, so a known history of flooding or a known location in a flood-prone area is disclosable on actual knowledge even though no statute separately commands a flood disclosure. Section 33-28-311 confirms the setting: in a rental the licensee is deemed to be working with the landlord as agent or intermediary and with the tenant as a customer unless the parties agree otherwise in writing. Section 33-28-310(b) adds that the licensee has no duty to inspect independently, so this is an actual-knowledge duty, not a diligence duty. If you self-manage, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-103(a)(i) exempts an owner and the owner’s regular employees from the licensing act altogether, so § 33-28-310 does not reach you — but it does reach your property manager if that manager is licensed.

Two other constraints matter in practice. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property, and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on “knowingly,” so affirmatively telling a prospective tenant the property does not flood when you know it does is exposure, with pre-suit notice and a cure period required by § 40-12-109. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) bars you from renting a unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, which an actively flooding or flood-damaged unit is not.

Recommended course. Disclose a known flood history or known flood-zone location in writing before signing, keep a copy signed by the tenant, and tell the tenant plainly that your insurance does not cover the tenant’s belongings and that ordinary renter’s insurance excludes flood. None of that is compelled by Wyoming statute; all of it is cheap protection against the licensing-act duty, a Consumer Protection Act claim and a fitness dispute. Local flood-plain ordinances adopted for National Flood Insurance Program participation are a separate layer that this corpus does not cover — check the city or county.

title: No Duty to Tell a Tenant the Property Is in Foreclosure
bodyText:
Wyoming imposes no foreclosure disclosure duty on a landlord. No statute requires you to tell an applicant or a tenant, before or after signing, that the property is the subject of a mortgage default, a notice of foreclosure or a pending foreclosure sale, and none requires you to disclose a redemption deadline. Wyoming's foreclosure chapters (Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-4-101 through 34-4-113, foreclosure by advertisement and power of sale) say nothing about tenants, and the residential rental article (§§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) contains no foreclosure disclosure.

What fills the gap is that the tenant gets the notice anyway, from the lender rather than from you. Wyo. Stat. § 34-4-104(a) requires the foreclosing mortgagee, before the first date of publication of the four-week notice, to serve a copy of the notice by certified mail with return receipt requested on the record owner, on 'the person in possession of mortgaged premises, if different than the record owner', and on subordinate recorded lienholders. Your tenant is the person in possession. Plan on the tenant learning of the foreclosure independently and early, and decide in advance how you will answer, because an evasive answer is the real risk (see below).

You keep the rent for a while after the sale. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-18-104(e), the mortgagor or owner is entitled to possession of the land sold and to the rents and profits for three months after the sale — twelve months if the property is agricultural real estate as defined in § 1-18-103(c) — and only at the expiration of that period is the purchaser entitled to possession. The redemption period itself is the same three months (§ 1-18-103(a)) or twelve months for agricultural real estate (§ 1-18-103(b)), with junior lienholders able to redeem for a further thirty days under § 1-18-104(a) and (d). So a foreclosure sale does not cut off your right to collect rent on the day of the sale; keep collecting and keep performing your Article 12 duties until possession passes.

After possession passes, the purchaser's route against a holdover occupant is the ordinary eviction chapter: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(ii) allows forcible entry and detainer after a judicial foreclosure sale where the judgment debtor was in possession, and § 1-21-1002(a)(iii) after a power-of-sale foreclosure once the purchaser or assignee has demanded possession. The § 1-21-1003 three-day notice to quit still applies.

Two cautions. First, saying nothing is lawful; saying something false is not. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing — 'merchandise' under § 40-12-102(a)(vi) includes property real, personal or mixed, and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110 — and § 40-12-105(a) makes it a deceptive trade practice to act 'knowingly' in any of the listed ways, including (a)(viii) misrepresenting the rights, remedies or obligations a consumer transaction involves and the (a)(xv) catch-all, 'engages in unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. Telling a prospective tenant the property is not in foreclosure when you know it is, or quietly taking a twelve-month lease and a deposit knowing the sale is set, is squarely inside that. Remedies include the § 40-12-108 private action (with the § 40-12-109 pre-suit notice and cure period) and the § 40-12-111 enforcement action. The safe practice, and the one we recommend, is to disclose a pending foreclosure in writing before signing even though no statute compels it, and to shorten the term rather than take a long lease you may not be able to honor.

Second, federal law fills part of the gap and is outside this corpus: FEDERAL: the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act generally requires the immediate successor in interest at a foreclosure sale to honor a bona fide lease and to give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. Confirm its current terms with counsel — it is not a Wyoming statute and nothing in the Wyoming Statutes restates it.

title: Wyoming Does Not Ban Foreign Ownership But Reports Conveyances Near Critical Infrastructure
bodyText: Wyoming has no alien land law and no ban on a foreign person, foreign entity or foreign adversary buying, owning or leasing residential property. Chapter 15 of Title 34 is still headed 'ALIEN LAND', but Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-15-101, 34-15-102 and 34-15-103 were all repealed by 2001 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 93, § 1, and only the empty heading survives. Do not read that heading as a live restriction. No Wyoming statute voids a lease because of a tenant's or an owner's nationality, and there is no lease-duration carve-out of the kind other states use, because there is no prohibition for a carve-out to sit inside. The one narrow survival is Wyo. Stat. § 2-4-105(a), a reciprocity rule in the probate code: a nonresident alien cannot acquire Wyoming real property by succession or testamentary disposition if their home country would not let a United States citizen take property there, and under § 2-4-105(c) the burden of proving reciprocity is on the alien. It reaches inheritance and wills only — not a purchase, not a lease, and not your tenant. What Wyoming does have is a reporting and investigation regime, and it can touch a long lease. Article 5 of Title 19 chapter 13, Wyo. Stat. §§ 19-13-501 to 19-13-503, lets the governor in consultation with the director of the department of homeland security designate 'critical infrastructure zones' by legal description. The definition of 'conveyance' at § 19-13-501(a)(i) is deliberately broad and expressly includes an interest in real property that is 'leased', excluding only wills. Under § 19-13-502(c), within fifteen days after a conveyance is RECORDED the county clerk must report it to the director and to the division of criminal investigation. Under § 19-13-502(d) they then determine whether it is within a critical infrastructure zone or up to five miles from one and, on reasonable suspicion, investigate whether it involves a 'designated country or person' — defined at § 19-13-501(a)(iv) as a foreign adversary specified in 15 C.F.R. § 791.4(a) or a state sponsor of terrorism — or otherwise threatens security. Wyo. Stat. § 9-1-618(a)(vi) gives the attorney general and the division subpoena power over witnesses and records to determine who the real parties to such a conveyance are, and § 19-13-502(e) keeps the investigation confidential. The practical trigger is recording. A residential lease for a term of three years or less is excluded from the Title 34 definition of 'conveyance' by Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 and so is not a recordable instrument in the ordinary course; a lease for a term exceeding three years is a conveyance and can be recorded, and a recorded one near a designated zone will be reported. So if you are leasing for more than three years anywhere near a refinery, a 69,000-volt or larger transmission line, a substation, a dam, a water or wastewater plant or any other critical system listed at § 19-13-501(a)(vi), expect the lease to be reported if you record it, and do not be surprised by an inquiry into who your tenant really is. Importantly, § 19-13-502(b), which was the substantive piece, was REPEALED by 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 52 (HB0097), effective July 1, 2025. What is left imposes no duty on you, no screening obligation, no disclosure and no penalty — the duties run to the county clerk, the director and the division. One more thing bears on you as an owner rather than as a landlord. Since 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 9 (HB0069), effective July 1, 2025, being 'owned or controlled by a foreign government or foreign nongovernment person determined to be a foreign adversary' under 15 C.F.R. § 791.4(a) — unless CFIUS has approved it — is a ground for the secretary of state to administratively dissolve or revoke a Wyoming entity: Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-16-1420(a)(vi)(D) and 17-16-1530(a)(viii)(C) for corporations and foreign corporations, §§ 17-19-1420(a)(v)(C) and 17-19-1530(a)(vii)(C) for nonprofits, § 17-29-705(c)(iii)(D) for limited liability companies, and § 17-30-904(h)(iii)(D). If the entity that owns your rental loses its charter or its certificate of authority, Wyo. Stat. § 17-16-1502(a) and, for foreign LLCs, § 17-29-114 bar it from maintaining any proceeding in a Wyoming court — which means it cannot maintain an eviction until the defect is cured. Keep the owning entity in good standing and keep its ownership disclosures accurate. Do not write a nationality screen into your lease or your application: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103 makes national origin a protected class in the sale and rental of housing, so refusing or conditioning a tenancy on a foreign tenant's nationality is a discriminatory housing practice regardless of anything in this section.

title: No Right to Pay and Stay After an Eviction Is Filed
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant no statutory right of redemption and no statutory right of reinstatement. There is no provision letting a tenant stop a filed eviction by paying the arrears and costs, no pay-before-the-hearing dismissal, no post-judgment window to pay and be restored to possession, and no statute letting a subtenant, a mortgagee or another interested party redeem the tenancy. The phrase "relief from forfeiture" appears nowhere in Wyoming law, and although "redemption" appears 333 times and "redeem" 183 times corpus-wide, not one of the Title 1 occurrences is in the forcible entry and detainer chapter — they are all in Chapter 18, the redemption of real estate sold on execution (§§ 1-18-103 to 1-18-106). Do not reason across from that chapter: an execution-sale redemption right has nothing to do with a tenancy.

The only pay-related breathing space Wyoming gives a tenant comes before you can file, not after. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows a forcible entry and detainer action against tenants holding over their terms "or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due". That is a three-day grace period measured from the due date, and rent paid inside it removes your ground. Keep it separate from the other three-day period: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003's three-day written notice to quit, served before you commence the action. They stack. In a nonpayment case you wait out the § 1-21-1002(a)(i) grace, then serve the § 1-21-1003 notice, then wait three more days, then file.

Once the three-day grace has run, nothing in the statute makes a later payment undo the default. Judgment is governed by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008: if the court finds the complaint true it "shall render a general judgment in favor of the plaintiff for restitution of the premises and costs", with no discretion to delay the writ for the tenant to pay, and no conditional or stay-on-payment judgment anywhere in the chapter. In a nonpayment case § 1-21-1008(b) requires the court to find the amount of rent due at the hearing and the terms of the parties' agreement as to amount and time of payment, and then to enter a money judgment for that rent "together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease", issuing execution separately from the writ of restitution. Two things worth noticing there. The attorney's fees come from the lease, not from the statute — Wyoming's eviction chapter shifts no fees of its own, so if your lease has no fee clause you recover costs only. And because the rent judgment and the writ of restitution travel on separate process, paying the money judgment does not stop the writ.

What Wyoming does have is the opposite of redemption: two places where the TENANT must put money up. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1007 the court may not continue the trial more than two days at the defendant's request unless the defendant gives a surety bond for rent accruing during the continuance. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1015(a) the tenant must deposit the rent found due as a condition of perfecting an appeal, on top of the appeal bond required by § 1-21-1014, and a missed later deposit means the judgment is affirmed.

Accepting rent after you have served the notice. This is the one question the statutes do not answer and you should handle carefully. Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 reverse the usual holdover rule in your favour, but only on their own facts: on the EXPIRATION of a term there is no implied renewal "either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent", and an expired lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by the parties; holding over plus acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance. Those sections are about a term that has run out. They say nothing about whether accepting rent after you have declared a forfeiture for breach waives the forfeiture, and that is a common-law waiver question decided by case law, which is outside this library's source material and has not been read. The cautious course is concrete: do not accept a partial payment after serving the notice to quit; if you decide to accept money, take it in full satisfaction of the arrears only after agreeing in writing, signed by both of you, either that the tenancy is reinstated on stated terms or that the money is accepted for use and occupancy without reinstating the tenancy and without waiving the notice. Put it in writing before you take the money, not after.

What fills the gap. Nothing in a lease can create a Wyoming redemption right and you would not want one. What a lease can usefully do is supply the attorney's-fee entitlement that § 1-21-1008(b) assumes but does not create, and state expressly that accepting any payment after a notice to quit is for use and occupancy and does not reinstate the tenancy or waive the notice unless Landlord agrees in a signed writing. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) the parties may modify any Article 12 duty by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so a term of that kind is good as between you and the tenant — but it cannot touch the Article 10 procedure, because § 1-21-1202(d) says "this article" and sits in Article 12.

title: Which Edition of a Code Actually Applies in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming points at outside technical standards in three different ways, and reading the newest national edition will give you the wrong answer more often than not. Before you rely on a code requirement, work out which of the three you are dealing with.

Fixed to a named edition. Wyo. Stat. § 16-6-501(a) requires accessibility features conforming to "the accessibility and supplemental accessibility requirements of the 2012 edition of the International Building Code" - frozen at 2012, and limited to buildings for general public use built by the state, a governmental subdivision, a school district, or another public administrative body, so it does not reach a private rental. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(d) sets state plan-review fees "in the amount provided in the 1997 Uniform Building Code and adjusted for inflation as adopted by rule," which keeps a 1997 edition alive purely as a fee schedule. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-803(a)(i) measures fire-safe cigarettes against ASTM standard E2187-04 "in effect on February 1, 2010," with a narrow mechanism letting the state fire marshal move to a later ASTM method only on a written finding that it does not change the test result.

Explicitly rolling. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(d) says the standards for liquefied petroleum gas installations "shall be the current edition of NFPA 58 Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code and ANSI Z223.1/NFPA 54 National Fuel Gas Code," and provides that those control over a conflicting International Fuel Gas Code. If you have propane at a rental, your obligation moves when NFPA publishes, with no act of the legislature. Wyo. Stat. § 16-6-501(b) likewise requires curb ramps designed in accordance with "the current Americans With Disabilities Act accessibility guidelines," and that subsection reaches curbs and sidewalks intended for public use "whether constructed with public or private funds" - the one part of that section that can touch a private owner.

Named with no edition at all. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) directs the council to adopt rules establishing minimum fire standards "not exceeding the standards prescribed by" the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code, and International Fuel Gas Code. Read that phrase carefully: those codes are a ceiling on what the council may require, not a floor you must independently meet. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-120(a) subjects the installation of electric equipment in or on buildings, mobile homes, and premises to "the applicable minimum requirements of the National Electrical Code," and provides that where any of the International codes conflicts with the NEC, the NEC controls. Neither section names an edition. The operative edition lives in Department of Fire Prevention and Electrical Safety rules, which are agency rules and are not in this review. Do not guess it from the newest published edition; pull the current rule.

Now the part that decides most of this for a residential landlord: Wyoming has no statewide residential building code, and the edition that governs your property is almost always a local choice. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(a) has the state fire marshal delegate complete enforcement and interpretation authority to any municipality or county that applies and qualifies, and § 35-9-121(a)(i) conditions the initial grant on the local governing body having adopted minimum standards by ordinance or resolution "equivalent to or more stringent than" the department's. Under § 35-9-121(a)(ii), a local government that fails to adopt new department standards within six months, or fails to maintain standards at least meeting the statewide ones, loses enforcement authority back to the department immediately. Under § 35-9-121(a)(iii), inspectors employed or contracted after July 1, 2010 to enforce fire and building codes must be certified by the International Code Council or the International Conference of Building Officials. The newest chapter says the quiet part out loud: Wyo. Stat. § 16-13-101, created by 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws (HB0002, Enrolled Act No. 16, House) and effective July 1, 2026, applies its residential building-permit deadlines only to a county or city "that has adopted a version of the International Residential Code," and Wyo. Stat. § 16-13-102(a)(i)(D) defines a covered application by reference to "the most recent version of the International Residential Code adopted by the local government entity." The statute itself treats IRC adoption as optional and local, and the version as whatever that locality last adopted. Flagged and not resolved here: you must check your city's or county's adopting ordinance to learn the edition and the local amendments. That is outside this corpus.

Two Wyoming rules cut in your favor. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-163(a) bars any state or local official enforcing that article - other than a county or municipality with delegated authority under § 35-9-121 - from interpreting or enforcing building codes or standards "in a way that is more stringent or burdensome than required by the standards or codes." And Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-163(b) provides that, notwithstanding any other law, short-term rental of detached one- and two-family dwellings and townhomes "shall not be regulated as a commercial use for purposes of fire, building and electrical standards and shall not be subject to regulation under the International Building Code." If you run short-term rentals in that building type, that sentence is worth knowing by heart. Separately, state-level plan review under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108(a) does not reach ordinary residential rentals; the list is governmental buildings, public buildings over 5,000 square feet, multistory public buildings, child care centers housing more than ten children, public bars, lounges, restaurants, night clubs, lodge halls, theaters, churches and public meeting places, and fuel dispensing facilities.

Finally, none of this defines your habitability duty. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires a unit "in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation" with operational electrical, heating and plumbing and hot and cold running water, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires that the unit be "reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy" with common areas, electrical, plumbing, heating and water maintained. Those sections use their own words and incorporate no code edition - the Residential Rental Property Act never mentions a building, housing, fire, or property-maintenance code. So you cannot discharge § 1-21-1203(a) by pointing to a code edition, and you do not breach it merely because an edition changed.

When you draft, decide deliberately. If your lease makes the tenant responsible for complying with "the fire code" or "applicable codes," a frozen reference can leave the lease out of step with what your inspector actually enforces, while a bare rolling reference changes the tenant's obligations without notice. The safer form ties the lease to the enforceable standard: refer to the applicable codes and standards as adopted and amended from time to time by the authority having jurisdiction, rather than naming an edition in the lease.

title: No Good Cause Eviction Rule in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law and no good-cause notice to give. Nothing in Wyoming law requires you to have a reason to let a lease run out, to decline a renewal, or to explain your reason to the tenant. What Wyoming law does instead is make the lease term do all the work, so read the three rules that actually govern. First, a lease that expires by its own limitation is not renewed by anything but an express written contract signed by the parties, whatever form the original lease took (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 34-2-129). Second, Wyoming recognizes no implied landlord-tenant relation except a tenancy by sufferance: on expiration of a term created by a verbal or written lease there is no implied renewal for any period whatever, not by the tenant holding over and not by your accepting rent for the holdover period, and holding over plus your acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 34-2-128). So in Wyoming, unlike most states, taking a holdover tenant's rent does not convert the tenancy into a new month-to-month term. Third, the eviction grounds are the forcible entry and detainer grounds in Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1002(a): a tenant holding over the term, or failing to pay rent for three days after it is due (paragraph (i)); and a renter in violation of any terms imposed under § 1-21-1204 (the renter's duties, including being current on all payments and complying with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement) or § 1-21-1205 (the renter's prohibited acts) (paragraph (vi)). Before you file, you must notify the adverse party to leave the premises, with service at least three days before the action is commenced, by leaving a written copy with the tenant or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003). That three-day notice to quit does not have to state a cause, and Wyoming requires no statutory language in it. Be careful about one real gap: Wyoming has no statute setting how much notice ends a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy. The statutes do not use the terms "month-to-month," "periodic tenancy" or "tenancy at will" at all. Put the notice period for ending a periodic tenancy in the lease in plain words — for example, that either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice delivered at least 30 days before the next rent due date — because without a lease term you are left to common law and a court's view of what is reasonable. And although Wyoming imposes no good-cause requirement, your reason still has to be lawful: the Wyoming Fair Housing Act forbids discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 40-26-103(b)). Finally, a city or county may have its own rule; local ordinances were not reviewed here.

title: Passing Government Fees to the Tenant
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute on this in either direction. Nothing authorizes you to bill a tenant for a government charge assessed against you, and nothing forbids it. There is also no state rental registration, rental licensing or rental inspection scheme to generate the fee in the first place -- the phrase does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. So whether you can recover a local fee from a tenant is purely a question of what the lease says, and if the lease is silent you absorb it.

Two cautions about the local side. First, a Wyoming city, town or county may still have its own rental registration, business license, inspection or service fee by ordinance, and ordinances are outside what this library verifies -- check the municipality where the unit sits before you assume there is no fee and before you assume you may pass it on, because an ordinance can impose the charge on the owner specifically and some impose it on the owner in terms that a lease cannot shift. Second, there is no Wyoming statute preempting local regulation of residential rents or rental fees, so a local rule in this area is not vulnerable to a state-preemption argument the way it would be in some states.

The one government charge Wyoming law does route through to the occupant is sales and lodging tax, and for ordinary residential tenancies it does not apply. Sales tax reaches "[t]he sales price paid for living quarters in hotels, motels, tourist courts and similar establishments providing lodging service for transient guests" (Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-103(a)(i)(G)), "lodging service" means sleeping accommodations provided to transient guests (§ 39-15-101(a)(i)), and a "transient guest" is "a guest who remains for less than thirty (30) continuous days" (§ 39-15-101(a)(xiv)). A tenant on a month-to-month or longer tenancy is not a transient guest, so no state sales tax and no state or local lodging tax attaches to their rent. If you run a short-term rental where stays are under 30 continuous days, the opposite is true and the law does the pass-through for you: § 39-15-107(b) levies the tax on the purchaser, requires the vendor to collect it, and requires you to give the purchaser a receipt displaying the tax separately. You also owe the statewide lodging tax under § 39-15-211 and any local lodging tax under § 39-15-204. Those are collected from the guest, not absorbed, and the 30-day line is what decides which regime a stay falls under.

Practical course: if you want the ability to recover a local fee, say so in the lease, in a clause that is specific about which charges it reaches and that excludes fines, penalties and anything tied to the condition or construction of the building -- those are your costs of ownership and a tenant will fight them. Quote the fee in writing when it is assessed rather than folding it silently into rent.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute that bars a landlord from making a tenant reimburse a government fine, and none that permits or caps one. Unlike Texas, which forbids charging a tenant for a fine unless the tenant or another occupant actually caused the condition, Wyoming is silent. The question is therefore one of contract and of ordinary damages.

What Wyoming does give you, and it is more useful than a pass-through clause in many cases, is that the fine may land on the tenant directly rather than on you.

• Cities and towns. Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xix) empowers a governing body to "[d]eclare and abate nuisances and impose fines upon parties who create, continue or permit nuisances to exist." The fine runs to the party who creates, continues or permits the nuisance — which can be your tenant. If a city cites you for something a tenant did, say so and ask the city to cite the occupant.
• Counties. Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-101(a)(viii) lets a board of county commissioners declare and abate nuisances it determines threaten health or safety, and provides that "[n]o person shall create, continue or permit nuisances to exist in violation of a final order." The abatement procedure at Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-115(b) requires written notice "to the owner OR OCCUPANT of the property describing with specificity the nature of the nuisance and the steps required for abatement," served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, filed with the clerk of the district court, and posted conspicuously on the property. The owner or occupant has twenty (20) days to file an answer with the clerk and serve the board, § 18-2-115(c); with no answer the order becomes final, and with an answer the court holds a hearing within twenty (20) days, § 18-2-115(d). Because the statute says "owner or occupant," a county order can be served on your tenant — but it can equally be served on you for something the tenant did, and the twenty-day clock is short. Diary it the day you are served.

Four Wyoming rules shape a reimbursement clause.

1. The tenant already owes you for damage. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(i) forbids a renter to intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly permit anyone to do so, and § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) forbids interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property. A nuisance your tenant creates generally breaches both, so you have a statutory hook before you reach your lease.

2. You cannot shift your own habitability duty by a general clause. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) makes you keep the unit safe, sanitary and fit for human habitation with operational electrical, heating and plumbing and hot and cold running water. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) does allow reallocation — "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties" — but note the two conditions in that sentence: the agreement must be explicit, in writing, and signed by the parties. A boilerplate "tenant pays all fines" line is not an explicit assignment of a named duty, and charging a tenant for a fine that arose from your own code failure invites an unfair-or-deceptive-practice claim under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a)(xv), since "merchandise" in § 40-12-102(a)(vi) includes real property.

3. Charge the real amount, not a markup. Wyoming has no liquidated-damages statute for rental fees, so a reimbursement equal to the fine you actually paid is on solid ground while a surcharge on top of it is not.

4. Collect it as a debt, not by self-help. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit at termination to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning and "other costs provided by any contract" — so a contractual fine reimbursement is deductible from the deposit at the end. During the tenancy, bill it; do not net it out of a rent payment, which muddies any later nonpayment case.

Use the library's optional clause `tenant-caused-fines-as`, which fits Wyoming law as written: it makes the tenant reimburse a fine, penalty or abatement cost caused by the tenant, the tenant's household or a person on the premises with the tenant's consent, within a set number of days after written notice with a copy of the citation, and expressly excludes a fine for a condition the landlord is responsible for. Nothing in Wyoming law contradicts it.

One gap to watch: Wyoming has no statute forbidding a lease term or a local ordinance that penalizes a tenant for calling police or emergency services, and no crime-free or chronic-nuisance statute at the state level. City ordinances are outside this library — check the ordinances where your property sits before relying on, or fearing, a nuisance-call rule.

title: Lease Guarantors and Renewals
bodyText: Wyoming has no guaranty statute aimed at leases and no provision limiting a guarantor to the original term the way Texas does, no requirement that a separate guaranty state a maximum liability and an end date the way Kentucky does, and no cap on what you may collect at move-in, so nothing limits a deposit or prepayment taken from a guarantor either. What Wyoming does have are two rules that decide most guarantor disputes. First, the guaranty must be in writing and signed. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(ii) voids 'every special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person' unless the agreement, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged. Paragraph (a)(i) adds the same requirement for any agreement that by its terms cannot be performed within a year, and paragraph (a)(vi) for a representation about another person's credit or ability made so that person can obtain credit. So the guarantor must sign — an oral promise from a parent, and a guaranty signed only by you or only by the tenant, is void, and an email the guarantor never subscribed is a fight you should not have to have. Second, and this is the part that decides renewals, Wyoming reverses the usual holdover rule. Under Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 a lease that has expired by its own limitation 'shall be again renewed except by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto' — no other way — and under Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 there is no implied renewal for any period whatever, not by the tenant holding over and not by you accepting rent; a holdover is only a tenancy by sufferance. Put those together: in Wyoming there is normally no such thing as an implied renewal for a guaranty to attach to. If the tenant holds over, what exists is a different tenancy, a tenancy by sufferance, and a guaranty of 'the Lease' is on shaky ground as to rent accruing under it. If there is a true renewal, it exists only because the parties signed a new express written contract — and the guarantor is a party to the guaranty, not to that lease, unless you bring the guarantor into the new writing. The practical rule is therefore simple and one-sided in your favor only if you act: get the guarantor's fresh signature on every renewal and every extension, and in the original guaranty say expressly that it covers renewals, extensions, holdover and any tenancy by sufferance. Do not assume a guaranty carries forward. Also name the guarantor as a defendant in any suit; Wyoming gives you no statutory shortcut for reaching a guarantor on a judgment entered only against the tenant.

title: Wyoming Gives Tenants No Statutory Guest Rights, So Your Lease Decides
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute giving a tenant a right to have guests, visitors, family, tradespeople, delivery people or suppliers of goods and services at the unit. There is no three-or-more-household rule, no non-waivability provision, and no prohibition on charging a guest fee. A search of all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws found nothing of the kind: "guest fee" and "social guest" return nothing anywhere, "supplier" and "guest" return nothing in Title 1 or Title 34, "tradesmen" and "tradespeople" return nothing, and no provision anywhere ties a right to buildings with three or more households.

So your lease governs. You may set a guest policy, cap how long a guest may stay before becoming an occupant who must be screened and added to the lease, require guests to park in designated spaces, and make the tenant responsible for the conduct of everyone the tenant lets in. If you want to charge for a guest's use of an amenity — a guest parking permit, a clubhouse booking, a pool pass — nothing in Wyoming law stops you, as long as the charge is in the lease.

Four Wyoming provisions do touch guests, and three of them help you.

First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c): you are not required to correct or remedy any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, or the renter's guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse of the property during the rental term or any extension of it. Damage done by a guest is not your repair problem.

Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii): before termination the renter must remove all property and garbage owned by or placed in the unit by the renter "or his guests," and clean the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning of the rental agreement. A guest's abandoned furniture is the tenant's problem to clear.

Third, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(i) makes it a prohibited act for a renter to intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit "or knowingly permit any person to do so," and § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) prohibits a renter from interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property. Between them, a tenant whose guests wreck the place or torment the neighbours is in breach of the statute, not just of your lease.

Fourth, on the limiting side, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) requires the renter to occupy the unit in the manner for which it was designed and not to increase the number of occupants above the number specified in the rental agreement without the owner's consent. That is the hook for a guest-becomes-occupant rule — but it only works if your rental agreement actually specifies a number of occupants. If you leave the number blank, there is nothing for the statute to measure against.

Two cautions. Wyoming has a state fair housing act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, and familial status is a protected class under § 40-26-103. A guest policy that in practice restricts children — stricter supervision rules, shorter stays for minors, a lower guest cap for households with children — is a familial-status problem. Write the policy about conduct and numbers, not about who the guest is. And because Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), with Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) making a more stringent local housing code prevail, a city may have occupancy or boarding rules of its own. Check the municipality before you set a hard cap.

The cautious course. Put a written guest policy in the lease; define "guest" by a number of consecutive or cumulative nights; specify the maximum number of occupants so § 1-21-1204(a)(v) has something to bite on; make the tenant responsible for guests' conduct and damage; and apply the policy the same way to every household.

title: No Habitability Presumption, and the Burden Sits on the Renter
bodyText: Wyoming creates no presumption that you have breached a habitability duty. There is no provision like California's, where an uncorrected code violation sixty days after an inspector's written notice presumes a breach and shifts the burden to the landlord; no Maryland-style presumption that more than thirty days is an unreasonable time to repair; and no Massachusetts-style rule that proof of a sanitary-code violation establishes a defence to an eviction. The phrase "warranty of habitability" appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and neither does "housing code." In fact the word "habitability" does not appear in Wyoming's landlord-tenant article at all — the single appearance of any "habitab" word in the whole of Title 1 is at Wyo. Stat. § 1-40-208(a), a crime-victims provision cross-referencing the hazardous-materials uninhabitability order in Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d). Wyoming's habitability duty is real but is written in different words. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires you, to protect the physical health and safety of the renter, to (i) not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; (ii) maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition; (iii) maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; and (iv) maintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement — that last one is opt-in, so an appliance you do not list in the lease is not yours to maintain. On the evidentiary question this topic is really about, Wyoming runs the opposite way from the presumption states. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) switches the whole notice-and-correct machinery on only "if the renter is current on all payments required by the rental agreement and has reasonable cause supported by evidence to believe" the unit does not comply. That phrase — reasonable cause supported by evidence — appears exactly once in the Wyoming statutes, and it puts the evidentiary burden on the renter at the threshold. The renter must also advise you in writing of the condition and specify the remedial action requested, and must serve that notice by certified mail or in the manner specified by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. You then have a reasonable time to either commence action to correct it or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim — and notifying the renter in writing that you dispute the claim is an answer the statute expressly allows, so do not ignore the notice. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a) stacks two more gates on the renter: the remedies in that section are available only to a renter in compliance with ALL of Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1204 (renter's duties) and 1-21-1205 (prohibited acts by renter), and only where the agreement has not been lawfully terminated under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d). A renter who has fallen behind in rent, damaged the unit, interfered with a neighbour's peaceful enjoyment, or unreasonably refused you access for repairs, inspection or showings under § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) has forfeited the remedy. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) adds that you need not correct a condition the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees caused by inappropriate use or misuse. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) bars claims under the article for mental suffering or anguish. There IS one statutory presumption in Wyoming's landlord-tenant article, and it runs your way, not the renter's: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210(a) provides that "Any property remaining within the rental unit after termination of the rental agreement shall be presumed to be both valueless and abandoned." That is the only presumption in the article, and it concerns abandoned property, not condition. None of this means you can neglect the unit. Wyoming has no presumption, but a renter who clears the § 1-21-1203(b) gate can serve a notice to repair under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(b) and go to court, and a court will decide condition on the ordinary evidence either side brings. Your practical protection is documentary: a dated, photographed move-in condition record signed by the renter, a written log of every repair request and your response, and a written dispute notice under § 1-21-1203(b) whenever you genuinely disagree. All of Article 12, including these provisions, applies only to a "residential rental unit" as defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and occasionally rented recreational property — and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty in the article be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, with no anti-waiver provision anywhere in the article.

title: The Lease Does Not Have to Promise a Habitable Unit
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires your lease to state that you will deliver the unit fit for habitation, or to recite the habitability standard in any form. Wyoming imposes exactly one mandatory piece of lease text, and it is about deposits, not habitability: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 provides that 'Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or his designated agent.' Note that § 1-21-1207 requires two things, not one — the statement in the agreement and a separate written notice when you take the money — and failing either is a real exposure. Beyond that single sentence, Wyoming tells you nothing you must put in a lease.

The duty exists whether or not you write it down. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) says each owner and his agent renting or leasing a residential rental unit 'shall maintain that unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation.' The next sentence adds that each unit 'shall have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties,' and a closing proviso says the section does not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins that are not intended to have those amenities. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) then lists the specific duties: do not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition; maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; and maintain other appliances and facilities only 'as specifically contracted in the rental agreement.' That last one is opt-in — listing a dishwasher or air conditioner in the lease is what creates your duty to maintain it, so be deliberate about what you list.

Wyoming is unusual in a way you should understand before you draft. The habitability duty is not a hard floor. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties,' and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12. Two narrower escape hatches sit alongside it: the hot-and-cold-water requirement in § 1-21-1202(a) is expressly subject to written agreement otherwise, and § 1-21-1202(c) says the article 'does not apply to breakage, malfunctions or other conditions which do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter.' Even so, do not try to disclaim habitability. The conditions in § 1-21-1202(d) are cumulative — explicit, written and signed — a broad boilerplate waiver will not satisfy them, no Wyoming court has blessed a wholesale disclaimer, and a term that leaves a family without heat invites a court to find it unconscionable or void as against public policy regardless of § 1-21-1202(d). Use the subsection for what it is plainly good for: shifting a defined, discrete maintenance task such as lawn care, snow removal or filter changes to the tenant in a signed, specific term.

The practical advice on drafting. Do not add a habitability statement you are not required to make. If you recite a promise in the lease, you create a contract term, and a tenant can sue you on it in ordinary contract outside the statutory scheme — which matters because the statutory scheme is comparatively narrow: the renter's remedies in § 1-21-1206 are gated by § 1-21-1206(a) on the renter being in compliance with §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205, and § 1-21-1203(e) provides that 'The owner is not liable under this article for claims for mental suffering or anguish.' A lease promise in your own words may hand back advantages the statute gives you. What is worth stating instead is the specific: exactly which appliances and facilities you maintain under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv), who handles which routine tasks, and how the tenant reports a defect.
