Remember that all of this turns off outside Article 12's gate — § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines a 'residential rental unit' as the renter's principal place of residence and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Contaminated Property and What You Must Tell a Tenant
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires you to tell a tenant that the property is contaminated, was contaminated, sits in a cleanup area, or carries a recorded environmental use restriction. Wyoming has no brownfield disclosure law, no Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, and no residential seller-disclosure act that a tenant could borrow from. Searching the whole corpus for any proximity between contamination and a tenant, renter or lessee returns nothing in either direction. That is a real gap, not an oversight on your part, and it does not mean saying nothing is safe.

Wyoming does have two contamination disclosure duties, and both of them run to buyers rather than tenants. The first is Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d). After a hazardous-material, weapons-of-mass-destruction or clandestine-laboratory incident, the incident commander may order that a building, structure or land is uninhabitable or contaminated. Property under such an order may be transferred or sold before remediation only if full written disclosure is made to the prospective purchaser, attached to the earnest money receipt if there is one, accompanying the sale documents but not forming part of the deed and not recorded; the seller must notify the incident commander of the transfer or sale within ten days. Note what that subsection then does: receipt of the full written disclosure constitutes a full release of liability for the seller and acceptance of liability by the buyer, unless they agree otherwise. There is no parallel duty, and no parallel release, for letting the same property to a tenant. The second is the Voluntary Remediation of Contaminated Sites article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-11-1601 and following. Its disclosure mechanism is recording, not telling: "institutional controls" are defined at § 35-11-103(g)(vii) as restrictions on the use of a site including deed notices, voluntary deed restrictions or other conditions, covenants or restrictions imposed by the property owner and filed with the county clerk, use control areas, and zoning restrictions. Long-term use restrictions are created as a use control area under § 35-11-1609, on the owner's own petition, after written notice to contiguous surface owners and four weeks of published notice. The law's assumption is that a future occupant finds out by searching the record.

So here is what to actually do. First, find out whether your property carries anything. Search the county clerk's records for a deed notice or recorded restriction, and ask the Department of Environmental Quality whether the site is in a use control area or under a remedy agreement. Second, if it is, carry the restriction into the lease. A recorded use restriction limits what the property may be used for, and nothing makes it reach your tenant automatically — if the restriction forbids disturbing soil, growing food, drilling a well or using a basement, your lease has to say so, or your tenant will do the forbidden thing and you will answer for it. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-11-1607(e), a violation of any use restriction, term or condition is a violation of the Environmental Quality Act, and the department may bring an action against the owner of the site at the time the violation occurs or against the person who violated the restriction; under § 35-11-1607(f) no person may change an engineering or institutional control contained in a remedy agreement or certificate of completion without the department's prior written consent. The liability lands on you as owner, not on the tenant who did it.

Third, disclose anyway. Wyoming's one real nondisclosure hook is the Consumer Protection Act. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include property "real, personal or mixed," so your rental is within the Act, and § 40-12-105(a) makes a knowing deceptive practice unlawful, with the catch-all in (a)(xv) broad enough to reach a lease or an advertisement that conceals a known contamination problem. The gate is "knowingly," which is precisely the position you are in once you have found a recorded restriction or received a remediation letter. Put the disclosure in writing, attach whatever document you have, and keep the tenant's signed acknowledgement. Finally, keep this separate from the federal lead-paint rule: for target housing built before 1978 the disclosure duty is FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d and its regulations, which apply to Wyoming landlords regardless of anything in this row.

title: Health Boards and Rental Units in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has local health boards, but it has none of the rental-specific machinery the Nevada-style rule assumes. There is no statute requiring you to give a tenant a copy of any health-district regulation on request, no statutory referral route sending a tenant's unanswered repair notice to a health board, no statutory board inspection triggered by a tenant complaint about a rental, and no provision letting a board recover its enforcement costs from a landlord as such. The phrase "rental dwelling" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code, and no provision anywhere links a tenant to a health officer.

What does exist, and what it means for you:

LOCAL HEALTH BOARDS AND THEIR RULES. Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-1-301 through 35-1-309 let counties, cities and multi-county districts establish health departments with a board of health. Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-303(a) gives those boards real rulemaking power: county, city and district boards of health "may enact rules and regulations pertaining to the prevention of disease and the promotion of public health in the area over which such respective boards have jurisdiction," subject to a floor - "in no instance shall such rules and regulations be less effective than, or in conflict with," state department of health rules. Under § 35-1-303(b) that jurisdiction covers all unincorporated areas and all municipalities in the county or district, except that a Class I municipality may keep its own health department. So a local board can regulate conditions in rental housing, and whatever it has adopted binds you. Those local rules are not in this review. Ask your county or city health department for its current rules in writing before you assume there are none, and do not assume a rule that applies in Laramie County applies in Natrona County.

THE 48-HOUR NUISANCE ORDER - THE SHORTEST COMPLIANCE WINDOW IN WYOMING LAW. Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-105(a)(vii) makes it an offence for the owner or occupant of private property on which a nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness exists to "willfully fail to remove the same at his own expense within forty-eight (48) hours after being ordered to do so by health authorities." Note the three features that matter to a landlord. The duty falls on the owner as well as the occupant, so a tenant-created condition is still your problem once the order lands. Removal is at your own expense. And the clock is forty-eight hours, not thirty days. Under § 35-1-105(b), conviction brings a fine of up to $100.00, imprisonment of up to six months, or both, AND liability for all expense health authorities incurred in removing the nuisance - and the subsection ends with a sentence worth reading twice: "No conviction under the penalty provisions of this act or of any other public health laws shall relieve any person from an action in damages for injury resulting from violation of public health laws." That preserves a private damages claim, which is one of the few routes by which a Wyoming tenant can reach you outside Article 12 of Title 1.

THE WIDER OFFENCES. Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-105(a)(i) separately makes it an offence to willfully violate, disobey or disregard the public health laws or "the terms of any lawful notice, order, rule or regulation issued pursuant thereto" - which picks up a local board's rules adopted under § 35-1-303. Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-106 adds a general penalty for violating the act, any lawful state health department rule, or any lawful order of a state, county or municipal health officer: a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $1,000.00, imprisonment of up to one year, or both. The two penalty provisions overlap and the larger one is not limited to the department's own rules.

A LIMIT ON HEALTH ORDERS THAT IS NARROWER THAN IT LOOKS. Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-310(a) provides that no public health order requested or issued by a county, municipal or district health officer "under this article" takes effect without notice to the public at least forty-eight hours in advance and an opportunity for written and electronic public comment, unless delay would cause immediate and life-threatening physical harm, exposure or transmission. Read the qualifier carefully: the first sentence says "under this article," meaning Article 3, where § 35-1-310 sits, so it does not plainly reach an order resting on Article 1, which is where the § 35-1-105(a)(vii) nuisance offence lives. The second sentence uses a wider phrase, "under this chapter," but it governs only orders restricting individuals' movements or activities to limit a contagious disease, capping those at ten days with extensions available only by majority vote of the county commissioners, the municipal governing body or the member political subdivision's governing body under § 35-1-310(a)(i)-(iii). Do not plan on § 35-1-310 giving you forty-eight hours' warning of an abatement order about your building, and note that the notice it does require is notice to the public, not personal notice to the owner.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. Because Wyoming hands you no statutory script, build one. Get your local health department's rental or nuisance regulations in writing and keep them with your property file. Give your tenants a written point of contact and a documented repair-request route, so a complaint comes to you before it goes to the county. Treat any communication from a health officer as a forty-eight-hour clock from the moment it is received, and respond in writing even if you dispute it. And remember that Article 12 of Title 1 runs in parallel: a tenant's written notice of noncompliance under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) starts a separate reasonable-time clock, and under § 1-21-1203(d) you may refuse to correct and terminate the tenancy where repair costs exceed what is reasonable in light of the rent and the property - but terminating the lease does not answer a health authority's order, because that order runs against you as owner.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Local board of health rules, state department of health rules, case law, court rules and municipal ordinances were not searched and may add requirements.

title: Heat is a listed owner duty in Wyoming, with no temperature standard and no season
bodyText:
Heat is one of the few things Wyoming names outright as your job. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) provides that each owner and his agent renting or leasing a residential rental unit shall maintain that unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, and that each residential rental unit shall have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water - "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties". Read that qualifier carefully: it sits at the end of the second sentence and attaches to the amenities list in that sentence, not to the fitness duty in the first. A third sentence then says the section does not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins that are not intended to have those amenities.

Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) states the ongoing duty: each owner shall maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. That is a closed list. Paragraph (a)(iv) picks up "other appliances and facilities" only "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement", so a window air conditioner, a wood stove you did not promise, or a supplemental heater is your problem only if your lease says it is. There is no Wyoming statute on cooling or air conditioning at all.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT SET. There is no minimum indoor temperature. The phrases "minimum temperature", "indoor temperature" and "heating season" do not appear in the statutes, and none of the eleven "Fahrenheit" references is a dwelling standard. There is no October-to-May heating season, no daytime and night-time set points, no 68-degree rule. There is also no statutory cold-weather moratorium on utility disconnection: the word "winter" does not appear in Title 37 at all. What "maintain ... heating" requires in practice is a working system that heats the unit, judged by ordinary reasonableness - so the sensible internal standard is the one the model codes use, and a system you can show was serviced annually.

HOW THE TENANT ENFORCES IT, AND WHEN YOU CAN WALK AWAY. The renter's route is § 1-21-1203(b), and it opens with a gate: it applies only "[i]f the renter is current on all payments required by the rental agreement" and the renter has reasonable cause supported by evidence. The renter must advise you in writing of the condition and specify the remedial action requested, served by certified mail or in the manner specified by § 1-21-1003. Within a reasonable time after you receive that notice you must either commence action to correct the condition or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim. Section 1-21-1203(c) relieves you of any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees through inappropriate use or misuse. Section 1-21-1203(d) is your exit: if the cost of repair exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement, you may refuse to correct and terminate the rental agreement - but you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance, give the renter no less than ten and no more than twenty days from the date of your notice to find substitute housing, prorate the rent to the date the renter vacates, and refund the balance along with any deposit due under § 1-21-1208. A failed furnace in an older low-rent unit is exactly the case § 1-21-1203(d) was written for. Section 1-21-1203(e) bars claims for mental suffering or anguish under the whole article, and the renter's remedies in § 1-21-1206 are available only to a renter who is in compliance with §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205 and only where the agreement has not been lawfully terminated under § 1-21-1203(d). The renter has duties on the other side too: § 1-21-1204(a)(iv) requires the renter to use all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner.

YOU CAN MOVE THE DUTY, BUT ONLY ONE WAY. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that any duty or obligation in the article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. The conditions are cumulative - explicit, written, and signed - and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12. So a tenant-supplied-heat arrangement is lawful in Wyoming if it is written into a signed lease in plain terms. Do not rely on an unsigned addendum, an oral understanding or a line in a handbook.

TWO LIMITS ON ALL OF THIS. First, § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines a "residential rental unit" as the renter's principal place of residence and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally, so the whole of Article 12, heat included, switches off outside that definition. Second, if you bill tenants for heat through a submeter, Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) withdraws the landlord's public-utility exemption for metered or direct sales of a utility commodity to tenants, and the fee-free allocation carve-out at (H)(VIII) and (IX) covers water only - there is no gas or electricity equivalent.

ONE THING WORTH TELLING TENANTS. Wyoming administers a low income home energy assistance and weatherization program under Wyo. Stat. § 42-2-501. At least twenty-five percent of the available funding must go to weatherization, and § 42-2-501(b)(iii), (iv) and (vi) expressly fund furnace and heating system modifications and repairs, furnace replacement, and repair or replacement of water heaters and heating systems for portions of a dwelling - for residential dwellings only. Section 42-2-501(c) sets eligibility at the lesser of 215 percent of the federal poverty level for Wyoming or 60 percent of state median household income. Pointing a struggling tenant there costs you nothing and may prevent an arrears.

title: Renting in a Condominium or Covenanted Community
bodyText:
Wyoming has no homeowners association statute and no common-interest community act. The phrases “unit owners’ association,” “common interest community,” “declaration of covenants” and “home owners association” appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes. There is no statutory association lien for assessments, no cap on an association’s approval or application fee, no statutory limit on what tenant information an association may demand, no right for an association to collect rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind on dues, no grandfather rule protecting owners who bought before a rental restriction was adopted, and no statutory procedure for association approval of a lease. If your lease library expects those rules, none of them exists here.

What Wyoming does have is thin and purely enabling. The Condominium Ownership Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-20-101 through 34-20-104, is four sections long. Section 34-20-102 recognizes condominium ownership as a fee simple estate in air space plus an undivided interest in common elements and makes the two inseparable. Section 34-20-103 defines the unit, the common elements and the declaration. Section 34-20-104(a) handles separate tax assessment of each unit and confines a tax or mechanic’s lien to the delinquent owner’s unit, so another owner’s default cannot reach your unit. Section 34-20-104(b) requires the declaration to be recorded with the county clerk and disapplies the rule against perpetuities and the rule against unlawful restraints on alienation to destruction and obsolescence provisions. Section 34-20-104(c) is the one that matters most to a landlord: to the extent the recorded declaration requires all unit owners to belong to an association, or provides for charges assessed by the association, those provisions are covenants running with the land binding on every owner and every successor in interest, any rule of law to the contrary notwithstanding. That is the whole of it. Outside condominiums, Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-306 and § 18-5-404 merely permit a county to require that a subdivision be subject to recorded covenants creating an entity such as a homeowners association, and expressly forbid the county board from mandating an entity able to interfere with an owner’s use of his private property except to collect an assessment. Associations themselves are ordinary nonprofit corporations under the Wyoming Nonprofit Corporation Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-19-101 et seq.

The practical consequence. Everything an association can do to you and to your tenant comes from the recorded declaration, the covenants and the bylaws, not from a statute, and § 34-20-104(c) makes those documents binding on you as a successor owner whether or not you negotiated them. Before you lease, read the recorded declaration for a leasing restriction, a minimum lease term, an owner-occupancy cap, an approval requirement, a tenant registration requirement, a fee, or a rule that the owner remains liable for the tenant’s violations — and assume it is enforceable, because Wyoming supplies no statutory override. Pull the recorded documents from the county clerk rather than relying on what a board member tells you. Put the association’s rules into your lease by reference and attach them, make the tenant responsible for compliance, and keep a right to terminate for a violation that exposes you to a fine; no Wyoming statute limits any of that.

One statutory check does exist on the content of covenants. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-154(a) lets a record owner, or an attorney or title company acting for one, record a new instrument removing a restrictive covenant that either has been held void and unenforceable by the Wyoming Supreme Court or the United States Supreme Court, or is in violation of the acts prohibited by Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109 — the Wyoming Fair Housing Act’s sale, rental, advertising, financing and disability provisions. Section 34-1-155 sets the filing process with the county clerk, and § 34-1-156 lets anyone who thinks the covenant was valid petition the court. Good-faith recording carries immunity under § 34-1-154(b), but that immunity is lost if you represent an unlawful covenant as valid or try to enforce one. So a covenant that discriminates on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin can be stripped from the chain of title, and you must not enforce it against an applicant or tenant in the meantime. Ordinary leasing restrictions, which discriminate on no protected class, are untouched by this route.

title: Money Taken Before the Lease Is Signed
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about holding deposits, earnest money, reservation fees or any other money taken from an applicant before a lease exists. The phrase 'holding deposit' appears once in the whole Wyoming Statutes, in the insurance code, and 'earnest money' appears only in real estate sales contexts. Nothing caps the amount, nothing says when you must decide, and nothing says you must refund it if you rent to someone else.

The reason this still needs care is that Wyoming's deposit statute is keyed to a rental agreement that has ended. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) operates 'Upon termination of the rental agreement' on 'property or money held as a deposit', and 'termination' is defined at § 1-21-1201(a)(v) as the lawful ending or cessation of a rental agreement. A 'renter' under § 1-21-1201(a)(iii) is a person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy the unit. An applicant who has signed nothing is not a renter and has no rental agreement to terminate, so the 30-day itemization clock, the 15-day new-address rule and the § 1-21-1208(c) remedy do not by their terms reach money you are holding before signing. Note too that the whole of Article 12 only applies to a 'residential rental unit', which § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis.

That silence cuts both ways, so take the cautious course. If the applicant signs, the money stops being a holding deposit: apply it to the security deposit or to rent, say so in the lease, and run the § 1-21-1208 clocks on it at the end like any other deposit. Section 1-21-1207 then bites — any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and separate written notice of that fact must also be given to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. That is Wyoming's only mandatory lease recital and it is two duties, not one. Give the written notice when you take the holding deposit, before you know whether the deal will close, and you have covered both timings.

If the applicant does not sign, you have nothing but your contract. Put the holding deposit in a short written agreement signed before you take the money, saying plainly: the amount, that you will take the unit off the market until a stated date, what you keep if the applicant backs out or fails screening after misrepresenting something, what you refund and when, and that the money becomes the security deposit on signing. Without that writing you are relying on general contract law, which is outside this corpus.

Three real constraints. First, do not describe the money dishonestly. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing — § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property and § 40-12-110 contains no real-property exemption — and § 40-12-105(a) makes it unlawful to act 'knowingly' in the listed ways, including (a)(viii), misrepresenting the rights, remedies or obligations a consumer transaction involves, and the (a)(xv) catch-all 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. Taking holding deposits from several applicants for one unit, or calling money refundable and then keeping it, is the exposure. Second, if a licensed real estate broker or a brokerage-managed company holds the money for you, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-122(a)(i) requires it to go into a designated trust or escrow account unless everyone with an interest agrees otherwise in writing, § 33-28-122(a)(ii) expressly contemplates lease transactions, and § 33-28-122(c) directs interest on withdrawn trust funds to 'the person from whom the trust funds were received' absent written agreement among all interested persons — so a broker-held holding deposit can owe the applicant interest even though a self-managed deposit never does. Third, money you hold for an applicant who disappears does not become yours by waiting: Wyoming's Unclaimed Property Act treats a security deposit as unclaimed property (§ 34-24-102(a)(x)(B)), and § 34-24-130(a) voids a contractual forfeiture deadline on an unclaimed deposit. Refund it to the last known address and keep the record.

title: Setting a Holdover Rate in a Wyoming Lease
bodyText: Wyoming lets you set a holdover rate, and it does not tell you what the rate may be. There is no statutory holdover damages measure, no multiplier, no cap, and no statute requiring or forbidding a stipulated sum. If you want a daily charge for a tenant who stays past the end of the term, the lease has to create it, because nothing else will. Four provisions make the clause work. First, Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 says that in Wyoming the landlord-tenant relation does not arise by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, that there is no implied renewal of an expired lease for any period whatever, and — this is the sentence out-of-state landlords get wrong — that no renewal arises either by the tenant holding over OR by the landlord accepting compensation or rent during the holding over. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 completes it: an expired lease is renewed only by express contract in writing signed by the parties, and no tenancy other than sufferance exists after the term ends. So taking money from a holdover tenant does not create a new tenancy against you, which is exactly what makes a daily holdover charge safe to collect in Wyoming when it would be risky elsewhere. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) grounds a forcible entry and detainer action 'against tenants holding over their terms' as a head of jurisdiction separate from nonpayment, so you can sue for possession on the holdover alone after the notice to quit required by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. Third, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to 'accrued rent, damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit ... and to other costs provided by any contract.' A holdover charge your lease creates is a cost provided by contract and is deductible from the deposit. Fourth, and the one most landlords miss: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008 splits the money judgment from the possession judgment. Under (a), if the court finds the complaint true it renders a general judgment for restitution of the premises and COSTS — nothing more. Only under (b), 'if the case is one based on failure to pay rent', does the court find the amount of rent due, 'together with the terms and conditions of the agreement between the parties in relation to the amount and time of payment of rent', and render a money judgment for the rent found due with 'costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease.' The practical consequence is concrete: in a pure holdover case you get possession and costs and no money, but if your lease defines the holdover charge as Rent and the tenant does not pay it, the case becomes one based on failure to pay rent and § 1-21-1008(b) reaches the charge in the same proceeding. Define the charge as Rent. The one place Wyoming names this kind of loss at all is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1014(b), which conditions a defendant's appeal bond on paying 'all damages which plaintiff may have sustained or may thereafter sustain in consequence of the wrongful detention of the premises during the pendency of the appeal' — the loss is recognized, but the statute supplies no measure for it. Now the limit, and it is a real one you should not be told the answer to. Wyoming has no liquidated-damages statute. 'Liquidated damages' appears fourteen times in the whole corpus and not once in the landlord-tenant chapter; the Title 1 hits are a garnishment provision and the structured-settlement transfer disclosures at Wyo. Stat. § 1-16-603, and nothing in Title 1 chapter 21 speaks to stipulated sums. Whether a stipulated holdover charge is enforced as liquidated damages or struck as a penalty is therefore governed entirely by Wyoming common-law penalty doctrine, which is CASE LAW. That case law was not read for this entry and is outside this library. Do not treat any figure here as cleared by a court. What you can do is draft the clause into the shape that is least exposed. Five drafting points follow from that. (1) Price the occupancy rather than substituting for damages. A term that fixes a daily price for the use and occupancy the tenant is actually taking is a different legal shape from a sum stipulated in place of damages, and the penalty objection is aimed at the second. (2) Keep the multiplier modest. States that legislate a ceiling cluster at 150% of the per diem of monthly rent, and at 100% in HUD-regulated units; a Wyoming lease that stays at or under 150% is at least in the range legislatures treat as compensatory. (3) Make it a floor, not a ceiling — preserve your right to prove actual loss instead, including what you owe an incoming tenant, rather than making the stipulated sum your exclusive remedy. (4) Never recover both the holdover charge and ordinary rent for the same day. (5) Say in the clause that the charge creates no tenancy and waives no notice. Two outside limits also apply. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases — Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property, there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110, and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct — so a charge pitched at a level no one could call compensatory is not merely unenforceable but a potential unfair-practice hook. And in a HUD-assisted unit the applicable federal model lease and program rules govern; those are federal and outside this library.

title: Home Businesses and Home Child Care
bodyText:
Wyoming has no home-based-business statute. There is no Wyoming equivalent of West Virginia's permitted-use law, and the phrases "home occupation", "home-based business", "home business" and "cottage food" appear nowhere in Wyoming law. For ordinary business use — a consultant, an online seller, a contractor storing tools, a stylist seeing clients — your lease decides, and local zoning decides on top of it. Wyoming does not protect the tenant's right to run a business from your rental, and nothing stops you restricting it.

CHILD CARE IS THE EXCEPTION, AND IT IS A TRAP IN THE DRAFTING. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-501, the only section in Title 34's Article 5 (Covenants), reads: "For residential property subject to a covenant that does not clearly and expressly prohibit child care, the provision of child care in a family day care home is a residential use of property and is a residential purpose." The section defines "family day care home" as a private residence or other structure in which day care is provided to not more than ten (10) children on a regular basis.

Read what that does and does not do. It is a construction rule about COVENANTS, and it sits in an article headed Covenants, in the chapter on conveyances — the natural target is a restrictive covenant recorded against the land, not a lease between you and your tenant. It does not grant anyone a right to run a day care; it says that where a covenant bars non-residential use without clearly and expressly prohibiting child care, child care for up to ten children counts as residential. And it carries its own escape: a restriction that DOES clearly and expressly prohibit child care is untouched.

Whether a court would treat a residential lease term as a "covenant" inside § 34-1-501 is not settled by the statute's words, and case law is outside this library's source material. So do not bet either way. The cautious course costs you one sentence and wins under either reading: if you do not want day care at the property, say so clearly and expressly, in those words, rather than relying on a general "residential use only" or "no business" clause. A general clause is exactly the kind § 34-1-501 reads around. If you are content to allow it, say that too, and set the terms — liability insurance, the number of children, parking and drop-off, and who bears the cost of any licensing or inspection.

HOMEMADE FOOD. The one business a Wyoming tenant can run from your rental with no state oversight at all is food. The Wyoming Food Freedom Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 11-49-101 through 11-49-104, exists "to allow for a producer's production and sale of homemade food or drink products for an informed end consumer" (§ 11-49-103(a)), and § 11-49-103(b) exempts compliant homemade food products from state licensure, permitting, inspection, packaging and labeling requirements. Transactions must be directly between producer and informed end consumer, occur only in Wyoming, and not involve interstate commerce (§ 11-49-103(c)). The practical consequence for you: a tenant running a home food business needs no state licence, so no regulator will ever tell you it is happening. Your lease, your inspections and your insurer are the only controls. If this matters to your property — kitchen load, grease, pests, deliveries, customer traffic, insurance — address it in the lease by name, because the Food Freedom Act will not. Currency note: 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 16 (SF0120) extended the Act to producer-raised homemade meat products and added a custom-slaughter-facility definition, with a delayed effective date contingent on the governor's certification based on federal action, so the meat provisions may or may not be operative — treat that part as uncertain.

ZONING AND INSURANCE, both outside this library. Wyoming leaves home occupations to local zoning — municipal under Title 15 and county under Title 18 — and local ordinances are not part of this library's sources. Check the city or county before allowing customer visits, signs, employees or commercial vehicles. Insurance is the other practical limit: a business run at the property can take the premises outside your landlord policy's terms, and that is a question for your insurer, not a question of Wyoming statute.

WHAT TO DO. Decide the point and write it down. A "residential use only" clause alone is not enough in Wyoming because of § 34-1-501. Name child care expressly, name food production expressly if it matters, and keep the right to require proof of any licence, permit or insurance the tenant's activity needs.

title: Why a Homestead Waiver Does Not Belong in a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming does have statutory homestead-waiver words, but they belong to a different kind of document than a lease, and putting them in your lease will not do what the clause is meant to do. Leave the waiver out.

The words exist in Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-121, titled "Conveyance and encumbrance of homesteads void unless spouse joins; exception." It says an owner or occupant of a homestead may voluntarily sell, mortgage, or otherwise dispose of or encumber it, provided the instrument of writing doing so contains in substance the words "Hereby releasing and waiving all rights under and by virtue of the homestead exemption laws of this state," and is freely and voluntarily signed and acknowledged by the owner and the owner's spouse. Read what that section governs: an instrument conveying, mortgaging, disposing of, or encumbering the homestead. A residential lease between you and a tenant is none of those things with respect to the tenant's homestead. The only carve-out is for a conveyance directly from husband to wife, which is not your situation either. So § 34-2-121 is a conveyancing formality for deeds and mortgages, not a general contract mechanism for waiving the exemption against a creditor.

The exemption itself is constitutional, not merely statutory, and that is the deeper reason to stay away. Wyo. Const. art. 19, § 9 provides that a homestead as provided by law "shall be exempt from forced sale under any process of law, and shall not be alienated without the joint consent of husband and wife, when that relation exists," subject only to taxes, obligations contracted for the purchase of the premises, and the erection of improvements on them. Rent is none of those three. And the joint-consent requirement means a waiver signed by one spouse alone is ineffective by its own terms, which is exactly the posture a lease signature page usually produces.

The statutory exemptions themselves contain no waiver provision at all. Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-20-101 through 1-20-109 neither authorize nor prohibit a contractual waiver; they are simply silent. The one exception the article does state is in Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-108(a): no property claimed as exempt under §§ 1-20-101 through 1-20-106 is exempt from attachment or sale on execution "for the purchase money of the property." Unpaid rent is not purchase money for the tenant's furniture or car, so that exception never helps a landlord. Because the article is silent on waiver, a lease term purporting to waive these exemptions sits on no authority, has to survive a public-policy challenge, and gains you nothing if it fails - the exemptions apply at execution whatever your lease says.

Know what you are actually up against when you collect, because that is the useful part. The homestead exemption is largely beside the point against a renter: Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-101 exempts a homestead up to $100,000 in value, but Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-102(a) makes it operative only while occupied as a homestead by the owner or the person entitled to it or their family, and your tenant does not own the unit they rent from you. Where it bites is if the tenant owns other Wyoming property they occupy, and note under § 1-20-102(b) that when two or more people jointly own and occupy the same residence, each gets a full exemption. Under § 1-20-104 a house trailer or other movable home counts, whether or not it still has wheels.

The personal-property exemptions are the real constraint, and they are generous on household basics. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-105, necessary wearing apparel up to $2,000 is exempt from levy or sale on execution, attachment, or any court process, excluding jewelry other than wedding rings. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-106(a), also exempt are the family bible, pictures and school books; a cemetery or burial lot; furniture, bedding, provisions and other household articles of any kind as the debtor selects, up to $4,000 in all, with a separate $4,000 exemption for each person occupying the same residence; the value in a motor vehicle up to $5,000; and up to three firearms worth $3,000 in all with up to 1,000 rounds of associated ammunition each. These stay exempt while the person or their family is moving from one Wyoming residence to another, so a move-out does not open a window. Under § 1-20-106(b), tools, team, implements or stock in trade used in a trade or business up to $4,000, or a professional's library, instruments and implements up to $4,000, are also exempt. Value is fixed under § 1-20-106(c) by three disinterested appraisers selected and sworn by the levying officer, so you do not get to assign the numbers yourself. Under § 1-20-108(b) the person claiming any of these must be a bona fide Wyoming resident.

Put all of that together and the arithmetic usually says a levy on a former tenant's household goods will not reach much. Collect the way the Residential Rental Property Act actually gives you: apply the deposit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning to move-in condition, and other contract costs, delivering the itemization on the statutory clock; pursue the balance under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b), which keeps the renter liable for damages beyond the deposit with ten percent annual interest on unpaid amounts and preserves any legal action available to you; and in a nonpayment eviction ask the court under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) for judgment for the rent found due together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease - which means your lease needs an attorney-fee clause, a term that is worth far more to you than a homestead waiver ever would be.

title: No Early Termination Right for Age, Illness or Disability
bodyText: Wyoming gives a tenant no statutory right to break a lease early because of age, illness, disability, or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. There is no physician-certification route, no sixty-day or two-month notice provision, no cap on what the tenant owes, and no rule about the death of a tenant or co-tenant either. The Wyoming statutes contain no "early termination" provision for residential tenancies at all. A tenant in that position is bound by the lease, and your remedies are the ordinary ones. What this means in practice: if a tenant tells you they must move into care, the move-out is governed entirely by your lease. The tenant stays liable for rent for the balance of the term unless the lease says otherwise or you agree to release them. Document any release in writing, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says a duty or obligation under the residential rental article may be assigned to a different party or modified only by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and a handshake release will be hard to prove. A "termination" for purposes of the deposit clock in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208 includes a voluntary termination by mutual agreement of the parties under the definition at Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(v), so the moment you agree to let the tenant out, your thirty-day itemization and refund deadline starts running off that date (extended by thirty days if there is damage to the unit, or until fifteen days after you receive the tenant's new mailing address, whichever is later). Four other things to keep in view. First, federal fair housing law still applies: refusing a reasonable accommodation, or treating a tenant worse because of disability or familial status, is a federal problem even though Wyoming's own statutes are silent here. FEDERAL: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. ss 3601-3619, including the reasonable accommodation duty at 42 U.S.C. s 3604(f)(3)(B). A request to end a lease early can itself be framed as a requested accommodation, so handle a refusal thoughtfully and in writing. Second, FEDERAL: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, 50 U.S.C. s 3955, does give a true statutory early-termination right, but only for military orders - it is not an infirmity right and it is not Wyoming law. Third, Wyoming does have one statutory early-exit, and it is unrelated to infirmity: under the Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303, a tenant who vacates because of a credible imminent threat of, or actual, domestic abuse or sexual violence has an affirmative defense to a rent claim if the seven-day written notice and evidence conditions are met, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 says that act may not be waived or modified in any lease. Do not let a request framed as a health move obscure a Safe Homes situation. Fourth, because nothing in Wyoming law forces your hand, you can decide your own policy - a written early-termination clause with a defined fee or notice period, applied consistently, is usually better business than case-by-case negotiation, and Wyoming law leaves you free to write one.

title: Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring you to give a tenant or an applicant a copy of an inspection order, a code citation or a condemnation order. There is no state housing code and no state property maintenance code to generate those orders in the first place -- the phrases "housing code," "property maintenance code" and "unfit for human habitation" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. Building and condemnation authority is delegated to municipalities: Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xxv) lets a city or town prescribe construction standards and provide for their inspection, and § 15-1-103(a)(xxvi) lets it "[p]rovide for the repair, removal or destruction of any dangerous building or enclosure." Whether an inspection regime exists where your unit sits, and whether its ordinance requires you to hand the paperwork to tenants, is a local question this library does not resolve -- check the ordinance.

One Wyoming regime does produce a condemnation order and does carry a disclosure duty, and it is worth knowing because it reaches rental housing. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d), after a hazardous material, weapons of mass destruction or clandestine drug laboratory incident, and until the incident commander declares the threat to public safety ended, the incident commander may issue an order on behalf of the political subdivision declaring any portion of a building, structure or land uninhabitable or contaminated, secure that portion, and take steps to minimize exposure. Property ordered uninhabitable or contaminated "shall only be transferred or sold prior to remediation if full, written disclosure is made to the prospective purchaser," attached to the earnest money receipt and accompanying the sale documents but not made part of the deed or recorded; the transferor must notify the incident commander within ten days of the transfer or sale, and the written disclosure releases the seller and shifts liability to the buyer unless they agree otherwise in writing.

Read that sentence carefully before you rely on it either way. It is written for a sale -- "prospective purchaser," "earnest money receipt," "sale documents" -- and the word "transferred" is not defined, so whether letting a contaminated unit is a "transfer" requiring disclosure is unsettled. The cautious course is to treat it as covered: do not re-let a unit under an uninhabitable or contaminated order before remediation, and if you let one at all, make the written disclosure to the tenant, keep it with the lease and tell the incident commander. The downside of disclosing where it was not required is nothing; the downside of not disclosing is a tenant moving into a space a government officer has declared unfit.

Your tenant will not be in the dark in any event. Under § 35-9-156(e) the order must be in writing, state its grounds, be filed with the clerk of the district court, be served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure on the owner AND any occupants of the building, and be posted conspicuously on the building. Under § 35-9-156(f) the owner OR the occupant may file an answer with the court within twenty days denying the allegations; if nobody answers the court affirms the order and fixes a time for enforcement, and if an answer is filed the court holds a hearing within eleven days (§ 35-9-156(g)) and either sustains the order and sets an enforcement date or annuls it. An appeal lies under the Wyoming Rules of Appellate Procedure (§ 35-9-156(h)). So your tenant has independent standing to contest an order on your building, and the twenty-day clock runs from service, not from when you get around to reading it. Diary that date.

Practical course: there is no general disclosure duty, so build one into your own process. Tell applicants about any outstanding order affecting the unit, put it in writing, and keep a copy in the file. The absence of a statute does not protect you from a misrepresentation or habitability claim built on what you did not say.

title: No Move-In or Move-Out Inspection Notice Rule in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no move-in walk-through, no move-out inspection, and no notice to the tenant that either is available — so there is no penalty for skipping one. There is no Wyoming counterpart to Minnesota's rule that a missed inspection notice costs you the withheld deposit twice over, or to Maryland's forfeiture of the right to withhold. The words "walk-through," "move-out," "joint inspection" and "condition of the premises" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes in a rental sense, and the only inspection language in Wyoming's residential rental article runs the other way: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) makes it a renter's duty not to "[u]nreasonably deny access to, refuse entry to or withhold consent to enter the residential rental unit to the owner, agent or manager for the purpose of making repairs to or inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale." That is a tenant obligation, not a landlord notice requirement, and Wyoming has no entry-notice statute at all.

That freedom cuts against you at move-out, because Wyoming's deposit rules are written in terms of a baseline you have to be able to prove.

• Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to "damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear" and to "the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement." Both measures are comparisons to the unit's starting condition.
• Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii) puts the matching duty on the renter: remove all property and garbage before termination "and clean the rental unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement."

Neither provision tells you how to establish what that beginning condition was. If the tenant disputes a deduction, your proof is whatever you created at move-in. So do voluntarily what Wyoming does not require: a dated, written condition report signed by both of you at move-in, with photographs or video, and the same again at move-out. Nothing in Wyoming law restricts that, and a signed report is the cheapest evidence you will ever buy.

The deposit penalty Wyoming does have attaches to the itemization and refund, not to any inspection. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) you must deliver or mail the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent, plus "a written itemization of any deductions from the deposit together with reasons therefor," without interest, within thirty (30) days after termination or within fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later — extended by another thirty (30) days if there is damage to the unit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) provides that if you "unreasonably fail" to comply with subsection (a) or the separate utilities-deposit cascade in subsection (b), "the renter may recover the full deposit and court costs." Note how that is framed: the exposure is the whole deposit, not double or treble it, and it turns on unreasonableness, which an itemization backed by a signed move-in report makes hard to establish. The same subsection gives you a shield — if you prevail and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs in addition to other relief.

Two related Wyoming notice duties exist but are not inspection notices, and should not be confused with one. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable AND requires separate written notice of that fact when the deposit is taken. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) sets the tenant-initiated condition-complaint route: the renter, if current on all payments, gives you written notice of the condition and the remedial action requested, served by certified mail or in the manner specified by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003, and within a reasonable time you must either commence corrective action or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim. Ignoring that notice, not skipping an inspection, is what exposes you under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(c) to costs, damages — including rent improperly retained or collected — and an order to repair or a court-ordered termination.

Practical course: build the move-in and move-out condition report into your own process and into the lease, keep the § 1-21-1208(a) deadlines on a calendar, and respond in writing to every § 1-21-1203(b) notice.

title: Jury Trials and Jury Waivers in Wyoming Leases
bodyText: No Wyoming statute prohibits a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and none authorizes one. Wyoming has no standard-form-contract statute making a jury or class-action waiver presumptively unconscionable, as Vermont does (9 V.S.A. § 6055): the only unconscionability provisions in the Wyoming statutes are in the Uniform Consumer Credit Code at Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-14-508 and 40-14-611, and that act's 'consumer lease' is defined at Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-206(a) as a lease of goods, so it does not reach a lease of a home. Wyoming's statute of frauds, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a), lists six kinds of agreement that must be written and signed, and waiving a constitutional right is not one of them, so Wyoming has nothing like Arkansas's rule (Ark. Code Ann. § 4-59-101(a)(7)). Two Wyoming points matter more than any of that. First, the state constitution is narrower than most. Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 9 says 'The right of trial by jury shall remain inviolate in criminal cases.' The word inviolate reaches criminal cases only; the rest of the section speaks to civil juries just to set their size at six or more. Nothing in the Wyoming constitution makes a civil jury right unwaivable. Second, and this is the practical answer, you very likely do not need a waiver to get a bench trial in an eviction. Wyoming's forcible entry and detainer article already defaults to the judge: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(a) provides that 'if neither party demands a jury, upon the return day of the summons the circuit court shall try the action,' and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1009 opens 'If a jury is demanded by either party.' So you get a bench trial by simply not demanding a jury. A lease waiver changes only one thing: whether the tenant can demand one. Be clear about what does not help you here. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties modify or reassign 'any duty or obligation in this article' by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and it is the master key to most of Wyoming landlord-tenant law — but 'this article' is article 12, the residential rental duties at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211. The jury right in an eviction comes from article 10 and from the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, not from article 12, so § 1-21-1202(d) is not authority for a jury waiver and should not be cited for one. Whether a Wyoming court will enforce a pre-dispute jury waiver signed by a residential tenant turns on case law and on W.R.C.P. 38 and 39, neither of which this library has reviewed. If you want a waiver, keep it narrow — possession only — say it operates only to the extent the law permits, put it in conspicuous type with its own signature or initial line, and never let it purport to waive any right under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211 or under the Wyoming Safe Homes Act, which Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 makes non-waivable.

title: No Key-Control or Staff-Screening Mandate in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring a landlord, of any size, to adopt a written key-control policy, to keep a key log, to limit master-key access, to rekey between tenancies, or to run criminal background checks on employees who can get into units. There is no unit-count threshold, no county-population trigger, and no enforcement provision of the kind Nevada has. The search was thorough: "rekey," "re-key," "rekeying," "master key," "keyless" and "deadbolt" return zero hits across all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws, and the word "key" in Title 1 appears only in the crime-victims chapter, about key witnesses.

Wyoming does not even require you to give the tenant a lock. There is no statutory lock, deadbolt or security-device standard. Your obligations under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) and § 1-21-1203(a) are about habitability — a safe, sanitary unit fit for human occupancy, safe common areas, and working electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. Locks are not on that list.

One real screening rule, with a gap you should know about. Property management for others is licensed activity in Wyoming under the Real Estate License Act, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-101 et seq. Anyone applying for a real estate licence must provide fingerprints and the other information needed for a criminal history record background check under Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-106(a) and § 7-19-201(a), and licences go only to people of good reputation for honesty, trustworthiness, integrity and competence under § 33-28-106(b). So if you hire a licensed management company, the licensed people in it have been checked by the state.

The gap is who is exempt. Section 33-28-103(a)(i) exempts an owner's regular employees, and § 33-28-103(a)(vi) exempts an on-site resident manager. Those are exactly the people most likely to hold a master key, and the state has not checked any of them. If you self-manage, nobody has screened your maintenance technician. That is your job, not the state's.

What to do, since nothing is mandated. Treat the Nevada model as good practice rather than law. Run a background check on anyone whose job gives access to unit keys or entry codes, and get the applicant's written authorization before you do, because the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act governs that check even though Wyoming does not. Keep master keys in a locked cabinet with a signed log of every key issued and returned. Rekey or recode between tenancies, and recover keys and deactivate codes the day an employee leaves. Record every entry into a unit. Write it down as a policy, because a written policy you follow is the thing that protects you if a tenant is burgled by someone with a key, and Wyoming's general negligence law — not a key-control statute — is where that claim will be fought.

Entry rules still apply. Wyoming has no statutory notice period for landlord entry, but Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) makes it a prohibited act for a renter to "unreasonably" deny access to, refuse entry to or withhold consent to enter the unit to the owner, agent or manager for making repairs, inspecting, and showing the unit for rent or sale. The word doing the work there is "unreasonably." That is a mutual reasonableness standard, not a licence to enter whenever you like, and the criminal trespass statute at § 6-3-303 does not shelter a landlord entering for repairs, inspection or showings. Set your own notice rule in the lease and keep to it.

Lockouts are not a key-control tool. Do not use a key or a lock change to put a tenant out. Wyoming's only self-help route is the unauthorized-occupant procedure in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, created in 2025, which runs through law enforcement and is for people who were never authorized to be there — not for a tenant in breach. Misusing it exposes you to actual damages, statutory damages of triple the fair market rental value for the period of wrongful removal, court costs and attorney fees under § 1-21-1403(c). A tenant goes out through the forcible entry and detainer process in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017.

Finally, local ordinances are not resolved here. Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), and Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) makes a more stringent local housing code prevail, so a city may have adopted a building code with lock or security-device requirements. Check yours.

title: No Penalty for a Prohibited Lease Term, But Watch the Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: Wyoming attaches no penalty to putting an unlawful term in a residential lease, for the simple reason that Wyoming does not have a list of prohibited lease terms. There is no Wyoming counterpart to Ohio's R.C. 5321.13 or Rhode Island's § 34-18-17, no section voiding confessions of judgment, exculpatory clauses, one-way attorney-fee clauses or waivers of statutory rights in a lease, and therefore no "knowing use" offence, statutory damages award or attorney-fee shift attached to using one. "Prohibited provision" and "contrary to public policy" return nothing in Title 1, and Title 1, Chapter 21, Article 12 contains no anti-waiver provision at all. The opposite is true: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that "Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." Those conditions are cumulative — explicit, written, signed — and they reach the whole of Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, which is habitability, owner duties, renter duties, deposits and abandoned property. So in Wyoming the usual question is not whether a term is penalised but whether it was properly agreed. Four real limits remain, and these are where your exposure actually sits. First, § 1-21-1202(d) says "this article." It sits in Article 12 and does not reach Article 10, so it is no authority for waiving the three-day notice to quit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 or any other Article 10 eviction procedure, and it does not reach the Safe Homes Act at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304. Second, a lease term cannot waive a right that comes from outside Article 12 — the Wyoming Fair Housing Act at Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, the assistance-animal rule at Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c), or federal law. Third, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a) makes certain agreements void unless in writing and subscribed by the party charged, including a lease for more than one year. Fourth, and this is the Wyoming-specific exposure landlords miss: the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114, has a knowing-conduct standard and is not limited to goods. "Merchandise" is defined in Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) to include "any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed," and a "consumer transaction" under § 40-12-102(a)(ii) is the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of merchandise to an individual for primarily personal, family or household purposes. The unlawful-practices section, Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a), is gated on acting "knowingly" in the course of business and in connection with a consumer transaction, and two of its paragraphs can reach lease drafting and marketing: § 40-12-105(a)(viii), representing that a transaction involves a warranty, a disclaimer of warranties, particular warranty terms, "or other rights, remedies or obligations" where the representation is false; and the catch-all at § 40-12-105(a)(xv), engaging in unfair or deceptive acts or practices. A clause that knowingly tells a tenant they have given up a right they cannot in fact give up, or an advertisement that misdescribes the unit or the charges, is the shape of claim to worry about. The remedy is real but gated: Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-108(a) gives a private action for actual damages, but only for an UNCURED practice, and Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-109 requires the consumer to give written notice stating fully the nature of the practice and the actual damage, within one (1) year of initial discovery or two (2) years of the transaction, whichever occurs first, and to sue within one (1) year of that notice. Section 40-12-108(b) allows a class action with attorney's fees to a successful class. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-113(a) lets the attorney general recover a civil penalty of up to five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) from a person who violates a permanent injunction. One shield matters: Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-110(a)(i) exempts acts or practices "required or permitted by state or federal law, rule or regulation or judicial or administrative decision" — so a lease term that does no more than what § 1-21-1202(d) expressly permits should fall outside the act. The practical course is therefore not to fear a prohibited-terms list that does not exist, but to make every modification of an Article 12 duty explicit, written and signed as § 1-21-1202(d) requires; never to draft a term that purports to waive an Article 10 procedure, a fair housing right or a Safe Homes Act right; and never to describe the tenant's rights inaccurately in the lease or in your advertising. A severability clause is still worth having, so that if a court strikes one term the rest of the lease stands.

title: What a Tenant Can Do If You Fail to Repair
bodyText:
Start with what a Wyoming tenant cannot do. There is no repair-and-deduct, no rent withholding, no rent escrow, no statutory rent abatement and no constructive-eviction statute anywhere in Wyoming law, and there is no landlord-retaliation statute at all. A tenant who stops paying rent because the furnace is broken is simply in default, and you may proceed under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002 and the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003. Do not let a habitability complaint talk you out of that, and do not invent a rent credit you are not obliged to give.

The tenant's one statutory route is a three-step ladder, and your job is to respond correctly at each rung. Step one, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b): a renter who 'is current on all payments required by the rental agreement' and 'has reasonable cause supported by evidence' may advise you in writing of the condition and specify the remedial action requested. Within a reasonable time after you receive that notice you must either commence action to correct the condition or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim. Those notices must be served by certified mail or in the manner specified by § 1-21-1003. Read the two preconditions — current on rent, and reasonable cause supported by evidence — because a tenant in arrears has not started the clock. But answer in writing anyway: a written dispute is itself a complete compliance step under the subsection, and silence is what the next rung punishes.

Step two, § 1-21-1206(b): if a reasonable time passes and you neither respond nor correct, the renter may serve a 'notice to repair or correct condition,' again by certified mail or in the manner specified by § 1-21-1003. That notice must recite the earlier § 1-21-1203(b) notice, state how many days have elapsed and that this constitutes a reasonable time, list the conditions still uncorrected, demand that they be corrected, and state that if you fail to commence reasonable corrective action within three (3) days the renter will seek redress in the courts. Three days is short. When one of these arrives, start work or get a written dispute out immediately.

Step three, § 1-21-1206(c): if you have not corrected or used due diligence to correct, or if you have told the renter the claim is disputed, the renter may sue in circuit court. The court endorses on the summons the time to appear and defend, not less than three (3) nor more than twenty (20) days from service — so you can be in court within a week. On a showing of unreasonable refusal to correct, or failure to use due diligence, the renter may be awarded costs, damages and affirmative relief as the court determines. Damages 'may include rent improperly retained or collected.' Affirmative relief may include a declaration terminating the rental agreement or an order directing you to make reasonable repairs. If the court terminates the agreement, § 1-21-1206(d) requires you to refund the balance of the rent and the deposit within thirty (30) days of the order, and the renter must vacate no sooner than ten (10) days nor later than twenty (20) days after termination.

Now the defences, which are substantial. Section 1-21-1206(a) makes the entire remedy available only to a renter 'in compliance with all provisions of W.S. 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205' and only when the agreement has not been lawfully terminated under § 1-21-1203(d). That is a strict gate: a renter who is behind on rent, who has exceeded the occupancy number in the lease, who has damaged the unit, who has interfered with another person's peaceful enjoyment, or who has unreasonably denied you access for repairs, inspection or showing, has forfeited the remedy. Document those breaches. Section 1-21-1203(c) means you need not correct any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family or the renter's guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse. Section 1-21-1202(c) takes the whole article off the table for 'breakage, malfunctions or other conditions which do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter.' Section 1-21-1203(e) provides that you are 'not liable under this article for claims for mental suffering or anguish.' And nothing in Article 12 shifts attorney's fees in either direction — § 1-21-1206(c) awards costs, not fees — so the tenant funds their own lawyer.

Two more things to know. Section 1-21-1203(d) gives you a lawful exit: you may refuse to correct the condition and terminate the agreement if the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the property or the agreement. To use it you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance and give sufficient time to find substitute housing, no less than ten (10) days and no more than twenty (20) days from the date of your notice; the rent is then prorated to the date the renter vacates and the balance plus any deposit due under § 1-21-1208 is refunded. Used properly this is often cheaper than a losing repair fight. And remember § 1-21-1202(d): any duty in Article 12 may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, with no anti-waiver provision to stop it — though the conditions are cumulative and a boilerplate waiver will not do. None of Article 12 applies at all unless the unit is the renter's principal place of residence under § 1-21-1201(a)(iv). Finally, Article 12 is not the only route a tenant has: an ordinary breach-of-contract claim on the lease and a claim under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114, both sit outside this scheme and are not limited by its gates.

title: No Insurance Mandate, and What You Can Require Instead
bodyText:
Wyoming does not require a landlord to carry liability insurance on a rental, in any amount, for any size of building. There is no rental registration scheme the state could hang an insurance condition on, no certificate to file with a municipality, and no penalty for going bare. Searching the whole corpus for any connection between a landlord and insurance turns up exactly one hit, and it is about real estate licensees. Carry insurance anyway, for the obvious reason: Wyoming also gives you very little statutory protection if something goes wrong, and nothing in the landlord-tenant article caps what a tenant or a tenant's guest can recover from you in an ordinary negligence claim.

What you can do instead is contract. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that any duty or obligation in the landlord-tenant article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in that article. Nothing in Wyoming law restricts requiring a tenant to carry renter's insurance, to name you as an additional insured, to carry a stated minimum limit, or to give you a certificate before move-in and at each renewal. No statute caps the limit you may demand or requires you to accept a particular carrier. Three cautions on how you write it. Make the requirement explicit, in writing, and signed, so it satisfies § 1-21-1202(d) if it is ever characterised as shifting a duty under the article. Remember the article only reaches a "residential rental unit," defined at § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) as the renter's principal place of residence and excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally, so for other property you are relying on ordinary contract law rather than on § 1-21-1202(d). And do not let an insurance requirement drift into a blanket exclusion of a protected class — Wyoming has its own fair housing act at §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, and a requirement applied unevenly is the kind of thing § 40-26-103 reaches.

One insurance mandate in this area does exist, and it is worth knowing which side of it you are on. Under Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-401(a), every real estate licensee must obtain and maintain errors and omissions insurance, through the commission's group program or individual coverage certified as meeting the commission's minimum requirements, and must submit proof on application, renewal or reactivation. So if you engage a licensed property manager, there is an E&O policy standing behind their work. If you self-manage, there is not: § 33-28-103(a)(i) and (a)(vi) exempt an owner's own employees and on-site managers from the licensing requirement, which means those people are also outside the E&O mandate. A landlord who manages through unlicensed staff has no statutory insurance layer at all, which is a reason to carry your own general liability cover and to consider requiring it of any contractor you engage.

Finally, local rules can exist where state law does not. Wyoming cities and counties can adopt ordinances, and an ordinance-based rental registration or insurance requirement would not appear in the state statutes. Check with your city or county before assuming nothing applies; this row resolves state law only.

title: No Landlord Lien on a Tenant's Property, With One Exception
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a residential landlord no general lien or security interest in a tenant's personal property to secure unpaid rent or damages. The phrase "landlord's lien" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code, there is no distress or distraint for rent, and Title 29, the liens title, contains no chapter for landlords of dwellings. So do not put a lien clause in a Wyoming residential lease and do not hold a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. A clause purporting to create a lien would at best be an unperfected consensual security interest in household goods, which is a federal unfair-practice problem under the FTC Credit Practices Rule, FEDERAL: 16 C.F.R. § 444.2, and holding goods you have no lien on is conversion.

THE ONE REAL EXCEPTION: HOUSE TRAILER SITES. Wyo. Stat. § 29-7-301(a) does give a lessor's lien, and landlords of mobile home lots routinely do not know it exists: "Any person leasing or renting space for a house trailer site shall have a lien on any house trailer thereon situated for unpaid lease or rental payments and for other unpaid charges due the lessor under the terms or conditions of any lease or rental agreement." Note how wide "other unpaid charges due the lessor under the terms or conditions of any lease or rental agreement" is - it picks up lease-created charges, not just rent. The mechanics: the lien becomes effective after the lessee has defaulted in payments as provided in the WRITTEN rental or lease agreement, so an oral lot tenancy does not support it; notice is given by posting written notice conspicuously on the mobile home; and the lien has priority over all other liens except a previously perfected security interest in the mobile home (§ 29-7-301(a)). Thirty days after notice you may remove the trailer from the site and keep the lien, assessing reasonable removal and storage charges against the trailer (§ 29-7-301(b)). But § 29-7-301(c) is the limit that matters most: "a house trailer shall not be removed pursuant to this section if it is occupied by the lessee. In this case the lessor has a remedy at law" - meaning you must evict first under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, and only an unoccupied trailer can be moved. Enforcement and foreclosure follow the UCC security-agreement route under §§ 34.1-1-101 through 34.1-10-104 (§ 29-7-301(d)), so this is a secured-party foreclosure with commercial-reasonableness duties, not a self-help sale. "House trailer" takes the Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-102(a)(xv) definition. This lien is for the SITE lessor. It does not help a landlord who rents out a dwelling.

WHAT YOU HAVE INSTEAD, AND IT IS BETTER THAN A LIEN. (1) The deposit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply property or money held as a deposit to accrued rent, damages, and "other costs provided by any contract" - so almost any lease-created charge is deductible if the lease creates it. Write the charges into the lease. (2) Abandoned property. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210 sets out what you may do with what the tenant leaves: on regaining lawful possession you may immediately dispose of trash and anything you reasonably believe hazardous, perishable or valueless and abandoned, and anything remaining in the unit after termination "shall be presumed to be both valueless and abandoned." Valuable property is handled on a 7-day notice (certified mail to an address the renter furnished in writing for this purpose, personal service under W.R.C.P. 4, or newspaper publication), with a further 7 days if the renter responds in writing - the statute then refers to "the additional fifteen (15) day period," which does not match the seven plus seven it has just described, so count generously and hold the goods the full fifteen days after the response. Crucially, § 1-21-1210(b) gives you payment of storage costs for the safekeeping period plus the cost of removal to storage - reasonable costs if you store it yourself, actual costs if stored commercially - and "[p]ayment of storage costs shall be made before the renter removes the property." That is a retention right over abandoned property, and it is the closest thing to a lien a Wyoming dwelling landlord has. Section 1-21-1210(c) adds that you are not responsible for loss to the renter resulting from storage. (3) Judgment collection. Sue, get a judgment, and execute or garnish.

TWO TRAPS. First, exemptions. Wyoming is a bankruptcy opt-out state: Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-109 disallows the federal 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) exemptions for a debtor domiciled in Wyoming for the 180 days before filing, so the Wyoming exemptions in Title 1 chapter 20 apply. No Wyoming statute says those exemptions cannot be waived in a contract, and no statute says they can - a lease clause waiving them is untested, and the cautious course is to leave it out, since a judgment debtor who is not told of the exemptions has ten days after seizure to claim them under the statutory notice. Second, the lien that runs AGAINST you: Wyo. Stat. § 29-2-105 gives anyone who works on or furnishes material for a tenant's improvement a lien on the LANDLORD's interest in the building and the land, if the landlord agreed to pay the cost of the improvement or the improvements were "specifically authorized by the landlord." Consent to a tenant alteration in writing, and say expressly that you do not authorize or agree to pay for the work and that the tenant must keep the property free of liens.
