This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: No rental registration in Wyoming, but three registrations can still catch you
bodyText:
Wyoming has no landlord or rental-property registration scheme. There is no filing with the county assessor as in Arizona, no state rental licence, no requirement to register a unit before it may be occupied, no tenant termination right for an unregistered owner, and no statewide business licence for residential renting. The phrase "rental registration" appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and the single occurrence of "residential rental property" in Title 1 is not a registration provision. Wyoming also has no general state business licence: the nineteen "business license" references sit in the alcohol, local government, motor vehicle, professional licensing, consumer protection and public assistance titles, none of them reaching a residential landlord as such.

Three things do require registration, and the first one can stop an eviction dead.

1. AN OUT-OF-STATE ENTITY THAT RENTS WYOMING PROPERTY. Wyo. Stat. § 17-16-1501(a) provides that a foreign corporation may not transact business in Wyoming until it obtains a certificate of authority from the secretary of state, and § 17-29-114 applies the same regime to a foreign limited liability company, which must comply with §§ 17-16-1501 through 17-16-1536 in the same manner as a foreign corporation. Section 17-16-1501(b) lists activities that do not count as transacting business, and the one landlords reach for is paragraph (ix): "Owning, without more, real or personal property." Read the words "without more". Advertising, leasing, collecting rent, maintaining the property and evicting tenants are all "more", and § 17-16-1501(c) says the list is not exhaustive. The consequence is in § 17-16-1502(a): a foreign corporation transacting business in Wyoming without a certificate of authority MAY NOT MAINTAIN A PROCEEDING IN ANY COURT IN THIS STATE until it obtains one, and § 17-16-1502(c) lets the court stay a proceeding while it decides the question and then until the certificate is obtained. That reaches a forcible entry and detainer action. Section 17-16-1502(d) adds money: liability to the state for all the fees and licence taxes that would have been imposed, plus eighteen percent interest, plus a $5,000 penalty, plus reasonable audit expenses and reasonable attorney fees, and the secretary of state may refuse the certificate until all of it is paid. Section 17-29-210(c) applies those same § 17-16-1502(d) penalties to an unregistered foreign LLC. The one piece of good news is § 17-16-1502(e): failure to register does not impair the validity of the entity's acts and does not prevent it from DEFENDING a proceeding - so your lease is still good, you just cannot sue on it. If you own Wyoming rentals through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, get the certificate of authority before you need to file anything.

2. A REGISTERED AGENT AND REGISTERED OFFICE, FOR EVERY ENTITY. Wyo. Stat. § 17-28-101(a) requires each business entity to continuously maintain in Wyoming both a registered office - at a street address in Wyoming which is a physical location where the registered agent, or a natural person with an agency relationship with the agent, can accept service of process and is physically present - and a registered agent who is either an individual at least eighteen years old residing in Wyoming whose business office is identical with the registered office, or one of the other categories the section allows. A post office box will not do.

3. SHORT-TERM RENTALS: A SALES TAX LICENCE AND THE LODGING TAX. If you rent for periods of less than thirty continuous days you are probably selling a taxable lodging service, not simply renting. Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-101(a)(xiv) defines a "transient guest" as a guest who remains for less than thirty continuous days, and § 39-15-101(a)(i) defines "lodging service" as the provision of sleeping accommodations to transient guests, including sites for tents, campers, trailers and mobile homes. Section 39-15-103(a)(i)(G) imposes sales tax on the price paid for living quarters in hotels, motels, tourist courts and similar establishments providing lodging service for transient guests, and § 39-15-104(h) adds a statewide lodging assessment of five percent on the sale of lodging services, three percent distributed under § 39-15-111(p)(i) and two percent under § 39-15-111(p)(ii). County and city lodging taxes may sit on top under § 39-15-204(a)(ii). To collect any of it you need the licence: § 39-15-106(a) requires every vendor to obtain a sales tax licence from the department of revenue, on an application stating the applicant's name and address, the names and addresses of all agents operating in the state, the character of the business and the location of all places of business, with a $60 fee for each new vendor. Thirty continuous days is the line. An ordinary month-to-month or year lease is not a lodging service; a weekend or week-long let is.

THE REAL REGISTRATION RISK IS LOCAL. Wyoming cities and towns can and do impose rental licensing, short-term-rental permits and local business licences, and nothing in state law preempts them for this purpose. Ordinances are outside what this review can resolve. Before you let a unit, check with the city or town clerk and, for anything short-term, with the county as well.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends Badly
bodyText:
POSSESSION. Wyoming’s only summary possession remedy is forcible entry and detainer, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017. It is filed in circuit court, which has exclusive original jurisdiction over it under Wyo. Stat. § 5-9-128(a)(v). Section 1-21-1002(a) lists the grounds; three matter to a residential landlord: (a)(i), against tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due; (a)(v), against a settler or occupier without color of title; and (a)(vi), against renters in violation of any terms imposed under § 1-21-1204 (the renter’s duties) or § 1-21-1205 (prohibited acts — damage, interference with another’s peaceful enjoyment, and unreasonably denying entry for repairs, inspection or showing). Keep the two three-day periods separate: the three days in § 1-21-1002(a)(i) is a grace period after rent is due, and § 1-21-1003 then requires a separate written notice to quit served at least three days before you commence the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found. You need both.

MONEY. What you can collect inside the eviction case is narrower than most leases assume. Under § 1-21-1008(a) a successful plaintiff gets a general judgment for restitution of the premises and costs — costs only. Rent and attorney’s fees appear only in § 1-21-1008(b), and only “if the case is one based on failure to pay rent,” where the court finds the amount of rent due and payable at the time of the hearing and the terms of the parties’ agreement, and renders judgment for that rent “together with costs and attorney’s fees as provided by the lease.” Read the limits. First, in a holdover or breach case that is not about unpaid rent, subsection (b) does not apply and you get possession and costs, not rent and not fees. Second, even in a nonpayment case the finding is rent due “at the time of the hearing” — this is not a vehicle for future rent or accelerated rent. Third, fees come from the lease or not at all; Wyoming has no fee-shifting statute anywhere in Articles 10 or 12. Once judgment enters, § 1-21-1012 lets the court issue a writ of restitution on the plaintiff’s request and § 1-21-1013 requires the officer to execute it within two days of receiving it, Sundays excepted, and to levy and collect the execution for rent and costs as upon other executions.

BOTH, AND SEPARATELY. You are not forced to choose. Section 1-21-1016 says the pendency of a forcible entry or detainer action does not bar an action of ejectment, and § 1-21-202(a) says the small claims remedy “is cumulative and not exclusive.” So you may take possession by FED and sue separately for money the eviction case cannot reach — future rent under an unexpired term, reletting costs, damage beyond the deposit, lease-created charges. Nothing in Wyoming law requires you to terminate before suing for rent already accrued: a suit for accrued rent is an ordinary contract action and does not itself end the tenancy.

WHICH COURT FOR A MONEY CLAIM ALONE. Three tiers. Small claims, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-201 through 1-21-205, for a claim not exceeding $6,000 exclusive of costs; you commence it by affidavit in circuit court reciting the defendant’s full address, the nature of the claim, the amount due and that demand was made and payment refused, and under § 1-21-202(b) a corporation, partnership, association or other organization may litigate in person or through authorized employees, with or without an attorney — though if you bring an attorney the other side gets a continuance to find one. Regular circuit court for any claim up to $50,000 exclusive of court costs, § 5-9-128(a)(i), which is exclusive original jurisdiction, not a ceiling you may ignore. District court above $50,000. Note the asymmetry in the FED case itself: under § 1-21-1017 a business entity may appear without a lawyer only if an owner, shareholder, member or partner appears (not an employee and not a property manager), the entity owns a majority interest, and written notice signed by every owner goes to the court and all parties — and § 1-21-1017(c) switches that off if the entity seeks more than the $6,000 small claims amount. Section 1-21-202(b) is the more generous rule, and it applies only in small claims.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT GIVE YOU. No statutory acceleration of rent and no statutory double or holdover rent — neither appears anywhere in the code. No statutory duty to mitigate your damages by reletting, and no statute excusing one either; treat mitigation as a common-law question your lease should address. No statutory late fee. No attorney’s fees except through § 1-21-1008(b) in a nonpayment case or through a separate contract suit.

TWO TRAPS ON TERMINATION. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 reverses the usual holdover rule: there is no landlord and tenant relation by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, and on expiration of a term there is no implied renewal for any period whatever, neither by the tenant holding over nor by the landlord accepting rent for the holdover period — holding over plus accepting rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance. Section 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is renewed only by express contract in writing signed by the parties, whether the original was written or oral. So accepting a check after expiry does not create a new term, and you cannot sue for a renewed term you never signed. And § 1-21-1202(d)’s power to modify duties by explicit written signed agreement is confined to Article 12 by its own words — it does not let your lease shorten or waive the § 1-21-1003 notice to quit or any other part of the Article 10 eviction procedure.

title: No Cap on Late Fees in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming does not regulate residential late fees. There is no cap, no percentage limit, no dollar limit, no mandatory grace period before a fee may be charged, no requirement that a fee be reasonable or bear a relation to your actual loss, and no requirement that the fee be disclosed in any particular way. The words 'late fee' and 'late charge' do not appear anywhere in Title 1, and the residential rental article (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) and the eviction chapter (§§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017) say nothing about them. A late fee in Wyoming is purely a creature of your lease, and it is only worth what the lease says.

That means the lease has to do all the work. Write the fee out in full: the day rent is due, the day a payment becomes late, the amount or the rate, whether it compounds or is charged once per late payment, whether partial payments are accepted and how they are applied, and whether a returned payment triggers a separate charge. If the lease does not create the charge, you cannot collect it and you cannot deduct it.

Do not confuse the three-day period in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) with a grace period for fees. That three days is a precondition to the nonpayment eviction ground — rent must be unpaid for three days after it is due before you have a forcible entry and detainer ground — and it says nothing about when a contractual late fee accrues. Your lease can make a fee accrue on day one if it says so.

Three Wyoming rules make a well-drafted late fee genuinely collectible. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to accrued rent, damages beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning to the original condition, 'and to other costs provided by any contract' — a late fee your lease creates is such a cost, so it is deductible from the deposit (subject to the 30-day itemization and the rest of § 1-21-1208, and only for a 'residential rental unit' as § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it). Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vi) makes it a renter duty to 'be current on all payments required by the rental agreement', and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 a ground for eviction — so unpaid late fees are, on the face of the statutes, an eviction ground. Be careful with that: a possession action over a small fee invites a fight and your own costs, and the cautious course is to pursue fees as money, not as a reason to evict. Third, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) requires the court in a nonpayment case to find the rent due and to render judgment for it 'together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease' — again, only if your lease provides for them.

The real limits on you are two, and neither is a number. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property, § 40-12-110 has no real-property exemption, and § 40-12-105(a) makes it unlawful to act 'knowingly' in the listed ways, including (a)(viii) misrepresenting the rights, remedies or obligations a transaction involves and the (a)(xv) catch-all, 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. A fee you advertise as one thing and charge as another, or a fee buried where the tenant could not find it, is the exposure — not the size of the fee as such. And a Wyoming court applying ordinary contract law may treat a fee grossly disproportionate to your loss as an unenforceable penalty rather than liquidated damages; that is case law, which is outside this corpus. Keep the fee defensible and documented.

Finally, the consumer credit statutes do not help a tenant here. Wyoming's Uniform Consumer Credit Code does cap delinquency charges — § 40-14-214(a) allows the greater of 5% of the unpaid installment or $10, only on an installment unpaid for ten days after its due date, and only once per installment — but that applies to a 'consumer credit sale', which § 40-14-204(a) defines as a credit sale of goods, services or an interest in land. An ordinary residential lease is none of those, and a UCCC 'consumer lease' under § 40-14-206(a) is a lease of goods only. The one place to watch is a rent-to-own or lease-purchase of the home itself: § 40-14-205(f) treats a lease in which the tenant has a purchase option and all or substantially all of the payments apply to the price as a sale of an interest in land, which can make the UCCC apply unless the credit service charge is 18% or less a year (§ 40-14-204(b)(ii)). If you offer lease-purchase, get that reviewed.

title: What Wyoming Actually Requires You to Report to Law Enforcement
bodyText: Wyoming has no crime-free housing law, no mandated crime-free or drug-free lease addendum, no statute requiring you to cooperate with police in general, no duty to give police a tenant list, keys or access, and — importantly for the other direction — no statute protecting a tenant from eviction or penalty for calling 911 or for being the subject of police calls. The words 'crime free' and 'crime-free' return zero in the entire Wyoming corpus. What Wyoming does impose are four specific duties, and three of them are criminal if you ignore them. First, child abuse. Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(a) is a UNIVERSAL mandatory reporting statute: 'Any person who knows or has reasonable cause to believe or suspect that a child has been abused or neglected, or who observes any child being subjected to conditions or circumstances that would reasonably result in abuse or neglect, shall immediately report it to the child protective agency or local law enforcement agency or cause a report to be made.' There is no occupational list to be on and no landlord exemption — you are inside it, and so is your on-site manager or maintenance technician who sees something in a unit. One qualifier is worth knowing: the statute says the fact that a child at least sixteen years old is homeless does not by itself support a neglect report. Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(b) adds that if the reporter is staff of an institution, school, facility or agency, they must also notify the person in charge, who then becomes responsible to make the report too — and expressly does not relieve the individual of reporting on their own behalf. Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(c) makes it a misdemeanor, up to six months and $750, for any employer to discharge, suspend, discipline or penalize an employee SOLELY for making a report, so do not retaliate against a technician who calls it in. Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-205(d) makes a knowingly false report, or coercing one, the same misdemeanor. Wyo. Stat. § 14-3-209 gives you immunity: anyone participating in good faith in any act required or permitted by §§ 14-3-201 through 14-3-215 is immune from civil and criminal liability, and good faith is presumed in any proceeding. Report in good faith and you are protected. Second, vulnerable adults, and here the failure to report is itself a crime. Wyo. Stat. § 35-20-103(a) requires 'any person or agency' who knows or has reasonable cause to believe a vulnerable adult is being or has been abused, neglected, exploited, intimidated or abandoned, or is self-neglecting, to report immediately to a law enforcement agency or the department, and gives good-faith civil immunity. Wyo. Stat. § 35-20-111(a) says that duty applies 'without exception'. Wyo. Stat. § 35-20-111(b) makes knowingly failing to report a misdemeanor punishable by up to ONE YEAR and $1,000 — a heavier penalty than most of Wyoming's landlord-tenant provisions carry. § 35-20-103(b) lists what to include where you know it, including the adult's name, age and address, who is responsible for their care, the nature of the condition, the basis of your knowledge and any evidence of previous injuries. § 35-20-114 is the immunity section and § 35-20-113 makes a knowingly false report a misdemeanor of up to one year. And watch Wyo. Stat. § 35-20-110: if access to the vulnerable adult is DENIED to law enforcement or the department investigating a report, the investigator may seek an injunction against the person obstructing it. A landlord who refuses entry to an investigator can be enjoined. Third, your own removal procedure. If you use Article 14, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 to 1-21-1403, to remove an unauthorized occupant, the whole mechanism runs through law enforcement: you file a sworn complaint, § 1-21-1402(b) requires ten sworn statements with (b)(x) putting the complaint under penalty of perjury under Wyo. Stat. § 6-5-303(a) — a felony — and under § 1-21-1403(a) you may ask law enforcement to stand by while you change the locks and remove property. Remember this route is CLOSED against a tenant: § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement, and § 1-21-1403(c) exposes you, and your authorized agent personally, to triple the fair market value of renting plus costs and attorney fees for misuse. Fourth, deaths. If you or your staff discover a death that appears to be a coroner's case (for example a tenant found dead from apparent violence, suicide, accident or overdose, from an unknown cause, or who had not been under a doctor's care in the last sixty days), you must report it immediately to law enforcement, who notify the coroner, and knowingly failing to do so is a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months and $750 (Wyo. Stat. §§ 7-4-104(a), 7-4-201(a)). Act on this as follows. Train anyone who enters units on the three reporting duties and on reporting in good faith rather than investigating first. Do not write a lease term that discourages a tenant from calling emergency services — Wyoming does not bar it, but it has no benefit and invites a fair-housing argument where the caller is a person with a disability or a domestic-violence victim, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(c) already bars terminating a tenancy based solely on victim status. Outside these four duties you may cooperate with police as a matter of judgment, not obligation. Where a police request goes beyond what a statute compels — tenant records, keys, entry to an occupied unit — the cautious course is to ask for a warrant, subpoena or court order, because nothing in Wyoming law authorizes you to give up a tenant's possession rights on request, and local crime-free or nuisance-abatement ordinances, which do exist in some Wyoming municipalities under Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xix), are outside this library and must be checked locally.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate to Attach to a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming has no lead law of any kind. There is no lead-safe certificate, no lead-free certificate, no inspection or clearance requirement, no registry of pre-1978 rentals, no childhood blood-lead screening statute, no abatement order power and no state lead disclosure. So there is nothing for you to obtain and nothing to attach to a Wyoming lease as an exhibit. This is a true zero, not a gap in our searching: "lead-based paint", "lead paint", "lead poisoning", "lead hazard", "lead-safe", "blood lead" and "lead level" each return nothing anywhere in the Wyoming statutes or the 2025 and 2026 session laws, and the only places the word "lead" sits near a child, a dwelling or a residence are two uses of the verb "lead to".

Your lead obligations in Wyoming are entirely federal, and they are real. FEDERAL: the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, 42 U.S.C. § 4852d, with the implementing disclosure rule at 24 C.F.R. part 35 subpart A and 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart F, requires that before a tenant is obligated under a lease for most housing built before 1978 you (1) give the EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet, (2) disclose any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the housing and give the tenant any records or reports you have about them, and (3) include in the lease, or attach to it, the prescribed Lead Warning Statement and the disclosure and acknowledgment language, signed. Keep the signed disclosure for three years. Separately, the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule, 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart E, requires a certified firm and certified renovators and the Renovate Right pamphlet for work disturbing painted surfaces above the de minimis thresholds in pre-1978 target housing. Wyoming has not been authorised to run those programs in place of the EPA, as far as this library's state-law sources show, so deal with the EPA and HUD, not with a Wyoming agency.

What that means for the lease. Use the library's federal lead disclosure form and attach it. Do NOT add a Wyoming lead-safe certificate exhibit — there is no such document, and a lease clause reciting one would be reciting something that does not exist. If you have had a private inspection or risk assessment done voluntarily, that report is a "record or report" you must give the tenant under the federal rule, so disclose it rather than filing it away.

Two Wyoming hooks worth knowing, neither of them a lead rule. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) requires the unit to be fit at the outset and § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) imposes a closed ongoing list of electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; peeling paint is not on that list, so a tenant's route in Wyoming runs through the § 1-21-1203(b) notice procedure and, for a condition that materially affects physical health or safety, § 1-21-1202(a)'s safe-and-sanitary duty — not through any lead statute. Second, if you tell a prospective tenant the property is lead-free or lead-safe and it is not, Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act can reach you: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines "merchandise" to include real property, § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct, and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110. Say nothing about lead beyond what the federal disclosure requires and what you actually know.

What fills the gap. Federal law fills it completely for pre-1978 housing. For post-1977 housing there is no lead obligation at all in Wyoming. Local ordinances are outside this library's sources; a Wyoming municipality could in principle adopt a lead ordinance, so check your city if the property is older housing in a city with its own housing code.

title: Wyoming Adds Nothing to the Federal Lead Paint Disclosure
bodyText:
Wyoming has no lead-paint law at all. Not a disclosure statute, not a state pamphlet or certificate, not a registration or inspection scheme for older rental stock, not an abatement-contractor licensing requirement, not a childhood blood-lead screening or reporting program that reaches landlords. The words "lead-based paint," "lead paint," "lead poisoning," "lead hazard," "lead abatement" and "blood lead" do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. Nothing you hand a Wyoming tenant about lead is required by Wyoming law, and there is no state form to use.

What fills the gap is entirely federal, and it binds you in Wyoming exactly as it does everywhere else. For any residential dwelling built before 1978, the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act requires you, before the tenant is obligated under the lease, to give the tenant the EPA-approved lead hazard information pamphlet, to disclose the presence of any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the unit, to provide any records or reports you have about lead-based paint or hazards in the housing, and to include in the lease a Lead Warning Statement with signed acknowledgments (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. S 4852d; 24 C.F.R. part 35 subpart A; 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart F). Keep the signed acknowledgment for three years from the start of the tenancy. Penalties are federal and are not small, and a knowing violation can expose you to treble damages. If you or a contractor disturb painted surfaces in a pre-1978 unit, the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule adds its own certification, work-practice, and pre-renovation notice requirements (FEDERAL: 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart E). Exemptions are also federal: housing built in 1978 or later, zero-bedroom units, short-term leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension, housing certified lead-free by a certified inspector, and designated elderly or disabled housing where no child under six resides.

Because Wyoming adds nothing, do not expect a state statute to tell you anything about lead, and do not let a lease template written for another state import a state-specific lead addendum, certificate, or registration recital into your Wyoming lease. A recital that your unit complies with a state lead program Wyoming does not have is at best meaningless and at worst a representation you cannot support. Use the federal disclosure form and pamphlet unmodified.

Two things this review does not resolve. A Wyoming municipality or county could adopt its own housing or lead provisions by ordinance; ordinances are outside this review and should be checked locally. And federally assisted housing carries additional lead safe housing requirements under 24 C.F.R. part 35 subparts B through R that go well beyond the disclosure rule, so if your unit takes a Housing Choice Voucher or other federal assistance, work from the program's rules rather than from this row.

One Wyoming point worth connecting. Although Wyoming imposes no lead duty by name, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) still requires you to maintain the unit "in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) forbids renting a unit unless it is "reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy." A known, unaddressed lead hazard in an occupied unit is the kind of condition a renter could use to trigger the written-notice and repair procedure in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) and then the judicial remedy in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(c). So the absence of a lead statute is not a licence to ignore a lead problem you know about; it just means your Wyoming exposure runs through the general habitability duty rather than through a lead-specific one.

title: What a Wyoming Lease Must Say
bodyText: Wyoming has no list of required lease contents. There is exactly one sentence in the statutes that tells you what a residential rental agreement must say, and it is about deposits. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 provides: any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or the owner's designated agent. Read that as two duties, not one - the statement goes in the lease, and a separate written notice goes to the tenant when you take the money. If you take only a fully refundable deposit, say so in the lease; if any part is nonrefundable, say which part, and hand over the notice at the same time you take it. Missing this is the single most common Wyoming lease-content failure, and the consequence runs through Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c): a renter may recover the full deposit and court costs where the owner unreasonably fails to comply with the deposit rules. Does the lease have to be written at all? Not always. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines a rental agreement as any agreement, written or oral, so an oral month-to-month tenancy is perfectly valid in Wyoming. But under the statute of frauds, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v), every agreement or contract for the sale of real estate, or the lease thereof, for more than one year is void unless the agreement, or some note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged. So a one-year lease may be oral; a fifteen-month lease must be written and signed by the party you want to hold to it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(i) points the same way for any agreement not to be performed within one year of its making. If you ever write a lease for more than three years, note that Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 excludes from the definition of a conveyance only leases for a term not exceeding three years - so a longer lease is a conveyance, and under Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-120 an unrecorded conveyance is void as against a later good-faith purchaser who records first. Beyond those, the rest of Wyoming's lease rules work the other way around: they do not require words in your lease, they give effect to words you choose to put there. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says any duty or obligation in the residential rental article may be assigned to a different party or modified only by explicit written agreement signed by the parties - so if you want the tenant to carry a duty the statute puts on you, the lease must say it plainly and both parties must sign. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes you maintain other appliances and facilities only as specifically contracted in the rental agreement, so what you list is what you owe. In the second sentence of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a), the requirement that each unit have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water applies unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties - that trailing qualifier belongs to that sentence, not to the first sentence of (a), which requires the unit be maintained in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation with no written-agreement escape. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) bars the renter from increasing the number of occupants above that specified in the rental agreement without your written permission, which only bites if the lease specifies a number. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to other costs provided by any contract, so a cost you never wrote down is a cost you cannot deduct. Practical course: state the deposit's refundability and give the separate notice; put the lease in writing and have both parties sign it whatever the term; specify the number of occupants, every appliance and facility you agree to maintain, every fee and charge, and who pays which utility.

title: No Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy of the Lease in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming does not require you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, sets no deadline for doing so, and gives the tenant no defense to enforcement if you never do. The phrase "copy of the lease" and "copy of the rental agreement" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and the Residential Rental Property article imposes no delivery duty. The real estate licensing law in Title 33 imposes none either, so using a broker or property manager does not add one. That said, give the tenant a signed copy anyway, because in Wyoming the written document is what your rights rest on. A lease of real estate for more than one year is void unless the agreement, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-23-105(a)(v)), and the same is true of any agreement that by its terms cannot be performed within one year (§ 1-23-105(a)(i)). Any duty or obligation under the Residential Rental Property article can be assigned to a different party or modified only by "explicit written agreement signed by the parties" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1202(d)) — so if you have shifted a maintenance duty to the tenant, you will have to produce that signed writing. An expired lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by the parties, and holding over creates no implied renewal (Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 34-2-128, 34-2-129). And eviction under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) reaches a renter who violates § 1-21-1204's duties, which include complying with "all lawful requirements of the rental agreement" — a requirement you will have to prove. There is one document Wyoming does require you to hand over: if any portion of the deposit is nonrefundable, the rental agreement must say so AND written notice of that fact must also be given to the tenant at the time the deposit is taken (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1207). That is a separate notice, not satisfied by the lease language alone. Practical course: have every tenant sign the lease, give each one a complete signed copy at signing, deliver the nonrefundable-deposit notice at the moment you take the money, and keep a signed acknowledgment of receipt in the file. None of that is compelled by Wyoming statute, but all of it is cheap, and it removes the tenant's "I never saw that term" argument in a forcible entry and detainer case that will be tried on a very short calendar.

title: No Initials Requirement for Lease Terms
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires a tenant to initial any lease term, and none requires a lease term to be in bold type, capital letters, a minimum point size or a separately signed rider to bind the tenant. There is no Wyoming equivalent of the states that make a longer-than-statutory notice period, an automatic-renewal clause or a liquidated-damages clause valid only if separately initialed. A term in your lease is enforceable on the ordinary contract footing: it was agreed to, and it is lawful.

Wyoming does not even require the lease to be written. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines "rental agreement" as "any agreement, written or oral, which establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules or any other provisions regarding the use and occupancy of a residential rental unit," so an oral month-to-month tenancy is a rental agreement with the full force of the statutes behind it.

The writing rules that do exist are about length and renewal, not about initials. First, the statute of frauds: under Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v), an agreement for "the sale of real estate, or the lease thereof, for more than one (1) year" is void unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged -- and under § 1-23-105(a)(i) the same is true of any agreement not to be performed within one year of its making. A thirteen-month lease you never reduced to a signed writing is unenforceable against the tenant. Second, renewal: Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 provides that "[n]o lease which shall have expired by its own limitation shall be again renewed except by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto, whether the original lease be written or verbal," and that no tenancy other than sufferance exists after the original lease ends unless created that way. Third, and in the same vein, § 34-2-128 provides that in Wyoming the landlord-tenant relation does not arise by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, that there is no implied renewal when a term expires, and that holding over plus the landlord's acceptance of rent "shall constitute only a tenancy by sufferance."

That combination is the practical point for a Wyoming landlord. Letting a fixed-term lease lapse and continuing to take rent does not roll the tenant into a new term or into a month-to-month tenancy on the old terms -- it produces a tenancy by sufferance, which is the weakest tenancy there is and carries none of the lease's protections for you, including any longer notice period you negotiated. If you want the lease terms to continue after the term ends, say so in a signed writing: either a renewal or extension signed by both parties under § 34-2-129, or an express holdover clause in the original lease stating what tenancy arises and on what terms.

So: initials are never legally required in Wyoming, but they remain good practice. Have the tenant initial the terms a court would call unusual -- a longer-than-ordinary notice period, an early-termination fee, an automatic renewal, a waiver, an attorney-fee provision -- not because a statute says so, but because initials make it much harder for a tenant to claim later that they never saw the term. Keep the signature page and any initialed riders with the lease and give the tenant a copy; Wyoming does not require you to furnish a copy either, and a tenant who has one argues less.

title: Recording a Residential Lease in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no lease registry and no rental registration scheme. Nothing requires you to file a residential lease with any state office, and nothing conditions any statutory right — eviction, deposit, habitability — on having filed one. There is no counterpart to American Samoa's Territorial Registrar. For an ordinary one-year apartment lease, record nothing.

What Wyoming does have is an ordinary recording act, and it draws a line at three years.

Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 defines "conveyance" for the recording chapter as "every instrument in writing by which any estate or interest in real estate is created, alienated, mortgaged or assigned, or by which the title to any real estate may be affected in law or in equity, except wills, leases for a term not exceeding three (3) years, executory contracts for the sale or purchase of lands," and certain paid-up purchase certificates. Read the exception as it is written: it is three years, not one. A residential lease of three years or less is simply outside the recording act. A lease longer than three years is a conveyance, and the recording rules bite.

For a lease over three years, three sections matter.
• Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-113 requires execution of a conveyance of land or any interest in land to be acknowledged by the party or parties executing it before a notarial officer, who must comply with Wyo. Stat. § 32-3-109.
• Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-118 makes the certificate of acknowledgment what entitles the instrument to be recorded in the office of the county clerk "in the county where the land lies." Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-119(a) adds that the clerk records originally signed documents (or properly certified copies, or electronic documents under the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act, §§ 34-1-401 through 34-1-407) and will not record until the grantee's address is supplied.
• Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-120 supplies the consequence: "Every conveyance of real estate within this state, hereafter made, which shall not be recorded as required by law, shall be void, as against any subsequent purchaser or purchasers in good faith and for a valuable consideration of the same real estate or any portion thereof, whose conveyance shall be first duly recorded." Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-121(a) is the mirror image: a recorded instrument touching any interest in lands is notice to, and takes precedence of, a later purchaser from the time it is delivered to the county clerk for record.

So an unrecorded long lease stays fully enforceable between you and your tenant — § 34-1-120 speaks only to subsequent good-faith purchasers — but a buyer or lender who records first can take free of it. If you are the landlord, that usually means the tenant, not you, carries the recording risk. Record a long lease anyway when you want the tenancy to survive a sale or a foreclosure, or when the tenant has a purchase option or a renewal right you want to bind later owners.

Separately from recording, Wyoming's statute of frauds makes the writing itself mandatory sooner. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v) makes void, unless in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged, "[e]very agreement or contract for the sale of real estate, or the lease thereof, for more than one (1) year." Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(i) adds any agreement not to be performed within one year of its making. Two different thresholds, then, and both matter: WRITE every lease longer than one year; RECORD only a lease longer than three years. Note that Wyoming's residential rental article accepts oral leases generally — Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines "rental agreement" as "any agreement, written or oral" — so for terms of a year or less the choice is yours, though a written lease is what makes almost every other right in this library usable.

One Wyoming consequence of letting a written lease simply run out: Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 reverse the usual holdover rule. No landlord-tenant relation is implied except a tenancy by sufferance, there is no implied renewal on expiration — not by the tenant holding over and not by your accepting rent — and an expired lease is renewed only by an express written contract signed by the parties. Put renewals in writing.

Finally, Wyoming has no statewide rental-registration, rental-licensing or periodic-inspection program; the terms do not appear in the statutes. Cities and towns may impose their own business licensing or rental registration by ordinance, and ordinances are outside this library — check the city where your property sits.

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText: Wyoming sets no maximum length for a private residential lease. The ninety-nine-year and other term caps you may find in the Wyoming statutes are in Title 36 (state lands) and Title 18 (county property) and do not touch a private landlord. What Wyoming does set are two thresholds you have to clear, at one year and again at three years. Over one year: the lease must be written and signed. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v) makes void 'every agreement or contract for the sale of real estate, or the lease thereof, for more than one (1) year' unless the agreement, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged. The party to be charged is whoever you are trying to hold to it, so get both signatures. Over three years: the lease becomes a conveyance of real estate. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 defines 'conveyance' to embrace every written instrument creating or assigning an interest in real estate, and expressly excepts 'leases for a term not exceeding three (3) years.' A lease longer than three years is therefore inside the recording act, and under Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-120 an unrecorded conveyance 'shall be void, as against any subsequent purchaser or purchasers in good faith and for a valuable consideration... whose conveyance shall be first duly recorded.' Under Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-121 recording is notice and takes precedence from the time of delivery to the county clerk. So for a lease over three years, have it acknowledged before a notary and record it, or record a short memorandum of lease, in the county where the property sits. If you do not, a buyer of the building can take free of the tenancy. Three formalities Wyoming does NOT require, in case you have seen them elsewhere. There is no seal: Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-125 says 'it shall not be necessary to use private seals on any instrument in this state,' and Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-126 says an unsealed writing has the same force as a sealed one. There is no rule that the owner personally sign rather than an agent; Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-104 simply lets a letter of attorney containing a power to convey lands be recorded once the owner has acknowledged it, which is what you would record alongside a long lease signed by an attorney-in-fact. And there is no trustee-consent rule. One spousal rule can bite, and only in one situation. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-121 makes a conveyance or encumbrance of a homestead void unless the instrument contains in substance the words 'Hereby releasing and waiving all rights under and by virtue of the homestead exemption laws of this state' and is freely and voluntarily signed and acknowledged by the owner and the owner's spouse, with an exception for a conveyance directly from husband to wife. A homestead is only a homestead while occupied by the owner or the owner's family (Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-102(a)), so an ordinary investment rental is not one. But if you are a married owner leasing out the home you yourself occupy or still claim as your homestead, and the lease runs more than three years so that it is a conveyance, get your spouse's signature and acknowledgment and include the release words. Finally, remember Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129: whatever term you choose, the lease will not renew itself. An expired Wyoming lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by the parties, and holding over, with or without your accepting rent, creates only a tenancy by sufferance.

title: You May Price and Write Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases Differently in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no lease-type parity rule. No statute bars terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant or the reverse, no statute caps the rent difference between lease types, and no statute limits rent increases at all. "Rent control" and "rent stabilization" return zero hits across all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws. You may charge a month-to-month premium, offer a discount for a twelve-month commitment, require a larger deposit on a short term, or attach a fee to one lease type and not the other, with no statutory ceiling on the gap.

The more surprising point is that Wyoming barely recognises the month-to-month tenancy as a legal category at all. "Month-to-month," "periodic tenancy" and "tenancy at will" appear nowhere in Title 1 or Title 34. There is no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy — no 30-day rule, no 7-day rule, nothing. Do not assume one exists. If you want a notice period, write it into the lease, because the statute will not supply one for you.

What Wyoming has instead, and it is unusual. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 says that in this state the relations of landlord and tenant do not exist by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance. When a lease term expires, there is no implied renewal "for any period of time whatever," not by the tenant holding over and not by the landlord accepting rent during the holdover. Holding over plus your acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance. Section 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is renewed only by express contract in writing signed by the parties, whether the original lease was written or verbal, and that no tenancy other than sufferance can exist after the original lease ends unless created that way.

Read together, those two sections mean a Wyoming landlord who takes rent after the term ends has not created a new month-to-month tenancy. The holdover tenant is a tenant at sufferance, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows forcible entry and detainer proceedings against tenants holding over their terms. This is the opposite of most states, and it is the single most valuable thing to know about lease types in Wyoming. Use it deliberately: if you actually want a month-to-month tenancy after the fixed term, create one by an express written agreement signed by both parties and state the notice each side must give. Do not drift into one.

Three practical consequences. First, if your lease's holdover clause says the tenancy "converts to month-to-month," that clause is doing all the work; the statute will not back it up unless both parties signed it. Second, a renewal needs signatures, so build renewal paperwork into your calendar rather than relying on an automatic rollover. Third, because there is no statutory periodic-tenancy notice, your own notice clause is the only notice rule — and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) any duty in the residential rental article can be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so your written terms carry real weight here.

Two limits to keep in mind when you do price lease types differently. Wyoming has a state fair housing act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, and § 40-26-103 protects race, colour, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin in the rental provisions. A lease-type policy applied selectively — short terms only for some households, the month-to-month premium waived for others — is a discrimination problem even though no parity statute exists. Apply the pricing the same way to everyone and keep the criteria written. And local ordinances are not resolved in this library: Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), and nothing in Wyoming law preempts local rental regulation, so check your municipality before assuming you are unconstrained.

The separate rent-timing rules that do apply to both lease types. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows a forcible entry and detainer action against a tenant after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires a separate three-day notice to quit before you file. Those are two different three-day periods stacked on each other, and they apply whatever the lease type.

title: No Minimum Type Size for a Wyoming Lease
bodyText: Wyoming sets no minimum type size, typeface, boldface or all-capitals requirement for a residential lease, for any clause in one, or for any notice a landlord gives a tenant. There is no Wyoming counterpart to N.Y. C.P.L.R. 4544, so there is no evidentiary sanction either — no rule that small or illegible print cannot be received in evidence on behalf of the landlord who prepared it, and no corresponding non-waiver rule. "Type size," "point type," "point font," "boldface," "typeface" and "capital letters" produce nothing anywhere in Title 1 or Title 34, and nothing in Wyoming's landlord-tenant law imposes any formatting requirement at all. Wyoming does have type-size rules in other consumer settings, which is why it is worth being clear they do not reach you. Wyo. Stat. § 40-19-107 and § 40-19-113 require ten (10) point bold type or an equivalently sized boxed digital disclosure for motor-vehicle liability damage waiver contracts; Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-303 requires ten (10) point boldface in written prize notices; the home-solicitation and roofing-contract cancellation notices in Title 40 require ten (10) and twelve (12) point boldface respectively. All of those are specific to their own transactions and none mentions a lease or a landlord. In practical terms the whole of Wyoming's content requirement for a residential lease is one sentence, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207: "Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or his designated agent." That is a content duty with no format attached — but note it imposes two things, a statement in the agreement and a separate written notice when the money is taken. Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v) requires a writing subscribed by the party to be charged for a lease of real property for more than one (1) year, and a lease for more than three (3) years falls inside the recording act because Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 excepts from "conveyance" only leases "not exceeding three (3) years" — two different thresholds, so do not merge them. Because nothing compels legibility, nothing protects you from the consequences of an unreadable lease either. A Wyoming court applying ordinary contract doctrine can still refuse to enforce a term the tenant could not reasonably have found or read, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) requires that any modification of an Article 12 duty be by EXPLICIT written agreement signed by the parties — a clause buried in six-point grey type is a poor candidate for "explicit." There is also the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act catch-all at Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a)(xv), unfair or deceptive acts or practices, which is gated on knowing conduct and could in principle reach a deliberately unreadable disclosure. The recommended practice, since no rule binds you: set the body of the lease in at least ten (10) point type, put the nonrefundable-deposit statement and any clause modifying an Article 12 duty in bold or in a separately initialled box, and keep a signed copy. None of that is required in Wyoming; all of it makes the terms easier to enforce.

title: How Long You Have to Sue a Tenant
bodyText:
Wyoming's limitation periods are long, and the one that matters most to a landlord is the longest. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-3-105(a)(i) an action 'upon a specialty or any contract, agreement or promise in writing' must be brought within ten (10) years after the cause of action accrues. A signed lease is a contract in writing, so you have ten years to sue a former tenant for unpaid rent, for damages beyond the deposit, and for the balance § 1-21-1211(b) says the renter still owes after you apply the deposit — plus the ten percent (10%) per annum interest that subsection adds. If there is no signed writing, § 1-3-105(a)(ii)(A) gives eight (8) years on a contract not in writing, express or implied. Get the lease signed: it is worth two extra years and a far easier proof.

The other periods you may need. Four (4) years under § 1-3-105(a)(iv) for trespass upon real property, for taking, detaining or injuring personal property, for an injury to the rights of the plaintiff not arising on contract and not otherwise enumerated — that is the ordinary negligence period — and for relief on the ground of fraud. Eight (8) years under § 1-3-105(a)(ii)(B) for a liability created by statute 'other than a forfeiture or penalty.' One (1) year under § 1-3-105(a)(v) for libel or slander, assault or battery, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment, and for an action 'upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture' unless that statute sets its own period. Ten (10) years under § 1-3-103 for recovery of the title or possession of lands. Ten (10) years under § 1-3-109 for any action not otherwise provided for. Two (2) years under § 1-3-115 for a liability created by a federal statute that sets no period of its own. Section 1-3-102 is the overriding rule: periods run from when the cause of action accrues, 'but where a different limitation is prescribed by statute, that shall govern.'

Partial payment restarts the clock, and this is the provision most worth knowing. Wyo. Stat. § 1-3-119 provides: 'When payment has been made upon any demand founded on contract or a written acknowledgment thereof, or promise to pay the same has been made and signed by the party to be charged, the time for commencing an action runs from the date of such payment, acknowledgment or promise.' Read the three triggers separately. A written acknowledgment must be written; a promise to pay must be made and signed by the party to be charged; but a payment is just a payment — no writing and no signature are required for it to restart the period from the date it is made. So a former tenant who sends you fifty dollars against an old balance hands you a fresh ten years from that date. Record the date of every payment on an old debt, keep the remittance, and never write off a balance because of its age without checking the last payment date. The same rule cuts the other way if you ever make a payment on something a tenant claims from you.

Three more provisions that quietly extend your time. Section 1-3-116: if a cause of action accrues against a person while he is out of the state, or he has absconded or concealed himself, the period does not begin until he returns or the concealment ends, and any later period of absence or concealment is not counted — a real advantage against a tenant who skips Wyoming owing rent. Section 1-3-118 is a savings statute: if you sued in time and the judgment is reversed, or you lose otherwise than on the merits after the period has run, you may commence a new action within one (1) year of that failure or reversal, and the same applies to a claim you assert as a defendant. Section 1-3-106 delays accrual: a cause of action for the wrongful taking of personal property does not accrue until the wrongdoer is discovered, and one on the ground of fraud does not accrue until the fraud is discovered. Two that can run against you: § 1-3-114 lets a person under a legal disability sue within three (3) years after the disability is removed or within any other statutory period, whichever is greater; and § 1-3-117 bars here any action already barred by the law of the state or country where it arose.

Two traps. First, if you own the building and someone is injured by a construction or design defect, § 1-3-111 is a statute of repose, not merely limitation: no action in tort, contract, indemnity or otherwise may be brought more than ten (10) years after substantial completion of the improvement against those who designed, built, altered, repaired, supplied materials for or supervised it — with § 1-3-111(b) allowing one (1) extra year where the injury occurs during the ninth year, and § 1-3-111(c) confirming it never extends a shorter period. Note its opening words, 'Unless the parties to the contract agree otherwise': your construction contract can change it, so read what you signed. Second, some claims against you carry far shorter clocks than the general ones. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act is the one to watch: under § 40-12-109 a consumer must give you written notice within one (1) year after initial discovery of the practice or within two (2) years following the transaction, whichever occurs first, and must sue within one (1) year after that notice.

One point you cannot settle from the statute. It is not clear whether a renter's claim under § 1-21-1208(c) for 'the full deposit and court costs' after you unreasonably fail to return or itemize a deposit is a 'liability created by statute' carrying eight (8) years under § 1-3-105(a)(ii)(B), or an action 'upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture' carrying one (1) year under § 1-3-105(a)(v)(D). The cautious course is to assume the tenant has eight years: keep deposit ledgers, itemizations, proof of mailing and the forwarding address for eight years, and do not treat a stale deposit claim as dead. As a general matter, keep the signed lease, the rent ledger and the move-out file for ten years, since that is how long your own best claim lives.

title: Fixed Damages Amounts in a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about liquidated damages in a residential lease. There is no provision voiding contract penalties, no test of impracticability like Oklahoma's, no cap on an early-termination fee, and no late-fee statute. The phrase "liquidated damages" appears fourteen times in the Wyoming statutes and none of them is about a lease: they are garnishment, structured settlement transfers and public contracting. "Penalty clause" appears nowhere. What governs the enforceability of a fixed damages figure in a Wyoming lease is common law — the familiar line between a reasonable advance estimate of hard-to-measure loss, which is enforceable, and a penalty designed to compel performance, which is not. That is case law, which this review could not reach, so treat the common-law rule as the real constraint and do not read the statutory silence as permission.

The statute that matters most to you is on the deposit side. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) says that on termination the deposit may be applied to accrued rent, to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, to the cost of cleaning the unit to its condition at the beginning of the rental agreement, "and to other costs provided by any contract." That last phrase is unusually generous: almost any charge your lease creates is deductible from the deposit, which means the practical question in Wyoming is rarely whether you may deduct a fixed charge but whether the charge itself would survive challenge. Write the charge into the lease explicitly, or you cannot deduct it at all.

The risk runs in one direction and it is worth taking seriously. Under § 1-21-1208(c), if you unreasonably fail to comply with subsection (a), the renter recovers the full deposit and court costs — not the disputed amount, the whole deposit. So deducting a fixed sum that a court later calls a penalty does not just cost you that sum; it can cost you everything you were holding. The itemization machinery is strict too: the balance and a written itemization with reasons must be delivered or mailed within thirty days after termination or fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by a further thirty days if there is damage to the unit. There is a counterweight — if you are the prevailing party and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs — but do not plan around it. The cautious course is to charge actual, documented loss wherever you can measure it, and to reserve fixed amounts for the genuinely hard-to-measure cases, keeping the figure to an honest estimate of your expected loss rather than a round deterrent number. Keep the arithmetic you used; it is what makes the figure defensible.

Two other Wyoming provisions bear on fixed charges. First, § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in the landlord-tenant article be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so a well-drafted damages clause is on firm statutory ground as a matter of allocation — though that section says nothing about whether the amount is reasonable, and it reaches only Article 12, not the eviction procedure in Article 10. Second, if the arrangement is really a lease-purchase of the home rather than an ordinary tenancy, the consumer credit code can take over. Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-248 provides that, apart from reasonable expenses of realizing on a security interest, an agreement for a consumer credit sale may not provide for any charges resulting from the buyer's default other than those the act authorizes, and a provision violating that section is unenforceable; § 40-14-508 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause in a consumer credit sale, consumer lease or consumer loan. Those reach a lease-option home deal through § 40-14-204(a) and § 40-14-205(f) when the credit service charge exceeds eighteen percent per year, and § 40-19-108 separately prohibits a list of terms in a rental-purchase agreement for goods. Finally, remember the Consumer Protection Act: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) brings real property within "merchandise" and § 40-12-105(a) reaches knowing deceptive practices, so a charge described misleadingly in the lease or in advertising is exposed on that front as well as on enforceability.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has nothing like the Texas opt-in lock change. There is no statute letting you change a delinquent tenant's locks, no advance-notice-and-24-hour-key-access scheme you can switch on in the lease, and no self-help repossession right of any kind for a residential landlord. Do not put a lockout clause in a Wyoming lease and do not lock a tenant out, however far behind the rent is and whatever the lease says.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN JUST UNAUTHORISED. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-306 makes it a crime: "A person is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00), if he violently takes or keeps possession of land without authority of law." The statute is not limited to strangers, and a landlord who retakes a leased unit without a court order is taking possession without authority of law. Separately, Wyoming's forcible entry and detainer jurisdiction runs both ways: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1001 lets a circuit court inquire "against those who make unlawful and forcible entry into lands and tenements and detain the same," and on such a finding "the judge shall require restitution to the complaining party." The complaining party in a lockout is the tenant. So the same chapter you use to evict is the chapter a locked-out tenant uses to get back in.

THE ONE LOCK-CHANGE POWER WYOMING DOES GIVE, AND WHY IT IS NOT THIS. The word "lock" appears exactly once in all of Title 1, at Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(a): after law enforcement has given an unauthorized person notice to immediately vacate under the new Article 14 removal procedure, the owner may ask law enforcement to stand by to keep the peace while the owner changes the locks and removes the person's property to or near the property line. That power exists only inside the Article 14 sworn-complaint route, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) shuts that route off against anyone who is a current or former tenant under any written or oral rental agreement. A tenant behind on rent is a tenant. Article 14 can never be used against them, and using it against them exposes you under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(c) to actual damages plus triple the fair market rental value, court costs and attorney fees. Do not reach for Article 14 as a shortcut around an eviction.

WHAT YOU DO INSTEAD, IN ORDER. (1) Wait out the three-day grace period. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows a forcible entry and detainer proceeding against a tenant "holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due." That is three days after the due date, and it is not a notice period. (2) Serve the notice to quit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires the party wanting to bring the action to notify the adverse party to leave the premises, served at least three days before commencing the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found. These are two separate three-day periods stacked on each other; do not merge them. (3) File the forcible entry and detainer action in circuit court under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017 and get a judgment for restitution of the premises. Only a court order and the officer who executes it put you back in possession.

FOUR THINGS A LOCKOUT CLAUSE WILL NOT SURVIVE. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d), the provision that lets the parties modify duties by explicit signed writing, sits in Article 12 and says "this article" - it is not authority for contracting out of the Article 10 notice to quit or any part of the eviction procedure. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(c), the criminal trespass section, provides that "[t]his section does not supersede W.S. 1-21-1003," so a trespass warning does not substitute for the notice to quit and does not let you treat a paying-late tenant as a trespasser. Third, Wyoming has no statute authorising you to shut off or interrupt a tenant's utilities to force a move-out, and doing it risks the same forcible-detainer exposure plus, if you are billing the tenant, the utility-regulation problems in Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI). Fourth, the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches real property under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi), and a lease clause asserting a lockout right you do not have is the kind of knowing misrepresentation Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105 is written for, subject to the pre-suit notice and cure period in § 40-12-109.

One narrow situation that is not a lockout: if the tenant has genuinely surrendered and you have regained lawful possession, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210 governs what you may do with property left behind, and § 1-21-1210(b) entitles you to removal and storage costs payable before the tenant takes the goods back. Surrender must be real - keys returned, possession given up - not inferred from a tenant being away or behind on rent.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: Wyoming lets you move almost any rental duty to the tenant, on three conditions
bodyText:
Wyoming is unusually permissive here, and the whole of the answer is one sentence. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d): "Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties."

Read what that covers. "This article" is Article 12 of Title 1 chapter 21, which runs from § 1-21-1201 through § 1-21-1211 and contains every residential duty Wyoming imposes: the owner's safe-and-sanitary and operational-systems duty in § 1-21-1202(a), the owner's duties in § 1-21-1203 (including the ongoing electrical, plumbing, heating and hot-and-cold-water list at (a)(iii) and the common-areas duty at (a)(ii)), the renter's duties in § 1-21-1204, the prohibited acts in § 1-21-1205, the renter's remedies in § 1-21-1206, the nonrefundable-deposit recital in § 1-21-1207, the deposit rules in § 1-21-1208, the successor-owner provision in § 1-21-1209, the abandoned-property procedure in § 1-21-1210 and the owner's remedies in § 1-21-1211. Subsection (d) is not limited to maintenance, and there is NO anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12 - the article was read section by section and none exists, and the only two "shall be void" provisions in all of Title 1 are the statute of frauds at § 1-23-105 and the covenant-not-to-compete section, neither of them landlord-tenant. Nothing in Wyoming requires good faith on the face of the statute, a separate signed writing apart from the lease, conspicuous type, a dollar allowance to the tenant, or a different rule for single-family homes. North Dakota's separate-writing rule and New Hampshire's precondition for common-area garbage have no Wyoming counterpart: "separate writing" and "separate written" both return zero in Title 1.

THE THREE CONDITIONS ARE CUMULATIVE AND THEY ARE THE WHOLE PROTECTION. The agreement must be (1) EXPLICIT, (2) WRITTEN, and (3) SIGNED BY THE PARTIES. Each does work. Explicit means the duty being moved is named - "Tenant is responsible for maintenance" is not explicit as to anything; "Tenant is responsible for replacing furnace filters monthly and for clearing snow and ice from the front walk and the driveway" is. Written rules it out of an oral tenancy: § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines a "rental agreement" to include an oral agreement, so a Wyoming tenancy can be perfectly valid orally while shifting no duty at all. Signed by the parties means both signatures; a landlord cannot shift a duty unilaterally, and a house-rules sheet handed over at move-in, an unsigned addendum, or an email will not do it. If you want the shift, put it in the body of the lease both parties sign, or in an addendum both parties sign and the lease incorporates.

WHAT IS SENSIBLE TO SHIFT, AND WHAT IS NOT. Routine upkeep moves cleanly: lawn care, yard work, snow and ice clearing on the areas serving the tenant's unit, filter changes, light bulbs, smoke-alarm batteries, drain care, garbage to the kerb. Wyoming has no statute on any of these - "lawn" returns zero in Title 1 and all ten Title 1 "snow" hits are in the ski-safety act - so they are governed entirely by your lease. The duties you should think twice about shifting are the ones in § 1-21-1203(a)(iii): electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. They are shiftable in law, but a tenant has neither the access nor the competence to maintain a furnace or a water heater, and a landlord who shifts them is usually just creating an argument about causation after a failure, with § 1-21-1203(c) already protecting you against conditions the renter or the renter's family, guests or invitees caused by inappropriate use or misuse. The better use of § 1-21-1202(d) is to extend your coverage, not to retreat: § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes "other appliances and facilities" your duty only "as specifically contracted", so listing an appliance in the lease creates a duty you did not otherwise have. If you do not want the duty, do not list the appliance.

FOUR LIMITS YOU MUST HOLD IN MIND.

First, § 1-21-1202(d) says "this article" and sits in Article 12. It is NOT authority to waive or shorten anything in Article 10, the eviction procedure - not the § 1-21-1003 three-day notice to quit, not the § 1-21-1002 grounds, not the appeal bond.

Second, Article 12 only applies where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence: § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" that way and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis. Outside that definition there is no statutory duty to shift, and your lease is the only source of obligation in either direction.

Third, shifting a duty under the statute does not shift liability to a third party. A guest, a neighbour or a passer-by injured by uncleared ice is not party to your lease, and § 1-21-1202(d) moves the statutory duty between you and the tenant, not your exposure to the world. Carry insurance and say so to yourself before you hand snow clearing to a tenant on a busy frontage.

Fourth, § 1-21-1209 binds the holder of the owner's interest at the time of termination to §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208 - the deposit recital and the deposit accounting - so a buyer inherits those two whatever the parties agreed. If you sell, make sure your purchaser has the signed lease, because the duty allocation in it is the only record of what was moved.

title: No Energy Conservation Charge Notice Rule
bodyText:
Wyoming has nothing resembling an energy-efficiency or conservation charge attached to a rental meter, and therefore no landlord notice duty and no tenant rent deduction tied to one. The pattern in other states — the utility recovers the cost of a conservation or weatherization improvement through a surcharge on the meter, the landlord must tell each new tenant about it before the lease is signed, and the penalty for not telling is that the tenant may deduct the charge from rent — does not exist in the Wyoming code. There is no statute requiring you to disclose a conservation charge, a weatherization loan, an energy improvement assessment, a PACE-style assessment or any other energy-related amount appearing on the tenant’s utility bill, and no statute giving a tenant any rent offset for one.

What the code actually contains. “Energy conservation” appears only in Title 9, in the Wyoming energy conservation improvement program, Wyo. Stat. §§ 9-12-1201 and 9-12-1202 — a voluntary Wyoming business council program supporting energy performance contracts for facility owners, with no application to residential rentals and no charge passed to any occupant. “Weatherization” appears only in Title 42, in Wyo. Stat. § 42-2-501, the low income home energy assistance program administered under federal P.L. 97-35. That section directs that at least 25 percent of program funding go to weatherization assistance for residential dwellings only — needs assessments and audits, caulking, insulation, storm windows, furnace modification and replacement, water heater repair or replacement, and other measures the department finds necessary — with eligibility at the lesser of 215 percent of the federal poverty level or 60 percent of state median household income. It is a grant benefit to the household, not a charge, and it creates no landlord notice duty and no lien or repayment obligation in the statute. The phrase “conservation charge” appears nowhere, “conservation” within 100 characters of “meter” returns nothing, and “rent deduction” appears nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes.

The only statutory utility surcharge in Wyoming runs the other way and is not yours to disclose. Wyo. Stat. § 37-18-102 authorizes the Public Service Commission, where a public utility shows it will incur incremental costs to comply with the reliable and dispatchable low-carbon energy standard, to let the utility collect a surcharge from customers of not more than two percent of each customer’s total electric bill. That is a regulated rate component billed by the utility to its own customer; it is not a landlord charge, it carries no landlord notice duty, and if the tenant holds the utility account it is simply part of the tenant’s bill.

What this means for you. If you want to pass through an energy improvement cost, a conservation program charge or an efficiency-upgrade cost, no Wyoming statute lets you do it and none forbids it — it is purely a lease matter. Write it as an itemized additional charge in the rental agreement, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct from the deposit “other costs provided by any contract,” which rewards a clearly drafted charge and gives you nothing for one you never wrote down. Two cautions. First, if the improvement is an appliance or facility you now promise to maintain, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) turns that promise into an ongoing statutory duty — the duty exists only “as specifically contracted,” so do not contract for more than you intend. Second, do not try to recover the cost by metering and selling the utility commodity itself to tenants: Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) withdraws the landlord’s public-utility exemption for metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity to tenants, and the only carve-outs are water allocation at (H)(VIII) and (IX) and retail electricity sold for electric vehicle charging at (H)(X).

title: Meth Labs and Contaminated Property
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant or an applicant that the property was used as a methamphetamine lab, was contaminated, or has or has not been remediated.
