There is no pre-lease meth disclosure, no posted-notice regime, no duty to report a known or suspected lab to the police, and no penalty for leasing without a disclosure. Wyoming also has no seller-disclosure act for real estate generally. But it does have a clandestine-laboratory regime, and the parts that bite a landlord are the ones about money and possession, not disclosure.

What Wyoming actually has. 'Clandestine laboratory operation' is defined at Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-1058(a)(ii) — procuring chemicals, supplies, equipment or a location for the illegal manufacture of controlled substances, transporting them, setting up, or distributing or disposing of the chemicals, equipment, supplies or products. Under the Wyoming Emergency Response Act, §§ 35-9-151 through 35-9-159, the discovery of hazardous materials related to such an operation is an 'incident' (§ 35-9-152(a)(iv)), every incident involving a clandestine laboratory must be investigated as a crime until shown otherwise (§ 35-9-156(c)), and the incident commander may order that any portion of the building, structure or land is uninhabitable or contaminated, secure it, and take steps to limit exposure (§ 35-9-156(d)).

Read § 35-9-156(d) carefully, because two protections in it are for COMMERCIAL property only. The duty to confine the declaration to the affected areas rather than condemning the whole property, and the duty to give the owner written notice describing the extent of the contamination with specificity, are both written for 'commercial real estate' and the 'commercial real estate owner'. A residential rental can be declared uninhabitable in its entirety, and the specific written notice is not owed to you. What you do get is process: § 35-9-156(e) requires the order to be in writing, to state its grounds, to be filed with the clerk of the district court, to be served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure on the owner and any occupants, and to be posted conspicuously on the building; § 35-9-156(f) gives you twenty days from service to file an answer denying the allegations, and if you do not, the court affirms the order and fixes a time for enforcement; § 35-9-156(g) requires a hearing within eleven days of the answer; § 35-9-156(h) allows an appeal. Twenty days is the whole of your window — diary it the day you are served.

The money. Under § 35-9-158(a), the governing body must first claim remediation expenses against the party responsible for the lab and must apply any directly related asset-forfeiture proceeds to offset them. Only then may a claim be made against you as owner, and only through the court: the law enforcement agency accounts for the expenses and presents them to the court for approval (§ 35-9-158(a)(i)), and the court allows them to the extent they exceed what was recovered from the responsible party (§ 35-9-158(a)(ii)). The sentence that matters most to a landlord is in (a)(ii): if the owner 'did not know or could not with reasonable diligence have known' of the clandestine laboratory operation, the amount recoverable from the owner is capped at one percent of the fair market value, as determined by the county assessor, of the portion of the building, structure or land declared uninhabitable. If you did know, or should have, there is no cap. The allowed amount becomes a lien on the real property, and if you do not pay within six months after the court approves it, the sheriff may sell the property under court order as on execution (§ 35-9-158(a)(iii)). The clear lesson: respond to tenant and neighbour reports of chemical smells, unusual traffic and blacked-out windows, document what you did about them, and inspect when your lease allows — that record is what buys you the one-percent cap.

The one real disclosure duty, and its limit. The last part of § 35-9-156(d) says property ordered uninhabitable or contaminated 'shall only be transferred or sold prior to remediation if full, written disclosure is made to the prospective purchaser, attached to the earnest money receipt if any', and the disclosure must accompany the sale documents but not form part of the deed and must not be recorded. The seller or transferor must notify the incident commander of the transfer or sale within ten days. Receipt of the full written disclosure is a full release of the seller's liability and an acceptance of liability by the buyer, unless they agree otherwise in writing. Everything about the wording — purchaser, earnest money receipt, sale documents, deed, buyer — points at a conveyance rather than a lease, so this is probably not a leasing disclosure. But the operative word is 'transferred or sold', and a lease transfers a possessory interest. The cautious course, and the one we recommend, is: never re-let property that is under an unremediated uninhabitable order (occupying it is what the order forbids), and if you ever let contaminated property after an order is lifted or before one issues, give the tenant the same full written disclosure in writing before signing and keep the acknowledgement.

Two gap-fillers. First, the remediation standards are set by the state emergency response commission under § 35-9-153(h) — agency rules, which are outside this library; get the current standard before you certify anything as cleaned. Second, silence is lawful but a lie is not: the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing (merchandise includes real property, § 40-12-102(a)(vi); no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110), and § 40-12-105(a) makes it unlawful to act knowingly in the listed ways, including the (a)(xv) catch-all 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'. Telling an applicant the unit was never a lab, or that it was remediated, when you know otherwise is squarely within it. Local ordinances may add duties and are outside this corpus.

title: No Military Airport or Noise Zone Disclosure Required in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming requires no military air installation disclosure in a residential lease. There is no noise zone or accident potential zone disclosure, no military impact district, no distance-based disclosure around a named installation, and no thirty-day or other termination right triggered by one. The phrases 'accident potential zone', 'clear zone', 'noise zone', 'military impact', 'airport hazard' and 'airport approach' each return zero across the whole Wyoming corpus, and 'avigation' with a word boundary returns zero as well. Nothing changes this for F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Cheyenne, which is the installation a Wyoming landlord is most likely to be near. If anything, Wyoming has stepped back from it: Wyo. Stat. § 19-7-301(a) cedes EXCLUSIVE jurisdiction to the United States over the territory the United States owns within F.E. Warren Air Force Base and over later additions held for military purposes. Land inside the base is federal; land outside it is ordinary Wyoming land with no special lease duty attached. The only Wyoming airport land-use statute is a local enabling act, and it does not reach you. Article 3 of Title 10 chapter 5, Wyo. Stat. §§ 10-5-301 et seq., lets a municipality or county regulate by ordinance the number of stories, size of buildings and height of structures within one-half mile of the boundaries of airports OWNED OR CONTROLLED BY the town, city or county, and lets them zone airspace beyond that half mile to assure reasonable safety on approach and departure, confined to the current FAA approach zone and in no case extending beyond six nautical miles along the approach path from the end of the instrument runway. Read the three limits in that sentence carefully: it reaches municipally or county-owned airports, not military bases; it authorizes building-height and bulk regulation, not a disclosure to a tenant; and it operates through a local ordinance you would have to look up, because local ordinances are outside this library. Wyoming also has no general seller or landlord disclosure act to fall back on, so there is no residual statutory duty here either. What to do anyway. Two things make a short voluntary disclosure worth including when the property is genuinely affected by military or civil aircraft noise, overflight or a published approach path. First, Wyoming's silence does not create a licence to conceal: the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases, because Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include property 'real, personal or mixed', there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110, and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct, with the (a)(xv) catch-all available. A knowing misstatement about noise, or a knowing silence in the face of a direct question, is the exposure — not the omission of a form Wyoming never required. Pre-suit notice and a fifteen-day cure window apply under Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-109 and 40-12-102(a)(ix). Second, a plain written acknowledgment that the tenant is aware of aircraft noise and overflight, signed at the same time as the lease, costs you nothing and forecloses the argument later. Write it as a statement of fact and an acknowledgment, not as a waiver of habitability, and do not claim it is a statutorily required disclosure, because it is not. Finally, keep the federal layer in view: aircraft noise and overflight themselves are governed by federal aviation law and by the installation's own air installation compatible use zone study, neither of which is Wyoming law and neither of which is in this library.

title: Naming a Minor in a Wyoming Eviction
bodyText:
Wyoming runs the opposite way from Ohio, Minnesota and Illinois. There is no bar on naming a minor as an eviction defendant, no dismissal penalty, no fee award and no sealing rule. Wyoming instead has an express statute saying a minor CAN be sued, with one procedural step you must not skip.

Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-102, "Minors as parties to actions", reads: "Every person over fourteen (14) years of age and under the age of majority, when subject to no disability other than being a minor, may sue or be sued. When plaintiff he shall sue by a next friend selected by him before suit is commenced. The next friend is liable for the cost chargeable to the plaintiff. When the minor is sued he shall appear by guardian nominated by him and appointed by the court before further proceedings are had in the case, but judgment shall be against the minor defendant only. In either case, if plaintiff or defendant neglects or refuses to nominate a next friend or guardian, the court shall appoint a next friend or guardian, who shall file his consent in writing, with the court."

Four things follow for an eviction.

One: a tenant over fourteen and under eighteen may be named. The age window is literal — "over fourteen", so a person aged exactly fourteen or younger is outside the section. Nothing elsewhere in Wyoming law supplies capacity for someone that young, so do not name a child of fourteen or under as a defendant; name the adult tenant and treat the younger child as an occupant who leaves under the writ with the household.

Two: the case stops until a guardian is appointed. The statute says the minor "shall appear by guardian nominated by him and appointed by the court BEFORE FURTHER PROCEEDINGS ARE HAD IN THE CASE." In a forcible entry and detainer action, where Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1004 sets trial not less than three nor more than twelve days after service, that appointment is exactly what will blow your trial date. If the minor neglects or refuses to nominate, the court appoints, and the appointee must file written consent — more delay. Budget for it, or avoid the issue by not naming the minor at all when an adult tenant is on the lease and the minor is not.

Three: the judgment reaches the minor only. "[J]udgment shall be against the minor defendant only." Naming a minor does not give you a judgment against the parent, so there is no money reason to add a minor to the complaint. A writ of restitution removes the household from the premises; you do not need every occupant named to recover possession.

Four: this is the general civil-practice rule, in Title 1 Chapter 1, and the forcible entry and detainer chapter adds nothing about minors. Nothing in §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017 mentions minors at all.

CAN AN 18-TO-20-YEAR-OLD SIGN A LEASE? Yes, with no qualification. Wyo. Stat. § 14-1-101(a) makes eighteen the age of majority, at which "an individual reaches the age of majority and as an adult acquires all rights and responsibilities granted or imposed by statute or common law", and § 14-1-101(d) says "[a]ny competent adult may enter into a binding contract and shall be legally responsible therefor." Wyoming has no higher contracting age for housing and no youth-specific lease rule.

LEASING TO SOMEONE UNDER 18. Three routes make a minor capable of signing. Under Wyo. Stat. § 14-1-201(a)(i) a minor who is or was married, or who is in the military service of the United States, is emancipated by status, with no court order needed. The third route is a decree: under § 14-1-203 a district court may emancipate a minor who is at least seventeen, willingly lives apart from his parents with their consent or acquiescence, manages his own financial affairs, and whose income is not from unlawful means or from public assistance under § 42-2-104; the court holds a hearing within sixty (60) days of filing, with ten (10) days' certified-mail notice to the minor and the parents. Section 14-1-202(a)(i) then states exactly what the decree does, and it covers everything you care about: it recognises the minor as an adult for entering into a binding contract, suing and being sued, buying or selling real property, and establishing a residence, and under (a)(ii) and (a)(iii) it terminates parental support, control and tort liability.

That last point is the one to weigh. An emancipation decree cuts off the parents' liability, so emancipation makes the minor able to contract but takes the parent away as a source of recovery.

THE CAUTIOUS COURSE. Wyoming has no statute on a minor disaffirming a contract — "disaffirm" appears four times in the whole corpus and the only Title 14 use is § 14-1-101(c), about consent to health care, not leases. Whether an unemancipated minor could walk away from a Wyoming lease is a common-law question and case law is outside this library's sources, so we will not guess. Practically: do not lease to an unemancipated minor. If you choose to, get a copy of the emancipation decree, the marriage certificate or the military orders and keep it with the file, and have a creditworthy adult sign as a co-tenant or guarantor regardless — a guarantor's promise stands on the guarantor's own capacity, not the minor's.

title: No Wyoming Mold Disclosure, and What to Do Instead
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no mold disclosure. There is no state mold statute at all: no disclosure duty, no state mold pamphlet or information sheet, no permissible-exposure or remediation standard, no licensing of mold assessors or remediators, and no notice you owe a tenant about mold either at signing or when a problem appears. The word "mold" does not appear in the Wyoming statutes in this sense anywhere. Do not import a mold addendum from a state that does require one, and in particular do not include a recital that you have given the tenant "the mold information approved by the state," because Wyoming approves none and the recital would be false.

That said, mold is not outside Wyoming law; it just arrives through the general habitability duty rather than through a mold-specific rule, and the Residential Rental Property Act gives you a workable framework if you use it.

Your side of it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires you to maintain the unit "in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires that you not rent the unit unless it is "reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy," that you maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition, and that you maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. A roof leak, a failed supply line, or a plumbing defect that produces persistent mold is squarely within those duties. Note also Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(c): the article does not apply to breakage, malfunctions, or other conditions "which do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter." Cosmetic surface mildew on a bathroom grout line is not the same thing as a chronic water intrusion, and the statute's own threshold is physical health or safety of the ordinary renter.

The tenant's side, which is where mold claims usually turn. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a) obliges the renter to maintain the unit in a clean and safe condition, to maintain all plumbing fixtures in a condition as sanitary as the fixtures permit, and to use all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) is the provision to know: you are not required to correct or remedy any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, or the renter's guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse of the property during the rental term or any extension of it. Mold caused by a tenant who never runs the bathroom fan, blocks vents, dries laundry indoors, or lets a tub overflow and says nothing is a condition you are not obliged to fix.

The procedure matters as much as the duty. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b), a renter who is current on all payments and has reasonable cause supported by evidence to believe the unit fails the health and safety standards must advise you in writing of the condition and specify the remedial action requested; within a reasonable time after receiving that notice you must either commence action to correct the condition or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim. Those notices go by certified mail or in the manner specified by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. Answer in writing, every time, and keep the copy. If you dispute, say so in writing rather than going silent, because silence is what moves the renter to the next step: a "notice to repair or correct condition" under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(b), which gives you three days to commence reasonable corrective action, and then a civil action under § 1-21-1206(c) in which a court may award costs, damages, and affirmative relief including an order to repair or a declaration terminating the agreement. One statutory comfort: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(e) provides that you are "not liable under this article for claims for mental suffering or anguish" - which takes the emotional-distress component off a mold claim brought under the article, though not off an independent tort claim. And if the cost of repair exceeds what would be reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse the repair and terminate instead, on written notice giving the renter no less than ten and no more than twenty days to find substitute housing, with rent prorated and the balance and deposit refunded.

So draft for the gap rather than disclosing into it. Put a moisture clause in the lease that does the work the absent statute does not: require the tenant to ventilate, to run exhaust fans when bathing or cooking, to keep the unit reasonably heated in winter, not to block vents, and above all to give you prompt written notice of any water intrusion, leak, standing water, or visible mold growth. Tie the notice obligation to Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii)'s duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, so a tenant who conceals a leak for months has breached a lease term and not merely been careless. Document the unit's condition at move-in with dated photographs, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) puts the cause of the condition in issue and photographs are how you win that question. Where you do know of a past water event or a prior remediation, disclose it in writing even though no statute makes you: it costs nothing, it undercuts a later claim that you concealed a known defect, and it is consistent with the § 1-21-1203(a)(i) duty not to rent a unit that is not reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for occupancy.

Flagged and not resolved: a Wyoming municipality or county could address mold or moisture through a local housing code, and local ordinances are outside this review.

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid Utility or Cleanup Bill Lands on Your Property
bodyText: Wyoming has no single utility-lien statute, and no provision anywhere that protects you when the tenant, not you, is the account holder. Whether a tenant's unpaid bill can reach your land depends entirely on which body supplied the service, and the answers differ sharply. City or town sewer service: no lien. Wyo. Stat. § 15-7-509(a) says that if a sewerage service charge is not paid within thirty days after it is due, the amount, together with a penalty of ten percent and a reasonable attorney's fee, may be recovered in a civil action by the city or town. That is a lawsuit against the person who owes the charge, not an encumbrance on your title. Sanitary sewer district: yes, effectively. Wyo. Stat. § 35-3-122 lets a district's board of trustees set connection charges and rates for each person whose premises are served, and then provides that if the service charge is not paid when due, the sum may be recovered in an action for the recovery of money OR it may be certified to the county assessor and assessed against the premises served, and collected or returned in the same manner as other district taxes. Read that disjunctive carefully: the district chooses. If it certifies, your tenant's unpaid sewer bill arrives as a charge against the premises, collected like a tax, and your name is on the tax bill. The same section also lets the district contract with whoever supplies water so that water is turned off and refused to any user more than forty-five days delinquent on sewer rental or service charges, with notice of the discontinuance by registered mail - which can leave your unit without water on a tenant's default. Surface water drainage utility: yes, by statute. Wyo. Stat. § 16-10-110 provides that if any service charge is not paid within thirty days after it is due, the charge plus a ten percent penalty and a reasonable attorney's and collection agency's fee shall constitute a lien against the land served and may be recovered in a civil action against the landowner by the governing body. Note the two halves of that sentence: a lien on the land, and a personal action against the landowner - this one names you, whoever used the service. Garbage, rubbish and weeds: yes, in city-manager municipalities. Wyo. Stat. § 15-4-204, which sits in Title 15 Chapter 4 Article 2 and so applies in cities and towns with the city manager form of government, says that if the owner OR occupant deposits or allows the accumulation of garbage, offal, manure or rubbish of any kind, or permits weeds to grow and remain, in violation of any statute or ordinance, the manager serves notice on the occupant, or the owner or the owner's agent; if it is not removed within one day after service, the manager has it removed, and the cost of removal shall be assessed against the property and constitutes a lien thereon, collected like other special assessments. The one-day window and the fact that notice may go to the tenant alone are the trap: you can first learn of it when the assessment appears. Other municipalities have the general power to declare and abate nuisances under Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xix), and counties abate under Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-115 (which has its own twenty-day objection procedure and creates no statutory lien), so the mechanism outside city-manager towns is a matter of local ordinance. Water line extension agreements: a lien you sign up for. Under Wyo. Stat. § 15-7-601, landowners who want the city water system extended agree to pay a stipulated amount in installments for up to ten years regardless of use or nonuse, and to make the charges a lien on their lands; once the agreement is filed with the city or town clerk the charges become a lien. Check for one before you buy. Practical course: put every utility account you can in the tenant's own name directly with the provider, but understand that in Wyoming this does not by itself protect the property - there is no statute, as there is in some states, saying a lien shall not attach where service was contracted for by the tenant, and no affidavit you can file to cut off your liability. So also (1) ask each provider, in writing, whether it certifies delinquent charges against the premises, (2) require the tenant to show proof the account is open in their name and to notify you of any shutoff notice, (3) make the tenant contractually responsible for utilities, trash removal and yard upkeep in the lease and for reimbursing you for any charge assessed against the property on their account - under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) you may apply the deposit to other costs provided by any contract, so this has to be written down to be deductible - and (4) drive by. A cheap monthly look at the yard beats a lien you learn about from the county. LOCAL ORDINANCE: municipal nuisance, trash and utility billing ordinances vary and are not resolved here.

title: The Three-Day Notice Before Filing for Nonpayment in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming's nonpayment notice is short, plain and unforgiving about timing. Two separate three-day periods have to run before you file. First, forcible entry and detainer lies against a tenant only "after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1002(a)(i)), so rent must be at least three days late. Second, "[t]he party desiring to commence an action for forcible entry or detainer must notify the adverse party to leave the premises involved. The notice shall be served at least three (3) days before commencing the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003). Serve the notice no earlier than the fourth day after rent was due, then wait the full three days before you file. There is no prescribed wording. Wyoming has no statutory form, no state-agency form, no required bold or conspicuous type, no font-size rule, no warning or rights-advisory you must copy out, and no mediation program you must go through first. It also has no notice-service fee ban, no rule adding days for mailing, and no once-per-twelve-months limit on a tender-of-rent defense — none of those regimes exists in Wyoming. Watch the service method, because it is narrower than landlords expect: § 1-21-1003 authorizes leaving a written copy with the tenant, or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found. It does not authorize mail, and it does not authorize posting on the door. Compare § 1-21-1203(b), where the legislature did expressly allow certified mail for a habitability notice — it knew how to say so and did not say so here. So hand the notice to the tenant; if you genuinely cannot find the tenant, leave a written copy at the home or the workplace; and keep a dated, signed proof of service describing exactly what you did. Sending an extra copy by certified mail costs nothing and may help, but do not let it be your only service. Understand what this notice is. It is a notice to leave, not a pay-or-quit notice: Wyoming gives the tenant no statutory right to cure by paying within the three days, and nothing obliges you to take late rent. If you choose to accept payment and keep the tenant, do it in a signed writing that says the tenancy continues on the existing terms, because Wyoming has no statute on the effect of accepting rent after a notice to quit. Write the notice so a judge can see it is good: name the tenant and the premises, say the rent is unpaid and how much and for what period, state plainly that the tenant must leave the premises, date it, sign it, and state that it is given under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003. Then the rest of the calendar: the summons states the cause, the time and place of trial, and must be served not less than three nor more than twelve days before the trial date the judge sets (§ 1-21-1004); if the court finds the complaint true it enters judgment for restitution and costs, and in a nonpayment case also finds the amount of rent due and payable at the hearing (§ 1-21-1008(a), (b)); and unless the tenant appeals, the officer executes the writ of restitution within two days (§ 1-21-1013). Nothing in Wyoming law lets the lease substitute for the statutory notice or waive it, so serve it in every nonpayment case even when the lease says otherwise.

title: Out-of-State Owners and In-State Agents
bodyText:
Wyoming does not require a nonresident individual who owns rental property here to name a Wyoming agent in the lease, file a designation with any office, or do anything else before renting the property out. There is no statute conditioning your right to sue a tenant on having made such a designation, as several states do. Search the statutes for "nonresident owner," "nonresident landlord" or an out-of-state owner's agent and nothing in the landlord-tenant law comes back.

You also do not have a withholding problem. Wyoming imposes no individual income tax, so there is no rule requiring a tenant or a property manager to withhold state tax from rent paid to an out-of-state owner. The state constitution contemplates the possibility -- Wyo. Const. art. 15, § 18 provides that no tax shall be imposed upon income without allowing full credit for sales, use and ad valorem taxes paid in the same year -- but no income tax has been enacted, so there is nothing to withhold.

A tenant does not need your in-state agent to reach you in court. Under Wyo. Stat. § 5-1-107(a), a Wyoming court may exercise jurisdiction on any basis not inconsistent with the Wyoming or United States constitution, and § 5-1-107(b) allows service outside the state under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure. Owning and renting property in Wyoming will support jurisdiction; being out of state is not a shield, and you should not treat the absence of an agent-designation statute as one.

Two Wyoming rules do bite out-of-state owners, and both are easy to miss because neither is in the landlord-tenant article.

First, if you hold the property in an entity rather than in your own name -- an LLC, a corporation, a limited partnership -- Wyo. Stat. § 17-28-101(a) requires every business entity to continuously maintain in Wyoming both a registered office at a street address that is "a physical location where the business entity's registered agent, or a natural person who has an agency relationship with the registered agent, can accept service of process ... and is physically present at that location," and a registered agent, who must be an individual at least eighteen who resides in Wyoming, a domestic business entity, or a foreign business entity authorized to transact business here, in each case with a business office identical to the registered office. A post office box will not do, and letting the registered agent lapse puts the entity's good standing at risk. Most out-of-state owners of Wyoming rentals are in this category, and this -- not a landlord-tenant statute -- is the in-state agent requirement that actually applies to them. An out-of-state entity must also obtain a certificate of authority from the secretary of state before transacting business here; owning property "without more" does not count, but leasing it and collecting rent likely do, and until it has the certificate it may not maintain a proceeding in any Wyoming court, including an eviction, though its leases remain valid and it may defend a suit (Wyo. Stat. §§ 17-16-1501, 17-16-1502, 17-29-114; see `edu-landlord-registration-wy`).

Second, watch who can accept your tenant's notices. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) defines "owner" to mean the owner, lessor or sublessor, and then adds: "for purposes of notice and other communication required or allowed under this article, 'owner' includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement." So if you use a Wyoming property manager, a notice your tenant gives the manager is a notice to you by operation of statute -- including a notice of defective conditions under § 1-21-1206 and the forwarding-address notice that starts the deposit clock under § 1-21-1208(a) -- and the only way out is an express written carve-out in the rental agreement itself, made by the agent or manager. If you are out of state and relying on a manager, this is a feature, not a bug: it is what lets your tenant deal with someone locally. But make sure the manager actually forwards what they receive, because the statute has already treated it as served on you.

Practical course: if you own through an entity, keep the § 17-28-101 registered agent current. Whether or not you must, put your name and a mailing address for notices in the lease, and name your Wyoming manager if you have one -- there is no statute requiring the disclosure, and a tenant who does not know where to send a notice is a tenant who will say they sent it somewhere you did not see.

title: Charging a Tenant for Preparing or Serving a Notice in Wyoming
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute authorizes, sets or caps a fee for preparing or serving an eviction notice, and none forbids one. Utah and Idaho both have statutes that permit a notice-service fee and limit it; Wyoming has no such provision, so a notice fee in a Wyoming lease is pure contract with no statutory backing.

Start from what Wyoming's notice actually costs you. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 is the whole of it: "The party desiring to commence an action for forcible entry or detainer must notify the adverse party to leave the premises involved. The notice shall be served at least three (3) days before commencing the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found." Three days, a written copy, hand delivery to the tenant or to the usual place of abode or business. No form is prescribed, no sheriff or process server is required, no filing is involved and no fee is set. You can serve it yourself, so the real cost is usually a sheet of paper and a trip. A flat "$75 notice fee" is hard to defend as a reasonable estimate of that.

Who needs the notice, and when. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a), forcible entry and detainer is available against "tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due" (paragraph (i)), and separately "[a]gainst renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205" (paragraph (vi)) — the tenant-duty and prohibited-act sections. Read the two three-day periods separately: paragraph (a)(i) is a three-day grace after rent comes due before the cause of action exists at all, and § 1-21-1003's three days is the notice period that must then run before you file. They stack.

The better route to recovery, and the one Wyoming actually blesses, is the lease fee clause the eviction judgment picks up. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) directs that in a case based on failure to pay rent the court "shall render judgment in accordance with the findings for the amount of rent found due, together with costs and attorney's fees AS PROVIDED BY THE LEASE." The phrase "as provided by the lease" attaches to the fees. Without a lease clause you get nothing; with one, your attorney's fees and costs of pursuing the eviction come back in the judgment, which covers far more than a notice charge would. Note the limit: subsection (b) is for nonpayment cases. In a case under § 1-21-1008(a) on other grounds the court renders judgment for restitution and costs, and fees depend on your lease and the court.

If you still want a notice charge in the lease, three cautions. First, tie it to your actual, documented cost — a process server's invoice or certified-mail charge — rather than a round number, because Wyoming has no statute authorizing a flat fee and a charge above your real loss risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty (case law is outside this library). Second, do not double-recover: if the court awards you costs or fees for the same notice, waive the contractual charge. Third, do not treat the unpaid notice fee as rent and build the next eviction on it; Wyoming does not define "rent," and an eviction resting on a disputed fee rather than on rent is a weak case. Bill it, or deduct it at termination under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), which permits applying the deposit to "other costs provided by any contract."

One more Wyoming point that interacts with notice. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) makes "owner" include a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager for purposes of notice and other communication under the residential rental article, unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement. So notices your manager gives and receives count, which removes one common reason landlords pay someone else to serve papers.

title: The Three-Day Notice to Quit Cannot Be Waived or Shortened
bodyText: Do not put a notice-to-quit waiver in a Wyoming lease. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 says that 'The party desiring to commence an action for forcible entry or detainer must notify the adverse party to leave the premises involved. The notice shall be served at least three (3) days before commencing the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found.' That is a condition on your right to start the case, directed at you as plaintiff, and nothing in it is made subject to the rental agreement. Four things make that reading hard to argue with. First, the Wyoming legislature plainly knows how to let a lease override a statute and did not do it here. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) ends 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties'; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) ends 'unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement'; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 has no such clause. Second, the master key does not fit this lock. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets 'any duty or obligation in this article' be reassigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and it is how most Wyoming landlord-tenant defaults get changed — but 'this article' is article 12, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211. The notice to quit lives in article 10, the forcible entry and detainer article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017. Section 1-21-1202(d) is not authority to waive it and should not be cited for that. Third, the legislature has twice blocked an end run around this section. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(c), in the criminal trespass statute, says in full: 'This section does not supersede W.S. 1-21-1003.' And the 2025 unauthorized-occupant removal procedure at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, which lets an owner ask law enforcement to remove a squatter immediately, is closed to tenants: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) and (b)(v) require that the person be 'not a current or former tenant pursuant to a written or oral rental or lease agreement authorized by the owner, the owner's predecessor or the owner's authorized agent,' and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(c) exposes an owner who uses it wrongly to restoration of possession, actual damages, triple the fair market rent for the period of wrongful removal, costs and attorney fees. Fourth, a waiver would not help you anyway, because the obligation runs to the court's power to order restitution, not to the tenant personally. Remember the separate second three days. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) lets you proceed against a tenant 'after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due' — that is a grace period before a cause of action exists, and it is not the same three days as the notice. On nonpayment the two stack: rent is due, three days pass, then you serve the notice to quit, then three more days pass, and only then may you file. The lease cannot shorten either period, because both are in article 10. What you may lawfully do: give more notice than three days; require the tenant to give you notice of intent to vacate; state a service address; and make clear that any contractual default-and-cure notice in your lease is in addition to, not instead of, the Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 notice.

title: No Content Rules for a Wyoming Notice to Quit, and No Ban on Work While One Is Pending
bodyText:
Wyoming has neither of the rules this topic asks about.

There is no required warning on a notice-to-vacate document. Wyoming has no statute like Kansas's, which makes a bold-type warning mandatory when a landlord's move-out form carries terms that are not already in the lease and voids the added terms without it. The phrases "notice to vacate" and "intent to vacate" do not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes or constitution, and nothing in Title 1 or Title 34 sets type size, boldface or required language for any landlord-tenant notice. That does not make a surprise term in a move-out form safe. A term added to a form the tenant signs on the way out is still a contract modification, and ordinary contract defences — lack of consideration, lack of assent, unconscionability — are where a tenant will attack it. If you want the tenant to agree to something new, put it in a separate signed document that says plainly what it is.

There is no rule against doing work while a notice is pending. Wyoming has no statute forbidding alterations or repairs that make a unit uninhabitable while a notice to vacate is outstanding, and no equivalent of the District of Columbia's regime. "Uninhabitable" and "unfit for habitation" appear 12 times corpus-wide, 11 of them in Title 35 and the twelfth in the crime-victims chapter cross-referencing Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-156(d) — none is a landlord-tenant restriction.

What Wyoming actually requires of your notice to quit is very little. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 says the party desiring to commence a forcible entry or detainer action must notify the adverse party to leave the premises involved; the notice must be served at least three days before commencing the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant, or at the defendant's usual place of abode or business if the defendant cannot be found. That is the whole section. No prescribed form, no prescribed words, no type size, no certified mail. Keep the notice to the facts — who, which premises, that they must leave, the date — and keep proof of how and when you served it.

Keep the two three-day periods apart. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) permits forcible entry and detainer against tenants holding over their terms, or after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due. That is a grace period that has to run before the default matters. Section 1-21-1003 is a separate three-day notice that has to run before you file. They stack; do not count them as one.

Your habitability duties do not pause because a notice is outstanding. Nothing in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211 suspends the owner's duties under § 1-21-1202(a) or § 1-21-1203(a) while a notice to quit, a holdover or an eviction case is pending. While the tenant is still in possession the unit must still be reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, the common areas must still be maintained, and the electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water must still work. Do not start a renovation around a tenant who has not yet left.

There is one lawful way to stop repairing and end the tenancy, and it has its own procedure. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse to correct a condition and terminate the rental agreement if the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement. You must notify the tenant in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the tenant's notice of noncompliance, and you must give the tenant no less than 10 days and no more than 20 days from the date of your notice to find substitute housing. On termination, prorate the rent to the date the tenant vacates, refund the balance, and return the deposit under § 1-21-1208. Done properly this also closes off the tenant's statutory remedies: § 1-21-1206(a) makes those remedies available only when the rental agreement "has not been lawfully terminated pursuant to W.S. 1-21-1203(d)." Done improperly — by simply letting conditions decay — it does the opposite, and § 1-21-1206(c) lets a court award the tenant costs, damages (including rent improperly retained or collected) and affirmative relief, including an order to repair or a declaration terminating the lease.

The cautious course. Serve a plain § 1-21-1003 notice with nothing extra in it. Keep any new agreement on a separate signed page. Keep repairing until the tenant is actually out. And if a repair is genuinely uneconomic, use the § 1-21-1203(d) route in writing, with the 10-to-20-day window, rather than letting the unit deteriorate.

title: Nuisance Abatement and Your Exposure as the Owner
bodyText: Wyoming has four separate nuisance regimes that can reach a landlord, and in three of them the ORDER IS SERVED ON THE OWNER, not just on the tenant whose conduct caused the problem. None of them requires you to put anything in a lease — Wyoming has no counterpart to Nevada's requirement that a lease summarise the nuisance statute — but all four are reasons to have a nuisance covenant and to act on complaints. First, and most serious, the criminal nuisance article at Wyo. Stat. §§ 6-6-201 through 6-6-208. Section 6-6-201 provides that whoever maintains, uses, OWNS OR LEASES any structure for the purpose of lewdness, assignation, prostitution or gambling, or for the manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of intoxicating liquor or any controlled substance in violation of law, is guilty of a nuisance — and the structure, the ground it sits on, and the furniture, fixtures and contents are declared a nuisance and shall be enjoined and abated. Note the verbs: owning or leasing the structure is enough to be inside the definition. Under Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-202 the county attorney OR ANY CITIZEN OF THE COUNTY may sue in the name of the State to perpetually enjoin the nuisance, the person maintaining it, AND the owner or agent of the building or ground — so a neighbour can bring you into court, and the court shall allow a temporary writ on presentation of a petition alleging the nuisance exists. Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-203 makes evidence of the general reputation of the place admissible to prove the nuisance, and taxes costs to a citizen complainant only where the court finds there was no reasonable ground for the action. If the nuisance is established, Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-204 requires an order of abatement as part of the judgment: removal and execution sale of the movable property used in conducting the nuisance, and CLOSURE OF THE STRUCTURE for a period the court specifies — your building, shut, with no rent coming in. Breaking and entering a closed building is punishable under Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-208. Your way out is Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-206: if the OWNER appears, pays all costs of the proceeding and files a bond with approved sureties in the full value of the property, conditioned on immediately abating the nuisance and preventing its recurrence for a time the court specifies, the court may cancel the order of abatement as to the property if satisfied of the owner's good faith — but the release does not clear any judgment, lien or liability the property is already subject to. And Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-207 assesses a tax of three hundred dollars ($300.00) against the building, the ground and the owner or agent whenever a permanent injunction issues, assessed by the county assessor within three (3) months, collected like any tax, and a PERPETUAL LIEN on all property used to maintain the nuisance. Appearing and bonding under § 6-6-206 is therefore the step that saves the building. Second, the fire-hazard nuisance at Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-9-111 through 35-9-113. A building is a public nuisance if it is especially liable to fire and endangers people, buildings or property in the vicinity; the state fire marshal, county fire warden or a fire chief shall order it repaired, torn down or demolished. The order must be in writing, state its grounds, be filed with the clerk of the district court, be served on the owner AND any occupants under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure, and be posted conspicuously on the building. You have twenty (20) days under § 35-9-112 to file an answer with the court clerk denying the allegations; if you do not, the court affirms the order of condemnation and fixes a time for enforcement. If you do answer, § 35-9-113 gives a hearing within twenty (20) days of the filing. Third, the public health nuisance at Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-105(a)(vii): the owner or occupant of private property on which a nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness exists must remove it at his own expense within forty-eight (48) hours after being ordered to do so by health authorities. Willful failure is an offence under § 35-1-105(b), punishable by a fine up to one hundred dollars ($100.00) or imprisonment up to six (6) months, or both, and leaves you liable for all expense the health authorities incur in removing it — and conviction does not relieve you from a damages action by anyone injured. Forty-eight hours is a very short fuse; treat a health-authority notice as urgent. Fourth, local abatement. Counties: Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-101(a)(viii) lets a board of county commissioners declare and abate nuisances it determines threaten health or safety, and Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-115 sets the procedure — standards fixed by resolution first, then a written order describing with specificity the nature of the nuisance and the steps required for abatement, filed with the district court clerk, served on the owner or occupant under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure and posted on the property, with twenty (20) days to answer, a hearing within twenty (20) days of the answer, and appeal under the Wyoming Rules of Appellate Procedure. Municipalities: Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xix) lets a city or town declare and abate nuisances and fine parties who create, continue OR PERMIT nuisances to exist — permitting is enough, and the detail is in local ordinances, which you must check where the property sits. Several things other states have, Wyoming does not. There is no nuisance receivership taking the rents ahead of the mortgage; no statute making you a necessary defendant so the court can order the lease terminated; no drug-nuisance suit by tenants or neighbours that escrows rents, suspends subsidies or seals the property; and no requirement that your lease summarise any criminal statute. Your tools are ordinary ones, and they are good ones if you use them. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) already makes it a prohibited act for a renter to "interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a) denies the renter's statutory remedies to anyone not in compliance with § 1-21-1205 — so a nuisance tenant loses the habitability remedies as well. Put an express nuisance and unlawful-use covenant in the lease, act on the first credible complaint and document what you did, and if a § 6-6-202 action is filed, appear and bond under § 6-6-206 rather than waiting for the closure order.

title: Terms Wyoming Law Leaves to Your Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a landlord unusually wide drafting freedom, and it builds that freedom into the statutes themselves. There is no statutory list of prohibited lease terms, no anti-waiver provision anywhere in the residential landlord-tenant article, and no 'void as against public policy' clause aimed at leases. What there is instead is a set of places where the statute expressly makes the result depend on what your lease says. Those are your levers, and if you leave them blank the default usually runs against you.

The master lever is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d): 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' That reaches the whole of Article 12 — habitability, owner duties, renter duties, deposits, abandoned property. Three conditions are cumulative: explicit, written, and signed by the parties. A general 'tenant accepts the premises as is' recital will not satisfy them. Name the specific duty you are shifting. Note the limit of its words: it says 'this article', and it sits in Article 12, so it is not authority to waive the § 1-21-1003 notice to quit or anything else in Article 10's eviction procedure.

Seven more lease-dependent provisions, each worth a deliberate decision. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes you maintain 'other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement' — appliance maintenance is opt-in, so every appliance you list is a duty you take on and every one you omit is a duty you do not have. Second, § 1-21-1204(a)(v) bars the renter from increasing the number of occupants 'above that specified in the rental agreement' without your written permission; if you specify no number, you have no occupancy limit. Third, § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit be applied to 'other costs provided by any contract,' which means almost any charge your lease creates is deductible and any charge it does not create is not. Fourth, § 1-21-1202(a) makes the hot-and-cold-running-water requirement subject to being 'otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties.' Fifth, § 1-21-1201(a)(i) provides that for notice and other communication under the article 'owner' includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager 'unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement' — so your manager is a valid recipient of a tenant's habitability notice by default, and note carefully that it is the agent or manager who must specify otherwise, in the rental agreement itself. Sixth, § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines the 'residential rental unit' to include 'any other area or facility provided to the renter in the rental agreement,' so writing a storage locker, yard, shop or barn into the lease pulls it inside your habitability and maintenance duties; leave out what you do not intend to maintain. Seventh, § 1-21-1210(a)(i)(A) lets you serve an abandoned-property notice by certified mail to 'an address furnished to the owner by the renter in writing specifically for this purpose' — collect that address in the lease, on its own line, with those words, and you will have a cheap service route later.

Two terms are not optional. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires that 'Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable,' and separately that written notice of that fact be given to the renter when the deposit is taken. That is the only mandatory recital in Wyoming's landlord-tenant law, and it is two duties, not one. And under the statute of frauds, § 1-23-105(a)(v), every agreement for the lease of real estate 'for more than one (1) year' is void unless it or a memorandum of it is in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged — so a two-year oral lease is unenforceable. Section 1-23-105(a)(i) adds the same requirement for any agreement not to be performed within one year, and § 1-23-105(a)(ii) requires a writing for 'every special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person,' which is your guarantor or co-signer: get the guaranty in writing and signed by the guarantor, not just by the tenant.

Finally, keep in mind what switches the whole scheme off. Section 1-21-1201(a)(iv) limits Article 12 to a unit that is the renter's principal place of residence and expressly excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis. Outside that definition you get no statutory habitability, deposit or abandoned-property framework at all, and your lease is the only law between you — which is a reason to draft it fully, not a reason to relax. And although § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines 'rental agreement' to include an oral agreement, § 1-21-1202(d) requires a signed writing to modify any duty, so nothing you agree verbally will shift a statutory obligation.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meters
bodyText:
California requires three pre-signing disclosures that often travel together — a former ordnance location near the property, a pending demolition permit, and a tenant's meter that also serves areas outside the unit. Wyoming requires none of them. There is no Wyoming lease-disclosure statute for any of the three, and no general pre-signing disclosure provision in the landlord-tenant article to borrow from. Each strand still has something worth knowing.

Ordnance. The word "ordnance" does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes, nor do "unexploded," "munitions," "military ordnance" or "former military." There is no state registry of formerly used defense sites and no duty to tell a tenant about one. If you happen to know the property sits on or near a former range or ammunition site, say so in writing anyway and keep the acknowledgement. Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches real property under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on acting "knowingly," which is precisely your position once you know. Federal cleanup records on formerly used defense sites are maintained by the Army Corps of Engineers and are a federal matter outside anything Wyoming law requires of you.

Demolition. No Wyoming statute requires you to disclose a demolition plan or permit application to a tenant, or to give any particular advance notice before demolishing. Two consequences follow. First, your lease has to do the work: Wyoming has no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy, so if you may need possession for demolition or redevelopment, build in a termination right with a notice period you can live with, or you will be negotiating for a surrender. Second, do not assume Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) is a demolition exit. It lets you refuse to repair and terminate when repair costs exceed what is reasonable in light of the rent and the nature of the property, but it is reactive — the right and its ten-to-twenty-day substitute-housing period both run from your receipt of the renter's written notice of noncompliance under § 1-21-1203(b), and a renter must be current on all payments to give that notice. It is not a provision you can invoke because you have decided to redevelop.

There is one demolition rule that genuinely helps, and it is money from someone else. If a public agency is behind the acquisition, rehabilitation or demolition, the Wyoming Relocation Assistance Act of 1973, Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-7-101 through 16-7-121, treats a displaced residential tenant as a displaced person: § 16-7-102(a) covers a person displaced from real property on which they are a residential tenant as a direct result of rehabilitation, demolition or other displacing activity in an agency program where the displacement is permanent. Under § 16-7-105 the displacing agency must pay a tenant who lawfully occupied the dwelling for at least ninety days before negotiations began, in an amount sufficient to rent a comparable replacement dwelling for up to forty-two months, capped at $5,250, with the computation for a low-income person taking their income into account, and the tenant may elect to apply it to a down payment instead. Advisory services come with it under § 16-7-106. This is the agency's obligation, not yours. Tell your tenant it exists and point them at the agency; it costs you nothing and it is the difference between a cooperative move-out and a fight.

Shared meters. Wyoming has no shared-meter disclosure duty — "shared meter," "shared utility," "single meter," "submeter" and "individually metered" all return nothing. But Wyoming regulates the underlying conduct harder than most states, so the practical rule is stricter than a disclosure rule would be. Under Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI), furnishing electricity, gas, water or steam for the use of your tenants is outside the definition of a public utility, except that "[s]uch exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." The only carve-backs, at (H)(VIII) and (H)(IX), both begin "Metered and other direct sales of water," so they cover water alone, and (VIII) applies only where the metering is solely to allocate usage among tenants and carries no additional fees or charges. So if a tenant's meter also serves a common area, a laundry room or another unit, do not simply pass the bill to that tenant: you are selling them a utility commodity you supply, and in Wyoming that is the thing that costs you the exemption. Put common-area and shared service in your own name and your own account, or fold it into rent as a flat amount, and say in the lease exactly which utilities the tenant pays and which you pay.

title: Facilities Wyoming Requires Beyond the Basic List
bodyText:
Wyoming's landlord-tenant article is short on supplied facilities. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires only that you not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; that you maintain common areas sanitary and reasonably safe; that you maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water; and that you maintain other appliances and facilities "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." There is no statutory requirement for window screens, storm windows, a mail receptacle, a telephone jack, trash receptacles, window shades, a minimum number of electrical outlets, minimum window sizes, water-closet ratios or an elevator. None of those words appears in the landlord-tenant law, and most appear nowhere in Wyoming's statutes at all.

But Wyoming has one old, live and widely overlooked facilities mandate that falls squarely on apartment landlords, and it is enforced by criminal penalty. It is in Title 35, it never uses the word "landlord," and it is easy to miss for exactly that reason.

FIRE ESCAPES ON BUILDINGS OF THREE OR MORE STORIES. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-501 requires that every building used in whole or in part as - among other things - a hotel, apartment house, boarding house or tenement house, three or more stories in height, "shall be provided with safe and suitable metallic, tunnel, iron or fireproof ladders or stair fire escapes with guard rail of sufficient strength, attached to the outside walls thereof and extending from or suitably near the ground to the uppermost story thereof, with platforms not less than six by three (6 x 3) feet," positioned near the windows of each story above the first so that access from each story is easy and safe. The same section imposes a posting duty on "every proprietor, custodian, superintendent or person or persons having charge and control" of the building: post notices in every hall and in a public and conspicuous place designating where on each floor the fire escapes are located.

TWO WAYS OUT IN SMALLER BUILDINGS WITH TWELVE OR MORE ROOMS. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-502 requires that every apartment house, boarding house or tenement house two stories or less in height having twelve or more rooms be provided with at least two stairways, hallways or means of exit or escape from each story. Count rooms, not units - the trigger is twelve or more rooms in the building.

KEEPING THEM USABLE, AND THE RED LIGHT. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-504 requires that all such ladders, stair fire escapes, stairways, hallways or means of egress "shall at all times be kept free from any obstruction, in good repair and ready for use; and at night, or where lights are necessary in the daytime, a red light shall be provided with the words inscribed thereon 'FIRE ESCAPE'." That is a maintenance duty and a lighting-and-signage duty, and it runs continuously, not just at installation.

THE PENALTY IS REAL AND IT COMPOUNDS. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-506 makes every person, firm or corporation, or its agents, officers, directors or trustees, "owning or having the management or control of" such a building guilty of a misdemeanor for failing, neglecting or refusing to comply - punishable by imprisonment in the county jail for not less than three nor more than six months, or a fine of not less than $100.00 nor more than $500.00, or both. The compliance deadline the section recites is October 1, 1917, so there is no grace period left. And the last sentence is the one that bites: "Each month or fraction thereof in which any building designated in this act shall remain in violation thereof shall constitute a separate offense." The exposure accumulates monthly.

THE EXEMPTION TO CHECK FIRST. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-507 provides that §§ 35-9-501 through 35-9-507 "shall not be applicable in any incorporated city or town that has by ordinance adopted a uniform building code which provides among other things adequate and safe means of inside fire escapes, smoke towers and fireproof inclosed stairways and further fixes the types of occupancies and types of buildings subject to the said code." So in most incorporated Wyoming municipalities with an adopted building code, the local code displaces this article entirely - but the exemption is conditional on what the ordinance actually provides, and it does nothing for a building in an unincorporated area. Find out in writing which regime your building is under before you rely on either. Local ordinances are outside this review.

WHAT ELSE FILLS THE GAP. Because Wyoming's statutes are thin here, three other things do the work. First, your lease: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes any facility beyond the named four your duty only if the rental agreement specifically contracts for it, so listing a facility is what creates the obligation - and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets you assign or modify any Article 12 duty by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Second, local building, fire and housing codes, which under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) prevail where more stringent than the state codes. Third, fair housing: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(i) requires you to permit a disabled tenant's reasonable modification at the tenant's expense, with a rental carve-out allowing a restoration condition "when it is reasonable to do so," and § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation in rules and policies - so a facility you are not obliged to supply generally may still have to be permitted for a particular tenant.

Remember the gate on Article 12: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally. The §§ 35-9-501 to 35-9-507 fire escape duties have no such limit - they turn on the building, not on the tenancy.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Agency rules, model codes, case law, court rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: No owner move-in statute, and in Wyoming you do not need one at the end of a term
bodyText:
Wyoming has no owner move-in or owner-occupancy termination statute, in either direction. Nothing gives you a statutory right to end a tenancy so that you or a relative can occupy the unit, and nothing conditions, limits or penalises such a termination - no notice content rules, no relocation payment, no minimum occupancy period, no re-offer obligation, no holding period. The phrases "owner occupancy", "intends to occupy" and "personal use" are absent from the Wyoming statutes, and none of the twenty-five "just cause" references is a tenancy provision. Wyoming also has no just-cause eviction law at all, which is the reason the statute is missing: there is nothing for an owner-occupancy exception to be an exception to.

AT THE END OF A TERM YOU NEED NO REASON AND NO CLAUSE. Two Wyoming provisions make this unusually clean. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that in Wyoming the relation of landlord and tenant does not exist by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, that on the expiration of a term created by lease, verbal or written, there is NO implied renewal for any period whatever - not by the tenant holding over and not by the landlord accepting compensation or rent during the holding over - and that such holding over and acceptance of rent constitute only a tenancy by sufferance. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that no lease which has expired by its own limitation may be renewed except by express contract in writing signed by the parties, whether the original lease was written or verbal, and that no tenancy other than sufferance exists after the original lease ends unless so created. So a fixed-term Wyoming lease simply ends on its last day. You do not have to give a reason, and you do not have to invoke any clause. If the tenant stays, the tenant is a tenant at sufferance and you proceed under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i), which allows forcible entry and detainer against tenants holding over their terms, after serving the three-day notice to quit required by § 1-21-1003 - a written copy left with the tenant, or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found, at least three days before you commence the action. Circuit court has jurisdiction under § 1-21-1001.

MID-TERM IS DIFFERENT, AND THE LEASE IS YOUR ONLY SOURCE OF A RIGHT. Wyoming gives you no statutory route to cut a fixed term short so you can move in. If you want that option you must reserve it in the lease before it is signed, and the library's optional Owner Occupancy clause does exactly that. Nothing in Wyoming law forbids such a term: § 1-21-1201(a)(v) defines "termination" to include expiration of the rental period, voluntary termination by mutual agreement, termination under § 1-21-1203(d), abandonment and termination by court order, and Wyoming's permissive § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties allocate Article 12 duties by explicit written signed agreement. But be realistic about what the clause buys you: it gives you a contractual right to end the term, not a way to take possession. If the tenant does not leave on the termination date, your route is still a forcible entry and detainer action, with the three-day notice to quit. Wyoming's Article 14 removal procedure for unauthorized occupants, §§ 1-21-1401 to 1-21-1403, cannot be used - § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement, and § 1-21-1403(c) exposes an owner who misuses it to triple the fair market value of renting plus fees.

PERIODIC TENANCIES: BEWARE THE ASSUMPTION. There is no statutory notice period for ending a month-to-month tenancy in Wyoming - "month-to-month", "periodic tenancy" and "tenancy at will" all return zero in Titles 1 and 34. Do not assume a thirty-day rule exists. Whatever notice your lease specifies is the notice that governs, so write one in.

RELOCATION MONEY: ONE NARROW CASE THAT IS NOT YOURS. Wyoming's Relocation Assistance Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 16-7-101 to 16-7-121, does pay displaced residential tenants, including up to 42 months' rent differential capped at $5,250 under § 16-7-105 - but it is payable by the displacing AGENCY in a public rehabilitation, demolition or acquisition project. It has nothing to do with a private owner moving back into his own house, and you owe a displaced tenant nothing.

TWO CAUTIONS. First, however clean the statutory position, an owner-occupancy termination that in fact follows a tenant's complaint, repair request or discrimination claim is exposed on other grounds - not through a Wyoming retaliation statute, since there is none, but through the federal Fair Housing Act and Wyoming's own fair housing act at §§ 40-26-101 to 40-26-145. Keep a contemporaneous record of why and when you decided. Second, your city or town may have its own rules, and ordinances are outside what this review can resolve.

title: Parking and Towing Rules
bodyText:
Wyoming imposes no parking-rules notice duty on a landlord. There is no requirement to deliver written parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, no prescribed heading or type size, no limit on changing the rules mid-term, no limit on the vehicle information you may ask a tenant for, and no rule making a parking permit coterminous with the lease. None of that exists in the Wyoming code. What does exist is a clear grant of authority to make the rules in the first place, and a slow statutory process for getting rid of a vehicle that will not leave.

YOUR AUTHORITY TO SET PARKING RULES. Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-111(a) provides that nothing in the Motor Vehicle Act prevents the owner of real property used by the public for vehicular travel by permission of the owner, and not as a matter of right, from prohibiting that use, from requiring other, different or additional conditions than the act specifies, or from otherwise regulating use of the real property as the owner determines. That is your statutory footing for assigned spaces, permits, guest-parking limits, a bar on commercial vehicles, boats, trailers or inoperable cars, and any other rule you want. Nothing conditions it on notice, signage or a particular form. Because the authority is unconditioned, the discipline has to come from your lease: put the rules in the rental agreement or in rules incorporated by reference, because § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes a renter comply with “all lawful requirements of the rental agreement” and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action. A rule that lives only on a sign in the lot gives you no eviction ground.

ACCESSIBLE PARKING IS THE ONE PLACE WYOMING PRESCRIBES FORM. Under § 31-5-111(b) a private property owner may reserve parking spaces for the handicapped and erect signs, but only “with the approval of the board of county commissioners or the local governing body having jurisdiction.” The signs must comply with § 31-5-501(b): durable material, the international symbol of accessibility, no smaller than twelve by eighteen inches, mounted above ground level so they are visible at all times and not obscured by a parked vehicle; the space must sit on the shortest possible accessible circulation route to an accessible entrance, allow easy wheelchair entry and exit including signage and any adjacent cross-hatched access markings, and be on a level surface. The two-percent-of-spaces minimum in § 31-5-501(b) is written for “public parking lots of ten (10) or more parking spaces,” so it does not by its terms set the count for a private residential lot — but once you reserve a space, the construction and placement requirements apply. Section 31-5-501(c) makes a sign erected under § 31-5-111(b) an official sign, so willfully parking in violation of it is unlawful and locally enforceable, and (c) protects a driver displaying an out-of-state accessible plate or card. Reserving accessible parking without county or municipal approval leaves you with an unenforceable sign. Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices and services where necessary to afford a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling — a reserved or relocated space for a tenant with a mobility disability is the classic example, and your parking rules must bend for it.

TOWING IS SLOW AND YOU MUST NOT RUSH IT. Wyoming has no private-property towing statute, no signage precondition, no immediate-tow authority and no vehicle immobilization or booting statute — “immobiliz” and “boot” return nothing in the whole code. The only route to remove a vehicle from your lot runs through the abandoned vehicle act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 31-13-101 through 31-13-112. Under § 31-13-101(a)(x)(C), a vehicle is abandoned when it is left unattended or unclaimed on private property for more than thirty days without the oral or written consent of the owner or person in lawful control of the property, or for more than thirty days after that consent expires — and § 31-13-109(a) says the thirty days begins on the first day you have knowledge the vehicle is there without consent or after consent expired. Then § 31-13-109(b) requires a written report to the Department of Transportation on its prescribed form listing make, year, model, plate and VIN, the owner, driver and lienholders if known, your name and address, the date consent lapsed, removal details and the vehicle’s current location; (c) has the department try to identify the owner and lienholders and report back; and (d) requires written notice of sale, after the thirty days and at least ten days before the sale, to the county sheriff and by certified mail return receipt requested to the owner and any lienholder identified, plus published notice once a week for two consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county. Only then may you sell at public auction, or proceed by court action under § 31-13-112(e). Note § 31-13-111 bars payment of private-property abandoned vehicle expenses from the county abandoned vehicle account — the cost is yours.

THE PRACTICAL WARNING. The immunity in § 31-13-112(a) runs to a person who removes or stores a vehicle “under this act or otherwise at the request of a police officer.” A tow on day two of a parking violation is neither, so you are outside the protection and exposed to a conversion claim by the vehicle owner. If you intend to tow before the thirty days, do it only through a written lease term the tenant signed consenting to removal at the tenant’s expense, use a licensed towing and recovery service, and understand that § 31-13-104(g) requires that service to notify the county sheriff within thirty minutes of completing the tow and to report a full description of the vehicle. For a tenant’s own vehicle, the cheaper and safer lever is usually the lease: a parking violation is a breach you can notice and enforce, and § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct “other costs provided by any contract” from the deposit if your lease creates the charge.

title: What a Wyoming Lease Can and Cannot Waive
bodyText:
Wyoming has no general anti-waiver statute for residential tenancies. There is nothing like a URLTA Part 5 rule voiding any agreement that waives a tenant right, no provision making the habitability duties non-waivable, and no list of prohibited lease terms. Wyoming runs the opposite way, and you need to understand both halves of that.

The waiver rule. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says: 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' Those words — 'this article' — reach the whole of Article 12, §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211. That includes the owner's safe-and-sanitary duty in § 1-21-1202(a), the four owner duties in § 1-21-1203(a), the renter notice and cure sequence in § 1-21-1203(b) and (d), the renter duties in §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205, the renter's remedies in § 1-21-1206, the nonrefundable-deposit recital in § 1-21-1207, the deposit accounting in § 1-21-1208, the successor-owner rule in § 1-21-1209, and the abandoned-property procedure in § 1-21-1210.
