There is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12 — 'shall not be waived' and 'may not be waived' each return exactly one hit in all of Title 1, and neither is in Article 12.

The three conditions in § 1-21-1202(d) are cumulative, and courts read reallocation clauses strictly, so meet all three on the face of the document: the agreement must be EXPLICIT (name the section or the duty you are moving — a general 'tenant accepts the premises as-is' is not explicit), WRITTEN, and SIGNED BY THE PARTIES. Do not try to do it by a house-rules booklet, a move-in checklist, a later email or a clause that merely says the tenant waives 'all statutory rights'. And remember Article 12 only applies at all to a 'residential rental unit', which § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis.

Now the four things you cannot waive. First, the Wyoming Safe Homes Act. Section 1-21-1304 says in one sentence: 'The provisions of this act shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant.' That is the only express anti-waiver rule in Wyoming landlord-tenant law, and it covers all of §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304 — so no lease term may condition, shorten, penalize or buy out the domestic violence and sexual violence affirmative defense in § 1-21-1303, and none may let you terminate a tenancy based solely on a person's status as a victim (§ 1-21-1303(c)). A separate agreement is caught as squarely as the lease itself, so a move-out agreement or settlement cannot do it either. Second, eviction procedure. Section 1-21-1202(d) says 'this article' and sits in Article 12, so it is not authority for anything in Article 10, §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017. You cannot shorten or waive the three-day notice to quit in § 1-21-1003, the three-to-twelve-day summons window in § 1-21-1004, the no-written-answer-required rule in § 1-21-1004, or the appeal bond and rent-deposit rules in §§ 1-21-1014 and 1-21-1015. Nor can you contract for self-help: taking or keeping possession by force is a crime under § 6-3-306, and the FED chapter at § 1-21-1001 runs against a landlord who locks a tenant out. Third, fair housing. Nothing in Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145 can be waived by a lease, and § 40-26-144(b) makes it a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with a person in the exercise of any right granted by the chapter — a lease term purporting to waive fair-housing rights is itself exposure, and § 40-26-144(c) makes the offense a misdemeanor. Fourth, if your lease sends disputes to arbitration, § 1-36-108 provides that a party may be represented by an attorney at any arbitration proceeding and 'a waiver of representation prior to the proceeding is ineffective'.

A practical caution. Because Wyoming lets you move almost every Article 12 duty onto the tenant, the temptation is to move all of them. Resist it. Section 1-21-1203(e) already bars claims for mental suffering under the whole article, and § 1-21-1202(c) already switches the article off for breakage and malfunctions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter, so the exposure you are drafting around is narrower than it looks. A lease that shifts electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water maintenance onto the tenant may be enforceable under § 1-21-1202(d), but it leaves you relying on the tenant to keep the property habitable, exposed under the nuisance and fire-hazard statutes that run against owners regardless of the lease (§§ 6-6-201 through 6-6-208, §§ 35-9-111 through 35-9-113, § 35-1-105(a)(vii)), and exposed under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act if the reallocation was presented deceptively. Shift specific, discrete duties for specific, stated reasons, and keep the signed writing.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services Needs to Be Written Into a Wyoming Lease
bodyText: Wyoming has no landlord entry statute in the shape other states use. There is no notice period, no twenty-four or forty-eight hour rule, no hours-of-entry limit, no emergency exception written out, and no provision about regularly scheduled services. What Wyoming has instead is a single sentence written as a prohibition on the TENANT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) says no renter shall 'unreasonably deny access to, refuse entry to or withhold consent to enter the residential rental unit to the owner, agent or manager for the purpose of making repairs to or inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale.' Read it carefully, because three things follow. First, it is not a grant of a right of entry to you — it is a limit on the tenant's right to refuse, and your entry right is only the mirror image of it. Second, it names exactly three purposes: making repairs to the unit, inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale. A regularly scheduled service that is not a repair and not an inspection — routine pest control, filter or smoke-alarm battery changes on a schedule, interior landscaping or window cleaning, a scheduled HVAC service visit — is not clearly inside any of the three, and you should not assume a court will stretch 'making repairs' to cover preventive work done on a calendar rather than in response to a fault. Third, the standard is 'unreasonably', not 'without notice'. Nothing in the statute requires you to give notice at all, and nothing tells the tenant how much notice makes a refusal reasonable. That ambiguity is the problem: you can be right about your entry right and still lose the argument about whether the tenant's refusal was unreasonable. Fix it in the lease, and Wyoming gives you a clean mechanism to do that. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' § 1-21-1205 sits inside that article, so the entry duty is one you may modify. The three conditions are cumulative and strict — EXPLICIT, WRITTEN, and SIGNED BY THE PARTIES — and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12 to cut against it. So a lease term that names your scheduled services, sets the notice you will give (or states that no further notice is needed because the schedule itself is the notice), and fixes reasonable hours is enforceable on its own terms. An oral tenancy will not do it: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) makes an oral agreement a 'rental agreement', but § 1-21-1202(d) requires a written and signed one, so an oral Wyoming tenancy shifts nothing and leaves you with the bare statutory three purposes. Two limits on the whole of this. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) gates all of Article 12 to a 'residential rental unit', meaning the renter's PRINCIPAL PLACE OF RESIDENCE, and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally — outside that definition § 1-21-1205 does not apply and your entry rights come from the lease alone. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) makes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager an 'owner' for notice purposes unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement — note that it is the AGENT who must specify otherwise, not you. The teeth are real. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) allows a forcible entry and detainer action 'against renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205', so a tenant who unreasonably refuses entry can be evicted on that ground alone, after the three-day notice to quit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. Do not take the other route. Wyoming's criminal trespass provision, Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(c), says it does not supersede § 1-21-1003, but that carve-out is about the notice to quit — it does not shelter a landlord who lets themselves in for repairs, an inspection or a showing over the tenant's objection, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) separately bars the tenant from interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment, which cuts both ways in practice. Put the schedule in the lease, give the notice the lease promises, keep a record of each visit, and if the tenant refuses, document the refusal and use § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) rather than the door.

title: No Pesticide Notice Owed to a Wyoming Tenant
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no pesticide notice to a residential tenant — not before signing, not before an application, and not by posting. There is no periodic-service disclosure, no advance-notice period, no caution statement, no adjacent-unit notice and no pest-control addendum. Unusually, you can also stop worrying about a local rule, because Wyoming expressly preempts one.

The statute that comes closest is about schools, not homes. Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-375 requires a commercial applicator licensed under § 35-7-359, "or any other person", to give notice of any pesticide application on or within any building or other real property used by a school district primarily for educating students, including student-activity property and playgrounds: at least seventy-two (72) hours to the district, which then notifies students, teachers and staff; each notice marked with a distribution date and stating the date of application, the location or treatment area, the pest to be controlled, the name and type of pesticide and a contact for more information; notices retained two (2) years. Subsection (b) adds posting — signs at main entrances and at the entrance to the specific treatment area not less than twelve (12) hours before an indoor application, signs immediately adjacent to an outdoor treated area and at the entrance to district property, left up for seventy-two (72) hours. Subsection (c) exempts anti-microbial pesticides such as disinfectants and sanitizers used for cleaning, and insect or rodent bait stations of the type available for home use. None of this reaches a rental dwelling. Do not borrow the school timings and present them to a tenant as law; if you adopt them voluntarily, say in writing that you are doing so as a courtesy.

THE PREEMPTION IS THE VALUABLE PART. Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-374(c) provides: "Except as otherwise provided by the Wyoming Environmental Pesticide Control Act of 1973, no political subdivision of this state shall adopt or enforce any ordinance, resolution, rule or regulation regarding pesticides storage, sale, distribution, notification of use, or use that is more stringent than the Wyoming Environmental Pesticide Control Act of 1973 or rules promulgated thereunder." "Notification of use" is named in terms. So a Wyoming city or county cannot impose a tenant pesticide-notice ordinance stricter than state law. This library normally flags local ordinances and does not resolve them; here the state statute resolves them for you. Note the two limits on that comfort: the preemption bars only rules MORE STRINGENT than the Act and the rules under it, and the Act's own rules are made by the department of agriculture and are agency rules, which are outside this library's sources — so a department rule on notification could exist and would not be preempted.

WHAT STILL APPLIES TO YOU. Three things. First, federal label law: Wyo. Stat. § 35-7-374(a)(iv) makes it unlawful to use any pesticide in a manner inconsistent with its labeling, and a restricted-use pesticide may be used only by or under the direct supervision of a certified applicator (§ 35-7-374(a)(iii), (a)(vii), (a)(viii)). The label is the law — if it says to vacate the area, ventilate, or keep children and pets off a treated surface for a stated period, that instruction binds you, and telling the tenant is how you comply. Second, § 35-7-360(c) preserves civil liability: nothing in the Act relieves any person from liability for damage to the person or lands of another caused by the use of pesticides, even where the use conformed to the Act's rules. Third, if an application makes the unit unfit, you are back in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a)'s duty to maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation.

WHO DEALS WITH THE PESTS. Wyoming's landlord duty list does not mention pests. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) is a closed ongoing list — electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water — and § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) sweeps anything else in only "as specifically contracted". So an infestation is your problem only to the extent it makes the unit unsafe or unsanitary under § 1-21-1202(a), or to the extent your lease says it is. The tenant's side is § 1-21-1204(a)(i) (maintain the unit in a clean and safe condition and not unreasonably burden any common area) and § 1-21-1204(a)(ii) (dispose of all garbage and other waste in a clean and safe manner). Because § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties assign or modify any Article 12 duty by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, your lease is where the allocation actually gets decided. Say who pays for treatment, who schedules it, and what preparation the tenant must do.

ENTRY. Wyoming gives you no statutory notice period for entry. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) makes it a prohibited act for the renter to unreasonably deny access, refuse entry or withhold consent to enter for making repairs to or inspecting the unit and showing it for rent or sale — a treatment visit sits most comfortably under repairs or inspection. There is no stated hours-of-notice figure in the statute, so write one into the lease. Twenty-four hours' written notice, with an emergency exception, is the cautious course and makes the entry far easier to defend as reasonable.

WHAT FILLS THE GAP. Your lease, entirely. Set the notice you will give, the preparation the tenant must do, who pays, and the access rule. See also the library's bed-bug cooperation row for the tenant-side obligations.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Is Required With a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no pet fact sheet, pet notice, or pet-related disclosure with a lease or renewal, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat. There is no state publication to hand over and no statute directing you to tell tenants what happens to an animal if they are evicted. Wyoming's statutes mention pets only in the animal-cruelty provisions of Title 6 and the commercial-feed labeling provisions of Title 11; nothing in the Residential Rental Property Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, or in the eviction article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, says a word about pets. Do not carry a pet-and-eviction fact sheet addendum over from another state's lease template; there is no Wyoming equivalent to point to and the recital would be describing a program that does not exist.

So pets in Wyoming are purely a matter of your lease, and the lease is where you should do the work. Write the pet terms yourself: whether animals are allowed at all, which species, how many, size or breed limits, where the animal may be on the property, leash and waste rules, and what happens if an unapproved animal appears. Those terms are enforceable the ordinary way, and there is a specific path to enforce them. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter's statutory duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 a ground for forcible entry and detainer. So a pet-clause breach reaches eviction only through that chain, and you should plead it that way: the pet term, the breach, § 1-21-1204(a)(vii), § 1-21-1002(a)(vi). A nuisance animal can also come in under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii), which prohibits a renter from interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property, and animal damage under § 1-21-1205(a)(i). Either way the notice is the ordinary one: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires written notice to leave the premises served at least three days before you commence the action, and Wyoming gives no statutory cure period, so if you want to give the tenant a chance to rehome an animal you must write that chance into the lease.

On pet money, Wyoming has no pet-deposit or pet-rent statute, no cap, and no special rules. What does apply is the ordinary deposit regime. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires that any rental agreement state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and that written notice of that fact also be given to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. If you charge a nonrefundable pet fee, that section is mandatory and it is the one disclosure a pet arrangement actually triggers in Wyoming: put it in the lease and give the separate written notice at the moment you take the money. A refundable pet deposit is governed by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), so it must be accounted for with the rest of the deposit on the same clock - the balance plus a written itemization of deductions and the reasons for them, delivered or mailed within thirty days after termination or fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by another thirty days if there is damage. Animal damage beyond reasonable wear and tear is a proper deduction under § 1-21-1208(a), and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b) keeps the renter liable for damage beyond the deposit with ten percent annual interest.

One thing your pet clause must not do is sweep in assistance animals, because Wyoming has a statute on that and it is not in the Title 1 landlord-tenant law where you would look for it. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) provides that a person shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, which shall be permitted in leased or rented residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act; the same subsection makes the person liable for any damage the assistance animal does to the premises or facilities. An "assistance animal" is defined in Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-205(a)(iv) as an animal that works, provides assistance or performs tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, or that provides emotional support alleviating one or more identified symptoms or effects of a person's disability - so emotional-support animals are inside the definition. Write your pet clause so that breed, size, number, fee, and deposit terms expressly do not apply to an assistance animal, and handle those requests as reasonable-accommodation requests under the Fair Housing Act rather than as pet applications. You keep the damage remedy either way, because § 35-13-201(c) preserves it. Wyoming also makes it a misdemeanor under Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(b) to knowingly and intentionally misrepresent an animal as a service or assistance animal to obtain the rights in that article, punishable by a fine of up to $750 - a provision worth knowing, though it is enforced by prosecutors and is not a self-help remedy for you.

Flagged and not resolved: a Wyoming municipality or county may regulate animals by ordinance - licensing, leash, dangerous-dog, and number limits are common - and local rules are outside this review.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: Wyoming puts no limit on what you charge for a pet. There is no pet deposit cap, no pet rent cap, no ban on a nonrefundable pet fee, and in fact no security deposit cap of any kind - the phrase "security deposit" does not appear anywhere in Wyoming's residential rental statutes. But the money is not unregulated, and the trap is in how Wyoming words its deposit statute. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) speaks of "property or money held as a deposit," not of a defined "security deposit," so there is no narrow definition for a pet deposit to fall outside of. Treat a refundable pet deposit as a deposit under that section: on termination you may apply it to accrued rent, damages to the unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning, and to other costs provided by any contract, and you must deliver or mail the balance with a written itemization of every deduction and the reasons for it within thirty days after termination, or within fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by another thirty days if there is damage to the unit. The renter must tell you within thirty days of termination where payment and notice may be sent. Note that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) gives a separately identified utilities deposit its own distinct timetable; the legislature carved out utilities deposits and no others, which is a further reason not to assume a pet deposit sits outside subsection (a). Get the nonrefundable part right, because this is the one hard Wyoming requirement. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 provides that any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and that written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. Those are two separate duties. If you charge a nonrefundable pet fee, say so in the lease in plain words, identify the amount, and hand the tenant a separate written notice when you collect it. If you skip either step, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs where the owner unreasonably fails to comply - so an undisclosed nonrefundable pet fee can cost you the whole deposit, not just the fee. Monthly pet rent is a different animal: it is rent, not a deposit, so § 1-21-1207 does not reach it, but state the amount and due date in the lease anyway - Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) ties your fastest eviction ground to failure to pay rent for three days after it is due, and you want pet rent to be unmistakably rent. Service and assistance animals are not pets and you may not charge for them. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) says a person shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, and that the animal shall be permitted in leased or rented residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act. Because that subsection incorporates the federal standard, the federal no-fee rule for assistance animals comes with it: do not charge a pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent for an assistance animal, and do not apply a breed, size or weight restriction to one. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-205(a)(iv) defines an assistance animal broadly, to include an animal that provides emotional support alleviating one or more identified symptoms or effects of a person's disability, so an emotional support animal is covered; § 35-13-205(a)(viii) defines a service animal by reference to 28 C.F.R. 35.104 and 36.104, includes service miniature horses, and since a 2025 amendment expressly includes a dog being trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. The same subsection that protects the tenant also protects you: § 35-13-201(c)'s second sentence says the person shall be liable for any damage done by his assistance animal to the premises or facilities. You cannot charge in advance, but you can charge for actual damage afterward. And if someone fakes it, Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(b) makes it a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $750, to knowingly and intentionally misrepresent that an animal is a service animal or assistance animal in order to obtain the rights set out in that article. FEDERAL: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. ss 3601-3619, and HUD's assistance animal guidance, which Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) incorporates by reference. LOCAL ORDINANCE: municipal dog licensing, breed and number-of-animals rules are not resolved here.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Requirement in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no plain-language contract act and no consumer-contract statute that dictates how a residential lease must be written. There is no readability score to hit, no requirement that the lease be divided and captioned by sections, no minimum type size, no front-page summary of landlord-protective terms, and no dollar threshold above or below which different drafting rules apply. The phrases "plain language," "plain English," "consumer contract" and "readability" appear nowhere in Wyoming law in a way that touches a lease. Wyoming's consumer statute, the Consumer Protection Act at Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114, is a deceptive-trade-practices law, not a drafting law: it lists knowing misrepresentations made "in the course of his business and in connection with a consumer transaction" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 40-12-105(a)) and says nothing about contract format, captioning or vocabulary. Whether it reaches a residential lease at all is an open question in Wyoming: "merchandise" is defined broadly enough to include real property (§ 40-12-102(a)(vi)), but "consumer transactions" is defined as "the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any merchandise to an individual for purposes that are primarily personal, family or household" (§ 40-12-102(a)(ii)), and that definition does not name a lease or a rental. Do not count on being outside it. The safe assumption is that a knowingly false statement you make while advertising or renting a unit — about the condition of the property, the existence of a warranty, the reason a unit is available, or the price — could be reached by the Act, and the Act has a cure mechanism and attorney general enforcement. So although no statute makes you write plainly, three Wyoming rules reward it. Any duty or obligation under the Residential Rental Property article may be assigned to a different party or modified only "by explicit written agreement signed by the parties" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1202(d)) — "explicit" is a drafting standard, and a buried or convoluted clause will not meet it. If any portion of the deposit is nonrefundable, the rental agreement must state that and a separate written notice must go to the tenant when the deposit is taken (§ 1-21-1207), which is a clarity duty in substance. And eviction for an ordinary lease breach runs through § 1-21-1204(a)(vii), the tenant's duty to comply with "all lawful requirements of the rental agreement" — a requirement a judge cannot find the tenant violated if the judge cannot tell what it means. Write short captioned sections in ordinary words, define the few terms you must, put the deposit and nonrefundable-portion language where it cannot be missed, and have the tenant sign. Ambiguity in a lease is generally construed against the party who drafted it, which is you.

title: No Plain-Language Requirement for Leases
bodyText:
Wyoming has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts or residential leases. There is no readability test to pass, no Flesch score, no required type size or sentence length, no "statement of consumer restrictions" you must include, no option to submit a lease to the Attorney General for preapproval, and no dollar threshold above which a different rule applies. The words "plain language" appear twice in the entire Wyoming code, in Titles 26 and 39, and neither is about contracts with tenants. "Plain English," "Flesch," "clear and coherent" and "everyday words" return nothing at all. The legislature knows how to impose a readability rule when it wants one -- Wyo. Stat. § 26-22-105(h) lets the insurance commissioner adopt readability standards for health coverage forms -- and it has not done so for leases.

So your lease is judged as an ordinary contract. It binds the tenant because they agreed to it, not because it was easy to read, and a tenant cannot escape a term by arguing it was written in legalese. Note the flip side, though: Wyoming also has no statute telling a court how to construe an ambiguous lease, so if a term is genuinely unclear you are relying on general contract principles and on how a Wyoming court applies them -- which this library's sources do not settle. An ambiguity you wrote is an ambiguity you are litigating.

There is one consumer statute in the background worth not tripping over. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114, makes it unlawful to engage in a deceptive trade practice "in the course of his business and in connection with a consumer transaction" when done knowingly, and the list in § 40-12-105(a) includes, at (a)(viii), representing "that a consumer transaction involves a warranty, a disclaimer of warranties, particular warranty terms, or other rights, remedies or obligations if the representation is false." The act's reach is broad on its face: "merchandise" is defined at § 40-12-102(a)(vi) to include "any service or any property, tangible or intangible, real, personal or mixed," so real property is in. Whether a residential lease is itself a "consumer transaction" is less clear, because § 40-12-102(a)(ii) defines that term as "the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any merchandise to an individual for purposes that are primarily personal, family or household" -- renting is not obviously a sale, and "distribution" is undefined. What is clear either way is that advertising a rental unit to the public is squarely "advertising ... of any merchandise."

The cautious course follows from that, and it costs nothing. Do not knowingly misstate the law in your lease or your listing -- do not tell a Wyoming tenant they have waived a right they cannot waive, that you may enter without limit, that a deposit is nonrefundable when § 1-21-1208 says what you may keep, or that the unit has a feature it does not. Write the lease so a tenant can follow it: short sentences, headings, numbers rather than words for amounts and days, and a plain statement of what the tenant pays, when, and what happens if they do not. No Wyoming statute makes you do this. It makes the lease easier to enforce, it makes a deceptive-practice argument harder to mount against you, and it is the single cheapest thing you can do to reduce disputes.

title: Political Canvassers, Candidates and Signs at Wyoming Rentals
bodyText:
Wyoming gives political candidates, campaign workers and petition circulators no right of access to a rental property, and gives tenants no statutory right to display political signs. There is no Wyoming counterpart to Minnesota's Minn. Stat. § 211B.20, which makes it unlawful to deny a candidate access to a multiple-unit residence. The phrases "political sign" and "political literature" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and Wyoming's election code, Title 22, contains no reference to apartments, multiple-unit buildings or door-to-door canvassing of residences.

The one campaign-placement statute Wyoming has runs the other way. Wyo. Stat. § 22-25-115 bars written campaign advertising on the real or personal property of the state or its political subdivisions, with exceptions for state and county fairgrounds, and for the University of Wyoming, community colleges and school districts (which may permit it subject to time, place and manner rules that must "provide for equal access to opposing political views"). On municipal street rights-of-way, campaign materials may be placed only "[s]ubject to the approval of the landowner" and any municipal rules. The statute governs public property; it says nothing about private rental property, and nothing in it obliges a private owner to allow anything.

So in Wyoming this is your property right plus your lease, and the controlling authority is trespass law. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(a) makes it criminal trespass to enter or remain on the land or premises of another "knowing he is not authorized to do so, or after being notified to depart or to not trespass," with notice given either by "[p]ersonal communication to the person by the owner or occupant, or his agent, or by a peace officer" or by "[p]osting of signs reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders." It is a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months, a fine of up to $750, or both. Two features matter here. First, you may post "no soliciting" signage at the common entrances and exclude canvassers from halls, lobbies and grounds. Second — and landlords often miss this — the statute names the "owner OR OCCUPANT, or his agent." Your tenant is an occupant. A tenant may invite a canvasser to their own door and may exclude one, and a general building rule cannot override the tenant's control of the unit they have exclusive possession of. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iii) defines a renter as a person entitled under the rental agreement "to occupy a residential rental unit to the exclusion of others."

Practical course. You may lawfully adopt and enforce a written no-solicitation rule covering common areas and grounds, post it, and ask a canvasser to leave; after that, § 6-3-303 backs you. But apply the rule neutrally to every cause, candidate and party. Selective enforcement — letting one campaign in and turning another away — is where trouble starts, and the same even-handedness is the only safe course for a sign rule: a blanket, content-neutral limit on window and yard signs (size, number, location, no damage to the premises, removal at move-out) is far more defensible than one that singles out political content. Nothing in Wyoming's statutes stops a tenant from displaying a sign inside their own unit, and a lease term purporting to bar that would be unusual and unenforceable in practice.

The Wyoming Constitution does not change this. Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 20 provides that "[e]very person may freely speak, write and publish on all subjects, being responsible for the abuse of that right," and art. 1, § 21 protects the right of petition and peaceable assembly. Both are guarantees against government action; neither imposes a duty on a private landlord, and Wyoming has no statute extending them to private property. Whether a Wyoming court would ever read a quasi-public-forum exception into a large residential complex is untested in this research — case law is outside this library — so the cautious course is the neutral, written, evenly enforced rule described above.

Finally, check your city. Municipalities may license and regulate solicitors and peddlers by ordinance, and ordinances are outside this library.

title: Pools and Spas at a Wyoming Rental
bodyText: If your rental property has a shared pool or hot tub, assume you need a state or local license for it. Wyoming's Public Pool and Spa Health and Safety Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-28-101 through 35-28-110, is administered by the department of agriculture with the department of health, and Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-108(a) provides that 'Any person operating a public pool or spa shall obtain a license from the department of agriculture or a local health department... No public pool or spa shall operate without a valid license.' The license is not transferable, must be renewed annually and must be prominently displayed. Two definitions decide whether this reaches you, and they are broad. Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-101(a)(vii) defines a 'pool' as an artificial structure containing water used for swimming, bathing, diving, surfing, wading or a similar use 'and operated by an owner, lessee, operator, licensee or concessionaire regardless of whether a fee is charged for use.' Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-101(a)(viii) then defines a 'public pool' as 'a pool that is open to the public or a segment of the public.' The tenants of an apartment complex or rental community are a segment of the public, and the no-fee language removes the obvious escape, so an apartment or complex pool is very likely covered. A 'spa' under paragraph (a)(x) expressly includes a hot tub or whirlpool that is not drained and refilled for each use, so a shared hot tub is covered on the same footing as a pool. The statute sets no minimum size, no dwelling-unit threshold and no exemption for small properties, and Wyoming has no counterpart to the owner-occupied duplex or single-family carve-outs you find in Washington's water recreation rules. The statute itself contains no fence, barrier, gate, self-closing latch, lifeguard, depth-marking or shut-off requirement — those live in the department of agriculture's rules under Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-102(a)(iii), and in whatever building code your city or county has adopted. This library does not resolve agency rules or ordinances, so for each property with a pool, call the local health department (or the department of agriculture where there is none) before the season, get the license, and ask them for the current barrier and signage requirements in writing. Enforcement has teeth: under Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-109 a regulatory authority may summarily suspend your license without prior warning or a hearing on finding an imminent health hazard, and under Wyo. Stat. § 35-28-110 it may revoke the license for uncorrected conditions, a history of noncompliance or a refusal to grant access. There is no Wyoming statute requiring you to give a tenant a pool safety notice at lease signing, so Arizona's approved-notice model has no Wyoming equivalent — but you still owe the ordinary duty under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) to maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition, and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) a pool held out for renters generally is part of the rental unit. Last, do not count on the recreational-use immunity in Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-19-101 through 34-19-107. It withdraws protection where the owner charges the persons who enter the land (Wyo. Stat. § 34-19-105(a)(ii)), and a tenant who pays rent for a unit with pool access is not the unpaid public visitor the act was written for.

title: Wyoming Requires Heat, Not Cooling, and Gives No Right to a Portable Air Conditioner
bodyText:
Wyoming has no portable-cooling-device statute. There is no tenant right to install a window or floor air conditioner, no bar on charging a fee for one, no notice period before installation, and no requirement that a lease restricting window units say so in a particular way or place. A search of all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws found nothing: "window unit," "swamp cooler," "evaporative cooling," "extreme heat" and "excessive heat" all return zero, and the words "portable" and "cooling" never appear together in a landlord-tenant context — "portable" appears 143 times corpus-wide but not once in Title 1.

Wyoming also does not require you to supply cooling at all. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) obliges you to maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. Cooling is not on that list, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires only operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water. Air conditioning falls under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv), which makes you maintain "other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." So an air conditioner becomes your obligation only if your lease says it is. If you list a window unit or central air in the lease as included, you have taken on the duty to maintain it. If you do not list it, you have not.

That means the whole question is yours to decide by lease. You may allow window units, ban them, allow them only in certain windows, require a particular mounting, require the tenant to carry the cost and the electricity, charge for an inspection, or require removal at move-out. Nothing in Wyoming law constrains any of that.

Four things to put in the lease if you allow them. First, say who pays for the unit, the electricity and any damage. Second, specify mounting and support — a unit that falls out of a second-storey window is a serious liability, and Wyoming's recreational and premises-liability rules will not help you there. Third, require removal and restoration at move-out, which lines up with Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii), under which the tenant must remove property placed in the unit and clean it to the condition it was in at the beginning of the tenancy. Fourth, remind the tenant of § 1-21-1204(a)(iv), the duty to use electrical and other facilities in a reasonable manner — a window unit on an extension cord through an old circuit is the real risk in most Wyoming housing stock.

The one rule that can override your ban. Wyoming has a state fair housing act, and Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107 deals specifically with disability. Under § 40-26-107(c)(i), it is discrimination to refuse to permit, at the disabled individual's own expense, a reasonable modification of the premises if the modification may be necessary to afford that individual full enjoyment of the premises — though in a rental you may, when it is reasonable to do so, condition permission on the renter agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Under § 40-26-107(c)(ii), it is discrimination to refuse to make a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services if the accommodation may be necessary to afford the individual equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. A tenant with a medical condition aggravated by heat can therefore ask you to waive a no-window-unit rule, and a flat refusal is a fair housing risk. Treat such a request as an accommodation request, ask for the limited verification the law allows, and document your response.

Two more limits. If you provide and advertise air conditioning, Wyoming's consumer protection law and ordinary contract law still hold you to it even though no habitability statute does. And local ordinances are not resolved here: Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), and Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) makes a more stringent local housing code prevail, so a municipality may have adopted a building code with window-unit or egress-window requirements. Check yours before you write the rule.

title: No Tenant Right to Install Solar in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming gives a tenant no right to install a plug-in solar device, a portable panel, a battery or any other solar equipment, and nothing requires you to allow one. There is no Virginia-style tenant installation right, no Maine-style provision letting a tenant install without utility approval, no Vermont-style notice-and-reasonable-restrictions scheme, and no statute voiding a lease term that forbids solar equipment. The proximity searches that would find such a rule — solar near lease, tenant or renter, in both word orders — return nothing at all in the Wyoming statutes, and "solar easement" and "solar covenant" return nothing either. So your consent requirement stands on ordinary contract terms, which means you should actually write one. Wyoming does have a Solar Rights Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-22-101 through 34-22-106, and it is worth understanding so you do not mistake it for something it is not. It is a solar ACCESS statute — a prior-appropriation style right to unobstructed sunlight as between neighbouring properties — not an installation right. Wyo. Stat. § 34-22-103(a) declares the beneficial use of solar energy a property right, and § 34-22-103(b)(i) makes beneficial use the basis, measure and limit of the right "except as otherwise provided by written contract," with priority in time giving the better right under (b)(ii). Wyo. Stat. § 34-22-104 restricts it: sun before 9:00 a.m. or after 3:00 p.m. Mountain Standard Time is de minimis and may be infringed without compensation; a solar right not beneficially used for five (5) years or more is deemed abandoned; and no solar right attaches to a collector that would be shaded by a ten (10) foot wall on the property line on a winter solstice day, unless the local government permits otherwise. Two points make this almost irrelevant to a plug-in panel. First, "solar collector" is defined in Wyo. Stat. § 34-22-102(a)(i) to require a device capable of collecting, storing or transmitting at least twenty-five thousand (25,000) BTU's on a clear winter solstice day — a small plug-in panel will not meet that threshold, so it is not a solar collector within the Act at all. Second, the Act is expressly subject to written contract, so your lease governs between you and your tenant regardless. Wyo. Stat. § 34-22-105 gives counties and municipalities the land-use and permitting role, and § 34-22-105(b) says the local government SHALL establish permit systems for the use and application of solar energy — so any installation question has a local permit dimension you must check where the property sits. Wyo. Stat. § 34-22-106 requires solar permits and transfers of solar rights to be recorded under Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-1-101 through 34-1-140. The net metering statute, Wyo. Stat. §§ 37-16-101 through 37-16-104, likewise gives a tenant nothing against you. It imposes duties on the ELECTRIC UTILITY: under § 37-16-102(a)(i) the utility must offer a bidirectional meter to an eligible customer-generator who has installed a net metering system. A qualifying net metering system is defined in § 37-16-101(a)(viii) as one fuelled by solar, wind, biomass or hydropower, of not more than twenty-five (25) kilowatts generating capacity, located on the customer-generator's premises and operating in parallel with the utility. Under § 37-16-104(a) it must meet the national electrical code, IEEE and Underwriters Laboratories standards, and under § 37-16-104(b) the customer-generator must provide lockable switching equipment at its own expense. Nothing in the chapter requires a landlord to permit an installation, and § 37-16-101(b) merely says a customer-generator is not a public utility. Because the law is silent, the risks of an uncontrolled installation fall on you: roof penetrations and the warranty on them, wind loading in a state that has plenty of it, electrical safety and insurance, the removal and restoration question at move-out, and who owns the equipment and any net metering credit if the tenant leaves it behind. Say all of that in the lease. Note also that Wyoming has no common-interest or HOA statute, so there is no statutory override of a declaration's solar restriction either — a condominium under the Condominium Ownership Act at Wyo. Stat. § 34-20-101 et seq. is governed by its own declaration, which you should read before consenting. One narrow accommodation point: if a tenant frames a solar request as a disability accommodation, handle it under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(i) and (c)(ii), not under this heading.

title: Rules That Change With the Size of Your Portfolio
bodyText:
Start with the half of this that is simple. Wyoming's landlord-tenant statutes contain no unit-count threshold of any kind. Habitability, deposits, notices, abandoned property and eviction procedure in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1211 apply identically whether you own one house or four hundred, with no small-landlord exemption and no extra duties for larger owners. Nor does the Real Estate License Act turn on portfolio size: the exemptions in § 33-28-103(a) are keyed to role, not to unit count — an owner, a member of the owner's immediate family, the owner's regular employees, and under (a)(vi) a resident manager who resides on the premises and leases in connection with that employment, each exempt unless the individual is already a licensee.

The thresholds that do exist are in fair housing, and they matter a great deal. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(a) exempts the sale or rental of a single family house sold or rented by the owner from §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109 — but only if every one of several conditions holds together. The owner must not own more than three (3) single family houses at any one time, and must not own any interest in, or have owned or reserved on the owner's behalf under any express or voluntary agreement, title to or any right to any part of the proceeds from the sale or rental of more than three (3) single family houses at any one time. The house must be sold or rented without using the sales or rental facilities or services of a licensed real estate broker, an agent, a person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or an employee or agent of any of them, and without the publication, posting or mailing of a notice, statement or advertisement prohibited by § 40-26-104. Read those two as cumulative, not alternative: use a broker and you lose the exemption; run a discriminatory advertisement and you lose it too. And if you were not the most recent resident of the house, the exemption applies to only one (1) sale or rental in a twenty-four (24) month period.

The same subsection contains a trap that catches ordinary landlords. Section 40-26-110(a) defines who is 'in the business of selling or renting dwellings,' and being in that business destroys the exemption. You are in the business if, within the preceding twelve (12) months, you have participated as principal in three (3) or more transactions involving the sale or rental of any dwelling or interest in one; or within the preceding twelve (12) months have participated as agent, other than in the sale of your own personal residence, in providing sales or rental facilities or services in two (2) or more such transactions; or — and this is the one that surprises people — if you are the owner of any dwelling designed or intended for occupancy by, or occupied by, five (5) or more families. Own a single five-plex anywhere and you are in the business, which means the three-house exemption is closed to you for every other property you own. Note also that three transactions in twelve months is a low bar for anyone with normal turnover.

The second threshold is the owner-occupied small-building exemption at § 40-26-110(b): §§ 40-26-103 and 40-26-105 through 40-26-109 do not apply to the sale or rental of the rooms or units in a dwelling containing living quarters occupied or intended to be occupied by not more than four (4) families living independently of each other, if the owner maintains and occupies one of those living quarters as the owner's residence. Count the owner's own unit in the four. Both conditions must hold: four families or fewer, and the owner actually living there.

Now the three limits that make these exemptions far narrower than they look, and that you must not get wrong. First, § 40-26-110(b) skips § 40-26-104. The list of disapplied sections is '40-26-103 and 40-26-105 through 40-26-109,' and § 40-26-104 is the publication provision: no person may make, print or publish a notice, statement or advertisement about the sale or rental of a dwelling indicating any preference, limitation or discrimination, or the intention to make one, because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. That prohibition binds you however small you are. Second, both exemptions reach only §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109. They do nothing about § 40-26-144, the intimidation-and-interference offence, which carries a longer list of protected characteristics — race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance — for conduct by force or threat of force under § 40-26-144(a)(i), makes coercion or interference with any chapter right a discriminatory practice without any force element under § 40-26-144(b), and makes either a misdemeanor under § 40-26-144(c). Third, these are Wyoming exemptions only. The federal Fair Housing Act has its own, differently drafted exemptions, and nothing in Wyoming law excuses you from federal law. If you are close to any of these lines, comply as though no exemption applied; the cost of compliance is far below the cost of being wrong about which side of a four-family or three-house line you were on.

One threshold outside fair housing is worth knowing if you supply water. Under Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(IX), metered and other direct sales of water by a person operating a water system escape public-utility regulation only if all four conditions hold: the system has less than fifteen (15) potential service connections; it is not owned, controlled or otherwise affiliated with a water utility or any other utility providing water service; it is not a centralized water supply system associated with a subdivision; and it is not located within the established service territory of a water utility or within the corporate limits of a municipality. Fail any one and the exemption is gone.

title: No Possession Bond, and the Bonds Wyoming Does Use
bodyText:
Wyoming has no possession bond. There is no device by which a tenant binds themselves in advance to deliver possession at the end of the term with a confessed judgment behind it, as Tennessee allows in its non-URLTA counties, and no landlord's bond that buys immediate possession before trial, as some states permit. The phrase does not exist in Wyoming law, and no bond anywhere in the statutes is posted by a landlord in an eviction. Do not put a possession-bond clause in a Wyoming lease: it has no statutory footing, and the confessed-judgment half of it runs into Wyo. Stat. § 1-16-201, which contemplates the debtor appearing personally in court with the creditor's assent, not signing in advance.

You do not need one, which is the point. Wyoming's forcible entry and detainer procedure is already fast and costs you no bond. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1012, once a circuit court enters a judgment of restitution the court shall issue a writ of restitution at the request of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's agent or the plaintiff's attorney — it is on request, not in the court's discretion. Under § 1-21-1013, unless the defendant appeals, the officer must execute the writ within two days after receiving it, Sundays excepted, by restoring you to possession, and must levy and collect the execution for rent and costs. Remember the two stacked three-day periods that come earlier and keep them distinct: § 1-21-1002(a)(i) gives a three-day grace period after rent falls due, and § 1-21-1003 requires a separate three-day notice to quit before you file.

Every bond in the Wyoming eviction statute is posted by the tenant, and knowing them is worth more to you than a possession bond would be. Under § 1-21-1007, no continuance may be granted to the defendant for longer than two days unless the defendant gives a bond to you, with good and sufficient surety approved by the circuit court, conditioned on paying the rent that may accrue and costs if judgment goes against them. If a tenant asks for a longer continuance, ask the court for the bond. Under § 1-21-1014(b), an appeal by the tenant does not stay proceedings unless, within forty-eight hours after judgment and Sundays excepted, the tenant executes and files a bond to you with two or more sufficient sureties approved by the court, conditioned on paying all costs accrued or to accrue and all damages you sustain from the wrongful detention of the premises during the appeal. That is a short, strict window, and the requirement of two or more sureties is easy for a tenant to miss. The same subsection lets the appellate court require a new bond in a larger amount if needed to secure the parties' rights, so ask if the first bond looks thin.

The provision most worth knowing is § 1-21-1015. On an appeal from a judgment for rents due and payable, the tenant must deposit with the court the amount of rent specified in the judgment, in addition to the § 1-21-1014 bond; unless that deposit is made the appeal is not perfected. Then, under § 1-21-1015(b), as further rent falls due the tenant must keep depositing it with the clerk of the appellate court, and if at any time before final judgment the tenant fails to make a deposit when the judgment specifies, the appellate court shall affirm the judgment with costs on your motion and proof of the failure — and the deposited rent is paid over to you on the court's order. So a tenant who appeals to buy time has to pay as they go, and the moment they miss a deposit you can move to end the appeal. Diary each rent due date during an appeal and watch the clerk's record. One caution runs the other way: under § 1-21-1014(a), if the court notifies the officer that proceedings are stayed on appeal and you have already been restored to possession, the officer must immediately put the tenant back in. Do not re-let the unit until the appeal window has closed.

title: Well Water Testing and What You Must Tell Tenants
bodyText:
Wyoming has no Private Well Testing Act. There is no statute requiring you to test a private well on a periodic cycle because you rent the property out, no duty to give a tenant a copy of test results at move-in or within any number of days of receiving them, and no seasonal-rental posting alternative. The phrase "private well" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code.

But Wyoming does have a testing duty, and it catches far more rental properties than landlords expect, because the trigger is only TEN service connections.

THE TEN-CONNECTION RULE. Wyo. Stat. § 35-4-220(a)(ii) defines a "sanitary public water supply" as "any water supply being distributed by ten (10) or more service connections, such connections being utilized to furnish water for human consumption either in preparing foods or beverages for inhabitants of residences or business establishments." A "service connection" is defined in § 35-4-220(a)(i) as any water line or pipe connected to a distribution supply main or pipe for the purpose of conveying water to a building or dwelling. So a single well serving ten or more dwellings - a ten-unit apartment building, a small mobile home park, a cluster of cabins or duplexes on one system - is a sanitary public water supply under Wyoming law. Ten is lower than the fifteen-connection figure used elsewhere in Wyoming statutes for utility purposes, so do not reason across from Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(IX).

MONTHLY BACTERIOLOGICAL SAMPLING. Wyo. Stat. § 35-4-221(a) places on "any public or private utility engaged in the development, storage and distribution of a sanitary public water supply" the duty to provide for the safety and purity of the supply to every service connection and "to collect samples of such water for bacteriological analysis at least once monthly or oftener as required by the state board of health." Samples go in special containers furnished by the state health department division of laboratories and must be returned to that laboratory; examination and reporting follow the United States public health service drinking water standards, and results are reported back to the owners or persons responsible for operating the supply. Monthly, not annually. If you are not already in this programme and your well serves ten or more connections, call the Wyoming Department of Health and the Department of Environmental Quality before your next rent run.

DO NOT TRY TO ARGUE YOUR WAY OUT ON THE WORD "UTILITY." The sampling sentence in § 35-4-221(a) is addressed to a "public or private utility," and a landlord might be tempted to say it is not one. Two things close that door. First, § 35-4-221(b) imposes the corrective duty on different people: when laboratory examination, inspection and report of the state department of health determine the water to be unsafe for human consumption, "the owners or persons responsible for the operation of such water supply shall take immediate action to correct sanitary defects, improve operation, provide necessary water treatment, or make any other changes or additions necessary to provide assuredly safe water." An owner is an owner. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 35-4-222 directs the department's written notice of danger to health to "the owners or persons responsible for the operation of such sanitary public water supply." So even on the narrowest reading of the sampling sentence, the correction duty and the notice land on you.

COMPLIANCE IS NOT A SHIELD. Wyo. Stat. § 35-4-223 says so expressly: "Compliance with the requirements of this act shall in no way release the owners or persons responsible for the operation of a sanitary public water supply from any liability for damage to persons or property caused by or resulting from the installation, operation or maintenance of a sanitary public water supply." Testing on schedule does not answer a tenant's claim if someone is harmed.

MOBILE HOME PARKS. Wyo. Stat. § 35-4-224 removes the department of health's authority to regulate or make rules about the DESIGN AND CONSTRUCTION of sewerage and water facilities inside a mobile home park - but it expressly preserves the department's power to make and enforce rules about the health of persons within the park and to inspect sewerage and water facilities once construction is complete. Read the second sentence as carefully as the first; park owners routinely read only the heading.

UNDER TEN CONNECTIONS. If your well serves fewer than ten connections, no Wyoming statute requires you to test it or to tell a tenant anything about it. That is not a reason to do nothing. Your habitability duty under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) is not to rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, and § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) requires you to maintain plumbing and hot and cold water - a contaminated supply is a problem under both. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires hot and cold running water "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties," so a seasonal or no-water arrangement must be in a signed writing. Test annually, keep the lab reports, give every new tenant a copy with the lease, and put the well, the system and who maintains what into the lease. None of that is required; all of it is cheap, and under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) a facility becomes your maintenance duty only when the rental agreement specifically contracts for it, so the lease is where this gets settled either way.

ONE MORE THING TO CHECK ON THE WATER RIGHT. A domestic well in Wyoming is an appropriation. Wyo. Stat. § 41-3-905 requires a permit from the state engineer for a well constructed after the act's effective date, and under § 41-3-906 the state engineer may, on the complaint of a domestic or stock well operator, order an interfering appropriator to cut back. Confirm the well is permitted and that the permitted use covers the number of dwellings you are serving before you add units to it.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Department of Health and Department of Environmental Quality rules, the federal Safe Drinking Water Act programme, case law, court rules and local ordinances were not searched and will add requirements, particularly above the federal public-water-system thresholds.

title: No written-promise rule, but an unkept repair promise has two Wyoming consequences
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute or rule requiring a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be put in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be given before the lease is signed. There is no Wyoming counterpart to Wisconsin's ATCP § 134.07. The words "promise" and "repair" never appear within thirty characters of each other anywhere in the Wyoming statutes, in either order, and none of the six "completion date" references is a tenancy provision. There is also no state agency rule on the point, because Wyoming's residential landlord-tenant law is statutory only.

That does not make an oral promise safe to give. Two things happen in Wyoming when you promise work and do not do it.

FIRST, A PROMISE IN THE LEASE CREATES A STATUTORY DUTY THAT DID NOT OTHERWISE EXIST. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) is a closed ongoing list - electrical systems, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water. Paragraph (a)(iv) then requires you to "[m]aintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement". Those four words are the hinge. Write into the lease that you will service the dishwasher, resurface the deck, replace the carpet or keep the garage door opener working, and you have imported that item into your § 1-21-1203 duties, with the tenant's notice machinery in § 1-21-1203(b) and the remedies in § 1-21-1206 attached to it. Leave it out and the item is not a statutory duty at all. So be deliberate: list what you genuinely intend to maintain, and do not list the rest. A promise of a one-off repair before move-in is different in kind from a promise of ongoing maintenance, and the lease should say which one you are making.

SECOND, A KNOWING MISREPRESENTATION IS A DECEPTIVE TRADE PRACTICE. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines "merchandise" to include property "real, personal or mixed", and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110. Section 40-12-105(a) makes it an unlawful deceptive trade practice when, in the course of his business and in connection with a consumer transaction, a person KNOWINGLY does any of the listed things. Two paragraphs bite here. Paragraph (a)(v) covers representing that merchandise has been supplied in accordance with a previous representation when it has not. Paragraph (a)(xv) is a bare catch-all: "Engages in unfair or deceptive acts or practices". Paragraph (a)(viii) can also catch a false statement about warranty terms or other rights, remedies or obligations. Everything is gated on "knowingly", so a promise you intended to keep and could not is not within the section; a promise made to close the letting, with no intention or means of performing, can be.

The Act's procedure is as important as its substance, and it favours a landlord who responds quickly. Under § 40-12-109 a consumer may not sue unless written notice was given to the alleged violator within one year after initial discovery of the practice or within two years following the consumer transaction, whichever comes first, and the notice must state fully the nature of the practice and the actual damage suffered - and unless the practice has become an "uncured unlawful deceptive trade practice". Section 40-12-102(a)(ix) defines that: a practice for which the consumer has given § 40-12-109 notice and either no offer to cure was made within FIFTEEN DAYS after that notice, or the practice was not cured within a reasonable time after the consumer accepted the offer. Section 40-12-102(a)(viii) says what curing means - offering in writing to adjust or modify the transaction to conform to the reasonable expectations the practice generated and performing that offer if accepted, or offering in writing to rescind and performing if accepted. Then § 40-12-108(a) limits the private action to a person relying on an UNCURED practice, and to actual damages, with attorney's fees available only in a class action under § 40-12-108(b). An action must be started within one year after the notice is furnished. The practical lesson: if a tenant sends you a written complaint that you promised work and did not deliver, you have fifteen days to make a written offer to cure, and making one and honouring it is a complete answer to a private claim.

A THIRD POINT, ABOUT FORM. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(i) is Wyoming's statute of frauds and makes void, unless in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged, every agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within one year from the making of it. A promise of work to be done next month is outside it; a multi-year maintenance commitment is not.

WHAT TO DO. Put every promise in the lease, item by item, each with a date or a period. Say in the lease that no promise outside it binds you. Where something is genuinely uncertain, say what you will do and by when you will tell the tenant more, rather than promising an outcome. And keep the correspondence: with no writing requirement and no case law in this review, a dispute over an oral promise comes down to whose account the court accepts.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Requirement
bodyText:
Wyoming has no Proposition 65 analog and no chemical exposure warning requirement for rental housing. There is no state list of chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, no duty to post or deliver a warning to tenants or visitors, no prescribed warning language or symbol, and no private right of action or bounty provision. The phrases “known to the state,” “reproductive harm,” “reproductive toxicant” and “birth defects” appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and “chemical” never appears within 100 characters of “warning” in either word order. The only three “carcinogen” references in the whole code are Wyo. Stat. § 27-15-102, the firefighter occupational disease presumption, and two risk-based cleanup standards in the Environmental Quality Act at Wyo. Stat. § 35-11-1609 and the surrounding voluntary remediation provisions — none of which touches a landlord or a tenant.

Wyoming also has none of the chemical disclosures that commonly travel with a Prop 65 row. There is no state lead-based paint disclosure (“lead-based paint” returns nothing), no radon disclosure or testing requirement (“radon” returns nothing in the entire code), no mold disclosure or remediation standard, and no methamphetamine contamination disclosure, decontamination standard or registry. The only methamphetamine provision that reaches a dwelling is criminal and is aimed at whoever exposes a child: Wyo. Stat. § 6-4-405(a) makes it an offense to knowingly and willfully cause or permit a child to ingest methamphetamine or fentanyl, to remain in a room, dwelling or vehicle where the person knows the drug is being manufactured or sold, or to enter and remain in one the person knows is used to manufacture or store the drug or the hazardous waste from manufacturing it. That is a crime, not a disclosure duty, and it does not tell you what to do with a contaminated unit.

WHAT ACTUALLY APPLIES. First, FEDERAL: the Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act, 42 U.S.C. § 4852d with 24 C.F.R. part 35 subpart A and 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart F, requires you, for target housing built before 1978, to give every prospective tenant the EPA pamphlet, disclose any known lead-based paint and hazards and provide any records or reports you have, and include the prescribed Lead Warning Statement and acknowledgment in the lease. That duty applies in Wyoming because it is federal; it does not depend on anything Wyoming enacted. It is the one chemical warning a Wyoming landlord genuinely owes. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) bars you from renting a residential rental unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy — a unit with a live chemical hazard is not, and § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) requires you to keep common areas sanitary and reasonably safe. Third, the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on “knowingly,” so affirmatively denying a hazard you know about is exposure, subject to the § 40-12-109 pre-suit notice and cure period. Fourth, if a real estate licensee is involved in the rental, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-102(b)(viii) makes a tenant a “buyer,” which brings § 33-28-310(a)(i)(F) into play: the licensee must disclose to prospective buyers adverse material facts actually known, including environmental hazards affecting the property that are required by law to be disclosed.

RECOMMENDED COURSE. Do not import a California-style warning into a Wyoming lease; it is not required, it is not tailored to Wyoming law, and a warning that overstates or misstates a hazard is itself a representation you can be held to. Do comply with the federal lead rule for pre-1978 housing, keep the signed disclosure for three years, disclose in writing any chemical hazard you actually know about, and remediate rather than paper over anything that makes the unit unfit under § 1-21-1203(a)(i). Local health ordinances may add requirements and are outside the state statutes.

title: No Property Tax Statement Owed to Tenants
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no property-tax disclosure to a residential tenant. There is no annual statement showing how much of each rent payment represents the property taxes you paid, no July deadline, no duty to re-issue the statement when rent changes, and no apportionment rule for taxes you pay on several properties together. Wyoming has nothing resembling NRS 118.165. The residential rental article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, contains one mandatory lease recital and one mandatory notice, both in § 1-21-1207 and both about nonrefundable deposits — nothing about taxes.

There is also nothing on the other side of the transaction to drive such a disclosure. Wyoming has no individual income tax, so there is no renter's credit, no property-tax circuit breaker for tenants and no 'certificate of rent paid' for a tenant to file — those phrases return no hits in the Wyoming Statutes. Property taxes are the owner's liability and are administered under Title 39, chapter 13.

Two things are worth knowing anyway. First, if you want the tenant to bear property taxes, the lease has to say so; nothing makes a residential tenant liable for them by default, and a tax pass-through you did not write into the lease is not collectible and is not deductible from the deposit (Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) permits deducting 'other costs provided by any contract', which means costs your contract creates). If you do pass taxes through, write out how the amount is calculated, when the tenant is billed and what proof you will give — because your tenant will ask, and the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act supplies the penalty for a charge described one way and billed another (§ 40-12-105(a) is gated on 'knowingly' and includes the (a)(xv) catch-all, with merchandise defined at § 40-12-102(a)(vi) to include real property and no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110).

Second, a pass-through has a consequence you may not want. Wyoming counties may run a property-tax deferral program under Wyo. Stat. § 39-13-107, letting a qualifying person defer collection of up to half the real estate ad valorem taxes on a principal residence. Subparagraph (J) of that deferral paragraph provides that if a residence is under rental and the terms of the rental contract require payment of the taxes by the renter, the RENTER may apply for the deferral — provided the property owner or an authorized agent also cosigns the affidavit to defer before a notarial officer or the county assessor or deputy. Deferral is not free money: under subparagraph (B) a granted deferral is a perpetual tax lien against the property with priority over any other lien, and the deferred taxes become due on sale or transfer of the property, among other triggers, with interest compounding under subparagraph (D). So a lease that makes your tenant pay the taxes also gives your tenant standing to ask you to cosign a lien against your own property. The cautious course if you use a tax pass-through is to address the deferral in the lease: say that the tenant will not apply for a § 39-13-107 deferral without your prior written consent, and that you are not obliged to cosign.

Local governments may impose their own notice or billing requirements and are outside this library; check the municipality and county where the property sits.

title: Wyoming Does Not Separately Ban Asking About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Wyoming's fair housing act contains no inquiry ban and no record-keeping ban. Unlike states that make the QUESTION itself unlawful regardless of what you do with the answer, Wyoming prohibits conduct and statements, not curiosity. All forty-five sections of the act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145, were checked for an inquiry provision and there is none; 'inquir' returns three hits in the whole of Title 40 and not one is in the fair housing chapter, and 'elicit' returns zero. Do not take that as permission to ask. What Wyoming does prohibit is wide enough that an application question will usually land inside it anyway, and the sequence matters. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(a) bars refusing to sell or rent after a bona fide offer, refusing to negotiate, 'or in any other manner mak[ing] unavailable or deny[ing] a dwelling' to an individual because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. § 40-26-103(b) bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in providing services or facilities in connection with one, on the same seven grounds. Those are the only seven classes in the core provisions — there is no source-of-income, sexual-orientation, gender-identity, age or marital-status class in §§ 40-26-103 to 40-26-109. The provision that comes closest to an inquiry ban is Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-104: a person may not make, print or publish, or cause the making, printing or publishing of, 'a notice, statement or advertisement that is about the sale or rental of a dwelling and that indicates any preference, limitation or discrimination OR THE INTENTION to make a preference, limitation or discrimination' on those seven grounds. Read 'statement' and 'intention' together: a question on your application form, in a showing, or in an email that signals you care about an applicant's religion, national origin, disability or whether they have children is a statement indicating an intention, and § 40-26-104 can reach it even where no one was turned away. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-105 adds that you may not represent to an individual, because of those grounds, that a dwelling is not available for inspection when it is. So the practical rule in Wyoming is the same as in an inquiry-ban state even though the statute is shaped differently: ask every applicant the same questions, ask only about the things you will actually decide on — income, rental history, credit, references, occupancy against the number in the lease under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) — and keep the answers out of your notes. Four specific traps. First, § 40-26-104 reaches you even when the rest of the act does not. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(a)'s three-house owner exemption covers §§ 40-26-103 through 40-26-109 but is expressly conditioned on NOT publishing a notice, statement or advertisement prohibited by § 40-26-104, and § 40-26-110(b)'s owner-occupied four-family exemption covers § 40-26-103 and §§ 40-26-105 through 40-26-109, deliberately leaving § 40-26-104 out. An exempt Wyoming landlord is still bound by the publication rule. And under § 40-26-110(a)(iii) a person who owns any dwelling intended for five or more families is 'in the business' and loses the three-house exemption across their whole portfolio. Second, disability. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services. Wyoming's act does NOT contain the federal disability-inquiry rule, so the cautious course on an accommodation request is the federal one: ask only whether the person has a disability-related need for the accommodation and for reliable confirmation of that need where it is not obvious — never for a diagnosis, medical records or the nature of the condition. That restraint comes from federal law, not Wyoming's. Third, the longer class list. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i), the intimidation-and-interference offence, lists MORE classes than the rest of the act — race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance — but only for conduct 'by force or threat of force'. § 40-26-144(b) makes coercing or interfering with any right granted by the chapter a discriminatory practice with no force element, and (c) makes either a misdemeanor. Do not state Wyoming's class list without saying which provision you mean. Fourth, federal law supplies the inquiry ban Wyoming lacks.
