The Fair Housing Act and HUD's rules — notably 24 C.F.R. § 100.202(c), which bars inquiring into whether an applicant or a person intending to reside in the dwelling has a disability, or into the nature or severity of one — apply in Wyoming and were not searched here. Keep one application form, use it for everyone, and record the reason for every denial in business terms.

title: Limiting the Property to Its Intended Use
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute voids, annuls or rescinds a lease because the premises were used for a prohibited purpose. There is no Wyoming equivalent of Rhode Island's annulment provisions and no North Dakota-style rule letting you treat the lease as rescinded for use outside a stated purpose. "Lease shall be void" and "void the lease" each return nothing in Wyoming law, and the one voiding statute that sounds close — Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-106, "Gambling contracts void" — reaches only contracts whose CONSIDERATION is money or property won by gaming or lent at the place of play. A residential lease's consideration is rent, so it is untouched even if the tenant gambles in the unit.

WHAT WYOMING GIVES YOU INSTEAD IS BETTER, AND MOST LANDLORDS MISS IT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) makes it a statutory duty of every renter to "[o]ccupy the residential rental unit in the manner for which it was designed and shall not increase the number of occupants above that specified in the rental agreement without written permission of the owner." That first limb is a purpose limitation written into Wyoming law, and it operates without any lease clause at all. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) then allows a forcible entry and detainer action "[a]gainst renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205". So occupying a dwelling as a workshop, a kennel, a storage depot, a short-term-rental business or anything else it was not designed for is a statutory breach with a statutory eviction ground attached. You still serve the three-day written notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 first, and the Article 12 duties reach only a "residential rental unit" as § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

Two more hooks sit beside it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter's duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, so a use restriction you write into the lease gets the same § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) eviction ground. And § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) prohibits interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property, which covers a use that spills onto neighbours even if the unit itself is undamaged.

NUISANCE USE — THE CONSEQUENCE RUNS TO THE PROPERTY, NOT TO THE LEASE. Wyo. Stat. § 6-6-201 declares that whoever maintains, uses, OWNS OR LEASES any structure for lewdness, assignation, prostitution or gambling, or for the manufacture, possession, sale or disposition of intoxicating liquor or any controlled substance in violation of law, is guilty of a nuisance — and the structure, the ground it stands on, and the furniture, fixtures and contents are declared a nuisance too, to be enjoined and abated. Note the breadth: mere POSSESSION of a controlled substance is inside the definition, and owning or leasing is inside the list of culpable acts. Under § 6-6-202 the county attorney or ANY citizen of the county may bring the action, and a temporary injunction issues without bond on three (3) days' written notice to the defendant. Under § 6-6-204 the abatement order directs removal and execution sale of the fixtures, furniture and movable property used in conducting the nuisance, and orders the structure CLOSED for a period the court sets; breaking into a closed building is itself punishable under § 6-6-208. Section 6-6-207 assesses a $300 tax against the building, the ground and the owner or agent whenever a permanent injunction issues.

Read that sequence carefully, because it is the real answer to this topic. Wyoming does not void the lease — it closes the building. The tenancy survives on paper while the premises become unusable, and the loss falls on you. Your escape is § 6-6-206: if the owner appears, pays all the costs of the proceeding and files a bond with approved sureties in the full value of the property, conditioned on immediately abating the nuisance and preventing its recurrence for a period the court sets, the court may cancel the abatement order as to the property if satisfied of the owner's good faith — but the release does not discharge any judgment, lien or liability. Good faith is proved by what you did and when, so act on what you learn and keep the record.

WHAT TO DO. Write a purpose clause anyway. The statutory duty in § 1-21-1204(a)(v) is framed around what the unit was "designed" for, which invites argument about an unusual use that is still residential; a lease that states the permitted use plainly, and names the uses you will not allow, removes that argument and brings § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) into play as a second, independent ground. Under § 1-21-1202(d) the parties may modify or assign any Article 12 duty by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so your clause can also sharpen the statutory duty rather than merely repeating it. Do not write that a prohibited use makes the lease automatically void — in Wyoming it does not, and a clause claiming an automatic forfeiture or a self-help remedy risks the Consumer Protection Act, which reaches residential leasing under § 40-12-102(a)(vi) and is gated on knowing conduct under § 40-12-105(a). Terminate, serve the § 1-21-1003 notice, and file.

title: Wyoming Requires No Recycling Notice to Tenants
bodyText:
Wyoming imposes no recycling duty on landlords and requires no recycling notice. You do not have to tell tenants where or how to recycle, provide recycling containers, list accepted materials, or post anything about collection. The word "recycling" does not appear anywhere in Wyoming's landlord-tenant law, and the recycling provisions Wyoming does have are environmental-permitting rules about solid-waste and advanced-recycling facilities in Title 35, which regulate facility operators rather than housing providers. There is also no state statewide collection list to reference, so a recycling clause copied from a state that has one will point at nothing.

What Wyoming does give you is the waste side of the tenant's statutory duties, and that is what your lease should build on. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(ii) requires each renter to "[d]ispose of all garbage and other waste in a clean and safe manner." Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii) requires the renter to remove all property and garbage owned or placed in the unit by the renter or the renter's guests before termination of the rental agreement, and to clean the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(i) separately requires the renter to maintain the unit in a clean and safe condition and "not unreasonably burden any common area," which is the provision that reaches overflowing bins, bags left in a shared hallway, or a dumpster filled with one tenant's move-out debris. These are statutory duties, so they apply whether or not your lease repeats them. They are also enforceable: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 a ground for forcible entry and detainer, on the ordinary three-day written notice to leave the premises under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003.

On your side, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) requires you to maintain common areas of the residential rental unit in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition, which is where a neglected shared waste enclosure would land. Where tenants fail at move-out, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, "the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement," and other costs provided by any contract - so hauling and disposal charges are a proper deduction if your lease says so, and you should say so. Itemize them in writing on the statutory clock: within thirty days after termination or fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by another thirty days if there is damage. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210(a) lets you immediately dispose of any trash or property you reasonably believe is hazardous, perishable, or valueless and abandoned once you lawfully regain possession, with anything still in the unit after termination presumed valueless and abandoned; only property you treat as valuable needs the seven-day notice procedure in § 1-21-1210(a)(i) through (iii).

So if recycling matters to you - because your hauler charges by contamination, or your building has a shared enclosure, or a local program exists - put it in the lease as a house rule rather than waiting for a statute to require it. Specify which containers take what, where they live, when they go out and come back in, and that the tenant must follow the collection program serving the property. Tie it to Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii), the renter's duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, so that a persistent violation is a lease breach and not merely an annoyance. Keep the rule lawful and reasonable, and give it to the tenant in writing with the lease.

Flagged and not resolved: Wyoming municipalities and counties run their own solid-waste and recycling programs and some impose requirements on property owners or on multifamily buildings by ordinance. Local ordinances are outside this review, so check the city or county serving the property before you promise a tenant that recycling is or is not available.

title: No Tenant Right to Pay and Stop an Eviction
bodyText: Wyoming gives a residential tenant no statutory right of redemption. There is no provision letting a tenant pay the rent, costs and fees and have a nonpayment eviction dismissed, no pay-before-the-lockout window, no once-per-lease-period limit to manage, and no rule telling you to accept a charity's or an agency's check. Wyoming's redemption statutes, in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-18-102 through 1-18-114, are about redeeming real property after an execution or foreclosure sale - a mortgagor's remedy, not a tenant's - and nothing in the forcible entry and detainer article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, or the residential rental article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, creates a cure or redemption right of any kind. The timeline runs the other way, and it runs fast. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) lets you bring the action against a tenant holding over, or after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires you to notify the tenant to leave the premises at least three days before you commence the action, by leaving a written copy with the tenant or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found. Once judgment of restitution is entered, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1012 says the court shall issue the writ of restitution at your request, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1013 says that unless the defendant appeals, the officer shall execute the writ within two days after receiving it, Sundays excepted, and shall levy and collect the execution for rent and costs. The only statutory way a tenant stops that clock is an appeal, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1014(b) requires the appellant to file a bond with two or more sufficient sureties within forty-eight hours after judgment, Sundays excepted; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1015(a) adds that in appeals from a judgment for rents due the appellant must also deposit the judgment rent with the court, and that unless the deposit is made the appeal is not perfected. Under § 1-21-1015(b) the appellant must keep depositing rent as it comes due, and if a deposit is missed the appellate court shall affirm the judgment with costs and the deposited rent is paid over to you. So the practical answer to "can my tenant pay their way out of this?" is: only if you let them. Because no statute requires you to accept a late payment, you have a real choice to make - and that is exactly where the risk sits, because Wyoming has no statute telling you what accepting rent after you have served a notice to quit does to your case. Under general landlord-tenant principles a landlord who accepts rent for a period after serving a termination notice may be held to have waived the forfeiture and reinstated the tenancy, and Wyoming's statutes neither codify that rule nor abolish it. The cautious course, since this cannot be settled from the statutes, is: decide before the money arrives. If you want the tenancy to continue, take the payment and serve a fresh notice later if you need one. If you want possession, either decline the payment outright, or accept it only under a signed written agreement that says the payment is applied to past-due rent, does not create a new tenancy, does not waive the notice or the pending action, and does not reinstate the lease - and get the tenant's signature before you deposit the check. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) supports doing it in writing: any duty or obligation under the residential rental article may be assigned or modified only by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Note finally that accepting partial payment is not the same as redemption in any event: Wyoming has no statute requiring reservation wording on a partial payment, and none limiting how often a tenant may catch up. Your own lease is the only place those limits can come from.

title: No Religious or Cultural Display Right in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming gives tenants no statutory right to display religious or cultural items on the entry door, the doorframe or anywhere else in or on the dwelling, and it sets no size limits, no exceptions and no procedure of the kind some states have written for mezuzahs, crosses, wreaths or similar items. There is no Wyoming flag-display right for tenants either. That means your house rules control, subject to two real limits. The first is discrimination law. Religion is a protected class under the Wyoming Fair Housing Act: you may not discriminate against an individual "in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a sale or rental of a dwelling" because of religion (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 40-26-103(b)), and you may not publish any notice or statement about a rental indicating a preference, limitation or discrimination on that basis (§ 40-26-104). A rule that bans a mezuzah or a crucifix while you tolerate wreaths, sports pennants and seasonal decorations, or that you enforce against one tenant's faith and not another's, is exactly the kind of term-and-condition discrimination the Act reaches, and the federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq., independently applies. Wyoming's fair housing exemptions in §§ 40-26-110 and 40-26-111 are narrow and fact-specific; do not assume one covers you. The second limit is the lease itself. Wyoming makes the renter responsible for not intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging, impairing or removing any part of the rental unit (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1205(a)(i)) and for complying with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement (§ 1-21-1204(a)(vii)), and it lets you apply the deposit to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear and to the cost of cleaning the unit back to its starting condition (§ 1-21-1208(a)). So your legitimate interest is in the holes, adhesive and paint damage, not in the symbol. The sound rule is neutral on its face, written in the lease or house rules, and enforced the same way for everyone: permit a small item affixed to the entry door or doorframe, cap its size, require a mounting method that does not damage the surface, keep required exits and door operation clear, prohibit anything that violates a fire or building code, and require removal and repair of any damage at the end of the tenancy with those costs chargeable to the deposit. Write the rule that way and you can enforce it; write it to single out religious items and you cannot. City and county ordinances were not reviewed and may add their own display rules.

title: Free Rent and Move-In Concessions
bodyText:
Wyoming regulates rent concessions not at all. There is no statute requiring a concession to be stated in the lease, no rule about how a concession must be advertised, no "net effective rent" disclosure rule, no cap on what you may claw back if the tenant defaults, and no provision making an unstated concession unenforceable. The word "concession" appears eleven times in the whole Wyoming code and every one is about a vendor stand or a state-land lease. "Free rent" returns nothing.

That means the lease is the whole of the law here, and that cuts both ways. A concession you did not write down is a gift, and a clawback you did not write down does not exist. Wyoming's statute of frauds, Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v), requires a lease of real estate for more than one year to be in a signed writing, and there is no Wyoming statute making an oral side promise about free rent enforceable against either party. Put the concession and its conditions in the lease itself, not in an email, a listing or a move-in sheet.

The clawback is worth thinking about structurally, because Wyoming's eviction statute gives you two different routes and you should know which one you are on. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i), a forcible entry and detainer action lies against tenants "holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due." Under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi), it also lies "[a]gainst renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205" -- and § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter's duty to "[c]omply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement." So a lease obligation to repay a concession on default is enforceable through the same summary process whether or not you call the repayment "rent." Either way, § 1-21-1003 requires you to serve a written notice to quit at least three days before you file, left with the tenant or at their usual place of abode or business if they cannot be found.

Be careful about calling the clawback "additional rent" reflexively. Doing so gives you the three-day nonpayment route in § 1-21-1002(a)(i), but it also means a dispute over whether the clawback was owed becomes a dispute over whether your notice correctly stated the rent due, and a defective notice sinks the case. The cleaner structure is the one in the clause that accompanies this note: state the concession, state exactly what event triggers repayment, state the amount or the formula, and state when it is due -- then enforce it as a lease obligation.

One more Wyoming-specific point. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 says there is no implied renewal when a lease term expires and that a tenant holding over with the landlord's acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance, and § 34-2-129 says an expired lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by both parties. A concession tied to completing a full term therefore does not carry forward into a holdover by itself. If you want the concession, and the clawback, to survive into a renewal, put them in the signed renewal.

Practical course: describe the concession precisely, in dollars and in dates; say whether it is a waiver of specific months' rent or a credit applied to the ledger; tie repayment to defined events rather than to "default" at large; and do not advertise a discounted monthly figure that is really an annual concession spread out, since misrepresenting the price of merchandise is one of the deceptive trade practices listed at Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a)(vii) and advertising a rental is within the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act on the face of § 40-12-102(a)(ii).

title: Rent Control and Local Rental Rules in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no rent control and no rent stabilization. It also has no statute preempting rent control — and that second point is the one worth knowing, because most landlords assume a state without rent control must have banned it. Wyoming has not. The phrases "rent control," "rent stabilization," "maximum rent" and "rent increase" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes, in either direction.

Set rent freely, and raise it freely. No Wyoming statute caps rent, limits an increase, requires notice before an increase, or treats recurring fees as rent for any cap. Wyoming also has no statutory notice period for ending a month-to-month tenancy, so the lease is what governs both the amount and the timing — write the increase and notice mechanics into it, because the statutes will not supply them.

On preemption, know where Wyoming actually stands. Compare South Dakota, which bars every local government from controlling the rent charged for private residential property. Wyoming has no such statute. What Wyoming has instead is a constitutional home-rule grant: Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b) provides that "[a]ll cities and towns are hereby empowered to determine their local affairs and government as established by ordinance passed by the governing body, subject to referendum when prescribed by the legislature, and further subject only to statutes uniformly applicable to all cities and towns, and to statutes prescribing limits of indebtedness." So a Wyoming city or town starts with broad ordinance power over local affairs and is cut back only by statutes that apply uniformly to all cities and towns. There is no uniformly applicable statute on rents to do the cutting. Whether a Wyoming court would uphold a municipal rent-control ordinance is untested — case law is outside this library — but you should not tell yourself it is impossible, and you should watch the city council where you own.

Counties are different. A board of county commissioners has only the powers the legislature grants, chiefly under Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-101; there is no county home rule in the Wyoming Constitution. A county rent ordinance would have to be traced to a statutory grant, and none exists.

What your city CAN already do, and does, is regulate around the edges — and those powers are explicit. Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xix) lets a governing body "[d]eclare and abate nuisances and impose fines upon parties who create, continue or permit nuisances to exist." A county may declare and abate a nuisance threatening health or safety under Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-101(a)(viii), following the procedure in Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-115, which requires written notice to "the owner or occupant" served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure and filed with the district court clerk, with a twenty (20) day window to answer. And a municipality or county may take on fire and building code enforcement under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121, enforcing the International Fire Code, International Building Code and related codes the state fire prevention and electrical safety council adopts under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i). Municipal ordinances — rental registration, rental licensing, periodic inspections, lead-safe certificates, short-term rental rules, crime-free housing programs — are outside this library and must be checked locally. Note that Wyoming has no STATEWIDE rental registration, rental licensing or periodic rental inspection program, and no statute limiting a locality from creating one.

Three related gaps to be clear about:
• No source-of-income protection and no preemption of one. Wyoming has no statute requiring you to accept a housing choice voucher, and no statute barring a city from requiring it. The one place public-assistance status appears in Wyoming housing law is Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i), which makes it an offense to intimidate or interfere with someone by force or threat of force because of, among other things, "status with respect to marriage or public assistance." That is a harassment offense, not an acceptance mandate.
• No emergency price control over rent. Wyoming has no price-gouging statute at all ("price gouging" appears nowhere in the statutes), and no emergency power that freezes dwelling rent during a declared disaster. There is no Wyoming counterpart to Puerto Rico's Ley 52-2019.
• No statute letting a locality sue a landlord over habitability on tenants' behalf. Wyoming's habitability remedies at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1203 and 1-21-1206 run to the renter, who must be current on all payments required by the rental agreement and must give written notice before using them. A city's route against a bad property is code enforcement and nuisance abatement, not a tenants' suit.

Practical course: price your units to the market, put a clear rent-adjustment and notice provision in the lease since no statute supplies one, and check your city's ordinances annually — Wyoming's home-rule structure means your local government, not the legislature, is where any rental regulation will appear.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for Property Conditions
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute that stops you from demanding or collecting rent because of the condition of the property. There is no rent escrow, no rent withholding, no repair-and-deduct, no rent abatement and no suspension of rent under a code order — none of those phrases appears anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. There is also no state rental registration or licensing scheme whose absence could bar your rent. Wyoming in fact runs the other way: paying rent is the price of the tenant's own remedies. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) a renter may give you written notice of a health-and-safety noncompliance only '[i]f the renter is current on all payments required by the rental agreement' and has reasonable cause supported by evidence. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a) the renter's remedies 'are available to a renter in compliance with all provisions of W.S. 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205,' and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vi) requires the renter to 'be current on all payments required by the rental agreement.' A renter who stops paying generally loses the statutory remedy, and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) you may proceed in forcible entry and detainer after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due. There is one real exposure and you should plan around it. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(c) lets a renter who has served the two statutory notices — the Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) notice of the condition, then the 'notice to repair or correct condition' under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(b) — bring a civil action in circuit court, and '[u]pon a showing of an unreasonable refusal to correct or the failure to use due diligence to correct a condition described in this article, the renter may be awarded costs, damages and affirmative relief as determined by the court. Damages awarded to the renter may include rent improperly retained or collected.' So Wyoming does not bar the demand up front; it lets a court take the rent back afterwards, and it can also terminate the lease or order you to make repairs. If the court terminates, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(d) gives the renter a refund of the balance of the rent and the deposit within thirty days. The practical answer is to treat a written Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) notice as a deadline. Within a reasonable time you must either start correcting the condition or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim — doing neither is what produces the clawback. Two limits in your favour: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(c) puts breakage, malfunctions and conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter outside the article entirely, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) says you need not correct a condition the renter, the renter's family or the renter's guests or invitees caused by inappropriate use or misuse. One other thing a landlord sometimes expects to see here: there is no Wyoming rule making rent uncollectible for want of a certificate of occupancy. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-108 requires a state fire marshal certificate of occupancy or letter of compliance before a newly constructed or remodeled building may be used or occupied, and the sanction is an order that the use and occupancy cease — not a forfeiture of rent.

title: Raising Rent in Wyoming - No Caps, No Notice Rule, No Retaliation Statute
bodyText:
Wyoming does not regulate rent in any way. There is no cap on the amount of an increase, no limit on how often you may increase, no statutory notice period before an increase takes effect, and no index or formula you must use. "Rent control," "rent stabilization," "maximum rent" and every form of "rent increase" return zero hits across all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Your lease is the only rule.

And Wyoming has no landlord-retaliation statute at all. This matters because the sub-questions this topic usually asks — whether the retaliation statute's safe harbour for a market-rate increase applies only if the lease provides for it, and whether the retaliation presumption reaches an increase scheduled in the lease itself — have no Wyoming answer, because there is no presumption and no safe harbour to be inside or outside of. The word "retaliat" does not appear once in Title 1, Title 34 or Title 40. Every one of its 32 appearances in Wyoming law is elsewhere: criminal law, insurance, education, elections, corrections, and a long-term care facility rule at Wyo. Stat. § 35-2-1306(a) about electronic monitoring. None of it reaches a residential landlord.

So you do not need a safe harbour, and you should not draft toward one. Do not import another state's "increase to comparable market rent is not retaliation" language; it has nothing to attach to here and invites an argument that Wyoming recognises a retaliation doctrine it does not.

There is one real limit, and it is not in the landlord-tenant chapter. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(b) makes it a discriminatory practice to "coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, or on account of the individual having exercised or enjoyed, or on account of the individual having aided or encouraged any other individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, any right granted or protected by this chapter." Note that subsection (b), unlike the criminal offence in § 40-26-144(a), has no force-or-threat-of-force element. An offence under (a) or (b) is a misdemeanour under § 40-26-144(c). So a rent increase aimed at a tenant because that tenant complained of housing discrimination, requested a disability accommodation, or helped a neighbour do either, is actionable — not as retaliation under a landlord-tenant statute, but as interference under the Wyoming Fair Housing Act. That is the exposure to manage, and the way to manage it is to apply increases by a written, uniform, documented policy.

The mid-term increase question has a clear Wyoming answer. During a fixed term, rent stays as the lease wrote it. There is no statute letting you raise it, so a mid-term increase is possible only if the lease itself provides for it. Put the escalation in the lease at signing — either a schedule of stated amounts and dates, or an index formula — or you are stuck with the rent you wrote until the term ends.

At the end of the term, the Wyoming rule is unusual and works in your favour. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that there is no implied renewal of a lease on expiration "for any period of time whatever," not by the tenant holding over and not by the landlord accepting rent during the holdover; holding over plus acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by the parties. So a tenant who stays on past the term has not locked in the old rent — but neither have you created a new tenancy at a new rent. If you want the tenancy to continue at a higher rent, get a signed written renewal or a signed written month-to-month agreement stating the new rent. If you do not, you have a tenant at sufferance and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) lets you bring forcible entry and detainer against a tenant holding over the term.

Four drafting points. First, under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) any duty or obligation in the residential rental article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so a signed escalation term is firmly within the landlord's power. Second, name your own notice period in the escalation clause, because no statute supplies one. Third, if you index the rent, name the exact published index and series, pick a base month, and say what happens if publication stops. Fourth, if you escalate for taxes, insurance or utilities, show the calculation in the notice — and if you escalate for a utility you meter or resell, check Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) first, because metered or direct sales of a utility commodity to tenants withdraw the landlord's public-utility exemption, and the fee-free allocation carve-out at (H)(VIII) and (IX) is for water only.

Finally, local ordinances are unresolved. Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b) and nothing in Wyoming law preempts local rental regulation, so confirm your municipality has not adopted anything before relying on the absence of state limits.

title: Rent Security and Counterclaims in an Eviction Case
bodyText:
Wyoming does not make a tenant pay rent into court to defend an eviction, and it has no compulsory counterclaim rule in a forcible entry and detainer case. The tenant may raise any defence without depositing a dollar. Indeed Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1004 states that 'The defendant shall not be required to file a written answer to the complaint as a condition of being allowed to participate fully in the trial,' and § 1-21-1006 repeats that the defendant 'may, but is not required to, file a written answer,' with either party allowed to amend. Expect to meet defences you have had no written notice of, and go to the first hearing with your ledger, the lease, the notice to quit and proof of service in hand.

But Wyoming does have two rent-security provisions, and both run in your favour. Ask for each by name, because neither is automatic.

The first is the continuance bond. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1007 provides: 'No continuance shall be granted the defendant for longer than two (2) days unless he gives a bond to the adverse party, with good and sufficient surety approved by the circuit court, conditioned for the payment of the rent that may accrue and costs if judgment is rendered against him.' This is the direct Wyoming answer to the question of whether a long adjournment requires rent security: it does. Two days is the free period; anything longer is conditioned on a surety bond running to you and covering rent accruing during the delay plus costs. When the tenant asks for a two-week postponement, do not simply agree — say on the record that you do not object provided the court sets the § 1-21-1007 bond, and ask that the amount cover the rent that will accrue.

The second bites harder, on appeal. Under § 1-21-1014(b), a defendant's appeal does not stay proceedings on the judgment unless, within forty-eight (48) hours after judgment, Sundays excepted, the appellant executes and files a bond to you with two (2) or more sufficient sureties approved by the court, conditioned that the appellant will pay all costs accrued or thereafter accruing and all damages you have sustained or may sustain in consequence of the wrongful detention of the premises during the appeal. The court in which the appeal is pending may require a new bond in a larger amount if needed to secure the parties' rights, so ask for an increase if the first bond is thin. Then § 1-21-1015(a) adds a separate cash requirement: in appeals from a circuit court judgment for rents due and payable, 'in addition to the bond required by W.S. 1-21-1014, the appellant shall deposit with the court the amount of rent specified in the judgment. Unless the deposit is made, the appeal is not perfected and proceedings upon the judgment shall be had accordingly.' In plain terms, no deposit means no appeal and you may proceed to enforce. Section 1-21-1015(b) keeps the obligation running: as each rent falls due during the appeal the appellant must deposit it with the clerk of the appellate court, and if the appellant fails to make any such deposit, then upon your motion and proof of that fact the appellate court 'shall affirm the judgment appealed from with costs,' with the deposited rent money paid over to you on the court's order. That is a mandatory affirmance, not a discretionary one — but it is triggered only by a motion from you, so diary every rent due date during an appeal and move the moment one is missed.

The rest of the enforcement timeline is quick. Under § 1-21-1012 the court shall issue a writ of restitution at your request once a judgment of restitution is entered, and under § 1-21-1013, unless the defendant takes an appeal, the officer shall execute the writ within two (2) days after receiving it, Sundays excepted, restoring you to possession, and shall levy and collect the execution for rent and costs. Note the two grounds most often used: § 1-21-1002(a)(i) reaches tenants holding over their terms or holding over after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due, and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) reaches renters in violation of any term imposed under § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205. Keep those three days distinct from the separate three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003, which is a different period and must still be given. Section 1-21-1002(b) confirms that the eviction article does not limit §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1210, and § 1-21-1016 confirms that a pending forcible entry and detainer action does not bar an action of ejectment.

Two cautions. First, § 1-21-1202(d), which lets Article 12 duties be modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, speaks only of 'this article' and sits in Article 12 — it gives you no power to contract around the Article 10 notice to quit or any of these bond and deposit provisions, and you should not try. Second, these are the statutory rules only. Counterclaim and setoff practice in circuit court is governed by the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure and the circuit court rules, which are not statutes; the general setoff provision at § 1-1-106 (cross demands are deemed compensated so far as they equal each other) exists, but whether a tenant may litigate a damages counterclaim inside a possession action, rather than separately, is a matter of court rule and practice. Ask your Wyoming counsel before assuming a counterclaim must be severed.

title: What Accepting Rent Does and Does Not Waive
bodyText:
Wyoming reverses the usual rule, and it is strongly in your favour — but only in one situation, and landlords get into trouble by stretching it.

Accepting rent after the lease expires. In most states, taking rent from a tenant who stays past the end of the term creates a new periodic tenancy by implication. Wyoming says the opposite, twice and in plain words. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that in this state the relations of landlord and tenant do not exist "by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance"; that on expiration of a term created by a lease, verbal or written, "there shall be no implied renewal of the same, for any period of time whatever, either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent for or during any period of such holding over"; and that holding over plus acceptance of rent "shall constitute only a tenancy by sufferance." Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is renewed only "by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto," and that no tenancy other than sufferance exists after the original lease ends unless created that way.

So, plainly: after the term has expired, accepting rent from a holdover tenant does not renew the lease, does not create a month-to-month or any other periodic tenancy, and does not give the tenant any new term of any length. It leaves a tenancy at sufferance, and nothing more. You can take the money and still proceed, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows forcible entry and detainer "[a]gainst tenants holding over their terms." Serve the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 and file. Note the flip side: because no periodic tenancy arises and Wyoming has no statutory notice period for ending one, a holdover tenant has no statutory right to thirty days' notice either. Note too that a renewal you actually want must be in a signed writing — an oral agreement to extend will not renew an expired lease under § 34-2-129, so put every extension in writing and have both parties sign.

Now the limit, and this is the part that catches people. Both sections are written about what happens "[u]pon the expiration of a term" and "after the termination of the original lease." Neither says anything about accepting rent while the term is still running. So if you serve a three-day notice for non-payment or for another default and then accept rent from a tenant whose term has not expired, §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 do not protect you. That situation is governed by the ordinary common-law doctrine that accepting rent with knowledge of a breach can waive the forfeiture — a doctrine Wyoming has not displaced by statute and which this review, limited to the statutes, cannot resolve. Treat that as real authority cutting the other way. The cautious course during a term: do not accept rent after serving a notice to quit unless you first get the tenant's signature on a written agreement stating that the payment is accepted for use and occupancy only, that it does not waive the default or the notice, and that it does not reinstate the tenancy. A clause in the original lease saying acceptance of rent never waives a default helps, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) supports writing one, but do not rely on it alone against a specific later acceptance.

The separate question: can rent be split from the duties? Kansas and a few other states forbid a lease, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument from permitting anyone to receive rent free of the habitability obligations. Wyoming has no such provision — "receipt of rent," "assignment of rents," "mortgagee in possession" and "free of the obligation" all appear nowhere in the statutes. Wyoming leans the other way. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says any duty or obligation in the landlord-tenant article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in that article. What ties the duties down instead is the definition: § 1-21-1201(a)(i) defines "owner" as the owner, lessor or sublessor of a residential rental unit, so the § 1-21-1203 duties attach to whoever occupies the landlord's role, not to whoever happens to receive the money. A lender taking an assignment of rents as collateral, or a receiver collecting during a default, does not become the "owner" merely by receiving rent. Two practical consequences. If you assign rents to a lender, you keep the duties, so do not assume the assignment moves them. And if you are buying, or stepping in as a receiver or manager, your exposure turns on whether you have become the lessor — get that allocated expressly and in a signed writing, which is exactly what § 1-21-1202(d) contemplates. All of this applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence, since § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" that way and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

title: No Duty to Give a Rent Receipt in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring a landlord to give a tenant a receipt for rent, in cash or any other form. There is no cash-receipt duty, no record-book requirement, no penalty for refusing a receipt, no rule that failing to give one is a defence to a nonpayment eviction, and no evidentiary presumption that a receipt for a later month proves earlier months were paid. Wyoming also has no statute requiring you to accept cash rent, and none permitting you to refuse it - the method of payment is whatever the lease says.

Give receipts anyway, and make the lease do the rest. Four Wyoming-specific reasons.

FIRST, THE THREE-DAY GRACE PERIOD TURNS ON THE DATE OF PAYMENT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows a forcible entry and detainer proceeding against a tenant "after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due." Whether the tenant paid, and on what day, is the whole case. A dated receipt or a bank record settles it; a cash payment with no record does not, and the absence cuts against whoever carries the burden on that point.

SECOND, THE TENANT'S OWN REMEDIES DEPEND ON BEING CURRENT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) gives a tenant the habitability-notice route only "[i]f the renter is current on all payments required by the rental agreement," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a) conditions every tenant remedy on compliance with §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205, which include § 1-21-1204(a)(vi), being current on all payments. Your payment records are therefore as useful to you defensively as offensively - they are how you show a complaining tenant was not current.

THIRD, DEPOSIT DEDUCTIONS RUN THROUGH THE SAME LEDGER. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to accrued rent, damages and "other costs provided by any contract," and § 1-21-1208(b) requires the deposit, less deductions, plus prepaid rent, with a written itemization, to be delivered or mailed within thirty days after termination or fifteen days after you receive the tenant's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by thirty days if there is damage. A clean running account of what was paid and when is what makes that itemization defensible.

FOURTH, THE CONSUMER PROTECTION HOOK. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches real property under Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi), and Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105 is gated on knowing conduct. A landlord who takes cash, issues nothing, and then sues for the same rent is exactly the fact pattern that invites a claim, subject to the pre-suit notice and cure period in Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-109.

WHAT TO PUT IN THE LEASE, SINCE NO STATUTE DOES IT FOR YOU. Name the permitted payment methods and say whether cash is accepted. If you do accept cash, require it to be handed to a named person at a named place and say that a written receipt will be issued at the time and that a payment is not treated as made until the receipt is issued - that protects you as much as the tenant. State where and to whom rent is paid; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) makes a property manager or agent a proper recipient of notices unless the rental agreement specifies otherwise, and the same clarity should apply to money. Say that partial payments are applied in a stated order and that accepting a partial payment is not a waiver of the right to the balance or to possession - no Wyoming statute supplies that rule, and without it accepting part of the rent can be argued as a waiver. Keep every receipt, bank record and ledger entry for at least the limitation period on the lease.

One point that is NOT the law in Wyoming and is in some other jurisdictions: there is no rule that producing a receipt for a later instalment creates a presumption that earlier instalments were paid. Wyoming has no such provision in its statutes, so a receipt proves only the payment it records.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched.

title: No rent-reporting rule in Wyoming, so federal law is the whole of it
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about reporting a tenant's rent payments to a credit bureau. Nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting as California and Maryland do, nothing sets a form of election or a fee cap, there is no state rent-reporting program a tenant could be pressed to join as in Nevada, and nothing requires you to notify a tenant before you report late rent as Puerto Rico does. The phrases "rent reporting", "credit bureau", "credit reporting agency" and "positive rent" produce no Wyoming tenancy provision at all, and "rental payment" never appears within sixty characters of "report" in either direction.

So if you choose to report, FEDERAL law governs you and Wyoming adds nothing. Reporting makes you a furnisher of information under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2 imposes the furnisher duties - do not furnish information you know or have reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate, correct and update information you have reported that you determine is incomplete or inaccurate, and investigate when a consumer disputes an item through the consumer reporting agency. FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 1681b governs the permissible purposes for pulling a report in the first place, which for a landlord is the tenant-screening purpose. Those are not Wyoming obligations and nothing in Wyoming law softens them.

THREE WYOMING POINTS THAT DO BEAR ON THIS.

First, how you describe the programme matters. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords - § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines "merchandise" to include real property and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110 - and § 40-12-105(a) makes it an unlawful deceptive trade practice to do any of the listed things knowingly in the course of business in connection with a consumer transaction, including under § 40-12-105(a)(viii) representing that a transaction involves particular rights, remedies or obligations when the representation is false, and under the § 40-12-105(a)(xv) catch-all engaging in unfair or deceptive acts or practices. Telling a tenant that reporting will raise their credit score, or that enrolment is required, or charging a fee you did not disclose, is where a Wyoming landlord gets into trouble on this subject. Note the cure mechanism: under §§ 40-12-109 and 40-12-102(a)(ix) a private claim lies only for an uncured practice, and you have fifteen days after a consumer's written notice to make a written offer to cure.

Second, a tenant's credit freeze does not stop you screening. Wyoming's security-freeze article, §§ 40-12-501 through 40-12-509, lets a consumer freeze a credit report under § 40-12-503, but § 40-12-505 carves out, among other things, a consumer reporting agency whose database consists entirely of public records and is used solely for criminal record information, TENANT SCREENING, employment screening or fraud prevention or detection, and a database or file consisting solely of information adverse to the consumer used for fraud prevention or detection, tenant screening, employment screening or any purpose permitted by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1681b. So a frozen file is not a reason you cannot run a tenant check.

Third, if you hold tenant data you have a breach-notification duty, and it is easy to miss because Wyoming does not use the phrase "data breach". Section 40-12-502(a) provides that an individual or commercial entity that conducts business in Wyoming and owns or licenses computerized data including personal identifying information about a Wyoming resident shall, when it becomes aware of a "breach of the security of the data system" as defined in § 40-12-501(a)(i), conduct in good faith a reasonable and prompt investigation into the likelihood that the information has been or will be misused, and if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely to occur, give notice as soon as possible to the affected Wyoming resident, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement and with measures needed to determine the scope of the breach and restore the integrity of the system. Section 40-12-502(b) allows delay only where a law enforcement agency determines in writing that notice may seriously impede a criminal investigation. Rent-reporting files - names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, bank details - are exactly the kind of data this covers, and a small landlord using a spreadsheet is "an individual ... that conducts business in Wyoming".

PRACTICAL ADVICE. If you want to offer rent reporting, make it genuinely optional, put the election and any fee in writing, say plainly that reporting may help or may hurt the tenant's credit depending on payment history, let the tenant withdraw, and report accurately and consistently for every enrolled tenant - selective reporting of only late payers is both an FCRA accuracy problem and the kind of practice § 40-12-105(a)(xv) was written for. Keep the data secure, because § 40-12-502 is the duty that will actually find you.

title: Taxes on Rent in Wyoming
bodyText:
RESIDENTIAL RENT IS NOT TAXED. Wyoming levies no sales tax, excise tax or gross receipts tax on residential rent, and no state or local tax on rent that you must collect from a tenant or state separately in the lease. The sales tax imposition section, Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-103(a)(i), lists the taxable events one by one, and renting real property is not among them. Subparagraph (B) taxes “The gross rental paid for the lease or contract transferring possession of tangible personal property” — that is equipment and furnishings rented on their own, not a dwelling. The only lodging-related item is subparagraph (G), “the sales price paid for living quarters in hotels, motels, tourist courts and similar establishments providing lodging service for transient guests.” Wyoming also has no individual income tax: Title 39 chapter 7 is headed “Income Taxes” and contains a single section, § 39-7-101, which reads “Repealed By Laws 1998, ch. 5, § 4.” So rent you receive is not subject to a Wyoming income tax either.

THE LINE IS THIRTY CONTINUOUS DAYS, AND IT IS A DEFINITION, NOT AN EXEMPTION. Everything turns on two definitions in Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-101(a). Paragraph (a)(xiv) defines a “transient guest” as “a guest who remains for less than thirty (30) continuous days.” Paragraph (a)(i) defines “lodging service” as the provision of sleeping accommodations to transient guests, and expressly includes providing sites for the placement of tents, campers, trailers, mobile homes or other mobile sleeping accommodations for transient guests. A tenant who stays thirty continuous days or more is therefore not a transient guest, what you provide is not a lodging service, and no lodging tax applies. Note that the test is continuous occupancy, not the stated term of the lease and not the frequency of rent payments — a written twelve-month lease occupied for three weeks and abandoned is not protected by the lease term, and a series of short stays is not aggregated into one.

WHEN YOU DO OWE TAX — SHORT-TERM AND MOBILE-HOME SITES. If you let a unit, a cabin, a room or a vacation rental to guests for less than thirty continuous days, you are providing a lodging service and three layers can apply. First, the state sales tax under Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-103(a)(i)(G) at the § 39-15-104(a) rate. Second, the statewide lodging assessment in Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-104(h): “In addition to the sales tax under subsections (a) and (b) of this section there is imposed an assessment upon the sale of lodging services of five percent (5%),” of which three percent goes to the Wyoming tourism account under § 39-15-111(p)(i) and two percent is distributed to counties and municipalities under § 39-15-111(p)(ii). Third, a county, city or town may impose its own lodging tax under Wyo. Stat. § 39-15-204(a)(ii), but only after the proposition is approved by the qualified electors at an election noticed once a week for thirty days, and if a countywide lodging tax passes, a city or town within the county may not add its own on top. If you rent mobile home, trailer or camper SITES, read § 39-15-101(a)(i) again: a site provided to a transient guest is a lodging service even though you supply no building. A permanent mobile home lot tenancy of thirty continuous days or more is not.

WHAT YOU STILL PAY. Ad valorem property tax on the real property is yours as owner, assessed under Title 39 chapters 11 and 13; nothing in Wyoming law bars you from recovering it through the rent you charge, and nothing requires you to itemize it. Wyoming has no statute banning the pass-through of a repealed or any other local tax to tenants — no such provision exists in the code. If you do pass a tax or a tax increase through as a separate charge rather than in the base rent, create it expressly in the lease: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) allows deduction from the deposit of “other costs provided by any contract,” which rewards a written charge and gives you nothing for an unwritten one. And if you run short-term lettings, register for a sales tax license and remit; the sales tax is a tax on the guest that you collect, and failing to collect it does not move the liability off you.

title: Government Inspections of Rental Property
bodyText:
Wyoming has no rental inspection program. There is no state proactive-inspection scheme, no rental inspection district, no rental licensing or registration requirement, no periodic certificate-of-occupancy renewal for a dwelling already in use, and no statute authorizing a housing inspector to enter an occupied rental unit. The phrases 'rental inspection', 'housing inspector' and 'administrative warrant' return no hits anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and 'rental licen', 'rental registr' and 'landlord licen' are all zero as well. Nobody from the state will knock on your tenant's door on a schedule.

What can reach an occupied rental is complaint-driven and runs through three channels, all of them outside the landlord-tenant article. Fire hazard: under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-111(a) the state fire marshal, a county fire warden or the chief of a fire department or district may declare a building a public nuisance if it is especially liable to fire and endangers people, buildings or property in the vicinity, and order it repaired, torn down or demolished. The order must be written, state its grounds, be filed with the clerk of the district court, be served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure on the owner AND any occupants, and be posted conspicuously on the building (§ 35-9-111(b)); you have the objection window in § 35-9-112 to answer. Public health: Wyo. Stat. § 35-1-105(a)(vii) makes it an offense for the owner or occupant of private property on which a nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness exists to willfully fail to remove it at his own expense within forty-eight hours after being ordered to do so by the health authority. Forty-eight hours is the shortest compliance window in Wyoming law — treat any such order as drop-everything. Code enforcement: Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(a) requires the state fire marshal to delegate complete authority to municipalities and counties that apply and qualify to enforce and interpret local or state fire, building, existing building standards and electrical safety standards, provided the local body has adopted minimum standards at least as stringent as the department's. The inspection powers your property is actually subject to therefore come from your city or county ordinance, not from a state statute, and local ordinances are outside this library — check them. Note that Wyoming's adopted model-code list at § 35-9-106(a)(i) is exhaustive (IFC, IBC, IMC, IEBC, IFGC) and omits plumbing, while electrical has a statewide floor under § 35-9-120(a).

Entry into an occupied unit is the hard part, and Wyoming does not solve it for anyone. The only statutory access right in the residential rental article runs to you, not to the government: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) prohibits the renter from unreasonably denying access to, refusing entry to or withholding consent to enter the unit 'to the owner, agent or manager' for repairs, inspection, and showing it for rent or sale. That list does not include a public inspector. An inspector who wants in over the tenant's objection needs the tenant's consent or a warrant; Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 4 secures people in their houses against unreasonable searches and requires a warrant on probable cause supported by affidavit. That protection belongs to the tenant as occupant, and you cannot waive it for them.

So can the lease authorize an inspector to enter? You can write the clause, and it is worth writing — nothing in Wyoming law forbids it, § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, and a violation of § 1-21-1204 is an eviction ground under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi). But understand what it buys. It is a promise by the tenant to you, enforceable by you; it is not consent given to the government, and an inspector relying on it rather than on the tenant's own consent or a warrant is taking a constitutional risk you do not control. The cautious course is to use the clause, give the tenant notice of the inspection, and attend with the inspector yourself so that your own § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) access right is the one being exercised.

Finally, a 2026 change on the permitting side, not the inspection side: 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 16 (HB0002) requires local government entities to meet deadlines for reviewing specified residential building permits, with suspension and extension rules, notice requirements and penalties, and applies to permit applications for construction of a dwelling filed on or after July 1, 2026. It does not create or restrict any inspection of an occupied rental.

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming does not regulate renter's insurance in a residential lease. There is no statutory advisory you must give, no written statement that you will not insure the tenant's property, no requirement that the tenant be free to choose the carrier, no proof deadline before you may force-place a policy, no cap on a force-placed premium or administrative fee, and no pre-signing insurance-and-flood notice. The phrase "renter's insurance" returns zero across the whole Wyoming corpus, 'force-placed' in either spelling returns zero, and the only Title 26 provisions that pair insurance with a renter are the rental-CAR waiver provisions in Wyo. Stat. § 26-20-102. You may therefore require renter's insurance, set the amount and the coverage, require yourself to be named as an additional interested party, and make a lapse a lease default — all by contract. Three Wyoming provisions make the contract work and one sets a real trap. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) says any duty or obligation in Article 12 may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in that article, so allocating risk of loss to the tenant by requiring insurance is squarely permitted — but the three conditions are cumulative, EXPLICIT, WRITTEN and SIGNED, and an oral tenancy shifts nothing even though Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) treats an oral agreement as a rental agreement. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit to 'other costs provided by any contract', so a premium you advance under a lease term that says you may is deductible from the deposit. And Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a forcible entry and detainer action available against a renter in violation of terms imposed under §§ 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205, while an insurance requirement is an ordinary lease covenant enforceable as a default under the lease and the three-day notice to quit in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. The trap is licensing. Wyo. Stat. § 26-9-203 says 'A person shall not sell, solicit or negotiate insurance in this state for any class or classes of insurance unless the person is licensed for that line of authority in accordance with this chapter', and Wyo. Stat. § 26-1-102(a)(xxxv) defines an insurance producer as a person required to be licensed to sell, solicit or negotiate insurance, agents and brokers included. If your renter's-insurance programme goes beyond requiring the tenant to get their own policy — if you place tenants into a master or force-placed policy, present a specific product at signing, take a commission, override or marketing fee, or advise an applicant on coverage — you are close to soliciting or negotiating insurance and you need to check your position with a licensed producer or the Wyoming insurance department before you run it. Charging a tenant a marked-up premium through the rent ledger is the version most likely to attract attention. Two more limits. Because you may require it, you must require it evenly: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(b) bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental on the seven classes in Wyoming's fair housing act, so one insurance standard for everyone, applied the same way, with any exception documented. And Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases — Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include real property, § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct, and there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110 — so do not describe a force-placed policy as protecting the tenant's belongings when it protects only your interest. The cautious course, and the one worth writing into the lease: require the tenant to carry liability coverage in a stated amount, let the tenant pick any admitted carrier, ask for a certificate and for notice of cancellation, state plainly that your own policy does not cover the tenant's property or liability, and if you want a backstop, reserve the right to buy a policy covering YOUR interest only and recover the actual cost, naming the cost rather than a fee.

title: No Repair Escrow, So No Exemption Notice
bodyText:
There is nothing for a Wyoming landlord to notice here, because there is no remedy to be exempt from. Wyoming has no rent escrow, no repair-and-deduct right, no rent withholding and no small-landlord carve-out, so there is no equivalent of Ohio's three-or-fewer-units notice and no exemption statement to put in your lease. "Repair and deduct" returns nothing in Wyoming law; "escrow" returns 198 hits of which the nineteen in Title 1 are structured-settlement transfers and the crime-profits escrow under § 1-40-303, not housing; and no provision anywhere exempts a landlord by unit count.

WHAT A WYOMING TENANT ACTUALLY HAS, so you can recognise it when it starts. It is a notice sequence, and it ends in court rather than in an escrow account.

Step one — the tenant's notice. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) opens with a condition that is easy to overlook and often decisive: "If the renter is current on all payments required by the rental agreement" and has reasonable cause supported by evidence to believe the unit does not comply with the article's health and safety standards, the renter advises you in writing of the condition and specifies the remedial action requested. A tenant in arrears cannot start the sequence at all. The notice must go by certified mail or in the manner specified by § 1-21-1003.

Step two — your response, within a reasonable time. Section 1-21-1203(b) gives you two choices and only two: commence action to correct the condition, or notify the renter IN WRITING that you dispute the claim. Doing nothing is the one answer that loses. Note that your duty to respond is reactive — it runs from receipt of the tenant's notice; § 1-21-1203(d) is not a free-standing obligation.

What you owe in the first place is a short list. Section 1-21-1203(a) requires you to (i) not rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, (ii) maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition, (iii) maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water, and (iv) maintain other appliances and facilities AS SPECIFICALLY CONTRACTED in the rental agreement. Paragraph (iii) is a closed ongoing list; paragraph (iv) sweeps everything else in only if your lease put it there. Section 1-21-1203(c) relieves you of any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse during the term or any extension.

Step three — your exit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse to correct and terminate the rental agreement if the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement. If you take that route you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance, and give sufficient time to find substitute housing — no less than ten (10) days nor more than twenty (20) days from the date of your notice. Rent is then prorated to the date the renter vacates and the balance refunded with any deposit due under § 1-21-1208. This is Wyoming's real alternative to an escrow regime: the landlord may walk away from an uneconomic repair by ending the tenancy, which no escrow state allows.

Step four — the tenant escalates. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a) the remedies are open only to a renter who is in compliance with all of §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205 and only where the agreement has not been lawfully terminated under § 1-21-1203(d). If a reasonable time has passed and you have neither responded nor corrected, § 1-21-1206(b) lets the renter serve a "notice to repair or correct condition" by certified mail or in the § 1-21-1003 manner, which must recite the earlier § 1-21-1203(b) notice, state how many days have elapsed and that this is a reasonable time, list the uncorrected conditions, demand correction, and state that if you fail to commence reasonable corrective action within three (3) days the renter will go to court.

Step five — court, not escrow. Section 1-21-1206(c) lets the renter file a civil action in circuit court if you have not corrected or used due diligence to correct, or if you disputed the claim. The court endorses on the summons the number of days you have to appear and defend, not less than three (3) nor more than twenty (20) days from service — a very short fuse. On a showing of unreasonable refusal to correct or failure to use due diligence, the renter may be awarded costs, damages and affirmative relief, and the statute says damages "may include rent improperly retained or collected" and affirmative relief may include a declaration terminating the rental agreement or an order directing you to make reasonable repairs. Note what that means: rent comes back to the tenant only by judgment, after a hearing — it is never withheld or escrowed along the way. If the court terminates, § 1-21-1206(d) gives the renter a refund of the balance of rent and the deposit within thirty (30) days and requires the renter to vacate no sooner than ten (10) and no later than twenty (20) days after termination. One limit in your favour: § 1-21-1203(e) bars claims for mental suffering or anguish under the whole article.

CAN YOU CONTRACT OUT? Partly, and this is the nearest thing Wyoming has to an exemption. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties", and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12. The conditions are cumulative — explicit, written, signed — and an oral tenancy shifts nothing, because § 1-21-1202(d) requires a signed writing even though § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) recognises oral rental agreements. But read the subsection for what it says: it reaches a DUTY OR OBLIGATION, and the § 1-21-1206 remedies are remedies, not duties. The sound way to use § 1-21-1202(d) is to shape the underlying duty — for instance to allocate a specific appliance or facility under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv), or to assign a maintenance obligation to the tenant — rather than to purport to abolish the tenant's remedy. The cautious course: never touch § 1-21-1203(a)(i), the duty not to rent a unit that is not reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. Modifying that one invites the Consumer Protection Act (§ 40-12-102(a)(vi) brings real property inside "merchandise", § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct) and leaves you defending the indefensible.

The whole of this applies only to a "residential rental unit" as § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally. Outside that definition Article 12 and all of the above switch off.

title: The Only Disclosure Wyoming Requires in a Lease
bodyText:
Wyoming requires exactly one disclosure in a residential lease, and it is about the deposit. Everything else you may have seen in another state's template is optional here, and several of those items describe programs Wyoming does not have.

The one requirement is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207: "Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or his designated agent." Read it as two obligations, not one. First, the rental agreement itself must state whether any part of the deposit is nonrefundable - and note the statute says "whether," so a lease that is simply silent does not comply even if nothing is nonrefundable. Second, you must separately give the renter written notice of that fact at the time you take the deposit. Doing one and not the other misses half the statute. The timing word is "at the time the deposit is taken," so if you collect a holding deposit before signing, the written notice goes out then, not at move-in. Note also that § 1-21-1207 applies to "any rental agreement," which Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines to include oral agreements - so even on an oral tenancy the written notice is required. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209 makes whoever holds the owner's interest at termination bound by §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208, so a buyer inherits the consequences of a seller's sloppy paperwork. Get this one right: it is the only disclosure trap in the Wyoming statute, and the deposit-accounting penalty in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) - the renter recovers the full deposit plus court costs if you unreasonably fail to comply - sits right next to it.

Here is what Wyoming does not require, so you can stop looking. There is no just-cause or rent-increase coverage notice for leases and renewals. There is no state-prescribed form that must be the first page of the lease, and no font-size, bold-type, or placement rule for any lease term; the only typographic rule in Title 1 is the fourteen-point bold requirement for structured-settlement transfer disclosures in Wyo. Stat. § 1-16-603, which has nothing to do with housing. There is no state mold, lead, radon, methamphetamine, flood, sex-offender, utility, recycling, pet, or property-condition disclosure. There is no statutory duty to disclose the owner's or agent's name and address. There is no requirement that the lease be in writing at all. If a template hands your tenant a state pamphlet, a state certificate, or a recital of compliance with a state program, delete it - Wyoming has no such program and the recital is a representation you cannot support.

One drafting point hides in a definition rather than in a disclosure section. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i) provides that for purposes of notice and other communication required or allowed under the article, "owner" includes a managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager "unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement." That is an opt-out that only works if it appears in the lease. If you want notices - habitability complaints under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b), deposit addresses under § 1-21-1208(a) - to go to you rather than to your property manager, or vice versa, say so in the rental agreement. Say nothing and the manager is a proper recipient by operation of the definition, and a notice served on them starts your clocks.

On the lease-with-option-to-buy question, Wyoming is safe. The state's only seller disclosure statute is Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-151, and subsection (d) defines the "vacant land" it applies to as land with no habitable dwelling, not within the boundaries of a platted subdivision or a city or town, and less than 140 acres. A residential rental has a habitable dwelling on it, so adding a purchase option to a dwelling lease cannot pull you into § 34-1-151(a). Two cautions if the option is actually exercised and a sale happens. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-151(e) requires every seller of land outside the corporate boundaries of a city or town to disclose in writing whether fee ownership of the wind estate has been severed in the chain of title, including any wind energy agreement under W.S. 34-27-102(a)(i) - that applies at the sale, by acreage-free rule, and a buyer may waive it under § 34-1-151(b). And Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-1-142 through 34-1-144 require a sworn statement of consideration to accompany an instrument transferring title when it is presented to the county clerk for recording, with a misdemeanor penalty for falsifying it. Neither of those is a lease disclosure; they attach to the conveyance.

Finally, the federal layer is real even though Wyoming adds nothing to it. For any dwelling built before 1978 you must give the EPA lead hazard pamphlet, disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, provide any records or reports you have, and include the Lead Warning Statement with signed acknowledgments in the lease (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. S 4852d; 24 C.F.R. part 35 subpart A; 40 C.F.R. part 745 subpart F). Flagged and not resolved: Wyoming municipalities and counties may impose their own rental-registration or disclosure requirements by ordinance, which are outside this review.

title: Fees You May Charge and Where They Must Appear
bodyText: Wyoming has no fee statute. There is no list of permitted fees, no cap on a late fee, no required grace period, no application or screening fee limit, and no rule - as Utah, Idaho and Oregon have - saying every fee must be named in the rental agreement before you can charge it. You are largely free to set fees by contract. Two Wyoming rules nevertheless make the lease the place where your fees have to live. First, the deposit rule. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply property or money held as a deposit to accrued rent, damages to the unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning of the rental agreement, "and to other costs provided by any contract." That last phrase is the operative one: a cost you did not provide for in the contract is not a cost you can take out of the deposit. An unwritten late fee, cleaning charge, re-letting fee, lock-change charge, pet fee or administrative fee is money you may end up suing for rather than deducting - and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c), if the court finds you unreasonably failed to comply with the deposit rules, the renter recovers the full deposit and court costs. Second, the nonrefundable rule. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires that any rental agreement state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and that written notice of this fact also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken.
