Any up-front charge you intend to keep belongs in both places: named in the lease as nonrefundable, and named again in the written notice you hand over when you collect it. Returned payments are the one fee Wyoming actually legislates, and it is generous. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-115(a), where a check is not paid because it has been dishonored for any reason, you may make written demand - mailed by United States postal service certificate of mailing to the address shown on the check or the drawer's last known address, or served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure - for the amount of the check plus a collection fee of up to $30; the demand must state that the drawer is required to pay the value of the check and the collection fee, and must state the collection fee the section provides. If the drawer does not pay within thirty days of that demand, Wyo. Stat. § 1-1-115(b) makes the drawer liable for three times the amount of the check, but never less than $100, plus a $30 collection fee and court costs; § 1-1-115(c) allows reasonable attorney fees in extraordinary cases, including where the court finds dilatory or bad faith defenses; and § 1-1-115(e) lets you bring the claim in small claims court if it is within that court's jurisdiction. Follow the demand mechanics exactly - the three-times-damages entitlement depends on the demand having been made and stated correctly. Two further points. Unpaid damages beyond the deposit carry statutory interest: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b) says that where the renter damages the property you may apply the deposit, the renter remains liable for damages beyond what the deposit pays, plus interest at ten percent per annum on any unpaid amounts, and you may take any legal action available to recover damage caused to the unit. And Wyoming's consumer credit code does not reach an ordinary residential lease: Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-206(a) defines a consumer lease as a lease of goods, so the code's delinquency-charge limits do not cap your late fee. The exception matters if you do lease-to-own - Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-205(f) says a sale of an interest in land includes a lease in which the lessee has an option to purchase and all or a substantial part of the rental or other payments previously made are applied to the purchase price, which can pull such a deal into the consumer credit sale rules at Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-204. Practical course: list every fee and charge in the lease with its amount, when it is due and what it is for; mark any nonrefundable amount as nonrefundable and give the separate written notice when you take it; keep late fees in a range you could defend as reasonable, since nothing in Wyoming blesses a particular number; and handle bounced checks through the § 1-1-115 demand rather than a lease-invented NSF fee, because the statute pays better than most lease clauses do.

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming publishes no official landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide, and no statute requires you to give a tenant one — not before signing, not at renewal, and not at any other time. There is no signed acknowledgment to collect, no summary of the law to attach, and no consequence for not handing anything over, because there is nothing to hand over. The words "pamphlet," "brochure," "handbook" and "rights and responsibilities" appear nowhere in the title that governs residential rentals. The one place Wyoming does assign an education role, it assigns it to the state, not to you: the enforcing authority under the Wyoming Fair Housing Act is directed to "foster prevention of discrimination under this chapter through education for the public, landlords, publishers, real estate licensees, lenders and sellers on the rights and responsibilities provided under this chapter" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 40-26-114). That is a duty on the agency to educate you; it creates no duty for you to distribute anything to a tenant. Two documents you do have to deliver in Wyoming, and they are easy to confuse with a rights guide. First, if any portion of the deposit is nonrefundable, the rental agreement must state that fact and separate written notice of it must be given to the tenant at the time the deposit is taken (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1207) — two duties, one in the lease and one as a standalone notice at the moment you take the money. Second, federal law, not Wyoming law, requires the EPA and HUD lead-based paint disclosure and the "Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home" pamphlet for most housing built before 1978 (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d; 24 C.F.R. part 35, subpart A; 40 C.F.R. part 745, subpart F). Beyond those, anything you give the tenant about their rights is voluntary. Voluntary is not pointless: a short, accurate one-page summary of how notices are served, when the deposit is returned and what the tenant's maintenance-notice route is under Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 1-21-1203 and 1-21-1206 heads off disputes, and nothing in Wyoming law penalizes you for providing it — but write it accurately, because a knowingly false statement about the transaction could expose you under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act. Check the city or county where you rent; local rental-licensing programs can require their own handouts, and local ordinances were not reviewed here.

title: When Your House Rules Are Enforceable
bodyText:
Wyoming gives you an unusually free hand with house rules, and the freedom comes from a definition rather than a rules statute. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines "rental agreement" as "any agreement, written or oral, which establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules or any other provisions regarding the use and occupancy of a residential rental unit." Rules are rental-agreement material by definition. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) then makes it a renter's statutory duty to "[c]omply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) allows a forcible entry and detainer action "[a]gainst renters in violation of any terms imposed under W.S. 1-21-1204 or 1-21-1205." So a rule the tenant agreed to is enforceable, and a serious breach of it is a ground for eviction -- after a written notice to quit served at least three days before filing under § 1-21-1003.

What Wyoming does not have is just as important. There is no statutory reasonableness test for a rule, no requirement that a rule serve a legitimate purpose or be reasonably related to it, no requirement that rules apply equally to all tenants, no specificity standard, no notice period for adopting or changing rules, and no "substantial modification of the bargain" limit on mid-tenancy changes. There is also no landlord-retaliation statute in Wyoming at all, so the retaliation presumption that polices rule changes in other states does not exist here.

The real constraint on changing rules mid-tenancy is contractual, not regulatory, and it is a strict one. Section 1-21-1201(a)(ii) speaks of an "agreement" that establishes or modifies rules -- a rule you post on the laundry room door is not an agreement. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that in Wyoming the relations of landlord and tenant do not arise "by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance," and § 34-2-129 provides that an expired lease is renewed only "by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto." Wyoming does not imply terms into a tenancy. So a new rule you announce in the middle of a term does not bind the tenant unless the lease already reserved your right to adopt and amend rules, or the tenant signs the new rule. Build the reservation into the lease at signing; it is far easier than getting a signature later.

There is one further piece of Wyoming freedom of contract that bears on rules generally. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." That reaches the whole of Article 12, §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211. It is why a Wyoming lease can reallocate maintenance duties, and it is the reason rules written into a signed lease carry so much weight here. Note the conditions in the statute's own words: the modification must be explicit, in writing, and signed by the parties. An unsigned rules addendum does not meet it.

The limits that do bind your rules come from outside Title 1. The Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-101 et seq., makes it unlawful under § 40-26-103(b) to "discriminate against an individual in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a sale or rental of a dwelling because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin." House rules are terms, conditions and privileges of a rental and are squarely covered. Familial status is the one that catches landlords out: rules restricting children's use of a pool, playground, common area or parking, or imposing curfews on minors, are classic familial-status problems. Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) provides that a person "shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, which shall be permitted in leased or rented residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act," with the person liable for damage the animal does. A no-pets rule must yield to that; a damage-responsibility rule may stand. Federal law applies independently: FEDERAL: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. §§ 3601-3619.

Practical course: put the rules in the signed lease or in a rules addendum the tenant signs, reserve the right to adopt and amend rules in the lease itself, make each rule specific enough to enforce and to prove, apply rules uniformly and document that you do, and run any rule touching children, disability, assistance animals, religion or national origin past the fair housing standard before you adopt it. The absence of a Wyoming reasonableness statute is not a licence to write an arbitrary rule -- it only means that when a rule is challenged, you will be arguing contract and fair housing rather than a statutory checklist.

title: Code Variances and What You Must Tell Tenants in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no state sanitary code for dwellings, so it has nothing like the Massachusetts rule that a board-of-health variance must be given to the tenant and attached to the rental agreement. The phrases "sanitary code," "housing code" and "health code" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes. There is no disclosure duty here to comply with.

Wyoming does grant code variances — just under the fire, building and electrical codes, with no tenant-notice string attached. Two routes exist, and a landlord who has one in hand should know which it is.

First, the state route. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) directs the council on fire prevention and electrical safety in buildings to adopt minimum fire standards not exceeding those prescribed by the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code and International Fuel Gas Code. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(c) then gives the council power to "hear appeals to determine the suitability of alternate materials and type of construction and to interpret and grant variances from rules and regulations of the council." A separate electrical board hears appeals and grants variances from the National Electrical Code.

Second, the local route. Where a municipality or county has taken on code enforcement authority, Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(d) requires it to "create its own appeals boards to determine the suitability of alternate materials and types of construction and to interpret and grant variances from adopted codes or standards," appointed and removed by the governing body, with the person whose decision is on appeal barred from sitting on the board. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(e), that board's decision may be appealed to the state council, and the council's decision to the appropriate district court. Note also Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b): "If local code provisions are more stringent than adopted state codes, the local code prevails." A city may demand more than the state does.

None of those provisions requires you to tell a tenant that a variance exists, to attach it to the lease, or to file it anywhere the tenant will see. That is the statutory answer, and it is a genuine gap rather than a hidden duty.

What you should still do, and why. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) makes every owner "maintain that unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation," with "operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties." Read that qualifier carefully: the "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing" attaches to the second sentence — the utilities list — not to the first sentence's safe-and-sanitary-and-fit duty, which stands regardless. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) separately forbids renting the unit at all "unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy." A code variance from a city appeals board does not excuse either duty: the variance is between you and the code authority, not between you and your tenant. If the condition the variance covers is one a tenant would reasonably care about — a non-standard egress window, a stair rail that does not meet current code, an alternate fire-separation detail — disclose it in writing anyway and attach a copy of the variance. Three reasons: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) only lets a duty be reallocated "by explicit written agreement signed by the parties," so a written acknowledgment is the only way to make the arrangement explicit; knowingly staying silent about a material condition risks a claim under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, where "merchandise" includes real property (Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi)) and § 40-12-105(a)(xv) reaches "unfair or deceptive acts or practices"; and a signed disclosure is your best answer if the tenant later serves the written condition notice that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) requires before using the repair remedies in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206.

One limit on this answer: the adopted code editions themselves and the councils' and local boards' rules are agency material, and municipal ordinances are local — neither is in this library. If a city granted you a variance, ask that city whether its own ordinance imposes any posting or notice condition.

title: Seasonal, Recreational and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Wyoming addresses seasonal and recreational rentals in two places, and both are easy to miss because they are single clauses inside longer sentences. First, the definition. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) says a 'residential rental unit' means 'a renter's principal place of residence' and includes its appurtenances, grounds, common areas and facilities, 'excluding a mobile home lot or recreational property rented on an occasional basis.' Two things follow. A unit that is not the renter's principal place of residence is not a residential rental unit at all, and recreational property rented on an occasional basis is excluded by name. Because the definitions in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a) apply 'As used in this article', the whole of article 12 — the habitability duties in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1202 and 1-21-1203, the renter duties in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204, the renter's remedies in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206, the nonrefundable-deposit notice in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207, the thirty-day deposit cascade in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208 and the abandoned-property procedure in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1210 — falls away for a genuine occasional recreational rental. Second, the amenities proviso. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires every residential rental unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water, and then adds: 'Provided, however, this section shall not prevent the rental of seasonal rental units such as summer cabins which are not intended to have such amenities.' Read it narrowly. 'Such amenities' means the utilities listed in the sentence before it, so the proviso lets you rent out a cabin with no running water or no heat where the unit was never intended to have them. It does not switch off the first sentence of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a), which requires the unit to be maintained in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, and it does not exempt a seasonal unit from the rest of the article. Three warnings. (1) The article 12 exclusion does not touch evictions. The forcible entry and detainer article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, is not limited to residential rental units: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) reaches 'tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due.' A seasonal guest who will not leave still has to be removed by a court action, after the three-day notice to quit required by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. Do not treat a seasonal renter as a trespasser. The 2025 removal procedure for unauthorized occupants at Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403 is closed to anyone who is a current or former tenant under a written or oral rental agreement, and misusing it exposes you to triple the fair market rent plus costs and fees under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(c). (2) 'Occasional' and 'principal place of residence' are fact questions, and no Wyoming case in this library defines them. A cabin you rent out all summer every summer to a series of guests may be occasional as to each of them; a cabin you rent to one household for nine months is not. If you cannot say with confidence that the exclusion applies, comply with article 12 anyway — the deposit timetable in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208 is the expensive one to get wrong. (3) Two other Wyoming provisions use their own definitions, so do not borrow them into the lease. Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-102(b)(liv), in the Real Estate License Act, defines 'short term rental' as the rental of real estate for thirty-one days or less — that is a licensing definition, not a landlord-tenant one. And Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-163(b) provides that 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, short term rental of detached one (1) and two (2) family dwellings and townhomes shall not be regulated as a commercial use for purposes of fire, building and electrical standards and shall not be subject to regulation under the International Building Code' — useful if a local inspector treats your cabin or townhome as commercial, and no help at all on tenancy questions.

title: How You May Hold a Wyoming Security Deposit
bodyText:
If you own and manage your own Wyoming rental, you may hold the deposit however you like. There is no escrow or trust account requirement, no separate-account requirement, no bond alternative, no duty to tell the tenant where the money is, no interest obligation, and no unit-count threshold that switches any of that on. Wyoming's deposit statutes, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1207 through 1-21-1209, say nothing at all about where the money sits. You may put it in your operating account.

Wyoming goes further than merely being silent on interest. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) says the balance of any deposit and prepaid rent, with a written itemization of deductions, "shall be delivered or mailed WITHOUT INTEREST to the renter." The statute affirmatively says no interest is owed. You keep whatever the money earns.

What the statute does require of you. Section 1-21-1208(a) lets you apply the deposit at termination to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning of the rental agreement, and other costs provided by any contract. The balance of the deposit AND of any prepaid rent, plus a written itemization of deductions with reasons, must be delivered or mailed within 30 days after termination, or within 15 days after you receive the tenant's new mailing address, whichever is later. If there is damage to the unit, that period is extended by a further 30 days. The tenant has a reciprocal duty: within 30 days of termination the tenant must tell you where payment and notice may be made or mailed. Do not overlook the prepaid-rent limb — a landlord who returns the deposit balance but keeps prepaid rent has not complied with the sentence.

A separately identified utilities deposit runs on its own clock under § 1-21-1208(b): refund within 10 days of a satisfactory showing that all the tenant's utility charges have been paid; if no such showing within 45 days of termination, apply the utilities deposit to the outstanding utility debt within the next 15 days; and pay any refund within 7 days after applying it, or within 15 days after receiving the new mailing address, whichever is later. That cascade only applies to a deposit you held and separately identified as a utilities deposit, so label it in the lease or it is an ordinary deposit on the 30/15 clock.

The penalty for getting it wrong. Under § 1-21-1208(c), if you or your agent "unreasonably" fail to comply with (a) or (b), the tenant may recover the full deposit and court costs. Read that carefully: the penalty is the full deposit — not two or three times it — plus court costs, and it is gated on unreasonableness, not on any failure. The same subsection cuts the other way: if you are the prevailing party and the court finds the tenant acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs in addition to any other relief. Attorney fees are not in this subsection at all. Wyoming awards fees only where the lease provides for them, and even then § 1-21-1008(b) ties the award to a nonpayment case, so put a fee clause in your lease if you want one.

One required disclosure, at the front end. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 says a rental agreement "shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable," and written notice of that fact must also be given to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. That is two separate acts — the lease text and a notice at the moment of payment — so do both.

If you sell, the duty follows the property. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209 provides that the holder of the owner's or designated agent's interest in the unit AT THE TIME OF TERMINATION of the rental agreement is bound by §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208. A buyer who takes over mid-tenancy inherits the obligation even if the seller never handed the money across, so if you are buying, get the deposits transferred and reconciled at closing; if you are selling, transfer them and document it.

The one situation where a trust account IS required. Property management for others is licensed activity in Wyoming under the Real Estate License Act. If a licensed responsible broker manages your property, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-122(a)(i) requires the broker to maintain an account at a financial institution in this state designated as a trust or escrow account, into which all trust funds received on behalf of a principal or any other person must be deposited, unless everyone with an interest in the funds has agreed otherwise in writing; the account must permit immediate withdrawal. A broker may use a "funds holder" instead. Under § 33-28-122(a)(ii) the broker must notify the Real Estate Commission of the institution and account name, and if a funds holder is used, the intention to use one and the funds holder's name must be disclosed to all parties to any lease or lease agreement the broker negotiates. Under § 33-28-122(c) the trust account may be interest bearing or not, and in the absence of a written agreement among everyone with an interest, accrued interest is paid out to the person from whom the trust funds were received, proportionally where there are several. Section 33-28-122(e) bars commingling with the broker's personal funds, with a narrow exception for a minimum balance identified at the time of deposit, and § 33-28-102(b)(xxvi) and (xxvii) make failure to keep others' funds in escrow, or to deposit financial instruments within one banking day, grounds for discipline.

The gap you should notice. Those broker rules do not reach you if you self-manage, because § 33-28-103(a)(i) exempts an owner's regular employees and § 33-28-103(a)(vi) exempts an on-site resident manager from licensing. So the tenant's deposit is protected by a state-supervised trust account only when a licensed broker is in the chain.

The cautious course, even though nothing compels it. Hold deposits in a separate account anyway. It makes the § 1-21-1208(a) itemization easy to prove, it stops a deposit being swept into an operating overdraft, and if the property is ever sold or the business fails it is the difference between a bookkeeping entry and a dispute. Keep the deposit, prepaid rent and any utilities deposit identified separately in your ledger, because the statute treats them differently. And check your municipality: Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b) and nothing preempts a local deposit rule.

title: No Interest Owed on a Wyoming Security Deposit
bodyText: Wyoming does not merely leave deposit interest unregulated — it says the opposite in the statute itself. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) directs that the balance of any deposit and prepaid rent, together with the written itemisation of deductions, "shall be delivered or mailed WITHOUT INTEREST to the renter." Those two words are in the statute. So you owe the tenant no interest, you need not hold the deposit in an interest-bearing or escrow account, there is no separation or commingling rule, no federally insured account requirement, no annual accounting, no obligation to disclose where the money is held, and whatever interest the funds do earn is yours. There is also no Wyoming equivalent of the problem some states have, where the interest rate is pegged to a federal body that no longer exists — no rate is set because no interest is owed. The rest of § 1-21-1208(a) is what you must actually get right. On termination you may apply the deposit to accrued rent, to damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, to the cost of cleaning the unit to the condition it was in at the beginning of the rental agreement, and to "other costs provided by any contract" — that last phrase makes almost any lease-created charge deductible, provided the lease creates it. You must deliver or mail the balance and the written itemisation of every deduction with reasons within thirty (30) days after termination of the rental agreement, or within fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is LATER; and if there is damage to the unit, that period is extended by a further thirty (30) days. The renter has their own duty under the same subsection: within thirty (30) days of termination, to tell you where payment and notice may be sent. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) is a separate and faster cascade for money "held and separately identified as a utilities deposit" — refund within ten (10) days of a satisfactory showing that the renter's utility charges are paid; absent that showing within forty-five (45) days of termination, apply it to the utility debt within fifteen (15) days thereafter; then pay any refund within seven (7) days of applying it, or within fifteen (15) days of receiving the new mailing address, whichever is later. If you do not separately identify a utilities deposit, you do not get the (b) treatment. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) is the penalty, and it is mild and reciprocal: if you unreasonably fail to comply with (a) or (b), the renter may recover the full deposit and court costs — no multiple damages — and if you are the prevailing party and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs too. Do not overlook Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207, which is separate from all of this: the rental agreement SHALL state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, AND written notice of that fact must also be given to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. Two duties, both easy to miss. Interest in Wyoming's deposit scheme runs the other way. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b) provides that where the renter damages the rental property, you may apply the deposit to the damages under § 1-21-1208(a) and "the renter shall remain liable for any damages beyond the damages paid by the deposit, plus interest at ten percent (10%) per annum on any unpaid amounts," and you may take any legal action available to recover. So the only statutory deposit-related interest rate in Wyoming is ten percent per annum in the landlord's favour on an unpaid damages balance. Finally, two scope points. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209 provides that the holder of the owner's or designated agent's interest in the unit at the time of termination is bound by §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208 — so if you buy the property, you inherit these duties. And all of Article 12 applies only to a "residential rental unit" as defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv): the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Deposit Standards Depend on Who Holds the Money
bodyText:
If you hold deposits yourself, Wyoming imposes almost no standards on you. There is no requirement to post or disclose how you calculate a deposit, no obligation to use uniform standards across your units, and no portfolio trigger of the kind some states apply to owners of more than four adjoining units. There is no deposit cap, no separate or escrow account requirement, no bonding option and no duty to pay interest. The phrase 'security deposit' does not appear in Title 1 at all; Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208 governs 'property or money held as a deposit,' which is a broad formula with no narrow definition that a pet, cleaning or redecorating deposit could slip through. You may hold the money in your operating account.

What Wyoming does require of every landlord is short. Section 1-21-1207 requires two things: 'Any rental agreement shall state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable,' and separate 'written notice of this fact shall also be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken by the owner or his designated agent.' Do both. Section 1-21-1208(a) then sets what you may keep and when you must account: the deposit may be applied to accrued rent, damages to the unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement, and 'other costs provided by any contract' — so name in the lease every charge you intend to deduct. The balance of the deposit and prepaid rent, with a written itemization of every deduction and the reasons for it, must be delivered or mailed without interest within thirty (30) days after termination or within fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by a further thirty (30) days if there is damage; the renter must give you that address within thirty (30) days of termination. Section 1-21-1208(b) runs a separate and faster clock for money 'held and separately identified as a utilities deposit': refund within ten (10) days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges are paid; absent that showing within forty-five (45) days of termination, apply it to the outstanding utility debt within fifteen (15) days thereafter; then pay any refund within seven (7) days after application, or fifteen (15) days after receiving the new address, whichever is later. If you want that faster track, identify the utilities deposit separately in writing when you take it. Under § 1-21-1208(c), an unreasonable failure to comply with (a) or (b) lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs — the full deposit, not merely the part wrongly withheld — though if you prevail and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action you may be awarded court costs too.

Now the part landlords miss. If a licensed real estate broker or a licensed property management company holds the deposit for you, a whole regime attaches that would not apply if you held it yourself. Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-122(a)(i) requires every responsible broker to maintain an account in a financial institution in this state designated as a trust or escrow account into which all trust funds received on behalf of a principal or any other person are deposited, unless all persons having an interest in the funds have agreed otherwise in writing; the account must permit immediate withdrawal, and a funds holder may be used instead. Section 33-28-122(a)(ii) requires notice to the real estate commission of the institution and account name, and if a funds holder is used, disclosure of that fact and the holder's name to all parties to any contract, purchase agreement, lease or lease agreement. Section 33-28-122(a)(iii) opens the trust accounting records to commission examination, and (a)(iv) requires the account to be maintained until all deposits are properly disbursed if the licence is cancelled. Section 33-28-122(e) forbids commingling with personal funds, though it is not commingling to leave an identified sum in the account to keep it open or avoid minimum-balance charges. Related grounds for discipline sit at § 33-28-111(a): failing to keep the funds of others in an escrow or trust account unless everyone with an interest has agreed otherwise in writing, (a)(xxvi); failing to deposit all financial instruments in such an account within one (1) banking day in a financial institution in this state, (a)(xxvii); and failing, on consummation or termination of the transaction, to give a full accounting showing dates of deposit, management and withdrawals, (a)(xxviii).

The interest rule inside that regime is the one to settle in writing. Section 33-28-122(c) says the trust account may be interest bearing or noninterest bearing and that any interest accrued shall be paid out as agreed in writing by all persons having an interest in the deposit — but 'in the absence of a written agreement among all persons having an interest in the deposit,' when any portion of the deposit is withdrawn and paid out, the interest accrued on the funds withdrawn must also be paid out 'to the person from whom the trust funds were received,' pro rata where more than one person is entitled. The person from whom a tenant's deposit was received is the tenant. So where a broker holds the money in an interest-bearing account and nobody has signed an agreement about interest, the interest belongs to the tenant by default, even though § 1-21-1208(a) requires the deposit itself to be returned 'without interest.' If you want a different result, get it in writing and signed by everyone with an interest before the money goes in.

Three closing points. Whether this broker regime applies to you turns on § 33-28-103(a), whose exemptions are keyed to role and not portfolio size: an owner, a member of the owner's immediate family, the owner's regular employees, and under (a)(vi) a resident manager who lives on the premises and leases in connection with that employment, are each outside the Real Estate License Act unless already a licensee. Second, a successor matters: § 1-21-1209 binds whoever holds the owner's interest at termination to §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208, so buying a building buys its deposit liabilities. Third, do not rely on a lease clause making an unclaimed deposit forfeit after a fixed time; Wyo. Stat. § 34-24-130(a) provides that the expiration of any period specified by contract, statute or court order during which a claim for money can be made does not prevent the money from being deemed abandoned under the Unclaimed Property Act or affect your duty to report and deliver it. And remember that all of Article 12 applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence, § 1-21-1201(a)(iv).

title: Locks and Security Devices
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no security devices at all. There is no deadbolt mandate, no peephole or door-viewer requirement, no window latch or sliding-door rule, no keyless bolt, and no duty to rekey between tenants. The words "deadbolt," "dead bolt," "peephole," "door viewer," "keyless," "rekey," "window latch" and "sliding door" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. There is no Texas-style schedule of devices a tenant can demand and no remedy for failing to install one. Nothing in Wyoming law obliges you to change the locks when a tenancy ends, though you should, for reasons that have nothing to do with statute.

The nearest Wyoming hook is the owner's duty section, and it needs reading carefully because it is narrower than landlords assume. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(i) says you shall "[n]ot rent the residential rental unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy." A missing or broken lock on an exterior door is a sound candidate for not reasonably safe, so get the locks working before a tenancy starts. But notice the shape of the rest of the subsection. Paragraph (a)(ii) is about keeping common areas sanitary and reasonably safe. Paragraph (a)(iii) is the ongoing maintenance duty and its list is closed: electrical systems, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water. Locks are not in it. Paragraph (a)(iv) then requires you to maintain "other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement" — which makes ongoing lock maintenance opt-in. If your lease promises to maintain locks, you have created that duty for yourself; if it is silent, your clear statutory obligation is the one at the start of the tenancy under (a)(i). The practical answer is still to fix locks promptly, both because the (a)(i) standard is a poor thing to argue about and because an unrepaired broken lock is an obvious negligence exposure, but know which duty you are actually under.

Three related points. First, if a tenant does send you a written notice of noncompliance about a lock under § 1-21-1203(b) — which they can only do while current on all payments — you must, within a reasonable time, either begin correcting it or tell them in writing that you dispute the claim, served by certified mail or in the manner of § 1-21-1003. Do not simply ignore it. Second, Wyoming's Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304, does not give a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence any right to have the locks changed. What it gives is an affirmative defence to a rent claim for the period after the tenant vacates, on the conditions in § 1-21-1303, and § 1-21-1304 makes that act the one provision in Wyoming landlord-tenant law that cannot be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement. If a tenant asks you to change the locks after an incident, that is a request you may grant or refuse as a matter of good practice, not a statutory entitlement — and granting it is usually the right call. Third, never change the locks on a tenant to force them out. The lock-change procedure in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403, where law enforcement stands by while the owner changes the locks, belongs to the unauthorized-occupant process in Article 14 and § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) expressly excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement. Against a tenant your route is forcible entry and detainer, and misusing Article 14 exposes you to triple the fair market value of renting plus fees under § 1-21-1403(c).

Finally, the absence of a state rule does not mean no rule. Local building and fire codes do reach locks and egress hardware, and under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121 the state fire marshal delegates complete enforcement authority to qualifying municipalities and counties, whose standards may be more stringent than the state's. Ask your city or county building department which code edition they enforce before you replace door hardware, particularly on a multi-unit building where egress requirements apply.

title: No Work Card for Staff in 55-and-Older Housing
bodyText:
Wyoming has nothing like Nevada's work card. No statute requires a sheriff-issued or any other card, permit, registration or background check for people who work in housing intended and operated for occupants 55 and older - or in any other rental housing. There is no hours-per-week trigger, no access-to-all-units trigger, no five-year renewal, no change-of-employer rule and no exemption list, because there is no scheme. "Work card" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code.

STAFF SCREENING GENERALLY. Wyoming imposes no screening mandate on apartment staff. The one adjacent requirement, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-106(a), requires a criminal-history record check for a real estate licence applicant, and the Real Estate License Act exempts exactly the people who hold your keys: Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-103(a)(i) and (a)(vi) take the owner's own employees and on-site managers outside the licensing requirement. So the one Wyoming provision that does require a background check is the one your maintenance technician and resident manager are exempt from. Whatever screening you do is your own policy under general employment law, and it is worth having a written one.

WHAT WYOMING DOES REGULATE ABOUT 55-AND-OLDER HOUSING, AND IT IS NOT STAFFING. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-112 is the familial-status and age exemption in the state fair housing act, and it is the provision that lets you operate age-restricted housing at all. Section 40-26-112(a) says the chapter's provisions relating to familial status and age do not apply to housing that: the federal secretary of housing and urban development determines is specifically designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a federal programme; the enforcing authority determines is specifically designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a state programme; is intended for, and solely occupied by, individuals sixty-two years of age or older; or is intended and operated for occupancy by at least one individual fifty-five years of age or older for each unit, as determined by enforcing authority rules. For that last route the statute requires the enforcing authority to adopt rules demanding at least two things: § 40-26-112(a)(i), that at least eighty percent of the units are occupied by at least one individual aged fifty-five or older per unit; and § 40-26-112(a)(ii), "[t]he publication of, and adherence to, policies and procedures which demonstrate an intent by the owner or manager to provide housing for individuals fifty-five (55) years of age or older." Read (a)(ii) as a working instruction: it is not enough to be 80 percent over fifty-five in fact. You must have written, published age policies and you must follow them. Publish them, apply them to every applicant, and keep the age verification records.

TWO SAFE HARBOURS INSIDE THE EXEMPTION. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-112(b)(i) protects you against existing under-age residents - housing is not in violation by reason of individuals residing there as of July 1, 2015 who do not meet the age requirement, provided new occupants do. Section 40-26-112(b)(ii) protects unoccupied units, provided they are reserved for occupancy by qualifying individuals. Note what the exemption does NOT do: it lifts only the familial status and age provisions. Race, colour, religion, sex, disability and national origin apply in full, and the disability provisions in Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107 - reasonable modification at the tenant's expense under (c)(i), with a rental carve-out allowing a restoration condition "when it is reasonable to do so," and reasonable accommodation in rules and policies under (c)(ii) - matter more in senior housing than anywhere else.

THE PROVISION THAT SHOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE HOW YOU RUN SENIOR HOUSING. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-111 sits in the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, which reaches real property through the definition of merchandise in Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi). It provides that a person who willfully uses a method, act or practice violating the act which victimises or attempts to victimise an "older person" or a "person with disabilities," and who commits the violation knowing or having reason to know the conduct was unfair or deceptive, must make restitution or reimbursement "including reasonable attorney fees and costs," and in addition is liable for a civil penalty of up to fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000.00) for each violation, recoverable by the office of the attorney general. "Older person" is defined in § 40-12-111(a)(iv) as a person over sixty years of age - a lower bar than fifty-five-and-older housing, so in practice most of your residents qualify. "Person with disabilities" is defined in (a)(i) to (a)(iii) and expressly includes an educational deficiency substantially affecting a person's ability to read and comprehend the terms of a contract. Two consequences. First, this is one of the very few routes to attorney fees against a Wyoming landlord; fees otherwise come from the lease under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) or not at all. Second, the per-violation penalty is $15,000 and is enforced by the attorney general, not only by the resident. Keep your lease, your fee schedule, your advertising and your renewal letters plain and accurate, and train anyone who signs residents up.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Adopt a written staff screening policy even though none is required, because nothing in Wyoming law will supply one for you. Document the age policy § 40-26-112(a)(ii) effectively requires, and audit the eighty percent figure annually. And treat every written communication to a resident over sixty as something the attorney general could read.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. The enforcing authority's fair housing rules under § 40-26-112 are agency rules outside this corpus; case law, court rules and local ordinances were not searched. Federal law, including FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b), runs in parallel and is flagged, not resolved here.

title: Refusing an assistance animal in a Wyoming rental is a crime
bodyText:
Wyoming is one of the states that attaches a criminal penalty to the LANDLORD, and it is easy to miss because the provision sits in the public health title, not in the landlord-tenant article. Read these two sections together.

Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c): "A person shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, which shall be permitted in leased or rented residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act." The same subsection adds that the person "shall be liable for any damage done by his assistance animal to the premises or facilities of the leased or rented residential property." Separately, § 35-13-201(a)(iii) provides that a person with a disability shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of apartments and other private residential property because of the disability.

Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(a): "Any person denying or interfering with admittance to or enjoyment of any place or facility referenced in W.S. 35-13-201(a) through (c) or otherwise interfering with the rights of the blind, partially blind, deaf, hearing impaired person or other person with a disability is guilty of a misdemeanor and may be fined not more than seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00)." The cross-reference runs through subsection (c), so the residential assistance-animal right is inside the offence. Denying an assistance animal in a Wyoming rental, or interfering with the tenant's enjoyment of it, is a misdemeanor.

THE DEFINITION IS BROAD, AND IT COVERS EMOTIONAL SUPPORT ANIMALS. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-205(a)(iv) defines "assistance animal" as an animal that works, provides assistance or performs tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, OR provides emotional support that alleviates one or more identified symptoms or effects of a person's disability. It is not limited to dogs and it has no training requirement. "Service animal" is defined separately at § 35-13-205(a)(viii) by reference to 28 C.F.R. §§ 35.104 and 36.104, includes service miniature horses under 28 C.F.R. §§ 35.136 and 36.302(c), and - since a 2025 amendment - expressly includes a dog that is being trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability. "Person with a disability" is defined at § 35-13-205(a)(ii) as an individual with a mental or physical impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, and § 35-13-205(a)(iii) defines those as functions associated with the normal activities of independent daily living such as caring for oneself, performing manual tasks, walking, seeing, hearing or speaking. So the residential provision reaches well beyond guide dogs.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR LEASE AND YOUR PRACTICE. A no-pets or no-animals clause cannot be applied to an assistance animal. Do not charge a pet fee, pet deposit or pet rent for one, and do not apply breed, weight or size limits to one: those are the commonest ways a landlord "interferes with" the right. Grant the request, document it, and rely on § 35-13-201(c)'s own last sentence - the tenant is liable for damage the animal does to the premises or facilities - rather than on a deposit. Wyoming's own fair housing act reinforces all of this: § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services where necessary to afford a person with a handicap equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and § 40-26-107(c)(i) deals with reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense. Section 40-26-144 adds its own offences for intimidation, interference and coercion.

THE PROTECTION THAT RUNS YOUR WAY. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(b) makes it a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $750, for any person who KNOWINGLY AND INTENTIONALLY misrepresents that an animal is a service animal or an assistance animal for the purpose of obtaining any of the rights or privileges set forth in the article. That is a real deterrent you may fairly mention in a written accommodation policy. It does not, however, let you demand medical records or a certificate: the gate is the federal Fair Housing Act standard that § 35-13-201(c) points to, which allows you to ask for reliable documentation of the disability-related need only where the disability or the need is not obvious.

TWO MORE SECTIONS TO KNOW. Section 35-13-206(a) makes it a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment for less than one year, a fine of up to $5,000, or both, for a person knowingly, willfully and without lawful cause to inflict - or to permit or direct an animal under his control or ownership to inflict - serious bodily harm, permanent disability or death on a service or assistance animal, and § 35-13-206(b) requires the court to order restitution for veterinary bills, replacement or retraining costs and other reasonable expenses. If you keep a dog on site, that is your exposure. Section 35-13-201(d) gives a public accommodation that admits a service animal, or an animal believed in good faith to be one, immunity from liability for damage or injury the animal causes - note that this immunity is written for public accommodations, not for residential landlords, so do not rely on it in the rental context.

title: Faking a Service or Assistance Animal Is a Crime in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has a misrepresentation-penalty statute, and it DOES reach housing. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-203(b) provides that any person who knowingly and intentionally misrepresents that an animal is a service animal or an assistance animal “for the purpose of obtaining any of the rights or privileges set forth in this article” is guilty of a misdemeanor and may be fined not more than $750. The scoping is by ACT, not by a list of places, and that is why it covers rentals: the rights set forth in the same article include Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(a)(iii), the right of a person with a disability not to be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of apartments and other private residential property, and § 35-13-201(c), the right not to be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal. A tenant or applicant who lies about an animal to get it into a no-pets unit is obtaining a right set forth in the article and is within § 35-13-203(b).

Understand what the statute gives you and what it does not. It is a criminal offense prosecuted by the state, not a civil claim you can bring, and the maximum is a $750 fine. It gives you no right to refuse the animal, no right to charge a pet fee or pet deposit for a genuine assistance animal, no right to demand documentation beyond what the federal Fair Housing Act allows, and no defense to a discrimination complaint. The practical use is narrow: it is a reason to document an obviously false claim, and a deterrent you may describe neutrally in your rules.

THE DUTY SIDE IS MUCH SHARPER, AND MOST LANDLORDS MISS IT. Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-201(c) says a person shall not be discriminated against in the leasing or rental of residential property because the person has an assistance animal, which shall be permitted in leased or rented residential property in accordance with the federal Fair Housing Act. And § 35-13-203(a) makes it a MISDEMEANOR, fine up to $750, for any person denying or interfering with admittance to or enjoyment of any place or facility referenced in § 35-13-201(a) through (c) — which includes residential property under (a)(iii) and (c) — or otherwise interfering with the rights of a person with a disability. Refusing an assistance animal in Wyoming is not merely a fair housing exposure; it is a crime. Section 35-13-205(a)(iv) defines “assistance animal” broadly: an animal that works, provides assistance or performs tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability, OR provides emotional support that alleviates one or more identified symptoms or effects of a person’s disability. Emotional support animals are squarely inside the Wyoming definition. “Service animal” at (a)(viii) takes the federal ADA definitions at 28 C.F.R. 35.104 and 36.104, includes service miniature horses, and since 2025 expressly includes a dog being trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability.

WHAT YOU DO KEEP. The last sentence of § 35-13-201(c) is yours: “The person shall be liable for any damage done by his assistance animal to the premises or facilities of the leased or rented residential property.” That is a statutory damage liability, separate from your lease, and it survives whatever the animal’s status is. Combined with Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a), which lets you deduct damages, unpaid rent and other costs provided by any contract from the deposit, you can charge actual animal damage against the deposit — you simply cannot charge a pet fee, pet deposit or pet rent up front for an assistance animal. Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii), the Wyoming Fair Housing Act’s disability section, requires reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices and services where necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling — the state-law home of the accommodation analysis, and richer than § 40-26-103 for any animal question. Finally, do not harm the animal: Wyo. Stat. § 35-13-206(a) makes knowingly and willfully inflicting serious bodily harm, permanent disability or death on a service or assistance animal a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment for less than one year, a fine of up to $5,000, or both, with mandatory restitution under (b) for veterinary bills and the cost of replacing or retraining the animal.

title: Servicemember Tenants in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no state lease-termination statute for servicemembers. There is no Wyoming analog of the SCRA's housing-lease provision, no state early-termination notice period, no rule about refunding prepaid rent after a military termination, and no application-decision deadline for a servicemember applicant. The early-termination right your tenant will rely on is FEDERAL: the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, which is outside this corpus and should be applied from its own text.

What Wyoming adds is a reach-extension and a set of teeth. Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(a) gives members of the Wyoming national guard ordered to active state service, by either the state or the federal government, for more than thirty consecutive days 'all protections afforded to persons in the armed forces of the United States under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Public Law 108-189'. 'Active state service' is defined by cross-reference to § 19-7-101(a)(v): service on behalf of the state in aid of civil authorities, under martial law, at encampments ordered by state authority, or any other duty requiring the entire time of the person, including state active duty and Title 32 duty, but excluding call into federal service under Title 10. So a Guard member activated by the Governor for a flood or a fire for more than thirty days gets the same protections as a soldier on federal orders — and a landlord who treats state orders as 'not real military orders' is wrong.

The teeth are three, and you should price all of them. First, § 19-11-122(b): any person who knowingly violates the protections provided to a Wyoming Guard member under subsection (a) or under § 19-11-125 is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000. Second, § 19-11-122(c): those protections may serve as the basis for an action or as a defense, and Wyoming courts that would otherwise have jurisdiction have jurisdiction over SCRA, USERRA and § 19-11-125 proceedings under ordinary rules; § 19-11-122(d) requires the courts to give scheduling preference on the motion of a person in the uniformed services who certifies their service. Third, and most expensive: § 19-11-123 provides that 'In any proceeding employed to enforce any of the provisions of this act, the court shall award reasonable litigation expenses including reasonable attorney's fees.' That is mandatory, not discretionary — a rare thing in Wyoming, where there is no attorney-fee shifting anywhere in the eviction chapter or the residential rental article.

One provision needs a careful read and a cautious answer. Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-125 lets a person ordered to active service in the uniformed services (or already in service and transferred) suspend a 'service contract' for orders of more than 30 but not more than 180 consecutive days, and terminate or suspend one for orders of more than 180 days, at any time after receiving military orders. Subsection (b) lists the contracts covered — telecommunication, internet, television, athletic club or gym memberships, satellite radio or communication services — and then adds (b)(vi), 'Other services provided pursuant to a contract that requires periodic and ongoing payments'. A residential lease is a conveyance of a possessory interest, not a service, and every named item in the list is a consumer subscription service, so the better reading is that a lease is outside § 19-11-125. But (b)(vi) is written broadly and no Wyoming authority in this corpus settles it, and the consequences if a tenant is right are severe: under § 19-11-125(c), effective on the date specified in the notice or ten days after it is sent, whichever is later, and 'A service member who terminates, suspends or reinstates services may not be charged any penalty, interest, fee, loss of deposit or other cost because of the termination' — no early-termination fee and no deposit forfeiture — all enforced by the § 19-11-122(b) misdemeanor and the mandatory § 19-11-123 fee award. The cautious course: when a tenant hands you written or electronic notice with a copy of military orders, do not charge an early-termination fee, do not keep the deposit as a penalty, and do not threaten eviction. Treat the termination as effective, settle rent to the effective date, and run the deposit through § 1-21-1208 on its ordinary terms (you may still deduct for actual damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, unpaid rent accrued to the effective date, cleaning and other costs your contract creates). If you want to contest it, get advice before you charge anything.

Practical handling. Ask for written or electronic notice plus a copy of the orders; that is what § 19-11-125(c) requires and it mirrors what the federal SCRA expects. Diary the effective date. Put your acceptance in writing. Do not condition release on the tenant finding a replacement, paying a re-letting fee or forfeiting any part of the deposit. And remember § 1-21-1304: the Safe Homes Act's anti-waiver rule shows Wyoming knows how to write one and did not write one here — but a lease term purporting to waive a servicemember's SCRA protections would still run straight into § 19-11-122(b) if you acted on it knowingly.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty in Wyoming, But a Residency Rule You Must Know
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no sex offender disclosure on a landlord. There is no required registry notice in the lease, no duty to tell a prospective tenant that a registered offender lives nearby, no duty to answer if one asks, and no statute making registry information off limits in screening. Wyoming's answer is that the information is public and the tenant can look it up. Wyo. Stat. § 7-19-303(a)(iii) directs the division of criminal investigation to make a public registry available to the public through internet technology, including the offender's name and aliases, physical address, date and place of birth, date and place of conviction, the crime of conviction, photograph, physical characteristics and the full history of qualifying convictions, excluding only internet identifiers, telephone numbers and delinquency adjudications. Wyo. Stat. § 7-19-303(k) directs the division to facilitate access without assessing anyone's individual risk, and to post a disclaimer that no determination has been made that any listed individual is currently dangerous, that people are listed solely by virtue of their conviction record and state law, and that the purpose is accessibility rather than a warning about any specific individual. That disclaimer is worth repeating to a tenant who asks you to interpret the registry: Wyoming's legislature has said in terms that the registry is not a risk assessment. The real Wyoming rule here is not about disclosure at all — it is a residency restriction that can make your unit unlawful for a particular tenant, and it changed on July 1, 2026. Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-320(a)(iv) makes it an offence for a registered offender eighteen or older to reside within 1,000 feet of the property on which a SCHOOL is located, measured from the nearest point of the exterior wall of the offender's dwelling unit to the school's property line, with the paragraph not applying if the residence was established before July 1, 2010. Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-320(a)(v), added by 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. __ (SF0088) effective July 1, 2026, extends the same 1,000-foot rule to a CHILD CARE FACILITY, measured the same way, and does not apply if the residence was established before July 1, 2026 or before the date the facility was established at that location. 'Child care facility' is defined at § 6-2-320(e)(iii) and covers a facility licensed as a child care provider by the department of family services and a facility administered, owned or supervised by a governmental entity that provides care for children for consideration at the parents' or an agency's request. A violation of subsection (a) is a misdemeanor under § 6-2-320(c), up to six months and $750. Two carve-outs matter to housing providers: § 6-2-320(b)(iii) exempts an offender residing at a state licensed or certified facility for incarceration, health or convalescent care within 1,000 feet of a school, and § 6-2-320(b)(ix) exempts an offender who stays at a homeless shelter or resides at a recovery facility within 1,000 feet of a school if the shelter or facility has been APPROVED FOR SEX OFFENDERS BY THE SHERIFF OR POLICE CHIEF. Note that both of those carve-outs are written against the school rule; if you operate a shelter or recovery residence, get the approval and get it in writing. There is a mechanism for checking: Wyo. Stat. § 7-19-302 provides that upon an offender's request the sheriff or the division shall determine whether an address is within 1,000 feet of a child care facility as defined by § 6-2-320(e)(iii). That request is the offender's to make, not yours, but you can tell an applicant it exists. Act on this as follows. You may screen on criminal history and you may use the public registry, but screen every applicant the same way and record the business reason for every denial — Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(a) and (b) bar refusing, making unavailable, or discriminating in the terms of a rental on Wyoming's seven protected classes, and § 40-26-103(c) protects only one criminal exception by name, a conviction for the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance, so a blanket criminal-history bar is not blessed by the Wyoming statute. Do not volunteer registry information about a neighbour or another tenant as a selling point or a warning; you have no duty to and Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act, which reaches residential leases through Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) with no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110 and a knowing-conduct gate in § 40-12-105(a), is the exposure if you get it wrong. If a prospective tenant asks you directly, the clean answer is to point them at the public registry and the § 7-19-303(k) disclaimer rather than to characterise anyone. And if you rent anywhere near a school or a licensed child care facility, be aware that § 6-2-320(a)(iv) and (a)(v) can make your unit an unlawful residence for a particular applicant regardless of what you are willing to rent to them.

title: Registered Offenders and Where They May Live
bodyText:
Wyoming puts the whole duty on the offender and none of it on you. No Wyoming statute makes it an offence for a landlord to rent to a registered offender, none bars two registered offenders from sharing a dwelling, none requires you to screen, none requires you to disclose a nearby registrant to a prospective tenant, and none gives you a safe-harbour lease statement of the Birmingham kind. "Landlord" and "offender" never appear within two hundred characters of each other anywhere in Wyoming law, in either word order.

What exists is a residency restriction on the registrant, and in 2026 it grew. Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-320(a) provides that, except as subsection (b) allows, no person eighteen or older who must register as a sex offender under § 7-19-302 shall:

— (a)(iv) reside within one thousand (1,000) feet of the property on which a SCHOOL is located, measured from the nearest point of the exterior wall of the registered offender's dwelling unit to the school's property line, "except that this paragraph shall not apply if the registered offender's residence was established prior to July 1, 2010"; and

— (a)(v), added by 2026 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 52 (SF0088) effective July 1, 2026, reside within one thousand (1,000) feet of the property where a CHILD CARE FACILITY is located, measured the same way to the facility's property line, "except that this paragraph shall not apply if the registered offender's residence was established before July 1, 2026 or before the date when the child care facility was established at the location."

THE TWO GRANDFATHER CLAUSES ARE NOT THE SAME, and the difference decides whether your tenancy survives. The child care paragraph has a second limb: a registrant is also safe if his residence was established before the facility was established at that location. So a day care opening across the street next year does not put a sitting tenant in breach. The school paragraph has no such limb — its only exception is a residence established before July 1, 2010. On the literal words, a registrant who moved in during 2015 and finds a new school built within a thousand feet in 2027 is caught. Keep the two apart; do not reason from one to the other.

"CHILD CARE FACILITY" IS NARROWER THAN IT SOUNDS. Section 6-2-320(e)(iii) defines it as (A) a facility licensed as a child care provider by the department of family services, or (B) a facility administered, owned or supervised by a governmental entity — including the state, local governments and school districts — that provides care for children in exchange for consideration at the request of parents, guardians or a responsible agency, expressly excluding an elementary, middle or high school. An unlicensed private home day care that falls outside DFS licensing, and a private facility that is not governmental, are in neither limb. So the restriction does not attach to every place children are minded. Measure from a licensed or governmental facility, not from a neighbour's informal arrangement.

A DRAFTING QUIRK TO KNOW. Subsection (b) lists nine exceptions, but its stem reads "The provisions of paragraphs (a)(i) and (ii) shall not apply to the extent the registered offender:". Two of the nine are plainly about residing — (b)(iii), residing at a state licensed or certified facility for incarceration, health or convalescent care within a thousand feet of a school, and (b)(ix), staying at a homeless shelter or residing at a recovery facility within a thousand feet of a school that the sheriff or police chief has approved for sex offenders. On the literal text those exceptions do not reach (a)(iv) or (a)(v) at all, because the stem confines subsection (b) to paragraphs (a)(i) and (ii). We are not resolving that; we flag it. If your property is a licensed care facility, a shelter or a recovery residence within a thousand feet of a school or a child care facility, do not rely on (b)(iii) or (b)(ix) without advice.

PENALTY AND WHO ENFORCES. A violation of § 6-2-320(a) is a misdemeanour under § 6-2-320(c) — imprisonment up to six (6) months, a fine up to seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00), or both. It is prosecuted against the offender. You are not an accessory for having rented the unit, and nothing in the section imposes a duty on an owner.

HOW DISTANCE GETS DETERMINED, AND WHY YOU CANNOT ASK. Section 7-19-302(w), also added by 2026 ch. 52, directs the division to verify a registrant's residential address to decide whether he lives near a child care facility as defined by § 6-2-320(e)(iii) and whether an exception applies. The second sentence is the practical one: "Upon request by an offender, the sheriff or the division shall determine whether an address provided by the offender is within one thousand (1,000) feet of a child care facility." The request right belongs to the OFFENDER. A landlord cannot demand that determination. What you can do is make it a condition of the tenancy that the tenant obtain it and give you the answer in writing before moving in.

WHAT NOTICE YOU MIGHT GET. Under § 7-19-303(c)(ii) the sheriff notifies residential neighbours within at least seven hundred fifty (750) feet of the offender's residence, and community organisations including schools and religious and youth organisations, but only where the conviction was for an offence specified in § 7-19-302(h) or (j); and the division must notify each child care facility within at least one thousand (1,000) feet. You get nothing in your capacity as the landlord of the unit. If you happen to live within 750 feet you may be notified as a neighbour.

FAIR HOUSING — DO NOT ASSUME A SHELTER. Wyoming's Fair Housing Act has a conviction carve-out, but it is narrow and it does not cover this. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(c) says only that "[t]his section does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been convicted under federal law or the law of any state of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance." It is confined to § 40-26-103 by its own opening words, it requires a conviction, and it covers only drug manufacture or distribution. A sex offence is outside it entirely. Whether a blanket registry-based exclusion creates unlawful disparate impact is a question of federal Fair Housing Act case law and HUD guidance, which are outside this library's sources and have not been read — we make no prediction. The cautious course is to tie any restriction to the statute's own geography, as the clause below does, rather than to registry status at large.

PRACTICAL COURSE. Find out once whether your property sits within a thousand feet of a school or of a licensed or governmental child care facility, and write the answer in your file. If it does, use the occupancy clause. If it does not, you have nothing to administer here.

title: No Single-Family Occupancy Notice in Wyoming, but Name the Occupants Anyway
bodyText:
Wyoming has no single-family-residence occupancy disclosure and no occupancy standard of any kind. There is no notice you must put at the top of a lease for a single-family rental, no rebuttable presumption about lawful occupancy, no requirement that the lease be notarized or signed by a permitted property manager, no requirement to print your address and telephone number in the lease, and no state limit on how many people may live in a unit - no persons-per-bedroom rule, no square-footage formula, nothing. The terms "single-family" and "single family" do not appear in Title 1 or Title 34 at all, and "occupancy limit," "maximum occupancy," "occupancy standard" and "persons per bedroom" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes.

Wyoming also imposes no typographic rule on any residential lease term. There is no relative font-size requirement, no "larger than any other font in the lease" rule, no first-page placement rule, and no all-capitals requirement. If you are adapting a lease from a state that demands an oversized first-page notice, drop the notice and drop the formatting; neither is required here, and a notice describing a presumption Wyoming does not have will only confuse a Wyoming tenant and a Wyoming judge.

What Wyoming does have is a single occupancy provision, and it only works if your lease does its part. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) requires each renter to "[o]ccupy the residential rental unit in the manner for which it was designed and shall not increase the number of occupants above that specified in the rental agreement without written permission of the owner." Read the second half carefully. The statutory ceiling is not a number the legislature chose; it is "that specified in the rental agreement." If your lease does not specify a number of occupants, there is no figure for the tenant to exceed and this duty gives you nothing. So state it: name every adult occupant, give a total permitted occupant count including children, and say that any additional occupant requires your prior written permission. The statute's own remedy mechanism is written permission, so make clear that permission must be in writing and that an unapproved long-stay guest counts as an added occupant - otherwise you will be arguing about where a guest ends and an occupant begins.

Doing that converts overcrowding into an enforceable eviction ground without any special notice. A violation of § 1-21-1204 is a ground for forcible entry and detainer under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi), on the ordinary written notice to leave the premises served at least three days before you file under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003. Plead the chain expressly: the occupant number stated in the lease, the increase, § 1-21-1204(a)(v), and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi). The first half of the paragraph - occupying the unit "in the manner for which it was designed" - is a separate duty, and it is the one that reaches a tenant running a business out of the house, partitioning rooms, or using a garage or basement as sleeping space it was not built for.

Two cautions on how high or low you set the number. Federal fair housing law limits occupancy restrictions: an unreasonably restrictive limit can discriminate on the basis of familial status (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. S 3604). Do not set a number that would effectively exclude families with children, and do not write the clause to count children differently from adults. Flagged and not resolved: Wyoming municipalities and counties commonly set occupancy and unrelated-persons limits through zoning and housing ordinances, and those are outside this review - check the city or county, because a lease that permits more occupants than local zoning allows creates a problem you will own.

One place Wyoming does single out this building type is worth knowing even though it is not a disclosure. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-163(b) provides that, notwithstanding any other law, short-term rental of detached one- and two-family dwellings and townhomes "shall not be regulated as a commercial use for purposes of fire, building and electrical standards and shall not be subject to regulation under the International Building Code." That is a shield against commercial code treatment, not a notice duty, and it imposes nothing on your lease.

title: No Shoreline or Waterfront Access Disclosure
bodyText: Wyoming has no shoreline access disclosure. No statute requires a lease of waterfront property to carry a notice about the public's rights along a shore, a beach, a lake edge or a riverbank, and the statutes contain no "beach," "coastal," "littoral" or "lakeshore" provision at all. Wyoming is landlocked, and the few statutory uses of "shoreline" are county boundary descriptions tracing the edge of Yellowstone Lake. The closest thing Wyoming has to a water-rights disclosure runs to land sales, not leases: in the subdivision statutes, Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-415 for municipal annexation and subdivision plats and Wyo. Stat. §§ 18-5-306 and 18-5-316 for county subdivision permits, a subdivider's plat materials must state that the owner does not warrant to a purchaser any rights to the natural flow of a stream within or adjacent to the subdivision, and must further state that Wyoming law does not recognize any riparian rights to the continued natural flow of a stream or river for persons living on its banks. That is a useful sentence to know even though it is not yours to give: a Wyoming tenant on a riverbank gets no right to the water simply by living there. Water itself is not yours either. Wyo. Const. art. 8, § 1 declares the water of all natural streams, springs, lakes and other collections of still water within the state to be the property of the state, and Wyoming allocates it by appropriation through the state engineer and board of control under Wyo. Const. art. 8, § 2 - not by riparian ownership. So a lease cannot grant a tenant a water right, and you should not imply one. Practical course, if you rent a place on or near water: say in the lease what the tenant may actually use and what they may not - whether any dock, boat slip, mooring, irrigation ditch, well or pond use is included, and whether the tenant may draw, divert or impound water (they generally may not without a permit). Say whether any recorded easement, ditch right-of-way, public fishing easement or access agreement crosses the property, because the tenant will meet the people using it. And if you rely on the property being private, know what backs that up: under Wyo.
