Stat. § 6-3-303(a) a person commits criminal trespass by entering or remaining on the land or premises of another, knowing he is not authorized, or after being notified to depart or not to trespass, where notice is given either by personal communication from the owner, occupant or their agent or a peace officer, or by posting signs reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders; § 6-3-303(b) makes it a misdemeanor carrying up to six months, a fine of up to $750, or both. Posting, in other words, is what makes the boundary enforceable, and the statute lets the occupant - your tenant - give that notice as well as you. One caution the statutes cannot settle: whether members of the public may float or wade a stream where it crosses private land, and where the bed and banks stop being public, depends on navigability and on Wyoming case law rather than on any section of the code, and case law is outside what was searched here. Do not promise a tenant exclusive use of a watercourse; describe what you know, and say that public use of the water itself is not within your control. LOCAL ORDINANCE: county and municipal shoreline setback, dock and public access rules are flagged and not resolved here.

title: No Rent Protection During a Government Shutdown
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant no special treatment because a government shutdown has interrupted their pay. There is no statute delaying rent, suspending a late fee, pausing an eviction, or requiring you to accept rent after the due date for a federal, state or tribal employee or contractor. The word "shutdown" standing alone appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and "government shutdown," "lapse in appropriation" and "essential worker" return nothing at all. Wyoming also has no eviction-moratorium statute and no emergency rent provision tied to a declared state of emergency.

So a shutdown changes nothing about the mechanics. Rent is due when the lease says it is due. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) a forcible entry and detainer action lies against a tenant "after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due," and under § 1-21-1003 you must serve a written notice to quit at least three days before you commence the action. Those two three-day periods are separate and they stack. Nothing suspends either of them because a paycheck is late.

One Wyoming provision in this neighborhood does bind you, and it has nothing to do with shutdowns -- it is about call-ups. Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(a) provides that "[m]embers of the Wyoming national guard ordered to active state service by the state or federal government for a period of more than thirty (30) consecutive days shall have all protections afforded to persons in the armed forces of the United States under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Public Law 108-189." That pulls the full federal package across to a state-activated Guard member -- including the SCRA's residential lease termination right and its bar on evicting a servicemember or their dependents from a covered residence without a court order (FEDERAL: Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, 50 U.S.C. §§ 3951, 3955). This matters in Wyoming in practice, because Guard activations for wildfire, flood and winter-storm response can run past thirty days. If your tenant is a Guard member on active state service of more than thirty consecutive days, treat them as an SCRA-protected servicemember.

Take that seriously: under Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(b), "[a]ny person who knowingly violates the protections provided to members of the Wyoming national guard pursuant to subsection (a)" is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000. Section 19-11-122(c) makes those protections available to the tenant either as a claim or as a defense in your eviction case, and § 19-11-122(d) requires the court to give scheduling preference to a servicemember who certifies their service -- so the defense is both available and fast-tracked. Section 19-11-122(a) also provides that, apart from the subsection (b) misdemeanor, nothing in it authorizes imposing the SCRA's own penalties for a violation of the Guard member's state-conferred protections.

Practical course: during a shutdown you are free to do nothing, but you are also free to agree to something, and in Wyoming that agreement is what creates the right. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in the residential rental article be modified "by explicit written agreement signed by the parties," so if you want to give a furloughed tenant a payment plan or defer a month, write it down and have both of you sign it -- a verbal accommodation you later deny is a dispute, and a signed one is a record. Keep it specific: what is deferred, when it is repaid, and whether late fees accrue. And before you serve a notice on a tenant you know to be in uniform, check whether § 19-11-122 or the federal SCRA applies.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones in Wyoming
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute limits renting out a home in a single-family zone, and none conditions a rental on the owner living on the lot. There is nothing like the Kentucky provision, KRS 383.199, that bars leasing a single-family home in a traditional single-family zone in Jefferson County unless the owner occupies the property. Wyoming has no statewide owner-occupancy requirement for rentals, no statewide short-term rental law, and no accessory-dwelling-unit statute at all — "accessory dwelling" appears nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes.

Zoning in Wyoming is entirely local, and the enabling statutes are broad. For cities and towns, Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-601(a)(i)(E) lets the governing body by ordinance "[r]egulate and restrict the ... [l]ocation and use of buildings, structures and land for trade, industry, residence or other purposes," and § 15-1-601(b) lets it divide the municipality into districts and regulate the use of buildings, structures or land within them. Section 15-1-601(c) is the main constraint and it is a weak one: regulations may differ from district to district "but shall be uniform for each class or kind of buildings within a district." For counties, Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-201(a) lets each board of county commissioners "regulate and restrict the location and use of buildings and structures and the use, condition of use or occupancy of lands for residence, recreation, agriculture, industry, commerce, public use and other purposes in the unincorporated area of the county" — note that county power reaches "occupancy of lands for residence" expressly, and reaches only unincorporated areas; the same subsection says nothing in §§ 18-5-201 through 18-5-208 may be construed to contravene a city's or town's zoning authority.

So the restriction you need to worry about is a city ordinance or county resolution, not a statute — and because Wyoming gives cities and towns constitutional home rule under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b) ("[a]ll cities and towns are hereby empowered to determine their local affairs and government as established by ordinance ... subject only to statutes uniformly applicable to all cities and towns"), and because the legislature has preempted nothing in this area, a Wyoming municipality can and sometimes does regulate rentals, short-term rentals and occupancy. Ordinances are outside this library. Before you buy or rent out a house in a Wyoming single-family district, read the zoning ordinance for that city, or the county zoning resolution if the property is unincorporated, and ask the planning office in writing whether a long-term rental is a permitted use and whether any owner-occupancy, registration or licensing condition applies.

The few statutory limits on local zoning that do exist have nothing to do with rentals: Wyo. Stat. § 18-5-201(a) bars a county from preventing a use reasonably necessary to mineral extraction, from requiring consistency with a local land use plan unless the plan's provisions are in the zoning regulations, from using minimum lot sizes to prevent residential or agricultural uses on land divisions exempt under § 18-5-303(a)(i), and from treating a qualifying private school differently from a public school. Wyoming also has no statutory protection placing group homes or community residences in single-family zones as of right, and no statewide family-definition or unrelated-occupants rule — so a local "family" definition capping unrelated occupants is a genuine risk, and a federal Fair Housing Act familial-status or disability issue is the usual route for challenging one.

Two Wyoming points to keep in view if a local rule does bite. First, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) caps occupants only at "that specified in the rental agreement" — state law supplies no number, so write one in, and write it to match whatever the local ordinance allows. Second, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-113(a) says the Wyoming Fair Housing Act "does not affect a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling or a restriction relating to health or safety standards" — so a reasonable local occupancy cap survives the Act, but an unreasonable one, or one applied to exclude families with children, does not.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute regulating smart locks, keypads, key fobs, app-based entry or biometric entry in a residential rental. The words 'smart lock', 'electronic lock' and 'keyless' appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and there is no Wyoming counterpart to Washington's smart access system law (RCW 59.18.750 to 59.18.760, effective January 1, 2027) requiring an alternative non-app, non-biometric key on request or a written privacy policy at lease signing. Nor does Wyoming have a general consumer data privacy act. Four things fill the gap, and the third is the one landlords miss. First, Wyoming also has no statute restricting landlord entry, so the lock technology does not change your entry rights — they come from the lease. The only entry provision in Wyoming landlord-tenant law is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii), which bars a renter from unreasonably denying entry for repairs, inspection and showing the unit; it is a tenant prohibition, not a grant of remote access, and it says nothing about using a system log or a remote unlock. Second, the lock is part of the unit. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) the unit must be kept in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation and must have operational electrical service, and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) and (a)(iii) you must maintain common areas in a reasonably safe condition and maintain the electrical system. A smart lock that will not open because its battery, WiFi or server is down is a habitability and safety problem, not a technology inconvenience, so always leave the tenant a working physical override. Third, and the real exposure: a biometric or app-based lock makes you the keeper of data Wyoming regulates. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-502(a) provides that 'An individual or commercial entity that conducts business in Wyoming and that owns or licenses computerized data that includes personal identifying information about a resident of Wyoming shall, when it becomes aware of a breach of the security of the system, conduct in good faith a reasonable and prompt investigation to determine the likelihood that personal identifying information has been or will be misused,' and must then notify the affected Wyoming resident as soon as possible. 'Personal identifying information' is defined at Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-501(a)(vii) as a person's first name or initial plus last name together with any of the data elements in Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-901(b)(iii) through (xiv), and that list expressly includes, at paragraph (b)(xiii), 'Unique biometric data, meaning data generated from measurements or analysis of human body characteristics for authentication purposes,' and, at paragraph (b)(viii), 'Shared secrets or security tokens that are known to be used for data based authentication.' A fingerprint or face template tied to a tenant's name, or an access token or entry code tied to a tenant's name, is therefore regulated data in your hands. Read your vendor contract to see who is the data owner, and get the vendor to carry the notification obligation in writing. Fourth, Wyoming's electronic surveillance and eavesdropping offences are in Title 6 and are not displaced by a lease, so a camera or intercom built into an entry system must not be pointed or used in a way that records inside the unit. The practical course, which no Wyoming statute compels but all of this recommends: give every tenant a physical key or a non-biometric credential as well, do not make biometric enrollment a condition of the tenancy, tell the tenant in writing what the system records and for how long, do not use entry logs to monitor a tenant's comings and goings, and put all of it in the lease.

title: Wyoming Has No Indoor Smoking Ban at All, So Your Lease Is the Smoking Policy
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statewide smoking ban. Not for workplaces, not for public places, and not for the enclosed common areas of apartment buildings. There is therefore no smoke-free workplace law that could reach a common hallway where your building staff work, and the question this topic asks has no Wyoming hook to attach to.

The search is unusually clean. "Smoke-free," "smokefree," "clean indoor air," "secondhand smoke," "environmental tobacco" and "no smoking" return zero hits across all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws. The word "smoking" appears just seven times in the whole corpus, and every one of them is in Title 30, the mining and oil chapter, restricting smoking near explosives magazines and in underground workings. Wyoming's 170 "tobacco" references are about importation and labelling (Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-7-1501 and 35-7-1502), taxation, and sales to minors — none of them is an indoor-air rule.

Wyoming also has no smoke-drift waiver statute, no disclosure requirement for a building where smoking is allowed, and no statute validating or invalidating a tenant's waiver of a tobacco-nuisance claim. Utah's waiver clause, which is where this topic usually comes from, has no Wyoming equivalent either way.

So the lease is your policy, and you have wide latitude. You may make the whole property smoke-free, including inside units, balconies, patios and common areas; you may allow smoking; you may allow it outdoors only and set a distance from doors and windows; and you may treat vaping and cannabis separately. None of that needs statutory authority. Say what is prohibited, where, and by whom — tenant, occupants and guests — and say what the consequence of a breach is.

Four things that still bite.

First, a waiver of a nuisance claim is a contract term, and Wyoming has given you no statute that validates one. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) does let any duty or obligation in the residential rental article be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and there is no anti-waiver provision in that article — but a tobacco-nuisance claim between neighbours is not a duty in the article, so § 1-21-1202(d) does not carry it. A smoke-drift acknowledgement is still worth having: it defeats a claim that the tenant was misled about the building, and it documents disclosure. Do not draft it as a blanket release of all liability, because an exculpatory clause reaching personal injury is a different and riskier thing, and Wyoming courts' treatment of those is case law, which is outside this library.

Second, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) makes it a prohibited act for a renter to interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property, and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) allows forcible entry and detainer against renters in violation of any term imposed under § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205. If one tenant's smoking genuinely makes a neighbour's unit unusable, that is your enforcement route, and it exists whether or not your lease has a smoking clause.

Third, if you employ on-site staff, note Wyo. Stat. § 27-9-105(a)(iv). It is an unfair employment practice for an employer to require, as a condition of employment, that an employee or prospective employee use or refrain from using tobacco products outside the course of his employment, or otherwise to discriminate in compensation or the terms, conditions or privileges of employment on the basis of use or nonuse of tobacco outside employment, unless not using tobacco outside the workplace is a bona fide occupational qualification. You may ban smoking on the job and on the property; you may not make off-duty abstinence a condition of the job. A limited exception lets you price health, disability or life insurance by tobacco use if the differential rates reflect an actual differential cost to you and you give employees written notice of the rates.

Fourth, smoking policy touches fair housing. Wyoming's fair housing act protects disability at Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107, and § 40-26-107(c)(ii) makes refusal of a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services a discriminatory practice where the accommodation may be necessary to give the individual equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling. A tenant with a respiratory disability may ask you to enforce a smoking rule, relocate them, or seal a shared duct. Handle it as an accommodation request rather than a complaint.

The cautious course. Decide the policy before you advertise, put it in the lease in plain words, disclose honestly whether smoking is permitted elsewhere in the building, use an acknowledgement rather than a release, and apply the rule uniformly. And check your municipality: Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), nothing in state law preempts a local smoking ordinance, and Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) makes a more stringent local code prevail — several Wyoming towns have adopted smoking ordinances of their own, and this library does not resolve them.

title: No Benefit-Delay Defence to a Wyoming Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Wyoming gives a tenant no defence to a nonpayment eviction based on a late, reduced or terminated government benefit. There is no California-style Social Security hardship stay, no Massachusetts-style requirement that the court continue the case and reinstate the tenancy when a benefit or voucher payment is late, and no pay-and-stay or cure-on-the-courthouse-steps right of any kind. "Public assistance," "government benefit," "housing assistance payment" and "pay and stay" return nothing in Title 1, and no Wyoming provision ties a rent default to a benefit interruption. Wyoming's forcible entry and detainer statutes run the other way, and you should know the shape of them. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows the action after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires a separate written notice to quit served at least three (3) days before the action is commenced — two stacked three-day periods, not one. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1006 the tenant may, but is not required to, file a written answer. Then comes the provision that most directly answers this topic: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1007 provides that "No continuance shall be granted the defendant for longer than two (2) days unless he gives a bond to the adverse party, with good and sufficient surety approved by the circuit court, conditioned for the payment of the rent that may accrue and costs if judgment is rendered against him." So a Wyoming tenant waiting on a delayed benefit cannot simply be given time — beyond two days the court must require a surety bond covering accruing rent and costs. That is the opposite of a benefit-delay continuance right. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(a) the circuit court tries the action on the return day of the summons if it is not continued, the place of trial is not changed, and neither party demands a jury; if the complaint is found true the court renders a general judgment for restitution of the premises and costs, and if true only in part, restitution of that part with costs taxed as deemed equitable. In a nonpayment case Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) requires the court to find the amount of rent due and payable at the time of the hearing together with the terms of the parties' agreement about the amount and time of payment, to render judgment for that amount "together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease," and to issue execution for the rent and costs separately from the writ of restitution. Note that attorney's fees come from the lease, not from the statute — if your lease has no fee clause, you get no fees. On appeal, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1015(a) requires the appellant in an appeal from a judgment for rents due to deposit the rent with the court in addition to the bond required by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1014. None of this means a benefit interruption is irrelevant in practice, and there are two real constraints you should respect. First, if the tenant participates in a federal housing programme, the federal programme rules and the HAP contract govern what you may do about the subsidy portion and when, and those are federal, not Wyoming, obligations. Second, if you obtain a money judgment, you may well be unable to collect it from benefits: Wyoming's own exemption notices at Wyo. Stat. § 1-15-107 (attachment and garnishment) and Wyo. Stat. § 1-17-102 (property seized under execution) both list, as exemptions the debtor may claim, Social Security benefits pursuant to 42 U.S.C. 407 and supplemental security income, veteran's benefits and black lung benefits. Garnishing a benefit-dependent tenant is usually a dead end, which is a practical reason to take a payment plan rather than a judgment. Wyoming also has no source-of-income discrimination class — the Wyoming Fair Housing Act classes under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103 are race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin — but note that Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i), the intimidation-and-interference offence, carries a longer list that includes "status with respect to marriage or public assistance," though only for conduct by force or threat of force. So threatening a tenant over their public assistance status is a different and more serious matter than simply declining to accept a voucher.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Wyoming Lease
bodyText:
No Wyoming statute requires a residential lease to state that the property sits inside a special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, plans, design criteria or restrictions. There is no bold-type acknowledgment of the kind Puerto Rico imposes, no district disclosure form, and no obligation to attach a district's rules to the lease. Wyoming also has no residential seller-disclosure act that might generate a parallel duty, and no common-interest or homeowners'-association statute. The only mandatory recital in a Wyoming residential lease is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207, which requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable and requires separate written notice of that fact when the deposit is taken.

That is not because Wyoming lacks special districts. It has a great many — improvement and service districts, water and sewer districts, fire protection, hospital, cemetery, weed and pest, conservation and others — and their costs reach property through special assessments. Those assessments run against the land and against you, not against your tenant. Under Wyo. Stat. § 15-6-406(a), when a local-improvement assessment roll is confirmed the charge on the assessed lots and parcels becomes a lien on the property from the time the roll reaches the collecting officer, and that lien is 'paramount and superior to any other lien or encumbrance created before or after, except a lien for assessments for general taxes.' Section 15-6-606(a) does the same for a lighting district, creating a lien from the date the levying resolution finally passes. Section 15-6-426 gives a city, a certificate-of-delinquency holder or anyone else entitled to collect ten (10) years from delinquency to sue on an assessment or enforce its lien. A superior lien that outranks your mortgage is worth knowing about whether or not you have to tell a tenant.

So the practical question is not disclosure but allocation. If you want a tenant to bear any part of a district assessment, your lease must create the charge. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit be applied to 'other costs provided by any contract,' and the general Wyoming position is that a charge the lease does not create is not collectible. Write it as a specific, named escalation or reimbursement term identifying the district and the kind of charge, and state how the amount is calculated and when it is billed. A vague clause letting you pass through 'any governmental charges' invites a dispute and gives the tenant no way to verify the number. Check the clause 'tax-escalation' for the shape.

Two cautions. First, do not add a district representation you are not required to make. A statement about a district's boundaries, charges or plans is a representation you can be held to, and if it turns out to be wrong you have a problem under the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-101 through 40-12-114 — § 40-12-105(a)(i) reaches knowingly representing that merchandise has 'accessories or uses it does not have,' and § 40-12-105(a)(xv) is a general unfair-or-deceptive-practices catch-all, with 'merchandise' defined at § 40-12-102(a)(vi) to include real property. If a prospective tenant asks about a district, answer accurately or say you do not know and point them to the county assessor. Second, districts are frequently creatures of local action, and municipal ordinances and district resolutions are outside the scope of this research. A city, town or district could adopt its own notice or acknowledgment requirement, so if your property is in a newly formed improvement district check with the clerk of the municipality or county before you assume nothing applies.

title: Sprinkler Systems in Wyoming - No Notice Required, Two Traps
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no sprinkler disclosure. There is no equivalent of New York's notice stating whether the premises have a maintained and operative sprinkler system, and no equivalent of Maryland's high-rise notice that a building lacks a complete system. Nothing in Wyoming law requires you to tell a tenant that a system exists, that it does not exist, or when it was last inspected. Searching for any connection between a sprinkler and a tenant, a lease, a rental or a disclosure returns nothing in either direction.

Wyoming also has no statute requiring sprinklers in a residential rental. Where sprinkler requirements come from in Wyoming is the model codes: under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) the fire prevention and electrical safety council adopts minimum fire standards not exceeding the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code and International Fuel Gas Code, and under § 35-9-121(a) the state fire marshal delegates complete enforcement authority to any municipality or county that qualifies, whose own standards may be equivalent to or more stringent than the state's. So whether your building needs a system, and how often it must be inspected and tested, is answered by your city or county building department and the code edition it has adopted, not by the statutes.

Sprinklers appear in the Wyoming statutes in exactly two places, both procedural, and both are worth knowing if you are building or renovating. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-107(a)(iii)(F), acceptance testing on fire alarm systems, fire sprinkler systems and kitchen hood and duct suppression systems is part of the fire prevention division's function — budget time for it. Under § 35-9-108(s), plans for fire alarm systems and fire sprinkler systems shall be submitted as successive phase plans after the initial plans are approved, so do not bundle your sprinkler drawings into the first submission; they go in afterwards, and sending them early will not speed anything up. Both of those only engage if your project is within state plan review at all, and § 35-9-108(a) limits that to state and local government buildings, public buildings over 5,000 square feet, multistory public buildings, child care centers over ten children, public assembly premises and fuel dispensing facilities — with "public building" defined at § 35-9-102(a)(xvii) as one "intended for access by the general public," which an ordinary apartment building is not. If you do engage a sprinkler contractor from out of state, Wyo. Stat. § 16-6-1101 recognises manufacturer and industry certifications for fire systems installation, testing and maintenance, including those of the national institute for certification in engineering technologies and the American and national fire sprinkler associations, so a qualified out-of-state contractor need not retest to be recognised.

Two things to actually do. First, disclose anyway, in writing, if the building has a system or conspicuously does not. It costs nothing, it is the kind of fact a tenant's insurer and your own will ask about, and once you know it, Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act is the exposure: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) brings real property within "merchandise" and § 40-12-105(a) reaches knowing deceptive practices. Second, deal with maintenance expressly in the lease, because Wyoming's default is not what you would expect. The owner's ongoing maintenance duty in § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) is a closed list — electrical systems, plumbing, heating, and hot and cold water — and a sprinkler system is not on it. Under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) you maintain "other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement," so the statutory duty to maintain a sprinkler system is opt-in. Do not treat that as a reason to stay silent. A sprinkler system is a life-safety system; local code will require periodic inspection and testing regardless of your lease, § 1-21-1203(a)(i) still forbids renting a unit that is not reasonably safe, and silence in the lease will not help you in a negligence claim after a fire. Say plainly in the lease that you maintain and test the system, that the tenant must not hang anything from, paint, obstruct or tamper with a sprinkler head, and that the tenant must report damage at once — and keep the inspection records.

title: When a Wyoming Lease Must Be Written, Signed and Recorded
bodyText:
Wyoming has two different lease-length thresholds, one year and three years, and they do different jobs. Mixing them up is the common mistake.

ONE YEAR - THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS, A VALIDITY RULE. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a) provides that in the listed cases "every agreement shall be void unless such agreement, or some note or memorandum thereof be in writing, and subscribed by the party to be charged therewith." Paragraph (a)(v) covers "[e]very agreement or contract for the sale of real estate, or the lease thereof, for more than one (1) year." Paragraph (a)(i) independently covers "[e]very agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within one (1) year from the making thereof," which can catch a one-year lease that does not start until a later date. Three points on the wording. The sanction is "void," not merely unenforceable, which is stronger language than most states use. A note or memorandum is enough - the whole lease need not be the signed document - but it must be "subscribed by the party to be charged," so a lease you want to enforce against the tenant must carry the tenant's signature; your own signature does not cure its absence. And § 1-23-105 does not require notarisation, witnesses or any particular form.

THREE YEARS - THE RECORDING RULE, A PRIORITY RULE. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 defines "conveyance" for the purposes of Title 34 chapter 1 as "every instrument in writing by which any estate or interest in real estate is created, alienated, mortgaged or assigned, or by which the title to any real estate may be affected in law or in equity, except wills, leases for a term not exceeding three (3) years, executory contracts for the sale or purchase of lands," and certain paid-up purchase certificates. So a lease for more than three years IS a conveyance in Wyoming, and the recording machinery applies to it. Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-120 then provides that every conveyance of real estate not recorded as required by law "shall be void, as against any subsequent purchaser or purchasers in good faith and for a valuable consideration of the same real estate or any portion thereof, whose conveyance shall be first duly recorded." Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-121(a) gives the converse: a recorded instrument touching any interest in lands is notice to, and takes precedence of, any subsequent purchaser from the time it is delivered to the county clerk for record. To record, Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-113 requires the conveyance to be acknowledged by the party or parties executing it before a notarial officer, who must comply with Wyo. Stat. § 32-3-109.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE. A three-year-or-shorter residential lease needs no notary and no recording; nothing is lost by not recording it, because it is not a conveyance. A lease longer than three years - a long tenancy, a ground lease, a lease with options that take the term past three years - should be signed, acknowledged before a notary and recorded, or a memorandum of it recorded, because an unrecorded one is void against a later good-faith purchaser for value who records first. The tenant loses the leasehold, not you, but you have promised them something you may be unable to deliver, and the buyer's title insurer will ask. A three-year lease sits exactly on the line, since the exclusion is "not exceeding three (3) years" - a lease of exactly three years is excluded, a lease of three years and a day is not. If you record, note that under Wyo. Stat. § 19-13-502(c), added by 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 32 (HB0097), the county clerk must report every recorded conveyance to the director of homeland security and the division of criminal investigation within fifteen days, for the critical-infrastructure-zone screening in §§ 19-13-501 and 19-13-502. The duty is the clerk's, not yours, but recording is no longer a purely private act.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT DO. There is no long-term lease exclusion from tenant-protection coverage. Article 12 of Title 1 applies by reference to Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv), which gates it on the unit being the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally - there is no term-length cut-off anywhere, so a five-year residential lease gets the full Article 12 treatment. There is also no statute requiring a lease to be in writing below the one-year threshold, no requirement to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no required lease form.

THE RENEWAL TRAP THAT SITS ON TOP OF THIS. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 provides that a lease which has expired by its own limitation may be renewed only "by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto, whether the original lease be written or verbal," and Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 removes any implied renewal from holding over or from your accepting rent, leaving only a tenancy by sufferance. So in Wyoming a writing requirement reappears at every renewal, regardless of the length of the new term. Get a signed renewal or extension every time.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched - in particular, whether part performance takes an oral long lease out of § 1-23-105 is a case-law question not resolved here, and the cautious course is to assume it does not.

title: Wyoming's money limits at a glance, and the ones that do not exist
bodyText:
Wyoming is one of the thinnest-statute states in the country on money terms. Almost every cap a landlord expects simply is not there, which means your lease is doing the work - and where your lease is silent, nothing fills the gap.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT CAP OR REGULATE. No security deposit cap of any kind, and no narrow definition of "deposit" that a pet, cleaning or last-month-rent payment could escape through: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) speaks simply of "property or money held as a deposit". No deposit interest requirement - § 1-21-1208(a) says the balance is delivered "without interest". No late fee cap, no grace period beyond the three days in § 1-21-1002(a)(i), and no late-fee statute at all. No application or screening fee cap. No returned-check fee cap binding a landlord beyond the figure in § 1-1-115. No convenience-fee or card-surcharge rule in either direction. No rent control and no rent-increase cap. No cap on holdover damages and no statutory holdover formula. No cap on attorney's fees a lease may shift. No required deposit escrow or separate trust account for a self-managed landlord. The battery behind that list is in the notes; in short, no Wyoming statute puts a ceiling on a residential deposit or a residential fee.

THE NUMBERS WYOMING DOES SET, ALL VERIFIED.

Deposit accounting, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a): on termination, the balance of any deposit and prepaid rent, plus a written itemization of deductions with reasons, must be delivered or mailed to the renter without interest within THIRTY DAYS after termination of the rental agreement, or within FIFTEEN DAYS after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is LATER. If there is damage to the unit, the period is extended by a further THIRTY DAYS. The renter must, within thirty days of termination, tell you where payment and notice may be sent. Deductions permitted are accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost of cleaning the unit to its condition at the beginning of the rental agreement, and "other costs provided by any contract" - that last phrase is broad, so almost any lease-created charge is deductible IF the lease creates it.

Utilities deposit, § 1-21-1208(b), a separate cascade: a deposit held and SEPARATELY IDENTIFIED as a utilities deposit must be refunded within TEN DAYS of a satisfactory showing that all the renter's utility charges are paid. Absent that showing within FORTY-FIVE DAYS of termination, you must within FIFTEEN DAYS after that apply the utilities deposit to the outstanding utility debt. Any refund then due is paid within SEVEN DAYS after the application, or within fifteen days after receipt of the new mailing address, whichever is later.

Deposit penalty, § 1-21-1208(c): if you unreasonably fail to comply with (a) or (b), the renter may recover THE FULL DEPOSIT and court costs - no multiplier, but you lose the deductions entirely. If you are the prevailing party and the court finds the renter acted unreasonably in bringing the action, you may be awarded court costs.

Bounced rent check, § 1-1-115: a written demand mailed by certificate of mailing or personally served starts a THIRTY DAY clock; the demand may claim the check plus a collection fee of up to THIRTY DOLLARS; if unpaid after thirty days the drawer is liable for THREE TIMES the check amount, with a MINIMUM OF $100, a $30 collection fee and court costs, and attorney fees in extraordinary or bad-faith cases.

Judgment interest, § 1-16-102: ten percent per year from the date of rendition until paid - EXCEPT that under § 1-16-102(b), if the judgment is founded on a contract and all parties agreed to a certain rate, the judgment rate corresponds to the contract. Put an interest rate in your lease and it will carry through to the judgment.

Attorney's fees in an eviction, § 1-21-1008(b): in a nonpayment case the court renders judgment for the rent found due "together with costs and attorney's fees as provided by the lease". There is no fee-shifting anywhere in Articles 10 or 12 of Title 1 chapter 21. If your lease does not provide for fees, you get costs only.

Small claims threshold, § 1-21-201: $6,000, exclusive of costs. This also gates § 1-21-1017(c), which switches off an entity's right to appear in an eviction without a lawyer if it seeks more than that amount.

Appeal and continuance security: § 1-21-1007 - no continuance for the tenant beyond TWO DAYS without a surety bond for accruing rent and costs; § 1-21-1014(b) - no stay on appeal unless a bond with two or more sureties is filed within FORTY-EIGHT HOURS after judgment, Sundays excepted; § 1-21-1015 - the judgment rent must also be deposited, and a missed later deposit means the appellate court SHALL affirm.

Penalties that run against you. § 1-21-1403(c): misusing the Article 14 unauthorized-occupant removal procedure exposes you to restoration of possession, actual costs and damages, STATUTORY DAMAGES EQUAL TO TRIPLE the fair market rental value for the period of wrongful removal, court costs and reasonable attorney fees. § 6-6-207: a $300 tax assessed against the building, the ground and the owner or agent when a permanent nuisance injunction issues. § 35-9-158(a)(ii): clandestine-lab remediation recoverable from an owner is capped at ONE PERCENT of assessed fair market value of the portion declared uninhabitable only if the owner neither knew nor with reasonable diligence could have known - otherwise uncapped. § 35-13-203: $750 for denying or interfering with an assistance animal in a rental. § 35-13-206(a): up to one year and $5,000 for seriously harming a service or assistance animal. § 35-9-506: $100 to $500 and three to six months for a fire-escape violation, with each month a separate offence. § 19-11-122(b): $1,000 for knowingly violating a Wyoming National Guard member's Servicemembers Civil Relief Act protections. § 17-16-1502(d): back fees and licence taxes plus EIGHTEEN PERCENT interest plus a $5,000 penalty plus audit expenses and attorney fees for an out-of-state entity that rents here without a certificate of authority.

Short-term letting: § 39-15-104(h) imposes a statewide lodging assessment of FIVE PERCENT on lodging services to guests staying less than thirty continuous days, and § 39-15-106(a) requires a sales tax licence, with a $60 fee for each new vendor.

THE PRACTICAL POINT. Because Wyoming caps so little, and because § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties reallocate any Article 12 duty by explicit written signed agreement, your lease is the only document that limits anything. Set your own figures, state them plainly, and keep them defensible - the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, § 40-12-105(a), still reaches a knowingly deceptive charge, and a charge nobody disclosed is the one that gets challenged.

title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant only a short list of statutory escapes, and two of the three are narrower than they look.

1. DOMESTIC ABUSE OR SEXUAL VIOLENCE — A DEFENCE, NOT A TERMINATION RIGHT. The Wyoming Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304, does not say a tenant “may terminate.” It says that in an action you bring to recover rent for breach of lease, the tenant has an affirmative defense and is not liable for rent for the period after vacating, if the court finds the elements by a preponderance of the evidence. Section 1-21-1303(a) covers a credible imminent threat of domestic abuse or sexual violence at the premises, demonstrated by medical, court or police evidence, with seven days’ written notice before vacating stating that reason. Section 1-21-1303(b) covers abuse that already occurred on premises you own or control, with the same seven days’ written notice, which must also state the date of the violence and that the tenant gave you medical, court or police evidence, and the violence must have occurred within sixty days before the notice unless hospitalization or seeking shelter or counseling made that impracticable. Section 1-21-1303(d) preserves your claim for rent accrued before the notice and vacating, and preserves a forcible entry and detainer action for that earlier nonpayment. Section 1-21-1303(c) separately bars terminating a tenancy based solely on victim status. Section 1-21-1304 makes none of it waivable in any lease or separate agreement — this is the one hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law, and § 1-21-1202(d)’s general power to modify duties sits in a different article and does not reach it.

2. YOUR FAILURE TO REPAIR — ONLY A COURT CAN TERMINATE. Wyoming has no repair-and-deduct, no rent withholding and no self-help termination for conditions. The only route is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206, and it is tightly gated. Subsection (a) makes the remedies available only to a renter who is in compliance with ALL of §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205 — which includes § 1-21-1204(a)(vi), being current on all payments — and only where you have not already lawfully terminated under § 1-21-1203(d). The sequence is: the tenant’s written § 1-21-1203(b) notice of the condition; a reasonable time; then a “notice to repair or correct condition” served by certified mail or in the § 1-21-1003 manner, which under § 1-21-1206(b) must recite the earlier notice, state the days elapsed and that they are a reasonable time, list the uncorrected conditions, demand correction, and warn that the renter will go to court if you do not commence reasonable corrective action within three days. Only then, under (c), may the renter sue in circuit court, where the summons sets your appearance at not less than three nor more than twenty days. On a showing of unreasonable refusal or failure to use due diligence, the court may award costs, damages and affirmative relief, including rent improperly retained or collected, and “a declaration terminating the rental agreement” or an order to make reasonable repairs. If the court terminates, § 1-21-1206(d) entitles the renter to a refund of the balance of rent and the deposit within thirty days and requires the renter to vacate no sooner than ten and no later than twenty days after termination. Note § 1-21-1203(e): you are not liable under the article for claims of mental suffering or anguish.

3. MILITARY SERVICE. The lease-termination right for servicemembers who receive permanent change of station or deployment orders is FEDERAL — the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, 50 U.S.C. § 3955 — and it applies in Wyoming regardless of state law. Wyoming adds a state layer for its own Guard: Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(a) gives members of the Wyoming National Guard ordered to active state service by the state or federal government for more than thirty consecutive days all protections afforded under the SCRA. Cite the whole section: § 19-11-122(b) makes a knowing violation of those protections a misdemeanor punishable by a fine up to $1,000, and (c) makes them a basis for an action or a defense in Wyoming courts, with (d) giving scheduling preference.

THE LANDLORD’S OWN EARLY EXIT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse to correct a condition and terminate the rental agreement where the cost of repairs exceeds an amount that would be reasonable in light of the rent charged, the nature of the rental property or the rental agreement. It is reactive, not free-standing: the notice runs from your receipt of the renter’s § 1-21-1203(b) notice of noncompliance, and you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving it and allow sufficient time to find substitute housing — no less than ten and no more than twenty days from the date of your notice. On termination you prorate the rent paid to the date the renter vacates and refund the balance plus any deposit due under § 1-21-1208.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT GIVE. There is no statutory termination right for a landlord’s fraudulent misrepresentation — the phrase appears only in Titles 31 and 33, on vehicle titles and real estate licensing. There is no provision forfeiting accrued rent because you omitted a prescribed sentence from the lease; Wyoming’s only mandatory lease recital is § 1-21-1207, and its sanction is not forfeiture of rent. There is no casualty or destruction-of-premises termination statute — “destroyed by fire,” “untenantable” and “destruction of the premises” return nothing — so fire, flood and casualty are purely lease matters and your lease must address them. There is no job-relocation, health-condition or senior-housing termination right, no early-termination fee cap, and no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy at all: “month-to-month,” “periodic tenancy” and “tenancy at will” appear nowhere in Titles 1 or 34. Do not assume a thirty-day rule; write the notice period into the lease.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no steam radiator cover law. There is no duty to cover or insulate a steam or hot-water radiator, no right for a tenant to request a cover, no mandatory lease rider, no annual written notice, no posting requirement and no penalty. The word 'radiator' appears exactly once in the entire Wyoming Statutes, in the Title 40 antifreeze-labeling definitions, and 'radiator cover', 'scald' and 'lease rider' return nothing at all. Nothing in the residential rental article (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) or anywhere else obliges you to install one, and nothing stops you from installing one voluntarily.

What does apply to heating equipment is general and modest. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires each owner and agent renting or leasing a residential rental unit to maintain it in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, and requires each unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water unless both parties otherwise agree in writing — with an express carve-out for seasonal rentals such as summer cabins not intended to have those amenities. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) puts 'electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water' on the closed list of ongoing owner duties. Those are duties to keep the heating working, not duties to make its surfaces safe to touch, and § 1-21-1202(c) switches the article off for breakage, malfunctions or conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter. Do not call this a warranty of habitability — the word 'habitability' appears nowhere in Wyoming's landlord-tenant article; describe the duties the statute actually imposes.

The fire and building codes are where any surface-protection requirement would come from, and Wyoming sets them by reference. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) directs the fire prevention and electrical safety council to adopt minimum fire standards not exceeding the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code and International Fuel Gas Code — that list is exhaustive and notably omits a plumbing code. Those codes, and whatever your city or county has adopted and enforces under the delegation in § 35-9-121(a), are the only place a guard, shield or clearance requirement for a hot surface could live. They are agency and local material and are outside this library; if the question matters for your building, ask your local building or fire official in writing.

The practical course. Because no statute requires covers, the exposure if a child is burned is ordinary premises-liability case law, which is also outside this corpus, and Wyoming gives you no statutory safe harbour against it. Section 1-21-1203(e) limits the damage somewhat — the owner is not liable under the whole article for claims of mental suffering — but that bars a category of claim under Article 12, not a negligence claim. So: if a unit has exposed steam or high-temperature radiators and you rent to families, fit covers or guards even though no law makes you, keep the receipt and the date, and inspect them. If a tenant asks for a cover, treat it as a maintenance request and answer in writing either way. And if a tenant with a disability asks for one as an accommodation, that is a different question governed by Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107 — § 40-26-107(c)(i) covers a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense, with an express rental carve-out allowing a restoration condition when it is reasonable to do so, and § 40-26-107(c)(ii) covers a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services. Do not refuse that request on the ground that no radiator statute exists.

title: Wyoming Has No Stigmatized Property Rule in Either Direction
bodyText: Wyoming has no stigmatized-property statute, and the point to grasp is that it is missing in BOTH directions. There is no duty to tell a prospective tenant that someone died, was murdered or died by suicide in the unit, that a former occupant had HIV or AIDS, or that the property has any other psychological history. But there is also no safe harbour — Wyoming has not enacted the provision most states pair with the silence, the one declaring that such a fact 'is not a material fact' and gives rise to no cause of action. 'Stigmatiz' and 'psychologically impacted' each return zero across the whole corpus, and so does 'not a material fact'. Wyoming also has no seller-disclosure act of any kind to anchor a residual duty. So you are in open common-law territory, and the cautious course is not silence-at-all-costs but honesty on request. Four things actually govern. First, if a licensed real estate professional is involved in your leasing, a statutory disclosure duty attaches and most landlords miss it because it sits in the licensing title. Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-311(a) provides that for the purposes of Article 3 of the Real Estate License Act a licensee is deemed to be working with the LANDLORD as an agent or intermediary pursuant to a written agreement, and with the TENANT as a customer unless otherwise provided in writing — which imports the Article 3 duties into residential leasing. Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-303(c) then says a licensee acting as a seller's agent owes the other side no duty 'except that a licensee shall disclose to any prospective buyer all adverse material facts actually known by the licensee', and that those facts 'may include adverse material facts pertaining to the title and the physical condition of the property, any material defects in the property and any environmental hazards affecting the property which are required by law to be disclosed.' Two things follow. The enumerated categories are physical and title facts, not psychological ones, which is the best Wyoming textual argument that a death in the unit is outside the duty — but the statute says 'may include', so the list is illustrative rather than closed, and nobody should treat that as settled. And § 33-28-303(c) adds that the licensee 'shall not perpetuate a material misrepresentation of the seller which the licensee knows or should know is false', so your manager cannot repeat a denial you have made. Note the licensing boundary: Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-103(a)(i) and (a)(vi) exempt an owner's own employees and on-site managers, so a self-managing landlord is not a licensee and § 33-28-303(c) does not reach them directly — it reaches the third-party brokerage. Second, a direct question changes everything. Wyoming has no statute authorising you to answer falsely, and the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leases: Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include property 'real, personal or mixed', there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110, and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct with an (a)(xv) catch-all. A knowing false answer to a direct question is the exposure, and it is a much bigger exposure than the non-disclosure. If you are asked, answer truthfully or say you will not discuss prior occupants, and apply the same policy to everyone. Pre-suit notice and a fifteen-day cure window apply under Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-109 and 40-12-102(a)(ix). Third, HIV and health status are a discrimination question, not a disclosure question. Wyoming has no HIV housing statute — 'HIV' with a word boundary returns zero in the corpus — but Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(a) and (b) bar discriminating in the rental of, or in the terms, conditions or privileges of, a dwelling because of the disability of the renter, of an individual residing or intending to reside there, or of any individual associated with them, and § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires reasonable accommodation. Never disclose a current or former tenant's health information to a prospective tenant and never let it bear on a rental decision; the federal Fair Housing Act treats HIV as a disability and that interpretation, which is outside this library, is the governing one. Fourth, the one Wyoming provision that does attach stigma to a property runs TOWARD you, not from you. Under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-158(d), where law enforcement discovering a clandestine laboratory operation finds no immediate and substantial threat, it must give WRITTEN NOTICE OF THE DISCOVERY TO THE OWNER, who then has ninety days to remediate to the § 35-9-153(h) standards, with an extension available on a good-faith showing under (d) and an appeal under (e) via Wyo. Stat. § 16-3-114. An innocent owner's remediation cost is capped at one percent of assessed value by § 35-9-158(a)(ii); a knowing owner is uncapped and faces a lien and sheriff's sale under (a)(iii). That notice is a duty to clean, not a duty to disclose, but once you have it you know a fact about the physical condition of the property, which is squarely inside the § 33-28-303(c) category — so disclose it. Practical rule: adopt one written policy on prior-occupant questions, apply it to every applicant, disclose anything physical you know, never lie, and keep health information out of it entirely.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or a Refrigerator
bodyText:
Wyoming does not require you to supply a stove, a range, an oven or a refrigerator, and has no rule about who maintains one if you do supply it beyond what your own lease says. The word "stove" appears three times in all of Wyoming law — in the agriculture, insurance and taxation titles — and never in a housing context; "refrigerat-" appears thirteen times, the closest being the Condominium Ownership Act's list of central services in a condominium's common elements, which is about a building's central plant, not a tenant's kitchen; "oven" as a standalone word appears nowhere; and "cooking" appears eleven times, none of it a landlord duty.

What Wyoming does say about appliances is the opposite of a supply mandate. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) sets out the owner's duties, "[t]o protect the physical health and safety of the renter": (i) not to rent the unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy; (ii) to maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition; (iii) to "[m]aintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water"; and (iv) to "[m]aintain other appliances and facilities AS SPECIFICALLY CONTRACTED in the rental agreement."

Read paragraphs (iii) and (iv) together, because the structure is the whole answer. Paragraph (iii) is a closed ongoing list of four systems — electrical, plumbing, heating, hot and cold water — and a stove and a refrigerator are on none of them. Paragraph (iv) is the only route by which any other appliance becomes your responsibility, and it is opt-in: the duty arises only "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement". So in Wyoming you create your own appliance duty by writing it down, and you have none if you do not. That cuts both ways and is worth being deliberate about. A lease that lists "refrigerator, range, dishwasher, microwave" under a heading like "Appliances Provided" may well be the specific contracting that § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) refers to, and if it is, you have taken on a maintenance duty enforceable through the § 1-21-1203(b) notice sequence and ultimately through § 1-21-1206. If you mean to supply an appliance without warranting it, say so in terms: that it is provided as a convenience, in its present condition, that Landlord does not undertake to maintain, repair or replace it, and that the parties do not intend it to be specifically contracted under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv).

Two limits on how far you can push that. First, the floor underneath everything is § 1-21-1202(a): each owner and agent renting a residential rental unit "shall maintain that unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation", with operational electrical, heating and plumbing and hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed in writing by both parties — and the proviso at the end of that subsection exempts seasonal rentals such as summer cabins not intended to have those amenities. A missing stove is unlikely to make a unit unfit; a stove you supplied that leaks gas is a safety problem, not an appliance problem, and § 1-21-1202(c) only disapplies the article to breakages and malfunctions that do NOT materially affect physical health or safety. Second, § 1-21-1203(c) relieves you of any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse — so a tenant who ruins a supplied appliance is not your problem.

YOU CAN ALSO MOVE THE DUTY THE OTHER WAY. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties", and Article 12 contains no anti-waiver provision. The conditions are cumulative — explicit, written, signed — and because § 1-21-1202(d) demands a signed writing, an oral Wyoming tenancy shifts nothing even though § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) recognises oral rental agreements. So you may put the maintenance of a tenant-used appliance on the tenant, but only in a signed writing that says so plainly.

IF THE TENANT BRINGS THEIR OWN. Wyoming has no acknowledgment form of the California kind and no notice-back right. Handle it in the lease: say the appliance is the tenant's property, that the tenant maintains it and bears the cost, that the tenant is responsible for any damage it causes including water damage from an ice maker or a washer, that the tenant removes it at the end of the tenancy, and that anything left behind is dealt with under the lease and Wyoming's abandoned-property rules.

THE PRACTICAL COURSE. Decide for each appliance whether you want the duty, then write the answer down. An appliance list with no words about responsibility is the worst of both worlds, because § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) may read it as the contract that creates the duty. See also the library's appliance-exclusion rows for the clause language.

All of this applies only to a "residential rental unit" as Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

title: Wyoming Has No Student Housing Rules, Which Creates One Real Question
bodyText:
Wyoming has no student-housing law. There is no licensing or certification scheme for landlords who rent to students, no student-housing registration, no special deposit, lease-term, or disclosure rule, no regulation of per-bed leases or roommate arrangements, and no exemption or special treatment for housing near the University of Wyoming or a community college. The phrase "student housing" does appear in the Wyoming statutes, but only in the state capital-construction provisions in Titles 9 and 21, which exclude student housing, student unions, and auxiliary services areas from the square-footage formulas used to fund major maintenance of university and community college buildings. Those are appropriations rules about state facilities; they say nothing about a private landlord and a student tenant.

So the ordinary Residential Rental Property Act governs, and renting to students is renting. But there is one genuine question Wyoming's definitions create, and you should decide how to handle it rather than discover it in court.

Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" as "a renter's principal place of residence," including appurtenances, grounds, common areas and facilities held out for the occupancy of residential renters generally and any other area or facility provided to the renter in the rental agreement, and excluding a mobile home lot or recreational property rented on an occasional basis. The whole Act - the habitability duties in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1202 and 1-21-1203, the deposit-accounting rules and deadlines in § 1-21-1208, the nonrefundable-deposit disclosure in § 1-21-1207, the abandoned-property procedure in § 1-21-1210, and the renter's remedies in § 1-21-1206 - hangs on that phrase. A student who lives in your unit year-round and has no other home is plainly covered. A student who occupies during the academic year, keeps a permanent address at a parent's house, votes and registers a car there, and goes home each summer is a harder case, and a literal reading of "principal place of residence" could put that tenancy outside the Act altogether.

Do not try to exploit that. Treating a student tenancy as outside the Act would mean no § 1-21-1208 obligations for you, which sounds attractive until you consider the other side: it would also mean the Act's protections for owners do not apply either, including the abandoned-property safe harbor in § 1-21-1210 that lets you dispose of leftover belongings after a seven-day notice, the mental-suffering bar in § 1-21-1203(e), the ten-percent interest and residual damage liability in § 1-21-1211(b), and the storage-loss disclaimer in § 1-21-1210(c). Losing the § 1-21-1210 procedure in a building that empties out every May would be a genuine problem, because end-of-term abandoned property is exactly the situation that procedure solves. The cautious and practical course is to comply with the Act for every residential tenancy you have, student or not, and to write the lease so it does not depend on the answer. Note also that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets the parties assign or modify duties in the article by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, which gives you a lawful way to allocate specific responsibilities without betting on a definitional argument.

Everything else about student rentals is pure lease drafting, because no statute fills any of it in. Wyoming has no rule on joint and several liability among roommates, so say expressly that each tenant is jointly and severally liable for all rent and all damage, not merely for a share. Wyoming has no guarantor statute, so if you take a parent co-signer, make the guaranty a signed written obligation in its own right and say it survives renewals and holdovers. Wyoming has no rule on subletting or assignment, so state whether a summer sublet is permitted and on what conditions - and remember Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(v) caps occupants at the number "specified in the rental agreement," so if your lease names no number you have no occupancy ceiling to enforce against an extra summer roommate. Noise and party complaints run through Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(ii), which prohibits a renter from interfering with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property, and a violation of § 1-21-1205 is an eviction ground under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) on the ordinary three-day notice to leave the premises under § 1-21-1003.

One trap specific to this market: age. Under Wyo. Stat. § 14-1-101(a) a person reaches the age of majority at eighteen, and incoming first-year students are sometimes seventeen. A lease signed by a minor is voidable at the minor's election under ordinary contract law, so do not sign one without an adult co-signer who is primarily, not merely secondarily, obligated.

Flagged and not resolved: the University of Wyoming and community college boards of trustees set their own housing rules for institutionally owned housing, and Wyoming municipalities regulate occupancy, unrelated-persons limits, parking, and nuisance by ordinance in the towns where student rentals cluster. Institutional regulations and local ordinances are outside this review.

title: Voucher Inspections and a Tenant Who Refuses Entry
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute about subsidized housing inspections - nothing letting you refuse a voucher tenancy because of the program's inspection, and nothing giving you a special remedy when a subsidized tenant refuses to let the inspector in. The phrases "housing choice voucher," "subsidized housing" and "rental assistance" do not appear in the landlord-tenant statutes at all. Two separate questions sit under this topic, and Wyoming answers them differently. Whether you must take a voucher at all: Wyoming does not protect source of income. The Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(a), bars refusing to sell or rent, refusing to negotiate, or otherwise making a dwelling unavailable to an individual because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin, and § 40-26-103(b) bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental on those same grounds. That list is closed and does not include participation in a rental assistance program, so declining to enter a voucher tenancy - including because you do not want the program's inspection and contract - is not a Wyoming fair housing violation. Three cautions on that. First, the reason has to be real: if "I don't take vouchers" is a stand-in for a refusal based on disability, familial status or another listed ground, it is a violation, and Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-114 directs that the enforcing authority's substantive rules impose obligations, rights and remedies the same as federal fair housing regulations. Second, if the applicant has a disability, the separate duty in Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107 still applies on its own terms. Third, one Wyoming provision does mention public assistance, and you should not step on it: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i) makes it an offense, whether or not the person acts under color of law, to intentionally intimidate or interfere with an individual BY FORCE OR THREAT OF FORCE because of that individual's race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin or status with respect to marriage or public assistance, where the individual is or has been renting, occupying or negotiating for the rental or occupation of a dwelling; § 40-26-144(b) adds that it is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with an individual in the exercise or enjoyment of any right granted or protected by that chapter, and § 40-26-144(c) makes an offense under either subsection a misdemeanor. So quietly declining a voucher application is one thing; threatening or strong-arming a voucher holder is another, and that one is a crime. Fourth, LOCAL ORDINANCE: a Wyoming municipality could add source-of-income protection by ordinance; that is flagged and not resolved here. What happens once you are in the program is federal, not state: the housing quality inspection, the re-inspection, abatement of the housing assistance payment and termination of the HAP contract are creatures of the federal program documents you sign. FEDERAL: Section 8 housing choice voucher program, 42 U.S.C. s 1437f and 24 C.F.R. part 982. Wyoming law adds nothing and takes nothing away. Whether you can act when the tenant blocks entry: yes, but only on the ordinary track. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) says no renter shall unreasonably deny access to, refuse entry to or withhold consent to enter the residential rental unit to the owner, agent or manager for the purpose of making repairs to or inspecting the unit, and showing the unit for rent or sale. Read that list of persons carefully: it names the owner, the agent and the manager. A housing authority inspector arriving alone is not within the statute's words, so schedule the inspection so that you or your agent are present and are the ones seeking entry - then a refusal is a refusal of entry to you, which is what the statute reaches. A violation of § 1-21-1205 is a listed ground for a forcible entry and detainer action under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi), and a tenant in breach of § 1-21-1205 also loses the renter's remedies in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206(a). But there is no shortcut: you still serve the three-day notice to quit required by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 and proceed on the ordinary timetable, with service of summons not less than three nor more than twelve days before trial under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1004. Wyoming has nothing resembling the two-refusals-in-thirty-days emergency track some states give subsidized housing. Practical course: put the entry and inspection terms in the lease in writing, including that the tenant will permit inspections required by any housing assistance program and will cooperate with scheduling; give written notice of each inspection date and keep the proof; attend the inspection yourself or send your agent; and if the tenant refuses twice, document both refusals in writing before you serve the notice to quit, since "unreasonably" in § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) is the word you will have to prove.

title: No Subsidy Rent Proration Rule in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute reducing rent when part of a rental becomes uninhabitable, and no rule at all about how a housing subsidy figures into such a reduction. There is no automatic abatement, no proportional-to-the-affected-area formula, and nothing saying whether a reduction is calculated on the tenant's share or on the total contract rent including the subsidy-paid portion. Wyoming landlord-tenant law uses the word "prorated" exactly once, and not for this: if you terminate the rental agreement because the cost of repairs would exceed what is reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property, "the rent paid shall be prorated to the date the renter vacates the unit and any balance shall be refunded to the renter along with any deposit due in accordance with W.S. 1-21-1208" (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1203(d)). That is a refund of prepaid rent on termination, not a reduction for a unit that is partly unusable, and it makes no mention of a subsidy. The only route to a rent reduction in Wyoming runs through the courts and only after the tenant has followed the statutory notice chain: the tenant who is current on all payments gives you written notice of the condition and the remedial action requested (§ 1-21-1203(b)); after a reasonable time without correction or dispute the tenant serves a "notice to repair or correct condition" (§ 1-21-1206(b)); and only then may the tenant sue in circuit court, where on a showing of unreasonable refusal to correct or failure to use due diligence the court may award "costs, damages and affirmative relief," and "[d]amages awarded to the renter may include rent improperly retained or collected" (§ 1-21-1206(c)). If the court terminates the agreement, the tenant gets the balance of rent and the deposit within 30 days and must vacate between 10 and 20 days after termination (§ 1-21-1206(d)). Nothing in that chain distinguishes a subsidized tenancy. Two things fill the gap. First, the subsidy contract. If you have signed a housing assistance payments contract with a public housing agency, that contract and the federal program rules, not Wyoming law, decide whether the agency abates its share after a failed inspection and what happens to the tenant's share — and an abated subsidy payment is generally not collectible from the tenant. Read your HAP contract and the agency's notices; this review covers Wyoming statutes only and does not resolve federal program terms. Second, your lease. Wyoming lets any duty or obligation under the Residential Rental Property article be assigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties (§ 1-21-1202(d)), so if you want a rent-adjustment mechanism for a partly unusable unit, write one — but note that the article does not apply to breakage or malfunctions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of an ordinary renter (§ 1-21-1202(c)), so most minor problems are not habitability matters at all. One more Wyoming fact worth knowing: source of income is not a protected class under the Wyoming Fair Housing Act, whose classes are race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 40-26-103), so state law does not compel you to accept a voucher — but a city or county ordinance might, and local ordinances were not reviewed here.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about late fees on subsidized rent, and in fact has no residential late-fee statute at all. There is no cap on the amount, no mandatory grace period, no notice requirement before a late fee may be charged, and no rule barring a late fee on the portion of rent a housing authority is responsible for paying. The phrase "late fee" appears nowhere in Title 1 and nowhere in Title 15. Wyoming has not adopted the Housing Choice Voucher program into its own statutes either -- the phrase returns nothing, and neither does any reference to the federal housing act that creates it.

That means two things for a Wyoming landlord with a voucher tenant. First, whatever rules govern the late-payment side of the subsidy come from the federal program and from your Housing Assistance Payments contract with the public housing authority, not from Wyoming law. The HAP contract is a contract you signed; read it, because it will typically forbid charging the family for the authority's share and will fix what you may charge the family for a late payment of the family's own portion. FEDERAL: Section 8 housing choice voucher program, 42 U.S.C. § 1437f, and the HUD regulations and HAP contract issued under it, govern that relationship. Second, nothing in Wyoming law does the work for you, so if your lease does not provide for a late fee, you do not have one.

The practical rule is the one the federal program would impose anyway, and it is simply sound: charge a late fee only on the tenant's own share of the rent, and only after the tenant's share is actually late. A fee computed on the full contract rent when the tenant owes only a fraction of it is both likely to breach your HAP contract and hard to defend. Keep the tenant's portion stated separately in the lease and on every ledger and notice, so the amount you say is overdue is the amount the tenant actually owes.

This matters for eviction too. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) a forcible entry and detainer action lies "after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires a written notice to quit served at least three days before you file. If your notice demands the full contract rent when the authority's payment is what is missing, the tenant has not failed to pay and your notice overstates the debt. Serve a notice for the tenant's share only.

One more Wyoming point, because it comes up alongside voucher tenancies. Source of income is not a protected class in Wyoming. The Wyoming Fair Housing Act lists only race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin (Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103), so Wyoming law does not require you to accept a voucher. But once you do accept one, you are in the federal program and bound by its terms, and the fair housing classes that do exist apply to how you treat a voucher tenant exactly as they apply to anyone else. A local ordinance could add a source-of-income protection; ordinances are outside what this library verifies, so check the municipality.
