Practical course: state the tenant's portion of rent as a separate, named figure in the lease; state the late fee as a fee on that portion; say when it accrues; and never serve a three-day notice for an amount that includes the authority's share.

title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Substandard Rentals in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no substandard-rental receivership statute. Nothing in Wyoming law requires a city or county to act when a two-or-more-unit rental violates a habitability or building standard, and nothing authorizes a court to install a receiver to collect your rents and fix the building. There is no Wyoming counterpart to the Nevada scheme. The word "dilapidated" appears nowhere in the statutes, and the receivership statutes that do exist are about banks, insurers, corporations and judgment enforcement, not housing.

Four things can still happen to a bad Wyoming rental, and you should know each of them.

1. Municipal dangerous-building power. Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-103(a)(xxvi) empowers the governing body of a city or town to "[p]rovide for the repair, removal or destruction of any dangerous building or enclosure." Related powers in the same subsection let a municipality prescribe construction standards and provide for inspection (paragraph (xxv)) and cause the destruction or removal of a building constructed or repaired in violation of an ordinance (paragraph (xxvii)). The statute is an enabling grant — the actual procedure, notice and cost recovery live in the city's ordinance, which is outside this library.

2. County nuisance abatement. Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-101(a)(viii) lets a board of county commissioners declare and abate a nuisance it determines threatens health or safety. The procedure at Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-115 is specific and fast: the board must first adopt standards by resolution (§ 18-2-115(a)); it may then issue a written order describing the nuisance "with specificity" and the steps required for abatement, filed with the clerk of the district court and served under the Wyoming Rules of Civil Procedure "upon the owner or occupant," with a copy posted conspicuously on the property (§ 18-2-115(b)); the owner or occupant has twenty (20) days to file an answer with the court clerk and serve the board (§ 18-2-115(c)); with no answer the order becomes final, and with an answer the court holds a hearing within twenty (20) days and, if it sustains the order, fixes a time for enforcement (§ 18-2-115(d)); appeal lies under the Wyoming Rules of Appellate Procedure (§ 18-2-115(e)). Calendar the twenty days the moment you are served.

3. Fire and building code enforcement. The state council on fire prevention and electrical safety adopts the International Fire Code, International Building Code and related codes by rule under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i), and a municipality or county may assume enforcement authority under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121, which also provides that a more stringent local code prevails (§ 35-9-121(b)) and requires a local appeals board that may grant variances (§ 35-9-121(d)), appealable to the council and then to district court (§ 35-9-121(e)).

4. Your tenant's own remedies — the real risk in Wyoming. The enforcement pressure in Wyoming comes from the renter, not from a receiver. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a) requires you to keep the unit reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy, maintain common areas, and maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. A renter who is current on all payments and has reasonable cause supported by evidence serves written notice under § 1-21-1203(b), by certified mail or in the manner of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003, specifying the condition and the remedial action requested; within a reasonable time you must either commence corrective action or notify the renter in writing that you dispute the claim. If you do neither, § 1-21-1206(b) lets the renter serve a "notice to repair or correct condition" that must state you have three (3) days to commence reasonable corrective action, and § 1-21-1206(c) then lets the renter sue in circuit court, where the court endorses on the summons a response time of not less than three (3) nor more than twenty (20) days. On a showing of unreasonable refusal or failure to use due diligence, the court may award costs, damages — expressly including "rent improperly retained or collected" — and affirmative relief, which "may include a declaration terminating the rental agreement, or an order directing the owner to make reasonable repairs." A court-ordered repair order is the closest thing Wyoming has to the receivership other states use, and it is the tenant who gets it, not the city.

Two defenses worth knowing. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) says you are not required to correct a condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees by inappropriate use or misuse. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d) lets you refuse to repair and terminate the agreement if repair costs exceed what is reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property — but you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the noncompliance notice and give no less than ten (10) nor more than twenty (20) days to find substitute housing, prorate the rent to the day the renter vacates, and refund the balance with any deposit due under § 1-21-1208. And § 1-21-1203(e) bars claims under the whole article for mental suffering or anguish.

Finally, receivership is not impossible in Wyoming, just not a housing tool. Wyo. Stat. § 1-33-101(a) lists the cases in which a district court may appoint a receiver — fraudulent purchase, a creditor subjecting property to a claim, a co-owner where property is in danger of being lost or materially injured, a mortgagee foreclosing where the property is in danger or the debt undersecured, enforcement of a judgment, corporate insolvency, and the catch-all at § 1-33-101(a)(viii), "[i]n all other cases where receivers have been appointed by courts of equity." Habitability is not on that list. The realistic receivership risk to a neglected Wyoming rental is your LENDER invoking § 1-33-101(a)(iv), not the city.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: No Wyoming statute addresses a lease clause that passes a property tax increase to a residential tenant. Wyoming neither authorizes nor forbids one, and it imposes none of the conditions other states attach. There is no requirement that the clause state the tenant's exact percentage share, and no requirement that you refund a share of any later abatement — Massachusetts imposes both (Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15C) and Wyoming has no counterpart. There is also no rent-increase notice statute in Wyoming at all, so no notice period governs the charge; whatever notice the lease gives is the notice the tenant gets. Because the whole subject is contract, the lease has to carry the entire arrangement: the base year, the tenant's share as a stated percentage or fraction, what evidence you will give, when payment is due, and whether a reduction or refund is credited back. A term you did not write is a term you do not have. Two Wyoming points are worth knowing. First, the deposit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit be applied on termination 'to the payment of accrued rent, damages to the residential rental unit beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit to the condition at the beginning of the rental agreement and to other costs provided by any contract.' That last phrase is what makes an unpaid tax-escalation charge deductible from the deposit — but only if the lease provides for the charge in the first place. Make the lease say the charge is additional rent, and the deduction follows; leave it out and you have nothing to deduct, because the statute does not supply the obligation. Second, the increase you can pass on is capped for most houses. Under Wyo. Stat. § 39-11-105(a)(xliii) a single family residential structure is exempt from tax on any assessed value above the prior year's assessed value plus four percent, and Wyo. Stat. § 39-11-105(a)(xliv) does the same for the improved land associated with it. Neither exemption depends on the owner living there — 'single family residential structure' is defined in subparagraph (D) as a house, modular home, mobile home, townhouse or condominium that is a privately owned single family dwelling unit — so your single-family rental gets the cap too. The cap drops away in two situations: where the increase is attributable to structural changes including new construction or additions (§ 39-11-105(a)(xliii)(B)(I)), and where the owner acquired the property during the prior calendar year (§ 39-11-105(a)(xliii)(B)(II), (a)(xliv)(B)), with listed exceptions for transfers between spouses, by court order, to a trust for the prior owner, or to an entity the prior owner owns. So the year after you buy a rental, expect a full-value jump and expect your tenant to feel it. One exemption you cannot pass through as a saving: the long-term homeowner exemption at Wyo. Stat. § 39-11-105(a)(xlv) requires the claimant to occupy the property as a primary residence for at least eight months of the year, so a rented unit does not qualify.

title: No Wyoming Cable or Satellite Access Law for Rental Buildings
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute giving a tenant a right of access to cable television, satellite or broadband service, no bar on taking payment from a provider for access to your tenants, no rule against charging subscribers and non-subscribers different rent, and no mandatory-access or forced-wiring provision for multifamily buildings. A search of all 44 Wyoming titles, the constitution and both the 2025 and 2026 session laws found none: "satellite dish," "satellite antenna" and "direct broadcast" return zero hits anywhere, and no provision anywhere ties cable, broadband or telecommunications to a landlord, a tenant or a multiple dwelling.

What Wyoming does have about cable is not about you. The handful of references are elsewhere: Wyo. Stat. § 34-24-102(a)(xvii), the Unclaimed Property Act's definition of "utility," which includes a person transmitting communications including cable television; Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-131, which governs a municipality's cable franchise and franchise fee and exempts a holder of a federal cable franchise under 47 U.S.C. § 541 from parts of the section; Wyo. Stat. § 37-15-413, which limits a city or town from entering an exclusive agreement for telecommunications or broadband internet access service; and various pole-attachment and underground-facility provisions in Title 37. None of them reaches a private landlord.

So the lease decides, with one important federal exception. You may choose which providers you let into the building, negotiate a bulk or marketing agreement, require conduit and wiring to be installed to your specification, charge for installation and restoration, require insurance and indemnity from the installer, and prohibit holes through exterior walls and roof penetrations. There is no Wyoming rule against any of that.

The federal exception matters, so do not write around it. FEDERAL: the Federal Communications Commission's over-the-air reception devices rule, 47 C.F.R. § 1.4000, generally preempts a lease term or rule that unreasonably delays, prevents or increases the cost of installing, maintaining or using a satellite dish one metre or less in diameter, a television antenna, or a fixed wireless antenna, in an area within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony, patio or fenced yard the tenant alone uses. It does NOT give the tenant any right in common areas, on the roof, on an exterior wall, or anywhere else outside the tenant's exclusive space, and it does not override safety and historic-preservation restrictions that are narrowly tailored. The practical consequence: you may ban a dish on the roof or the building's exterior wall, but a flat ban on a small dish on a tenant's own balcony is likely unenforceable. Federal regulation is outside this library, so confirm the current text of the rule before you rely on the detail.

The Wyoming points that do touch installation. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(i) a renter may not intentionally or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the unit, or knowingly permit any person to do so — which covers an installer drilling through siding. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(viii) the renter must remove property placed in the unit and clean it to the condition it was in at the beginning of the tenancy, which supports a removal-and-restoration term. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) you are not required to correct a condition the renter or the renter's guests or invitees caused by inappropriate use or misuse, which covers damage done by the tenant's chosen installer. And under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) you maintain "other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement" — so if you list wiring, a dish or an internet service as included, you have taken on a duty to maintain it. Be deliberate about that.

If you resell or bundle service, check the utility rules first. If you meter or make direct sales of a utility commodity to tenants, Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) withdraws the landlord's public-utility exemption, and the carve-out at (H)(VIII) and (IX) is for water only, as fee-free allocation. Bundled internet billed as a separate charge is a different animal from reselling electricity, but the same instinct applies: a charge you collect for a third party's service invites scrutiny, so disclose it in the lease as a separate itemised amount rather than folding it into rent.

Two closing cautions. A rent differential between subscribers and non-subscribers is not barred in Wyoming, but if it correlates with a protected class it becomes a fair housing problem under Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145. And local ordinances are unresolved: Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), municipalities do franchise cable under § 15-1-131, and nothing preempts a local building or access requirement.

title: Wyoming Has No Tenancy at Will, Only Tenancy by Sufferance
bodyText: Wyoming does not recognise a tenancy at will, and the phrases "tenancy at will," "estate at will," "periodic tenancy" and "tenancy from" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. Wyoming abolished implied tenancies outright. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides: "In this state there shall not exist the relations of landlord and tenant, by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance. Upon the expiration of a term created by lease, either verbal or written, there shall be no implied renewal of the same, for any period of time whatever, either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent for or during any period of such holding over. Such holding over by the tenant and acceptance of rent by the landlord shall constitute only a tenancy by sufferance, with the rights, duties, obligations and incidents of such tenancy." Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 completes it: "No lease which shall have expired by its own limitation shall be again renewed except by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto, whether the original lease be written or verbal. Nor shall any other tenancy than that by sufferance exist after the termination of the original lease, unless created as aforesaid, by express contract in writing." Read those together and three practical consequences follow, and all three favour you. First, accepting rent after the term expires does NOT renew the lease or create a month-to-month tenancy in Wyoming, which is the opposite of the rule in most states. You can take the money without extending the tenancy. Second, there is no such thing in Wyoming as a tenancy that rolls over by default; the only thing that exists after expiry is a tenancy by sufferance, and the only way to get a real renewed tenancy is an express contract in writing signed by both parties, even where the original lease was oral. If you want a month-to-month arrangement after the fixed term, you must sign one; do not assume a holdover clause in the expired lease does it unless it is drafted as an express written renewal both parties signed. Third, because a holdover tenant is only a tenant at sufferance, you do not owe them a thirty-day notice — Wyoming has no statutory notice period for ending any tenancy. There is no provision anywhere in Title 1 or Title 34 setting a notice period to terminate a tenancy, and none setting a notice period for a rent increase either. What you must give instead is the eviction notice. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows a forcible entry and detainer proceeding "Against tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due," and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires you to notify the party to leave the premises by written notice served at least three (3) days before you commence the action, by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found. So the practical sequence against a holdover is: the term expires, the tenant becomes a tenant at sufferance, you serve the three-day notice to quit, and after three days you file. Note that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d), which lets Article 12 duties be modified by explicit signed written agreement, does NOT reach this — it is confined to Title 1, Chapter 21, Article 12, so it is no authority for shortening or waiving the § 1-21-1003 notice. Be careful with the two matching-but-different writing thresholds. Wyo. Stat. § 1-23-105(a)(v) makes an agreement void unless in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged where it is a lease of real property for more than ONE (1) year. Separately, Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102 excepts from the definition of "conveyance" only leases "not exceeding three (3) years," so a lease for more than THREE years falls inside the recording act at Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-1-120 and 34-1-121. One year for the writing, three years for recording — do not merge them. Finally, be clear what a tenancy by sufferance does and does not change. The holdover remains liable for compensation for occupancy, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(b) still lets you apply the deposit to damage and leaves the renter liable for damage beyond it plus interest at ten percent (10%) per annum on any unpaid amounts. Whether the Article 12 duties in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211 continue to bind you during a sufferance tenancy is not settled by the statutes — the article applies to a "residential rental unit," defined in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) as the renter's principal place of residence, which a holdover's home still is, so the cautious course is to assume habitability and deposit duties continue to apply until possession is actually returned.

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText:
Wyoming has no landlord-tenant bankruptcy rule. No statute says what a tenant's filing does to the lease, whether a bankruptcy clause in your lease is enforceable, how the automatic stay interacts with a forcible entry and detainer action, or what you may do with the deposit. Bankruptcy itself is federal and the Bankruptcy Code supplies all of that. In broad terms, FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362 imposes an automatic stay the moment the petition is filed, and it stops an eviction in its tracks; § 362(b)(22) and § 362(l) create a narrow exception and a certification procedure where you already held a judgment for possession before the filing; § 365 governs whether the trustee or debtor assumes or rejects an unexpired lease of residential real property; and § 525(a) restricts discriminatory treatment by governmental units. Those provisions are outside the scope of this Wyoming research and they are unforgiving of mistakes. The moment you learn of a filing, stop every collection step — no demand letters, no late notices, no lockouts, no filing or advancing an eviction — and get bankruptcy counsel before you do anything else, including before you apply a deposit against a prepetition balance, because a setoff can itself violate the stay.

Where Wyoming law does bite is on what you can collect afterwards, and the single most important provision is Wyo. Stat. § 1-20-109. Wyoming has opted out of the federal exemption schedule: 'In accordance with 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(1), the exemptions from property of the estate in bankruptcy provided in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d) are not authorized in cases where Wyoming law is applicable on the date of the filing of the petition and the debtor's domicile has been located in Wyoming for the one hundred eighty (180) days immediately preceding the date of the filing of the petition or for a longer portion of the one hundred eighty (180) day period than in any other place.' So a Wyoming tenant uses the Wyoming exemptions below, not the federal list, and those are the figures to run before you spend money chasing a judgment.

The Wyoming exemptions a judgment for unpaid rent will meet. Section 1-20-101 gives every resident a homestead not exceeding one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000.00) in value, exempt from execution and attachment arising from any debt, contract or civil obligation; § 1-20-102(a) makes it operative only while occupied as a homestead by the owner or the person entitled to it or their family, and § 1-20-102(b) gives each of two or more persons who jointly own and occupy the same residence a separate exemption, so a couple can shelter two hundred thousand dollars. Section 1-20-104 is broad about what counts: a house on a lot or other lands of any number of acres, or a house trailer or other movable home, whether or not it has wheels or rests on immovable support. Section 1-20-105 exempts necessary wearing apparel up to two thousand dollars ($2,000.00), excluding jewelry other than wedding rings. Section 1-20-106(a) exempts the family bible, pictures and school books; a cemetery lot; furniture, bedding, provisions and other household articles the debtor selects up to four thousand dollars ($4,000.00) in all, with a separate exemption for each of two or more persons occupying the same residence; the value in a motor vehicle up to five thousand dollars ($5,000.00); and not more than three (3) firearms up to three thousand dollars ($3,000.00) in all with up to one thousand (1,000) rounds of ammunition each. Section 1-20-106(b) adds four thousand dollars ($4,000.00) for the tools, team, implements or stock in trade of a trade or business, or the same amount for a professional's library, instruments and implements. Value is fixed under § 1-20-106(c) by three (3) disinterested appraisers summoned and sworn by the levying officer. Section 1-20-110 exempts retirement funds and accounts from execution, attachment, garnishment or any other legal process, though § 1-20-110(b) withdraws that protection from a contribution made to a retirement plan within ninety (90) days before the individual files for bankruptcy, and § 1-20-111 exempts contributions to a qualified medical savings account. Two limits run your way: § 1-20-108(a) denies these exemptions against a debt for the purchase money of the property itself, and § 1-20-108(b) requires anyone claiming them to be a bona fide resident of Wyoming.

Garnishment, if you get that far. Both the post-judgment writ under § 1-15-408(b) and continuing garnishment under § 1-15-511(a) cap the reachable portion of aggregate disposable earnings at the lesser of twenty-five percent (25%) of the debtor's disposable earnings for that week, or the amount by which those weekly disposable earnings exceed thirty (30) times the federal minimum hourly wage under the Fair Labor Standards Act. 'Disposable earnings' under § 1-15-401 means what remains after deducting all amounts required by law to be withheld. Section 1-15-408(a) extends the same exemption to money the debtor deposited in a financial-institution account within twenty (20) calendar days before service of a writ on the account, on the day of service, or within ten (10) business days after — so you cannot garnish the bank account to capture wages you could not garnish from the employer. An income withholding order for child support takes priority over any other garnishment.

Finally, understand what you do not have. Wyoming gives a residential landlord no lien on a tenant's goods — the phrase 'landlord's lien' appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and the only landlord-related lien, Wyo. Stat. § 29-2-105, runs against you, letting a contractor who improved the premises at a tenant's request reach your interest where you agreed to pay or specifically authorised the work. Your claim for unpaid rent is an ordinary unsecured claim, and your only property remedy is the abandoned-property procedure in § 1-21-1210, which operates only after you have regained lawful possession and which the automatic stay will suspend. Section 1-21-1211(b) keeps the renter liable for damages beyond the deposit with interest at ten percent (10%) per annum, but that too is just an unsecured claim in a bankruptcy. The practical conclusion is to screen well and to require a written guaranty where you are uneasy, remembering that under § 1-23-105(a)(ii) a promise to answer for another's debt must be in writing and subscribed by the guarantor.

title: Tenant Information in Wyoming - No Confidentiality Rule, But a Real Breach Duty
bodyText:
Wyoming has no tenant-confidentiality statute. Nothing bars you from disclosing a tenant's, former tenant's or applicant's information, there is no consent requirement, no list of protected data, and no exception framework like Oregon's. Searching for any connection between a tenant and confidentiality returns nothing in either direction. Wyoming's Safe Homes Act imposes no confidentiality duty either — it gives a victim of domestic abuse or sexual violence an affirmative defence to a rent claim, nothing more. That absence is not permission to be careless, because a different Wyoming law does apply to you, and most landlords do not know it.

Wyoming's data breach notification law reaches landlords squarely. Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-502(a) applies to "[a]n individual or commercial entity that conducts business in Wyoming and that owns or licenses computerized data that includes personal identifying information about a resident of Wyoming." If you keep tenant applications, screening results or payment details in a computer, a spreadsheet, a cloud property-management system or an email account, that is you — whether you own one house or two hundred units, and whether or not you are incorporated.

What counts as personal identifying information is defined by a chain you have to follow. Section 40-12-501(a)(vii) defines it as a person's first name or first initial and last name together with one or more of the unredacted data elements listed in Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-901(b)(iii) through (xiv). Those elements are: social security number; driver's license number; an account, credit card or debit card number in combination with a security code, access code or password allowing access to a financial account; a tribal identification card; a federal or state government issued identification card; shared secrets or security tokens used for data based authentication; a username or email address in combination with a password or a security question and answer permitting access to an online account; a birth or marriage certificate; medical information; health insurance information; unique biometric data; and an individual taxpayer identification number. Note what the chain leaves out: the statute's list begins at paragraph (iii), so a tenant's address at (b)(i) and telephone number at (b)(ii), though they are personal identifying information for the identity-theft offence, are not within the breach-notification definition. Most rental files contain several of the elements that are covered — the driver's licence number on the application and the bank details on the autopay authorisation are the usual ones.

What you must do if there is a breach. Under § 40-12-502(a), once you become aware of a breach you must conduct in good faith a reasonable and prompt investigation into the likelihood that the information has been or will be misused; if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, you must notify the affected Wyoming resident as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay, allowing only for law enforcement's legitimate needs and for the steps needed to scope the breach and restore the system. Notice may be written, by electronic mail, or by substitute notice if you can show the cost would exceed $10,000 for a Wyoming-based business, that the affected class exceeds 10,000 people, or that you lack sufficient contact information — thresholds a typical landlord will never meet, so plan on individual notice. Under § 40-12-502(e) the notice must be clear and conspicuous and must include a toll-free number for contacting you and for obtaining the credit reporting agencies' numbers and addresses; the types of information involved; a general description of the incident; the approximate date if reasonably determinable; in general terms what you have done to protect the system from further breaches; advice to the person to stay vigilant by reviewing account statements and monitoring credit reports; and whether notice was delayed by a law enforcement investigation. Notification may be delayed only if a law enforcement agency determines in writing that it would seriously impede a criminal investigation. Under § 40-12-502(f) the attorney general may sue for any violation, for compliance, for damages, or both, and that section expressly does not displace other law. And under § 40-12-502(g), if you hold computerized personal identifying information on behalf of another business entity, you must tell that entity of a breach as soon as practicable.

The practical upshot. Collect only the data elements you actually need, redact what you keep, and remember that under § 40-12-501(a)(vii) redacted data falls outside the definition. Keep tenant files out of shared drives and personal email. If you use a property management platform, your contract should require it to tell you of any breach promptly, which is the § 40-12-502(g) duty running toward you. Beyond the breach law, treat tenant information as confidential as a matter of policy even though no statute compels it: Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches real property under § 40-12-102(a)(vi) and § 40-12-105(a) reaches knowing deceptive practices, so a privacy promise in your lease or advertising that you do not keep is an exposure you created. Do not promise more than you will deliver, and do not put a blanket consent-to-disclose clause in the lease that you would be embarrassed to read aloud.

title: No Tenant Right to Display Flags or Signs in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant no statutory right to display anything. There is no flag-display right, no political-sign right, no religious-display right, no size or quantity rules you must allow, no prevailing-party attorney fee provision attached to any such right, and no provision barring you from restricting displays. "Political sign" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code, nor does "American flag" or any religious-display term.

WHAT THE FLAG PROVISIONS ACTUALLY DO. Wyo. Stat. § 8-3-110(a) adopts the Federal Flag Code, P.L. 94-344, as the flag code for Wyoming, and § 8-3-110(b) adds Wyoming Day, December 10, and July 10 to the dates on which the United States flag may be displayed in the state. That is a protocol statute - how and when the flag is properly displayed - not a tenant right and not a limit on a private landlord. The rest of Title 8 chapter 3 is about the state flag, the state territorial flag and the POW/MIA flag on state and local government buildings. None of it reaches a rental.

THERE IS ALSO NO ASSOCIATION BACKSTOP. In several states the display right comes from a common-interest community statute rather than landlord-tenant law. Wyoming has none: there is no unit owners' association act, and the Condominium Ownership Act at Wyo. Stat. § 34-20-101 et seq. says nothing about signs or flags. So if your property is in a covenanted subdivision or a condominium, what your tenant may display is governed by the recorded declaration and covenants, which are private documents outside this review - read them, because they bind you and you can be the one in breach if your tenant posts something they forbid.

WHAT THIS MEANS. You may restrict or prohibit flags, political signs, banners, window displays, holiday decorations and religious items in and on the premises, and you set the rules. Three real limits.

FAIR HOUSING. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103 protects race, colour, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin in the sale and rental provisions. A display rule applied evenly to everyone is not a problem; a rule enforced against a mezuzah, a crucifix or a head covering but not against other decorations is religious discrimination, and so is a rule written to reach only one faith's observance. Under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) you must also make reasonable accommodation in rules and policies where necessary for a disabled tenant - a rule banning all window attachments may have to bend for an assistive device. Note that Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i), the intimidation-and-interference offence, carries a longer protected list than § 40-26-103 - it adds age and status with respect to marriage or public assistance - but only for conduct "by force or threat of force"; § 40-26-144(b) makes coercion or interference with any right under the chapter a discriminatory practice with no force element, and (c) makes either a misdemeanor. Enforcing a display rule by threats, not by notice, is how a rules dispute becomes a criminal one.

ADVERTISING. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-104 is the fair housing advertising provision, and it is worth remembering that the general exemptions in Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110 do not reach it: subsection (a) covers §§ 40-26-103 to 40-26-109, but subsection (b) covers § 40-26-103 and §§ 40-26-105 to 40-26-109, deliberately omitting § 40-26-104. So even an otherwise-exempt owner is caught by the advertising rule. A "no signs" policy is not advertising, but a sign or notice at the property indicating a preference is.

FEDERAL LAW. FEDERAL: the Freedom to Display the American Flag Act of 2005 restricts condominium, cooperative and residential real estate management associations, not landlords, so it does not give your tenant a right against you - but it may bind an association your property sits in. FEDERAL: 47 C.F.R. § 1.4000, the FCC over-the-air reception devices rule, does limit what you can prohibit in the way of antennas and satellite dishes in a tenant's exclusive-use area, and is the one real federal constraint on a Wyoming landlord's display and attachment rules. Both are flagged, not resolved here. The First Amendment and Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 20 restrain government, not a private landlord.

So put your display rules in the lease or in written rules the lease incorporates, make them content-neutral, apply them to everyone, and allow for accommodation requests. Wyoming will not supply any of this for you.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules, recorded covenants and local ordinances were not searched.

title: Housing your own employee in Wyoming, where the landlord-tenant act does not step aside
bodyText:
Wyoming has no employee-housing statute. Nothing requires an employer-landlord to give a signed disclosure of the occupancy and vacating conditions as Delaware does, nothing requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends, there is no filing with any agency, and there is no sponsor liability for a worker's rent. "Employee housing", "company housing", "conditioned on employment" and "guest worker" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and "employment" and "occupancy" never appear within sixty characters of each other in either direction.

THE IMPORTANT POINT IS WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT DO. Many states exclude employee occupancy from the landlord-tenant act - Alaska and Hawaii both switch the act off for an employee whose right to occupy is conditioned on employment. WYOMING HAS NO SUCH EXCLUSION. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines a "residential rental unit" by one test only: the renter's principal place of residence, including appurtenances, grounds, common areas and facilities held out for the occupancy of residential renters generally and any other area or facility provided to the renter in the rental agreement, excluding only a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis. Employment is not mentioned. Section 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines a "rental agreement" as ANY agreement, WRITTEN OR ORAL, which establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules or any other provisions regarding the use and occupancy of a residential rental unit, and § 1-21-1201(a)(iii) defines a "renter" as any renter, lessee, tenant or other person entitled under a rental agreement to occupy a residential rental unit to the exclusion of others. An employment arrangement that fixes who lives where, on what terms, is capable of being a rental agreement on those words. So plan on the footing that your caretaker, ranch hand, motel manager or on-site maintenance employee living in a unit you own IS a renter with the full Article 12 protections - habitability under §§ 1-21-1202 and 1-21-1203, deposit rules under §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208, and the abandoned-property procedure in § 1-21-1210 - and that ending the job does not end the occupancy.

AND YOU MUST USE THE COURT. Ending the employment does not give you possession. There is no self-help in Wyoming. The forcible entry and detainer route in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 to 1-21-1017 is what you have, after the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003. Two grounds fit: § 1-21-1002(a)(i) against a tenant holding over the term, and § 1-21-1002(a)(v) "[i]n cases where the defendant is a settler or occupier of lands or tenements, without color of title, to which the complainant has the right of possession" - which is the ground designed for an occupier whose right never rested on a lease at all. Do NOT reach for the Article 14 removal procedure. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(a)(ii) requires that the unauthorized person "has unlawfully entered", which an employee you housed did not, and § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or ORAL rental or lease agreement authorized by the owner. Misusing it exposes you under § 1-21-1403(c) to restoration of possession, actual damages, statutory damages equal to TRIPLE the fair market rental value for the period of wrongful removal, court costs and reasonable attorney fees.

THE WAGE SIDE, WHERE WYOMING IS GENEROUS TO YOU AND THEN EXPENSIVE. Wyo. Stat. § 27-4-104(a) provides that when an employee quits or is discharged, the employee shall be paid whatever wages are due no later than the employer's usual practice on regularly scheduled payroll dates, or at a time specified in a collective bargaining agreement - AND that "[t]he employer may offset from any monies due the employee as wages, any sums due the employer from the employee which have been incurred by the employee during his employment." Unpaid rent incurred during the employment is such a sum, so the offset is expressly available. But get it wrong and § 27-4-104(b) is severe: where a former employee sues for wages earned and due and establishes the amount justly due, the court SHALL allow interest at EIGHTEEN PERCENT per annum from the date of discharge or termination, or from when the wages were due, together with a reasonable attorney fee and all costs of suit. Offset only amounts that are genuinely due and documented. Section 27-4-101(b) separately requires you to furnish, with each payment of wages, an itemized written statement showing all deductions made - so the rent deduction has to appear on the pay statement.

TWO MORE WYOMING POINTS. Minimum wage: Wyo. Stat. § 27-4-202(a) sets the Wyoming rate at $5.15 an hour, so the federal rate governs in practice, and the Wyoming act contains NO board-or-lodging credit at all - do not assume you may count the housing toward the wage floor; that is a federal question under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Payroll taxes: both the unemployment and workers' compensation "wages" definitions in Title 27 exclude the value of lodging furnished by and for the convenience of the employer where the employee is required to accept lodging on the employer's business premises as a condition of employment - a real exclusion worth knowing about, and one that depends on the housing being genuinely required and on the premises.

FINALLY, THE LICENSING EXEMPTION. If your on-site manager holds keys and shows units, Wyo. Stat. § 33-28-103(a)(i) and (a)(vi) exempt the owner's own employees and on-site managers from the real estate licensing requirement, so you do not need a licensed broker for that role.

WHAT TO DO. Put the arrangement in a written lease separate from the employment contract, state the rent (even if it is offset against wages), state that occupancy continues only while the employment does and that the term ends when the employment ends, take and account for any deposit under § 1-21-1208, and authorise the wage offset in writing. None of that is required by a Wyoming statute. All of it is required by the fact that Wyoming will otherwise treat your employee as an ordinary tenant.

title: No Duty to Forward Notices, and No Attornment Rule
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring a tenant to forward you notices, summonses or court papers served on the tenant in a proceeding against the property, and no penalty for failing to do so. Several states impose that duty and forfeit a multiple of rent if the tenant ignores it; Wyoming has nothing of the kind. Wyoming also has no attornment statute: the word “attornment” does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and neither does any form of the verb “attorn” standing alone. There is no provision voiding an attornment clause and none requiring one, so an attornment or subordination clause in your lease is governed by ordinary contract law, not by a statute you need to match.

What makes this mostly a non-problem in Wyoming is that your tenant usually will not be the only one notified. Under Wyo. Stat. § 34-4-103(a)(iv), a mortgagee may not foreclose by advertisement and sale unless written notice of intent to foreclose has been served, by certified mail with return receipt, on the record owner AND on “the person in possession of the mortgaged premises if different than the record owner,” mailed to each one’s last known address at least ten days before publication of the notice of sale begins, with proof of compliance by affidavit. That means you, as record owner, get your own certified-mail notice; the tenant’s copy is additional, not a substitute. Section 34-4-104 then requires publication for four consecutive weeks, at least once a week, in a newspaper in the county. So a Wyoming foreclosure by advertisement will reach you directly.

What happens to the tenancy after a sale. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(iii) lets a purchaser or assignee bring forcible entry and detainer where real estate has been sold under a power of sale in a mortgage or trust deed and the purchaser has demanded possession, and § 1-21-1002(a)(ii) does the same after a judicial or execution sale where the judgment debtor was in possession. Nothing in Wyoming law requires a tenant to attorn to the purchaser or preserves the lease against the purchaser; what protects a bona fide tenant is FEDERAL — the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, 12 U.S.C. § 5220 note, made permanent in 2018 — which generally gives a bona fide tenant ninety days’ notice to vacate and lets a bona fide lease run to the end of its term, subject to the exception for a purchaser who will occupy the unit as a primary residence. Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 cut the other way for anyone hoping a tenancy continues by implication: there is no landlord and tenant relation by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, there is no implied renewal on expiration of a term either by holding over or by a landlord accepting rent, and an expired lease is renewed only by express contract in writing signed by the parties.

THE PRACTICAL POINT. Because no statute obliges the tenant to tell you anything, put the duty in the lease. A short clause requiring the tenant to notify you immediately and deliver any written notice received about a proceeding affecting the property costs nothing and is enforceable as a lease term: § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes a renter comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 an eviction ground. Also mind the mirror image of the problem: under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i), for purposes of notice and other communication under the landlord-tenant article, “owner” includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager “unless the agent or manager specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement.” Notice served on your manager is notice to you, and only the agent or manager — not you unilaterally — can switch that off, and only in the rental agreement.

title: Renters Insurance and Insurance Claims
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute about tenant insurance. Nothing says whether you may require renters insurance, whether you may require a tenant to submit a claim on their own policy, or whether you may file a claim against a tenant's policy yourself. The phrases 'renters insurance' and "renter's insurance" return no hits anywhere in the Wyoming Statutes, and the residential rental article (Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211) does not mention insurance at all. Wyoming also has no Colorado-style prohibition on pushing habitability repairs onto a tenant's carrier, and no statute voiding an exculpatory, indemnity or hold-harmless term in a residential lease — the only anti-indemnity public-policy statute in the Wyoming Statutes is § 40-17-102, which voids indemnity clauses in motor carrier transportation contracts and has nothing to do with leases. There is no bar on your insurer subrogating against your tenant, and no statute on waiver-of-subrogation clauses.

So you have wide latitude here — wider than in most states — and the risk is overreach rather than prohibition.

What you can do. Require renters insurance in the lease. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) makes it a renter duty to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement, and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 a ground for a forcible entry and detainer action, so a properly drafted insurance requirement has real force. Specify the coverage type and minimum limits, require you to be named as an additional interested party so you get lapse notices, and require proof at move-in and at each renewal. You may also require a waiver of subrogation in the tenant's policy and include a mutual waiver in the lease; nothing in Wyoming law forbids it.

What you should not do, even though no statute forbids it. Do not make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of your doing a repair, and do not delay a repair while a claim is pending. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) puts electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water on the owner, and § 1-21-1202(a) requires the unit to be maintained in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation. It is true that Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty or obligation in Article 12 be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, so in Wyoming you could in principle move those duties by contract — but that is a reallocation of the duty itself, done explicitly in a signed writing, not a licence to leave the duty with yourself and fund it from the tenant's policy. A tenant who is current on all payments can start the § 1-21-1203(b) notice sequence, and if you do not commence corrective action or dispute the claim in writing within a reasonable time the tenant has the § 1-21-1206 route; forcing an insurance claim instead of acting does not stop that clock. It also invites a Wyoming Consumer Protection Act problem — § 40-12-105(a) is gated on 'knowingly' and includes the (a)(xv) catch-all 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices', with merchandise defined to include real property at § 40-12-102(a)(vi) and no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110.

For damage the tenant caused, you do not need their insurer. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1205(a)(i) forbids a renter intentionally or negligently destroying, defacing, damaging, impairing or removing any part of the unit or knowingly permitting another to do so, and § 1-21-1211(b) lets you apply the deposit to the damage under § 1-21-1208(a), leaves the renter liable for damage beyond what the deposit covers plus interest at ten percent a year on unpaid amounts, and preserves 'any legal action available to recover damages caused to the unit by the renter'. Pursue the tenant; the tenant's liability coverage is then their problem and their carrier's, which is the clean way to reach the policy. Filing directly against a tenant's policy yourself is unregulated in Wyoming but you have no statutory standing to do it, and attempting it without the tenant's written authorization is a poor idea.

Two limits to keep in view. Section 1-21-1203(e) bars claims for mental suffering under the whole of Article 12, which narrows what either side can recover there. And Article 12 applies only to a 'residential rental unit' as § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it — the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented on an occasional basis. Whether a Wyoming court would enforce a broad exculpatory clause in a residential lease is a question of case law, which is outside this library; the statutes do not void one.

title: What a Wyoming Lease Can and Cannot Force Through a Tenant Portal
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute about tenant portals, online rent payment or electronic signatures in a lease specifically. It does have the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-21-101 et seq., and that act decides most of the question — including one thing your lease cannot override. Start with what is permitted. Wyo. Stat. § 40-21-107 says a record or signature may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is electronic, a contract may not be denied effect solely because an electronic record was used in its formation, an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature. So an e-signed Wyoming lease is a lease, an emailed notice can be a written notice, and portal records are records. Now the two limits. First, consent, and it is not automatic. Wyo. Stat. § 40-21-105(a) says the act does not REQUIRE anyone to use electronic means, and § 40-21-105(b) says the act 'applies only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means', with whether they agreed 'determined from the context and surrounding circumstances, including the parties' conduct.' Get the agreement in the lease rather than relying on conduct. Second, and this is the one most portal clauses get wrong: Wyo. Stat. § 40-21-105(c) provides that 'A party that agrees to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct OTHER transactions by electronic means. The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement.' Read it precisely. It is not a right to opt out of what the tenant already agreed to, and it does not undo an e-signed lease or a portal payment the tenant has made. It is a forward-looking, non-waivable right to decline the NEXT electronic transaction. A lease term saying the tenant irrevocably agrees that all future notices, signatures, renewals and payments will be electronic and that the tenant waives any right to paper is, to that extent, unenforceable against § 40-21-105(c) — the non-waiver sentence is express. Draft the clause as a default with a stated paper alternative instead, and it does everything you actually need. Third, and separately from UETA, two Wyoming notices cannot go through a portal at all. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires that a notice to quit be served at least three days before the action 'by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found.' That is a manner-of-service requirement, not merely a writing requirement, and § 40-21-107(c) only converts a writing requirement. Serve the notice to quit physically, every time, however good your portal is. The same caution applies to the renter's noncompliance sequence: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) and § 1-21-1206(b) each require service 'by certified mail or in the manner specified by W.S. 1-21-1003'. Those sit inside Article 12, so Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) — 'Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties' — can reach them, and an explicit, written, signed lease term could substitute portal delivery. § 1-21-1003 itself is in Article 10 and § 1-21-1202(d) says 'this article', so it cannot be changed that way. Fourth, know when a portal posting counts as received. Wyo. Stat. § 40-21-115(b) says that unless otherwise agreed an electronic record is received when it enters an information processing system 'that THE RECIPIENT has designated or uses for the purpose of receiving electronic records or information of the type sent, and from which the recipient is able to retrieve' it, in a processable form. Your own portal is your system, not the tenant's. Posting a notice to it and nothing more is a weak receipt argument. The fix is in the same words 'unless otherwise agreed': have the tenant designate an email address in the lease, send the notice to that address as well as posting it, and keep the delivery log. Finally, the mechanics. Wyoming has no statute requiring you to accept cash or to offer a non-electronic payment method, no cap on a convenience or portal fee, and no statute requiring a rent receipt. A portal fee is a lease-created charge — state it as a dollar amount, make it optional by offering a free method, and remember it is recoverable from the deposit only if the lease creates it, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) allows deduction of 'other costs provided by any contract'. Two outside constraints: apply the portal policy evenly, because Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103(b) bars discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental on Wyoming's seven protected classes and a mandatory-portal rule can disadvantage an applicant with a disability for whom Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii) requires a reasonable accommodation in rules and policies; and your portal holds personal data, so Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-501 to 40-12-511 impose breach-notification duties on you, under an article confusingly headed 'CREDIT FREEZE REPORTS'.

title: Tenant Records and the Data You Hold
bodyText:
Two different questions, two different answers.

RENT LEDGERS AND RECORD REQUESTS — nothing. Wyoming imposes no duty to keep a rent ledger, none to give a tenant a statement of account on request, none to attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice, and no confidentiality rule about who you may show a tenant's file to. "Rent ledger" returns nothing in Wyoming law, and the forty "ledger" hits are banking, business-entity and tax provisions. There is no Wyoming equivalent of Virginia's disclosure list or its records-request right.

That does not mean records do not matter — it means they matter as evidence rather than as compliance. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1008(b) requires the court in a nonpayment case to find "the amount of rent due and payable at the time of the hearing, together with the terms and conditions of the agreement between the parties in relation to the amount and time of payment of rent", and then to enter judgment accordingly. A payment ledger is how you prove that. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) separately requires a written itemization of every deposit deduction with reasons, within thirty (30) days of termination or fifteen (15) days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by thirty (30) days if there is damage — and under § 1-21-1208(c) an unreasonable failure lets the renter recover the full deposit plus court costs. The documents behind that itemization are the only thing standing between you and that penalty. Keep the signed lease, the move-in and move-out condition records, the payment ledger, every notice with proof of how it was served, and the receipts behind every deduction.

YOUR DATA OBLIGATIONS — real, and most landlords do not know they are covered. Wyoming's breach statute is Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-501 through 40-12-509, and it is easy to miss for two reasons: it is filed under an article headed around credit freezes, and Wyoming does not use the phrase "data breach". Its term is "breach of the security of the data system".

Who it covers: § 40-12-502(a) applies to "[a]n individual or commercial entity that conducts business in Wyoming and that owns or licenses computerized data that includes personal identifying information about a resident of Wyoming". A landlord with a spreadsheet, a property-management system or a scanned application folder is squarely inside it. There is no small-business exemption and no unit-count threshold.

What counts as personal identifying information: § 40-12-501(a)(vii) defines it as a person's first name or first initial and last name in combination with one or more of the data elements in § 6-3-901(b)(iii) through (xiv), unredacted. Those elements are: social security number; driver's licence number; an account, credit card or debit card number in combination with a security code, access code or password that would allow access to a financial account; tribal identification card; a federal or state government issued identification card; shared secrets or security tokens used for data-based authentication; a username or email address in combination with a password or security question and answer permitting access to an online account; a birth or marriage certificate; medical information; health insurance information; unique biometric data; and an individual taxpayer identification number. A rental application captures several of those on page one. Note two limits: § 40-12-501(a)(viii) treats data as redacted where no more than five digits are accessible, and § 40-12-501(b) excludes information contained in government records or in widely distributed media lawfully available to the public.

What you must do on a breach: § 40-12-502(a) requires you, when you become aware of a breach, to conduct in good faith a reasonable and prompt investigation into the likelihood that the information has been or will be misused, and, if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely, to notify the affected Wyoming resident as soon as possible, in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay. Under § 40-12-502(b) notice may be delayed only if a law enforcement agency determines in writing that it would seriously impede a criminal investigation. Notice may be written, by email, or by substitute notice on the cost and volume thresholds in § 40-12-502(d)(iii) — over $10,000 in cost or over 10,000 affected persons for a Wyoming-based business. Section 40-12-502(e) fixes the contents: a toll-free number to contact you and from which the person can get the credit reporting agencies' numbers and addresses; the types of information involved; a general description of the incident; the approximate date if reasonably determinable; in general terms what you have done to protect the system from further breaches; advice to stay vigilant by reviewing account statements and monitoring credit reports; and whether notice was delayed for a law enforcement investigation.

If your property manager or software vendor holds the data: § 40-12-502(g) makes the holder disclose any breach to you as soon as practicable, and lets the two of you agree who gives the resident notice — only one notice per breach is required — but if you cannot agree, the duty falls on whoever has the direct business relationship with the Wyoming resident. For a tenant, that is you. Put the allocation in your management or software contract now, not after a breach.

Enforcement: § 40-12-502(f) lets the attorney general bring an action in law or equity for any violation, for other appropriate relief, to recover damages, or both, and says the section is not exclusive and does not relieve you from any other applicable law.

WHAT WYOMING DOES NOT REQUIRE, which is as useful to know. There is no written information security program requirement — "information security program" appears once in all of Wyoming law, in a state-agency provision in Title 9, not in a duty on private holders. There is no encryption mandate, no records-destruction or shredding duty, and no data-minimisation rule. So the statute is reactive: it tells you what to do after a breach, not how to prevent one. Doing it well before the breach is nevertheless the cheapest insurance, because § 40-12-502(e)(v) will make you describe, in your own notice letter, the actions you took to protect the system.

THE OTHER HOOK. Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing — § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines "merchandise" to include real property, there is no real-property exemption at § 40-12-110, and § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct. If you promise applicants that their information is secure or will be destroyed and it is not, that promise is the kind of representation the Act is aimed at. Say only what you actually do.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to a Wyoming Tenant
bodyText:
Wyoming is one of the most permissive states in the country on this, and the permission comes from one sentence. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d): "Any duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." Three things about that sentence decide everything.

First, its reach. It says "this article," not "this section," so it covers every duty in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211 - including the habitability duties in § 1-21-1202(a) and § 1-21-1203(a), the common-area duty in § 1-21-1203(a)(ii), and the deposit mechanics in § 1-21-1208. There is no carve-out for code compliance, no carve-out for health and safety, and no "this does not diminish your obligations to other tenants" proviso. If you are adapting a clause written for a state that follows the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, strip those recitals out or keep them as a deliberate choice; they are not Wyoming law.

Second, what Wyoming does not require. There is no separate-writing rule - a clause inside the signed lease satisfies "written agreement signed by the parties," and Wyoming never uses the phrase "separate writing" in this context at all. There is no consideration requirement, no good-faith formality, and no rule that the arrangement must not be a device to evade your obligations. Most importantly for a multifamily owner, there is no dwelling-type distinction: Wyoming does not limit duty-shifting to single-family residences or to properties with four or fewer units. The same rule reaches every residential rental unit in the state.

Third, the one condition that does bite: "explicit." That word is the whole of Wyoming's formality and you should treat it as a real constraint rather than a throwaway. A general "Tenant accepts the premises as-is," a catch-all "Tenant is responsible for all maintenance," or a duty buried in a list of housekeeping rules is not an explicit assignment of a named statutory duty. Name the duty, cite the subsection it comes from, say plainly that the duty is assigned to the tenant or modified, describe exactly what the tenant must do, and get both signatures. Also keep in mind Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(i): a managing agent, leasing agent, or resident manager counts as the "owner" for notice purposes unless the rental agreement says otherwise, so make sure the right person signs.

The Act actually gives you two different mechanisms with two different formalities, and knowing which one you are using matters.

The general mechanism is § 1-21-1202(d), described above: explicit, written, signed by the parties. Use it to move an existing statutory duty onto the tenant.

The narrower, opt-in mechanism is Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv), and it works in the opposite direction. Your duty under that paragraph is to "[m]aintain other appliances and facilities as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." So beyond the core items the statute lists for you - not renting a unit that is not reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy under § 1-21-1203(a)(i), maintaining common areas under (a)(ii), and maintaining electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water under (a)(iii) - you have no statutory duty to maintain an appliance or facility at all unless your lease specifically contracts for it. The dishwasher, the washer and dryer, the garage opener, the sprinkler system: if the lease is silent, § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) imposes nothing on you. You do not need to shift those duties away, because they never attached. Conversely, if you do promise to maintain them, you have created a statutory duty enforceable through the § 1-21-1203(b) notice procedure and the § 1-21-1206 judicial remedy. List what you will maintain, deliberately and no more.

There is also a third, very narrow formality sitting in § 1-21-1202(a) that is easy to misread. That subsection's second sentence requires every residential rental unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties." That trailing qualifier belongs to that sentence only - it does not reach back to the first sentence's duty to maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, nor forward to the third sentence's seasonal-rental carve-out for summer cabins and the like. Note that this formality is written differently from § 1-21-1202(d): it says "in writing by both parties" without the words "explicit" or "signed." Do not rely on the looser wording. Where both could apply, satisfy both: make it explicit, in writing, and signed by both parties. That costs you nothing and removes the argument.

Two limits worth stating plainly. The statute lets duties be "assigned to a different party or modified" - not extinguished. A clause that leaves nobody responsible for a safe and sanitary dwelling is a different animal from one assigning the duty to the tenant, and it is the version a court is most likely to refuse to enforce. And none of this touches the renter's own statutory duties in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 or the prohibited acts in § 1-21-1205, which apply regardless; nor does it reach outside the article, so it cannot modify the eviction procedure in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017 or the Wyoming Safe Homes Act, which Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 makes unwaivable. Building, fire and electrical codes and any municipal housing ordinance are also unaffected by a private agreement; local ordinances are flagged here and not resolved.

One practical caution. Because the corpus holds no Wyoming case law, how far a court will let § 1-21-1202(d) go against the core habitability duties is untested. The safer uses are the ordinary ones - lawn care, snow and ice removal from the tenant's own walks and drive, filter changes, light bulbs, pest control, gutter clearing, taking waste to the collection point, pool or spa care. The aggressive use - assigning the tenant responsibility for the furnace, the water heater, the roof, or common areas shared with other tenants - is where you are relying on untested ground, and where a rent reduction or other stated consideration, though not required by the statute, is worth including to show the assignment was a genuine bargain.

title: No Statutory Tenant Organizing Right
bodyText: Wyoming gives tenants no statutory right to organize. There is no tenant association statute, no duty to let organizers canvass the building or distribute literature, no right to meet in a common room, and no rule about keeping management out of a tenants' meeting. The phrases "tenant union," "tenant association" and "tenants' organization" appear nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes. Just as important for you to know: Wyoming also has no landlord retaliation statute of any kind. The word "retaliation" does not appear in Title 1 at all, so there is no Wyoming provision making it unlawful to raise rent, cut services, refuse to renew or bring a possession action because a tenant complained, joined with other tenants, called a code officer or testified against you. That is not an invitation to do those things, and here is why. First, the forcible entry and detainer grounds in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a) are a closed list, so an eviction still has to rest on holding over, nonpayment after three days, or a violation of Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205 - organizing is none of those, and a judge will want to see the ground you actually pleaded. Second, FEDERAL: the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. s 3617, makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with a person's exercise or enjoyment of fair housing rights or because they aided or encouraged others in exercising them, so retaliation that tracks race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin is a federal problem; the Wyoming Fair Housing Act's own interference provision runs the same way: Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a) makes it an offense to intimidate or interfere with a renter by force or threat of force on listed grounds, § 40-26-144(b) makes it a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone in the exercise or enjoyment of a right granted or protected by that chapter, or because they aided or encouraged another in exercising it, and § 40-26-144(c) makes either a misdemeanor. Third, FEDERAL: if the building takes HUD subsidy, federal tenant-organizing rules attach to the program (24 C.F.R. part 245 for multifamily projects), independent of Wyoming law. Fourth, if the tenants' complaint concerns habitability, the written notice procedure in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) and the renter's remedies in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206 operate whatever you think of the group that organized it - responding on the merits, in writing, within a reasonable time is both the statutory duty and the better answer. A word on the state constitution: Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 21 says the right of petition, and of the people peaceably to assemble to consult for the common good and make known their opinions, shall never be denied or abridged. That provision constrains government, not a private landlord, so it does not give your tenants a right to assemble in your building - but it does mean a city cannot stop a tenants' group from meeting or petitioning in public. Practical course: because Wyoming law neither grants nor denies these rights, your written house rules decide the question on your property, and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) a renter must comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement. Write common-area and solicitation rules that are content-neutral - the same booking rules, notice periods and limits for every gathering, whether it is a birthday party, a church group or a tenants' meeting - and apply them that way every time. A rule aimed at tenant meetings alone is the one that will look like pretext if a federal interference or discrimination claim is ever brought.

title: No Statement of Tenant Rights Required in Wyoming
bodyText: No Wyoming agency publishes a statement of tenant rights and responsibilities, and no Wyoming statute requires you to give one to a tenant, attach one as the first page of the lease, have the tenant sign or initial each page, or collect an acknowledgment of receipt. There is also no Wyoming rule barring you from suing or filing an eviction until you have provided such a statement — that whole regime does not exist here. The phrases "statement of tenant rights" and "tenant rights" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. The only condition precedent Wyoming puts on an eviction is the notice to quit: before commencing a forcible entry and detainer action you must notify the tenant to leave the premises, with the notice served at least three days before you file, by leaving a written copy with the tenant or at the tenant's usual place of abode or business if the tenant cannot be found (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003). Satisfy that and nothing else stands between you and the courthouse on the disclosure side. One thing Wyoming does require you to hand over, and it is easy to overlook because it is not a rights statement: if any portion of the deposit is nonrefundable, the rental agreement must say so and a separate written notice of that fact must be given to the tenant at the time the deposit is taken (Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1207). The holder of the owner's interest at termination is bound by that section and by the deposit-return section (§ 1-21-1209), so a buyer inherits the consequences. Separately, federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for most pre-1978 housing (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 4852d). Everything else you give the tenant about their rights is voluntary. Giving a short, accurate summary is still smart: Wyoming's habitability remedy depends on the tenant serving you written notice first (§ 1-21-1203(b)) and then a second "notice to repair or correct condition" (§ 1-21-1206(b)), and a tenant who knows that route is more likely to use it than to stop paying rent. If you write such a summary, keep it accurate — a knowingly false statement about the transaction could be reached by the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act. Finally, check the city or county where you rent; a local rental-licensing program can impose its own tenant-information requirement, and local ordinances were not reviewed here.

title: Changing Rent or Other Lease Terms
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute telling you how to change a lease term, and no statute telling you how much notice to give before raising the rent. "Rent increase" appears nowhere in the Wyoming code, and neither does any proximity of "increase" and "rent" in a tenancy context. There is also no month-to-month tenancy, periodic tenancy or tenancy at will in Wyoming's statutes -- all three phrases return nothing -- so there is no 30-day modification notice to piggyback on and no statutory notice period to end a tenancy either. Do not assume a 30-day rule. It does not exist here.

What exists instead is a strict rule against implying anything, which is the opposite of what most landlords expect. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides that in Wyoming "there shall not exist the relations of landlord and tenant, by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance," that on the expiration of a term "there shall be no implied renewal of the same, for any period of time whatever, either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent," and that holding over plus acceptance of rent "shall constitute only a tenancy by sufferance." Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is not renewed "except by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto, whether the original lease be written or verbal."

So you cannot change a term by sending a notice. A notice is an offer. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) treats a modification as an "agreement" -- the definition of "rental agreement" is "any agreement, written or oral, which establishes or modifies the terms, conditions, rules or any other provisions regarding the use and occupancy of a residential rental unit." And where the change touches a duty under the residential rental article, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) is explicit about the form: "[a]ny duty or obligation in this article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." Explicit, written, signed. A posted notice, an email or an unsigned addendum does not meet that standard.

That leaves you three clean routes, and you should pick one deliberately.

First, reserve the power in the lease at signing. A lease may give you the right to adopt and amend rules on stated notice, or to adjust a specified charge on stated notice. This works because the tenant agreed to it when they signed. It is the only way to get a mid-term change without going back for a signature, and its reach is limited to what you actually reserved -- a rules-amendment power is not a rent-increase power.

Second, amend by signed agreement. Write the change, state its effective date, and have both parties sign. This is the route § 1-21-1202(d) contemplates, and it is the only safe route for a rent increase during a term.

Third, do not renew. Let the term run out and offer a new lease on new terms. Because § 34-2-129 requires a signed writing to renew, the new terms travel in the new signed lease. If the tenant stays without signing, they are a tenant by sufferance -- not a month-to-month tenant on the old terms and not a tenant on your new terms -- and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) a forcible entry and detainer action lies against "tenants holding over their terms," after the written notice to quit that § 1-21-1003 requires at least three days before filing.

The cautious course, since Wyoming sets no period: give at least thirty days' written notice before the end of a term that you will not renew or that renewal is offered on new terms, deliver it the way the lease requires, and keep proof. Thirty days is not a legal minimum in Wyoming; it is a practical floor that gives the tenant time to accept or move and gives you a clean record. And whatever you do, do not keep accepting rent at the old figure after announcing a new one -- in a state that refuses to imply a renewal, a course of dealing argument is the one thing you want to avoid handing the tenant.

One statutory termination notice does exist in the article, for a different situation. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(d), if a renter has given you written notice of a condition under § 1-21-1203(b) and the cost of repair exceeds what would be reasonable in light of the rent charged and the nature of the property, you may refuse to correct it and terminate the rental agreement -- but you must notify the renter in writing within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance and give sufficient time to find substitute housing, "which shall be no less than ten (10) days nor more than twenty (20) days." That is a repair-refusal termination, not a term-change notice, and it is the only numbered notice period of its kind in Article 12.

title: No Rent-Cap or Just-Cause Exemption Notice in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no notice telling a tenant that a property is exempt from a rent cap, from just-cause eviction rules, or from a tenant purchase right — because Wyoming has none of those rules to be exempt from.
