California's Tenant Protection Act notice under Civ. Code § 1946.2(e)(8)(B)(iii) has no Wyoming counterpart, and nothing in it should be copied into a Wyoming lease: it recites California Civil Code sections that have no force here, and a statement in a Wyoming lease that misdescribes the law is worse than no statement at all.

What Wyoming lacks, specifically:
• No rent cap or rent stabilization, and no preemption of one — "rent control," "rent stabilization," "maximum rent" and "rent increase" appear nowhere in the statutes.
• No just-cause eviction requirement. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) makes forcible entry and detainer available "[a]gainst tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due," and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) against renters violating Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205. Holding over past the term is itself a ground; no reason need be given for letting a term expire.
• No tenant right of first refusal and no tenant opportunity to purchase on sale. The phrase "right of first refusal" appears twice in the whole corpus, in Title 31 (motor vehicles) and in a Title 34 real-estate-transfer-fee definition; "opportunity to purchase" twice, in Titles 36 and 37, neither a tenant right.
• No condominium-conversion tenant notice or purchase right. Wyoming has a Condominium Ownership Act at Wyo. Stat. § 34-20-101 et seq., but Title 34 uses the word "tenant" only in conveyancing senses — tenant for life, joint tenants, tenants by the entirety — plus the holdover sections, and contains no conversion protections.
• No good-cause or exemption notice of any kind tied to termination.

What Wyoming has instead, and it cuts the landlord's way, is Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129, which reverse the usual holdover rule. Section 34-2-128 provides that "[i]n this state there shall not exist the relations of landlord and tenant, by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance," and that on expiration of a term created by lease, verbal or written, no implied renewal arises. A tenant who stays past the term, and a landlord who accepts rent afterward, do not create a renewed tenancy; under § 34-2-129 an expired lease is renewed only by an express written contract signed by the parties. So in Wyoming the expiration of the term, not a notice of exemption from anything, is what ends the tenancy — and you should put renewals in writing precisely because nothing is implied.

Practical course: say nothing in the lease about rent caps, just cause or exemption from them. If you use a multi-state lease form, strike any California-style Tenant Protection Act notice, any "this property is exempt from local rent regulation" recital, and any tenant right-of-first-refusal language you did not intend to grant — a right of first refusal written into a Wyoming lease is enforceable as a contract term even though no statute requires one. The one place to be careful is your own city: Wyoming gives cities and towns home rule under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b) and has preempted nothing in this field, so a local rent or just-cause ordinance, if one ever appeared, could carry its own notice duty. Ordinances are outside this library; check locally.

title: No Tenant Right to Buy When You Sell
bodyText: Wyoming gives a tenant no statutory right or opportunity to purchase the property when you sell it, and no notice is owed to the tenant because of the sale. There is no tenant opportunity-to-purchase act, no tenant right of first refusal, no right to match a third-party offer, no notice of intent to sell, no condominium conversion notice and no sale-of-the-park notice for a mobile home park. The phrases 'opportunity to purchase' and 'right of first refusal' appear in the Wyoming statutes only in a state-lands provision, a utility provision, the motor vehicle dealer franchise act and the private transfer fee chapter — never in landlord-tenant law. California's Tenant Protection Act notice and Maryland's tenant right to offer to purchase have no Wyoming analogue, and none of that text belongs in a Wyoming lease. What actually matters on a Wyoming sale is what travels with the property. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209, 'The holder of the interest of the owner or designated agent in the residential rental unit at the time of termination of the rental agreement shall be bound by the provisions of W.S. 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208' — so the nonrefundable-deposit notice duty and the whole deposit itemisation and refund timetable attach to whoever holds the owner's interest when the tenancy ends. Transfer the deposits to the buyer at closing, get a written acknowledgement of the amount transferred and of the buyer's assumption of the obligation, and tell the tenant in writing who holds the deposit and where to send the new address required by Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) — none of that is required by statute, but § 1-21-1209 is what you are managing. Watch the recording rule too. A lease for a term of more than three years is a conveyance under Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-102, and under Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-120 an unrecorded conveyance is void as against a later good-faith purchaser for value who records first; so a long unrecorded lease may not survive the sale, which can be a problem for a buyer who wants the tenancy and a problem for you if you warranted it. And Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 continue to apply: a buyer who accepts rent from a holdover tenant renews nothing and gets only a tenancy by sufferance. You may of course give a tenant a right of first refusal by contract, and many Wyoming landlords do as a way to sell without a broker. If you do, put it in the signed lease, state the notice you will give, the time the tenant has to accept, and that the right ends if the tenancy ends. One drafting caution if you ever want to charge for releasing such a right: Wyoming's private transfer fee chapter, Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-28-101 et seq., regulates fees payable on transfer of an interest in real property, and the definition at Wyo. Stat. § 34-28-101(a)(ii) excludes consideration payable to the holder of a right of first refusal for waiving, releasing or not exercising it — so that particular payment is outside the chapter, but anything broader needs checking against it.

title: No Wyoming Landlord-Tenant Statute Is on a Repeal Clock
bodyText:
As of October 24, 2026, nothing in Wyoming's landlord-tenant law is scheduled to expire. There is no tenant-protection act on a sunset clock, no dated repeal in the residential rental article, and no date after which any of the rules in this library stops applying. You can plan a lease term, a renewal and a multi-year holding period without a statutory expiry hanging over it.

That is a real finding, not an assumption. Wyoming's core landlord-tenant provisions were each checked for a repeal or expiry date: the forcible entry and detainer article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017; the residential rental property article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211; the Safe Homes Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1301 through 1-21-1304; the removal of unauthorized occupants article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403; the holdover and renewal provisions at Wyo. Stat. §§ 34-2-128 and 34-2-129; and the Wyoming Fair Housing Act, Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145. None carries a sunset.

The searches behind that. "Sunset" appears 33 times across the Wyoming statutes, and "repealed effective" 27 times, so Wyoming does use sunset drafting — it is simply not used here. In Title 1, the title that holds all of Wyoming's landlord-tenant procedure, those terms produce exactly one hit, and it is a temporary restraining order that "shall expire within a time fixed by the court," nothing to do with landlords. In Title 34, the property title, they produce zero. In Title 40, which holds the Fair Housing Act, they produce 12, and every one is a licence renewal date or a pawn-transaction maturity date, none of them in the fair housing chapter.

The newest piece of Wyoming landlord-adjacent law is also permanent. The removal of unauthorized occupants article, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, was created by 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws (SF0006). Its only dating provision is section 3, "This act is effective July 1, 2025." There is no repeal date and no review clause.

No recent act has touched the rules either. A search of all 171 enrolled acts from the 2025 general session and all 107 from the 2026 budget session found no act amending or repealing Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017, §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, or the Fair Housing Act at §§ 40-26-101 through 40-26-145. The only 2025 or 2026 act in this neighbourhood is SF0006, which added law rather than ending any.

What this does not mean. Wyoming's rules are durable but not frozen. The legislature meets every year — a general session in odd years and a budget session in even years — and could change any of this. The practical point for your lease is a different one: because no statute is set to lapse, you do not need a clause saying what happens if the law changes on a known date, and you should not copy one from a state that has a sunsetting tenant-protection act. What you should do instead is write your lease to the law as it stands and re-check before each renewal cycle, which for Wyoming means after each session adjourns in March.

One genuine dated item sits outside landlord-tenant law but can reach a rental. Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), and nothing in state law preempts local rental regulation; Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) expressly makes a more stringent local housing code prevail. A municipal ordinance can carry its own sunset or review date, and this library does not resolve ordinances. If your city has adopted a rental registration, inspection or short-term rental ordinance, check its expiry and review provisions directly.

title: No Lease Translation Duty in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming imposes no duty to translate a residential lease into any language, in any circumstance. There is no California-style rule requiring a translation where you advertised or negotiated primarily in another language, no prescribed verbatim statutory lease text in any language, no minimum type size paired with a translation requirement, and no two-official-text priority rule of the kind Puerto Rico has. "Translation" near lease, rental, tenancy or contract returns nothing anywhere in the Wyoming statutes in either word order, "negotiate" near "language" returns nothing in either word order, and the word "Spanish" appears exactly once in the entire Wyoming code, in a revenue provision in Title 39. Wyoming's stated policy runs the other way. Wyo. Stat. § 8-6-101(a) provides that "English shall be designated as the official language of Wyoming," and that except as otherwise provided by law no state agency or political subdivision shall be required to provide documents, information, literature or other written materials in any language other than English. That section binds state agencies and political subdivisions, NOT you — it imposes nothing on a private landlord and it does not forbid you from translating anything. Its practical significance for you is that you cannot expect the state to supply a translated lease, notice or disclosure form, and no state body is obliged to produce one on request. Wyo. Stat. § 8-6-101(b) lists eight purposes for which a state agency or political subdivision MAY act in another language anyway, including providing information orally in the course of delivering services, complying with federal law, protecting public health or safety, and protecting the rights of parties and witnesses in a civil or criminal action or an administrative proceeding — so a court interpreter in an eviction case is expressly contemplated. Because nothing requires a translation, nothing regulates one either, and that cuts both ways. If you choose to provide a translated lease and the two versions conflict, no Wyoming statute says which prevails; the lease itself must say, so include a clause naming the English text as controlling and recording that the translation was provided only as an accommodation. Three outside constraints still apply and are the real exposure. First, the Wyoming Fair Housing Act. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103 makes it unlawful to discriminate in the rental of a dwelling because of national origin, among the other listed classes, and Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-104, the publication provision, is the one that survives even the owner-occupied exemption in Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-110(b). A blanket refusal to deal with anyone who does not speak English, or screening applied more harshly to people who do not, is a national-origin problem whatever the translation rules say. Second, the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, which has a knowing-conduct standard and is not limited to goods: Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-105(a)(viii) reaches a knowing false representation about the rights, remedies or obligations a transaction involves, and the catch-all at § 40-12-105(a)(xv) reaches unfair or deceptive acts or practices. Describing the lease orally in one language and then handing over an English document that says something different is squarely within that shape. Third, federal fair housing law applies independently. The sensible practice, since no rule binds you: negotiate and sign in the same language you advertised in; if the tenant does not read English well, let them bring their own adult interpreter and note in the file who it was; give a courtesy translation where you can, with an English-controls clause; and never sign up a tenant who plainly does not understand what the document says, because an unenforceable lease is worse than a slow one.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText:
Wyoming gives you a usable criminal trespass tool, and it is drafted more broadly than most states' versions. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-303(a): 'A person is guilty of criminal trespass if he enters or remains on or in the land or premises of another person, knowing he is not authorized to do so, or after being notified to depart or to not trespass.' Notice is given either by 'personal communication to the person by the owner or occupant, or his agent, or by a peace officer' under (a)(i), or by 'posting of signs reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders' under (a)(ii). The offence is a misdemeanor punishable under § 6-3-303(b) by imprisonment for not more than six (6) months, a fine of not more than seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00), or both.

Three features of that text are worth pausing on. First, the offence covers remaining as well as entering, so someone who was welcome when they arrived commits the offence by staying after you tell them to go. Second, the statute contains no list of defences. Unlike the neighbouring criminal entry offence, § 6-3-303 has no guest, invitee, business-purpose or open-to-the-public defence written into it. Third, notice may come from the 'owner or occupant, or his agent,' which means your property manager can issue a no-trespass notice in your name — and it also means your tenant, as the occupant, can issue one for their own unit.

That third point cuts both ways and sets the boundary of this tool. A person your tenant has invited into the tenant's unit is authorized by the occupant to be there, so you cannot make them a trespasser from the unit by your own say-so. Your route against a tenant's problem guest runs through the tenant and the lease: § 1-21-1204(a)(v) caps occupants at the number specified in the rental agreement and requires your written permission to exceed it; § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) requires the renter to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement; § 1-21-1205(a)(ii) forbids a renter to interfere with another person's peaceful enjoyment of the residential property; and § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) makes a violation of § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205 a ground for forcible entry and detainer. Common areas, parking lots, laundry rooms and hallways are a different matter: there you are the owner and the person in control, and a written no-trespass notice to a former tenant, an ex-partner or a persistent nuisance is exactly what § 6-3-303 contemplates.

You cannot use trespass against your own tenant, and the statute says so. Section 6-3-303(c) reads: 'This section does not supersede W.S. 1-21-1003.' A tenant leaves by notice to quit under § 1-21-1003 and a forcible entry and detainer action, never by a trespass complaint. Nor is there a shortcut in Wyoming's non-judicial removal procedure for unauthorized occupants at §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403: § 1-21-1402(a)(ii) requires that the person have 'unlawfully entered and remain[ed]', and § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes any current or former tenant under a written or oral agreement. Getting it wrong is expensive — § 1-21-1403(c) lets a wrongfully removed person be restored to possession and recover actual costs and damages plus statutory damages equal to triple the fair market rental value of the dwelling for the period of wrongful removal. And § 6-3-306 makes it a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00) for anyone who 'violently takes or keeps possession of land without authority of law,' which is a description of a self-help lockout.

How to do it properly. Put the ban in writing, date it, identify the person by name and description, describe the property and the areas covered, state plainly that the person is not authorized to enter or remain and is notified not to trespass, and deliver it personally or have a peace officer deliver it — § 6-3-303(a)(i) requires personal communication, so a letter left in a mailbox is weaker than a hand delivery you can prove. Keep a copy with a note of who delivered it, when and how, and give a copy to your local police department or sheriff so an officer responding later can see the notice already exists. Post signs at the entrances and in the parking area as well, since § 6-3-303(a)(ii) makes posting an independent method of giving notice to intruders generally. If the person is in a building rather than on open ground, the separate offence of criminal entry under § 6-3-302 may also apply to entering a building, occupied structure, vehicle or a separately secured or occupied portion of those enclosures without authority — but note that § 6-3-302(b) does supply affirmative defences, including that the enclosure was open to the public and the person complied with all lawful conditions of access, and that the person reasonably believed the owner 'or other person empowered to license access' would have authorized entry. A tenant is such a person, so expect that defence from a tenant's visitor. Section 6-3-307 covers the worst case, unlawful entry into an occupied structure where the person commits or attempts battery or domestic battery.

One thing Wyoming does not give you is a statutory civil remedy. There is no statute awarding damages, attorney's fees or punitive damages for trespass on premises; the two trespass damages provisions in Wyoming law are for computer trespass and for trespassing to collect resource data, neither of which applies here. Your civil claim is common-law trespass, and under § 1-3-105(a)(iv)(A) an action for trespass upon real property must be brought within four (4) years after the cause of action accrues.

title: No Truth in Renting Act and No Banned-Terms List
bodyText:
Wyoming has no Truth in Renting Act. There is no state-published statement of tenants' and landlords' rights that you must give out or post, no required notice in the lease telling the tenant that a lease cannot waive their rights, and no plain-language mandate for the lease itself. The phrase "truth in renting" appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and neither do "plain english" or any readability requirement for a rental agreement. Do not reach for New Jersey's or Michigan's model: there is no Wyoming handbook to hand over and no Wyoming agency charged with producing one.

There is also no list of lease terms Wyoming declares void. This is the part that most distinguishes Wyoming, and it cuts in your favour while placing the responsibility on you. Michigan's act voids specified clauses and gives the tenant damages for including one; Wyoming does nothing of the kind. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) runs the other way, providing that any duty or obligation in the landlord-tenant article may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in that article. The conditions are cumulative — explicit, written, and signed by the parties — so a term buried in a rules addendum nobody signed does not get the benefit of it. The one hard floor in Wyoming landlord-tenant law sits elsewhere: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1304 provides that the Safe Homes Act "shall not be waived or modified in any lease or separate agreement between a landlord and tenant." Note two further limits on § 1-21-1202(d). It says "this article," so it reaches Article 12 only and is no authority for contracting around the eviction procedure in Article 10, including the three-day notice to quit under § 1-21-1003. And Article 12 itself applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence, because § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines "residential rental unit" that way and excludes a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

So what actually polices your lease wording? One thing, and it is worth respecting. The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches landlords: § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines merchandise to include property "real, personal or mixed," there is no real-property exemption, and § 40-12-105(a) makes it a deceptive trade practice to do the listed things "knowingly" — including, at (a)(viii), misrepresenting that a consumer transaction involves rights, remedies or obligations that it does not, and at (a)(xv), engaging in unfair or deceptive acts generally. A lease clause that tells a tenant they have given up a right they cannot give up, or that describes your obligations in a way you know is wrong, is squarely within (a)(viii). That is the Wyoming analogue of a truth-in-renting violation, and the "knowingly" gate means the risk grows the moment you are told a clause is inaccurate and leave it in. There is a meaningful procedural protection for you: under § 40-12-109 a consumer generally cannot sue without first giving you written notice stating fully the nature of the alleged practice and the actual damage, within one year after discovering it or two years after the transaction, whichever comes first, and the practice must have become uncured. Treat such a notice as the opportunity it is and fix the clause.

Two practical conclusions. First, because no statute makes your lease readable and no statute voids an overreaching term, the quality of the lease is entirely on you — and a term a court will not enforce is worse than useless, because you will have relied on it. Write in ordinary language, put anything that shifts a statutory duty in its own clearly headed clause, and get a signature on every addendum you intend to rely on. Second, do not expect the state to translate anything. Wyo. Stat. § 8-6-101(a) makes English the official language of Wyoming and provides that, except as otherwise provided by law, no state agency or political subdivision is required to provide documents, information, literature or other written materials in any language other than English. If you rent to tenants who do not read English well, any translation or plain-language explanation is yours to arrange, and arranging one is a sensible way to reduce exactly the § 40-12-105(a)(viii) risk described above.

title: Removing an Unauthorized Occupant Without an Eviction
bodyText:
Wyoming now has a non-judicial route for removing a squatter. It is new: Article 14 of Title 1 chapter 21, Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1401 through 1-21-1403, created by 2025 Wyo. Sess. Laws ch. 20 (SF0006), effective July 1, 2025, with a companion criminal offence at Wyo. Stat. § 6-5-309 and a new felony at Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-201(b)(iv). Read the next paragraph before anything else.

THIS CANNOT BE USED AGAINST A TENANT. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(a)(iv) excludes from the procedure anyone who "is not a current or former tenant pursuant to a written or oral rental or lease agreement authorized by the owner, the owner's predecessor or the owner's authorized agent." Current OR former. Written OR oral. Authorized by you, by whoever owned the property before you, or by your agent. A tenant who stops paying, a tenant who holds over after the term, a tenant in breach of any rule - none of them can be removed this way. For them the only route is forcible entry and detainer: the three-day grace period in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i), the separate three-day notice to quit in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003, and an action in circuit court under Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1001 through 1-21-1017. Using Article 14 against a tenant is not a shortcut; it is the mistake the statute is built to punish, and the penalty is set out below.

THE FIVE CONDITIONS, ALL OF WHICH MUST BE MET. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(a) an owner or the owner's authorized agent may ask law enforcement in the county where the property is located for the immediate removal of a person unlawfully occupying or possessing the owner's residential dwelling only "if all of the following conditions are met": (i) the person requesting removal is the owner or the owner's authorized agent; (ii) the unauthorized person "has unlawfully entered and remains or continues to reside in" the dwelling - both limbs, so lawful original entry defeats the procedure; (iii) there is no known pending litigation related to the dwelling between the owner and any known unauthorized person; (iv) the person is not a current or former tenant under any written or oral rental or lease agreement authorized by the owner, the owner's predecessor or the owner's agent; and (v) the person is not an immediate family member of the OWNER or in a cohabiting relationship with the OWNER. Note two things about (v): "immediate family member" is defined narrowly in Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1401(a)(i) as a spouse, child or parent, and the relationship that matters is to the owner, not to the tenant. What actually bars Article 14 against a tenant's overstaying guest is condition (ii): a guest the tenant let in did not unlawfully enter.

WHO AND WHAT COUNT. "Law enforcement" means the sheriff, the sheriff's deputies or peace officers of a city or town (§ 1-21-1401(a)(ii)). "Residential dwelling" is broad - a dwelling or property, real or otherwise, serving as a place of residence or other facilities held out for a person's occupancy, including the real property where the dwelling sits (§ 1-21-1401(a)(iv)). "Unauthorized person" is a person not authorized to maintain presence or residency in the dwelling (§ 1-21-1401(a)(v)).

THE SWORN COMPLAINT, AND WHAT IT MUST SAY. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(b) requires you to submit to law enforcement in that county a complaint for removal stating at a minimum ten things: (i) that you are the owner or the owner's authorized agent; (ii) that an unauthorized person has unlawfully entered and is remaining or residing unlawfully in the dwelling; (iii) that the person is not an owner or co-owner and has not been listed on title, unless the person has engaged in title fraud; (iv) that there is no known pending litigation related to the property between you and the person; (v) the current-or-former-tenant negative; (vi) the immediate-family-or-cohabitant negative; (vii) your acknowledgment that a person removed under the section may sue you for false statements in the complaint or for wrongfully using the procedure, and that you may be liable for actual damages, penalties, costs and reasonable attorney fees; (viii) that you are requesting immediate removal; (ix) a copy of your valid government-issued identification, or of the documents authorizing an agent to act for you; and (x) that the information is true and correct and the complaint is submitted under penalty of perjury. Paragraph (b)(iii), the title and co-owner point, appears only in the complaint list and not among the (a) conditions - so check it anyway, because the complaint is sworn. And because (b)(x) puts the whole complaint under penalty of perjury, getting it wrong is not merely a civil risk: a knowingly false certificate or declaration under a lawfully administered oath outside a judicial or administrative proceeding is a felony under Wyo. Stat. § 6-5-303(a), punishable by up to two years and a $2,000.00 fine.

WHAT LAW ENFORCEMENT DOES. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1402(c) law enforcement must verify that you are the record owner or the owner's authorized agent and that you are entitled to relief, and if they cannot verify it they have no obligation to give notice or to clear the dwelling. On verification, § 1-21-1402(d) requires them, without delay, to give notice to immediately vacate to all unauthorized persons and to put you in possession. Notice may be by hand delivery to the occupant or by posting on the front door or entrance. They must also attempt to verify and must document the identities of everyone occupying the dwelling, and may arrest anyone found there for trespass, outstanding warrants or any other legal cause. There is no waiting period and no court hearing.

LOCKS AND BELONGINGS. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(a) lets you, after the notice to vacate has been given, ask law enforcement to stand by to keep the peace while you change the locks and remove the unauthorized person's personal property from the premises "to or near the property line." Do it with the officer present - that is the only lock change Wyoming law authorises anywhere in Title 1. Under § 1-21-1403(b) law enforcement is not liable for loss, destruction or damage to property removed, and you are not liable either, with two exceptions written into the same sentence: unless the removal was wrongful, or unless the property is wantonly destroyed or damaged. So move the goods out; do not break them.

THE PRICE OF GETTING IT WRONG. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(c) creates a civil cause of action against the owner or the owner's authorized agent for wrongful removal. A person harmed "may be restored to possession of the residential dwelling" and may recover (i) actual costs and damages incurred; (ii) statutory damages equal to TRIPLE the fair market value of renting the dwelling during the period of wrongful removal; (iii) court costs; and (iv) reasonable attorney fees. Attorney fees are rare against a Wyoming landlord - there is no fee-shifting anywhere in Article 10 or Article 12 - and here they are automatic on a wrongful removal, on top of triple the fair market rental value and restoration of possession. Note also that your authorized agent is exposed alongside you, so a property manager who files the complaint is personally in the frame.

WHAT ARTICLE 14 DOES NOT DISPLACE. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1403(d) preserves the rights of an owner, a peace officer's authority to arrest for trespassing, vandalism, theft or any other criminal offence, and remedies available under Title 1 chapter 21 or any other law. So Article 14 sits alongside forcible entry and detainer, not in place of it. If any one of the five conditions is doubtful, use the court route.

TWO NEW CRIMES THAT CAME WITH IT, AND ONE OF THEM CAN CATCH YOU. Wyo. Stat. § 6-5-309(a) makes it a misdemeanor, up to six months and a $750.00 fine, for a person who, with intent to detain or remain on real property or in a residential dwelling, knowingly presents to another a false document purporting to be a valid lease agreement, deed or other instrument conveying real property rights - the fake-lease squatter. Section 6-5-309(b) is a felony, up to two years and a $5,000.00 fine, for a person who lists or advertises residential real property for sale knowing the purported seller has no legal title or authority to sell, "or who rents or leases the property to another person knowing that he has no lawful ownership or leasehold interest in the property." Read that second limb as directed at you as well as at a fraudster: if your right to let the property has ended - a foreclosure completed, a head lease terminated, an authority withdrawn - continuing to let it is within the words of a felony. And Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-201(b)(iv), added by the same act, makes property destruction and defacement a felony punishable by up to ten years and a $10,000.00 fine where the person unlawfully detains or occupies a residential dwelling as defined by § 1-21-1401(a)(iv) and knowingly defaces, injures or destroys property in or on it, regardless of the cost of restoration or the value destroyed. Photograph the condition of the dwelling when you recover it; that felony has no damage threshold, so the evidence is what makes it chargeable.

HOW TO DECIDE, IN ONE LINE. Was there ever a rental agreement with this person, written or oral, with you or any predecessor or agent? If yes, or if you are not certain, it is a forcible entry and detainer case. Only a person who broke in, who never had an agreement, who is not your spouse, child, parent or cohabitant, and against whom nothing is pending, goes to the sheriff.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local ordinances were not searched; no Wyoming court has yet construed Article 14 so far as this corpus shows.

title: No unbundled parking rule, and wide authority to set your own parking terms
bodyText:
Wyoming has no statute requiring or regulating the separation of parking charges from residential rent. There is no Wyoming counterpart to California's Civil Code § 1947.1: no mandatory unbundling for new or larger buildings, no required separate parking agreement, no tenant right of first refusal to spaces, no rule that an unpaid parking fee cannot support an eviction, and no cap on what you may charge for a space. The word "unbundled" appears once in the entire Wyoming statutes, in Title 37, in a utility context. You may include parking in the rent, charge for it separately, or do both for different tenants, as you choose.

WHAT WYOMING DOES GIVE YOU IS BROAD CONTROL OF THE LOT. Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-111(a) provides that nothing in the Motor Vehicle Act prevents the owner of real property used by the public for vehicular travel BY PERMISSION OF THE OWNER, and not as a matter of right, from prohibiting that use, from requiring other, different or additional conditions than the Act specifies, or otherwise regulating use of the real property as the owner determines. A residential parking lot is exactly that kind of property. So your parking rules - who may park, where, in what, for how long, with what permit - are yours to set, subject to the lease and to any ordinance.

ACCESSIBLE PARKING IS THE ONE PLACE WYOMING SETS SPECIFICATIONS, AND IT WORKS DIFFERENTLY FROM WHAT YOU MIGHT EXPECT. Under Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-111(b), a private real property owner may reserve parking spaces for the handicapped and erect signs in accordance with § 31-5-501(b), BUT ONLY WITH THE APPROVAL of the board of county commissioners or the local governing body having jurisdiction - and once approved, those signs are enforceable under § 31-5-501(c) or under any existing municipal ordinance. Section 31-5-501(b) sets the specifications: signs of durable material, carrying the international symbol of accessibility, no smaller than twelve inches by eighteen inches, placed above ground level so as to be visible at all times and not obscured by a parked vehicle; spaces located on the shortest possible accessible circulation route to an accessible entrance of the building; spaces that allow easy wheelchair entry and exit, including signage and any adjacent cross-hatched access markings, and located on a level surface. The two percent minimum - at least two percent of the total available spaces, and never fewer than one - is written for "public parking lots of ten (10) or more parking spaces", so whether it reaches your residential lot depends on whether that lot is a public parking lot, which the section does not define. Section 31-5-501(c) makes the signs official signs and makes it unlawful to willfully park in violation of them, which is the practical benefit: without local approval and conforming signs, your reserved accessible space is not enforceable as a traffic matter at all. Get the approval.

FAIR HOUSING REACHES PARKING EVEN WHERE THE MOTOR VEHICLE ACT DOES NOT. Wyoming's own fair housing act applies. Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(b) bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of rental of a dwelling or in the provision of services or facilities in connection with it because of a disability. Section 40-26-107(c)(ii) makes it discrimination to refuse a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services if the accommodation may be necessary to afford the individual equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling - which is the provision an accessible or closer parking space request runs on, and the usual answer is yes, including waiving a parking fee where the space is needed because of the disability. Section 40-26-107(c)(iii) makes it discrimination to fail to design and construct a covered multifamily dwelling so that the public use and common use portions are readily accessible to and usable by individuals with a disability; § 40-26-107(d) treats compliance with the referenced American national standard as satisfying the adaptive design requirements, and § 40-26-107(e) exempts from subparagraph (c)(iii)(A) ONLY - not from the whole of (c)(iii) - a building first occupied on or before March 13, 1991. Section 40-26-107(c)(i) covers reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense, with an express rental carve-out allowing you to condition permission on restoration "when it is reasonable to do so".

THREE DRAFTING POINTS. First, how you label the money matters. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines the "residential rental unit" to include the appurtenances, grounds, common areas and facilities held out for the occupancy of residential renters generally AND any other area or facility provided to the renter in the rental agreement. A space you assign in the lease is therefore part of the unit, and your § 1-21-1203(a)(ii) duty to maintain common areas in a sanitary and reasonably safe condition covers it. Unbundling into a separate agreement does not make the lot stop being a common area held out generally. Second, if the parking fee is defined in your lease as rent, non-payment is a nonpayment case under § 1-21-1002(a)(i) with its three-day grace; if it is not rent, non-payment is a breach of a lease term, enforceable under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) through the renter's duty in § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement. Decide which you want and say so. Third, if you would rather be able to withdraw a space than to evict over it, keep parking in a separate, revocable agreement and say in the residential lease that no parking is included.

TWO LIMITS. If the building is a condominium, parking areas are within the common areas and facilities described in Wyoming's Condominium Ownership Act, so the declaration, not you, may control their assignment. And towing, parking minimums and lot standards are overwhelmingly municipal: Wyo. Stat. §§ 15-1-801 et seq. gives cities and towns power over off-street parking facilities, and ordinances are outside what this review can resolve.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText:
Wyoming has NO statutory unconscionability doctrine for a residential lease. There is no provision letting a court refuse to enforce a rental agreement or strike a clause as unconscionable, no list of presumptively unconscionable terms, and no statute declaring any particular lease clause enforceable notwithstanding unconscionability. Nothing in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1201 through 1-21-1211, the landlord-tenant article, or in Title 34, the property title, speaks to unconscionability at all — the word does not appear in either title. Every one of the 27 appearances of “unconscionab” in the Wyoming code is in Title 40 chapter 14, the Uniform Consumer Credit Code, and none of them reaches an ordinary residential lease.

WHY THE UCCC DOES NOT HELP A TENANT. Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-508(a) does give a court the familiar powers — refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest without the unconscionable clause, or limit the clause to avoid an unconscionable result — with § 40-14-508(b) guaranteeing the parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence of the clause’s setting, purpose and effect, and § 40-14-508(c) providing that a charge or practice expressly permitted by the act is not in itself unconscionable. But § 40-14-508(a) applies only “with respect to a consumer credit sale, consumer lease, or consumer loan,” and each of those is a defined term that excludes renting a home. Section 40-14-206(a) defines “consumer lease” as a lease of GOODS — so a dwelling is out. Section 40-14-204(a) defines “consumer credit sale” as a sale of goods, services OR AN INTEREST IN LAND meeting five conditions, which is the one door that opens onto real property.

THE ONE REAL EXPOSURE: RENT-TO-OWN AND LEASE-OPTIONS. Wyo. Stat. § 40-14-205(f) provides that a “sale of an interest in land” includes a lease in which the lessee has an option to purchase the interest and all or a substantial part of the rental or other payments previously made are applied to the purchase price. If you write a rent-to-own or lease-purchase arrangement on those terms, you may have made a consumer credit sale rather than a lease, and § 40-14-508 unconscionability can then apply to the whole agreement. Read the carve-out carefully, because it is counterintuitive: § 40-14-204(b)(ii) says “consumer credit sale” does NOT include a sale of an interest in land if the credit service charge does not exceed eighteen percent per year on the actuarial method, “except as provided for disclosure and debtors’ remedies in W.S. 40-14-520.” And § 40-14-520(a) pulls a land sale back in only for the civil liability for disclosure violations under § 40-14-522 and the debtor’s right to rescind — it does not pull back in § 40-14-508. So the practical result is a split: a lease-option carrying an effective credit charge over eighteen percent is a consumer credit sale fully subject to the unconscionability section, while one at or under eighteen percent escapes § 40-14-508 but still faces the UCCC disclosure liability and rescission rules. If you do any rent-to-own business, price it below that line and give the disclosures. Note too that § 40-14-106(a) bars a buyer, lessee or debtor from waiving UCCC rights, and § 40-14-106(d) voids a settlement waiving them if the court finds the settlement unconscionable when made, weighing the person’s competence, any deception or coercion, the legal advice received and the value of the consideration.

WHAT ACTUALLY POLICES A WYOMING LEASE. First, common-law unconscionability. Wyoming courts apply the ordinary contract doctrine, which comes from case law, not statute; case law is not in this statutory corpus, so treat it as a live litigation risk rather than a rule you can read off a page. Second, the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act, which is the only real statutory hook: Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi) defines “merchandise” to include property “real, personal or mixed,” there is no real-property exemption in § 40-12-110, and § 40-12-105(a) reaches conduct done “knowingly,” with (a)(viii) and the (a)(xv) catch-all able to reach lease wording and advertising. The WCPA does not use the word “unconscionable,” so it is an unfairness-and-deception statute, not an unconscionability statute, and § 40-12-109 requires the consumer to give pre-suit notice and a cure period. Third, go the other way and remember how much Wyoming lets you do: § 1-21-1202(d) permits any duty in the landlord-tenant article to be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, Article 12 has no anti-waiver section, and the only non-waivable provision in the field is § 1-21-1304, the Safe Homes Act. A one-sided Wyoming lease is far more likely to be enforced than struck.

ONE GAP YOU SHOULD KNOW ABOUT. Wyoming codifies its Uniform Commercial Code separately as Title 34.1, which was not part of the statutory set searched for this library. UCC § 2-302, the general sale-of-goods unconscionability section, and Article 2A on leases of goods therefore were not checked. That gap does not change the answer for a lease of a dwelling — the UCC governs goods, not real property — but if your transaction involves furnishings, appliances or equipment leased separately, assume a UCC unconscionability rule exists and verify it.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant in Wyoming
bodyText:
Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Wyoming property law does not use. The word 'usufruct' appears nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes or the Wyoming Constitution, so the civil-law rule about a lease granted by a usufructuary does not arise here. The closest Wyoming interest is a life estate — for example a surviving spouse who holds the home for life while the children hold the remainder — and Wyoming does have one statute directly on point.

Wyo. Stat. § 34-1-111 reads: 'A conveyance made by a tenant for life or years, purporting to grant a greater estate than he possessed or could lawfully convey, shall not work a forfeiture of his estate, but shall pass to the grantee all the estate which such tenant could lawfully convey.' A lease is a conveyance of a possessory interest, so this answers both halves of the question. First, granting a lease whose term could outlast your life estate does not forfeit the life estate — you are not penalized for overreaching. Second, the lease passes only what you could lawfully convey, which is your own interest. When the life estate ends, so does the tenant's right to possession derived from it. Nothing in the statute makes the remainder owners take the lease, and no Wyoming statute makes you liable to the tenant for the shortfall the way La. Civ. Code art. 2716 makes a Louisiana usufructuary liable — but the absence of a statute is not a defense to a misrepresentation claim, and the Wyoming Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing (merchandise includes real property, Wyo. Stat. § 40-12-102(a)(vi); no real-property exemption at § 40-12-110; § 40-12-105(a) is gated on 'knowingly' and includes the (a)(xv) catch-all). Renting out a term you know you may not be able to deliver, without saying so, is the exposure.

What happens next is quick and public. Under Wyo. Stat. § 2-9-101, when a person dies seized of a life estate that terminates by reason of death, an interested person may petition the court, and on hearing the court enters a decree, recorded with the county clerk, that is presumptive evidence of the creation and termination of the estate and of who now holds it. Wyo. Stat. § 2-9-102 provides a simpler route by affidavit of survivorship with a death certificate attached. Your tenant will find a new owner of record with a recorded decree or affidavit, and will need to be told where to pay rent.

If the remainder owners let the tenant stay on, understand what Wyoming makes of that. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 says that in Wyoming the relation of landlord and tenant does not exist by implication or operation of law except a tenancy by sufferance, and that on expiration of a term there is no implied renewal 'either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent' — holding over plus acceptance of rent creates only a tenancy by sufferance. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-129 adds that an expired lease is renewed only by express written contract signed by the parties. So the new owners do not become bound to your lease by taking rent; whoever wants a real tenancy after the life estate ends must sign a new written lease.

The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease (use the optional Landlord's Status clause filed with this row), keep the term short or make it month to month, and — if the tenant needs certainty — have the remainder owners sign the lease too, or sign a written agreement that the lease continues if your life estate ends first. Keep the deposit and prepaid rent accounted for, because the deposit obligations in Wyo. Stat. §§ 1-21-1207 and 1-21-1208 bind 'the holder of the interest of the owner or designated agent in the residential rental unit at the time of termination of the rental agreement' under § 1-21-1209, which means the person holding the property when the tenancy ends — potentially the remainder owners rather than your estate. Tell them, in writing, what you are holding and for whom.

What Wyoming does not have: no statute apportioning rent between a deceased life tenant's estate and the remainder owners, no emblements statute, and no notice duty to the tenant on the death of a lessor. Those are matters of case law and of the terms of the instrument that created the life estate, both outside this library.

title: Wyoming's Real Limit on Charging Tenants for Utilities
bodyText: Wyoming has no utility-allowance statute and no cap on an allowance figure, and nothing in the landlord-tenant article says anything about utility billing. But do not conclude that you may bill utilities however you like, because the binding constraint lives in the public utilities title, which never uses the word 'landlord' at all. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H) opens 'None of the provisions of this chapter shall apply to:' and then lists ten independent non-applications. Subparagraph (VI) exempts the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, the manufacture or distribution of gas, the furnishing or distribution of water, and the production, delivery or furnishing of steam or any other substance, by a person 'for the sole use of a producer or other person, or FOR THE USE OF TENANTS of a producer or other person and not for sale to others' — and then takes much of it back: 'Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants.' That clawback sentence is internal to (VI): it says 'Such exemptions', meaning the several stated in (VI), and it closes at the semicolon before (VII). It does not reach the later carve-outs. The practical result is the rule you must build your lease around. FURNISHING a utility to your tenants is exempt. SELLING it to them by meter, or by any other direct sale, is not — and if you are not exempt, you are inside the chapter as a public utility, subject to public service commission rate regulation and tariff filing. For electricity and gas there is no tenant carve-out at all, so a submetered per-kilowatt-hour or per-therm charge to a residential tenant is the exact conduct the clawback names and is genuinely dangerous. For WATER there is a narrow carve-out and it is itself a cap, written in the statute's own words. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VIII) exempts 'Metered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants WHEN the metered or other direct sales are SOLELY FOR PURPOSES OF ALLOCATING USAGE AMONG TENANTS and INCLUDES NO ADDITIONAL FEES OR CHARGES.' Three conditions in one sentence: it must be water, the purpose must be solely allocation among tenants, and there must be no additional fee or charge of any kind. Pass the bill through at cost and nothing more. A billing fee, an administration fee, a meter-reading fee, a third-party biller's fee passed on, a markup, a minimum charge or a profit margin each defeat the exemption on the face of the words, and defeating it does not just invalidate the fee — it removes your exemption from the whole chapter. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(IX) is a second, different water carve-out, for a person operating a water system that has fewer than FIFTEEN potential service connections, is not owned, controlled or affiliated with a water or other utility providing water service, is not a centralized water supply system associated with a subdivision, and is not within a water utility's established service territory or a municipality's corporate limits. Do not reason across from the ten-connection threshold in Wyoming's drinking-water statutes at Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-4-220 to 35-4-224 — the numbers are different and so are the subjects. Two more carve-outs exist and neither helps with tenant utilities: (H)(VII) covers the retail sale of compressed natural gas as motor vehicle fuel by a person not otherwise regulated, and (H)(X) covers the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person not otherwise regulated. (X) IS an electricity carve-out, so do not say flatly that Wyoming has none — but it reaches EV charging only and does nothing for submetered household electricity. So the lawful shapes for a Wyoming residential lease are these. Build the utility cost into the Rent and furnish the service — that is 'furnishing for the use of tenants' and is squarely inside the (VI) exemption. Or have the tenant take service in their own name directly from the utility, which takes you out of it entirely. Or, for WATER only, allocate the actual bill among tenants with no fee or charge added, under (H)(VIII). An allowance-plus-overage structure, where you absorb a stated amount and bill the tenant the excess measured by a submeter, is the structure to avoid for electricity and gas: it is a direct sale measured by meter and it is what the (VI) clawback catches. If you want the economics of an allowance without the risk, set the Rent to include the expected utility cost and raise the Rent at renewal rather than billing usage mid-term. Three related points. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) treats a deposit 'held and separately identified as a utilities deposit' on its own cascade — refund within ten days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges have been paid, and absent that showing within forty-five days of termination, apply it within fifteen days thereafter — so if you take a utilities deposit, identify it separately in writing or it falls back into the ordinary thirty-day deposit rule in § 1-21-1208(a). Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets you deduct 'other costs provided by any contract', so an unpaid utility charge your lease creates is deductible. And Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-402 is NOT your remedy against a tenant who diverts a utility: § 37-12-402(a) opens 'a utility may bring a civil action', and the double damages in (c) are gated on willful or intentional conduct — the claim runs to the utility, not to you.

title: Billing Tenants for Utilities That Are Not Separately Metered
bodyText:
Wyoming has no landlord-tenant rule on this at all. No statute makes unenforceable a term charging a tenant for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit, none prescribes an allocation formula, none caps an administrative or late charge on a utility bill, none requires you to give the tenant a copy of the underlying bill, and none bars you from disconnecting for nonpayment of a utility charge. There is no Connecticut-style effective date to watch for. "Separately metered", "submeter", "ratio utility" and "master meter" (outside one noncodified Gillette water project) return nothing in Wyoming law.

THE LIMIT COMES FROM UTILITY REGULATION, NOT FROM LANDLORD-TENANT LAW, and it is a serious one. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H) opens "None of the provisions of this chapter shall apply to:" and then lists ten independent non-applications. Three of them decide this topic.

Paragraph (H)(VI) exempts "the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, or to the manufacture or distribution of gas, or to the furnishing or distribution of water, nor to the production, delivery or furnishing of steam or any other substance, by a producer or other person, for the sole use of a producer or other person, or for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others." Then comes the sentence that matters: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." That clawback is internal to paragraph (VI) — it says "Such exemptions", meaning the ones (VI) itself grants, and it closes before paragraph (VII) begins. It does not reach (VIII), (IX) or (X).

So the shape is this. Furnishing electricity or gas to your tenants as part of what they pay for the premises is exempt. SELLING it to them is not. And read the clawback's words: it covers "metered or other direct sales". The phrase is not limited to submetering. Paragraph (VIII) confirms the drafter's usage by describing an allocation as a species of "other direct sales". The cautious conclusion, and the one we recommend acting on, is that a ratio-based allocation of an electricity or gas bill — charging each unit a share of the master bill by square footage, occupancy or any other formula — is a "direct sale" inside the (VI) clawback just as a submeter reading would be. Doing it puts you outside the exemption and exposes you to being treated as a public utility, with the Public Service Commission's rate, tariff and reporting apparatus behind it. Do not do it.

WATER IS DIFFERENT, AND THE CARVE-OUT IS NARROW. Paragraph (H)(VIII) exempts "[m]etered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants when the metered or other direct sales are SOLELY for purposes of allocating usage among tenants and includes NO ADDITIONAL FEES OR CHARGES." Both conditions are cumulative and both are strict. "Solely for allocating usage" means you may divide the actual bill among the tenants and no more — no margin, no rounding up, no recovery of anything beyond the water itself. "No additional fees or charges" kills an administrative fee, a billing fee, a meter-reading fee, a third-party billing company's charge passed through, and a late fee attached to the water line. Add any one of those and you are outside (VIII) and back inside the (VI) clawback. If you allocate water, pass through the exact bill, show the arithmetic, and charge nothing else.

Paragraph (H)(IX) is a separate and unrelated water exemption for a person operating a water SYSTEM that has fewer than fifteen (15) potential service connections, is not owned, controlled or affiliated with a water or other utility providing water service, is not a centralized water supply system associated with a subdivision, and is not within a water utility's established service territory or a municipality's corporate limits. Note the number: fifteen here, but TEN service connections is the threshold for the public-drinking-water duties at Wyo. Stat. §§ 35-4-220 to 35-4-224, which include monthly bacteriological sampling. Do not reason across from one to the other.

Paragraph (H)(X) exempts "the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under this title." That is a genuine electricity carve-out, but it covers EV charging only. It does not help with household submetering, and the two must not be run together.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. Three clean routes, in order of preference. (1) Have the tenant be the utility's own customer, with the account in the tenant's name — then no sale by you occurs at all. (2) Include the utility in the rent as a single, undifferentiated rent figure, with no separate utility line; you are then furnishing for the use of tenants under (VI) and not selling. (3) For water only, allocate under (VIII) on the strict terms above. A fourth route some landlords reach for — a fixed monthly "utility charge" on top of rent — is the dangerous middle ground, because a separately stated charge for a commodity looks like a sale. If you want the economics of route (2) with the transparency of route (3), raise the rent and say in the lease that rent includes the utility.

THREE WYOMING POINTS THAT GO WITH THIS. First, deposits: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) gives a SEPARATELY IDENTIFIED utilities deposit its own refund cascade — refund within ten (10) days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges have been paid; absent that showing within forty-five (45) days of termination, apply the deposit to the outstanding utility debt within fifteen (15) days thereafter; and pay any refund within seven (7) days after application, or fifteen (15) days after receiving the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later. That cascade runs only if the deposit is separately identified as a utilities deposit, so label it or lose it. Second, tampering damages: Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-402(a) opens "a utility may bring a civil action", so the double damages in (c) run to the UTILITY, not to you and not to the tenant. Third, if you misstate what a tenant will pay for utilities, Wyoming's Consumer Protection Act reaches residential leasing (§ 40-12-102(a)(vi) brings real property inside "merchandise", § 40-12-105(a) is gated on knowing conduct, and there is no real-property exemption at § 40-12-110).

See also the library's electric submetering disclosure row for Wyoming, which covers the electricity side in more detail.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment in Wyoming, but Three Rules Still Bite
bodyText:
Wyoming requires no utility disclosure attachment. There is no statute making you attach a utility addendum to the lease, disclose which utilities serve the unit or who pays for them, provide historical consumption or average-cost figures, explain an allocation formula, or give notice before shifting a utility from your account to the tenant's. The words "submeter," "shared meter," "ratio utility" and "utility allocation" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes. But three real Wyoming rules bear on utilities in a residential lease, and two of them are easy to walk into.

First, and most important if you bill utilities through to tenants: you can become a regulated public utility. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) exempts the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, the manufacture or distribution of gas, the furnishing or distribution of water, and the production, delivery or furnishing of steam or any other substance by a person "for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others" - and then takes the exemption straight back: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." So furnishing utilities to your tenants as part of the rent is outside public-utility regulation, but metering and selling a utility commodity to them is not. There is one carve-out, and it is narrow. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VIII) exempts "[m]etered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants when the metered or other direct sales are solely for purposes of allocating usage among tenants and includes no additional fees or charges." Read every limit in that sentence. It covers water only - not electricity, not gas. It covers allocation of usage only. And it fails the moment you add any fee or charge: an administrative fee, a billing-service charge, a markup over what the utility charged you, a rounding-up, or a minimum. If you submeter water and pass through exactly what the meters show with nothing added, you are inside the exemption. Add a $5 billing fee and on the face of the statute you are not. A separate exemption in Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(IX) covers metered water sales by a person operating a water system with fewer than fifteen potential service connections that is unaffiliated with a water utility, is not a subdivision's centralized supply, and is not inside a water utility's service territory or a municipality's corporate limits - relevant to a rural property on its own well, not to a town apartment building. The cautious course for electricity and gas is plain: either include them in rent, or have the tenant take service in their own name directly from the provider, and do not meter and sell.

Second, the utilities deposit. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) creates a wholly separate regime from the ordinary deposit rules, and it applies only to "property or money held and separately identified as a utilities deposit." That phrase is a drafting instruction. If you want the utilities-deposit timetable, say in the lease and on the receipt that the money is held separately as a utilities deposit and state the amount; if you do not, the money is an ordinary deposit governed by § 1-21-1208(a) and its thirty-day clock. The utilities timetable runs in four steps. The deposit must be refunded within ten days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges the renter incurred have been paid. If no such showing is made within forty-five days of termination, you must within fifteen days after that apply the utilities deposit to the renter's outstanding utility debt. Any refund then due must be paid within seven days after the deposit has been applied, or within fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later. Calendar those dates, because Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(c) lets the renter recover the full deposit plus court costs if you unreasonably fail to comply with subsection (a) or (b), and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1209 binds whoever holds the owner's interest at termination to § 1-21-1208.

Third, if any part of a utilities deposit is nonrefundable, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 applies in full: the rental agreement must state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, and you must also give the renter separate written notice of that fact at the time the deposit is taken. That is Wyoming's only genuinely mandatory deposit-related disclosure, and it reaches a utilities deposit like any other.

On service itself, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires each residential rental unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water - but that sentence carries its own qualifier, "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties." The qualifier belongs to that sentence only; it does not reach the first sentence's duty to keep the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) separately requires you to maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water, and that duty can be reallocated only through Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d), by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. Nothing in Wyoming law addresses shutting off a utility to force a tenant out, so do not do it: an interruption you cause would put you straight into the § 1-21-1203(b) notice procedure and the § 1-21-1206(c) judicial remedy, where a court may award costs, damages and an order to repair or a declaration terminating the agreement.

So while no attachment is required, write the utility terms into the lease anyway: name each utility, say who holds the account and who pays, state the allocation method exactly if you allocate water, state any utilities deposit as separately identified with its amount, and confirm in writing that the tenant must place service in their own name before possession where that is the arrangement. Flagged and not resolved: municipal and county utility ordinances and the tariffs and rules of the serving utility and the Wyoming Public Service Commission are outside this review, and a municipal water provider may have its own rules about landlord liability for a tenant's unpaid bill.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute letting a tenant authorize the utility to warn you before the tenant's own service is cut off, and none requiring a utility to copy a landlord on a disconnection notice. There is no Wyoming equivalent of the Wisconsin owner-notification authorization, no third-party designee statute, and no winter or cold-weather shutoff moratorium in the statutes. You are not without a way to find out - it just has to come from the lease and from the utility's own procedures rather than from a statute. Why you should care more than most landlords: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) says each residential rental unit shall have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water, and that requirement applies unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties. The habitability duty in the first sentence of that subsection - maintaining the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation - carries no such written-agreement escape at all, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) separately requires you to maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. A Wyoming winter in a unit whose heat has been shut off for nonpayment is the kind of condition those sections are about, so a tenant's unpaid utility bill can become your problem even though you did not run it up. Learning late is the risk; the lease is where you fix it. One statutory shutoff you can be blindsided by: under Wyo. Stat. § 35-3-122 a sanitary sewer district may contract with whoever supplies water to the district's inhabitants so that water is turned off and refused to any water user more than forty-five days delinquent on sewer rental or service charges, with notice of the discontinuance given by registered mail to the supplier and the water user. That notice goes to the user, not to you. Practical course, since no statute supplies the warning: (1) make the lease require the tenant to keep every utility account the lease assigns to them current, in the tenant's own name, and to give you a copy of any disconnection, shutoff or final notice within a set number of days of receiving it - Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1204(a)(vi) requires the renter to be current on all payments required by the rental agreement and § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) requires compliance with all lawful requirements of the agreement, and a breach of § 1-21-1204 is a listed ground for a forcible entry and detainer action under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(vi); (2) make the tenant authorize you, in a separate signed document rather than buried in the lease, as a person the utility may notify, and have the tenant file it with the utility - Wyoming does not require the utility to honor that, but most will act on a customer's written consent, and the signed authorization costs you nothing; (3) ask the serving utility and the sewer district in writing, before the tenancy starts, what their own rules allow by way of third-party or landlord notification; (4) take and separately identify a utilities deposit, which Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) treats on its own timetable - refundable within ten days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges incurred by the renter have been paid, and if no such showing is made within forty-five days of termination, applied by you to the outstanding utility debt within fifteen days thereafter, with any refund due paid within seven days after it is applied or fifteen days after you receive the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later; and (5) if you learn of a pending shutoff, act at once - restoring service yourself and recovering it from the tenant as a contract cost is usually cheaper than a habitability claim, and under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) you can deduct it from the deposit only if the lease provided for it. LOCAL ORDINANCE and AGENCY RULES: Public Service Commission service rules and municipal utility tariffs may allow third-party notification; those are flagged and not resolved here, because they are not in the statutes.

title: Do Not Cut Off Submetered Electricity in Wyoming
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute letting a landlord who submeters or reallocates electricity interrupt a tenant's service for nonpayment, and no regime of advance notices, prohibited weather days or medical exceptions of the kind states with such a right have written. The absence cuts against you, not for you: with no statute authorizing interruption, you are left with the owner's duties, and those duties point the other way. Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1202(a) provides that each residential rental unit "shall have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties," and § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) requires each owner, to protect the physical health and safety of the renter, to "[m]aintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water." Cutting the power to an occupied unit over an unpaid bill would put you in breach of both. The tenant's remedy is real: written notice of the condition and the requested remedy (§ 1-21-1203(b)), then a "notice to repair or correct condition" after a reasonable time (§ 1-21-1206(b)), then a circuit court action in which the tenant may be awarded "costs, damages and affirmative relief," including rent improperly retained or collected, and an order directing repairs or terminating the tenancy (§ 1-21-1206(c), (d)). Note one limit on that remedy chain in your favor: the article does not apply to breakage, malfunctions or conditions that do not materially affect the physical health or safety of the ordinary renter (§ 1-21-1202(c)) — but a unit with no electricity is not that. There is a second reason to be careful about submetered electricity in Wyoming, separate from interruption. Under Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI), the Public Service Commission chapter does not apply to the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity by a person "for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others" — but that sentence is followed immediately by its own exception: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." So master-metered electricity whose cost is simply built into the rent is outside the chapter, while metered or other direct sales of electricity to your tenants are not. Wyoming wrote tenant carve-outs for metered WATER sales — sales solely to allocate usage among tenants with no additional fees or charges (§ 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VIII)), and small systems under § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(IX) — and wrote no equivalent carve-out for electricity. Treat a submetered electric resale program as potentially regulated and get advice before running one. The practical course: include electricity in the rent or have the tenant put the account in the tenant's own name with the serving utility; if you do submeter, bill it as a separate charge and collect it the way you collect rent — by demand, by applying the deposit at termination under § 1-21-1208(a), or by a forcible entry and detainer action under § 1-21-1002(a)(vi) for the tenant's failure to be current on all payments required by the rental agreement (§ 1-21-1204(a)(vi)) — never by flipping the breaker. Note too that a separately identified utilities deposit has its own faster refund clock under § 1-21-1208(b). Local utility ordinances were not reviewed here.

title: When the Utility Account Is in Your Name
bodyText:
Wyoming gives a tenant none of the statutory tools that other states provide when the landlord holds the utility account. There is no statute barring a utility from shutting off service to a building because the landlord did not pay. There is no requirement that the utility notify each unit before a building-wide shutoff. There is no tenant right to pay the landlord's bill and deduct it from rent -- Wyoming has no pay-and-deduct, no repair-and-deduct and no rent-escrow statute of any kind, and "withhold rent," "rent escrow" and "repair and deduct" all return nothing in the entire code. There is no rent receivership a tenant can petition for. And there is no master-metering notice duty: the phrase "master meter" appears four times in Wyoming law, all in a noncodified water-district provision about a city's pipeline. Shutoff and reconnection practice in Wyoming is set by Public Service Commission rules and by each utility's tariff, and agency rules are outside what this library verifies -- so do not tell a tenant what the utility will or will not do; point them to the utility and the Commission.

What Wyoming does regulate, and this is the part that can catch a landlord badly, is whether billing your tenants for utilities turns you into a regulated utility. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) exempts from the public utility chapter the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, the manufacture or distribution of gas, the furnishing or distribution of water, and the production or furnishing of steam, by a person "for the sole use of a producer or other person, or for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others." Then comes the sentence that matters: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." So supplying utilities to your tenants is exempt -- but metering them and selling the commodity to them is not.

Wyoming wrote a way back in for water only. Section 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VIII) exempts "[m]etered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants when the metered or other direct sales are solely for purposes of allocating usage among tenants and includes no additional fees or charges," and (H)(IX) adds a further water exemption for a person operating a very small water system -- fewer than fifteen potential service connections, not affiliated with a water utility, not a subdivision's centralized supply. Read (H)(VIII) narrowly, because it is narrow: pure allocation of actual usage, and not one dollar of additional fee, administrative charge or markup. Add a billing fee and you are outside it.

There is no equivalent carve-out for electricity, gas or steam. On the face of the statute, a Wyoming landlord who submeters electricity or gas and bills tenants for it is making "metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity ... to his tenants" and has lost the exemption -- which would put them in the public utility chapter, with everything that implies about Commission jurisdiction. Whether the Commission would actually assert jurisdiction over a small apartment building is a question of agency practice that this library cannot answer from the statutes.

So take the cautious course. If you want tenants to bear utility costs for electricity or gas, either have each unit on its own account directly with the utility in the tenant's name, or include utilities in the rent as a flat amount that is not presented as a metered sale of the commodity. If you submeter water, bill pure allocation of measured usage with no added fee and keep the arithmetic documented so you can show it is allocation. Before you submeter electricity or gas and bill for it, get Wyoming-specific advice; the statutory text does not support it.

Two more practical points. First, if you hold the account, the bill is yours and the risk of a shutoff is yours. A shutoff in a unit you must keep habitable is your problem: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires each owner to maintain the unit "in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation" with "operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties," and § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) requires the owner to "[m]aintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water."
