Note the "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties" in § 1-21-1202(a) -- that qualifier attaches to the hot-and-cold-running-water sentence, and § 1-21-1202(d) separately allows any duty in the article to be reassigned or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties. That is how a Wyoming lease shifts utility responsibility, and it has to be explicit, written and signed.

Second, deposits. If you take a deposit for utilities, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) puts it on its own clock: property or money "held and separately identified as a utilities deposit" must be refunded within ten days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges incurred by the renter have been paid -- much faster than the thirty-day general deposit deadline in § 1-21-1208(a). The words "separately identified" do real work; if you do not identify it separately, it is an ordinary deposit on the ordinary clock.

title: Utility Shutoffs and Submetering in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming's statutes contain no utility-disconnection rules for residential customers. There is no statutory notice period before a utility shuts off service for nonpayment, no winter or cold-weather moratorium or extension ("cold weather" appears nowhere in the Wyoming Statutes), no medical-certificate protection, and no ban on disconnection during a declared storm or disaster. Those rules, where they exist in Wyoming, are Public Service Commission rules made under Title 37, and agency rules are outside this library — check the PSC's current service rules for the utility serving your property, and the municipality's own rules if the water or electric provider is a city.

The only disconnection notice in the Wyoming Statutes has nothing to do with nonpayment: Wyo. Stat. § 37-13-132 requires ten (10) days' written notice, left at the principal building on the lot, before overhead electric or communication facilities are disconnected because the owner failed to make service-entrance changes or provide a trench during an overhead-to-underground conversion.

Now the part that matters most to a landlord: you must not shut utilities off yourself, and Wyoming gives a tenant several ways to make that expensive even though there is no statute aimed squarely at it.

• It breaches your core duty. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires each owner to maintain the unit "in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation" and requires each unit to "have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties." Read the qualifier precisely: "unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties" sits in the second sentence, so a written agreement can shift who supplies and pays for those utilities, but it does not dissolve the first sentence's safe-sanitary-and-fit duty. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) separately requires you to "[m]aintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water."
• The tenant's remedy is real. After written notice under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(b) and a second "notice to repair or correct condition" under § 1-21-1206(b) giving you three (3) days, the renter may sue in circuit court, and under § 1-21-1206(c) the court may award costs, damages "may include rent improperly retained or collected," and affirmative relief that "may include a declaration terminating the rental agreement, or an order directing the owner to make reasonable repairs." Where the shutoff is an emergency, expect the court to use the short end of the three-to-twenty-day summons window that subsection sets.
• Eviction in Wyoming is judicial, full stop. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1211(a) has the SHERIFF remove a renter's possessions and bar reentry, and only after a court order under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1001 et seq. Cutting power or water to force someone out is a substitute for that process, not a part of it. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-306 makes it a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to seven hundred fifty dollars ($750.00), to "violently take[] or keep[] possession of land without authority of law."
• Pulling a meter is its own problem. Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-401(a)(iv) defines "unauthorized metering" as "removing, moving, installing, connecting, reconnecting or disconnecting any meter or metering device for utility service by a person other than an authorized contractor, employee or agent of the utility." Under § 37-12-402(a) and (c) the utility may sue anyone who commits, authorizes, solicits, aids or abets it, and on proof of willful or intentional conduct may recover two (2) times its actual damages plus all reasonable expenses — investigation, disconnection, reconnection, service calls, employees and equipment, expert witnesses, costs of suit and reasonable attorney fees — within three (3) years. That provision cuts both ways: it is also your remedy, through the utility, if a tenant bypasses or tampers with a meter.

Submetering: water yes, electricity no. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) exempts a person who furnishes electricity, gas, water or steam "for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others" from public-utility regulation, BUT the same subparagraph adds: "Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants." Submeter and sell, and you have stepped out of the exemption and into Public Service Commission jurisdiction. Wyoming wrote a carve-out for metered WATER only, and wrote it narrowly. Subparagraph (H)(VIII) exempts "[m]etered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants when the metered or other direct sales are solely for purposes of allocating usage among tenants and includes no additional fees or charges" — both conditions must hold, so allocation at cost is fine and any markup, administrative fee or billing charge forfeits it. Subparagraph (H)(IX) separately exempts a small water system with fewer than fifteen (15) potential service connections that is not owned, controlled or affiliated with a water utility, is not a subdivision's centralized supply, and is not within a water utility's service territory or a municipality's corporate limits — all four conditions required. There is no electricity or gas equivalent. The one electricity carve-out Wyoming did write, at § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(X), is for "the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under this title" — EV charging, not tenant submetering, so it does not help here. If you want tenants to pay for electricity, put the account in the tenant's name or build the cost into rent; do not submeter and bill it.

One more: Wyo. Stat. § 18-2-116 bars any county from enacting or implementing a resolution or policy that prohibits, or has the effect of prohibiting, the connection or reconnection of electric, natural gas, propane or other energy utility service provided by a public utility, municipality or cooperative.

Practical course: say in writing which utilities you supply and which the tenant puts in their own name, never interrupt a service you supply, and if a tenant is not paying for a utility in your name, pursue it as a debt or as a lease breach through the § 1-21-1003 notice and an eviction — never through the meter.

title: Submetering and Billing Tenants for Utilities
bodyText: Wyoming has no utility submetering disclosure statute. The word 'submeter' does not appear anywhere in the Wyoming statutes. There is no prescribed disclosure, no type-size rule, no building-size threshold, no cap on an administrative or billing fee, and no late-fee limit on a utility charge. What Wyoming has instead is a regulatory line, and it is in the public utilities title, which never uses the word 'landlord' at all. The line is in the definition of 'public utility' at Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi). Subparagraph (H)(VI) takes you out of Title 37 for 'the generation, transmission or distribution of electricity, or to the manufacture or distribution of gas, or to the furnishing or distribution of water, nor to the production, delivery or furnishing of steam or any other substance, by a producer or other person, for the sole use of a producer or other person, or for the use of tenants of a producer or other person and not for sale to others.' Then it takes it back: 'Such exemptions shall not apply to metered or other direct sales of a utility commodity by a producer or other person to his tenants.' Read that sentence carefully, because it is the whole topic. Furnishing a utility for the use of your tenants is exempt. Metering it and selling it to them is not — and a person who is not exempt is a public utility, which in Wyoming means the public service commission's jurisdiction over certificates, tariffs and rates. Electricity and gas have no carve-back. There is no Wyoming provision that lets a landlord submeter electricity or gas and bill tenants for it. Water has two carve-backs, and both are narrow. Subparagraph (H)(VIII) exempts 'Metered and other direct sales of water by a person to his tenants when the metered or other direct sales are solely for purposes of allocating usage among tenants and includes no additional fees or charges.' Both conditions are cumulative: the billing must be solely to allocate usage, and it must add nothing. No administrative fee, no billing fee, no per-unit markup, no service charge, no late fee on the water line — any of those is an 'additional fee or charge' and puts you outside the exemption. Subparagraph (H)(IX) separately exempts metered and direct water sales by a person operating a water system that has fewer than fifteen potential service connections, is not owned, controlled or otherwise affiliated with a water utility or any other utility providing water service, is not a centralized water supply system associated with a subdivision, and is not located within a water utility's established service territory or a municipality's corporate limits — four conditions, all of which must hold. What to do with that. The two safe structures in Wyoming are to include utilities in the rent, or to have the tenant hold the account with the utility in the tenant's own name. If you want the tenant to bear a measured share of water, do it as a fee-free allocation under subparagraph (H)(VIII) and charge nothing for doing it. Before you submeter electricity or gas and bill for it, get advice — that is the step that can make you a public utility. Four Wyoming mechanics to get right in the lease. First, the allocation itself is a matter of written agreement: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires every unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water 'unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties,' and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) lets any duty in the residential rental article be assigned to a different party or modified 'by explicit written agreement signed by the parties.' Explicit, written and signed are cumulative; an unsigned utility addendum does not do it. Second, if you want to recover an unpaid utility charge from the deposit, the lease has to create the charge: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) lets the deposit be applied to accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, cleaning, 'and to other costs provided by any contract.' Third, if you take a utility deposit, hold it and identify it separately. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) gives a deposit 'held and separately identified as a utilities deposit' its own timetable — refund within ten days of a satisfactory showing that all utility charges have been paid; absent that showing within forty-five days of termination, you must apply it to the outstanding utility debt within the next fifteen days, and pay any refund within seven days after applying it, or within fifteen days after receiving the renter's new mailing address, whichever is later. A deposit you did not separately identify falls into the ordinary thirty-day cascade in subsection (a) instead. Fourth, never touch the utility's meter. Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-401(a)(iv) defines 'unauthorized metering' as removing, moving, installing, connecting, reconnecting or disconnecting any meter or metering device for utility service by someone other than an authorized contractor, employee or agent of the utility, and Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-402(c) lets the utility recover double its actual damages plus investigation, disconnection and reconnection costs, expert witnesses, suit costs and attorney fees on proof of willful or intentional bypassing, tampering or unauthorized metering. Install submeters through the utility or a contractor the utility authorizes, and keep the paperwork.

title: Wyoming Gives You No Right to Cut Off Utilities Still in Your Name
bodyText:
Wyoming has no transfer-or-cutoff statute. Nothing lets you terminate a utility that is still in your name because the tenant did not put it in theirs within three days, or within any other period. There is no Wyoming equivalent of the Tennessee provision this topic is built around. The searches are clean: "transfer" and "utility" within sixty characters of each other, in both word orders, produce two hits and both are rate-regulation provisions in Title 37; "terminate" and "utility" in both orders produce three, all rate regulation; and Title 37 contains the word "landlord" zero times.

But Wyoming does not prohibit it either, and that is the trap. Because there is no statute on the point, there is also no safe harbour. Wyoming has no general anti-self-help statute, no statutory damages for a utility cutoff, and no provision telling you when a cutoff is lawful. What you have instead is a set of duties and exposures that make a cutoff a bad idea anyway. Here they are, in the order they will hurt.

Your habitability duties do not depend on whose name is on the bill. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires each residential rental unit to have operational electrical, heating and plumbing, with hot and cold running water, unless otherwise agreed in writing by both parties. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) requires you to maintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water. A tenant who is in possession and loses power, gas, heat or water because you called the utility and closed the account has a straightforward argument that you broke those duties, and nothing in the statutes conditions them on the tenant having opened an account.

The tenant's remedy is real. Under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1206, a tenant who is in compliance with §§ 1-21-1204 and 1-21-1205, and whose tenancy has not been lawfully terminated under § 1-21-1203(d), may serve a written notice of the condition, then a "notice to repair or correct condition" giving you three days to begin reasonable corrective action, and then sue in circuit court. Section 1-21-1206(c) lets the court award costs, damages and affirmative relief on a showing of unreasonable refusal to correct or failure to use due diligence, and says expressly that damages "may include rent improperly retained or collected" and that affirmative relief may include an order directing you to make reasonable repairs or a declaration terminating the lease. The court endorses a short appearance deadline on the summons — not less than three nor more than twenty days from service — so this moves fast.

Touching the meter is the expensive mistake. Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-401(a)(iv) defines "unauthorized metering" as removing, moving, installing, connecting, reconnecting or disconnecting any meter or metering device for utility service "by a person other than an authorized contractor, employee or agent of the utility." A landlord pulling a meter or disconnecting it is squarely inside that definition. Under Wyo. Stat. § 37-12-402(a)(i) the UTILITY — not the tenant — may bring a civil action against any person who commits, authorizes, solicits, aids, abets or attempts unauthorized metering resulting in damages to the utility, and on proof of willful or intentional conduct § 37-12-402(c) lets it recover two times its actual damages plus all reasonable expenses, expressly including investigation, disconnection, reconnection, service calls, employees and equipment, expert witnesses, costs of suit and reasonable attorney fees. The limitation period is three years under § 37-12-402(b), and § 37-12-403 makes these remedies cumulative with everything else. So the meter is the utility's, not yours, and the double-damages exposure runs to the utility even if the tenant never sues.

The criminal statute is narrow, which is cold comfort. Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-306 makes it a misdemeanour, fine up to $750, to "violently" take or keep possession of land without authority of law. A quiet utility shutoff is probably not "violent," so the criminal exposure is small. That is not a reason to do it; the civil exposure is where the money is.

And if you become the utility, you inherit regulation. Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI) withdraws the landlord's exemption from public-utility status for metered or direct sales of a utility commodity to tenants, and the carve-out at (H)(VIII) and (IX) is for water only, and only as fee-free allocation. There is no electricity or gas equivalent. The one electricity carve-out Wyoming did write, at § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(X), is for "the retail sale of electricity for charging electric vehicles by a person that is not otherwise regulated under this title" — EV charging, not tenant submetering, so it does not help here. So a scheme where you keep the account and bill tenants for metered usage can make you a public utility, which is a bigger problem than an unpaid bill.

What to do instead, and it works. Make the transfer a lease obligation with a deadline. Make failure to transfer a breach. Price it: say that while a service remains in your name you will pay it and the tenant will reimburse the actual billed amount, and stop there. Do not add an administrative charge or any other markup, and do not call the reimbursement rent. A charge above the amount actually billed turns the arrangement into a direct sale of a utility commodity to your tenant under Wyo. Stat. § 37-1-101(a)(vi)(H)(VI), which costs you the public-utility exemption itself; for water, subparagraph (H)(VIII) allows the allocation but says 'no additional fees or charges'. And because no Wyoming statute makes a fee rent, calling it rent will not let you use the three-day nonpayment notice for it. That converts the problem into a rent problem, and rent problems in Wyoming have a clean route — Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1002(a)(i) allows forcible entry and detainer after a failure to pay rent for three days after it is due, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 requires a separate three-day notice to quit before filing. Those are two stacked three-day periods, not one. Section 1-21-1002(a)(vi) separately allows the action against renters in violation of any term imposed under § 1-21-1204 or § 1-21-1205, and § 1-21-1204(a)(vii) requires the renter to comply with all lawful requirements of the rental agreement. Also label any utilities deposit separately: under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(b) a deposit "held and separately identified as a utilities deposit" runs on its own 10/45/15/7-day cascade, which is far more useful to you than folding it into the general deposit.

The cautious course, stated plainly. Do not shut off, do not ask the utility to disconnect, and do not touch a meter while a tenant is in possession. Put the money question in the lease, bill it as additional rent, and if the tenant will not pay, evict for nonpayment. One narrow exception to consider with counsel: after you have regained lawful possession of an empty unit, closing an account in your own name is an ordinary act of ownership rather than a cutoff — but get advice before relying on that, and never do it while anyone is still living there.

Local ordinances are unresolved. Wyoming is a constitutional home-rule state under Wyo. Const. art. 13, § 1(b), municipal utilities are common here, and a city utility's own rules on account transfers and disconnections are outside this library. Check them.

title: No Wyoming Landlord Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Wyoming offers a landlord nothing for renting to a veteran. There is no tax credit, no deposit waiver or reimbursement, no vacancy-relief payment for holding a unit, no damage-loss fund, and no pilot programme of any kind. "Landlord incentive," "vacancy relief," "vacancy payment" and "HUD-VASH" return nothing anywhere in the Wyoming statutes, and "incentive" near "veteran" returns nothing. Wyoming also has no individual income tax, so a state income-tax credit is not even a structural possibility. The veteran tax relief Wyoming does have is for the veteran, not for you. Wyo. Stat. § 39-13-105(a) gives listed veterans who have been bona fide Wyoming residents for at least three (3) years the property tax exemption provided by Wyo. Stat. § 39-11-105(a)(xxiv), extended by § 39-13-105(h) to a surviving spouse during widowhood or widowerhood and to surviving parents where there is no surviving spouse, subject to residency conditions. Wyo. Stat. § 39-13-105(b) limits it to an annual exemption of six thousand dollars ($6,000.00) of assessed value, and § 39-13-105(c)(iv) requires the claimant to swear that the exemption for real property "shall only apply to the principal residence of the veteran or qualifying surviving spouse." That last condition is decisive: a rental unit you own is not the veteran's principal residence for your tax purposes, so renting to a veteran does not reduce your property tax, and the exemption cannot be assigned or passed through to you. A veteran tenant may of course claim it against property the veteran owns, and may also apply it as a county motor vehicle registration fee reduction, but none of that touches your bill. What you do need to know about military and veteran tenants is a set of protections, not incentives. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, 50 U.S.C. § 3901 et seq., lets a servicemember terminate a residential lease on qualifying orders and restricts default judgments and evictions. Wyoming extends those protections by state law: Wyo. Stat. § 19-11-122(a) provides that members of the Wyoming national guard ordered to active state service by the state or federal government for a period of more than thirty (30) consecutive days have all protections afforded to persons in the armed forces of the United States under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. Read § 19-11-122 carefully, because the penalty structure is unusual. Subsection (a) says that, except as provided in subsection (b), nothing in it authorises imposing an SCRA penalty for violating these state-extended protections — but subsection (b) then makes any person who KNOWINGLY violates them guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000.00), and subsection (c) provides that the protections may serve as the basis for an action or as a defence in Wyoming courts. "Active state service" takes the definition in Wyo. Stat. § 19-7-101(a)(v). So a Wyoming landlord who knowingly disregards a Guard member's SCRA-equivalent lease termination is exposed to a criminal fine as well as a civil claim. Note the thirty-consecutive-day threshold, and note that the protection runs to the Guard member on active state service even where the federal Act on its own terms would not reach them. Wyoming has no state source-of-income or veteran-status protected class in housing: the classes in Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103 are race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status and national origin. Veteran status is not among them, and is not among the longer list in the intimidation provision at Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-144(a)(i) either. You are therefore free to market to veterans, offer them a reduced deposit or waive an application fee if you wish — nothing in Wyoming law requires or rewards it, and nothing forbids it, provided the preference is not operated in a way that disadvantages a protected class. If you want the benefit, look to federal programmes such as HUD-VASH rather than to Wyoming law.

title: What Accepting Rent Does and Does Not Waive
bodyText:
Wyoming reverses the usual holdover rule, and the reversal is written into the statute books rather than left to the courts. Wyo. Stat. § 34-2-128 provides: 'In this state there shall not exist the relations of landlord and tenant, by implication or operation of law, except a tenancy by sufferance. Upon the expiration of a term created by lease, either verbal or written, there shall be no implied renewal of the same, for any period of time whatever, either by the tenant holding over or by the landlord accepting compensation or rent for or during any period of such holding over. Such holding over by the tenant and acceptance of rent by the landlord shall constitute only a tenancy by sufferance, with the rights, duties, obligations and incidents of such tenancy.' Section 34-2-129 completes it: 'No lease which shall have expired by its own limitation shall be again renewed except by express contract in writing, signed by the parties thereto, whether the original lease be written or verbal. Nor shall any other tenancy than that by sufferance exist after the termination of the original lease, unless created as aforesaid, by express contract in writing.'

So where your lease term has run out and the tenant stays on, here is plainly what accepting rent does and does not do. It does not renew the lease, for any period of time whatever. It does not create a month-to-month or any other periodic tenancy. It does not give the tenant a new term, a right to stay, or any entitlement to notice beyond what the eviction statute requires. It does not waive the expiration. What it does do is leave the tenant exactly where the holdover put them — a tenant by sufferance — and put money in your pocket for the period of occupation. There is no implied-renewal doctrine in Wyoming for a lease that has expired, and only an express contract in writing, signed by the parties, can renew one. Note how wide those two sections reach: they are in Title 34 and apply to every lease, verbal or written, and are not confined to the principal-residence rentals that Article 12 covers.

But do not over-read them, and this is where landlords get into trouble. Sections 34-2-128 and 34-2-129 are both keyed to a term that has ended: the operative words are 'Upon the expiration of a term created by lease' and 'No lease which shall have expired by its own limitation.' They say nothing about a tenancy that is still running. If the term has not expired and you served a three-day notice to quit under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003 because the tenant failed to pay, these sections do not answer the question of whether taking the money afterwards kills your case, and there is no Wyoming statute that does. The practical risk is real, because the ground you are relying on is defined by the default itself: § 1-21-1002(a)(i) permits a forcible entry and detainer proceeding 'Against tenants holding over their terms or after a failure to pay rent for three (3) days after it is due,' and once the arrears are paid in full it is open to the tenant to say there is no longer a failure to pay. The same caution applies to a notice grounded on § 1-21-1002(a)(vi), a violation of a duty under § 1-21-1204 or a prohibited act under § 1-21-1205: payment does not cure a non-rent breach, but a tenant can argue you elected to treat the tenancy as continuing.

The cautious course, in order of safety. First, during an unexpired term with a live notice to quit, the safest thing is to decline the payment and return it promptly, keeping proof. Second, if you take it, take it only under a short written agreement signed by the tenant stating that the sum is accepted for use and occupancy for a stated period, that it is not rent, that it does not waive the notice to quit or any default, and that it does not reinstate, renew or extend the tenancy. Third, put a non-waiver clause in every lease saying that accepting any payment after a default or after notice does not waive the default, the notice, or your right to possession — nothing in Wyoming law prohibits such a clause, there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in the residential landlord-tenant article, and it is ordinary contract. Be aware, though, that § 1-21-1202(d)'s power to modify duties by explicit written agreement signed by the parties speaks only of 'this article' and sits in Article 12, so it is not authority for contracting around the Article 10 notice to quit; a non-waiver clause works as contract, not as a statutory waiver. Fourth, if the term has already expired, you can accept rent from a holdover with much less anxiety, because § 34-2-128 answers the question for you — though even then, serve the § 1-21-1003 notice and keep your file clean.

Two footnotes. Wyoming does not define the incidents of a tenancy by sufferance anywhere in statute; § 34-2-128 simply refers to 'the rights, duties, obligations and incidents of such tenancy' and leaves them to the common law. There is also no statutory notice period for ending a periodic tenancy in Wyoming and no double-rent holdover penalty, so do not assume a thirty-day rule and do not expect a statutory multiplier on holdover rent. And the reinstatement-on-tender right you may have seen in Wyoming's rental-purchase provisions in Title 40 is part of the consumer rent-to-own law for goods; it has nothing to do with renting a home.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText:
Wyoming sets no water heater temperature, maximum or minimum, and imposes no duty to set or check one at turnover. There is no equivalent of Wisconsin's 125-degree rule or Washington's requirement to set an accessible single-unit heater at each new occupancy. "Scald," "anti-scald," "tempering valve," "mixing valve," "maximum temperature" and "water temperature" appear nowhere in the Wyoming statutes, and no provision connects hot water to a tenant at all.

More striking, and worth knowing before you call anyone: Wyoming has no state plumbing code. The model codes the fire prevention and electrical safety council may adopt under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) are named exhaustively — the International Fire Code, International Building Code, International Mechanical Code, International Existing Building Code and International Fuel Gas Code — and no plumbing code is among them. The phrases "plumbing code" and "International Plumbing Code" do not appear in the Wyoming statutes at all. Electrical work has a statewide floor, because Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-120(a) subjects electric equipment in or on buildings, mobile homes and premises to the National Electrical Code and makes the NEC control over the I-codes where they conflict. Plumbing has no such statewide floor. Whatever plumbing requirement applies to your property is local: Wyo. Stat. § 15-1-119 lets any city or town adopt by reference national fire prevention, building, plumbing and electrical codes, and § 35-9-121(a) delegates complete fire and building enforcement to municipalities and counties that qualify, with § 35-9-121(a)(i) allowing local standards equivalent to or more stringent than the state's. So the real answer to "what temperature must my water heater be?" in Wyoming is: ask the city or county building department which plumbing code edition, if any, they have adopted.

What Wyoming does require of you is the water itself. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) obliges you to "[m]aintain electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water." That is a short, closed list and it is the only ongoing maintenance duty the statute imposes — but hot water is squarely on it, so a unit without working hot water puts you out of compliance, and the fact that the failure is the water heater's fault is no answer. The list says nothing about temperature. Separately, § 1-21-1203(a)(i) forbids renting the unit at all "unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy," and a heater delivering scalding water is a credible candidate for not reasonably safe. Those two provisions, not a temperature statute, are where your exposure sits.

So set it yourself. The widely used figure is 120 degrees Fahrenheit, which is hot enough for ordinary household use and is the limit the model plumbing codes apply to bathing water through a temperature-limiting device. No Wyoming statute compels that number, but adopting it costs nothing and answers both halves of the problem — it is comfortably within "reasonably safe" and it still delivers the hot water § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) requires you to maintain. Check and record the setting at every turnover, note it on the move-in condition inspection, and keep the record. Where a heater is old or has no accessible thermostat, a thermostatic mixing valve at the heater outlet is the straightforward fix. Think twice before pushing below about 120 degrees in a building with long pipe runs, since very low storage temperatures raise their own health concerns, and that is a question for a licensed plumber rather than for this row.

Two drafting points. You may shift maintenance duties by agreement — Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) allows any duty in the landlord-tenant article to be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties, with no anti-waiver provision anywhere in the article. But do not shift responsibility for a water heater the tenant cannot reach: if it sits in a locked utility room, or serves more than one unit, the tenant has no way to comply and the clause will not help you. And remember the article reaches only a "residential rental unit," which § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines as the renter's principal place of residence, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally — so for a cabin let by the week, the § 1-21-1203 duties do not apply and your lease and ordinary negligence law are all there is.

title: No Waterbed Rule in Wyoming
bodyText:
Wyoming has no waterbed statute. The words "waterbed," "water bed" and "flotation bedding" appear nowhere in the Wyoming code. That means none of the machinery other states have: no rule barring you from refusing to rent to someone because they have a waterbed, no building-age cut-off, no required insurance amount, no certificate of installation, no extra security deposit allowance, and no notice-before-inspection right tied to a waterbed. The whole subject is yours to decide by contract, and if your lease says nothing you have agreed to nothing.

WHAT THAT MEANS IN PRACTICE. You may prohibit waterbeds and other liquid-filled furniture outright, or permit them on conditions you set. Four Wyoming points shape how to do it.

(1) PERMISSION IS A LEASE QUESTION, AND SO IS MAINTENANCE. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) makes you responsible for maintaining "other appliances and facilities" only "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement." So a waterbed heater, a liner or a pedestal that the lease does not name is not your maintenance problem. Do not list it.

(2) DAMAGE THE TENANT CAUSES IS NOT YOUR REPAIR DUTY. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c) provides that you are not required to correct or remedy any condition caused by the renter, the renter's family, guests or invitees "by inappropriate use or misuse of the property during the rental term or any extension of it." A burst bladder is the paradigm case.

(3) THERE IS NO DEPOSIT CAP, SO A HIGHER DEPOSIT IS AVAILABLE. Wyoming sets no maximum deposit, and Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a) permits applying "property or money held as a deposit" to accrued rent, damages and "other costs provided by any contract" - so any repair or cleaning charge your lease creates is deductible. If you do take an additional deposit for a waterbed, remember Wyoming's one mandatory lease recital: Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1207 requires the rental agreement to state whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable AND requires separate written notice of that fact to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. Both duties, not one.

(4) YOU CAN SHIFT THE DUTY, BUT ONLY IN WRITING AND ONLY IF SIGNED. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) provides that any duty or obligation in Article 12 "may be assigned to a different party or modified by explicit written agreement signed by the parties." The conditions are cumulative - explicit, written, and signed by the parties - and there is no anti-waiver provision anywhere in Article 12. An insurance requirement, an installation standard and an indemnity are enforceable in Wyoming for that reason, where in a URLTA state they often are not.

THREE LIMITS TO KEEP IN VIEW. First, a floor-load or building-code constraint may come from your local building code, adopted and enforced locally; under Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(b) a more stringent local code prevails over the state code, and local ordinances are outside this review. Second, fair housing: a blanket waterbed ban applied evenly is fine, but if a tenant asks for a flotation or water-filled mattress for a medical reason, that is a reasonable accommodation request under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-107(c)(ii), and a related alteration is a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense under § 40-26-107(c)(i), with an express rental carve-out allowing you to condition it on restoration "when it is reasonable to do so." Handle those on their own facts, in writing. Third, Article 12 applies only where the unit is the renter's principal place of residence as Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1201(a)(iv) defines it, excluding a mobile home lot and recreational property rented occasionally.

THE CLAUSE TO USE. Prohibit waterbeds and other liquid-filled or flotation furniture unless you give prior written consent; if you consent, require written proof of renter's insurance naming you as additional insured in a stated amount and kept in force while the bed is in place, a pedestal or frame distributing the weight, a liner, professional installation and removal, and restoration of any damage; make every associated cost a cost provided by the lease so it is deductible under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1208(a); and state that the tenant is responsible for all damage from the bed under Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1203(c). Have the tenant sign it, so Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(d) is satisfied.

This review covers Wyoming statutes and the 2025 and 2026 session laws. Case law, court rules, agency rules and local building codes were not searched.

title: No window guard requirement and no window-guard notice
bodyText:
Wyoming has no window-guard law. No statute requires you to install, provide or maintain window guards, window stops or any other window fall protection in a rental, whether or not children live in the unit, and none requires a notice, a bold-type lease recital, a tenant request form or a model text. There is no Wyoming counterpart to the New Jersey or New York City window-guard regimes. The phrase "window guard" appears nowhere in the Wyoming statutes; neither does "window fall", "fall prevention", "window screen", "window opening" or "egress window", and "window" never appears within thirty characters of "guard" in either direction. The twenty-eight "window" references in the Wyoming statutes are motor vehicle glazing and tinting in Title 31, a weatherization storm-window measure in Title 42, a search-warrant provision and the fire-escape platform specification in Title 35, and scattered unrelated uses.

WHAT FILLS THE GAP IS CODE AND YOUR OWN LEASE.

The model codes. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-106(a)(i) directs the state fire prevention and electrical safety council to adopt rules establishing minimum fire standards not exceeding the standards prescribed by the International Fire Code, the International Building Code, the International Mechanical Code, the International Existing Building Code and the International Fuel Gas Code, for all new construction or remodeling under § 35-9-108(a), for the prevention of fire and the protection of life and property from fire and panic in all existing buildings, and for hazardous substances. The International Building Code and International Residential Code contain window fall protection and sill-height provisions, so in practice those standards reach new construction and remodeling in Wyoming through the plan review and certificate-of-occupancy machinery in § 35-9-108. They are rules and model codes, not statutes, and this review covers statutes only.

Local enforcement, which is where the real answer usually is. Wyo. Stat. § 35-9-121(a) requires the state fire marshal to delegate complete authority to municipalities and counties that apply to enforce and interpret local or state fire, building, existing building standards or electrical safety standards. Before a local authority is granted that power the fire marshal must determine that the local governing body has adopted, by ordinance or resolution, minimum standards equivalent to or more stringent than the department's; and under § 35-9-121(a)(ii) if a locality that has been granted authority fails within six months of the department adopting new standards to adopt or maintain standards at least meeting the statewide standards, enforcement authority immediately reverts to the department. So your city or county may be enforcing something stricter than the state baseline. Ask the local building department before you assume there is no requirement.

Your general duties. Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1202(a) requires you to maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, and § 1-21-1203(a)(i) forbids renting a unit unless it is reasonably safe, sanitary and fit for human occupancy. A window that will not stay shut, has a broken sash cord or a rotted frame, or opens onto a drop with a failed guard, is a safety problem those provisions reach, even though no statute names window guards. Note that the ongoing maintenance list in § 1-21-1203(a)(iii) is closed - electrical systems, plumbing, heating and hot and cold water - and windows are not on it, so your ongoing window obligation is the one your lease creates under § 1-21-1203(a)(iv), which reaches other appliances and facilities only "as specifically contracted in the rental agreement".

THE TRAP IF YOU DO INSTALL GUARDS. Because § 1-21-1203(a)(iv) works on what the lease specifically contracts for, be deliberate. If you install window guards and your lease lists them among the facilities you maintain, you have created a maintenance duty enforceable through § 1-21-1203(b) and § 1-21-1206. If you install them and say nothing, you have installed a safety device with no statutory maintenance obligation attached - but you will still answer in ordinary negligence for a guard you installed badly or left broken after being told. The sensible middle course is to install them where there is a real fall risk, say in the lease that they are installed, that the tenant must not remove, disable or obstruct them and must report any defect in writing at once, and that you will repair them on notice.

ONE THING YOU MAY NOT DO. Do not use a fall risk as a reason to refuse or discourage families. Wyoming's fair housing act makes familial status a protected class under Wyo. Stat. § 40-26-103, and § 1-21-1204(a)(v) caps occupancy only at the number specified in the rental agreement - there is no Wyoming statutory occupancy standard and no statutory basis for an upper-floor policy against children. A "not suitable for children" line in an advertisement or a refusal to rent an upper unit to a family is a familial-status problem, not a safety measure.

This review covered the Wyoming statutes and constitution. It did not cover the fire council's adopted codes, other agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law, and any actual window-guard requirement in Wyoming would come from one of those.

title: Which Wyoming Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText:
Wyoming has no single statute listing notices that must be written. It does it provision by provision, and the list below is the complete set in the landlord-tenant chapters. Where a section says “written,” an oral notice does not start the clock, and a lease term permitting oral notice does not substitute — the statute fixes what the notice must be to have the effect the statute gives it.

NOTICES YOU MUST PUT IN WRITING. (1) Notice to quit, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1003: before commencing a forcible entry and detainer action you must notify the adverse party to leave, and the notice must be served at least three days before you commence the action “by leaving a written copy with the defendant or at his usual place of abode or business if he cannot be found.” This sits in Article 10, which § 1-21-1202(d) does not reach — that modification power says “this article” and lives in Article 12 — so no lease clause can waive or shorten it. (2) Your dispute of a tenant’s complaint, § 1-21-1203(b): after the renter’s written notice of a condition, you must within a reasonable time either commence corrective action or “notify the renter in writing that the owner disputes the renter’s claim,” and notices under that subsection are served by certified mail or in the § 1-21-1003 manner. (3) Your repair-cost termination, § 1-21-1203(d): if you refuse to correct and intend to terminate, you must notify the renter IN WRITING within a reasonable time after receiving the notice of noncompliance, allowing no less than ten and no more than twenty days to find substitute housing. (4) Permission to add occupants, § 1-21-1204(a)(v): a renter may not increase the number of occupants above the number specified in the rental agreement “without written permission of the owner” — so your consent must be written too, and a verbal yes you later regret still counts against you as evidence. (5) The nonrefundable deposit notice, § 1-21-1207: this is Wyoming’s only mandatory lease recital and it is two separate duties — the rental agreement SHALL STATE whether any portion of a deposit is nonrefundable, AND written notice of that fact shall ALSO be provided to the renter at the time the deposit is taken. Doing one does not do the other. (6) Deposit accounting, § 1-21-1208(a): the balance of the deposit and prepaid rent, together with “a written itemization of any deductions from the deposit together with reasons therefor,” must be delivered or mailed without interest within thirty days after termination or within fifteen days after you receive the renter’s new mailing address, whichever is later, extended by thirty days if there is damage. Under § 1-21-1208(c), unreasonable failure lets the renter recover the full deposit and court costs. (7) Abandoned property, § 1-21-1210(a)(i): WRITTEN notice describing the property and stating it will be disposed of after seven days, deemed served on the date of certified mailing to an address the renter furnished IN WRITING specifically for that purpose, or on the date of personal service under W.R.C.P. 4 with a copy of the written notice delivered personally, or on the date of publication in a county newspaper. (8) Modifying any Article 12 duty, § 1-21-1202(d): “explicit written agreement signed by the parties” — three cumulative conditions, explicit, written and signed. (9) Dispensing with hot and cold running water, § 1-21-1202(a): the requirement of operational electrical, heating and plumbing with hot and cold running water applies “unless otherwise agreed upon in writing by both parties.” Read that qualifier carefully: it attaches to the amenities sentence it sits in, not to the first sentence’s duty to maintain the unit in a safe and sanitary condition fit for human habitation, which no writing can switch off. (10) Renewing an expired lease, § 34-2-129: an expired lease is renewed only “by express contract in writing, signed by the parties,” whether the original was written or oral, and § 34-2-128 confirms that holding over and your acceptance of rent create only a tenancy by sufferance.

WRITTEN NOTICES THE TENANT OWES YOU. The renter’s notice of a noncompliant condition must be in writing, § 1-21-1203(b); the follow-up “notice to repair or correct condition” must be prepared and served by certified mail or in the § 1-21-1003 manner and must contain the five items in § 1-21-1206(b)(i)-(v); the renter must notify you within thirty days of termination where payment and notice may be sent, § 1-21-1208(a); a response claiming abandoned property must be in writing, § 1-21-1210(a)(ii)-(iii); and a Safe Homes Act tenant must give seven days’ WRITTEN notice before vacating that states the statutory reason and, under § 1-21-1303(b)(ii), also the date of the violence and that the evidence was provided, Wyo. Stat. § 1-21-1303(a)(ii) and (b)(ii).

TWO TRAPS. First, the § 1-21-1210(a)(iii) abandoned-property timeline contradicts itself: it says the property “shall be held for an additional period of seven (7) days after the written response is received,” then in the next sentence says the property is conclusively abandoned if the renter fails to take possession “within the additional FIFTEEN (15) DAY period.” The safe course is to hold for fifteen days after the written response before disposing. Second, under § 1-21-1201(a)(i), for purposes of notice and other communication under Article 12 “owner” includes a managing agent, leasing agent or resident manager unless THE AGENT OR MANAGER specifies otherwise in writing in the rental agreement — notice served on your manager is notice to you, and you cannot switch that off unilaterally.

WHAT IS NOT REQUIRED TO BE WRITTEN. There is no statutory notice period, written or otherwise, for ending a periodic tenancy — “month-to-month,” “periodic tenancy” and “tenancy at will” appear nowhere in Titles 1 or 34 — so the form and length of that notice come from your lease alone. A rental agreement itself need not be written: § 1-21-1201(a)(ii) defines “rental agreement” as any agreement, WRITTEN OR ORAL, and § 1-21-1302(a)(iv) likewise contemplates an oral lease. There is no written rent-increase notice requirement and no written entry notice requirement; § 1-21-1205(a)(iii) bars a renter from unreasonably denying entry for repairs, inspection or showing but names no notice at all. Finally, note what is NOT waivable: nothing in Article 12 is protected by an anti-waiver clause, so § 1-21-1202(d) can move or modify most of these duties by explicit signed writing — but it cannot touch Article 10’s § 1-21-1003 notice to quit, and § 1-21-1304 makes the Safe Homes Act provisions unwaivable in any lease or separate agreement.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Wyoming follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Wyo. Stat. § 34.1-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Wyo. Stat. § 34.1-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Wyoming's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Residential Rental Property Act and Wyoming's general lease statutes searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Wyoming's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
